CMS-2025-0050-110005♔CMS-2025-0050♔Daniel Taylor♔National Alliance for Care at Home♔♔♔♔The National Alliance for Care at Home strongly opposes the proposed removal of AI transparency requirements (model card disclosures) from the Decision Support Interventions certification criterion, arguing that home health clinicians have no othe...♔National Alliance for Care at Home⏎Comments on ASTP/ONC Deregulatory Actions To Unleash Prosperity: Health Data, Technology, and Interoperability⏎Submitted via regulations.gov⏎⏎MY CONCERN: REMOVING AI TRANSPARENCY REQUIREMENTS FROM THE CERTIFICATION PROGRAM⏎⏎The National Alliance for Care at Home submits these comments in response to the proposed rule's provisions that would remove or revise the Decision Support Interventions (DSI) certification criterion, specifically the requirements for model cards and transparency disclosures. Our organization represents home health agencies, hospice providers, and personal care organizations serving patients across the country. I want to be direct: this proposed change concerns me deeply, and I think the rationale offered for it does not hold up when you look at how AI-assisted clinical tools actually function at the point of care in home and community-based settings.⏎⏎The current DSI criterion, as established in the 2024 HTI-1 final rule (89 FR 1192), requires that health IT developers provide disclosure documentation including intended use, target population, known risks, training data characteristics, and evidence of external validation. These requirements exist because a clinician using a risk-stratification algorithm to decide whether a home health patient needs a skilled nursing visit does not have any other way to know whether that algorithm was trained on data that looks anything like their patient population. The South Bronx is not suburban Ohio. A model trained predominantly on data from large academic medical centers may perform very differently when applied to Medicare patients receiving post-acute wound care in underserved urban neighborhoods. That is not a hypothetical. A 2021 study published in NEJM Catalyst (Obermeyer et al., building on prior work from Science 2019) showed that widely-deployed commercial algorithms systematically underestimated the health needs of Black patients by roughly 26.3 percent because the training data used healthcare cost as a proxy for need. Without the model card disclosures required under 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11), a home health clinician has NO WAY to know whether the tool they are being handed has this problem or not!!⏎⏎The proposed rule suggests that removing these criteria reduces "administrative burden" on health IT developers. I genuinely don't understand what burden they are describing. Writing down what data your model was trained on is not a compliance nightmare. Publishing your intended use case is not an unreasonable ask. If a developer cannot answer these basic questions about their own product, that is itself important information for the clinicians and patients who are being asked to rely on it.⏎⏎WHAT THE CURRENT REQUIREMENTS ACTUALLY REQUIRE (AND WHY EACH MATTERS)⏎⏎The DSI transparency disclosures under 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11), as specified in 89 FR 1192 and further clarified in ONC's certification companion guide published March 2024, currently require developers to document:⏎⏎1. Intended use and scope of the intervention, including the clinical workflow context⏎2. Target patient population, with demographic and clinical inclusion/exclusion criteria⏎3. Known risks, including documented failure modes and performance degradation conditions⏎4. Training data characteristics, including source, time period, and known limitations⏎5. External validation results, where available, including validation population characteristics⏎⏎Each of these elements corresponds to a real gap that home health clinicians face when using certified health IT. Under 42 CFR 484.75 (the Conditions of Participation for home health agencies), agencies are responsible for ensuring that clinical decisions made in the home are appropriate and evidence-based. When an EHR-embedded DSI tool flags a patient as "low risk for rehospitalization" and a nurse follows that guidance without knowing the model has never been validated on patients over age 80 with multiple chronic conditions, the accountability falls entirely on the agency and the clinician. The developer faces no corresponding obligation to have disclosed the limitation. That asymmetry is the problem. The 21st Century Cures Act (Pub. L. 114-255, Section 4002) explicitly directed ONC to support the development of a health IT certification program that promotes patient safety and clinical decision support that is transparent and trustworthy. Removing model card requirements moves in the opposite direction from that statutory mandate.⏎⏎I also want to flag something that I don't see discussed enough in these rulemaking proceedings. The information blocking provisions at 45 CFR 171.300 et seq., as amended, work in tandem with certification criteria. When a home health agency requests structured clinical data from a hospital EHR system under the HIPAA right of access (45 CFR 164.524) or under an information blocking complaint framework (45 CFR 171.103), the quality and interpretability of that data depends in part on whether the sending system's DSI outputs are documented and standardized. If a hospital's discharge risk score is generated by a black-box algorithm with no disclosed parameters, and that score is transmitted to a home health agency in a FHIR R4 bundle (as contemplated under the USCDI v3 data class structure referenced in 89 FR 1192 at page 1347), the receiving clinician has a number but no context for what it means or whether it applies to their patient. This is exactly the scenario I have seen play out in practice in New York City. The technology exists. The obligation to make it interpretable is what is at risk here.⏎⏎ONC should retain the DSI certification criterion in full, including all model card disclosure elements. If there are specific documentation requirements within 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11) that developers find genuinely burdensome in ways that do not implicate patient safety, ONC should initiate a targeted request for information to identify those specific elements rather than removing the entire transparency framework. The American Medical Informatics Association (AMIA) submitted comments in the HTI-1 rulemaking in 2023 specifically supporting the model card requirements as consistent with emerging best practices in responsible AI deployment (AMIA 2023 RFI response, Docket ONC-2023-0004). The Coalition for Health AI (CHAI) blueprint published in April 2023 similarly identified training data disclosure and external validation reporting as baseline requirements for trustworthy health AI. Those positions have not changed. What has changed is the political framing around "deregulation," and that framing should not drive clinical safety policy.⏎⏎The National Alliance for Care at Home strongly urges ASTP/ONC to withdraw the proposed revision to the DSI criterion and to maintain the current transparency disclosure requirements. Comments or questions may be directed to our policy team at policy@nahc.org⏎⏎Daniel Taylor⏎Community Organizer, National Alliance for Care at Home⏎New York, NY♔♔2025-12-20T00:00:00Z♔2025-12-20T00:00:00Z♔2025-12-12T00:00:00Z♔2026-02-10T00:00:00Z♔3♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Retain the current Decision Support Interventions (DSI) certification criterion requiring AI model cards and transparency disclosures (intended use, target population, known risks, training data characteristics, external validation) to ensure patient safety, informed clinical decision-making, and accountability in AI-assisted healthcare.♔Removing transparency requirements creates unacceptable patient safety risks when AI systems make or influence high-stakes clinical recommendations without disclosed performance data or known limitations.♔advocacy_group♔high♔frustrated♔New York♔community organizer♔40♔Last spring, I spent three weeks helping a 67-year-old woman in the South Bronx fight to get her own discharge records transferred to her home health agency — records she needed to continue the wound care that was keeping her out of the hospital. CMS-2025-0050-110006♔CMS-2025-0050♔Richard Lopez♔The Society of Thoracic Surgeons♔♔♔♔The Society of Thoracic Surgeons strongly opposes ONC's proposed removal of the Decision Support Interventions (DSI) certification criterion, arguing that AI transparency requirements—including model cards, training data disclosures, and validatio...♔The Society of Thoracic Surgeons | Comments on ASTP/ONC Deregulatory Actions | Docket ONC-2025-0001 | Page 1⏎⏎The Society of Thoracic Surgeons (STS) submits these comments in response to the proposed rule titled "ASTP/ONC Deregulatory Actions To Unleash Prosperity: Health Data, Technology, and Interoperability." STS represents more than 7,800 cardiothoracic surgeons and allied health professionals across North America, and our members operate in some of the highest-acuity, highest-risk clinical environments in medicine. We have a direct and concrete stake in how health information technology certification standards are maintained, particularly as AI-assisted clinical decision support tools become more common in surgical planning, risk stratification, and postoperative management.⏎⏎Our comments focus specifically on the proposed removal of the Decision Support Interventions (DSI) certification criterion, specifically the provisions that require developers to disclose AI model cards, intended use statements, target population parameters, training data characteristics, known risk profiles, and external validation results. We believe removing these requirements would be a serious mistake, and the rationale offered in the proposed rule does not adequately address the patient safety implications for complex surgical populations.⏎⏎⏎THE DSI TRANSPARENCY REQUIREMENTS ARE NOT ADMINISTRATIVE OVERHEAD⏎⏎The preamble to this proposed rule frames the DSI model card requirements as a compliance burden, and suggests that market forces and voluntary disclosure practices can adequately substitute for certification-level requirements. We disagree with that framing, and we want to be specific about why.⏎⏎Cardiothoracic surgery involves patient populations with comorbidity profiles that are often dramatically underrepresented in the training datasets used for commercial AI tools. The Society of Thoracic Surgeons maintains the STS National Database, which as of the most recent reporting cycle includes data on approximately 7.9 million cardiac and thoracic surgical procedures going back to 1989. That database is one of the most comprehensive surgical registries in the world. And yet, even with that resource available, our members regularly encounter commercial AI decision support tools that were trained on general hospital admission data, or on datasets that skew heavily toward younger, healthier, lower-acuity patients, and that then get deployed in cardiothoracic surgery units without any disclosure of those limitations.⏎⏎Under the current DSI certification criterion at 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11), a developer seeking ONC certification must provide documentation of the intervention's intended use, the population the model was developed and validated on, known limitations and risks, and the nature of any external validation that was conducted. This is not a burdensome requirement. It is the minimum information a cardiothoracic surgeon needs to make a rational judgment about whether a given AI tool is appropriate for the patient in front of them.⏎⏎When ONC first finalized the DSI criterion in the 2024 HTI-1 final rule (89 Fed. Reg. 1192), the agency explained that the transparency requirements were designed to give clinicians and patients the information necessary to evaluate AI recommendations in context. That rationale has not changed. The clinical risks associated with opaque AI decision support have not changed. What has changed is the political framing around regulatory burden, and we are concerned that the substantive patient safety rationale is getting lost in that reframing.⏎⏎⏎THE SURGICAL CONTEXT IS SPECIFIC AND THE RISKS ARE REAL⏎⏎STS members who practice in Alaska, rural Montana, northern Minnesota, and other geographically isolated settings face a particular version of this problem. When a patient presents for an emergency cardiac procedure at a facility that has limited access to subspecialty consultation, the attending surgeon may be relying on an AI-assisted risk calculator or decision support tool to help inform the treatment plan. If that tool was trained primarily on data from large academic medical centers in urban settings, its predictions for a 67-year-old Alaskan Native patient with a history of rheumatic heart disease and limited prior diagnostic imaging may be poorly calibrated in ways the surgeon cannot detect without transparency disclosures.⏎⏎This is not a hypothetical. A 2023 study published in the Journal of the American College of Cardiology (Parikh et al., JACC Vol. 81, No. 14) documented systematic performance degradation in commercial AI cardiac risk tools when applied to populations with demographic and comorbidity profiles that differed from training populations, and noted that most commercial tools provided no documentation that would allow clinicians to identify this problem in advance. The DSI transparency requirements were a direct regulatory response to exactly this kind of evidence. Removing them now, before the market has demonstrated any meaningful voluntary adoption of equivalent disclosure practices, seems premature at best.⏎⏎The Society of Thoracic Surgeons | Comments on ASTP/ONC Deregulatory Actions | Docket ONC-2025-0001 | Page 2⏎⏎There is also a second-order problem here that the proposed rule does not address. When an AI decision support tool contributes to a poor surgical outcome, the absence of transparency documentation makes it extremely difficult to conduct meaningful quality review. STS participates in the national quality improvement infrastructure through the STS National Database and through our participation in the American College of Cardiology's National Cardiovascular Data Registry. Both programs depend on accurate attribution of outcomes to clinical decisions and clinical tools. If a certified EHR can deploy an AI decision support intervention without disclosing its training data or validation history, there is no reliable mechanism for post-market surveillance of that tool's performance in real-world surgical populations. The current DSI requirements, whatever their imperfections, at least create a documentation trail that quality improvement programs can work with.⏎⏎⏎SPECIFIC CONCERNS ABOUT THE PROPOSED CHANGES⏎⏎The proposed rule would remove the requirement that certified health IT include AI model card disclosures as a condition of certification. The alternative framework described in the preamble relies on developer voluntary disclosure and market transparency. We have the following specific concerns:⏎⏎1. Voluntary disclosure frameworks have not produced consistent transparency in the health IT market to date. ONC's own 2022 report on AI in health IT (ONC Data Brief No. 58) found that fewer than 30 percent of surveyed health IT developers provided documentation of training data characteristics for their AI-enabled clinical decision support tools. The current certification requirement was adopted partly in response to that finding.⏎⏎2. The proposed rule does not explain how clinicians are supposed to evaluate AI tools for appropriateness to their patient population if disclosure is voluntary and inconsistent. The preamble states that "market incentives will encourage transparency," but that assertion is not supported by any cited evidence.⏎⏎3. For surgical subspecialties in particular, the Food and Drug Administration's existing framework for Software as a Medical Device (SaMD) does not cover the full range of AI decision support tools used in cardiothoracic surgery. Many tools that qualify as clinical decision support under ONC's framework are explicitly excluded from FDA oversight under the 21st Century Cures Act provisions codified at 21 U.S.C. 360j(o). Removing ONC certification transparency requirements for these tools would leave a genuine regulatory gap with no offsetting oversight mechanism.⏎⏎4. The proposed rule does not address how the removal of DSI transparency requirements interacts with the information blocking provisions in 45 CFR 171. If a clinician cannot determine what AI tool was used in generating a clinical recommendation, or what population that tool was validated on, there is a reasonable argument that the absence of that information constitutes interference with a clinician's ability to make informed decisions using electronic health information. We would ask ONC to address this interaction explicitly in any final rule.⏎⏎5. STS is aware that some developers have raised concerns about proprietary training data and competitive sensitivity as reasons to resist model card requirements. We are not unsympathetic to those concerns. But the current DSI criterion does not require disclosure of proprietary model architecture or exact training datasets, it requires disclosure of the intended use, the population parameters, known limitations, and validation status. That is a narrower ask than some developers have characterized it as being, and we think ONC should be clearer in any final rule about exactly what the requirement does and does not mandate.⏎⏎⏎WHAT WE ARE ASKING ONC TO DO⏎⏎STS respectfully requests that ONC retain the DSI certification criterion at 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11) in its current form, including the model card and transparency disclosure requirements. If ONC believes there are specific elements of the current criterion that create disproportionate burden without corresponding clinical benefit, we would welcome a targeted revision process, and STS would be glad to participate in that process through our Health IT Task Force.⏎⏎We are genuinely open to discussing how the documentation requirements could be streamlined or standardized to reduce duplication for developers who are already complying with FDA SaMD guidance or with emerging voluntary frameworks like those being developed through the Coalition for Health AI (CHAI). But streamlining is different from removal, and the proposed rule as written goes much further than streamlining.⏎⏎STS also requests that ONC commission or cite specific evidence on the current state of voluntary AI transparency disclosure in certified health IT before finalizing any changes to the DSI criterion. The 2022 ONC Data Brief is now three years old and predates the HTI-1 final rule. An updated assessment of developer disclosure practices under the current certification requirements would give both ONC and the public a much clearer picture of whether voluntary alternatives are actually viable.⏎⏎The Society of Thoracic Surgeons | Comments on ASTP/ONC Deregulatory Actions | Docket ONC-2025-0001 | Page 3⏎⏎One more thing worth saying directly: the framing of certification requirements as obstacles to prosperity concerns us when it is applied to patient safety documentation in high-risk clinical settings. Reducing paperwork for administrative workflows is genuinely different from reducing transparency requirements for AI tools that inform surgical decisions. We are not arguing that every regulatory requirement is equally justified or that compliance burden is never a legitimate concern. We are arguing that the DSI transparency requirements were adopted for specific, well-documented patient safety reasons, and the proposed rule has not provided an adequate account of how those safety interests will be protected if the requirements are removed.⏎⏎STS appreciates the opportunity to submit these comments and is available to provide additional information or technical assistance to ONC staff. Inquiries may be directed to the STS Health Policy and Government Relations office at⏎⏎healthpolicy@sts.org♔♔2026-01-04T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-04T00:00:00Z♔2025-12-12T00:00:00Z♔2026-02-10T00:00:00Z♔5♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Retain the current Decision Support Interventions (DSI) certification criterion requiring AI model cards and transparency disclosures (intended use, target population, known risks, training data characteristics, external validation) to ensure patient safety, informed clinical decision-making, and accountability in AI-assisted healthcare.♔Removing DSI transparency requirements creates a dangerous regulatory gap where AI-based clinical decision support tools face fewer disclosure obligations than traditional medical devices, undermining consistent safety standards.♔advocacy_group♔high♔urgent♔Alaska♔executive director♔49♔Last February, a colleague of mine — a cardiothoracic surgeon in Fairbanks — spent nearly four hours on hold and fax machines trying to obtain a patient's prior imaging and catheterization records from a Lower 48 facility before an emergency valve replacement; the patient coded during that delay. CMS-2025-0050-110007♔CMS-2025-0050♔William Ramirez♔American College of Radiology (ACR)♔♔♔♔The American College of Radiology strongly opposes ONC's proposal to weaken or remove the Decision Support Interventions (DSI) certification criterion, arguing that AI transparency disclosures — including model cards, training data characteristics...♔ACR Comments | ONC Deregulatory Actions RFI | Page 1⏎⏎American College of Radiology⏎Comments on ASTP/ONC Deregulatory Actions To Unleash Prosperity: Health Data, Technology, and Interoperability⏎Submitted to the Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology, Department of Health and Human Services⏎⏎The American College of Radiology (ACR) respectfully submits these comments in response to ONC's proposed deregulatory actions affecting the Health IT Certification Program and information blocking framework. The ACR represents more than 40,000 radiologists, radiation oncologists, interventional radiologists, and medical physicists across the United States and maintains a long-standing commitment to patient safety, diagnostic quality, and evidence-based deployment of health information technology in clinical settings. We appreciate the opportunity to engage on these proposals, though we write with some concern about specific provisions that, in our view, move in the wrong direction.⏎⏎RETENTION OF DSI CERTIFICATION CRITERION: AI MODEL CARDS AND TRANSPARENCY DISCLOSURES⏎⏎ACR Comments | ONC Deregulatory Actions RFI | Page 2⏎⏎The ACR urges ONC to retain the Decision Support Interventions (DSI) certification criterion in its current form, specifically the requirement that certified health IT include model cards and transparency disclosures covering intended use, target population, known risks, training data characteristics, and external validation status. The proposal to weaken or remove this criterion, even in the name of reducing administrative burden, is one the College cannot support. Radiology is now one of the most heavily AI-integrated specialties in all of medicine. The ACR's own AI-LAB platform has catalogued more than 500 FDA-cleared AI algorithms as of early 2024, and the pace of deployment into clinical workflows at hospitals and outpatient imaging centers has outrun the capacity of many institutions to independently evaluate what they are deploying. The DSI transparency requirement is, at present, one of the few structural mechanisms that places a disclosure obligation on the vendor at the point of certification rather than relying entirely on post-market surveillance or voluntary best practices.⏎⏎What the ACR has observed, and what the published literature supports, is that AI tools certified without robust transparency requirements tend to produce documentation that is commercially oriented rather than clinically informative. A 2023 study published in npj Digital Medicine (Sendak et al.) reviewed 130 FDA-cleared AI devices and found that fewer than 30% disclosed sufficient training data characteristics for clinicians to assess potential demographic bias. That finding alone should give ONC pause before removing a certification criterion designed specifically to address this gap. The DSI model card requirement at 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11) is not a paperwork exercise. It is the mechanism by which a radiologist at a community hospital in, say, Elko, Nevada, can ask a vendor a basic question: was this nodule detection algorithm validated on a population that looks anything like mine? Without the certification requirement, the answer is "we'll get back to you," and often they don't.⏎⏎ACR Comments | ONC Deregulatory Actions RFI | Page 3⏎⏎We want to be direct about something. The framing of this proposal as burden reduction is not wrong on its face. Certification requirements do impose costs, and the ACR has in other contexts supported streamlining certification timelines where the clinical rationale for a specific criterion is thin. But the DSI transparency criterion is not thin. It was developed through extensive stakeholder engagement, informed by the 21st Century Cures Act's directive at Section 4002 to address clinical decision support in a way that protects patient safety, and shaped by public comments from physician organizations, patient advocates, and health equity researchers who documented specific harms from opaque algorithmic tools. The 2024 ONC HTI-1 final rule at 89 Fed. Reg. 1192 articulated the policy rationale for this criterion in considerable detail, and the current proposal does not, in the ACR's reading, offer a commensurate evidentiary basis for reversing course.⏎⏎The College's specific concerns are as follows:⏎⏎1. Intended use and target population disclosures. Without a certification requirement, vendors face no structured obligation to disclose whether an AI tool was designed for screening versus diagnostic use, or whether it was validated on adult versus pediatric populations. Radiology AI tools have been deployed in clinical environments outside their validated use cases with some frequency (see Gichoya et al., Radiology: Artificial Intelligence, 2023), and this type of mismatch is precisely what the DSI criterion is designed to surface.⏎⏎2. Known risks documentation. The requirement that certified DSI tools disclose known failure modes and risk profiles is consistent with FDA's own Software as a Medical Device (SaMD) guidance and with the ACR's Appropriateness Criteria framework. Removing it from the certification pathway creates a gap between what FDA expects at clearance and what ONC requires at certification, which is the opposite of regulatory coherence.⏎⏎3. Training data characteristics. This is perhaps the most consequential disclosure requirement. Algorithmic bias in medical imaging AI is well-documented. A 2021 JAMA Internal Medicine study (Obermeyer et al., though that specific study focused on a different domain, the methodological concern is directly applicable) and subsequent imaging-specific research (including work published in the Lancet Digital Health, 2022) have shown that training data composition directly affects diagnostic accuracy across racial and socioeconomic subgroups. Removing the obligation to disclose this information at certification does not make the bias go away. It just makes it harder to find.⏎⏎4. External validation status. The ACR's own Qualified Medical Imaging AI registry work has found that a significant proportion of commercially available radiology AI tools lack peer-reviewed external validation at the time of clinical deployment. The certification requirement to disclose validation status does not mandate that a tool be externally validated before deployment, but it does require transparency about whether it has been. That is a modest ask.⏎⏎ACR Comments | ONC Deregulatory Actions RFI | Page 4⏎⏎The College also wants to flag a practical concern that has come up in conversations with ACR member institutions over the past 18 months. When certification requirements are loosened, the burden of due diligence shifts entirely to the purchasing institution. For large academic medical centers with dedicated health IT and AI governance infrastructure, this is manageable, if annoying. For critical access hospitals, rural imaging centers, and smaller community practices, it is not manageable. These institutions typically rely on the certification framework as a proxy for a baseline level of vetting they cannot replicate internally. If ONC removes the DSI transparency criterion, the practical effect is not that vendors will voluntarily continue producing model cards. The practical effect is that the institutions least equipped to evaluate AI tools will have the least information with which to do so. The ACR does not think this outcome is consistent with ONC's stated goals around health equity or with the agency's obligations under Executive Order 13985 and subsequent HHS equity guidance.⏎⏎We would also note that the argument that model card requirements impose excessive burden on developers is not well-supported by what the ACR has seen in practice. Vendors who are building responsible AI tools are already producing this documentation for FDA submissions, for institutional procurement processes, and increasingly for international regulatory bodies (the EU AI Act's requirements for high-risk medical AI systems, which took effect in stages beginning in 2024, include disclosure obligations that are substantively similar to or more extensive than the DSI criterion). The developers who find the ONC requirement burdensome are, with some regularity, the ones who have the least documentation to show. That is a signal worth taking seriously.⏎⏎ACR Comments | ONC Deregulatory Actions RFI | Page 5⏎⏎The ACR recognizes that ONC is operating under significant pressure to reduce regulatory burden across the health IT ecosystem, and the College does not oppose deregulatory action as a general matter. There are provisions in the broader certification framework that could be streamlined without clinical consequence. But the DSI transparency criterion is not one of them. The timing is also worth noting. The period from 2024 through 2026 is likely to see accelerating deployment of large language model-based clinical decision support tools, multimodal diagnostic AI, and ambient documentation systems across inpatient and outpatient radiology. These tools are more opaque than their predecessors, not less. Removing transparency requirements at this moment, when the need for them is growing, would be a significant policy miscalculation.⏎⏎ACR Comments | ONC Deregulatory Actions RFI | Page 6⏎⏎The College's recommendation is straightforward: retain 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11) in its current form, including all model card and transparency disclosure sub-elements. If ONC believes that specific sub-elements impose disproportionate burden relative to their clinical value, the ACR would welcome a targeted stakeholder process to examine those sub-elements individually, with input from clinical specialty societies, patient advocates, and health equity researchers. What the College cannot support is a wholesale removal or significant weakening of the criterion based on a burden-reduction rationale that has not been tested against the clinical evidence.⏎⏎The ACR also urges ONC to clarify, in any final rule or guidance, the relationship between the DSI certification criterion and the information blocking framework. One concern that has surfaced in ACR member conversations is that loosened information blocking exceptions could, in combination with weakened DSI transparency requirements, make it harder for researchers and clinicians to access the information they need to evaluate AI tool performance in real-world populations. The experience of researchers attempting to access de-identified imaging datasets through FHIR-based pipelines, only to be blocked by contractual carve-outs that exploit ambiguities in the information blocking exceptions, is not hypothetical. It is a documented barrier to the kind of post-market surveillance and performance monitoring that compensates for whatever pre-market transparency requirements do not capture. The two policy levers interact, and ONC should treat them as connected rather than independent.⏎⏎www.acr.org | regulatory.comments@acr.org⏎⏎ACR Comments | ONC Deregulatory Actions RFI | Page 7⏎⏎The ACR thanks ONC for the opportunity to comment and reiterates its strong support for retaining the DSI certification criterion as currently structured. The College is available to provide additional technical input, including data from the ACR AI-LAB registry on current patterns of AI tool documentation and validation status, if that would be useful to the agency in evaluating this question. We would also note that the ACR's Data Science Institute has been working with member institutions since approximately 2019 on frameworks for AI governance in radiology that are directly relevant to the policy questions ONC is navigating here, and we would welcome a conversation about how that work might inform the final rule. Correspondence may be directed to the ACR's regulatory affairs office at the address above. I am a retired librarian living outside of Billings, Montana, and I want to say at the outset that I am not a physician or a health IT professional. I spent forty years helping people find information and understand what they were reading. That background is, I think, precisely why this particular proposed rule troubles me as much as it does.⏎⏎Last spring, my cardiologist retired abruptly. His practice transferred my records to a regional health network, and that network locked my own echocardiogram results behind a patient portal I could not access. Their system did not recognize my rural Montana address format. I failed authentication twice. When I finally reached a human being on the telephone, she told me my records were "not shareable in your current access tier." I still cannot parse what that phrase means, and I spent a career parsing bureaucratic language for other people. I waited eleven weeks for a new physician to request those records through official channels while managing a medication adjustment with incomplete information.⏎⏎I say all of that not to complain about my personal inconvenience, but because the experience made me pay close attention to what this agency does with health information rules. Which brings me to my specific concern.⏎⏎ON AI TRANSPARENCY AND THE DECISION SUPPORT CERTIFICATION CRITERION⏎⏎I understand this proposed rule would remove or revise certain certification requirements for health IT systems, including the criterion that currently requires what the agency calls Decision Support Interventions to come with documentation about how they work. From what I have read in the Federal Register notice, the agency is considering whether those transparency requirements, specifically the obligation to disclose an AI tool's intended use, target population, known risks, training data characteristics, and external validation status, are necessary going forward.⏎⏎I am asking the agency not to remove those requirements. I want to explain why, as plainly as I can.⏎⏎When a physician in a clinic is using a software tool that makes recommendations about my care, and that tool is built on an AI model I know nothing about, I have no way to know whether:⏎⏎1. The model was trained on patient populations that look like me (a 73-year-old man with a cardiac history living in a rural state with limited specialist access).⏎2. The model has been externally validated in settings similar to my clinic, or only in large urban academic medical centers.⏎3. The known failure modes of that model have been disclosed to my physician before she acts on its output.⏎⏎These are not hypothetical concerns. A 2021 study published in the New England Journal of Medicine (Obermeyer et al., though the original paper was 2019 in Science) documented how commercial algorithms systematically underestimated illness severity in Black patients because the training data used healthcare costs as a proxy for health needs. If the physician using that algorithm had access to a simple disclosure card explaining the training data and target population, she might have caught the problem. Without it, she had no way to know.⏎⏎The current certification criterion, as I understand it, requires developers to produce something like a model card: a plain-language document that describes what the tool was built to do, who it was tested on, and what its limitations are. This is the same principle behind the nutrition label on a box of cereal, or the package insert in a prescription medication. We do not tell the food industry that package labels are administrative burden and remove them. The label exists because the person consuming the product cannot otherwise evaluate what is in it.⏎⏎I genuinely do not understand why the agency would consider removing this requirement now, when AI tools are becoming more common in clinical settings, not less. The Federal Register notice mentions reducing administrative burden on developers. I take that concern seriously. Burden reduction is a legitimate goal. But there is a difference between reducing paperwork that serves no one and removing disclosures that a physician needs to make an informed decision about whether to follow an AI recommendation for a patient like me.⏎⏎A NOTE ON WHAT "ACCESS" ACTUALLY REQUIRES⏎⏎I want to say one more thing, because my experience last spring stays with me. Better access to my health information means very little if the clinical decisions being made about me are shaped by tools I cannot evaluate and my physician cannot evaluate either. Interoperability is important. Getting my records out from behind that portal is important. But if the records that move freely are then fed into an opaque AI model that makes recommendations based on training data nobody has disclosed, I have not actually gained meaningful access to my own care. I have just moved the opacity from one place to another.⏎⏎The agency cites 45 CFR Part 170 as the basis for the certification criteria at issue. Those criteria exist because Congress, in the 21st Century Cures Act, directed the agency to promote the safe and trusted use of health information technology. Removing transparency requirements for AI decision support tools is not consistent with that direction, in my reading.⏎⏎I recognize I am one retired librarian in Montana, and the agency will hear from many large organizations with more technical expertise than I have. I am not asking to make developers' lives difficult. I am asking the agency to keep a basic disclosure requirement in place so that the physicians making decisions about patients like me have the information they need to evaluate the tools they are using.⏎⏎If the concern is that the current model card format is too burdensome, the agency could work with developers to simplify the format. That seems like a reasonable middle ground. What does not seem reasonable is removing the requirement entirely and hoping that physicians will somehow independently assess the limitations of AI tools that developers are not required to explain.⏎⏎My new cardiologist, when I finally got one, told me she had no idea what training data the risk-scoring tool in her EHR system was built on. Comments on ASTP/ONC Proposed Deregulatory Rule⏎Docket: ONC-2025-0002⏎Submitted by: Ashley Adams, Chief Medical Officer, RubyWell, Inc.⏎⏎RubyWell, Inc. is a Washington-based digital health company serving primary care and specialty practices across rural and frontier communities in the Pacific Northwest. Our patient population skews older, geographically dispersed, and often underserved by the health IT tools that were built with urban academic medical centers in mind. We have been operating certified Health IT products under the ONC Health IT Certification Program since 2019 and have direct, daily experience with the clinical consequences of how these certification requirements are written and enforced.⏎⏎RubyWell, Inc. Comments | ONC-2025-0002 | Page 1⏎⏎POSITION ON DSI TRANSPARENCY REQUIREMENTS⏎⏎The proposed rule contemplates removing or substantially scaling back the Decision Support Interventions certification criterion at 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11), including the provisions that currently require AI model cards, transparency disclosures covering intended use, target population, known risks, training data characteristics, and documentation of external validation. We are writing specifically to urge ONC to retain those requirements in their current form.⏎⏎Our concern is straightforward. The clinical staff at RubyWell rely on DSI outputs to inform decisions that carry real patient risk. When an algorithm surfaces a recommendation about medication dosing or flags a patient for care escalation, the clinician acting on that recommendation needs to know, at minimum: what population the model was trained on, whether it has been externally validated, and what the known failure modes are. Without the model card requirement, that information has no guaranteed pathway to the point of care. The relevant literature supports this concern. A 2021 study in JAMA Network Open (Obermeyer et al., 2021) and prior work by the same group documented how algorithmic tools trained on biased historical data systematically underestimated illness severity in Black patients. The problem wasn't that the tools were malicious. The problem was opacity. Clinicians using those tools had no way to know what they didn't know.⏎⏎ONC's own 2023 report on AI in Health IT (ONC Data Brief No. 67) documented that fewer than 30 percent of health IT developers provide structured documentation of model training data to end users absent a regulatory requirement to do so. That figure alone makes the case for keeping 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11) intact. The argument that market incentives will fill this gap is not persuasive to us, because we have watched the market for several years now and the gap has not closed on its own.⏎⏎RubyWell, Inc. Comments | ONC-2025-0002 | Page 2⏎⏎The specific elements we are asking ONC to retain are:⏎⏎1. Disclosure of intended use and target population, consistent with FDA guidance on Software as a Medical Device (SaMD) and the 21st Century Cures Act, Pub. L. 114-255, Section 3060.⏎2. Documentation of training data characteristics, including known limitations related to race, ethnicity, age, and geographic setting (see also 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11)(iv) as currently written).⏎3. Known risks and contraindications, including any published evidence of differential performance across subgroups.⏎4. External validation status. A model validated only on the developer's internal dataset is a materially different product than one validated against an independent cohort, and clinicians deserve to know which they are using.⏎5. Version tracking so that when a model is updated, the clinical team receives notification, consistent with ONC's proposed approach to transparency in the 2020 ONC Cures Act Final Rule (85 FR 25642).⏎⏎We are not opposed to streamlining certification processes where the burden is genuinely disproportionate to the clinical benefit. We sat through an eighteen-month certification queue for a feature our clinical team built in six weeks, so we understand that frustration is real on both sides of this. But the transparency disclosures in the DSI criterion are not the source of that delay. In our experience, the bottleneck is in the testing and certification infrastructure, not in the documentation requirements themselves. Removing model card requirements would not make certification faster. It would just make the certified products less safe and less accountable.⏎⏎There is also a health equity dimension here that the proposed rule does not appear to weigh sufficiently. CMS-2025-0050-110012♔CMS-2025-0050♔Barbara Green♔♔♔♔♔Removing the Decision Support Interventions certification criterion — which requires AI developers to disclose how their tools were trained, what populations they were designed for, and where they may fail — would leave clinicians without critical...♔RE: ASTP/ONC Deregulatory Actions To Unleash Prosperity -- Health Data, Technology, and Interoperability⏎⏎⏎MY CONCERN ABOUT REMOVING AI TRANSPARENCY REQUIREMENTS⏎⏎What happened to my mother last spring is the reason I'm writing this. She was transferred between three separate facilities in six weeks -- a hospital in Denver, a rehabilitation center in Lakewood, then a skilled nursing home near us in Fort Collins -- and her medical records either arrived late, arrived incomplete, or didn't arrive at all. Each time. Her cardiologist at the Fort Collins facility was making decisions about her beta-blocker dosage without knowing what adjustments had already been tried in Lakewood. I was terrified. I kept asking the nurses, asking the discharge coordinators, and getting variations of "the records should have come with her." They hadn't.⏎⏎I eventually got her complete records myself by logging into an online patient portal, which took maybe twenty minutes. That's what got me thinking about all of this. If I, a retired teacher with no medical training, could pull together her full history in twenty minutes, why couldn't three professional facilities do it automatically during a transfer? And if the answer is "because the systems don't talk to each other," then the systems are broken in ways that need more rules and more accountability, not fewer.⏎⏎That's the context I'm coming from when I say I'm genuinely worried about one piece of this proposed rule. I understand that the stated goal is reducing administrative burden, and I don't doubt that there's real paperwork that slows things down without helping anyone. But I keep coming back to the proposal to remove or weaken what's called the Decision Support Interventions certification criterion -- the part that currently requires health IT developers to disclose things like how an AI tool was trained, what population it was designed for, what its known risks are, and whether it's been validated outside the lab. I want to explain why I think removing that would be a serious mistake, even for someone like me who doesn't follow regulatory policy for a living.⏎⏎⏎WHY THE AI TRANSPARENCY REQUIREMENT EXISTS IN THE FIRST PLACE⏎⏎From what I've read and understood, the current certification rules require that when a health IT system uses AI or algorithmic tools to support clinical decisions -- things like flagging which patients might need a follow-up, or recommending a medication, or predicting deterioration -- the developers have to provide what's sometimes called a "model card." That's a disclosure document explaining what the AI was trained on, who it was designed to work with, what the known failure modes are, and how it performed in testing on real-world populations.⏎⏎I'll be honest: I didn't know this requirement existed until I started looking into this rule. But when I read about it, my first thought was: of course that should be required. My mother's care team was already working without basic information about her history. The idea that they might also be working with AI tools that nobody has explained to them -- tools that might have been trained primarily on data from younger or healthier populations, or that perform differently for elderly patients with multiple cardiac conditions -- that's not a hypothetical worry. There's published research on this. A 2019 study in Science (Obermeyer et al.) found that a widely used commercial algorithm systematically underestimated the health needs of Black patients because it used healthcare costs as a proxy for health status. The algorithm was embedded in clinical workflows. Clinicians often didn't know it was there, let alone how it worked.⏎⏎Removing the requirement to disclose this kind of information doesn't make the AI go away. It just means the doctors using it have less information about what they're actually working with. I genuinely don't understand the reasoning there.⏎⏎⏎WHAT GETS LOST IF THIS GOES AWAY⏎⏎The argument I've seen for removing this requirement, as best I can tell, is that it imposes compliance costs on developers and may slow the adoption of helpful tools. I take that seriously. I'm not someone who thinks all regulation is good regulation. But the compliance cost here is documentation -- writing down what your tool does, who it was built for, and what the risks are. If a company can't or won't do that, I'm not sure I want that tool anywhere near my mother's care.⏎⏎What concerns me is that without this requirement, there's no standardized way for a physician in Fort Collins to know whether the AI tool flagging my mother's risk score was trained on a population that looks anything like her. Elderly women. History of atrial fibrillation and a recent hip replacement. Multiple medications. That's not an unusual patient profile, but it's also not the profile that tends to dominate clinical trial data or, I'd guess, a lot of training datasets.⏎⏎The transparency requirement as it currently exists creates a paper trail. It gives clinicians something to look at. It gives patients and family members something to ask about. If it goes away, the AI is still in the room, but it's invisible. That's not less burdensome -- it's just less visible.⏎⏎⏎A SPECIFIC THING THAT WORRIES ME ABOUT HOW THIS GETS IMPLEMENTED⏎⏎Even setting aside the policy question, there's a practical problem I keep thinking about. Right now, if a hospital or clinic uses a certified health IT product, they have some assurance that the AI components of that product met a certain disclosure standard. Physicians can request the model documentation. It might not always happen in practice, but the structure exists.⏎⏎If ONC removes the DSI certification criterion, or waters it down significantly, that structure goes away. And there's nothing in what I've read to suggest that anything replaces it. The Federal Register notice for this rule talks about reducing "unnecessary" certification criteria, but it doesn't explain how the agency determined that AI transparency is unnecessary. That's the part I'd like an answer to.⏎⏎I've read a little about what happened with early pulse oximeters and how their performance gaps in patients with darker skin tones weren't widely known for years because there wasn't a systematic requirement to test and disclose performance by subgroup. The FDA has since addressed some of that (there's a 2021 safety communication and ongoing rulemaking), but the lesson there is that the absence of disclosure requirements doesn't mean the problem doesn't exist. It means it stays hidden longer.⏎⏎AI tools in clinical decision support have the same potential for hidden, population-specific failure modes. The model card requirement is not a perfect solution to that -- I'm not claiming it is. But it's a start. It's a minimum. Removing it without replacing it with something equivalent or better seems like exactly the wrong direction.⏎⏎⏎WHY I'M ASKING ONC TO RECONSIDER⏎⏎I recognize that this comment is coming from someone without a medical degree or a background in health IT policy. I'm a retired teacher who spent a frightening spring managing my mother's care across three facilities and came out of it with a lot of questions about how these systems work. So I want to be clear that I'm not claiming to have the full technical picture here.⏎⏎But I do think patients and families have standing to weigh in on this, because we're the ones who bear the consequences when clinical AI fails quietly. When an algorithm underweights someone's risk because she's 78 and female and on six medications and the training data didn't include many people like her -- that's not a developer's problem. That's her problem. It's my family's problem.⏎⏎The current transparency requirement at least creates the possibility that someone in the care chain knows what the tool was built for and where it might fall short. A physician who knows that a sepsis-prediction model was validated primarily on ICU patients in large urban academic medical centers might think twice before relying on it heavily for a post-surgical patient in a smaller community hospital. That's exactly the kind of informed judgment we want clinicians to be making.⏎⏎Removing the requirement doesn't make the tool better. It just removes the information that would let a clinician use it wisely.⏎⏎⏎WHAT I'D LIKE TO SEE INSTEAD⏎⏎I'm not in a position to propose detailed regulatory language. But at a minimum, I'd ask ONC to explain publicly -- in the final rule, with actual reasoning -- why AI transparency disclosures are considered unnecessary, and what alternative mechanism will ensure that clinicians and patients have access to information about the AI tools influencing their care.⏎⏎If the argument is that the current model card requirements are too burdensome in their specific form, then revise the form. Require less paperwork but keep the core disclosures: intended use, target population, known performance gaps, and whether the tool was validated on data that actually resembles the patients it will be used with. That's not an unreasonable ask.⏎⏎I also want to say: the interoperability improvements in this rule, the parts about making it easier for patients to access their own records, those seem genuinely good to me. If my mother's records had moved with her the way they should have, her doctors in Fort Collins would have had what they needed from the start. I support that. But improving data flow and removing AI accountability requirements are two separate things, and I don't think doing the first justifies doing the second.⏎⏎My mother is 81. She's home now, doing reasonably well. Her cardiologist in Fort Collins has finally gotten a complete picture of her medication history, which took about four months longer than it should have. Reg. [forthcoming 2025])⏎⏎⏎Dental Standards Institute Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 1⏎⏎The Dental Standards Institute (DSI) submits these comments in response to the proposed rule issued by the Assistant Secretary for Technology Policy and the Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology. DSI is a nonprofit professional standards organization based in Manchester, New Hampshire, with a membership that includes approximately 4,200 dental practitioners, oral surgeons, dental hygienists, and health IT professionals operating in clinical and institutional settings across 38 states. Our policy work sits at the intersection of oral health, systemic disease management, and health information technology, which means we pay close attention to interoperability standards and certification criteria that shape how clinical decision support tools behave in practice. Our members use certified health IT systems daily, and those systems increasingly incorporate algorithmic decision support. What those algorithms do and do not tell the clinician using them matters enormously to the patients in the chair.⏎⏎We want to be direct: our central concern with this proposed rule is the proposed removal of the Decision Support Interventions (DSI) certification criterion as it relates to AI transparency disclosures, specifically the requirements that developers document and make available model cards, intended use statements, target population specifications, known risks, training data characteristics, and external validation status (45 CFR 170.315(b)(11), as established in the ONC Health IT Certification Program under the HTI-1 Final Rule, 89 Fed. Reg. 1192 (Jan. 9, 2024)). We believe removing or substantially weakening this criterion would be a serious error, and we want to explain why in some detail.⏎⏎⏎I. BACKGROUND ON THE DSI TRANSPARENCY REQUIREMENTS AND WHY THEY MATTER⏎⏎The HTI-1 Final Rule, published in January 2024, represented years of effort by ONC to bring meaningful accountability to the use of predictive algorithms and AI-driven decision support in certified health IT. The DSI criterion at 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11) required that health IT developers, as a condition of certification, make available to end users specific documentation about any AI or predictive model embedded in or connected to their certified product. That documentation included the model's intended use, the population on which it was trained, performance characteristics, known limitations and failure modes, and whether the model had been externally validated on populations outside the developer's own data environment.⏎⏎These are not exotic demands. Any clinician who has tried to interpret a risk-stratification score produced by a black-box model knows exactly why this information is necessary. When a decision support tool tells a dentist that a patient has an elevated risk for a systemic inflammatory condition based on periodontal presentation, the clinician needs to know whether that model was validated on a population that looks like the patient in front of them. If the training data came primarily from one demographic group, the model's predictions for patients from other groups may be unreliable in ways that are not visible at the point of care. The National Academy of Medicine has documented this problem repeatedly; see, for example, "Artificial Intelligence in Health Care: The Hope, the Hype, the Promise, the Peril" (2019), which specifically noted that algorithmic tools trained on non-representative data can produce systematically worse predictions for already-underserved populations.⏎⏎⏎Dental Standards Institute Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 2⏎⏎The DSI transparency requirements were ONC's attempt to give clinicians the minimum information they need to exercise professional judgment about whether and how to act on an AI recommendation. Removing those requirements does not make the AI go away. The algorithms will still be there. They will still be influencing prescribing decisions, referral patterns, care escalation choices. They will just be doing so with less accountability than they had under the rule that went into effect less than two years ago.⏎⏎We want to be honest about what we are not saying here. We are not arguing that the current certification framework is perfect or that compliance burdens are irrelevant. There are legitimate questions about how to structure model card requirements in ways that are practical for smaller developers and that avoid creating paperwork exercises that no one reads. Those are real implementation concerns and we do not dismiss them. But the answer to imperfect implementation is better implementation, not elimination of the underlying requirement.⏎⏎⏎II. THE SPECIFIC PROBLEM WITH REMOVING THE DSI AI TRANSPARENCY CRITERION⏎⏎The proposed rule frames the removal of certain DSI requirements as burden reduction and increased flexibility for developers. We understand the framing. But when we look at what specifically is proposed to be removed, we find that the "burden" at issue is largely the burden of documenting what a model does, who it was tested on, and whether it works. That is not an administrative burden in the way that duplicative reporting requirements are an administrative burden. That is the basic scientific accountability that any clinical tool should be expected to provide.⏎⏎Consider the parallel to pharmaceuticals. A drug manufacturer must document the populations in its clinical trials, known adverse effects, contraindications, and the specific indications for which the drug is approved. We do not consider that documentation a burden to be reduced; we consider it the minimum condition for safe prescribing. AI models embedded in clinical decision support are functionally analogous. They influence clinical choices. In some settings they drive those choices, particularly when time-pressured clinicians are working through high patient volumes and default to whatever the system recommends.⏎⏎The HTI-1 preamble itself acknowledged this concern. ONC wrote, in the discussion of the DSI criterion, that "the absence of transparent documentation about AI model characteristics creates asymmetric information between developers and clinicians that can undermine the clinician's ability to appropriately weigh algorithmic recommendations" (89 Fed. Reg. 1192 at 1287). We agree with that analysis. What we do not understand is why the agency is now proposing to remove the mechanism it created to address exactly that problem.⏎⏎⏎Dental Standards Institute Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 3⏎⏎There is also a patient safety dimension here that the proposed rule does not adequately engage. The Food and Drug Administration has been grappling with how to regulate AI-based Software as a Medical Device (SaMD) under its existing statutory authorities (see FDA's "Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning in Software as a Medical Device" discussion paper, January 2021). ONC's DSI transparency requirements operated in a different regulatory lane than FDA's device oversight, but they were complementary. FDA regulation focuses on whether a device is safe and effective for its intended use as determined by the developer. ONC's certification requirements, by contrast, were aimed at ensuring that the clinician at the point of care had enough information to make their own assessment. Those are different functions and both matter. Weakening ONC's transparency requirements while FDA's oversight of many AI decision support tools remains limited creates a gap that, frankly, no one in this regulatory ecosystem seems positioned to fill.⏎⏎We are also concerned about what removal of the DSI transparency criterion signals to the market. Certification criteria function partly as market signals. When ONC certifies a health IT product, it is communicating to purchasers, including hospitals, dental practices, and integrated delivery networks, that the product meets a defined standard. If AI transparency documentation is no longer a condition of certification, purchasers lose a lever they currently have to demand that information from vendors. A large health system with a sophisticated IT procurement team may still negotiate for model cards in its contracts. A 12-dentist group practice in rural New Hampshire almost certainly will not, because they do not know to ask, and even if they did, they do not have the bargaining power to get it. The certification program is supposed to level that playing field. Removing the DSI transparency requirements tilts it back.⏎⏎⏎III. THE ARGUMENT THAT MARKET FORCES WILL SUPPLY TRANSPARENCY IS NOT PERSUASIVE⏎⏎We have heard, in various forms, the argument that developers have reputational and commercial incentives to be transparent about their AI models, and that regulatory requirements are therefore unnecessary. We find this argument unpersuasive for several reasons.⏎⏎First, the health IT market does not operate like a consumer market where poor product performance quickly drives customers to alternatives. Electronic health record switching costs are enormous. A dental practice that has invested in a particular certified EHR system, trained its staff, migrated its records, and built its workflows around that system is not going to switch vendors because it learned that the vendor's embedded risk-stratification algorithm has a documented performance gap for patients over 70. The practice is going to keep using the system and, in the absence of any required disclosure, probably will not even know about the performance gap. This is a textbook case where market discipline is structurally unable to produce the outcome that regulatory requirements can.⏎⏎Second, the transparency requirements in the DSI criterion were specifically designed to address information asymmetries that exist even when developers are acting in good faith. A developer may genuinely believe its model performs well across populations, because its internal testing showed that. External validation on independent data sets sometimes reveals performance gaps that internal testing did not catch, as documented in a 2022 study published in The Lancet Digital Health finding that 71 of 232 AI clinical prediction models reviewed showed significant performance degradation when applied to populations outside the original training data (Collins et al., Lancet Digital Health, 2022). The disclosure requirement was a mechanism for surfacing that information. Removing it does not make the information irrelevant; it just makes it harder to obtain.⏎⏎Third, and this is something we feel strongly about, the patients whose care is affected by AI decision support tools are not parties to any market transaction between the EHR vendor and the clinical practice. The patient sitting in the exam room has no way to know that a recommendation they receive is being shaped by an algorithm with a known performance limitation for their age group or their demographic profile. The DSI transparency requirement was, in part, a proxy protection for patients who cannot protect themselves in this market.⏎⏎⏎Dental Standards Institute Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 4⏎⏎We want to be careful not to overstate the case here. The DSI criterion as implemented in HTI-1 had real practical limitations. The model card requirements as written were somewhat high-level, and there were legitimate questions raised in the comment process about whether the required disclosures would be detailed enough to be clinically useful, or whether they would end up as checkbox compliance documents that developers produced without meaningful review and clinicians never read. Those criticisms have some merit. But the response to inadequate disclosure is more specific and more useful disclosure requirements, not the elimination of disclosure requirements. A model card that tells a clinician "this model was trained on data from a single academic medical center in the Midwest between 2015 and 2019 and has not been externally validated on rural or elderly populations" is genuinely useful clinical information, even if it is imperfect. No model card at all is not an improvement over an imperfect one.⏎⏎⏎V. WHAT WE ARE ASKING ONC TO DO⏎⏎Our recommendation is straightforward: retain the DSI certification criterion as it applies to AI and predictive model transparency disclosures. If ONC concludes that specific elements of the current disclosure requirements are too burdensome or insufficiently useful, we encourage the agency to issue revised guidance or a supplemental rulemaking that refines the requirements rather than eliminating them. We would specifically support a process in which ONC convenes a technical working group, including clinical end users, patient advocates, and health IT developers, to develop more operationally specific model card standards that address the implementation concerns raised by developers while preserving the core transparency function. The Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality funded work in this space as recently as 2023, and there is a body of literature on how to structure AI transparency documentation to be both practical and clinically meaningful (see, e.g., Mitchell et al., "Model Cards for Model Reporting," Proceedings of the ACM Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency, 2019; Sendak et al., "Real-World Integration of a Sepsis Deep Learning Technology into Routine Clinical Care," NEJM Catalyst, 2020).⏎⏎We also ask ONC to be more explicit in the final rule about the patient safety rationale for retaining or modifying the DSI requirements. The proposed rule, as written, frames this primarily as a burden-reduction exercise. We think that framing misses the clinical stakes. When a physician or dentist acts on an AI recommendation and something goes wrong, the question of whether the clinician had adequate information about the model's limitations is not a paperwork question. It is a question about whether the standard of care was met. The DSI transparency requirements were, in part, ONC's effort to ensure that the information necessary to meet that standard was available. That purpose deserves explicit acknowledgment in the final rule, regardless of what ONC ultimately decides about the specific regulatory text.⏎⏎⏎Dental Standards Institute Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 5⏎⏎We also want to note, because we think it is relevant, that the proposed rule arrives at an unusual moment in the broader regulatory conversation about AI in healthcare. The White House Executive Order on AI (October 30, 2023) called for federal agencies to develop standards and guidelines for AI safety and transparency. HHS issued a concept paper in 2023 outlining a framework for responsible AI use in healthcare that included transparency as a core principle. The FDA has been developing guidance on predetermined change control plans and transparency obligations for AI-based SaMD. In this environment, proposing to remove ONC's existing AI transparency requirements in certified health IT seems to move in the opposite direction from where the rest of the federal government was heading as recently as 18 months ago. We are genuinely uncertain whether this proposed rule reflects a coordinated policy shift or whether it is the product of a narrower burden-reduction exercise that did not fully account for the broader AI governance context. If it is the latter, we would ask ONC to pause and assess.⏎⏎One more thing, and we recognize this is slightly outside the formal scope of the certification criterion question, but it bears mentioning. The proposed rule also includes modifications to information blocking exceptions that could, in some interpretations, give providers and developers more latitude to delay or decline to share clinical data in circumstances where current rules require sharing. We have not analyzed those provisions in full, and we are not prepared to offer a comprehensive position on them in this comment. But we are concerned that, read together with the proposed weakening of the DSI transparency requirements, the cumulative effect of this rule could be to reduce both the transparency of AI tools used at the point of care and the portability of the patient data those tools rely on. Those two things are connected. An AI model's performance depends on the quality and completeness of the data it receives, and a patient's ability to benefit from clinical AI depends in part on their data being available to the systems making recommendations about their care.⏎⏎We know from direct experience what happens when data is not available at the moment a clinical decision needs to be made. The consequences are not abstract. They are a physician making a medication decision without knowing what the patient was given at the previous facility. They are a dentist proceeding without knowing that a patient is on a bisphosphonate that changes the risk calculus for an extraction. These are not edge cases. They happen every day, and they happen precisely because the interoperability infrastructure we have been building for the past decade is still incomplete and fragile. This proposed rule, in our reading, would make it more fragile, not less.⏎⏎⏎Dental Standards Institute Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 6⏎⏎We want to be fair to ONC. The agency has done genuinely important work over the past decade to build the technical and regulatory infrastructure for health IT interoperability, and the HTI-1 rule itself was a serious and thoughtful effort to address emerging questions about AI in clinical settings. We do not think ONC is indifferent to the concerns we are raising. But the proposed rule as written would undo one of the more consequential things HTI-1 accomplished, and it does so in a way that we do not think the justification provided in the proposed rule adequately supports.⏎⏎The preamble to the proposed rule cites feedback from health IT developers that the DSI transparency requirements created compliance burdens and that the model card requirements were difficult to operationalize for some types of AI tools. We take that feedback seriously. Operationalizing model card requirements for continuously learning algorithms, for instance, is a genuinely hard technical problem, and the static documentation model contemplated in HTI-1 may not be well-suited to all AI architectures. Those are real issues. But the proposed rule's response, which is essentially to remove the requirements rather than to work through the implementation challenges, does not seem proportionate to the problem identified. The compliance challenges described by developers are the kind of thing that guidance documents, safe harbors, and phased implementation timelines are designed to address. They are not, in our view, a justification for eliminating the underlying transparency obligation.⏎⏎We would also ask ONC to consider the perspective of clinical end users more carefully in this rulemaking. The comment record for HTI-1 included extensive input from clinical organizations supporting the DSI transparency requirements, including the American Medical Association, the American Nurses Association, and a number of specialty societies (see 89 Fed. Reg. 1192 at 1283-1290 for ONC's discussion of those comments). We are not aware of a comparable record in this proceeding of clinical organizations asking for the transparency requirements to be removed. The impetus appears to have come primarily from the developer side of the market. That is not illegitimate; developer feasibility matters. But in a rulemaking that will affect patient safety and clinical decision-making, the clinical perspective deserves at least equal weight.⏎⏎⏎Dental Standards Institute Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 7⏎⏎DSI's formal request is that ONC retain 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11) in its current form, or, if the agency concludes that modifications are warranted based on implementation experience, that any modifications be made through a separate rulemaking with a full public comment process, rather than through this deregulatory action. We believe the transparency requirements in the DSI criterion are sufficiently important to patient safety and clinical accountability that they should not be removed or substantially weakened without a dedicated regulatory process in which ONC explicitly solicits and responds to evidence about the patient safety implications of doing so.⏎⏎We are available to provide additional technical input to ONC or to participate in any stakeholder process the agency convenes to address these issues. That expectation took years to establish and, based on what we know about how AI is being deployed in healthcare, it is becoming more important over time, not less. Removing or substantially weakening these requirements under the framing of burden reduction would be a mistake.⏎⏎The practical context here matters. Over the past eighteen months our team has worked alongside hospital systems and ambulatory EHR vendors deploying AI-assisted scheduling, risk stratification, and diagnostic flagging tools. In that work, we have seen, repeatedly, what happens when a clinical decision support module lacks adequate provenance documentation. A risk stratification model trained on a predominantly urban Medicare population gets deployed in a rural Idaho Medicaid context (see ONC's own 2023 Health IT Report, pp. 41-44, and the related commentary in JAMIA Vol. 30, No. 4, 2023). The model performs. The outputs look reasonable. Nobody in the workflow knows to ask whether the training data reflected their patient population because there is no place in the certified product that tells them to ask. That is the problem the DSI criterion was designed to address, and the Federal Register preamble at 88 FR 23746 (April 18, 2023) said as much explicitly.⏎⏎I sat in a sign-off meeting last spring watching my best developer stare at the ceiling with the particular exhaustion of someone who knows their work mattered to no one. That was $400,000 in contractor hours recertifying a scheduling module that hadn't changed a line of clinical logic. I understand burden. I am not arguing against burden reduction categorically. But there is a real difference between recertification overhead that produces no safety value and a disclosure requirement that tells a cardiologist in Twin Falls that the sepsis-prediction model flagging her patient was validated on data from 2017-2019, before COVID significantly altered baseline lab patterns (see Wynants et al., BMJ 2020;369:m1328, which documented this exact validation-currency problem across 232 prediction models).⏎⏎The specific requirements we urge ONC to retain, in full, under 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11):⏎⏎1. Intended use and scope statements, including explicit contraindications for off-label clinical deployment contexts.⏎2. Target population characteristics, with enough granularity that a deploying provider can assess demographic fit (see FDA AI/ML Action Plan, January 2021, pp. 8-9).⏎3. Known performance limitations and failure modes, documented in plain language accessible to non-data-science clinical staff.⏎4. Training data source characteristics, including date range, geographic coverage, and payer mix where relevant.⏎5. External validation status, including whether validation was performed on data independent of training data (45 CFR 170.315(b)(11)(v) as currently written).⏎⏎Cloudflare Inc.
