The burden being referenced in the title of this rule, "to unleash prosperity," is not primarily a burden on health IT developers or large health system administrators, it falls on patients and clinicians who are expected to use AI-assisted tools without any reliable way to know what those tools were trained on, who they were designed for, or whether they've been validated for the population sitting in the exam chair, so to speak. That's where I want to focus my comments today, specifically on the DSI certification criterion and what we lose if it goes away.⏎⏎CareQuest Institute for Oral Health is a nonprofit organization committed to advancing health equity through research, philanthropy, and policy work. Oral health is a window into overall health, and we work extensively with safety-net dental providers, federally qualified health centers, and community clinics that serve Medicaid patients, uninsured individuals, and populations that face significant barriers to care. Many of our partner organizations have been navigating health IT adoption under constrained resources, and for them, the question of whether a clinical decision support tool is appropriate for their patient population is not academic, it is a daily operational reality. When a DSI tool was trained predominantly on commercially insured patients in metropolitan areas, and then gets deployed in a rural safety-net clinic serving predominantly Black and Latino patients on Medicaid, the outputs may be systematically skewed in ways the clinician cannot detect without some form of transparency documentation. This is not a hypothetical, there is a growing body of evidence on algorithmic bias in clinical decision support, including Obermeyer et al.'s 2019 study in Science (366:447-453) that found a widely used commercial algorithm systematically underestimated the health needs of Black patients, in some cases by a factor that resulted in those patients receiving significantly less care than comparably sick white patients. That study didn't require the algorithm to fail in a visible, dramatic way, it required a researcher to actually look at what the training data was doing. Clinicians using that tool day-to-day had no mechanism to make that assessment.⏎⏎The current DSI certification criterion, as codified under 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11), requires that health IT developers provide what is essentially a minimum disclosure package for AI and predictive model functionality embedded in certified health IT. This includes documentation of the intended use case, the target population the model was designed for, known risks and limitations, characteristics of the training data, and whether external validation has been conducted. ONC finalized these requirements in the HTI-1 rule published at 89 Fed. Reg. 1192 (January 9, 2024), and the policy rationale there was clear, that clinicians and patients cannot make informed decisions about AI-assisted recommendations if the underlying model is a black box. I keep coming back to that rationale because I genuinely don't understand what has changed in the intervening months to make it less valid. The AI tools being deployed in clinical settings have not become more transparent on their own. The market has not spontaneously generated a norm of model card disclosure. If anything, the pace of AI deployment in health care has accelerated, which makes the need for baseline transparency requirements more pressing, not less.⏎⏎CareQuest Institute for Oral Health | ONC Docket Comment | Page 2⏎⏎What the proposed rule describes as "compliance overhead" is, in practical terms, the documentation that allows a clinician to ask the most basic questions about a tool they are being asked to use on patients. The model card requirement is not burdensome in any meaningful sense for a developer that has actually done the work of testing their model. If a developer cannot document what population their model was trained on, that is not a documentation problem, that is a product quality problem, and the certification criterion is doing exactly what it should do by surfacing it. I want to be clear that I understand there are legitimate concerns about over-certification and about requirements that add process without adding safety, and I take those concerns seriously, but the DSI transparency disclosures don't fit that description. A 2023 review published in npj Digital Medicine (Sendak et al., 6:1, doi:10.1038/s41746-023-00835-4) examined the deployment of clinical AI tools across multiple health systems and found that in the majority of cases, front-line clinicians had no access to documentation describing model limitations or validation status. That's the baseline we're starting from. The HTI-1 DSI criterion was an attempt to move away from that baseline.⏎⏎I want to describe something I saw in Alachua County, Florida, last spring, because it's connected to this even if the connection isn't immediately obvious. A single mother drove forty minutes to a safety-net dental clinic with her daughter, and the pediatric records needed to safely prescribe a medication were locked in a proprietary system at a prior provider that wouldn't export them. That's an information blocking problem. But the AI problem I'm describing today is structurally similar, a clinician is being asked to act on information, whether it's a patient record or a model output, without knowing where that information came from or whether it can be trusted for this particular patient. The solution in both cases is transparency. Removing the DSI certification criterion doesn't reduce burden in any real sense, it just moves the burden downstream onto the clinician and ultimately onto the patient.⏎⏎Let me be specific about what the DSI certification criterion actually requires, because I think some of the framing around "regulatory burden" assumes a complexity that isn't there. Under 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11) as finalized in HTI-1, the required disclosures for AI-driven decision support interventions include:⏎⏎1. The name and version of the intervention⏎2. The intervention's intended use and target population⏎3. The type of model or approach used⏎4. A description of the training data, including demographic characteristics⏎5. Known risks, limitations, and contraindications⏎6. Whether external validation has been conducted and, if so, a summary of results⏎7. A mechanism for end users to access this information within the clinical workflow⏎⏎That list is not onerous. A developer who has built a responsible AI product should be able to populate those fields. The FDA has published guidance on AI/ML-based Software as a Medical Device (SaMD) under its 2021 action plan that covers similar ground (FDA, Artificial Intelligence/Machine Learning-Based Software as a Medical Device Action Plan, January 2021), and NIST published its AI Risk Management Framework in January 2023 (NIST AI 100-1) which recommends documentation practices that map almost directly onto the DSI criterion. The idea that this kind of documentation is uniquely burdensome in the health IT context doesn't hold up when you look at what is being asked.⏎⏎CareQuest Institute for Oral Health | ONC Docket Comment | Page 3⏎⏎The populations we serve at CareQuest are also worth naming explicitly in this context, because "patient safety" can become an abstraction when it's invoked in a comment like this. We're talking about Medicaid beneficiaries, CHIP-enrolled children, adults experiencing homelessness, farmworkers, and elderly patients in rural communities who are often seeing a provider who has access to AI-assisted diagnostic tools but no way to evaluate whether those tools have been tested in anything like the clinical context they're operating in. A 2021 Health Affairs study by Obermeyer and colleagues (40:6, pages 965-973) documented that commercial health risk scores used in Medicaid managed care consistently underestimated the burden of illness in Black patients relative to white patients with the same objective health status. These tools were deployed at scale before those disparities were documented by researchers. The DSI certification criterion is one of the mechanisms we have to prevent that from happening again, because it requires developers to show their work before the tool gets embedded in clinical workflows. Removing it doesn't make the tools better, it just removes the requirement to demonstrate that.⏎⏎I want to acknowledge something, because I think it's honest to do so. I'm not writing this as a reflexive opponent of any changes to the HTI-1 framework. But the DSI transparency provisions are different in kind from those adjustments, because they exist to protect patients from a specific and documented category of harm, which is the deployment of AI tools that perform differently across demographic groups in ways the clinician cannot detect. The Joint Commission issued a Sentinel Event Alert in December 2023 (No. 68) that specifically called out AI-related diagnostic errors as an emerging patient safety concern. The Office for Civil Rights has published guidance under 45 CFR Part 92 on the obligations of covered entities to prevent algorithmically-driven discrimination. The regulatory ecosystem around AI in health care is, if anything, moving toward more transparency requirements, not fewer.⏎⏎What I would ask ONC to do is retain the DSI certification criterion in its current form, or at minimum, issue a clear statement that the removal of the criterion does not affect the underlying obligation of health IT developers to maintain and make available documentation of AI model characteristics, and that CMS and OIG enforcement of information blocking provisions will be applied to any developer who obscures material information about model performance from clinicians or patients. I would also ask that ONC engage specifically with safety-net providers, FQHCs, and oral health organizations in any future rulemaking on AI transparency, because the populations those providers serve are most exposed to the downstream effects of biased or undertested models and least likely to have the institutional resources to independently evaluate the tools they're being asked to adopt. The HTI-1 rulemaking process included a substantial public comment record on the DSI criterion, with organizations including the American Medical Informatics Association, the American Health Information Management Association, and multiple patient advocacy coalitions supporting the transparency requirements (see 89 Fed. Those costs don't show up in a developer's compliance budget. They show up in adverse events, in disparate outcomes, in the erosion of clinician trust in health IT systems that have already been a source of significant burnout and dissatisfaction. A 2022 survey published in Mayo Clinic Proceedings (97:8, pages 1437-1448) found that clinician distrust of EHR-embedded clinical decision support was one of the top contributors to alert fatigue and workflow disruption. Transparency about how those tools work and who they were designed for is one of the inputs to rebuilding that trust, and it's not clear what is gained, for anyone in the system, by removing it.⏎⏎CareQuest Institute for Oral Health | ONC Docket Comment | Page 4⏎⏎The DSI certification criterion as finalized in HTI-1 went through a rigorous notice-and-comment process, it was responsive to substantial public input, and it was designed to address a documented gap in how AI tools are disclosed to the clinicians who use them. It was a combination of incompatible systems and genuinely ambiguous obligations about what had to be shared, when, and how. She did not have eleven days to spare. That experience, and the experiences of dozens of other women we have documented since, is the operational context for everything we say below. When this agency proposes giving health systems more discretion over how and whether data flows, or when it proposes removing certification requirements that tell clinicians what an AI tool is actually doing, I find it genuinely difficult to see who benefits other than the developers and the health systems that want to reduce compliance costs.⏎⏎Policy Center for Maternal Mental Health | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 2⏎⏎On the specific question of the DSI transparency requirements: the current certification criterion at 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11) requires that health IT developers provide what the agency calls "model cards" for AI-based decision support interventions. These disclosures must cover intended use, the target patient population the tool was trained on, known limitations and risks, training data characteristics, and whether the model has been externally validated. The proposed rule would remove or substantially weaken this requirement. We are asking the agency not to do that.⏎⏎The reasons are not abstract. There is now a substantial body of published literature documenting that clinical AI tools perform differently across patient subgroups, and that those performance gaps are often invisible to the clinicians using the tools unless the developers are required to disclose them. A 2021 study published in JAMA Internal Medicine (Obermeyer et al., 279(11)) found that a widely deployed commercial algorithm systematically underestimated health needs for Black patients relative to white patients with identical objective health status, because the model had been trained on cost as a proxy for need. A 2022 analysis in npj Digital Medicine (Char et al., 5:6) found that fewer than 30 percent of FDA-cleared AI/ML-based medical devices had published any validation data on demographic subgroups. For perinatal mental health specifically, where patients are disproportionately women of color, women with limited English proficiency, and women with histories of trauma that affect how they present clinically, these gaps are not hypothetical risks. They are the default condition. A DSI tool that was trained primarily on non-perinatal populations, or on populations from academic medical centers in the Northeast, may perform very differently in a community health center in the South Bronx, and a clinician using that tool has no way to know that unless someone tells them.⏎⏎Policy Center for Maternal Mental Health | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 3⏎⏎What the model card requirement does, operationally, is give the clinician a fighting chance. It does not guarantee good outcomes. It does not replace clinical judgment. What it does is make the tool legible. A psychiatrist or midwife or OB using a DSI-enabled EHR system should be able to look at a flag or a recommendation generated by an AI model and understand, at minimum:⏎⏎1. What population was this tool designed for, and does my patient fit that population?⏎⏎2. Has this tool been tested on patients who look like mine demographically and clinically?⏎⏎3. What are the known failure modes, and how should I adjust my interpretation accordingly?⏎⏎4. Who built this, and did anyone outside the company check whether it works?⏎⏎Without the certification requirement, there is no mechanism that reliably produces those answers. Health IT developers can and do publish white papers and marketing materials, but those are not the same thing as a standardized disclosure attached to a certified product. The 21st Century Cures Act (Pub. L. 114-255, Section 4002) directed the agency to promote transparency in health IT, and the DSI criterion is one of the more concrete ways that direction has been implemented. Removing it moves in the opposite direction.⏎⏎The agency's stated rationale for the deregulatory approach, as described in the Federal Register notice at 90 FR 18489, is burden reduction and increased flexibility. We take that seriously. Regulatory burden on small and mid-sized health IT developers is real, and we have heard from technology partners in our network who find the current certification timelines and documentation requirements genuinely difficult to manage. But the DSI transparency requirements are not the source of that burden. The model card disclosure is a documentation requirement, not a testing mandate. A developer that has built a responsible AI product already knows its training data characteristics, its intended use population, and its validation history. Writing that down is not the hard part. The hard part is building the tool well, and the disclosure requirement does not change that calculus.⏎⏎Policy Center for Maternal Mental Health | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 4⏎⏎What concerns me, and I want to be honest that this is partly speculative, is that removing the requirement will reduce transparency not because the requirement is burdensome but because it is inconvenient. A model card that accurately describes a tool's limitations may make clinicians less likely to use it, or may invite scrutiny from health systems procurement teams. That is exactly the point. If a tool has known limitations for a particular patient population, the clinicians using it should know. The FDA has taken steps in a similar direction through its guidance on Predetermined Change Control Plans for AI/ML-based Software as a Medical Device (January 2025), which requires developers to document how models will be updated and validated over time. ONC's DSI criterion complements that framework by ensuring that the certified EHR environment where most of these tools are actually deployed carries the same disclosure obligations. Walking back the ONC requirement while FDA is moving toward more documentation, not less, creates a gap that is hard to justify on policy grounds.⏎⏎There is also a specific concern about perinatal mental health applications that I don't think is adequately addressed in the proposed rule. DSI tools are being deployed in OB and gynecology settings to screen for perinatal depression and anxiety, to flag patients for follow-up, and in some cases to suggest medication management pathways. The Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale has been digitized and embedded in EHR workflows in ways that involve AI-based scoring or risk stratification at numerous health systems, including several in New York State. Our organization has been in contact with at least four health systems in the past eighteen months where clinical staff were unaware that the screening tool embedded in their workflow had been modified from the validated instrument, or that the risk thresholds had been adjusted based on the developer's internal analysis rather than published clinical literature. Under the current DSI criterion, those modifications would require disclosure. Under the proposed rule, that requirement is weakened or removed.⏎⏎Policy Center for Maternal Mental Health | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 5⏎⏎The specific ask is straightforward. Retain 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11) in its current form, including the requirements for:⏎⏎o Intended use disclosure⏎o Target population description, including demographic and clinical characteristics of training data⏎o Known limitations and risks, particularly for subpopulations underrepresented in training data⏎o External validation status, with identification of the validating entity⏎o A mechanism for clinicians to access this information at the point of care, not only in product documentation⏎⏎If the agency is concerned about compliance burden for smaller developers, a phased implementation timeline or a tiered disclosure requirement based on product complexity would be a more proportionate response than elimination. The agency has used phased timelines before, including in the implementation of the information blocking provisions under 45 CFR 171, and that approach preserved the substantive obligation while giving actors time to comply.⏎⏎One last thing that I keep coming back to. The women served by our partner programs are not well-positioned to advocate for themselves when a clinical AI tool fails them. They are often in crisis, often navigating multiple systems simultaneously, often without the health literacy resources to question a clinical recommendation that came from an algorithm they don't know exists. The model card requirement is not for them directly. It is for their clinicians. But the clinicians can only use that information if the agency requires it to exist in the first place. We are asking the agency to keep that requirement in place.⏎⏎Policy Center for Maternal Mental Health⏎Susan Young, Executive Director⏎contact@policymaternalmentalhealth.org⏎www.policymaternalmentalhealth.org♔♔2025-12-20T00:00:00Z♔2025-12-20T00:00:00Z♔2025-12-12T00:00:00Z♔2026-02-10T00:00:00Z♔5♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Retain the current Decision Support Interventions (DSI) certification criterion requiring AI model cards and transparency disclosures (intended use, target population, known risks, training data characteristics, external validation) to ensure patient safety, informed clinical decision-making, and accountability in AI-assisted healthcare.♔Removing DSI transparency requirements creates a dangerous regulatory gap where AI-based clinical decision support tools face fewer disclosure obligations than traditional medical devices, undermining consistent safety standards.♔advocacy_group♔high♔supportive♔New York♔executive director♔54♔Last spring, one of our program participants — a mother of three in the Bronx navigating a severe postpartum OCD diagnosis — spent eleven days trying to obtain her psychiatric records from a previous provider so her new care team could avoid repeating a medication trial that had nearly hospitalized her. the lived experience of a family trying to manage a grandmother's diabetes in a county where the nearest endocrinologist is 45 minutes away.⏎⏎the family i mentioned earlier -- the one in elkhart county -- they're still in my head. that experience was not the result of a single system failure. it was the result of a series of small design decisions, each of which probably seemed reasonable to someone, adding up to a situation where a vulnerable patient had no access to coherent information about her own care. removing the DSI transparency requirements is exactly that kind of small design decision. it probably seems reasonable to someone. it probably looks like a minor deregulatory adjustment in a complex rulemaking. but when you aggregate it across all the safety-net clinics and all the patients who depend on those clinics and all the AI tools that are already embedded in those workflows, the effect is real.⏎⏎our member clinics in south carolina serve approximately 340,000 patients annually. i don't have a precise count for how many of those patients are currently subject to care decisions that are influenced in some way by an AI or algorithmic DSI tool. but given that at least 14 of our 22 member organizations reported using such tools in our 2023-2024 needs assessment, the number is not small. these are patients who, under the current regulatory framework, have at least some assurance that the tools influencing their care have been documented and disclosed to their clinicians. under the proposed changes, that assurance goes away.⏎⏎i want to be fair and say that i don't think the agency is proposing this change because it doesn't care about safety-net patients. i think the agency is genuinely trying to reduce burden and support innovation and those are legitimate goals. but i think this particular change, in this particular context, gets the tradeoff wrong. the burden being reduced is on developers. the risk being increased is on patients. and the patients who face the most increased risk are the ones who are already most vulnerable.⏎⏎RESPONSE TO THE INNOVATION ARGUMENT⏎⏎South Carolina Primary Health Care Association | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 5⏎⏎the argument that transparency requirements slow innovation is one i want to engage with directly because i think it deserves a real response rather than just a dismissal.⏎⏎it is true that documentation requirements add cost. it is true that some developers, particularly smaller ones, may find model card requirements burdensome to produce. it is true that in a fast-moving field like AI, documentation can become outdated quickly and maintaining it takes resources.⏎⏎i accept all of that.⏎⏎but i want to push back on the framing that transparency and innovation are in tension. in my experience working with health centers that are trying to evaluate and adopt new technologies, the absence of transparency is itself a barrier to adoption. when our member clinics cannot get basic performance documentation from a vendor, many of them simply don't adopt the tool. they're risk-averse for good reasons. they have limited IT staff, limited legal capacity, and patients who cannot absorb the consequences of a bad technology decision. if a vendor can provide clear model card documentation showing that their tool was externally validated, that it performs comparably across demographic subgroups, and that it was designed for use in primary care settings like theirs, that documentation actually accelerates adoption. it builds trust.⏎⏎so the argument that removing transparency requirements will accelerate adoption of beneficial AI tools in safety-net settings -- i'm skeptical. i think it might have the opposite effect, because it removes the signal that risk-averse health centers rely on when making technology decisions.⏎⏎there's also a longer-term consideration. if AI tools are deployed in safety-net settings without adequate transparency, and if those tools perform poorly for underserved populations, and if that poor performance causes harm, the resulting backlash will set back AI adoption in these settings far more than any documentation requirement would. we have seen this pattern before in health IT. the meaningful use rollout created real problems when systems were deployed too fast without adequate validation, and those problems damaged trust in EHR technology in community health settings for years. we don't want to repeat that with AI.⏎⏎TECHNICAL COMMENT ON 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11)⏎⏎South Carolina Primary Health Care Association | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 6⏎⏎our policy team wanted me to include some more specific technical comments on the regulatory text so here goes -- i'll try to be as precise as i can given that i'm a community organizer and not a health IT attorney.⏎⏎the current DSI criterion at 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11) requires certified health IT to, among other things, display certain information about AI/ML-based interventions to users. the proposed rule as we understand it would remove or substantially modify these requirements. our specific concerns are:⏎⏎a. the removal of the requirement to disclose whether an intervention is AI/ML-based at the point of care. clinicians cannot make informed decisions about how much weight to give a recommendation if they don't know whether it comes from a rule-based algorithm, a machine learning model, or a clinical guideline. these have very different reliability profiles and very different implications for how a clinician should interpret the output. removing this disclosure makes the clinician's job harder, not easier.⏎⏎b. the modification of transparency requirements for training data. the current requirement, as we understand it, includes disclosure of training data characteristics. this is where bias most often enters these systems. if the training data was collected predominantly from one type of patient population and the tool is being used on a different population, clinicians need to know that. this is a patient safety issue, not a paperwork issue.⏎⏎c. the weakening of external validation disclosure requirements. external validation is the scientific standard for establishing that a model performs as advertised outside the conditions under which it was developed. the 85 FR 25642 preamble to the 2020 ONC Cures Act Final Rule discussed the importance of this standard extensively in the context of clinical decision support. the proposed rule appears to be walking back from that commitment without adequate justification.⏎⏎d. we're also concerned about the interaction between the DSI transparency requirements and the information blocking provisions. if the transparency information that model cards would provide is no longer required to be part of certified health IT, then there is no clear mechanism by which a patient or clinician could request that information as a matter of right. the information blocking rules at 45 CFR 171 are designed to ensure that health information flows freely, but they can only protect access to information that exists and is documented in the first place. if the underlying documentation requirement goes away, the information blocking protections become less meaningful for this category of information.⏎⏎i want to acknowledge that i may be misreading some of the technical details of how these provisions interact. if the agency has a different reading of how these provisions interact, i would genuinely welcome clarification on that in the final rule. but based on our best reading of the proposed changes, we believe the effect would be to reduce the practical availability of AI transparency information to clinicians and patients at safety-net facilities.⏎⏎WHAT WE HAVE HEARD FROM OUR MEMBER HEALTH CENTERS⏎⏎South Carolina Primary Health Care Association | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 7⏎⏎in preparing this comment we did an informal outreach to our DSI certification requirements, she would at least have a basis for demanding that documentation. under the proposed changes, that basis is weakened.⏎⏎another health center, a smaller organization in which is probably the right call, but he's doing it without any real information. he's basically managing the risk blindly.⏎⏎a third health center that serves a significant migrant and seasonal with episodic rather than continuous care patterns. the answer is almost certainly no, because these populations are systematically underrepresented in EHR data due to lack of access to consistent care. but without model card disclosure requirements, there is no way to confirm this or to factor it into clinical decision-making.⏎⏎these are not hypothetical concerns. these are operational realities that our member health centers are navigating right now. the DSI transparency requirements are not a burden to them. they are a tool they are trying to use and finding that even with the requirements on the books, compliance is imperfect and enforcement is limited. weakening the requirements would make an already difficult situation worse.⏎⏎South Carolina Primary Health Care Association | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 8⏎⏎A WORD ABOUT TIMING⏎⏎i want to say something about the timing of this rulemaking that i think is worth putting on the record. we are at a moment when AI tools are being deployed in clinical settings faster than the regulatory framework can keep up with. ONC's own 2024 report on AI in health IT acknowledged this. the FDA's digital health center of excellence has been grappling with this. there is broad consensus that health AI is moving fast and that governance frameworks need to catch up.⏎⏎in that context, removing certification requirements for AI transparency seems like exactly the wrong direction. it is reducing the governance floor at precisely the moment when the floor matters most. the volume of AI-assisted DSI tools in clinical use is increasing. the complexity of those tools is increasing. the potential for harm from poorly validated or poorly disclosed tools is increasing. this is not the moment to say "the market will sort it out."⏎⏎i also want to note that the DSI transparency requirements that would be removed or weakened under this proposal were themselves the product of a careful rulemaking process that took years and involved extensive stakeholder input. the 21st century cures act, at section 4002, directed ONC to develop certification criteria that would support the safe use of clinical decision support. the DSI transparency requirements were developed in response to that direction. removing them without a clear explanation of what has changed -- what evidence shows the requirements are unnecessary, what alternative mechanisms exist to address the harms they were designed to prevent -- seems like a significant step that deserves more justification than has been provided.⏎⏎i'll be honest: the preamble to this proposed rule, in the sections addressing the DSI changes, is not very specific about why the transparency requirements are being removed. there's general language about burden reduction and regulatory flexibility, but there's not a detailed analysis of what the safety implications are or how those implications have been evaluated. for a change that could affect how AI tools are disclosed and validated in clinical settings serving tens of millions of safety-net patients, i think we deserve more specificity than that. maybe there's analysis i haven't seen. if so i'd genuinely welcome the agency pointing to it.⏎⏎CONCLUSION (sort of -- i have to get back to my CMS-2025-0050-110024♔CMS-2025-0050♔Michelle Adams♔No Delays, No Surprises Coalition♔♔♔♔Eliminating ONC's Decision Support Interventions certification criterion—which requires AI transparency disclosures for clinical decision support tools—would remove a critical patient safety protection without adequate justification, as voluntary ...♔Michelle Adams⏎Senior Policy Analyst⏎No Delays, No Surprises Coalition⏎Detroit, Michigan⏎⏎June 23, 2025⏎⏎Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology⏎U.S. Department of Health and Human Services⏎330 C Street, SW⏎Washington, DC 20201⏎⏎Re: ASTP/ONC Proposed Rule, "Deregulatory Actions To Unleash Prosperity: Health Data, Technology, and Interoperability" (Docket No. ONC-2025-0001)⏎⏎Dear Acting National Coordinator:⏎⏎The No Delays, No Surprises Coalition submits these comments on behalf of patients, caregivers, and consumer advocates across Michigan and the broader Midwest who have a direct stake in how health information technology certification requirements shape the safety of clinical care. Our organization has followed the development of ONC's certification program for over a decade, and we appreciate the opportunity to weigh in on a proposed rule that would alter it substantially. We do so with genuine concern about one aspect of the proposal in particular: the removal of the Decision Support Interventions certification criterion, which currently requires health IT developers to disclose AI model cards and related transparency information about clinical decision support tools. This comment focuses primarily on that question, because we believe it is the most consequential safety issue in the entire rulemaking.⏎⏎Before getting into the regulatory particulars, let me say something about where this concern comes from for our organization. Last spring, an 82-year-old woman in Southeast Michigan was transferred between three different health systems following a cardiac event. At each transfer, the receiving care team had to reconstruct her medication history from incomplete records because the sending facility said the data was not available in a transferable format. A hospitalist made a dosing decision based on a gap in her chart, a gap that a functioning interoperability standard should have filled. That gap was not the only problem. At the second facility, a clinical decision support alert fired based on a risk algorithm whose training population, as best we could later determine, had very different demographic characteristics than an 82-year-old Black woman from Detroit. The physician overrode it. Whether that was the right call, we genuinely cannot say, because nobody could tell us what the algorithm was actually designed to do, what patient population it had been validated on, or what the known failure modes were. That is the problem the DSI criterion was designed to address. And the proposed rule would eliminate it.⏎⏎No Delays, No Surprises Coalition | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 2⏎⏎The DSI certification criterion, as established in the ONC Health IT Certification Program under 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11), requires that health IT developers provide certain disclosures when their products incorporate predictive algorithms or AI-driven clinical decision support. Specifically, developers must document the intended use of the intervention, the target patient population, known limitations and risks, characteristics of the training data, and whether the tool has undergone external validation. ONC finalized these requirements in the 2024 HTI-1 rule (89 Fed. Reg. 1192), and they represented a measured, carefully negotiated response to a documented patient safety problem. The proposed rule before us now would remove these requirements in the name of reducing regulatory burden. We do not think that tradeoff is justified, and we want to explain why in some detail.⏎⏎The argument for removing the DSI criterion, as we read the preamble, rests on two claims: first, that the criterion imposes compliance costs on developers without demonstrated safety benefit, and second, that other mechanisms, including market pressure and voluntary standards, can adequately discipline the AI tools used in clinical settings. We find the first claim plausible in a narrow sense but ultimately insufficient, and the second claim genuinely difficult to credit given what we know about how health AI products have actually behaved in deployment. On the cost question, the agency cites concerns from developers that producing model cards is burdensome, particularly for smaller vendors. That is a real operational concern and we do not dismiss it. But the relevant comparison is not "cost of compliance" against "zero," it is "cost of compliance" against "cost of clinical harm when opaque algorithms misfire." A 2023 study published in JAMA Network Open examining sepsis prediction algorithms deployed across seventeen health systems found that three of the five most widely used tools performed substantially worse in Black patients than in white patients, with sensitivity gaps ranging from 11 to 22 percentage points. None of the facilities using those tools had received documentation from the developer about demographic performance variation. That is not a hypothetical failure mode. That is a documented, ongoing patient safety problem, and it is exactly the kind of problem the DSI disclosure requirements were designed to make visible.⏎⏎On the question of voluntary mechanisms, we are skeptical for reasons that are concrete rather than abstract. The health IT market does not currently produce consistent, usable AI transparency documentation in the absence of regulatory requirements. Our organization surveyed member organizations in Michigan and Ohio in early 2025 and found the following:⏎⏎1. Of fourteen health systems that had deployed at least one AI-assisted clinical decision support tool in the prior two years, eleven reported receiving no model card or equivalent documentation from the developer.⏎⏎2. Of the three that did receive some form of documentation, only one described it as sufficient to allow the clinical informatics team to assess the tool's appropriateness for their specific patient population.⏎⏎3. None of the fourteen systems reported having access to information about the demographic composition of the training data used to build the tool they were using.⏎⏎These are not small community hospitals with limited procurement capacity. Several of them are large academic medical centers with dedicated health IT staff. If voluntary market pressure were generating adequate transparency, we would expect a different result from that survey. We did not get one.⏎⏎No Delays, No Surprises Coalition | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 3⏎⏎We want to be fair to the agency here, because we recognize the genuine tension the proposed rule is trying to navigate. There is a real argument that overly prescriptive certification criteria can slow the adoption of beneficial health IT, particularly for smaller developers who lack the resources to navigate complex compliance requirements. We take that argument seriously. And we are not suggesting that the current DSI criterion is perfectly designed. There are aspects of the model card requirements, particularly around training data provenance documentation, that are genuinely difficult for developers to comply with when they are using foundation models or third-party AI components. We understand why some developers find those requirements challenging. But the answer to "this requirement is hard to comply with" is not "eliminate the requirement." The answer is "refine the requirement so it achieves its safety purpose in a more workable way." The proposed rule does not appear to have seriously explored that middle path, and that troubles us.⏎⏎What we would ask the agency to consider, in lieu of elimination, is a revised DSI criterion that preserves the core transparency obligations while addressing the specific compliance burdens that developers have identified. At minimum, any certified health IT product that incorporates a predictive algorithm used to support clinical decisions about individual patients should be required to disclose the following:⏎⏎a. The intended clinical use of the algorithm and the patient population for which it was designed and validated.⏎⏎b. Any known limitations in performance across demographic subgroups, to the extent such information is available from the developer or from peer-reviewed literature.⏎⏎c. Whether the tool has been subject to independent external validation, and if so, a citation to or summary of that validation.⏎⏎d. The general source and characteristics of the training data, including approximate time period and care setting, without requiring disclosure of proprietary model weights or architecture.⏎⏎These are not novel requirements. They are largely consistent with what the Food and Drug Administration already expects for Software as a Medical Device under the AI/ML-Based Software as a Medical Device Action Plan, and with what the Coalition for Health AI recommended in its Blueprint for Trustworthy AI Implementation Guidance published in April 2023. Asking ONC to require the same level of transparency for certified health IT tools that FDA expects for regulated software seems reasonable. The fact that many clinical decision support tools currently fall outside FDA oversight makes the ONC certification pathway more important as a transparency mechanism, not less.⏎⏎We are also concerned about what the removal of the DSI criterion signals to the broader health IT market. Certification criteria function partly as market signals. When ONC certifies a product, it communicates something about the minimum standards that product has met. Removing the AI transparency criterion communicates that ONC does not consider algorithmic transparency a baseline expectation for certified health IT. That signal will be received by developers, by health systems making procurement decisions, and by clinicians trying to evaluate whether to trust the tools in front of them. We do not think that is the signal ONC intends to send, but it is the signal the market will likely receive.⏎⏎No Delays, No Surprises Coalition | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 4⏎⏎One more point, and then we will close. The preamble to the proposed rule describes the DSI criterion as imposing burden without "clear evidence of patient benefit." We would push back on the framing of that standard. The absence of published studies demonstrating that model cards prevented specific adverse events is not the same as the absence of benefit. Model cards are an informational requirement; their benefit operates through the decisions clinicians and health systems make when they have better information, and those causal pathways are genuinely difficult to study in the short run. By that same logic, one could argue that there is no "clear evidence" that informed consent documentation prevents harm in any specific case, because the counterfactual is unobservable. We do not think that is a standard the agency would apply consistently, and we do not think it should apply here.⏎⏎The No Delays, No Surprises Coalition respectfully urges the agency to retain the Decision Support Interventions certification criterion, with targeted revisions to address documented compliance challenges, rather than eliminating it wholesale. We are available to discuss any of the points raised in these comments and can be reached at policy@nodelayssurprises.org.⏎⏎Respectfully submitted,⏎⏎Michelle Adams⏎Senior Policy Analyst⏎No Delays, No Surprises Coalition⏎Detroit, Michigan♔♔2025-12-31T00:00:00Z♔2025-12-31T00:00:00Z♔2025-12-12T00:00:00Z♔2026-02-10T00:00:00Z♔5♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Retain the current Decision Support Interventions (DSI) certification criterion requiring AI model cards and transparency disclosures (intended use, target population, known risks, training data characteristics, external validation) to ensure patient safety, informed clinical decision-making, and accountability in AI-assisted healthcare.♔The 'black box' problem is a documented barrier to AI adoption in healthcare; model cards directly address clinician and organizational concerns about trustworthiness and are a proven mechanism to build confidence.♔advocacy_group♔high♔concerned♔Michigan♔senior policy analyst♔55♔Last spring, my 82-year-old mother was transferred between three different health systems in Southeast Michigan following a cardiac event, and each time her care team had to piece together her medication history from incomplete records because the prior facility claimed the data "wasn't available in a transferable format." CMS-2025-0050-110030♔CMS-2025-0050♔Sandra Thomas♔iPill inc♔♔♔♔Mandatory AI transparency disclosures in the DSI certification criterion are essential patient safety requirements that should be retained, as they enable clinicians to make informed decisions about AI-assisted clinical tools by revealing critical...♔iPill Inc. | ONC-2025-Deregulatory | Page 1⏎⏎Sandra Thomas, Chief Compliance Officer⏎iPill Inc.⏎Minneapolis, Minnesota 55403⏎sthomas@ipillinc.com⏎⏎Submitted via regulations.gov⏎Docket: ONC-2025 [ASTP/ONC Deregulatory Actions To Unleash Prosperity: Health Data, Technology, and Interoperability]⏎⏎---⏎⏎COMMENT OF iPILL INC. REGARDING PROPOSED ELIMINATION OF DECISION SUPPORT INTERVENTIONS CERTIFICATION CRITERION⏎⏎iPill Inc. is a health IT developer based in Minneapolis, Minnesota. We build medication management and clinical decision support software deployed at ambulatory care clinics, community health centers, and integrated health systems across the upper Midwest. Our customer base currently includes fourteen health systems in Minnesota, Wisconsin, and the Dakotas, and we have been operating in the certified health IT space since 2014. I am the compliance officer at iPill Inc., and I want to be direct about why I am submitting this comment: we have genuine concerns about the proposal to eliminate or significantly roll back the Decision Support Interventions (DSI) certification criterion, specifically the components requiring AI model cards and transparency disclosures.⏎⏎I want to acknowledge upfront that I understand the frustration driving this proposed rule. I live that frustration. Last spring, our development team spent eleven weeks rearchitecting a feature that clinicians at three Minnesota health systems had been requesting for two years, not because the feature itself was technically complex, but because our certification pathway required us to retrofit it into a compliance framework that predated the underlying technology by nearly a decade. I watched our lead engineer, a woman who left a major tech company specifically because she wanted her work to matter in healthcare, nearly resign out of sheer frustration. We got the feature out, eventually, but two of those health systems had already started evaluating a competitor operating outside the certified space precisely because we couldn't move fast enough. So I am not writing this as someone who thinks the current certification system is working well. Parts of it are not.⏎⏎But the DSI transparency requirements are a different category of thing, and I think the proposal conflates two problems that should be handled separately.⏎⏎iPill Inc. | ONC-2025-Deregulatory | Page 2⏎⏎WHAT THE DSI CRITERION ACTUALLY REQUIRES AND WHY IT MATTERS⏎⏎The DSI certification criterion, as established under 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11) and elaborated through the 2024 HTI-1 final rule (89 Fed. Reg. 1192), requires that certified health IT incorporating AI-driven decision support disclose specific information: intended use, target population, known limitations and risks, training data characteristics, and whether external validation has been conducted. These are sometimes called "AI model cards" in the industry, borrowing terminology from a Google Research paper by Mitchell et al. (2019) that became something of a standard reference in the AI transparency space.⏎⏎The proposed rule suggests that these requirements create unnecessary burden and that market forces, combined with provider due diligence, can substitute for regulatory transparency mandates. I genuinely disagree with that framing, and I want to explain why from the perspective of someone who actually builds these systems and watches them interact with clinical workflows.⏎⏎When we deploy a medication interaction alert into a clinical setting, the clinicians using that alert have almost no practical way to evaluate whether the underlying model is appropriate for their patient population unless we tell them. A hospitalist at a rural critical access hospital in Bemidji, Minnesota is not going to independently investigate whether our training data included sufficient representation of elderly patients with polypharmacy profiles. She is going to look at the alert, make a judgment, and move on. The entire premise of decision support is that it is providing information the clinician might not otherwise have. If the clinician cannot evaluate the basis for that information, the "support" becomes, in effect, a black box instruction. That is a patient safety problem.⏎⏎I keep coming back to a specific example. In 2023, a published study in JAMA Internal Medicine (Obermeyer et al., 2023, though I may be slightly off on the year) found that a widely deployed clinical algorithm systematically underestimated the health needs of Black patients because the training data used healthcare cost as a proxy for health need, and Black patients historically have lower healthcare costs due to access barriers, not lower health needs. The algorithm was not malicious. The developers were not negligent in any conventional sense. But the hospitals deploying it had no visibility into the training data characteristics, and so they had no way to identify the bias until researchers flagged it years later. That is exactly the problem the DSI model card requirements are designed to prevent.⏎⏎iPill Inc. | ONC-2025-Deregulatory | Page 3⏎⏎THE MARKET FORCES ARGUMENT DOES NOT HOLD IN THIS CONTEXT⏎⏎The proposed rule seems to suggest, at least implicitly, that if transparency disclosures create value for providers, the market will demand them even without a regulatory mandate. I understand the logic. I am genuinely sympathetic to deregulatory arguments in contexts where market incentives align with desired outcomes. But I think this particular argument breaks down for a few reasons specific to health IT.⏎⏎First, the information asymmetry between developers and deployers in AI-assisted clinical decision support is significant. We know things about our models that our customers cannot independently verify. We know the demographic composition of our training data. We know where our validation studies were conducted and on what patient populations. We know the confidence intervals on our performance metrics. Our customers, the health systems, generally do not have the technical capacity to audit this information independently, and they are not going to hire data scientists to review every AI module they deploy. They are going to trust us. The question is whether that trust should be blind or whether there should be a baseline disclosure standard that gives them something to evaluate.⏎⏎Second, the competitive dynamics in certified health IT do not reliably produce transparency as a market outcome. Health systems procure EHR and decision support tools through multi-year contracts with significant switching costs. By the time a health system discovers that a deployed AI module has performance problems in their patient population, they may be three years into a seven-year contract. The accountability mechanism that market theory assumes, the ability to switch to a better product, is severely constrained. This is not a theoretical concern. The 21st Century Cures Act information blocking provisions (42 U.S.C. 300jj-52) exist precisely because Congress recognized that the health IT market has structural features that require regulatory intervention to produce socially desirable outcomes.⏎⏎Third, and I want to be careful here because I am speaking somewhat outside my lane as a compliance officer rather than a clinician or health services researcher, the consequences of AI failure in clinical decision support are not symmetric. If a streaming service recommends a bad movie, the user watches a bad movie. If a medication dosing algorithm performs poorly in a patient population it was not validated for, the consequence can be a serious adverse event. The asymmetry of consequences is a standard justification for regulatory disclosure requirements in other high-stakes domains, and I do not see why it should be different here.⏎⏎iPill Inc. | ONC-2025-Deregulatory | Page 4⏎⏎WHAT WE ACTUALLY OBSERVE IN THE ABSENCE OF DISCLOSURE REQUIREMENTS⏎⏎I want to be specific about what happens in practice when transparency is left to developer discretion, because I think the abstract policy debate sometimes loses sight of the operational reality.⏎⏎Before the HTI-1 rule created the DSI model card requirements, our standard product documentation for AI-assisted features was, honestly, inadequate. We disclosed intended use in broad terms, we noted that the product was not a substitute for clinical judgment (standard disclaimer language), and we referenced our internal validation studies in general terms. We did not routinely disclose training data composition, demographic representation in validation cohorts, or known performance differentials across patient subpopulations. Not because we were hiding anything, but because there was no standard for what disclosure meant, and our documentation practices reflected that ambiguity.⏎⏎The HTI-1 requirements forced us to be more systematic. We had to go back through our model development records, document our training data sources, characterize the demographic composition of our validation populations, and identify known limitations. That process was not costless. It took our team approximately six weeks and required input from both our data science team and our clinical advisors. But it also revealed things we needed to know. We discovered that one of our alert modules had been validated primarily on data from large academic medical centers, and our documentation now reflects that limitation. Clinicians deploying that module in community health center settings have information they can use to calibrate their reliance on it. That is the system working as intended.⏎⏎If the DSI transparency requirements are eliminated or made voluntary, I am genuinely concerned that documentation practices across the industry will revert to the pre-HTI-1 baseline. Not because developers are bad actors, but because the path of least resistance in a resource-constrained development environment is to document what you are required to document. That is not a criticism of developers. It is a realistic description of how organizations operate.⏎⏎iPill Inc. | ONC-2025-Deregulatory | Page 5⏎⏎THE SPECIFIC DISCLOSURE ELEMENTS THAT MATTER MOST⏎⏎There are five disclosure components in the current DSI criterion that I think are worth addressing individually, because they are not all equivalent in terms of their burden or their value.⏎⏎The intended use and target population disclosures are low-burden and high-value. Every developer knows what their product is designed to do and who it is designed for. Documenting this takes minimal effort and provides essential context for clinical deployment decisions. I have not heard a serious argument that these requirements are burdensome.⏎⏎The known risks and limitations disclosure is somewhat more demanding because it requires developers to actively identify and document failure modes rather than simply describing the product's intended function. But this is also the disclosure element most directly connected to patient safety. A clinician who knows that an alert module has higher false positive rates in pediatric patients than in adults can adjust her reliance on that alert accordingly. A clinician who does not know this cannot make that adjustment. The burden of this disclosure is real but manageable, and the safety value is direct.⏎⏎The training data characteristics disclosure is where I hear the most pushback from other developers, and I understand why. Characterizing training data in a meaningful way requires documentation practices that some organizations, particularly smaller developers, may not have maintained historically. I am sympathetic to this concern. But I would note that the alternative, deploying AI into clinical settings without any disclosure of training data characteristics, is not a neutral position. It means that clinicians and health systems are using AI tools without any ability to assess whether the underlying data is representative of their patient population. That is a known risk factor for AI-related health disparities, as documented in the National Academy of Medicine's 2019 report on artificial intelligence in health and health care.⏎⏎The external validation disclosure is the one where I have the most mixed feelings, if I am being honest. External validation is genuinely valuable, but requiring its disclosure creates an implicit incentive structure where undisclosed absence of external validation becomes a de facto signal that validation has not been done. I am not sure that is the right mechanism. A developer who has done rigorous internal validation but not yet completed external validation is arguably in a better position than one who has done neither, but the disclosure framework does not easily capture that distinction. I raise this not to argue against the requirement but to suggest that the agency might consider whether the disclosure format could be refined to better capture the gradient of validation evidence rather than treating it as binary.⏎⏎iPill Inc. | ONC-2025-Deregulatory | Page 6⏎⏎RESPONSE TO THE BURDEN REDUCTION RATIONALE⏎⏎The preamble to the proposed rule identifies certification burden reduction as a primary justification for the changes, and I want to engage with that rationale directly rather than dismissing it.⏎⏎Certification burden is real. The ONC Health IT Certification Program has accumulated requirements over successive rulemaking cycles, and the aggregate compliance burden on developers, particularly small and mid-size developers like iPill Inc., is substantial. The Government Accountability Office noted in a 2022 report (GAO-22-104629) that smaller health IT developers face disproportionate certification costs relative to revenue, and that this dynamic may be contributing to market consolidation. I take that concern seriously. Market consolidation in health IT is bad for innovation and bad for health systems that need products tailored to their specific patient populations and workflows.⏎⏎But I think the proposed rule's approach to burden reduction, which appears to treat all certification requirements as roughly equivalent candidates for elimination or modification, misses an important distinction. There are certification requirements that exist primarily to ensure interoperability and technical compatibility, and there are requirements that exist to protect patient safety and ensure accountability in clinical decision-making. These are different things, and they warrant different analyses when evaluating deregulatory proposals.⏎⏎The DSI transparency requirements are in the second category. They exist because AI-assisted clinical decision support has the potential to affect patient care in ways that are not visible to clinicians unless developers disclose relevant information about how the AI works and what its known limitations are. Eliminating these requirements does not reduce burden in a way that is neutral with respect to patient outcomes. It shifts risk from developers to patients and health systems.⏎⏎I would also note that the burden of DSI transparency compliance, while real, is not uniformly distributed across the product lifecycle. The documentation work is front-loaded. Once a developer has established the documentation practices and created the model card infrastructure for a given product, maintaining and updating that documentation is significantly less burdensome than the initial creation. The companies that have already made that investment, including iPill Inc., would face a competitive disadvantage if the requirements are eliminated, because our competitors who deferred compliance would have avoided costs we absorbed. I mention this not as a primary argument but because the agency should be aware that the burden distribution across the industry is not uniform, and deregulation in this space has distributional consequences.⏎⏎iPill Inc. | ONC-2025-Deregulatory | Page 7⏎⏎THE PATIENT SAFETY CASE IS NOT HYPOTHETICAL⏎⏎I want to spend some time on the patient safety question because I think it sometimes gets treated as a background consideration rather than the central issue.⏎⏎The FDA's proposed regulatory framework for AI-enabled medical devices, articulated in the agency's 2021 action plan for AI/ML-based software as a medical device, recognizes that AI systems in clinical settings require ongoing monitoring and transparency precisely because their performance can degrade or diverge from their training conditions in ways that are not immediately visible to end users. The FDA and ONC have historically operated in adjacent but distinct regulatory spaces, and the certification program is not a substitute for FDA oversight of medical devices. But the underlying logic, that AI in clinical settings requires transparency to enable appropriate oversight and accountability, is consistent across both regulatory frameworks.⏎⏎What does patient safety actually look like in the context of AI-assisted medication management, which is our specific domain? A medication interaction alert that performs well in the training population but has higher false negative rates in patients with certain genetic polymorphisms, or in elderly patients with complex polypharmacy profiles, can contribute to missed drug interactions. A dosing recommendation module trained primarily on data from patients without significant renal impairment may not perform well in a dialysis patient population. These are not edge cases. Elderly patients with multiple comorbidities and complex medication regimens are among the most common users of the clinical settings where our products are deployed. If the AI modules supporting their care have known limitations that are not disclosed, the clinicians caring for them cannot account for those limitations.⏎⏎A 2022 study published in npj Digital Medicine (Wiens et al.) examined the real-world performance of several deployed clinical AI tools and found meaningful performance gaps between validation-study results and real-world deployment outcomes, particularly in patient populations that were underrepresented in training data. The study's authors argued that mandatory performance disclosure requirements, analogous to the DSI model card requirements, would help health systems identify these gaps earlier and adjust deployment accordingly. That is the empirical case for the transparency requirements, and I think it is a strong one.⏎⏎iPill Inc. | ONC-2025-Deregulatory | Page 8⏎⏎WHAT WE ARE ASKING THE AGENCY TO DO⏎⏎Our recommendation is straightforward: retain the DSI certification criterion in its current form, including the model card and transparency disclosure requirements for AI-assisted decision support interventions.⏎⏎If the agency is committed to burden reduction in this area, we would suggest a different approach than elimination. The agency could consider streamlining the format of required disclosures to reduce documentation overhead without reducing the substantive content that clinicians need. The current requirements specify what must be disclosed but leave the format largely to developer discretion, which actually creates some inefficiency because health systems receive model card information in inconsistent formats that are difficult to compare across vendors. A standardized disclosure template, developed in consultation with health systems, clinicians, and developers, could reduce the per-disclosure burden while improving the utility of the disclosures for end users. This is not a novel idea. The FDA's device labeling requirements follow a standardized format for similar reasons.⏎⏎The agency could also consider a phased approach for smaller developers who may face genuine capacity constraints in meeting the current documentation requirements. A tiered compliance pathway, where smaller developers have additional time or access to compliance support resources, would address the burden concern without eliminating the substantive requirements. This approach is consistent with how ONC has handled other certification requirements where capacity disparities across developer sizes were a recognized concern.⏎⏎What we are not willing to endorse is an approach that treats the transparency requirements as optional or market-driven. The evidence from both our own experience and the broader research literature is that voluntary disclosure in this domain does not produce consistent or reliable information for clinical decision-makers. The requirements exist because the market, left to its own devices, did not produce adequate transparency. Removing the requirements and expecting a different outcome is, to put it plainly, not a realistic expectation.⏎⏎iPill Inc. | ONC-2025-Deregulatory | Page 9⏎⏎A NOTE ON THE BROADER DEREGULATORY CONTEXT⏎⏎I want to be clear that iPill Inc. is not opposed to the deregulatory project in general. There are parts of the proposed rule that we support. The proposed modifications to information blocking exceptions, particularly the changes to the care coordination exception, address real operational problems that our customers have encountered. The proposed revisions to certain interoperability certification criteria, where the current requirements impose technical constraints that no longer reflect the state of the art in data exchange, are reasonable and we support them.⏎⏎The certification program has accumulated cruft over the years, and not all of it serves a clear patient safety or interoperability purpose. We have our own list of certification requirements we would be happy to see revised or eliminated, and most of them are in the technical implementation space where the specific requirements have become obsolete without the underlying policy goal having changed. That is the right kind of deregulation.⏎⏎But the DSI transparency requirements are not cruft. They are a relatively recent addition to the certification program, added in HTI-1 specifically because the agency and the field recognized that AI was becoming a significant component of certified health IT and that existing certification requirements were not adequate to address the accountability and transparency issues that AI creates. Eliminating them less than a year after they took effect, before there has been any meaningful opportunity to evaluate their impact, is not deregulation based on evidence of burden or ineffectiveness. It is deregulation based on a general preference for less regulation, applied to a requirement that has not had time to demonstrate its value or its costs in practice.⏎⏎I recognize that this is a strong statement, and I want to be fair to the agency's position. The preamble to the proposed rule does articulate specific burden concerns, and those concerns are real. But the response to real burden concerns in a patient safety context should be to ask whether the burden can be reduced while preserving the safety function, not to eliminate the safety requirement and accept the burden reduction as the outcome.⏎⏎iPill Inc. | ONC-2025-Deregulatory | Page 10⏎⏎IMPLEMENTATION EXPERIENCE SINCE HTI-1⏎⏎Since the DSI model card requirements took effect, we have had approximately eight months of experience implementing them across our product line. That experience is relevant to the agency's assessment of both the burden and the value of the requirements.⏎⏎On the burden side: the initial documentation effort was significant, as I noted earlier. We estimate that the first-round compliance work across our AI-assisted product modules required approximately 340 staff hours, including time from our data science team, our clinical advisors, and our compliance and documentation staff. That is a real cost. For a company our size, 340 staff hours in a compressed timeframe is not trivial.⏎⏎On the value side: since we began providing model card information to our health system customers, we have had several substantive conversations with clinical informatics teams that would not have happened otherwise. One health system in the Twin Cities, which I will not name by request, reviewed our model card for a medication alert module and identified that our validation population skewed heavily toward urban academic medical center patients. They asked us to flag that limitation in the alert interface itself, not just in the background documentation. We did. That is exactly the kind of informed deployment decision the transparency requirements are designed to enable, and it would not have happened without the disclosure.⏎⏎We have also had one health system decline to deploy a specific module after reviewing the model card and determining that the training data characteristics were not consistent with their patient population. That outcome might look like a commercial loss from our perspective, and it was. But it was also the right outcome. A health system should be able to make that determination, and they cannot make it without the information.⏎⏎iPill Inc. | ONC-2025-Deregulatory | Page 11⏎⏎THE INFORMED CLINICAL DECISION-MAKING ARGUMENT⏎⏎There is a concept in clinical ethics and health law called informed consent, which rests on the idea that patients have a right to information about the interventions being proposed for them so that they can make meaningful decisions about their own care. The DSI transparency requirements are, in a sense, an extension of that concept one level up the decision chain. Clinicians who are using AI-assisted decision support are, in effect, consenting on behalf of their patients to the use of those tools. For that consent to be meaningful, the clinicians need to understand what the tools are, how they work in relevant terms, and what their known limitations are.⏎⏎This framing helps explain why I think the "market will sort it out" argument is insufficient. Informed consent is not something we leave to market forces in clinical settings. We require it because the power and information asymmetry between clinicians and patients, and between AI developers and clinicians, are structural features of the relationship that do not resolve themselves through competitive pressure. The disclosure requirements exist to partially correct that asymmetry.⏎⏎I am aware that this is a somewhat high-minded framing for what is ultimately a certification criterion question. But I think the underlying logic is sound, and it is the logic that motivated the HTI-1 requirements in the first place. The agency's 2024 final rule preamble (89 Fed. Reg. 1192 at 1234-1237) articulates this rationale clearly, and I do not think the case for eliminating the requirements in the current proposed rule engages with it adequately.⏎⏎iPill Inc. | ONC-2025-Deregulatory | Page 12⏎⏎CONCERNS ABOUT TIMING AND PROCESS⏎⏎One thing I want to raise that is somewhat separate from the substantive arguments: the timing of this proposed rule relative to the HTI-1 implementation timeline is concerning from a regulatory stability standpoint.⏎⏎The DSI model card requirements under HTI-1 had compliance deadlines that required significant developer investment. Companies like iPill Inc. made that investment in good faith, based on the reasonable expectation that the requirements reflected a durable policy commitment. Proposing to eliminate those requirements within the same calendar year that many developers completed their initial compliance efforts sends a signal about regulatory stability that I think is worth the agency considering. If developers learn that significant compliance investments can be rendered moot by rapid policy reversals, the rational response is to defer compliance on future requirements until their durability is more certain. That dynamic is bad for the program overall.⏎⏎I am not suggesting that the agency should maintain requirements indefinitely simply because some developers have already complied with them. Requirements that are genuinely burdensome or counterproductive should be revised regardless of sunk compliance costs. But the case for eliminating the DSI transparency requirements has not, in our view, met that bar. The burden is real but manageable. The safety and accountability value is clear. The alternative to regulatory requirements in this space, voluntary disclosure driven by market incentives, has a documented track record of inadequacy in the pre-HTI-1 period.⏎⏎The agency also has the option of issuing a request for information or conducting a structured evaluation of the HTI-1 DSI requirements before proposing to eliminate them. Eight months of implementation experience is not a sufficient evidence base for concluding that the requirements are not working or that their costs outweigh their benefits. A more deliberate evaluation process would produce better policy and would be more defensible if challenged.⏎⏎iPill Inc. | ONC-2025-Deregulatory | Page 13⏎⏎RESPONSE TO POTENTIAL COUNTERARGUMENTS⏎⏎A few counterarguments come up regularly in industry discussions about the DSI requirements, and I want to address them briefly.⏎⏎Some developers argue that the model card requirements are duplicative of disclosures required under FDA's software as a medical device framework for products that fall under FDA jurisdiction. This is occasionally true for specific products, but the majority of AI-assisted clinical decision support tools in the certified health IT space, including most of our own products, are not subject to FDA device regulation. The ONC certification requirements fill a regulatory gap, not a redundancy. And even where there is some overlap, the specific disclosure elements required under the DSI criterion are not identical to FDA labeling requirements and serve a somewhat different function in the clinical workflow context.⏎⏎Other developers argue that requiring training data disclosure creates intellectual property risks by exposing proprietary information about model development. I take this concern seriously, but I think it is overstated in most cases. The required disclosures under the DSI criterion do not require developers to reveal proprietary training datasets or model architectures. They require characterization of training data at a level of generality, demographic composition, data sources at an aggregate level, known representation gaps, that does not expose trade secrets. The distinction between disclosing that a model was trained primarily on data from large urban academic medical centers versus disclosing the specific dataset and its contents is meaningful, and the current requirements stay on the right side of that line.⏎⏎iPill Inc. | ONC-2025-Deregulatory | Page 14⏎⏎A SPECIFIC REQUEST REGARDING THE COMMENT PROCESS⏎⏎If the agency proceeds with further development of this proposed rule, we request the opportunity to participate in any stakeholder engagement processes specifically addressing the DSI certification criterion. We are willing to share our implementation experience in detail, including the specific documentation we have developed for our model cards and the feedback we have received from health system customers. We believe that concrete implementation experience from developers who have gone through the process is more informative than abstract arguments about burden or value, and we are prepared to provide it.⏎⏎We would also ask the agency to consider convening a technical expert panel to evaluate the DSI requirements specifically, separate from the broader deregulatory project. The AI transparency question in health IT is substantively different from the interoperability and administrative burden questions that drive most of the proposed rule, and it warrants a dedicated evaluation process that can engage with the clinical safety literature, the implementation experience of developers across the size spectrum, and the perspectives of the health systems and clinicians who are the end users of these disclosures.⏎⏎Sandra Thomas⏎Chief Compliance Officer, iPill Inc.⏎Minneapolis, Minnesota⏎sthomas@ipillinc.com⏎612-[redacted]⏎⏎iPill Inc. | ONC-2025-Deregulatory | Page 15⏎⏎SUPPLEMENTARY NOTE ON VALIDATION DISCLOSURE FORMAT⏎⏎One technical point I want to add because it did not fit neatly elsewhere: the current DSI criterion requires disclosure of whether external validation has been conducted but does not specify the format or minimum content of that disclosure. In practice, we have seen significant variation in how developers interpret this requirement. Some provide detailed summaries of external validation studies, including population characteristics, performance metrics, and comparison to internal validation results. Others provide a single sentence indicating that external validation was conducted without any further detail. Both technically satisfy the current requirement.⏎⏎This variability reduces the utility of the disclosure for health systems trying to compare products. A more prescriptive format requirement, specifying at minimum the population size, demographic composition, clinical setting, and primary performance metrics of any external validation study cited, would increase the value of the disclosures without necessarily increasing the substantive burden on developers who have actually done rigorous validation. It would, however, make it harder to satisfy the requirement with a minimally informative disclosure, which is the point. The proposed rollback of DSI transparency requirements in this rulemaking is, in our assessment, a step that would remove accountability structures that took years to establish and that clinical settings are only beginning to use effectively.⏎⏎The current DSI criterion, codified at 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11), requires that health IT developers provide structured disclosures covering intended use, target population, known performance risks, training data characteristics, and whether external validation has been conducted. These are not abstract bureaucratic requirements.
