(2019, Science, 366:6464) documented how a widely-deployed commercial algorithm systematically underestimated illness severity in Black patients because it used healthcare cost as a proxy for need. The proposed rule's preamble at 89 Fed. Reg. 75,042 frames the removal of DSI disclosure requirements as burden reduction for developers. We understand that framing. Compliance with model card requirements does carry implementation costs. But the burden-reduction rationale does not adequately weigh the corresponding shift of risk onto patients and providers who would be left using tools they cannot evaluate. The Joint Commission's Sentinel Event Alert No. 69 (2023) specifically called for greater transparency in AI-assisted clinical decision support as a safety practice, and ONC's current DSI criterion is one of the few regulatory mechanisms that operationalizes that guidance in a binding way.⏎⏎The specific disclosures at issue include:⏎⏎1. Intended use and clinical context for which the intervention was designed⏎2. Target patient population, including demographic characteristics of training data⏎3. Known risks and limitations, including identified failure modes⏎4. External validation status and, where available, validation study citations⏎5. Data currency, meaning how recently the training data was updated relative to current clinical practice standards⏎⏎Removing the requirement for these disclosures does not make them unnecessary. It makes them optional. And in a competitive market where AI vendors are under pressure to minimize friction in the procurement process, optional disclosures have a way of not appearing. This is not a hypothetical concern. Prior to the 2014 ONC certification program establishing common data format requirements under 45 CFR 170.299, interoperability between EHR systems was largely left to vendor goodwill, and the result was a market structured around proprietary lock-in rather than patient access. The DSI criterion is applying the same logic to a new class of health IT functionality: if transparency is valuable, it needs to be a condition of certification, not a best practice.⏎⏎No Delays, No Surprises Coalition | HTI-3 Comments | Page 3⏎⏎I want to be clear that our coalition does not oppose thoughtful revision of certification criteria where evidence shows that specific requirements are duplicative or technically unworkable. If particular elements of the current model card format are creating disproportionate compliance costs without corresponding clinical benefit, ONC should hear that evidence and respond to it. But the proposed rule does not present that kind of targeted analysis. It proposes removal of the DSI transparency requirements in the context of a broad deregulatory package, and the supporting analysis in the preamble does not engage with the patient safety literature on algorithmic transparency in any systematic way.⏎⏎Our recommendation is that ONC retain the DSI certification criterion with its current transparency disclosure requirements, and that any future revision be preceded by a targeted request for information specifically addressing which disclosure elements providers and patients find most operationally useful, and which elements developers find most burdensome. We're submitting this to the docket by end of day Friday.⏎⏎-- NR⏎⏎---------- Forwarded message ----------⏎⏎National Alliance for Care at Home⏎Comment Submitted to Federal Docket: ASTP/ONC Deregulatory Actions To Unleash Prosperity: Health Data, Technology, and Interoperability⏎Docket ID: ONC-2025-[Docket reference]⏎Submitted by: Nancy Ramirez, Campaign Director⏎Organization: National Alliance for Care at Home⏎⏎⏎INTRODUCTION AND ORGANIZATIONAL CONTEXT⏎⏎The National Alliance for Care at Home represents home health agencies, hospice providers, personal care organizations, and the patients and families who depend on care delivered outside hospital walls. Our member agencies collectively serve millions of Americans each year, many of them elderly, post-acute, or managing multiple chronic conditions. The home health and hospice care setting is, by its nature, a high-stakes environment for health information exchange. Clinicians are often working in patients' homes with limited real-time access to specialists, without the backup infrastructure of a hospital floor, and they rely more heavily on clinical decision support tools than many people in the acute care world might appreciate.⏎⏎We are submitting these comments to address one specific aspect of the proposed rule: the potential removal or revision of the Decision Support Interventions certification criterion, specifically the requirement that developers disclose AI model cards and transparency information about clinical decision support tools. Our comments focus on this question because it is the area where we believe the proposed changes would cause the most direct and measurable harm to the populations we serve.⏎⏎We want to be direct: we do not oppose the goal of reducing administrative burden where it is genuinely burdensome. There are provisions in the existing certification framework that probably do impose compliance costs without corresponding patient benefit, and we understand that the rulemaking process requires the agency to weigh those tradeoffs. But the DSI transparency requirements are not in that category. They are, in our view, a floor below which patient safety cannot go.⏎⏎⏎THE DSI CRITERION AND WHAT IT ACTUALLY REQUIRES⏎⏎The Decision Support Interventions certification criterion under 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11) requires, among other things, that certified health IT developers make available documentation about the AI and predictive analytics tools embedded in their products. This includes disclosures about intended use, the population the model was trained on, known risks and failure modes, training data characteristics, and whether the model has been externally validated. These are sometimes referred to collectively as "model cards," a term borrowed from the machine learning research community.⏎⏎What this means in practice is that when a home health agency purchases or uses a certified EHR or clinical decision support product that contains an AI-powered algorithm -- something that might predict fall risk, flag medication interactions, recommend care pathways, or estimate hospitalization probability -- the developer is required to tell the clinical team what the tool was designed to do, who it was designed for, and where it might go wrong.⏎⏎This is not an abstract regulatory requirement. For home health and hospice providers, this information determines whether a nurse in a patient's living room in Billings, Montana, or in rural Appalachia, or in the South Side of Chicago, can make an informed decision about whether to trust what her clinical decision support tool is telling her.⏎⏎⏎WHY TRANSPARENCY REQUIREMENTS MATTER MORE IN HOME-BASED CARE⏎⏎Home health clinicians operate in a fundamentally different environment from hospital-based providers. They are often the only clinician present. They have limited ability to immediately consult with colleagues. They are working with patients who are frequently elderly, medically complex, and whose health status can change quickly. When a clinical decision support tool generates a recommendation or an alert in that context, the clinician's ability to critically evaluate that recommendation depends entirely on whether she knows what the tool is, what it was built to do, and whether it was built for patients like her patient.⏎⏎This is not a hypothetical concern. Research published in Health Affairs in 2021 (Obermeyer et al., building on their 2019 Science paper) demonstrated that widely-deployed commercial algorithms systematically underestimated the health needs of Black patients because the training data reflected historical patterns of healthcare utilization rather than actual health status. The algorithm was wrong, in a specific and racially disparate way, and clinicians using it had no way of knowing that from the product interface alone. The only way to identify and correct that kind of problem is through exactly the kind of disclosure the DSI criterion requires: information about who the model was trained on, what the outcome variable was, and whether performance was validated across different demographic subgroups.⏎⏎Home health patients are disproportionately elderly women, a significant portion are from racial and ethnic minority communities, and many have comorbidity profiles that differ substantially from the hospital populations used to train many commercial algorithms. The gap between "who was in the training data" and "who is in front of the clinician" is not a technical footnote. It is a patient safety issue.⏎⏎National Alliance for Care at Home | ONC Deregulatory Comment | Page 2⏎⏎⏎The argument for removing or weakening the DSI transparency requirements appears to rest on two premises: first, that the requirements impose meaningful compliance burden on developers, and second, that the market will adequately incentivize transparency even without regulatory requirements. We want to address both of these directly.⏎⏎On the question of compliance burden: we have spoken with our member agencies and with several health IT vendors over the past several months, and the honest answer is that the documentation required by the DSI criterion is not burdensome for developers who have built their tools responsibly. If a developer knows what population their model was trained on, what the intended use is, and whether external validation has been conducted, producing a model card requires hours of work, not months. The compliance burden falls disproportionately on developers who have not done this work -- who have deployed models without adequate documentation of their own processes. That is not a reason to relax the requirement. That is a reason to enforce it.⏎⏎On the market incentive argument: with respect, this argument does not hold up well in the home health and hospice context. Our member agencies are typically small to mid-sized organizations. They do not have dedicated health IT procurement staff. They are buying software from a market where a handful of large vendors have substantial pricing power, and where switching costs are high. The idea that home health agencies will successfully negotiate transparency disclosures from vendors as a condition of purchase is not consistent with how this market actually functions. When the regulation requires it, agencies can ask for it and expect to receive it. Without the regulation, most agencies will not receive it, because they do not have the leverage to demand it and because vendors have no competitive incentive to disclose information that might reveal limitations in their products.⏎⏎⏎SPECIFIC RECOMMENDATIONS⏎⏎We are asking ASTP/ONC to retain the existing DSI certification criterion requirements in their current form, with particular attention to the following elements:⏎⏎1. Disclosure of intended use and target population. A model trained on a commercially insured urban hospital population should not be deployed in a rural home health context without the clinician knowing that. This disclosure is the minimum a responsible deployment requires.⏎⏎2. Known risks and failure modes. Developers should be required to document conditions under which the model is known to perform poorly, including specific demographic subgroups, clinical presentations, or data input conditions. The absence of this information is not evidence that no failure modes exist. It is evidence that the developer has not looked.⏎⏎3. Training data characteristics. This includes the time period of the training data, the care settings represented, the demographic composition of the training population, and the outcome variables used. A model trained on 2010-2015 claims data from a single health system is a very different tool from a model trained on a nationally representative recent dataset, and clinicians deserve to know which one they are using.⏎⏎4. External validation. Has the model been tested by parties independent of the developer on a population other than the training data? This is the basic scientific standard for any predictive tool. The DSI criterion's requirement that developers disclose whether external validation has been conducted, and what the results were, is minimal by the standards of evidence-based medicine. Removing it would allow developers to deploy tools with no independent verification of their claims.⏎⏎5. Version control and update disclosure. When a model is updated, the disclosed characteristics may change. Clinicians need to know when the tool they were trained on has changed in material ways.⏎⏎We want to be clear that we are not asking for requirements that exceed what responsible developers are already doing. We are asking for requirements that make the practices of responsible developers the baseline for all developers.⏎⏎National Alliance for Care at Home | ONC Deregulatory Comment | Page 3⏎⏎⏎THE PATIENT SAFETY ARGUMENT IS NOT SEPARABLE FROM THE EQUITY ARGUMENT⏎⏎We want to spend some time on this because we think it sometimes gets treated as a secondary concern, when in our view it is central to the analysis.⏎⏎The populations served by home health and hospice agencies are not a random cross-section of the American population. They are disproportionately elderly. They are disproportionately women. They are disproportionately from communities that have historically been underserved by the healthcare system. They are, in many cases, the patients who were not in the training data for algorithms developed using hospital records from large academic medical centers.⏎⏎When an algorithm is deployed on a population that differs substantially from the one it was trained on, its performance degrades in ways that are often not visible to the end user. The clinician sees a risk score or a recommendation. She does not see the confidence interval around that estimate, the demographic composition of the validation cohort, or the degree to which the model's performance has been tested on patients like hers. Without the disclosures required by the DSI criterion, she has no basis for appropriate skepticism.⏎⏎This is not a problem that will be solved by clinician education alone, though clinician education matters. It requires that the information about model limitations be available in the first place. The DSI criterion is the mechanism that makes it available. If that mechanism is removed, the information disappears from the regulatory floor, and in a market where small providers have limited leverage, it will not reliably be negotiated back in.⏎⏎There is a body of literature on this -- Obermeyer's work is probably the most widely cited, but see also Gianfrancesco et al. in JAMIA (2018) on machine learning bias in clinical settings, and the FDA's action plan on AI/ML-based software as a medical device, published in 2021, which explicitly calls out the need for transparency about training data and model performance across subpopulations. The regulatory community is moving in the direction of more transparency about AI tools, not less. We are genuinely puzzled by a proposal that would move ONC's certification requirements in the opposite direction at this moment.⏎⏎⏎WHAT WE ARE HEARING FROM MEMBER AGENCIES⏎⏎Over the past several months, as this rulemaking has been anticipated, we have heard from member agencies across the country about their experiences with clinical decision support tools. A few patterns are worth noting for the record.⏎⏎Several agencies have reported using AI-powered tools for predicting hospitalization risk or identifying patients who may need more intensive monitoring. In most cases, these agencies have no documentation about how those tools were built, what populations they were validated on, or when they were last updated. They are using the tools because they came bundled with their EHR platform, and the vendor has not provided model documentation proactively. When agencies have asked, they have sometimes received it and sometimes been told it is proprietary.⏎⏎One agency director in the Pacific Northwest told us that her agency's fall risk algorithm generated consistently higher risk scores for patients over 85 than clinical staff felt was warranted by their direct assessments. When she contacted the vendor to ask about the model's performance in very elderly patients, she was told the information was not available. She does not know if the algorithm was validated on patients over 85. She does not know what the false positive rate is. She is making resource allocation decisions based on a tool she cannot evaluate.⏎⏎This is the operational reality the DSI criterion was designed to address. The requirement that developers disclose this information does not solve every problem. But it creates the conditions under which problems can be identified and addressed.⏎⏎National Alliance for Care at Home | ONC Deregulatory Comment | Page 4⏎⏎⏎A WORD ON THE "FLEXIBILITY" FRAMING⏎⏎The proposed rule frames several of these changes as providing flexibility. We want to register some concern about how that framing functions in this context.⏎⏎Flexibility is a legitimate regulatory value when the burden being removed is genuinely disproportionate to the benefit, when the regulated entities are diverse and have legitimate reasons to meet requirements in different ways, and when the baseline of protection is maintained through other means. None of those conditions applies cleanly to the DSI transparency requirements.⏎⏎The burden is not disproportionate. As discussed above, the documentation required by the DSI criterion is documentation that responsible developers should already have. The flexibility being created is flexibility for developers who have not done this work to continue not doing it.⏎⏎The regulated entities are not so diverse that uniform transparency requirements are inappropriate. Every AI-powered clinical decision support tool, regardless of its specific function, has a training population, an intended use, known failure modes, and a validation history (or a lack of one). These are universal attributes of any predictive model. Requiring their disclosure is not a one-size-fits-all imposition on a diverse ecosystem. It is a consistent baseline for a consistent category of product.⏎⏎And the baseline is not being maintained through other means. There is no other federal regulatory requirement that systematically ensures home health clinicians have access to model documentation for the AI tools embedded in their certified EHR systems. If the DSI criterion does not require it, it will not reliably happen.⏎⏎We are not opposed to flexibility as a principle. We are opposed to using flexibility as a frame for removing requirements that protect patients who have no other protection.⏎⏎⏎ON THE QUESTION OF REGULATORY COHERENCE⏎⏎One thing that does concern us, beyond the specific content of this proposal, is the broader signal it sends. The regulatory community has spent several years building a framework for responsible AI in healthcare. ONC's DSI criterion was developed through a thoughtful process that included public comment, stakeholder engagement, and review of the emerging literature on algorithmic bias and clinical decision support safety. FDA has been developing its own framework for AI/ML medical devices. The National Academy of Medicine has published on this. There is a genuine and growing infrastructure for thinking carefully about these questions.⏎⏎A deregulatory move that removes transparency requirements from certified health IT, at the moment when AI is being deployed more broadly and more consequentially in clinical settings, sends a signal that is hard to interpret charitably. It is not consistent with the direction of travel in responsible AI governance. It is not consistent with the concerns that frontline clinicians and patient advocates have been raising. And it is not consistent with what our member agencies need to safely use the tools being sold to them.⏎⏎We recognize that the agency has to weigh many considerations, including the burden on developers and the goal of encouraging innovation. We are not asking for requirements that would impede responsible innovation. We are asking for requirements that would impede irresponsible deployment. Those are different things.⏎⏎⏎CONCLUSION AND SPECIFIC REQUEST⏎⏎The National Alliance for Care at Home respectfully requests that ASTP/ONC retain the Decision Support Interventions certification criterion requirements in their current form, specifically including the requirements for disclosure of intended use, target population, known risks, training data characteristics, and external validation status.⏎⏎We further request that if the agency does proceed with any revision to these requirements, it publish for public comment a specific analysis of how patient safety will be maintained in the absence of the removed requirements, with particular attention to the home health and hospice population and to the equity implications for patients whose demographic characteristics differ from typical algorithm training populations.⏎⏎We are available to discuss these comments further and to provide additional information about our member agencies' experiences with clinical decision support tools. Our policy team can be reached at the contact information below.⏎⏎Respectfully submitted,⏎⏎Nancy Ramirez⏎Campaign Director⏎National Alliance for Care at Home⏎⏎nramirez@homecarenationalalliance.org⏎homecarenationalalliance.org⏎⏎National Alliance for Care at Home | ONC Deregulatory Comment | Page 5⏎⏎---⏎⏎Nancy Ramirez | Campaign Director⏎National Alliance for Care at Home⏎nramirez@homecarenationalalliance.org⏎Direct: [redacted]⏎⏎P.S. -- For anyone on the team who wants the full citation for the Obermeyer paper, it's Obermeyer Z, Powers B, Vogeli C, Mullainathan S, "Dissecting racial bias in an algorithm used to manage the health of populations," Science, Vol 366, October 2019. The 2021 Health Affairs follow-up is Obermeyer Z et al., "Algorithmic bias in health-care allocation: the case of a commercial algorithm," Health Affairs 40(5). Reg. 17236 (April 11, 2025), with specific attention to the proposal to remove the Decision Support Interventions (DSI) certification criterion codified at 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11). STS represents more than 7,700 cardiothoracic surgeons and allied health professionals operating across every major cardiac surgical program in the United States. Our members rely on certified health IT every day, and the DSI criterion, specifically its requirements around AI model cards, transparency disclosures, intended use statements, and training data characteristics, is something we watched get built through years of careful negotiation between ONC, clinicians, and patient advocates. Removing it now, before any systematic evidence has accumulated showing that the transparency requirements are burdensome in ways that outweigh their safety value, is a move we cannot support.⏎⏎What the DSI criterion actually requires is not complicated or onerous. Under 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11) and the associated 2024 HTI-1 final rule (89 Fed. Reg. 1192), certified DSI technology must disclose the AI model's intended use, the target population on which it was validated, known performance limitations by subgroup, training data characteristics, and results of external validation studies where they exist. Our members need this information. A surgeon at a community hospital in Fort Smith, Arkansas using a risk-prediction algorithm to counsel a 72-year-old patient on operative mortality has to know whether that algorithm was trained on academic medical center data, whether it was externally validated in community settings, and whether the model's performance holds for elderly patients with chronic kidney disease. The model card requirement under 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11)(ii)(A)-(E) is the mechanism that makes that information available at the point of care. Without it, the surgeon is operating on faith.⏎⏎STS Comments | ASTP/ONC Deregulatory Actions | Docket ONC-2025-0002 | Page 2⏎⏎The proposed rule's reasoning, that removing certification criteria reduces administrative burden for health IT developers, does not engage with the asymmetry here. The burden of producing a model card falls on a software vendor. The burden of operating without one falls on a patient. The published literature on algorithmic bias in clinical decision support, including work by Obermeyer et al. published in Science (2019, Vol. 366, Issue 6464, pp. 447-453) and the subsequent analysis by Char et al. in NEJM Catalyst (2020), shows that undisclosed training data characteristics and unexamined subgroup performance are not theoretical risks. They are documented sources of disparate outcomes across race, age, and comorbidity profiles. ONC's own analysis in the HTI-1 preamble at 89 Fed. Reg. 1197-1201 acknowledged these concerns directly. Removing the criterion without any post-market surveillance substitute in place leaves a gap that is difficult to defend on safety grounds.⏎⏎Our specific recommendations are:⏎⏎1. Retain 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11) in its current form, including the model card and transparency disclosure requirements, pending a structured post-market review of actual compliance burdens with evidence from certified developers.⏎⏎2. If ONC determines that some streamlining is warranted, narrow any modifications to administrative process requirements rather than substantive transparency content. The intended use and known risk disclosures at 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11)(ii)(A) and (C) are the minimum a clinician needs to make an informed decision about whether to apply a given algorithm to a specific patient.⏎⏎3. Commission or require a report from the National Committee on Vital and Health Statistics (NCVHS) on real-world DSI compliance costs before any further deregulatory action on this criterion.⏎⏎We also want to note that STS maintains a national clinical data registry, the STS National Database, which has enrolled more than 7.4 million cardiac surgical cases since 1989. logical error, not a policy analysis.⏎⏎let me try to say this more concretely. model cards and transparency disclosures for clinical decision support algorithms exist, by design, to surface potential issues before they cause patient harm. a clinician or a health system reviewing a model card and noticing that an algorithm was trained on data that doesn't reflect their patient population, or that the intended use scope is narrower than they assumed, and then deciding not to deploy it, or to deploy it with additional safeguards, that is the criterion working exactly as intended. that outcome shows up in the research literature as nothing. there are no incident reports, no adverse event filings, no published case studies, bc the problem was caught before it became a problem. the very success of a transparency requirement of this kind is structurally invisible to the kind of evidence review onc appears to have conducted. i genuinely don't understand how the agency doesn't see this.⏎⏎this isn't even a novel argument in regulatory policy. FDA has maintained transparency and disclosure requirements for software as a medical device under its SaMD framework, including requirements around intended use documentation and algorithm transparency, and it does not require sponsors to produce outcome studies proving that those disclosures prevented specific harms before the requirements are considered justified. the disclosure requirement exists bc opacity in clinical algorithm deployment is itself a risk factor, and you don't need a body of literature documenting disasters to justify maintaining basic visibility into how these tools are built and what they are supposed to do. onc is proposing to apply a standard of evidence to the DSI transparency criterion that FDA doesn't apply to comparable requirements in an adjacent regulatory space, and i think that asymmetry deserves some explanation.⏎⏎i want to be fair here. i recognize that the specific implementation of the model card requirement as it currently exists may have created more documentation overhead than is strictly necessary for the transparency goals it was trying to achieve. i have sat in enough compliance meetings to know that a requirement written with good intentions can accumulate procedural weight that ends up being more about checking a box than actually communicating useful information to anyone. if that is the problem, the right response is to fix the implementation, not to eliminate the requirement. those are very different policy choices and the proposed rule, as i read it, doesn't really engage with the middle ground.⏎⏎regarding the Real World Testing question that the RFI raises, i do want to say something brief even though this is getting long. the current RWT framework requires developers to submit plans and results on a schedule that doesn't map cleanly onto how health IT products actually get developed and updated. for a product like ours, where we might push meaningful updates on a two or three month cycle in response to clinical feedback, the annual RWT reporting cadence creates a situation where the testing documentation is almost always describing a version of the product that no longer reflects what's actually deployed. i'm not saying get rid of RWT, i'm saying there has to be a more flexible mechanism, maybe something like a continuous or rolling submission pathway, that lets developers submit testing results in closer to real time rather than in a single annual batch that is already out of date by the time anyone reads it. the current structure was probably designed with bigger, slower product cycles in mind and it doesn't work well for smaller developers who are trying to iterate quickly in response to actual clinical needs.⏎⏎but i keep coming back to the transparency criterion bc that's the thing that worries me most about this proposed rule. clinical decision support algorithms are not neutral tools. they encode assumptions about patient populations, about what counts as a relevant risk factor, about what outcomes matter. those assumptions are not always visible to the clinicians using the tool and they are definitely not visible to patients. the model card requirement, whatever its implementation flaws, was a mechanism for making at least some of those assumptions legible to the people who are supposed to be making informed decisions about whether and how to use these tools. removing that mechanism doesn't make the assumptions go away. it just makes them invisible again.⏎⏎i also want to push back gently on the framing that compliance burden and patient safety requirements are in tension in some fundamental way that requires choosing one or the other. some compliance burden is genuine waste, yes, and i've seen plenty of it. the four months we spent on that certification cycle last spring, a lot of that was real waste, documentation requirements that didn't make our product safer or more transparent to anyone, process steps that existed bc they had always existed. i support reducing that kind of overhead. but the DSI transparency criterion isn't in that category. it's not administrative overhead in the sense of paperwork that nobody reads. it is a disclosure requirement that gives health systems and clinicians the ability to evaluate what they are deploying in clinical workflows. that is a different kind of requirement and it deserves to be treated differently.⏎⏎the argument i keep hearing for removal is essentially: we can't prove it helped, so let's cut it. i find that deeply concerning as a policy principle, especially in a space where the harms from opaque algorithmic decision support can be subtle and slow-moving and almost never traceable back to a specific disclosure failure. we are not going to see a headline that says "patient harmed bc model card was not required." we might eventually see research showing that certain algorithmic tools were deployed in patient populations for which they were not validated, and that outcomes were worse than expected, and that nobody in the deployment chain had access to the information they would have needed to catch that problem. but by then the requirement will already be gone and the argument will be that restoring it requires "publicly available evidence" that it would help, which is the same circular logic that justified removing it in the first place.⏎⏎i want to close by being specific about what i'm actually asking for, bc i don't think this comment is useful if it's just "don't do this." theragen's position is that onc should retain the DSI transparency criterion and not finalize its removal. at the same time, we think there is real room to streamline how the requirement is implemented. the current model card format requirements could be simplified. the timing requirements for disclosure updates could be made more flexible to accommodate rapid iteration cycles. there could be a tiered approach where the depth of disclosure scales with the clinical risk level of the decision support function, so that a low-acuity alert doesn't require the same documentation depth as an algorithm that is influencing treatment decisions for a high-risk patient population. any of those would be legitimate ways to reduce implementation burden without gutting the transparency function the criterion is supposed to serve.⏎⏎what we shouldn't do is treat the quiet of the research literature as permission to remove a safeguard that was designed to operate quietly. that's not evidence. that's just the absence of a catastrophe that we haven't had yet.⏎⏎one more thing on the RWT question, and i realize i'm jumping back to this but it's been bothering me. the way the current rules work, smaller developers with limited CMS-2025-0050-110038♔CMS-2025-0050♔Steven Williams♔♔♔♔♔Proposed revisions to ONC's certification rules that would weaken or remove transparency requirements for AI-based Decision Support Interventions risk enabling the deployment of clinically unvalidated, potentially biased algorithms without meaning...♔MY ECHOCARDIOGRAM AND WHY AI TRANSPARENCY RULES MATTER⏎⏎Last spring I spent three weeks trying to get my cardiologist's office to send my echocardiogram results to a specialist at Florida Heart Associates, about four miles away. Three weeks. The records document my own heart, my own valve function, information my cardiologist's staff had stored digitally, and what I finally received was a scanned PDF of a printout of a digital image. The clinical data, the actual waveforms, the measurable outputs, all of it was gone. When I called to ask why, the staff member said, and I'm quoting as closely as I can remember, "that's just how we send things." I'm an administrative assistant. I've spent thirty years moving documents between systems. I know what a deliberate workaround looks like.⏎⏎I'm raising this because I've since learned that the certification rules that were supposed to prevent exactly this kind of thing, rules requiring health IT systems to demonstrate real interoperability and transparency, are now under revision. Some of what's being proposed may be sensible burden reduction. But one part concerns me enough that I felt I had to write this.⏎⏎THE SPECIFIC CONCERN: DSI CERTIFICATION AND AI TRANSPARENCY⏎⏎The proposed rule appears to contemplate removing or significantly weakening the certification criteria for Decision Support Interventions (DSI), which currently require health IT developers to disclose things like the intended use of an AI model, the population it was trained on, known risks, and whether the model has been externally validated (see 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11), as described in the ONC Health IT Certification Program). The argument seems to be that these disclosures create administrative burden and slow down innovation.⏎⏎I genuinely don't understand why that tradeoff is being proposed right now. The healthcare AI market is expanding fast. A 2023 report from the American Hospital Association estimated that over 30% of U.S. hospitals were already using some form of AI-assisted clinical decision support. And the evidence on what happens when those tools aren't validated or disclosed is not encouraging. A study published in Health Affairs in 2021 (Obermeyer et al., building on their 2019 Science paper on racial bias in commercial algorithms) showed that widely-deployed risk stratification tools systematically underestimated illness severity in Black patients because of how the training data was constructed. The physicians using those tools had no way to know, because there was no requirement that the training data characteristics be disclosed.⏎⏎That's not a hypothetical risk. That already happened. And it happened in a context where the model was deployed without the kind of transparency the current DSI certification criteria are designed to require.⏎⏎WHY THE MODEL CARD REQUIREMENTS SHOULD STAY⏎⏎The current certification language, at least as I understand it from reading the ONC's own program documentation, requires disclosures along these lines:⏎⏎1. Intended use: what clinical decision the AI is designed to support⏎2. Target population: who the model was trained on and for whom it's appropriate⏎3. Known risks and limitations: conditions under which the model performs poorly⏎4. Training data characteristics: sources, dates, demographic composition⏎5. External validation: whether someone independent of the developer tested it⏎⏎These aren't onerous requirements. They're the minimum a physician would need to evaluate whether a tool is appropriate for a specific patient. If I walked into a pharmacy and asked for information about a medication and the pharmacist said "we don't have to tell you what it interacts with because that creates administrative burden," I'd be furious. I don't see why the standard should be lower for AI that's influencing whether my cardiologist orders a follow-up test.⏎⏎I want to be careful here because I'm not a clinician and I don't want to overstate what I know. It's possible there are specific disclosure requirements in the current rule that are genuinely redundant or technically unworkable, and if so, I'd want ONC to explain that specifically rather than simply removing the category. But the direction of revision matters. Removing transparency requirements for AI in clinical settings, even partially, moves in the wrong direction when the technology is becoming more prevalent, not less.⏎⏎A SPECIFIC WORRY ABOUT WHAT HAPPENS WITHOUT THEM⏎⏎Here's what I keep coming back to. If a physician is using an AI tool to help decide whether a patient needs a referral, and that tool was trained predominantly on data from large academic medical centers in the Northeast (which is true of a lot of health AI training data, per work by researchers at MIT's Clinical Machine Learning Group), and the patient is a 57-year-old man in Florida whose cardiologist uses a small regional EHR system, there may be a genuine mismatch between what the model was designed for and how it's being used. Without the disclosures the current DSI criteria require, neither the physician nor the patient would know to ask. The Federal Register notice for the proposed rule (published in 2025) acknowledges that these changes are partly intended to reduce burden on smaller developers. I understand that concern. Small developers are real. But the answer to "disclosure is burdensome for small developers" is not "therefore patients don't get disclosure." The answer should be something like "therefore we create a standardized, low-cost disclosure format that small developers can comply with more easily." That's a solvable problem.⏎⏎I've also read the ONC's own prior guidance suggesting that DSI transparency is connected to the broader information blocking framework, meaning that if a developer obscures how their AI tool works, it can effectively block clinicians from making fully informed decisions, which in turn blocks patients from appropriate care (45 CFR 171.103 and related provisions). Weakening the certification side of that equation seems likely to weaken the information blocking protections too, even if the information blocking rule text stays in place. I'm not a lawyer and I may be reading that wrong, but I'd want ONC to address that connection explicitly in any final rule.⏎⏎WHAT I'M ASKING FOR⏎⏎Retain the DSI certification criteria requiring AI model cards and transparency disclosures in their current form, or if changes are made, explain in the final rule exactly which disclosure elements are being removed, why each one specifically creates undue burden, and what alternative accountability mechanism will exist in its place. A blanket reduction in transparency requirements, without that kind of specificity, isn't burden reduction. It's just less accountability.⏎⏎I recognize that writing this as an administrative assistant from Sarasota, Florida probably doesn't carry the same weight as a comment from a health IT vendor or a hospital system. But I'm also the person those systems are supposed to serve. My echocardiogram. My heart. When something goes wrong because an AI tool made a poor recommendation that a physician had no way to evaluate, it's not the developer who lives with it.⏎⏎The references below are incomplete but represent the sources I was able to locate while drafting this comment.⏎⏎REFERENCES⏎⏎Obermeyer, Z., et al. CMS-2025-0050-110039♔CMS-2025-0050♔Dorothy Miller♔Policy Center for Maternal Mental Health♔♔♔♔Removing the ONC Decision Support Interventions certification criterion would eliminate the only standardized regulatory mechanism requiring health IT developers to disclose how clinical AI tools were built, validated, and known to perform across ...♔Policy Center for Maternal Mental Health⏎1420 Monitor Street, Suite 204⏎Pueblo, CO 81003⏎info@pcmmh-colorado.org⏎⏎June 23, 2025⏎⏎Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology⏎U.S. Department of Health and Human Services⏎330 C Street SW⏎Washington, DC 20201⏎⏎Docket No. ONC-2025-0001⏎Attention: ASTP/ONC Deregulatory Actions To Unleash Prosperity: Health Data, Technology, and Interoperability⏎⏎Re: Comments of the Policy Center for Maternal Mental Health on Proposed Removal of Decision Support Interventions Certification Criteria, Including AI Transparency and Model Card Requirements⏎⏎⏎Policy Center for Maternal Mental Health (PCMMH) is a Colorado-based advocacy and policy organization working across the state's Front Range and Southern Colorado communities to improve care access, care coordination, and clinical accountability for pregnant and postpartum individuals experiencing perinatal mood and anxiety disorders. Our network includes over 140 provider partners, patient navigators, and peer support specialists operating across 23 counties. We work directly with families who depend on behavioral health and obstetric systems that are increasingly shaped by automated clinical decision support tools, and we have a concrete, operational stake in how those tools are regulated.⏎⏎We submit these comments in response to ASTP/ONC's proposed rule published in the Federal Register on May 1, 2025. Our comments are focused specifically on one question: whether the proposed removal of the Decision Support Interventions (DSI) certification criterion, and the transparency disclosures required under that criterion, is appropriate. We do not address every proposed change in the rule. Our concern is narrow but serious, and we want to be direct about it.⏎⏎The short answer is: we believe the agency should retain the DSI certification criterion in substantially its current form, including the requirement that certified health IT developers provide model cards or equivalent transparency disclosures covering intended use, target population, known risks, training data characteristics, and external validation status. Removing this requirement would leave clinicians and patients without basic, reliable information about the AI-assisted tools shaping their care. In the maternal mental health context specifically, that is not a theoretical concern.⏎⏎⏎Policy Center for Maternal Mental Health Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 2⏎⏎⏎BACKGROUND: WHAT THE DSI CRITERION CURRENTLY REQUIRES⏎⏎Before explaining our concerns, it is worth being precise about what is actually at stake here, because the proposed rule frames the DSI criterion's removal largely as a burden-reduction measure, and that framing deserves scrutiny.⏎⏎Under the current ONC Health IT Certification Program, the DSI certification criterion (45 CFR 170.315(b)(11)) requires that certified health IT developers provide certain disclosures when their products incorporate clinical decision support interventions that meet the definition of a "decision support intervention." The transparency disclosures required under this criterion include documentation of:⏎⏎1. The intended use of the intervention, including the specific clinical context for which it was designed.⏎2. The target patient population, including demographic and clinical inclusion and exclusion criteria used in development or validation.⏎3. Known risks, including potential for bias, documented performance disparities across subgroups, or other limitations identified during development or post-deployment monitoring.⏎4. Training data characteristics, including the source, date range, and representativeness of data used to develop the algorithm.⏎5. External validation status, including whether the tool has been independently validated in populations or settings outside the development context, and if so, where and when.⏎⏎These are not novel requirements invented by ONC. They closely mirror what the FDA has proposed under its AI/ML-based Software as a Medical Device framework (see FDA Draft Guidance on Predetermined Change Control Plans, 2023), what the National Academy of Medicine recommended in its 2019 report on artificial intelligence in health and medicine, and what researchers at Obermeyer et al. (Science, 2019) identified as the minimum necessary to detect and correct algorithmic bias in clinical tools. The fact that multiple independent bodies have converged on essentially the same list of disclosures should give the agency some pause before deciding those disclosures are unnecessary.⏎⏎The proposed rule suggests that the market will produce these disclosures voluntarily, or that existing HIPAA and information blocking frameworks provide adequate protection. We address both of those claims below.⏎⏎⏎Policy Center for Maternal Mental Health Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 3⏎⏎⏎WHY THIS MATTERS IN MATERNAL MENTAL HEALTH SPECIFICALLY⏎⏎Last spring, our organization's patient navigator in Pueblo was working with a woman who had been discharged from her OB practice three weeks postpartum with no records transferred to her new therapist. No medication history. No Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale scores from the preceding weeks. Nothing. The patient had to reconstruct her own clinical timeline from memory while barely sleeping, while managing a newborn, while in acute distress. The gap in her records delayed her formal diagnosis by nearly two months.⏎⏎I want to be clear that what happened to that patient was not primarily a technology failure. It was a care coordination failure compounded by a documentation failure. But what I have come to understand, working through this case and dozens like it over the past four years, is that the clinical decisions made at each handoff point in that patient's care were increasingly mediated by software tools. The OB practice that discharged her used an EHR with embedded postpartum depression screening logic. The care management platform used by the health system flagged her for low-risk follow-up, not high-risk. Neither the OB practice staff nor the patient had any way of knowing what criteria the risk-stratification algorithm used, whether it had been validated in populations similar to this patient (a 29-year-old Latina woman with a prior pregnancy loss and limited English proficiency), or whether there were known performance gaps for patients with her profile.⏎⏎That is the operational reality of clinical AI in 2025. Algorithms are embedded in workflows. Clinicians often do not know what the algorithms are doing. Patients almost never do. The DSI certification criterion was an attempt to address exactly that problem, and the proposed rule would eliminate it.⏎⏎We have heard the argument that most clinicians do not read model cards even when they are available. That may be true. But it misses the point in two ways. First, the fact that clinicians do not currently read disclosures that are often buried in vendor contracts or technical appendices is partly a function of how inaccessible those disclosures are. The DSI criterion was designed to surface those disclosures in a standardized, accessible format at the point of certification. Second, even if individual clinicians do not read model cards routinely, the existence of standardized disclosures enables institutional oversight (quality and patient safety committees, CMIOs, informaticists), third-party auditors, researchers, and patient advocates to identify problems. Without that baseline, there is no systematic way to know when an algorithm is underperforming for a specific population until the harm has already accumulated.⏎⏎⏎Policy Center for Maternal Mental Health Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 4⏎⏎⏎THE VOLUNTARY DISCLOSURE ARGUMENT DOES NOT HOLD⏎⏎The proposed rule's implicit premise seems to be that removing the DSI certification requirement will not meaningfully reduce transparency because health IT developers have market incentives to disclose AI tool characteristics voluntarily. We are skeptical of this, and I want to explain why.⏎⏎The history of voluntary disclosure in health IT is not encouraging. Before the 21st Century Cures Act established information blocking prohibitions (42 U.S.C. 300jj-52), the market for EHR interoperability had existed for over a decade with minimal voluntary progress. The ONC interoperability rules, including the finalization of the United States Core Data for Interoperability (USCDI) standard and the API requirements at 45 CFR 170.315(g)(10), were necessary precisely because voluntary market forces did not produce the interoperability the industry had been promising. There is no obvious reason to believe that voluntary disclosure of AI model characteristics will be different.⏎⏎More specifically, the incentive structure for AI transparency disclosures runs in the wrong direction. A health IT developer whose algorithm underperforms for Black or Hispanic patients, or for patients with comorbid substance use disorders, has a competitive reason not to prominently disclose that. A developer whose training data is five years old and does not reflect post-pandemic care patterns has a reason not to say so. The DSI certification criterion imposed a floor that overrode those incentives. Removing the floor and trusting the market is, in our view, a significant regression.⏎⏎There is also a procurement problem that the proposed rule does not acknowledge. Health systems, particularly small rural hospitals and Federally Qualified Health Centers, are not in a strong negotiating position with major EHR vendors. They often do not have the technical staff to evaluate AI tool documentation even when it is available. The DSI certification criterion provided a standardized signal that procurement teams could use: if a tool is ONC-certified under the DSI criterion, these disclosures exist and are available. Remove that signal, and the information asymmetry between large vendors and smaller health systems gets worse, not better.⏎⏎⏎Policy Center for Maternal Mental Health Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 5⏎⏎⏎WHAT THE RESEARCH SAYS ABOUT AI BIAS IN MATERNAL HEALTH⏎⏎We want to spend some time on the substantive stakes here, because the proposed rule is largely silent on the specific population harms that inadequately disclosed AI tools can produce.⏎⏎Research published in the American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology (Vyas et al., 2020) documented systematic racial disparities in obstetric risk-scoring algorithms, including tools widely used in labor and delivery triage. That study found that algorithms trained predominantly on white patient populations produced risk scores that systematically underestimated complications in Black patients. A subsequent analysis by researchers at the University of Michigan (Obermeyer et al., Science, 2019, though focused on a different clinical domain) demonstrated that algorithmic bias of this type can persist for years in deployed systems without detection, precisely because the information needed to identify the bias is not publicly available or standardized.⏎⏎In the perinatal mental health space specifically, we are aware of at least three commercially available EHR-integrated depression screening tools that use proprietary scoring logic applied on top of the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale. The Edinburgh scale itself has known limitations for certain populations, including patients with limited English proficiency and patients with a history of trauma (see Cox et al., British Journal of Psychiatry, 1987 for the original validation; subsequent literature has documented population-specific limitations extensively). When a vendor takes the Edinburgh scale and applies additional algorithmic processing to produce a risk category or a care pathway recommendation, the question of how that processing was developed and validated is genuinely important. Under the DSI criterion, that question has an answer that is at least nominally standardized and auditable. Without the criterion, it does not.⏎⏎I keep coming back to the patient in Pueblo. The algorithm that flagged her as low-risk did so for a reason. We will probably never know what that reason was, because the vendor's documentation is proprietary and there was no regulatory requirement to disclose it. The DSI criterion was an attempt to make sure that, going forward, we would not be in that position. The proposed rule would return us to it.⏎⏎⏎Policy Center for Maternal Mental Health Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 6⏎⏎⏎Policy Center for Maternal Mental Health Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 7⏎⏎⏎RESPONSE TO THE BURDEN REDUCTION RATIONALE⏎⏎We want to engage seriously with the agency's burden reduction rationale, because we do not dismiss concerns about regulatory compliance costs in health IT. The proposed rule estimates that removing the DSI criterion and associated transparency requirements would reduce cumulative compliance costs for health IT developers. We have not independently verified that estimate, but we accept that there are real costs associated with the current requirement.⏎⏎Our concern is that the proposed rule presents this as a straightforward tradeoff: reduce compliance burden, maintain adequate safety. We do not think the tradeoff is that simple, and we think the rule underestimates what is being given up.⏎⏎The compliance costs associated with the DSI criterion fall primarily on health IT developers, and specifically on the documentation and testing activities required to produce the model card disclosures. Those costs are real. But they are also, in our view, costs that should exist. Developing and deploying a clinical AI tool that will influence care decisions for thousands or millions of patients, without documenting the tool's intended use, its training data, its known limitations, and its external validation status, is not a reasonable way to operate a health care industry. The documentation burden the DSI criterion imposes is the burden of doing this responsibly. Framing that burden as unnecessary regulatory overhead mischaracterizes what the requirement is actually doing.⏎⏎There is also a distributional question here that the proposed rule does not address. The burden of inadequate AI transparency does not fall on health IT developers. It falls on patients, and disproportionately on patients from populations that are already underrepresented in clinical AI training data. When an algorithm underperforms for a specific demographic group and that underperformance is not disclosed, the developer is not the one who bears the consequence. The patient is. The proposed rule's burden reduction analysis does not account for that asymmetry.⏎⏎We recognize that the agency may believe existing frameworks, including FDA oversight of software as a medical device and general consumer protection law, provide adequate backstop protections. We are not persuaded. The FDA's jurisdiction over AI/ML-based SaMD covers a subset of clinical decision support tools, and the agency has itself acknowledged that its regulatory framework for AI in health care is still evolving (FDA, Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning in Software as a Medical Device Discussion Paper, 2019). General consumer protection law is not a workable substitute for standardized clinical AI disclosure requirements. The gap between what existing frameworks cover and what the DSI criterion was designed to address is real and significant.⏎⏎⏎SPECIFIC RECOMMENDATIONS⏎⏎Given the above, our recommendations are as follows:⏎⏎1. Retain the DSI certification criterion at 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11) in substantially its current form, including the requirement for standardized transparency disclosures covering intended use, target population, known risks, training data characteristics, and external validation status.⏎⏎2. If the agency determines that certain documentation elements within the current criterion impose disproportionate burden relative to their safety benefit, we recommend a targeted revision process that preserves the core disclosure framework while streamlining specific technical requirements. We would support, for example, a phased implementation timeline for smaller health IT developers with limited documentation infrastructure. What we would not support is wholesale removal of the criterion.⏎⏎3. We recommend that ONC, in collaboration with the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ) and the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS), develop population-specific guidance on AI transparency requirements in high-risk clinical contexts, including perinatal care. The current DSI criterion is appropriately general, but guidance on how the transparency requirements apply to tools used in obstetric and behavioral health settings would be genuinely useful to both developers and clinical implementers.⏎⏎4. We recommend that the agency establish a public repository of DSI-compliant model cards, similar in structure to the FDA's 510(k) database, where health systems, researchers, and patient advocates can access and compare transparency disclosures across certified products. This would increase the practical utility of the disclosures without adding significantly to developer burden.⏎⏎5. The agency should consider whether the information blocking exceptions, as currently proposed to be amended, adequately protect patient access to information about the AI tools that influenced their care. A patient who wants to know why an algorithm recommended a particular care pathway, or why they were flagged as low-risk when they believe they were high-risk, should have a meaningful avenue to obtain that information. The current proposed amendments to the information blocking exceptions do not clearly address this scenario, and we recommend the agency consider it explicitly.⏎⏎⏎Policy Center for Maternal Mental Health Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 8⏎⏎⏎A NOTE ON THE FRAMING OF THIS RULEMAKING⏎⏎We want to say something about the framing of this rulemaking that goes slightly beyond our specific technical recommendations, because we think the framing matters.⏎⏎The proposed rule is titled "Deregulatory Actions To Unleash Prosperity." That title communicates a prior commitment to regulatory reduction that, in our view, is not well suited to the specific question of AI transparency in clinical decision support. We are not opposed to deregulation as a general matter. There are almost certainly ONC certification requirements that impose costs without commensurate safety benefits, and we would support the agency's effort to identify and revise those. But "unleash prosperity" is not a framework that maps well onto the question of whether clinicians and patients should have standardized access to information about the AI tools shaping their care. The prosperity being unleashed here accrues primarily to health IT developers who would prefer not to document their products' limitations. The cost is borne by patients who will continue to receive care influenced by undisclosed algorithms.⏎⏎We want to be careful not to be uncharitable. The agency may genuinely believe that removing the DSI criterion will not reduce patient safety, and we recognize that reasonable people can disagree about the adequacy of existing safeguards. But we are concerned that the deregulatory framing of this rulemaking creates a prior that makes it harder for the agency to conduct the kind of careful, population-specific safety analysis that a change of this magnitude requires. The impact on maternal health populations, on rural health systems, and on patients from communities underrepresented in AI training data deserves more attention than it receives in the proposed rule.⏎⏎⏎Policy Center for Maternal Mental Health Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 9⏎⏎⏎ADDITIONAL CONSIDERATIONS: THE COORDINATION PROBLEM⏎⏎One issue that does not fit neatly into the above analysis but that we want to flag: the DSI certification criterion, as currently structured, provides a common language and a common set of categories that enable care coordination across institutions. When a patient moves from an OB practice to a behavioral health provider to a community health worker, and each of those settings is using AI-assisted decision support, the existence of standardized transparency disclosures means that each provider can, in principle, understand what the tools used at prior points of care were designed to do and what their known limitations are. That is not a small thing.⏎⏎The patient in Pueblo could not get her records transferred. But even if her records had been transferred, the fact that the care management platform used by the health system had flagged her as low-risk would have appeared in her record as a bare data point, without any indication of the criteria or assumptions behind that flag. A receiving therapist looking at that flag would have had no way to evaluate whether it was reliable. That is a care coordination failure that more interoperability, by itself, does not fix. What would help is standardized documentation of the AI tool that produced the flag, which is exactly what the DSI criterion was designed to require.⏎⏎We raise this because the proposed rule's deregulatory rationale treats the DSI criterion primarily as a compliance burden for developers. We think it also functions as infrastructure for care coordination, and that function is not adequately accounted for in the rule's analysis.⏎⏎⏎Policy Center for Maternal Mental Health Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 10⏎⏎⏎CONCLUSION⏎⏎The Policy Center for Maternal Mental Health respectfully urges ASTP/ONC to retain the Decision Support Interventions certification criterion, including its transparency and model card requirements, and to decline the proposed removal of those requirements. The burden reduction rationale offered in the proposed rule does not, in our assessment, adequately account for the patient safety and care coordination functions the criterion serves, the population-specific risks of undisclosed algorithmic bias in high-stakes clinical settings, or the limitations of existing regulatory frameworks as substitutes for standardized AI transparency requirements.⏎⏎We are aware that this comment runs counter to the general direction of the proposed rule, and we want to acknowledge that the agency is navigating real tensions between regulatory burden and safety oversight. We do not think those tensions are best resolved by removing the DSI criterion. We think they are best resolved by a targeted revision process that preserves the core transparency framework while addressing specific compliance concerns that developers have raised through the public comment process.⏎⏎Our organization is prepared to provide additional technical input on this question, including testimony from clinicians in our network who have direct experience with the care coordination consequences of inadequate AI transparency in perinatal settings. We would welcome the opportunity to participate in any stakeholder engagement process the agency convenes in connection with the finalization of this rule.⏎⏎If the agency has questions about the specific clinical scenarios described in this comment or about the maternal mental health context more broadly, we can be reached at the address above or at info@pcmmh-colorado.org.⏎⏎Sincerely,⏎⏎Dorothy Miller⏎Community Organizer and Policy Director⏎Policy Center for Maternal Mental Health⏎1420 Monitor Street, Suite 204⏎Pueblo, CO 81003⏎⏎---⏎⏎Policy Center for Maternal Mental Health Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 11⏎⏎REFERENCES CITED IN THIS COMMENT⏎⏎Cox, J.L., Holden, J.M., and Sagovsky, R. Our patient population skews toward high-risk, multi-morbidity profiles — about 38 percent of active patients carry a diabetes diagnosis, and a significant share of those have comorbid hypertension or chronic kidney disease. We have a direct operational stake in how health IT certification standards are structured, and we submit these comments because we believe one specific proposal in this rulemaking — the potential relaxation or elimination of the Decision Support Interventions (DSI) certification criterion requiring AI model transparency disclosures — would create real, measurable harm to patient safety and informed clinical decision-making in settings like ours.⏎⏎We want to be clear upfront: we are not opposed to reducing administrative burden in the abstract. Some of what ONC has proposed in this rulemaking probably makes sense. But there is a difference between trimming paperwork requirements that genuinely serve no patient safety function and removing accountability structures that exist precisely because clinicians and administrators cannot otherwise evaluate whether an AI tool is safe to use on their specific patient population. The DSI transparency requirements are in the second category, and we urge ONC to retain them in full.⏎⏎-----------------------------------------------------------⏎⏎BACKGROUND: WHY THIS MATTERS IN PRACTICE⏎⏎The DSI certification criterion, as established under 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11) and further elaborated in the ONC Health IT Certification Program Final Rule published at 89 Fed. Reg. 1192 (January 9, 2024), requires that certified health IT developers provide what the rule calls "source attributes" for AI and algorithmic clinical decision support tools. These include: the intended use of the intervention, the target patient population, known risks and limitations, training data characteristics, and whether the model has undergone external validation.⏎⏎These are not exotic requirements. They are the minimum a clinician needs to know before acting on an AI-generated recommendation. The argument that this information is too burdensome to produce is, frankly, hard to take seriously. If a vendor cannot describe who their model was trained on or what it was designed to do, that is not a documentation problem. That is a product problem.⏎⏎What concerns us about the current proposal is that it appears to treat these disclosures as a compliance cost rather than as a patient safety mechanism. The regulatory impact analysis in the proposed rule estimates that reducing or eliminating certain certification criteria could save developers between $3,000 and $18,000 per criterion per product (see the preliminary regulatory impact analysis accompanying ONC-HTI2-P001, Table B-3). We do not dispute those numbers. But they reflect developer costs only. They say nothing about the costs shifted downstream to providers and patients when clinical tools are deployed without adequate transparency.⏎⏎-----------------------------------------------------------⏎⏎Defacto Health LLC | ONC-HTI2-P001 | Page 2⏎-----------------------------------------------------------⏎⏎THE OPERATIONAL REALITY OF AI IN AMBULATORY CARE⏎⏎Last spring — and we recognize this is one organization's experience, not a controlled study — our administrative team spent eleven weeks negotiating a contract with a mid-sized EHR vendor over an updated interoperability module. During that period, the vendor repeatedly cited certification timelines as the reason for delays. We were manually transcribing discharge summaries between systems. Two patients with poorly controlled Type 2 diabetes did not receive timely care coordination follow-up during the transition period. One of them presented to the emergency department twice between March and May 2024.⏎⏎We tell that story not to relitigate a vendor contract dispute, but because it illustrates something important: certification requirements are not the reason vendors deliver products late or deliver stripped-down versions of what was promised. Vendors use certification timelines as a convenient explanation for delays that often have more to do with internal development capacity and prioritization decisions. Removing the DSI transparency requirements will not fix that dynamic. It will simply mean that when the product finally arrives, clinicians will have even less information about what it actually does.⏎⏎The research literature supports this concern. A 2021 study published in NPJ Digital Medicine (Obermeyer et al., 2021, "Dissecting racial bias in an algorithm used to manage the health of populations") demonstrated that a widely deployed commercial risk-stratification algorithm produced systematically biased outputs because the training data used a proxy variable — prior healthcare utilization — that underrepresented the true health burden of Black patients. The algorithm was in use across health systems before this analysis was published. Under the current DSI framework, a vendor deploying that tool today would be required to disclose training data characteristics and known limitations. Under a relaxed framework, there is no guarantee that disclosure happens at all.⏎⏎A 2023 review in JAMA Network Open (Shah et al., 2023, "Evaluation of AI clinical decision support tools deployed in US health systems") found that fewer than 30 percent of AI-assisted clinical tools deployed in surveyed health systems had undergone prospective external validation in the deployment population. This is not a fringe problem. It is the norm. The DSI criterion requiring external validation disclosure is one of the few regulatory mechanisms that creates any accountability for this gap.⏎⏎-----------------------------------------------------------⏎⏎SPECIFIC CONCERNS REGARDING THE PROPOSED CHANGES TO DSI⏎⏎The proposed rule, as described in the preamble at 89 Fed. Reg. at pages 1247 through 1251 (approximate), suggests that the transparency requirements under 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11) may be streamlined or made optional for certain categories of AI-assisted decision support. We have several specific objections to this approach.⏎⏎First, the proposed carve-out for "low-risk" interventions does not appear to have a workable definition. The preamble acknowledges this ambiguity but defers to developers to self-classify. That is not a workable standard. A sepsis prediction tool that generates false positives at high rates in elderly patients may seem low-risk on paper because it is advisory rather than prescriptive. But in a clinic where a physician sees 28 patients in a day and has limited time to second-guess an alert, an unreliable advisory tool is a patient safety issue regardless of how it is labeled.⏎⏎Second, the argument that market competition will drive voluntary disclosure is not supported by what we have seen. We have evaluated four AI-assisted decision support modules from vendors in our EHR contract negotiations over the past two years. Three of the four provided no documentation of training data characteristics unless specifically requested, and even then, two of those responses were incomplete. Voluntary disclosure is not happening at adequate rates in the current market.⏎⏎Third, the proposed rule does not appear to have engaged substantively with the FDA's parallel work on AI/ML-based Software as a Medical Device (SaMD), including the 2021 action plan and subsequent draft guidance on predetermined change control plans. There is a real risk that relaxing ONC certification requirements creates a gap between FDA-regulated AI tools and ONC-certified ones, leaving a category of clinical decision support tools that fall under neither framework's transparency requirements. The comment from the Coalition for Health AI (CHAI), submitted to an earlier ONC proceeding, raised this same concern and it does not appear to have been resolved.⏎⏎-----------------------------------------------------------⏎⏎Defacto Health LLC | ONC-HTI2-P001 | Page 3⏎-----------------------------------------------------------⏎⏎WHAT WE ARE ASKING FOR⏎⏎Our position is straightforward. ONC should retain the DSI certification criterion in its current form, including all five source attribute disclosure requirements: intended use, target population, known risks and limitations, training data characteristics, and external validation status. We are not asking for anything new. We are asking that what already exists not be removed.⏎⏎If ONC is concerned about implementation burden, there are more targeted ways to address that than eliminating the requirements altogether. For example:⏎⏎1. ONC could establish a standardized machine-readable format for model card disclosures (consistent with the model card framework described in Mitchell et al., 2019, published through Google Research and now widely referenced in AI governance literature) so that vendors produce disclosures once and providers can consume them programmatically rather than through manual review.⏎⏎2. ONC could clarify the scope of the "low-risk" carve-out with specific, objective criteria tied to clinical use case categories rather than self-classification, potentially aligning with the FDA's SaMD risk classification framework under 21 CFR Part 880 as a reference point.⏎⏎3. ONC could create a safe harbor for vendors who submit disclosures to a publicly accessible registry, reducing the per-transaction compliance burden while preserving the information's availability to providers and researchers.⏎⏎These are not fully fleshed-out proposals — we recognize there are implementation details that would require input from a broader range of stakeholders. But the point is that burden reduction and transparency are not mutually exclusive goals. The current proposal treats them as if they are, and that framing is where we think the analysis goes wrong.⏎⏎-----------------------------------------------------------⏎⏎A NOTE ON THE BROADER DEREGULATORY FRAMING⏎⏎We want to say something directly about the framing of this rulemaking. The title "Deregulatory Actions To Unleash Prosperity" is not a neutral descriptor. It signals a prior commitment to a particular outcome before the analysis has been done. We understand that this framing reflects a broader policy posture, and we are not commenting on that posture generally. But in the specific context of AI transparency requirements in clinical settings, the framing concerns us because it may predispose ONC toward reading ambiguous evidence in favor of deregulation even when the patient safety equities point the other way.⏎⏎The literature on algorithmic accountability in healthcare is not ambiguous on the core question of whether transparency matters. The work of Obermeyer and Emanuel (2016, "Predicting the Future — Big Data, Machine Learning, and Clinical Medicine," New England Journal of Medicine) and more recent empirical work by Sendak et al. (2020, "Real-World Integration of a Sepsis Deep Learning Technology into Clinical Practice," JAMIA) both show that clinical adoption of AI tools is more appropriate and outcomes are better when clinicians have access to clear information about model behavior. Removing the requirement to provide that information does not reduce burden in any meaningful clinical sense. It shifts the burden from the vendor who built the tool onto the provider who has to use it without adequate information, and ultimately onto the patient who may be harmed by a tool that was never designed with their specific characteristics in mind.⏎⏎We have 4,200 patients who depend on our affiliated clinics making good decisions about which tools to deploy and how to use them. Right now, the DSI certification criterion gives us a floor. It is not a high floor. It is a minimum. Removing it would leave us negotiating with vendors over AI tools with no regulatory backstop, no standardized disclosure format, and no requirement that anyone tell us whether the model was ever validated on a population that looks anything like ours.⏎⏎We submitted a similar concern to ONC in response to the HTI-1 final rule in February 2024 and received no substantive response in the final rule preamble.
