Our clinical informatics team has worked directly with EHR partners, certification bodies, and health system clients across Illinois and the broader Midwest to bring AI-assisted tools through the ONC Health IT Certification Program. I am submitting these comments in my capacity as Chief Medical Officer, and I want to be direct about what is at stake in the proposals touching the Decision Support Interventions (DSI) certification criterion, specifically the provisions requiring AI model cards and transparency disclosures under 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11).⏎⏎⏎THE DSI TRANSPARENCY REQUIREMENTS SHOULD NOT BE WEAKENED OR REMOVED⏎⏎Last spring, our clinical informatics team spent eleven weeks renegotiating certification pathways with our EHR partner simply to deploy a predictive readmission algorithm that our hospitalists had been requesting for over a year. I will acknowledge that experience directly, because I think it matters here: that delay was real, it was frustrating, and it did have consequences. During that period I watched three patients cycle back through our ED within thirty days of discharge, patients whose outcomes data strongly suggested earlier intervention might have changed things. I am not going to overstate causation. But I will say that the compliance architecture in that specific case was not functioning the way it should.⏎⏎The question is what you conclude from that. My conclusion is that the certification pathway had process problems, not that the transparency requirements themselves were the problem. Those are different things, and I think the proposed deregulatory approach conflates them in ways that concern me.⏎⏎The DSI criterion as currently structured requires health IT developers to provide, at the point of algorithm deployment, disclosures covering intended use, target population, known limitations and risks, training data characteristics, and external validation status. See 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11) and the associated ONC certification companion guide published in the 2024 HTI-1 final rule (89 Fed. Reg. 1192). These requirements did not emerge from nowhere. They reflect years of documented evidence that clinical AI tools deployed without adequate transparency have caused patient harm, and in some cases, have exacerbated existing disparities in care. The literature on this is not ambiguous. Obermeyer et al. (2019) in Science demonstrated that a widely deployed commercial algorithm systematically underestimated illness severity in Black patients because of how the training labels were constructed (369 Science 447). That paper alone should be required reading for anyone proposing to relax model disclosure requirements in clinical settings.⏎⏎XSELL Technologies | ONC Deregulatory RFI Comments | DSI Certification | Page 2⏎⏎I want to address the burden argument directly, because I think it deserves a serious response rather than a dismissal. Certification timelines under the current DSI framework can be genuinely long. Our eleven-week renegotiation is not unusual; I have spoken with peers at other health systems who have experienced delays of similar or greater length. The Federal Register preamble to this proposed rule correctly identifies that compliance costs are real and that they fall disproportionately on smaller developers who cannot absorb them the way large EHR vendors can (see 89 Fed. Reg. at [relevant page]). I take that seriously.⏎⏎But the answer to process inefficiency is process reform, not disclosure elimination. There is a meaningful difference between streamlining how a developer submits model card information and eliminating the requirement to submit it at all. If ONC's concern is that the current certification pathway creates unnecessary friction, the appropriate response is to work with ACSI-accredited testing laboratories and authorized certification bodies to standardize templates and reduce duplicative review steps, not to remove the underlying transparency obligation from the criterion itself. The CHAI (Coalition for Health AI) has published model card frameworks that could be adapted for this purpose without requiring developers to build disclosures from scratch each time. Something like that, incorporated by reference into the certification companion guide, would reduce burden without creating a transparency gap.⏎⏎⏎WHAT CLINICIANS ACTUALLY NEED FROM AI TRANSPARENCY DISCLOSURES⏎⏎This is the part of the argument that I think gets lost when the discussion focuses primarily on developer burden. Clinicians using AI-assisted decision support tools in real clinical workflows need to know, at minimum, the following:⏎⏎1. What patient population was this model trained on, and is my patient population meaningfully different from that training set?⏎⏎2. What outcome was the model actually predicting, and is that outcome a reasonable proxy for the clinical question I am trying to answer?⏎⏎3. Has this model been externally validated in a setting similar to mine, and if so, what were the performance characteristics (sensitivity, specificity, calibration)?⏎⏎4. What are the known failure modes, and under what conditions has the model been observed to underperform?⏎⏎5. Who is responsible for monitoring model performance post-deployment, and is there a process for flagging degraded performance back to the developer?⏎⏎These are not abstract regulatory compliance questions. They are the questions my hospitalists ask me when I bring a new tool to the clinical committee for approval. Without model card disclosures as a certification requirement, there is no mechanism that ensures developers have even thought through these questions systematically before deployment. The alternative is that individual health systems bear the entire burden of independently auditing every AI tool they deploy, which is not realistic for most organizations and is especially not realistic for rural or safety-net hospitals that may lack dedicated clinical informatics staff. See 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11)(ii)(A)-(E) for the current required disclosure elements, which map closely to the questions above.⏎⏎XSELL Technologies | ONC Deregulatory RFI Comments | DSI Certification | Page 3⏎⏎The 21st Century Cures Act's information blocking provisions and the broader interoperability framework were built on a premise that transparency and accountability in health IT benefit patients and clinicians. See 42 U.S.C. 300jj-52. The DSI transparency requirements are an extension of that same premise applied specifically to AI. Removing them would be inconsistent with the legislative intent of the Cures Act, and it would be inconsistent with the direction that FDA, NIH, and the National Academy of Medicine have all moved in their respective AI governance frameworks over the past three years. The NAM's 2023 Special Publication on Artificial Intelligence in Health Care explicitly recommends that AI developers provide standardized documentation of model provenance, training data characteristics, and known limitations as a condition of clinical deployment. Weakening the ONC certification criterion in the opposite direction would create a confusing and potentially dangerous regulatory inconsistency across federal health AI oversight.⏎⏎I want to be honest about one thing that I am genuinely uncertain about. The current certification criterion does not specify a standardized format for model card disclosures, and in practice this means developers submit information in widely varying formats that can be difficult for clinicians to actually use. I have seen model cards that run to forty pages of technical documentation that no hospitalist is going to read before a clinical decision needs to be made, and I have seen model cards that are three paragraphs of marketing language that do not answer any of the five questions I listed above. Both of those are compliance failures of a different kind, and I am not sure the current criterion is well-designed to prevent them. That is a genuine criticism I would offer of the existing framework. But the solution is better specification of what disclosures must contain and how they must be presented, not removal of the disclosure requirement entirely. ONC could look to the work being done under the CHAI model card standard, or to the FDA's predetermined change control plan framework for AI/ML-based software as a medical device (see FDA Guidance, "Marketing Submission Recommendations for a Predetermined Change Control Plan," April 2023), as reference points for what more structured disclosure requirements might look like.⏎⏎⏎SPECIFIC RECOMMENDATION⏎⏎ONC should retain the current DSI certification criterion requirement for AI transparency disclosures in full. If the agency proceeds with deregulatory modifications to other aspects of the certification program, it should explicitly carve out the model card and transparency disclosure elements of 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11) from any reduction in scope. Specifically:⏎⏎o The requirement to disclose intended use and target population should be retained without modification.⏎⏎o The requirement to disclose training data characteristics, including any known demographic or clinical limitations of the training dataset, should be retained. This is the element most directly relevant to algorithmic bias risk, and it is the element most likely to be omitted if disclosure is made voluntary.⏎⏎o The requirement to disclose external validation status and performance characteristics should be retained. Deployment of AI tools with no external validation data should at minimum require affirmative disclosure of that fact.⏎⏎o The requirement to identify the responsible party for post-deployment performance monitoring should be retained and, if anything, strengthened to require a specific process description rather than a named entity alone.⏎⏎XSELL Technologies | ONC Deregulatory RFI Comments | DSI Certification | Page 4⏎⏎If ONC is concerned about burden, the appropriate mechanism is to work with the certification testing community to develop standardized disclosure templates that developers can complete more efficiently, and to allow incorporation by reference of third-party model card frameworks where those frameworks meet or exceed the criterion's requirements. That is a workable middle path that addresses the legitimate process concerns without creating a transparency gap in deployed clinical AI.⏎⏎I would also note, because I think it is worth saying plainly, that the health IT vendors most likely to benefit from removal of the DSI transparency requirements are not small innovative developers struggling with compliance costs. They are large EHR vendors and AI platform companies that have the resources to invest in robust internal validation processes but prefer not to be required to disclose the results. The burden argument, in this context, functions more as a rhetorical frame than as an accurate description of who bears compliance costs and who benefits from deregulation. Smaller developers with genuinely limited resources would, in my experience, benefit more from standardized templates and streamlined review processes than from elimination of the underlying requirements.⏎⏎⏎One more thing that keeps coming back to me as I write this: the patients who cycle back through the ED are not abstractions in this discussion. The transparency requirements exist because AI tools deployed without adequate disclosure have caused real harm to real patients, and the mechanism by which they caused harm was precisely the absence of the information that model card requirements are designed to surface. CMS-2025-0050-110043♔CMS-2025-0050♔Linda Perez♔Dental Standards Institute♔♔♔♔The Dental Standards Institute urges ONC to retain the mandatory Decision Support Interventions (DSI) certification criterion requiring AI transparency and model card disclosures, arguing that eliminating it would leave safety-net and dental clini...♔Dental Standards Institute⏎Comments on ASTP/ONC Proposed Rule: Deregulatory Actions To Unleash Prosperity⏎Docket No. ONC-2025-001⏎⏎Linda M. Perez, Executive Director⏎Dental Standards Institute⏎Albuquerque, New Mexico 87102⏎⏎lperez@dentalstandardsinstitute.org⏎⏎⏎ORGANIZATIONAL BACKGROUND⏎⏎The Dental Standards Institute (DSI) is a nonprofit standards and policy organization based in Albuquerque, New Mexico, focused on health information technology adoption across dental and integrated primary care settings. Our member network includes approximately 340 safety-net dental clinics, federally qualified health centers with oral health programs, and dental schools operating in rural and tribal communities across the Southwest. We work directly with health IT vendors, state Medicaid agencies, and clinical informatics teams to improve data quality and exchange in settings that are frequently overlooked by federal health IT policy discussions. These are not large academic medical centers with dedicated compliance staff. They are small clinics running on thin margins, often sharing EHR systems with primary care partners, and increasingly being asked to deploy AI-assisted clinical decision support tools they did not build and cannot independently audit.⏎⏎We appreciate the opportunity to comment on the proposed deregulatory rule published in the Federal Register at 90 Fed. Reg. 18347 (April 28, 2025). Our comments are focused on one specific area: the proposed removal of the Decision Support Interventions (DSI) certification criterion, specifically the AI transparency and model card disclosure requirements under 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11) as established in the ONC HTI-1 final rule (89 Fed. Reg. 1192, January 9, 2024). We are not commenting on the full scope of the proposed rule.⏎⏎⏎DSI Comments | ONC-2025-001 | Page 2⏎⏎⏎BACKGROUND ON THE DSI CERTIFICATION CRITERION AND WHY IT WAS NEEDED⏎⏎The HTI-1 final rule established the DSI certification criterion to address a real and documented problem: health IT systems were deploying predictive analytics and clinical decision support algorithms with almost no public-facing documentation about how those algorithms were built, who they were built for, or where they had been tested. ONC's own environmental scan, published in 2022 and referenced in the HTI-1 rulemaking, found that fewer than 30 percent of surveyed healthcare organizations could identify the source data used to train AI tools embedded in their certified EHR systems. Thirty percent. That is a low number for something that is directly influencing clinical decisions.⏎⏎The DSI criterion responded to this by requiring certified health IT developers to produce what the rule calls "source attributes" -- documentation covering intended use, the target patient population, known limitations, training data characteristics, and the existence (or absence) of external validation studies. This is not a novel concept. The FDA has required similar documentation for Software as a Medical Device under 21 CFR Part 820 since at least 2019. The National Academy of Medicine's 2019 report "Artificial Intelligence in Health Care" specifically called for model transparency documentation as a precondition for safe clinical deployment. The 2023 White House Executive Order on AI (EO 14110) directed HHS to develop guidance on AI safety standards in healthcare settings. The DSI criterion was ONC's operationalization of that broader policy direction.⏎⏎Our member clinics began seeing certified DSI tools deployed in their settings starting in late 2024. Several of them reached out to us specifically because, for the first time, they had documentation they could actually read. A clinic director in Las Cruces told me in February 2025 that she had finally been able to have an informed conversation with her EHR vendor about a sepsis-risk scoring tool -- because the model card told her the tool had been validated on adult inpatient populations at urban academic medical centers, and her clinic sees pediatric patients in a rural federally qualified health center. She was using it wrong, and nobody had told her. The model card told her.⏎⏎⏎DSI Comments | ONC-2025-001 | Page 3⏎⏎⏎THE PROPOSED REMOVAL AND WHAT IT WOULD ACTUALLY CHANGE⏎⏎The proposed rule would eliminate the DSI certification criterion entirely, or in the alternative, reduce it to a voluntary pathway. ONC's stated rationale, at 90 Fed. Reg. 18362-18365, is that the criterion imposes compliance costs on developers, that the market is evolving rapidly and prescriptive technical requirements may become outdated, and that other mechanisms (including voluntary frameworks like the Coalition for Health AI's CHAI model cards, and FDA oversight of high-risk AI) provide sufficient accountability.⏎⏎We understand that argument. I want to be honest that the compliance cost concern is not nothing. Smaller health IT developers have told us that producing full source attribute documentation for every DSI tool in their product suite is genuinely burdensome, particularly when training data provenance is held by a third-party model vendor rather than the EHR developer itself. That is a real operational problem. But the answer to that problem is probably not to eliminate the disclosure requirement entirely. It is to clarify liability allocation between EHR developers and upstream model vendors, and potentially to create a tiered documentation standard based on the clinical risk level of the tool, which ONC already gestured toward in the preamble to HTI-1 at 89 Fed. Reg. 1279-1282.⏎⏎What the proposed elimination would actually change, in practical terms:⏎⏎   1. Certified EHR developers would no longer be required to disclose the intended use population for embedded AI tools. A tool validated on commercially-insured adults in the Northeast could be deployed in a Medicaid clinic serving Indigenous patients in New Mexico with no disclosure requirement.⏎⏎   2. Known limitations and failure modes would no longer be required documentation. The developer's incentive structure does not favor voluntary disclosure of limitations. Without a certification floor, those disclosures will not happen at scale.⏎⏎   3. External validation status would become opaque again. The 2022 ONC environmental scan found that 61 percent of AI tools deployed in surveyed health systems had undergone no external validation. The DSI criterion created at least a disclosure obligation around that gap. Removing it removes the disclosure, not the gap.⏎⏎   4. Training data characteristics -- including whether the model was trained on data that is representative of the patient populations it will be used to serve -- would no longer be required disclosures. This is the piece that concerns me most for our member clinics.⏎⏎⏎DSI Comments | ONC-2025-001 | Page 4⏎⏎⏎ON THE QUESTION OF ALTERNATIVE ACCOUNTABILITY MECHANISMS⏎⏎ONC's proposal relies significantly on the argument that voluntary frameworks and FDA oversight provide sufficient accountability in the absence of the DSI criterion. This argument deserves direct engagement.⏎⏎The CHAI model card framework, referenced at 90 Fed. Reg. 18364, is a voluntary industry initiative. CHAI published its model card template in March 2023, and it is a well-designed document. The problem is adoption. As of the most recent CHAI public data (Q3 2024), fewer than 90 health IT products had completed CHAI model cards out of an estimated 800-plus AI-enabled clinical decision support tools currently marketed to U.S. healthcare providers (KLAS Research, "AI in Healthcare 2024," November 2024). Voluntary frameworks work when there is reputational or market incentive to participate. For safety-net clinics in New Mexico purchasing AI tools through state Medicaid procurement channels, that market incentive does not function the way it might in a large health system choosing among competing vendors.⏎⏎FDA oversight covers a defined subset of AI tools that meet the threshold for Software as a Medical Device under 21 CFR 880.3960 and related guidance. ONC itself estimated in the HTI-1 preamble (89 Fed. Reg. 1201) that a substantial share of clinical decision support tools embedded in certified EHRs fall outside FDA oversight because they are not intended to diagnose or treat a specific condition. Predictive risk-scoring tools, patient prioritization algorithms, documentation assistance tools -- these are the category of AI that is most widely deployed in ambulatory and dental settings, and they are the category least likely to be subject to FDA pre-market review. Relying on FDA oversight to fill the gap the DSI criterion would leave is, to be direct, an incomplete answer.⏎⏎There is also the question of 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11)'s role in the broader ONC certification ecosystem. Certification has historically served as the mechanism through which ONC creates a baseline floor for health IT capabilities and disclosures that apply uniformly across the market. Once a capability is removed from the certification program, it is very difficult to get it back -- the industry builds product roadmaps around certification requirements, and removing a criterion signals that ONC does not consider it a baseline expectation. We have seen this dynamic before with care coordination certification criteria that were made optional in earlier deregulatory cycles and then effectively disappeared from product offerings within 18 to 24 months.⏎⏎⏎DSI Comments | ONC-2025-001 | Page 5⏎⏎⏎SPECIFIC RECOMMENDATIONS⏎⏎DSI does not oppose all aspects of the proposed deregulatory rule. There are elements of the proposed revisions to information blocking exceptions, particularly around the Fees Exception at 45 CFR 171.302, where we think ONC has identified legitimate over-prescription in the current rule. But on the DSI criterion specifically, we recommend the following:⏎⏎   a. Retain the DSI certification criterion at 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11) as a mandatory certification criterion, not a voluntary one. The case for voluntary compliance in this area is not supported by current market behavior.⏎⏎   b. If ONC is concerned about compliance burden for smaller developers, consider a tiered documentation standard. Tools that are deployed in lower-acuity settings with lower clinical risk could meet a streamlined disclosure template. Tools that generate risk scores, treatment recommendations, or patient prioritization outputs should meet the full source attribute standard.⏎⏎   c. Clarify the allocation of documentation responsibility between EHR developers and upstream model vendors. The current rule places the obligation on the certified developer, but when the AI model is licensed from a third party (e.g., a foundation model vendor or a specialized clinical AI company), the developer may not have access to full training data documentation. ONC should address this in rulemaking rather than using it as a reason to eliminate the requirement.⏎⏎   d. Require that DSI documentation be machine-readable and accessible through standardized API endpoints consistent with the FHIR-based interoperability requirements at 45 CFR 170.315(g)(10). Currently, even where model cards exist, they are often buried in vendor documentation portals that are not accessible to the clinician at the point of care. Making them queryable through existing FHIR infrastructure would significantly reduce the practical friction of the disclosure requirement.⏎⏎   e. Coordinate with FDA's Digital Health Center of Excellence on a shared taxonomy for AI tool risk classification. The current situation, where FDA and ONC use different classification frameworks for what is essentially the same category of health IT tool, creates compliance confusion and leaves a meaningful coverage gap for the tools most widely used in ambulatory settings.⏎⏎⏎DSI Comments | ONC-2025-001 | Page 6⏎⏎⏎PATIENT SAFETY CONSIDERATIONS IN DENTAL AND INTEGRATED CARE SETTINGS⏎⏎One thing that tends to get lost in health IT policy discussions is that dental care is increasingly integrated with primary care, particularly in safety-net and tribal health settings. The Indian Health Service's integration of dental and medical EHR systems, which began in earnest with the 2017 IHS EHR modernization initiative, means that clinical decision support tools embedded in primary care EHRs are now surfacing in dental care encounters. A drug interaction alert, a diabetes risk flag, a medication reconciliation suggestion -- these tools are being seen by dental hygienists and dentists who may not have the clinical training to critically evaluate the tool's limitations or its population validity.⏎⏎We are not saying that is a problem unique to AI or to this proposed rule. But the DSI transparency requirements were one of the few mechanisms that gave those clinicians something concrete to work with. A model card that says "this tool was validated on patients with at least two prior primary care visits in the same health system" is actionable information for a dentist seeing a patient who has never had a primary care visit. Removing that disclosure does not make the tool safer. It just makes the limitation invisible.⏎⏎The literature on algorithmic bias in clinical decision support is now substantial enough that it should not require extended citation in a regulatory comment. Obermeyer et al. (Science, 2019) documented systematic underestimation of illness severity for Black patients in a widely deployed commercial risk-scoring algorithm. Gianfrancesco et al. (JAMIA, 2018) documented differential performance of EHR-based predictive models across racial and socioeconomic groups. A 2023 study in NEJM AI (Ballantyne et al.) found that 74 percent of commercially deployed clinical AI tools in the study sample had no published external validation on populations other than the original development cohort. These are not fringe findings. They are the mainstream of the peer-reviewed literature on this topic, and they are exactly the kind of known limitation that DSI source attribute disclosures are designed to surface.⏎⏎⏎DSI Comments | ONC-2025-001 | Page 7⏎⏎⏎We want to be clear that DSI does not read this proposed rule as an attempt to harm patients or to deliberately reduce transparency. The administrative burden concerns ONC has identified are real, and there are parts of the HTI-1 implementation that probably did move too fast for smaller vendors to absorb. But the solution to an implementation problem is an implementation fix, not the removal of the underlying requirement.⏎⏎The DSI criterion has been in effect for approximately 14 months as of the comment deadline for this proposed rule. Fourteen months is not enough time to assess whether it is working. Several of our member organizations are only now beginning to receive certified DSI documentation from their vendors, because many vendors requested and received compliance deadline extensions. Removing the criterion before it has been meaningfully implemented is not a deregulatory action in any analytically meaningful sense. It is a pre-emptive decision not to implement it.⏎⏎ONC has a strong track record of getting health IT certification right over time -- the Meaningful Use program, for all its growing pains, did move the needle on EHR adoption and basic interoperability in ways that mattered for patients. The 21st Century Cures Act information blocking rules have created real, measurable improvements in patient access to records (ONC's own 2023 annual report on information blocking complaints documents this). The DSI criterion is in that same tradition: a certification floor that creates a minimum standard for accountability in a rapidly changing technology environment.⏎⏎The proposed elimination of that criterion, at this particular moment in the deployment curve for clinical AI, is a decision that will be difficult to reverse once the market has adjusted to its absence. We urge ONC to retain the DSI criterion, to work with industry on implementation challenges through guidance and phased timelines rather than elimination, and to treat AI transparency as a baseline expectation in certified health IT rather than an optional feature.⏎⏎Submitted by:⏎Linda M. ONC's justification centers on administrative burden reduction for health IT developers, but we are genuinely uncertain this trade-off has been examined with sufficient rigor as it applies to patient safety outcomes at the point of care. The DSI criterion, finalized in the HTI-1 Final Rule (89 Fed. Reg. 1192, January 2024), requires that certified health IT present clinicians with specific disclosures about AI-driven decision support tools, including intended use, target population, known performance limitations, training data characteristics, and external validation status. These are not bureaucratic formalities. A cardiologist receiving an AI-generated risk score for a 68-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation needs to know whether that model was trained predominantly on data from male patients under 65, and whether it has ever been externally validated in a community hospital setting comparable to hers. Without the model card requirement, that information may simply not be available in any standardized form at the moment a clinical decision is being made.⏎⏎The literature on this point is not ambiguous. Obermeyer et al. (2019, Science, Vol. 366, pp. 447-453) documented substantial racial bias in a widely deployed commercial algorithm affecting approximately 200 million people annually. The FDA's proposed framework on AI/ML-based Software as a Medical Device (2021 Action Plan) and subsequent guidance on predetermined change control plans both contemplate transparency about model behavior as a baseline safety condition. The National Academy of Medicine's 2019 report on AI in health care (NASEM, "Artificial Intelligence in Health Care: The Hope, the Hype, the Promise, the Peril") was explicit that deployment transparency is a prerequisite for safe integration. Removing the DSI criterion moves directly against this body of evidence.⏎⏎Healthcare Leadership Council | ASTP-2025-ONC-DSI | Page 2⏎⏎---⏎⏎We acknowledge that some HLC members have raised concerns about the compliance costs associated with generating and maintaining model cards, particularly for smaller health IT developers. Those concerns are real. But the response to compliance burden should be standardization and technical assistance, not elimination of the requirement. ONC could reasonably:⏎⏎1. Develop a standardized machine-readable model card template that reduces per-product documentation time and allows for automated ingestion into EHR interfaces (see 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11)(ii) for the existing structural framework that could be extended rather than retired).⏎2. Establish a phased compliance timeline for developers below a defined revenue threshold, consistent with ONC's approach in the 21st Century Cures Act Final Rule (85 Fed. Reg. 25642).⏎3. Coordinate with the FDA's Digital Health Center of Excellence on a unified disclosure framework that satisfies both ONC certification requirements and FDA Software as a Medical Device (SaMD) transparency expectations, reducing duplicative burden across regulatory regimes.⏎4. Require that model cards be accessible via standardized FHIR R4 API endpoints (45 CFR 170.315(g)(10)) so that the disclosure burden does not fall on individual clinicians navigating multiple vendor interfaces.⏎⏎What we are not prepared to recommend is removing the requirement on the premise that the market will produce adequate transparency voluntarily. There is no historical basis for that assumption in health IT. The 2015 Edition certification requirements (45 CFR Part 170, Subpart C) were themselves a response to exactly that failure. Our members have spent the better part of a decade building workflows around the expectation that certified health IT meets minimum transparency standards.⏎⏎www♔♔2026-01-25T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-25T00:00:00Z♔2025-12-12T00:00:00Z♔2026-02-10T00:00:00Z♔2♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Retain the current Decision Support Interventions (DSI) certification criterion requiring AI model cards and transparency disclosures (intended use, target population, known risks, training data characteristics, external validation) to ensure patient safety, informed clinical decision-making, and accountability in AI-assisted healthcare.♔Removing DSI transparency requirements creates a dangerous regulatory gap where AI-based clinical decision support tools face fewer disclosure obligations than traditional medical devices, undermining consistent safety standards.♔advocacy_group♔high♔resigned♔Nevada♔director of government affairs♔40♔Last spring, I spent three weeks navigating a labyrinthine records request on behalf of my own mother after her cardiac event in Reno — watching a system that was technically "interoperable on paper" produce nothing actionable for her new cardiologist in time for her first follow-up. Our organization works directly with patient populations navigating complex care transitions, and our government affairs function has tracked federal health IT certification policy since the passage of the 21st Century Cures Act (Pub. L. 114-255). We have serious concerns about the proposal to remove or substantially revise the Decision Support Interventions (DSI) certification criterion, specifically the provisions requiring what are commonly called "model cards" for AI-based clinical decision support tools deployed in certified health IT. Those transparency requirements exist in 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11), and they are not administrative formalities.⏎⏎I want to be direct: the model card requirements that ONC finalized in the 2024 HTI-1 Final Rule (89 Fed. Reg. 1192, January 9, 2024) were the product of years of stakeholder input, including input from patient and consumer advocates who had watched AI-assisted tools make errors that went unexamined because no one was required to say what the tool was trained on, who it was validated for, or what populations it had been tested against. Removing or weakening those requirements now, before the field has even fully implemented them, makes little sense to us. The 2023 National Academy of Medicine discussion paper on AI in clinical settings (Matheny et al.) documented specific cases where algorithmic tools performed worse on minority patient populations precisely because training data characteristics were never disclosed. Under the proposed changes, a certified EHR vendor would have reduced obligation to surface that information to the clinicians relying on those tools.⏎⏎URAALI Refaluwasch Association Comments | ONC Deregulatory Rule | Page 2⏎⏎Our specific recommendations regarding the DSI criterion are as follows:⏎⏎1. Retain the requirement that certified health IT developers disclose intended use and target population for any AI or predictive model incorporated into DSI functionality, consistent with 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11)(iv) as finalized in HTI-1.⏎⏎2. Retain the requirement for disclosure of known risks and limitations, including documented performance disparities across demographic subgroups, with reference to the FDA's 2021 AI/ML-Based Software as a Medical Device Action Plan as a parallel regulatory framework that already expects this kind of transparency.⏎⏎3. Retain external validation disclosure requirements. The 2022 JAMA Internal Medicine study by Wong et al. on sepsis prediction models found that a widely deployed algorithm underperformed significantly outside its original training environment, with no external validation data available to the clinicians using it. That is the problem these requirements are designed to address.⏎⏎o If ONC is genuinely concerned about implementation burden on smaller developers, a tiered compliance timeline would be a more proportionate response than removing the requirement entirely. ONC used phased timelines in the 2015 Edition certification rule (80 Fed. Reg. 62602) and could do so again here.⏎⏎o We are also open to discussing whether the specific formatting of model card disclosures could be standardized in a way that reduces duplicative documentation work, but that conversation should happen with the requirement intact, not after it has been eliminated.⏎⏎What we cannot accept is the argument that transparency is itself the burden. Clinicians at small rural practices in Vermont, the kind our member families rely on, are increasingly encountering AI-generated risk scores and predictive alerts embedded in their EHR workflows. CMS-2025-0050-110047♔CMS-2025-0050♔Deborah Wilson♔♔♔♔♔A retired critical care nurse with 30 years of experience urges ONC to retain the Decision Support Interventions certification criterion's AI transparency requirements — including disclosures of intended use, target populations, known risks, train...♔COMMENT ON ASTP/ONC DEREGULATORY ACTIONS DOCKET⏎⏎My concern here is specific, so I want to be direct about it before getting into anything else. The proposed removal of the Decision Support Interventions certification criterion, specifically the part that requires what the industry calls "model cards" for AI tools, is something I genuinely cannot understand the rationale for. I spent thirty years in critical care nursing, and I watched what happens when clinicians work with tools they don't fully understand. It doesn't end well. I'm not opposed to reducing administrative burden in principle. Some of those burdens are real and they slow down care. But the transparency requirements attached to AI-based clinical decision support are not that kind of burden.⏎⏎PERSONAL BACKGROUND AND WHY THIS MATTERS⏎⏎I retired from nursing in 2021, and in my last several years I watched AI-assisted tools start appearing in clinical environments faster than most of my colleagues could absorb them. Sepsis prediction scores, readmission risk flags, medication dosing recommendations. Some of them were good. Some of them were trained on patient populations that looked nothing like the patients we were actually treating in Providence. That's not a hypothetical concern. A 2021 study published in the New England Journal of Medicine found that a widely deployed sepsis alert algorithm (the Epic Sepsis Model) had significantly lower sensitivity for Black patients than for white patients, a disparity that was only discovered through post-deployment external validation (Wong et al., NEJM Evidence, 2021). That's exactly the kind of information a model card is supposed to surface before a clinician acts on an alert.⏎⏎I keep coming back to a specific incident, not mine professionally but one that left an impression. A family member of a patient I knew spent three hours trying to piece together a medication history from a different hospital network after their mother arrived unresponsive. Meanwhile, the clinical decision support tool in the receiving hospital was flagging drug interactions based on incomplete data and no one at the bedside knew enough about how the algorithm worked to calibrate their confidence in it. That is the environment in which we are proposing to reduce AI transparency requirements.⏎⏎THE CERTIFICATION CRITERION IN QUESTION⏎⏎The current DSI certification criterion asks health IT developers to disclose:⏎⏎1. The intended use and target population for the AI model⏎2. Known risks and limitations, including performance disparities across demographic groups⏎3. Training data characteristics⏎4. Whether external validation has been conducted⏎⏎These are not unreasonable things to ask. A physician ordering a procedure has to explain the risks to a patient. A drug manufacturer has to disclose contraindications. I genuinely don't understand why an AI tool that influences clinical decisions should be exempt from equivalent disclosure. The argument that compliance costs are too high for smaller developers may have merit at the margins, but the solution to that is a tiered or simplified disclosure format, not no disclosure at all.⏎⏎CONCERNS ABOUT THE PROPOSED CHANGE⏎⏎The proposed rule, as I read it, would remove or substantially weaken the requirement that AI tools deployed in certified health IT include these transparency disclosures. The regulatory language around "flexibility" in the certification program is vague enough that I'm honestly not sure what would be required afterward (ONC, Proposed Rule, 89 Fed. Reg. 2024). That vagueness is itself a problem. Clinicians need to know what they're working with. Patients need some assurance that the tools influencing their care have been evaluated for safety in populations like them.⏎⏎A few specific things I'd ask the agency to consider:⏎⏎o If the goal is reducing burden, what evidence exists that the model card requirement is a disproportionate burden relative to its safety benefit? I haven't seen that analysis cited anywhere in the preamble.⏎⏎o External validation data is particularly important for AI tools used in high-acuity settings. Removing the requirement to disclose whether validation occurred removes the only reliable check on whether a tool performs as claimed outside the developer's own testing environment.⏎⏎o The target population disclosure matters for equity reasons that go beyond general fairness concerns. If a risk stratification tool was trained predominantly on one demographic and is being applied to another, that is a patient safety issue.⏎⏎WHAT I'M ASKING FOR⏎⏎Retain the DSI certification criterion in its current form, or if modifications are made, ensure that the core transparency elements (intended use, target population, known risks, training data, external validation) remain mandatory rather than optional or encouraged. "Encouraged" in regulatory language means "routinely skipped."⏎⏎I recognize that health IT regulation involves tradeoffs I'm not fully positioned to evaluate. I'm a retired nurse, not a health informaticist. But I've been in enough critical care situations to know that the question "what is this tool actually doing and how confident should I be in it" is not a bureaucratic question. It's a clinical one. The certification criterion as written gives clinicians at least a fighting chance of answering it.⏎⏎I would also note that the public comment period for this rule was 30 days, which for a proposal of this scope⏎⏎References:⏎⏎Wong, A., et al. CMS-2025-0050-110048♔CMS-2025-0050♔Michael Davis♔Dental Standards Institute♔♔♔♔The Dental Standards Institute urges ONC to retain the Decision Support Interventions certification criterion at 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11), arguing that its AI transparency disclosure requirements are essential patient safety protections that market f...♔Dental Standards Institute⏎1400 Crystal Drive, Suite 900⏎Arlington, Virginia 22202⏎⏎June 16, 2025⏎⏎Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology⏎U.S. Department of Health and Human Services⏎330 C Street, SW⏎Washington, DC 20201⏎⏎RE: ASTP/ONC Proposed Rule, "Deregulatory Actions To Unleash Prosperity: Health Data, Technology, and Interoperability" (Docket No. ONC-2025-0002)⏎⏎Dear Assistant Secretary and Staff:⏎⏎The Dental Standards Institute (DSI) is a Virginia-based nonprofit organization whose membership includes dental health systems, oral health informatics professionals, and integrated care networks operating across the mid-Atlantic and Southeast. Our work sits at an unusual intersection: we focus on how health data standards apply in dental and oral health contexts, which means our member organizations are often on the receiving end of health IT decisions made primarily with medical providers in mind. We have watched the ONC certification program develop over the years with genuine appreciation for what it has accomplished, even when specific provisions created implementation friction for our members. I raise that context because I want to be clear that DSI does not come to this comment as reflexively opposed to regulatory streamlining. There are provisions in this proposed rule that address real administrative burdens, and we recognize that.⏎⏎What I cannot support, and what I am asking the agency to reconsider, is the proposed removal of the Decision Support Interventions (DSI) certification criterion requiring transparency disclosures for AI-driven clinical decision support tools. That is the focus of these comments.⏎⏎⏎DSI COMMENTS | ONC-2025-0002 | Page 2⏎⏎⏎BACKGROUND: WHY THIS PARTICULAR CRITERION MATTERS⏎⏎Before addressing the specific regulatory question, I want to offer some context from our organization's work. Over the past eighteen months, DSI has been conducting informal assessments of how AI-assisted clinical decision support tools are being adopted by dental and integrated care providers in Virginia, Maryland, and North Carolina. What we have found is not reassuring. A significant number of these tools are deployed with almost no documentation available to clinicians about how the underlying models were trained, what patient populations were used to validate them, or what failure modes have been identified. A dental hygienist using a radiographic AI tool to flag potential carious lesions may have no idea whether that tool was validated on a patient population that looks anything like her patient panel. A periodontist using an AI-assisted treatment planning module may not know whether the model was trained on data from academic medical centers rather than community health settings, which would raise real questions about generalizability.⏎⏎This is not a theoretical concern. The literature on AI performance disparities across demographic groups in healthcare has grown substantially since 2019. Obermeyer et al. published findings in Science (2019, vol. 366, issue 6464) documenting how a widely used commercial algorithm systematically underestimated the health needs of Black patients due to the use of healthcare cost as a proxy for health need. That study looked at a general health management algorithm, but the methodological problem it identified applies directly to dental and oral health AI tools, where training datasets are often even less demographically representative than those used in general medicine. The FDA's 2021 action plan for AI/ML-based Software as a Medical Device noted the absence of standardized transparency requirements as a gap that needed to be addressed. ONC's DSI criterion, as currently written, was a meaningful step toward filling that gap within the certification program.⏎⏎The current criterion requires certified health IT to provide, at minimum, disclosures covering intended use, the target population the tool was designed for, known risks and limitations, characteristics of the training data, and whether external validation has been performed. See 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11) and the associated certification companion guide published in the 2024 HTI-1 final rule (89 Fed. Reg. 1192, Jan. 9, 2024). These are not burdensome disclosures. They are the kind of information that any responsible developer should be able to provide and that any clinician deserves to have before relying on a tool in patient care.⏎⏎The proposed rule would eliminate this criterion from the certification program on the grounds that it imposes unnecessary compliance costs on health IT developers and that market forces will drive adequate transparency over time. I find that reasoning genuinely difficult to accept, and I want to explain why in some detail.⏎⏎⏎DSI COMMENTS | ONC-2025-0002 | Page 3⏎⏎⏎THE MARKET FORCES ARGUMENT DOES NOT HOLD UP IN THIS CONTEXT⏎⏎The agency's premise appears to be that if clinicians demand AI transparency, developers will provide it voluntarily, and that certification requirements are therefore redundant. That argument might have some force in markets where buyers are well-informed, switching costs are low, and performance is observable after the fact. Health IT markets have none of those characteristics.⏎⏎Consider what actually happens when a dental group practice or a community health center evaluates an AI-assisted clinical decision support tool. The purchasing decision is typically made by an administrator or a technology committee, not by the individual clinicians who will use the tool daily. The clinicians themselves often have limited input into what tools are deployed. After deployment, the tool's outputs are woven into clinical workflows in ways that make it genuinely difficult to assess whether the AI is adding value or introducing systematic errors. If a radiographic AI tool is subtly underperforming on patients over 65 with dense enamel or on patients with certain restorative histories, the clinician may not notice for months or years, and may never attribute the performance gap to the model's training characteristics. There is no feedback loop that would naturally surface this problem and create market pressure for better disclosure.⏎⏎This is a well-documented feature of clinical AI deployment, not a hypothetical. A 2022 study in the Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association (JAMIA, vol. 29, issue 7, pp. 1149-1157) examining post-deployment performance of clinical decision support algorithms found that real-world performance degraded significantly compared to validation benchmarks in a majority of cases studied, and that clinicians were rarely aware of the degradation. The study recommended mandatory transparency mechanisms precisely because voluntary disclosure had not emerged organically.⏎⏎I am also not persuaded that the compliance costs of maintaining the DSI criterion are as prohibitive as the proposed rule suggests. The disclosures required under 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11) are documentation that responsible developers are already generating internally during the development and validation process. The marginal cost of making that documentation available in a standardized format is not large. What the criterion does is ensure that the documentation exists in the first place and that it reaches the people who need it. If a developer cannot produce information about their training data characteristics or external validation status, that is not a compliance burden. It is a signal that the tool may not be ready for clinical deployment.⏎⏎⏎DSI COMMENTS | ONC-2025-0002 | Page 4⏎⏎⏎THE PATIENT SAFETY DIMENSION⏎⏎My colleague's mother spent three weeks in the spring of 2024 cycling through urgent care visits across two different health systems in Northern Virginia. I watched my colleague spend evenings reconstructing his mother's medication history by phone and fax because her records were not portable between the platforms used by the two systems. She was eventually stabilized, but the fragmentation of her care record contributed directly to delays and to at least one medication dosing decision that had to be revisited. I raise this not to make a purely personal point but because it illustrates something I keep coming back to when I read the proposed rule: the costs of interoperability failures and transparency failures in health IT are not borne by developers or administrators. They are borne by patients. And they are often invisible to the people making the policy decisions.⏎⏎When a clinician uses an AI-assisted tool without knowing that the tool was validated primarily on patients from large academic medical centers, and the patient in front of her is a 72-year-old woman from a rural county in Southside Virginia who has never seen a specialist, the mismatch between the model's training population and the actual patient is invisible. The clinician has no reason to second-guess the tool's output. The patient has no reason to question the recommendation. The adverse outcome, if it comes, is attributed to something else. This is precisely the scenario that the DSI transparency criterion was designed to prevent. Removing it does not eliminate the risk. It just removes the mechanism that makes the risk visible.⏎⏎The agency should also consider the interaction between this proposed change and the broader information blocking provisions being modified elsewhere in the rule. The 21st Century Cures Act, at 42 U.S.C. 300jj-52, established information blocking prohibitions precisely because Congress recognized that health IT actors had both the incentive and the ability to restrict access to health information in ways that harmed patients and competition. The existing exceptions framework under 45 CFR 171.200 et seq. creates a careful balance between flexibility and accountability. Several of the proposed modifications to those exceptions would give health IT developers additional latitude to restrict or delay information sharing. If those modifications proceed alongside the removal of the DSI transparency criterion, the combined effect is a regulatory environment that gives developers more flexibility and patients less information. That combination is troubling.⏎⏎⏎DSI COMMENTS | ONC-2025-0002 | Page 5⏎⏎⏎SPECIFIC CONCERNS REGARDING THE PROPOSED REMOVAL⏎⏎DSI's objections to the removal of the DSI certification criterion fall into several categories, which I will address in turn.⏎⏎First, the removal eliminates a standardized mechanism for communicating model cards and AI transparency disclosures across the health IT ecosystem. Model cards, as described in the framework developed by Mitchell et al. (2019, Proceedings of the ACM Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency, pp. 220-229), are structured documents that summarize a machine learning model's intended uses, performance characteristics, and known limitations. The DSI criterion essentially operationalized this concept within ONC's certification framework. Without the criterion, there is no standardized format or minimum content requirement for these disclosures, and our member organizations tell us that in practice, what they receive from vendors varies enormously. Some provide detailed documentation. Many provide almost nothing. A certification requirement creates a floor below which no certified product can fall.⏎⏎Second, removing the criterion creates a two-tier market in which well-resourced health systems can negotiate for transparency disclosures contractually, while smaller providers cannot. A large integrated health system with a sophisticated legal team can include model card requirements in its vendor contracts and has the leverage to enforce them. A small dental group practice or a federally qualified health center does not have that leverage. The certification program has historically served as a way of ensuring that the protections built into the regulatory framework are available to all providers, not just those with the resources to negotiate for them privately. The proposed removal effectively means that AI transparency becomes a luxury available to large buyers.⏎⏎Third, the removal is premature given where the broader regulatory framework for AI in healthcare currently stands. The FDA's Center for Devices and Radiological Health has been working through its regulatory approach to AI/ML-based Software as a Medical Device since at least 2019, and that framework remains in development. The National Institute of Standards and Technology released its AI Risk Management Framework (NIST AI RMF 1.0) in January 2023, which provides a voluntary framework but not enforceable requirements. The Executive Order on AI (E.O. 14110, Oct. 30, 2023) directed HHS to develop guidance on AI in healthcare, but that guidance has not been finalized. In this environment, the ONC DSI criterion is one of the few concrete, enforceable transparency requirements that exists for clinical AI tools in certified health IT. Removing it now, before any of these broader frameworks have produced enforceable standards, leaves a gap that will not be quickly filled.⏎⏎Fourth, the proposed rule does not adequately address what replaces the criterion. The preamble suggests that industry best practices and voluntary frameworks will fill the void, but it does not identify which frameworks, how compliance would be assessed, or what recourse providers would have if a vendor's voluntary disclosures turned out to be incomplete or misleading. This is not a minor implementation detail. It is the entire mechanism of accountability, and the rule as proposed leaves it unaddressed.⏎⏎⏎DSI COMMENTS | ONC-2025-0002 | Page 6⏎⏎⏎WHAT DSI IS ASKING FOR⏎⏎Our organization's recommendation is straightforward. The agency should retain 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11) as currently structured, with the model card and transparency disclosure requirements intact. If the agency believes that specific elements of the criterion are creating disproportionate compliance burdens for smaller developers, we would welcome a targeted rulemaking to adjust those elements. What we cannot support is wholesale removal.⏎⏎If the agency is committed to some form of modification, we would ask that any revised criterion retain, at minimum, the following elements:⏎⏎1. A requirement that certified health IT disclose the intended use of any AI-driven decision support intervention, in plain language accessible to the clinician at the point of use.⏎⏎2. A requirement that the target population for which the tool was designed and validated be disclosed, including demographic characteristics of the training and validation datasets where those characteristics are known.⏎⏎3. A requirement that known limitations and failure modes be documented and made available to clinical users, updated at intervals that reflect meaningful changes to the model or its deployment environment.⏎⏎4. A requirement that any external validation study be identified by name, institution, and date, so that clinicians can locate and evaluate the underlying evidence if they choose to do so.⏎⏎5. A requirement that the developer disclose whether the model has been updated since initial certification and, if so, what the nature of the update was.⏎⏎These are not novel requirements. They reflect the minimum information that any clinician would want before relying on an AI tool in patient care, and they are consistent with the transparency standards being developed in adjacent regulatory contexts, including the FDA's predetermined change control plan framework described in its 2023 draft guidance for AI/ML-based Software as a Medical Device.⏎⏎⏎DSI COMMENTS | ONC-2025-0002 | Page 7⏎⏎⏎I want to say something directly about the framing of this rulemaking, because I think it matters. The title of the proposed rule, "Deregulatory Actions To Unleash Prosperity," reflects a particular view of what the health IT regulatory framework is for. Under that view, certification requirements are primarily costs imposed on developers, and reducing those costs produces economic benefits that outweigh whatever regulatory protections are lost. I understand the appeal of that framing, and I will concede that there are places in the ONC certification program where requirements have accumulated over time without a clear corresponding benefit.⏎⏎But the DSI criterion is not one of those places. The transparency disclosures it requires are not bureaucratic overhead. They are the mechanism by which clinicians can exercise informed judgment about whether to rely on an AI tool's output in a specific clinical situation. Removing them does not deregulate in any meaningful sense. It shifts the information asymmetry between AI developers and clinical users further in the developers' favor, at the expense of the patients those clinicians serve.⏎⏎The agency has cited 5 U.S.C. 610 and Executive Order 13771 in discussing the deregulatory rationale for this rulemaking. Those authorities are relevant to assessing regulatory costs, but they do not require the agency to remove protections that serve a genuine patient safety function. The agency retains discretion to maintain certification criteria that it concludes are necessary to protect public health, and we are asking it to exercise that discretion here.⏎⏎One additional point that I do not want to lose in the technical discussion: the HTI-1 final rule's preamble, at 89 Fed. Reg. 1192, made explicit findings about the patient safety rationale for the DSI transparency criterion. Those findings documented the specific harms that can arise when clinicians lack information about AI tool limitations, and they supported the conclusion that the criterion was appropriate under the agency's statutory authority. If the agency now proposes to remove the criterion, it needs to explain what has changed in the underlying factual record that would support a different conclusion. The proposed rule does not do that. It characterizes the criterion as a compliance burden without engaging with the safety findings that justified it in the first place. That is a gap in the administrative record that would need to be addressed before a final rule removing the criterion could withstand review under the Administrative Procedure Act, 5 U.S.C. 706.⏎⏎DSI appreciates the opportunity to submit these comments and asks that the agency treat this letter as a formal objection to the proposed removal of 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11). We are available to discuss any of these points further and can be reached at the address above or at policy@dentalstandardsinstitute.org.⏎⏎Respectfully submitted,⏎⏎Michael Davis⏎Executive Director⏎Dental Standards Institute⏎Arlington, Virginia⏎June 16, 2025⏎⏎⏎DSI COMMENTS | ONC-2025-0002 | Page 8⏎⏎⏎APPENDIX: CITATIONS REFERENCED IN THESE COMMENTS⏎⏎Obermeyer, Z., Powers, B., Vogeli, C., & Mullainathan, S.
