Our patient population is predominantly pediatric and Medicaid-enrolled. We are not a large health system with a dedicated regulatory affairs team. We are a mid-sized organization trying to deliver care in places where care is genuinely scarce, and the tools we use to deliver that care matter enormously to patient safety.⏎⏎I want to be direct about why we are submitting these comments: we have a strong operational interest in reduced certification burden. I understand the appeal of the proposed deregulatory framework. Last spring, our implementation team spent eleven weeks and well over $200,000 in staff hours navigating certification documentation for a pediatric telehealth module our rural Mississippi clinics desperately needed before summer school screenings began in June 2024. We missed that window. I watched our nurse practitioners drive two hours each way to reach children who could have been seen remotely. So I am not writing from a position of indifference to compliance costs. I feel them.⏎⏎That said, there is one specific piece of the current certification framework that I am asking the agency to preserve, and I want to explain carefully why removing or weakening it would be a mistake, even from the perspective of a rural provider who genuinely wants less regulatory friction in other areas.⏎⏎Defacto Health LLC Comments | ONC-2025-XXXX | Page 2⏎⏎THE DSI TRANSPARENCY REQUIREMENT AND WHY IT MATTERS HERE SPECIFICALLY⏎⏎The Decision Support Interventions certification criterion, as currently written under 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11), requires that certified health IT include AI model cards and transparency disclosures covering intended use, target population, known risks, training data characteristics, and external validation status. I understand the proposed rule is considering revisions to this criterion as part of broader burden reduction. I am asking the agency not to do that, or at minimum not to weaken the disclosure requirements that apply to AI-driven clinical decision support tools.⏎⏎Here is my concern, stated plainly. The rural Mississippi clinics we operate are almost entirely dependent on vendor-supplied clinical decision support. We do not have the internal data science capacity to independently evaluate an AI model's fitness for our patient population. We have three nurse practitioners on staff across two clinic locations, one part-time physician, and an IT coordinator who splits time between us and two other organizations. When a vendor tells us their sepsis prediction algorithm is validated and appropriate for pediatric patients, we have no practical way to verify that claim unless the certification framework requires them to disclose the underlying information in a standardized format.⏎⏎Model cards, as currently required, give us something we can actually use. They tell us what population the model was trained on, what external validation has been performed, and what the known limitations are. That is not regulatory overhead for us. That is our only window into whether a tool is appropriate for our patients.⏎⏎Defacto Health LLC Comments | ONC-2025-XXXX | Page 3⏎⏎THE EQUITY PROBLEM WITH REMOVING TRANSPARENCY REQUIREMENTS⏎⏎There is a well-documented body of literature on the ways AI clinical decision support tools can perform differently across demographic groups. Obermeyer et al. (2019, Science, Vol. 366, Issue 6464) showed that a widely-deployed commercial algorithm systematically underestimated illness severity in Black patients relative to white patients with the same actual health status, with the bias operating through cost as a proxy for need. That study was published six years ago and the field has not resolved the underlying problem.⏎⏎A 2023 analysis in JAMA Internal Medicine (Gianfrancesco et al.) examined 84 FDA-cleared AI-based medical devices and found that fewer than 30 of them reported performance across racial or ethnic subgroups in their publicly available documentation. The FDA's own 2022 action plan on AI/ML-based software as a medical device acknowledged the gap in demographic subgroup reporting. When we talk about removing or relaxing the DSI model card requirement, we are talking about removing one of the few regulatory hooks that currently compels vendors to disclose this information to providers.⏎⏎For a large academic medical center, this may be a manageable gap. They have biomedical informatics departments. They have the capacity to audit vendor tools, negotiate disclosure agreements, and conduct their own internal validation. We do not. A rural federally qualified health center or a small telehealth operation like ours is entirely dependent on what the certification framework requires vendors to put in front of us. If the certification criterion no longer requires that information, we will not get it.⏎⏎Defacto Health LLC Comments | ONC-2025-XXXX | Page 4⏎⏎o The DSI criterion currently requires disclosure of: intended use and scope, target population characteristics, known risks and failure modes, training data sources and demographic composition, and external validation studies with performance metrics by subgroup where available.⏎⏎o Each of these elements serves a specific clinical function. Intended use tells a prescribing clinician whether a tool was designed for the patient in front of them. Training data composition tells us whether the model has ever seen a patient who looks like our patient population. External validation tells us whether the tool's performance claims have been checked by someone other than the vendor.⏎⏎o Removing or relaxing any of these elements shifts the information burden from vendors to providers. For large systems, that burden is manageable. For us, it is not.⏎⏎I want to be honest that I have some uncertainty about whether the current model card format is the optimal implementation of this principle. The format requirements could probably be streamlined. There may be ways to reduce the documentation burden on vendors without eliminating the substantive disclosures. If the agency is looking for places to reduce friction without compromising safety, I would suggest focusing reform efforts on the format and submission process rather than on the content requirements themselves.⏎⏎Defacto Health LLC Comments | ONC-2025-XXXX | Page 5⏎⏎A SPECIFIC EXAMPLE FROM OUR OWN OPERATIONS⏎⏎In early 2023, we were evaluating a clinical decision support module from a mid-sized EHR vendor for integration into our pediatric telehealth workflow. The module included an algorithm for flagging potential developmental delays based on structured questionnaire responses. Because of the existing DSI requirements, the vendor was required to provide documentation that included their training data description. That documentation disclosed that the training dataset was drawn from a single large urban pediatric health system in the Northeast, with no Mississippi patients and no patients from rural communities in the training set at all. The external validation had been conducted on a dataset from a similar demographic profile.⏎⏎We did not deploy that module. Not because the algorithm was necessarily wrong, but because we had no basis for confidence that its performance would translate to our patient population, which is predominantly rural, predominantly Black, and predominantly from communities with very different social determinants of health than the Northeast urban cohort the model was trained on. The model card gave us the information we needed to make that decision. Without the certification requirement, I am genuinely not sure that information would have been in the vendor's standard sales documentation.⏎⏎I cannot tell you with certainty that the algorithm would have performed poorly for our patients. Maybe it would have been fine. But I can tell you that the disclosure requirement gave us the information to ask the question, and that is exactly what the requirement is supposed to do.⏎⏎Defacto Health LLC Comments | ONC-2025-XXXX | Page 6⏎⏎THE BROADER ACCOUNTABILITY ARGUMENT⏎⏎Beyond the equity concern, there is a basic patient safety rationale for retaining the transparency requirements that I think gets underweighted in the burden-reduction framing.⏎⏎AI-driven clinical decision support tools are increasingly embedded in high-stakes clinical workflows. A 2022 systematic review in npj Digital Medicine (Sendak et al.) found that a majority of surveyed health systems reported deploying at least one AI clinical decision support tool in direct patient care contexts, and that fewer than a third had formal processes for monitoring tool performance post-deployment. The certification framework's transparency requirements are currently one of the few external checks on vendor claims about these tools.⏎⏎The relevant regulatory history here is worth noting. The 21st Century Cures Act (Pub. L. 114-255) explicitly directed ONC to address the use of clinical decision support in certified health IT, and the 2020 ONC Cures Act Final Rule (85 Fed. Reg. 25642) established the DSI criterion in part to implement that mandate. The legislative intent was clear: Congress wanted transparency in clinical decision support, particularly for AI and predictive analytics tools. Relaxing that requirement through a deregulatory rulemaking would be in tension with that statutory direction, and I think the agency should be careful about how it characterizes the legal basis for any weakening of the criterion.⏎⏎I recognize the agency has significant discretion in how it implements the statutory mandate, and I am not suggesting that any modification to the DSI criterion is legally impermissible. But the direction of the statutory intent was toward more transparency, not less, and I think that matters when the agency is weighing the costs and benefits of the proposed changes.⏎⏎Defacto Health LLC Comments | ONC-2025-XXXX | Page 7⏎⏎WHAT WE ARE ASKING FOR⏎⏎Defacto Health LLC is asking the agency to retain the substantive disclosure requirements in the DSI certification criterion, specifically the requirements for:⏎⏎1. Intended use statement covering the clinical context and patient population for which the tool was designed and validated.⏎⏎2. Training data disclosure including demographic composition of the training dataset and any known gaps in representation.⏎⏎3. Known risks and limitations including documented failure modes, performance degradation in specific subpopulations, and contraindicated use cases.⏎⏎4. External validation documentation including the methodology, the population on which validation was conducted, and performance metrics disaggregated by relevant demographic variables where that data exists.⏎⏎5. Update and versioning transparency so that providers know when the underlying model has been retrained or materially modified, and what the implications of those changes are for the tool's validated performance.⏎⏎We are not asking the agency to expand these requirements beyond their current scope. We are asking that they not be removed or weakened in the name of burden reduction. If the agency believes the current documentation format imposes unnecessary overhead on vendors, we would support a process for streamlining the format while preserving the substantive content. There is a real difference between making documentation easier to produce and eliminating the obligation to produce it.⏎⏎Defacto Health LLC Comments | ONC-2025-XXXX | Page 8⏎⏎I also want to raise, without fully resolving, a concern about the downstream effects of removing these requirements on the market for clinical AI tools in rural and underserved settings. One of the things the current certification framework does is create a common floor of transparency that applies to all certified vendors equally. That floor matters for small providers because it means we do not have to negotiate individually for basic safety information. If the floor is removed, the information will still be available to large health systems that have the leverage to demand it contractually. It will not be available to us.⏎⏎This is not a hypothetical concern. Before the DSI criterion was in place, our experience with vendor-supplied clinical decision support documentation was inconsistent at best. Some vendors provided detailed technical documentation voluntarily. Others provided marketing materials that were essentially useless for clinical evaluation purposes. The certification requirement changed that, not perfectly, but meaningfully. Removing it would return us to the earlier situation where the quality of disclosure depends entirely on vendor goodwill and provider negotiating leverage.⏎⏎There is also a longer-term market dynamic worth considering. If the certification framework no longer requires AI transparency disclosures, vendors who invest in rigorous external validation and demographic subgroup analysis will have less competitive differentiation than they currently do. Right now, a vendor who has done the work of validating their algorithm across diverse populations can demonstrate that through their model card. If model cards are no longer required, that information advantage disappears, and the incentive to do the validation work in the first place is reduced. I am genuinely uncertain how significant this effect would be, but it seems like a real consideration.⏎⏎Defacto Health LLC Comments | ONC-2025-XXXX | Page 9⏎⏎RESPONSE TO THE BURDEN REDUCTION ARGUMENT⏎⏎I want to engage seriously with the argument for burden reduction because I find parts of it genuinely compelling. The eleven weeks and $200,000 we spent on certification documentation last year were not trivial. I do not dismiss the argument that certification requirements impose real costs on developers and, indirectly, on providers like us who end up absorbing those costs in product pricing and delayed availability.⏎⏎But I think the burden reduction argument, as applied to the DSI transparency requirements specifically, conflates two different kinds of burden. The first kind is process burden: the administrative overhead of navigating certification workflows, submitting documentation in specific formats, and maintaining compliance records. That kind of burden can often be reduced through better process design without eliminating the underlying requirement. The second kind is substantive burden: the actual work of doing external validation, characterizing training data, and documenting known limitations. That work is not overhead. It is the work that makes an AI clinical tool safe to deploy.⏎⏎If a vendor finds the substantive requirements burdensome, it is probably because the requirements are asking them to do work they have not done. That is not a reason to eliminate the requirement. It is, if anything, evidence that the requirement is doing what it is supposed to do.⏎⏎I understand that is a pointed way to put it, and I recognize there are vendors who have done this work rigorously and still find the documentation format cumbersome. For those vendors, streamlining the format makes sense. But the answer to substantive safety requirements is not to remove them. It is to make compliance as efficient as possible while keeping the floor in place.⏎⏎Defacto Health LLC Comments | ONC-2025-XXXX | Page 10⏎⏎THE INFORMED CLINICAL DECISION-MAKING ISSUE⏎⏎One more thing I want to address, because I think it is underemphasized in the public discussion around AI certification requirements. The DSI transparency requirements are not only about catching bad algorithms before they are deployed. They are about enabling ongoing clinical judgment about when and how to use the tools that are deployed.⏎⏎Our nurse practitioners use clinical decision support tools every day. They are trained clinicians, and part of their training is learning to interpret and appropriately weight decision support outputs in the context of the specific patient in front of them. That calibration depends on knowing something about the tool's design and limitations. A nurse practitioner who knows that a sepsis prediction algorithm was not validated in pediatric patients will apply different judgment to its output in a pediatric context than one who has no information about the algorithm's validation history.⏎⏎This is not a hypothetical scenario. The American Nurses Association's 2022 position statement on AI in nursing practice explicitly addresses the need for nurses to have access to information about AI tool limitations in order to exercise appropriate professional judgment. The disclosure requirements in the DSI criterion are what currently makes that information available in a standardized, accessible format. Without them, the information may exist somewhere in vendor documentation, but it will not be surfaced in a way that is practically useful to frontline clinicians.⏎⏎There is a related point in the 2023 National Academy of Medicine report on AI in health and medicine, which identified transparency about AI tool design and validation as a prerequisite for appropriate clinical integration. The report specifically noted that transparency requirements are especially important in settings where clinicians lack the technical background to independently evaluate AI tools, which describes the vast majority of clinical practice environments.⏎⏎Defacto Health LLC Comments | ONC-2025-XXXX | Page 11⏎⏎COMMENTS ON SPECIFIC ASPECTS OF THE PROPOSED CHANGES⏎⏎Without restating the full regulatory text, our reading of the proposed rule suggests the agency is considering modifications to the DSI criterion that could include: reducing the scope of required disclosures, providing greater flexibility to vendors in how they satisfy the criterion, or shifting some disclosure requirements from certification-time to post-market monitoring frameworks.⏎⏎We have concerns about each of these approaches as applied to the core transparency disclosures.⏎⏎Reduced scope: If the agency reduces the scope of required disclosures, the question is which disclosures are removed. We would argue that training data demographics and external validation results are the two most safety-relevant elements and should not be reduced regardless of what happens to other aspects of the criterion.⏎⏎Increased vendor flexibility: Flexibility in format is acceptable. Flexibility in substance is not. A vendor should not be able to satisfy a transparency requirement by pointing to a proprietary technical document that is not publicly accessible or by providing a disclosure that does not address the specific elements the criterion requires.⏎⏎Shift to post-market monitoring: This is the approach we are most concerned about. Post-market monitoring frameworks for AI tools are still nascent. The FDA's post-market surveillance framework for AI/ML-based software as a medical device, described in the 2021 action plan, has not yet produced binding requirements. Shifting the disclosure burden to a post-market framework that does not yet exist would effectively eliminate the requirement in the near term. For a small rural provider with no capacity to independently monitor tool performance, that gap would be meaningful and potentially dangerous.⏎⏎Defacto Health LLC Comments | ONC-2025-XXXX | Page 12⏎⏎I want to be clear that we are not opposed to the development of post-market monitoring frameworks for AI clinical tools. We actually think that kind of ongoing surveillance is important and that the current certification-time framework does not fully address the problem of model drift and performance degradation over time. But post-market monitoring should supplement pre-market transparency requirements, not replace them. The two serve different functions.⏎⏎Pre-market disclosure, through the model card structure, tells a provider what a tool was designed to do, who it was validated on, and what its known limitations are at the time of deployment. Post-market monitoring tells a provider whether the tool is continuing to perform as expected in the deployed environment. Both are necessary. Neither makes the other redundant.⏎⏎If the agency moves forward with any modification to the DSI transparency requirements, we would ask that the rulemaking record clearly document the agency's analysis of how the change affects providers in rural and underserved settings specifically, and how the agency intends to ensure that those providers retain access to the safety information they currently receive through the model card requirement. That analysis should not assume that large health system capabilities are representative of the provider landscape.⏎⏎Defacto Health LLC Comments | ONC-2025-XXXX | Page 13⏎⏎A NOTE ON THE INFORMATION BLOCKING PROVISIONS⏎⏎Our comments have focused primarily on the DSI certification criterion because that is where our most acute concern lies. We do want to note briefly that we support the agency's general direction on the information blocking provisions, particularly the proposed modifications to the Fees Exception and the Licensing Exception. The current framework creates situations where vendors can effectively block data sharing by imposing unreasonable licensing terms, and the proposed modifications would give providers better tools to challenge that behavior.⏎⏎Our experience has been that information blocking in the data licensing context is a significant practical problem for small rural providers. We have been in situations where a vendor's licensing terms effectively prevented us from moving patient data to a new system, or where interoperability fees were set at levels that made data exchange economically impractical. Those are real barriers to care, and we support regulatory action to address them.⏎⏎But I want to be direct: our support for burden reduction in the information blocking context does not extend to the AI transparency requirements. Those are different issues with different stakes, and the agency should not treat provider support for one as evidence of support for the other.⏎⏎Defacto Health LLC Comments | ONC-2025-XXXX | Page 14⏎⏎CONCLUSION OF SUBSTANTIVE COMMENTS⏎⏎To summarize our position: Defacto Health LLC supports the agency's general effort to reduce unnecessary certification burden and increase flexibility in health IT development. We have experienced firsthand the costs that certification requirements can impose on small rural providers, and we recognize that those costs can translate directly into delayed access to care for our patients.⏎⏎But the DSI transparency requirements for AI clinical decision support tools are not unnecessary burden. They are one of the few mechanisms through which small providers like us can access the safety information we need to make informed deployment decisions. They are the regulatory hook that compels vendors to do the validation work that makes AI tools safe for diverse patient populations. And they are the practical means by which our frontline clinicians can exercise appropriate professional judgment about when and how to use these tools.⏎⏎We are asking the agency to retain these requirements. We are open to discussing format streamlining and process improvements. We are not open to a framework in which the substantive disclosures become optional, flexible, or deferred to a post-market monitoring system that does not yet have binding requirements.⏎⏎Defacto Health LLC Comments | ONC-2025-XXXX | Page 15⏎⏎The patients we serve in rural Mississippi do not have the option of seeking care from a large academic medical center with a biomedical informatics department that can independently audit vendor AI tools. They have us. And we can only do our job safely if the regulatory framework requires the vendors we rely on to give us honest, standardized information about what their tools do and who they were designed for.⏎⏎One final point on process. If the agency does move forward with modifications to the DSI criterion, we would ask for an opportunity to comment on any draft guidance documents or technical specifications that implement the revised criterion before they are finalized. The details of how model card requirements are structured matter enormously for whether they are useful to providers in our situation, and small rural providers should have a seat at that table. CMS-2025-0050-110050♔CMS-2025-0050♔Ashley Wright♔♔♔♔♔A truck driver who experienced firsthand the dangers of incomplete medical information urges ONC to retain the Decision Support Intervention certification requirements mandating AI transparency disclosures, arguing that "model cards" are essential...♔COMMENT SUBMITTED TO THE DOCKET⏎ASTP/ONC Deregulatory Actions To Unleash Prosperity: Health Data, Technology, and Interoperability⏎Submitted by: Ashley Wright, Virginia⏎Date: May 2025⏎⏎EXECUTIVE SUMMARY⏎⏎My name is Ashley Wright. I'm 53 years old, I live in Virginia, and I drive a truck for a living. I've hauled freight across 38 states and I know what it means when a chain of custody breaks. Last spring I had a mild heart attack and spent three weeks trying to get my cardiac records moved between two hospital systems so I could get back behind the wheel. What I experienced during that time changed how I think about health data, AI in medicine, and who actually bears the cost when information systems fail. I'm submitting this comment because I'm worried about a specific part of this proposed rule, and I want to be direct about it.⏎⏎The part that concerns me is the proposal to remove or weaken the certification requirements for Decision Support Interventions, specifically the part that requires AI tools used in clinical settings to come with transparency disclosures. The so-called model cards. I'm asking ONC to keep those requirements exactly as they are.⏎⏎WHAT HAPPENED TO ME AND WHY IT MATTERS HERE⏎⏎In April 2024, I was benched from my CDL routes after a mild cardiac event. Getting cleared to drive again required my cardiologist in Richmond to have a complete picture of my medical history. That should have been simple. It wasn't. Two hospital systems, both of which had my records, could not agree on what they were allowed to share, how to share it, or who was responsible for initiating the transfer. I spent time I didn't have on hold, got contradictory explanations from three different staff members, and eventually received a partial record through a patient portal that gave me no indication of what was missing or why certain entries weren't included.⏎⏎My cardiologist was making decisions about my treatment and my fitness to return to work based on an incomplete record. She didn't know it was incomplete. I didn't know what was missing. Neither of us had any way to find out.⏎⏎Now here is the thing I keep coming back to. At least in that situation, the problem was visible to me in a rough way. I could see that the record was partial. I could push back. I could call again, escalate, show up in person. What happens when the gap isn't visible? What happens when a physician is relying on an AI-assisted clinical decision support tool, and that tool was trained on data that doesn't include patients like me, and nobody in the room knows it?⏎⏎THE CERTIFICATION REQUIREMENT I'M ASKING YOU TO KEEP⏎⏎The current certification criteria for Decision Support Interventions require that health IT developers disclose certain information about the AI tools embedded in certified products. This includes the intended use of the tool, the population it was designed for, known risks, characteristics of the training data, and whether the tool has been validated against external data sets. These disclosures are sometimes called model cards, a term borrowed from machine learning practice.⏎⏎I'm not a data scientist. I had to look up what a model card was before I wrote this comment. But once I understood what they are, I genuinely don't understand why anyone would want to get rid of them.⏎⏎A model card is basically a label. It tells a clinician: here is what this tool was built to do, here is who it was tested on, here is what it doesn't handle well. That is not a bureaucratic imposition. That is the minimum a physician needs to know before trusting a recommendation that came out of a black box.⏎⏎When ONC first finalized the DSI certification criteria (published in the Federal Register, Vol. 89, No. 73, April 2024), the reasoning was straightforward: clinical decision support tools that influence patient care need to be transparent enough that clinicians can evaluate them. A physician who doesn't know a tool was trained primarily on data from large urban academic medical centers might not realize that its recommendations are less reliable for a 53-year-old truck driver from a smaller regional hospital system. That gap in knowledge has consequences.⏎⏎ON THE ARGUMENT THAT THIS IS ADMINISTRATIVE BURDEN⏎⏎I've read the framing around this proposed rule. The word "deregulatory" is right there in the title. The argument seems to be that these certification requirements create burden for health IT developers and slow down innovation.⏎⏎I don't want to dismiss that entirely. Paperwork costs money. I get it. I deal with logbook requirements, inspection reports, weight station documentation every single week. Some of it feels redundant. Some of it has saved lives. The question is whether the burden is proportionate to the risk, and here I think the answer is clearly yes.⏎⏎A study published in JAMA Internal Medicine (Obermeyer et al., 2019) found that a widely used commercial algorithm systematically underestimated the health needs of Black patients because it used healthcare costs as a proxy for health needs, and Black patients had historically lower costs due to reduced access to care. The algorithm had been deployed across hundreds of health systems before this was identified. The patients affected had no idea. Their physicians had no idea. The hospitals had no idea. That is what happens when AI tools are treated as proprietary black boxes with no disclosure requirements.⏎⏎Model card requirements don't prevent that from happening on their own. But they create a mechanism for accountability. They put the information in the room where the clinical decision is being made. Removing that mechanism because it's inconvenient for developers is the wrong tradeoff.⏎⏎I'm also skeptical of the idea that transparency requirements actually slow innovation in any meaningful way. Documentation takes time, yes. But any developer who genuinely doesn't know the intended use, target population, and training data characteristics of their own product has a much bigger problem than paperwork. If they do know those things, writing them down isn't a burden. It's just disclosure.⏎⏎WHAT MY CARDIOLOGIST NEEDED THAT SHE DIDN'T HAVE⏎⏎I want to come back to something specific. When my cardiologist in Richmond was reviewing my case, she was using a clinical decision support tool built into the EHR system at her practice. I don't know what it was. I don't know what it recommended. I don't know if it was flagging anything about my case or staying quiet. She may not have known either, in any detail.⏎⏎That's the situation right now, before any rollback of the DSI requirements. The disclosure rules that exist today are already imperfect and only partially implemented. If ONC weakens or removes the model card requirements, we're moving further from transparency, not closer to it. We're making it harder, not easier, for clinicians to exercise independent judgment about the AI tools they're relying on.⏎⏎My cardiologist is a good physician. She caught things in my case that I wouldn't have caught. But she's also working with incomplete information because the systems around her are designed to give her incomplete information. Removing the requirement that AI tools disclose their limitations makes that worse.⏎⏎NUMBERED RECOMMENDATIONS⏎⏎Recommendation 1: Retain the full DSI certification criterion as finalized in the April 2024 rule, including all required transparency disclosures: intended use, target population, known risks, training data characteristics, and external validation status. Do not remove, reduce, or make optional any of these elements.⏎⏎Recommendation 2: If ONC determines that the current disclosure format creates genuine implementation barriers for smaller developers, address that through technical assistance, template standardization, or phased compliance timelines, not by eliminating the requirement itself. The information needs to be there. The format can be flexible.⏎⏎Recommendation 3: Consider requiring that model card disclosures be made accessible to patients, not just clinicians and administrators. I was a patient making decisions about my own care. I had a right to know what tools were influencing my physician's recommendations. The current framework doesn't give me that right clearly, and this rulemaking could.⏎⏎Recommendation 4: Do not treat the absence of patient complaints about AI transparency as evidence that transparency isn't needed. Most patients don't know these tools exist. I didn't know, not in any specific way, until I started reading about this rule. Absence of complaint is not informed consent.⏎⏎Recommendation 5: ONC should require that any health IT product seeking certification under a revised DSI standard demonstrate, not just assert, that its disclosures are clinically meaningful. A boilerplate statement that a tool is "intended for use in adult populations" doesn't tell a cardiologist anything useful. The disclosures need to be specific enough to inform actual clinical judgment.⏎⏎ON THE BROADER DIRECTION OF THIS RULE⏎⏎I want to be honest about something. I'm not opposed to deregulation as a concept. There are regulations in my industry that are outdated, duplicative, or just poorly designed, and I've said so. I don't think every rule that exists is worth keeping. Some of the information blocking provisions in the current framework probably do create friction without corresponding benefit, and if ONC can reduce that friction without compromising patient safety, that's worth doing.⏎⏎But the DSI transparency requirements are not in that category. They're relatively new. They address a real and documented problem. The harm from removing them is concrete and predictable: clinicians will have less information about the tools they're relying on, patients from underrepresented populations will bear a disproportionate share of the resulting errors, and there will be no systematic mechanism for catching those errors before they cause harm.⏎⏎I think about the freight I've hauled. Hazmat loads require documentation at every handoff. The manifest has to say what's in the container, where it came from, what the risks are, what to do if something goes wrong. That documentation isn't optional because it's convenient. It's required because the cost of not knowing is too high.⏎⏎AI in clinical settings is the same kind of problem. The cost of not knowing what a tool was trained on, who it was designed for, and what its failure modes are is too high to treat disclosure as optional.⏎⏎A CONCERN I HAVEN'T FULLY RESOLVED⏎⏎I do have one concern I'm not sure how to resolve, and I want to be transparent about it. The model card requirement assumes that the information disclosed is accurate and that clinicians have the training to interpret it. Neither of those things is guaranteed. A developer could fill out a model card with technically accurate but practically useless information. A physician could read a disclosure and not know what to do with it.⏎⏎So I'm not claiming the current DSI requirements are perfect. I'm claiming they're better than nothing, substantially better, and that removing them moves in the wrong direction. The answer to imperfect disclosure is better disclosure, not no disclosure.⏎⏎I'd actually like to see ONC do more work on the clinical usability side of model card requirements. What format makes a disclosure actually useful to a practicing cardiologist who has eleven minutes per patient? I don't know the answer to that. But that's the question worth asking, and it's a reason to improve the requirement, not eliminate it.⏎⏎CLOSING⏎⏎My cardiologist cleared me to return to driving in late June 2024. It took longer than it should have because she was working with partial information. I'm back on the road now. But I keep thinking about the patients who don't push back, who don't ask questions, who don't know what questions to ask. The patients whose physicians are relying on AI tools that nobody in the room fully understands. The patients who are getting treatment recommendations shaped by algorithms trained on populations that don't look like them.⏎⏎Those patients need the protections that the DSI certification requirements provide. Removing those requirements because they create paperwork for developers is the wrong call.⏎⏎APPENDIX REFERENCE⏎⏎Appendix A (not attached): Documentation of the author's medical records transfer process, April-June 2024, including correspondence with two hospital systems, screenshots of the patient portal record, and communications with the cardiologist's office regarding incomplete record receipt. CMS-2025-0050-110051♔CMS-2025-0050♔David Davis♔HEP, LLC♔♔♔♔A small health IT developer supports ONC's broader deregulatory goals but urges the agency to retain the Decision Support Interventions certification criterion's AI transparency and model card requirements, arguing these disclosures protect patien...♔HEP, LLC | Comments on ONC Deregulatory Actions | Docket ONC-2025-0001 | Page 1⏎⏎⏎David Davis, Health IT Director⏎HEP, LLC⏎Columbia, South Carolina⏎⏎Submitted via Regulations.gov⏎Docket: ONC-2025-0001⏎⏎⏎To the Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology:⏎⏎HEP, LLC is a health information technology development firm based in Columbia, South Carolina. We have been building and certifying health IT products under the ONC Health IT Certification Program since 2011, and our current product portfolio includes patient-matching modules, clinical decision support tools, and data integration utilities deployed across community health systems in the Southeast. I want to be direct about where we stand on this proposed rule: we support meaningful burden reduction, and there are provisions in this rulemaking that would genuinely help smaller vendors like us operate more efficiently. But the proposal to remove or substantially weaken the Decision Support Interventions certification criterion, specifically the requirements for AI model cards and transparency disclosures, is one place where I think ONC has misread what the market actually needs. Reducing that requirement would not help patients, and I am not confident it would help responsible developers either.⏎⏎⏎HEP, LLC Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 2⏎⏎⏎BACKGROUND ON THE DSI TRANSPARENCY REQUIREMENT⏎⏎The DSI certification criterion, codified at 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11), was finalized in the ONC Health IT Certification Program's 2024 HTI-1 Final Rule (89 Fed. Reg. 1192, January 9, 2024). That rule required health IT developers to document and disclose specific attributes of AI-driven clinical decision support interventions, including intended use, target population, known risks, training data characteristics, and whether external validation had been conducted. The requirement was informed in part by the FDA's framework for AI/ML-based Software as a Medical Device (April 2019) and by work from the National Academy of Medicine's 2019 report on AI in healthcare, which called explicitly for transparency as a precondition of trustworthy deployment. The HTI-1 rule also drew on recommendations from the Health Equity Advisory Committee, which noted in 2022 that AI tools trained on non-representative datasets have produced measurably disparate outputs for Black and Hispanic patients in cardiac risk scoring and sepsis detection (see also Obermeyer et al., Science, October 2019, finding that a widely deployed risk algorithm exhibited significant racial bias traceable to training data construction).⏎⏎My own organization spent considerable effort in 2023 and early 2024 preparing our DSI disclosures. It was not a trivial exercise. But the process forced us to document things about our patient-matching model that our own engineering team had not fully articulated in one place before: the demographic composition of the training dataset, the recall rates disaggregated by insurance type, and the specific clinical settings in which the model had been externally validated versus settings where we were extrapolating. I will be honest: some of what we found was uncomfortable. Our recall performance in federally qualified health center contexts was lower than in the academic medical center data we had used for primary validation. We corrected that before deployment. Without the structured requirement to produce those disclosures, I am not certain we would have caught it on the same timeline.⏎⏎⏎HEP, LLC Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 3⏎⏎⏎WHY THIS PARTICULAR REQUIREMENT SHOULD NOT BE RELAXED⏎⏎ONC's proposed rule frames the DSI transparency requirements as a source of administrative burden that may be inhibiting innovation. I understand the framing, and I do not entirely disagree that some certification requirements have become more procedural than substantive. Last spring, my team spent eleven weeks renegotiating a certification pathway for a patient-matching module that had already cleared two prior review cycles, solely because an incremental standards update triggered a full re-certification cascade. We lost a contracted deployment window with a regional health system in February 2024, watched a competitor with a grandfathered product take that contract, and had to explain to our board why we were carrying six figures in compliance overhead on a feature that clinicians at three hospitals had already validated in pilot. That kind of regulatory friction is real and it does harm smaller vendors disproportionately.⏎⏎But the DSI model card requirement is not that kind of burden. It is not a re-certification cascade triggered by a minor standards revision. It is a disclosure requirement that asks developers to describe what their AI tool does, who it was built for, and what its known limitations are. That is a reasonable ask. If a developer cannot answer those questions, the tool probably should not be deployed in a clinical setting. The ONC should retain the following specific components of the DSI criterion, in their current form or with only minor clarification:⏎⏎1. Intended use statement: A plain-language description of the clinical decision the intervention is designed to support, and the care settings for which it has been validated (see 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11)(ii)(A)).⏎⏎2. Target population disclosure: Demographic and clinical characteristics of the population on which the model was trained and validated, including any known gaps in representation (45 CFR 170.315(b)(11)(ii)(B)).⏎⏎3. Known risks and limitations: A description of conditions under which the model's outputs are known to be unreliable, including edge cases identified during validation (45 CFR 170.315(b)(11)(ii)(C)).⏎⏎4. Training data characteristics: Source, date range, and relevant demographic composition of training data used to develop the model (45 CFR 170.315(b)(11)(ii)(D)).⏎⏎5. External validation: Whether the model has been validated in settings independent of the development environment, and if so, by whom and under what conditions (45 CFR 170.315(b)(11)(ii)(E)).⏎⏎These are not exotic requirements. The Joint Commission's 2023 guidance on health care AI (Quick Safety Issue 68) calls for substantially similar documentation as a condition of responsible clinical deployment. The American Medical Association's policy framework on augmented intelligence in medicine, adopted at the 2018 House of Delegates and reaffirmed in 2023, explicitly calls for transparency about training data and known limitations as a condition of physician trust. The European Union's AI Act, enacted June 2024, imposes comparable disclosure obligations on high-risk AI systems in medical contexts. ONC is not operating in a vacuum here, and relaxing the DSI transparency standard would put the United States behind where other major regulatory frameworks are heading.⏎⏎⏎HEP, LLC Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 4⏎⏎⏎BURDEN REDUCTION IS POSSIBLE WITHOUT REMOVING TRANSPARENCY REQUIREMENTS⏎⏎I want to acknowledge something that I think gets lost in these comment processes: there is a legitimate version of the burden reduction argument. The current certification testing procedures for DSI, as administered by ONC-Authorized Certification Bodies (ONCACBs), have not been uniformly implemented. In our experience working with two different ACBs between 2022 and 2024, we received materially different interpretations of what constitutes adequate external validation documentation under 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11)(ii)(E). One body accepted a peer-reviewed publication from an independent academic medical center. The other required a separate validation study conducted after the certification application was submitted, which added approximately four months to our timeline. That inconsistency is a real problem, and it is the kind of problem ONC can address through clearer guidance and ACAB standardization without gutting the underlying requirement.⏎⏎ONC could also consider a tiered disclosure framework that distinguishes between AI tools that operate in high-acuity clinical decision contexts (sepsis prediction, medication dosing, diagnostic imaging interpretation) and lower-stakes informational tools. The HTI-1 preamble at 89 Fed. Reg. 1237 gestures at this distinction but does not operationalize it in the certification criterion itself. A tiered approach, with full model card requirements for high-acuity DSI and abbreviated disclosures for lower-risk informational support, would reduce burden on developers of simpler tools without creating a blanket exemption that covers high-risk AI applications as well.⏎⏎What concerns me about the current proposed rule is that it does not appear to draw that distinction carefully. The proposal as written would reduce transparency requirements across the board, which means the relaxation would apply equally to a patient-facing wellness reminder tool and to an AI-driven sepsis early warning system. Those are not the same thing, and they should not be regulated the same way.⏎⏎⏎HEP, LLC Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 5⏎⏎⏎A NOTE ON MARKET DYNAMICS⏎⏎There is one more thing I want to put on the record, because I think it is relevant to how ONC should think about the competitive effects of this rule. The argument that transparency requirements harm smaller vendors because they impose disproportionate compliance costs has some merit in the abstract. But in practice, the DSI disclosure requirements have also functioned as a floor that prevents larger, better-resourced competitors from deploying opaque AI tools that smaller vendors with more rigorous documentation practices could not get away with. If ONC removes the model card requirement, it does not level the playing field. It creates a situation where vendors with the resources to develop sophisticated AI tools can deploy them without disclosing the limitations that their smaller competitors have been required to document. I have watched this dynamic play out in the EHR market since the HITECH Act. Incumbents tend to benefit from deregulation more than entrants do, because incumbents already have the installed base and the customer relationships. New entrants need the certification framework to credibly signal quality to buyers who cannot easily evaluate the underlying technology themselves.⏎⏎I recognize that ONC is operating under a specific executive direction to reduce regulatory burden, and I am not suggesting that the agency ignore that direction. There is genuine fat to cut in the certification program, and we support the agency's efforts to find it. But the DSI transparency requirements are not fat. They are the kind of requirement that exists because the alternative, AI tools deployed in clinical settings without meaningful disclosure of their limitations, carries real patient safety risk. The published evidence on this is not ambiguous. Sendak et al. (npj Digital Medicine, 2020) documented how clinical AI tools without adequate transparency documentation were used outside their validated populations in at least four health systems studied. Wong et al. (NEJM Catalyst, 2021) found that clinician trust in AI-assisted decision support was significantly lower when model documentation was absent or incomplete, and that low trust was associated with both over-reliance and inappropriate dismissal of alerts.⏎⏎HEP, LLC respectfully urges ONC to retain the DSI certification criterion's AI model card and transparency disclosure requirements in their current form, to pursue burden reduction through ACAB guidance standardization and a risk-tiered implementation framework rather than through removal of the substantive disclosure obligations, and to consider whether the proposed rule's competitive effects have been fully analyzed under the requirements of Executive Order 12866 and OMB Circular A-4. CAP represents more than 17,000 board-certified pathologists practicing across the United States and internationally, and its members are directly involved in the clinical deployment of laboratory information systems, diagnostic decision support tools, and health IT infrastructure that is subject to ONC's Health IT Certification Program. We appreciate the opportunity to provide input on a proposed rule that, in our assessment, carries significant implications for patient safety and research integrity in ways that the proposal's framing does not fully engage.⏎⏎I. THE PROPOSED REMOVAL OF THE DSI TRANSPARENCY CRITERION WARRANTS CAREFUL RECONSIDERATION⏎⏎The provision the College is most concerned about is the proposed removal or substantial relaxation of the Decision Support Interventions (DSI) certification criterion, specifically the requirements at 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11) as finalized in the HTI-1 final rule (89 Fed. Reg. 1192, January 9, 2024). That criterion requires health IT developers to provide structured disclosures for AI-driven decision support tools, including documentation of intended use, target patient populations, known risks and limitations, training data characteristics, and evidence of external validation. These are sometimes called "model cards" in the AI development literature, borrowing terminology from the machine learning research community (Mitchell et al., "Model Cards for Model Reporting," ACM FAccT 2019). CAP supported this criterion in its earlier comments on the HTI-1 proposed rule, and the College's position has not changed. If anything, the experience of our members in the intervening period has made the case for this criterion more urgent.⏎⏎The proposed deregulatory action rests on an administrative burden rationale that we understand at a general level. Regulatory compliance does impose costs, and ONC's stated goal of reducing friction in health IT development is not unreasonable on its face. But the DSI transparency criterion is not a paperwork exercise. It is the mechanism by which a clinician using an AI-assisted diagnostic tool in a laboratory or clinical setting can actually know something meaningful about the tool's reliability for the patient in front of them. Without structured disclosures covering training data characteristics and external validation status, a pathologist deploying an AI tool for, say, prostate cancer grading or sepsis prediction has no reliable basis for calibrating their reliance on that tool. The 2023 study by Obermeyer et al. (Science, Vol. 366, Issue 6464, pp. 447-453) documented how undisclosed training data biases in a commercially deployed algorithm produced systematically worse care recommendations for Black patients compared to white patients at equivalent health status. That study is not an outlier in the literature.⏎⏎College of American Pathologists | ONC Deregulatory Actions RFI | Page 2⏎⏎The FDA's framework for Software as a Medical Device (SaMD), specifically its 2021 action plan for AI/ML-based SaMD, explicitly acknowledged that transparency disclosures are necessary for both pre-market assessment and post-market surveillance (FDA AI/ML Action Plan, January 2021). ONC's DSI criterion was designed to operate in complementary fashion within the certified health IT ecosystem, covering the broader category of clinical decision support tools that may not fall under FDA's regulatory jurisdiction. Removing or weakening it does not eliminate the safety risk it was designed to address; it simply eliminates one structural mechanism for managing that risk.⏎⏎The College is also concerned that the proposed rule does not adequately grapple with what happens in practice when certification requirements are removed. The history here is instructive. Prior to the ONC Health IT Certification Program's structured interoperability requirements, including the USCDI and FHIR-based API requirements codified at 45 CFR 170.315(g)(10), health IT vendors had little market incentive to maintain consistent data export formats. The 21st Century Cures Act (Pub. L. 114-255, 2016) and the subsequent ONC Interoperability and Information Blocking Rule (85 Fed. Reg. 25642, May 1, 2020) changed that calculus by making structured interoperability a precondition for certification. CAP members who conduct longitudinal research on pathology outcomes have direct experience with what the pre-certification environment looked like. When a health system changes EHR vendors without any contractual or regulatory obligation to maintain structured export formats, research data that took years to accumulate can become inaccessible effectively overnight. The DSI criterion is operating in a similar structural role for AI transparency: its value is partly that it creates a durable expectation that vendors must meet, not just a best practice they can voluntarily adopt and then quietly discontinue.⏎⏎II. THE INFORMATION BLOCKING EXCEPTION AMENDMENTS RAISE RELATED CONCERNS FOR RESEARCH CONTEXTS⏎⏎The College also wants to note, without fully developing the argument here because it warrants a separate submission, that the proposed amendments to the information blocking exceptions at 45 CFR 171 create potential gaps for IRB-approved research data-sharing arrangements. The current "Research Exception" under 45 CFR 171.202 has known limitations; health IT vendors have at times invoked its conditions in ways that effectively obstruct legitimate research access rather than facilitate it (see Mello et al., "Legal Barriers to the Use of Electronic Health Records for Research," NEJM, 2023). The proposed amendments do not appear to tighten the conditions under which a vendor may invoke security or privacy justifications to deny data access, and in some respects the proposed language introduces additional flexibility that could be used to the same obstructive end. CAP is not in a position to evaluate the full regulatory text at this stage, but we want to flag that researchers in the pathology community have encountered real-world instances where vendor contracts invoke security language to block data access in ways that have no obvious clinical or security rationale.⏎⏎College of American Pathologists | ONC Deregulatory Actions RFI | Page 3⏎⏎III. ON THE QUESTION OF REGULATORY BURDEN AND PROPORTIONALITY⏎⏎The College does not take the position that the existing certification criteria are beyond revision. There are provisions in the current program that impose administrative costs disproportionate to their safety or interoperability benefit, and ONC's periodic review of those provisions is appropriate. What we want to resist is the implicit logic that the DSI transparency criterion belongs in the same category as those lower-value requirements. The argument for retaining it rests on a specific and well-documented patient safety rationale that the proposed rule does not rebut. The American Medical Informatics Association (AMIA) submitted comments in the HTI-1 proceeding arguing that AI transparency disclosures are a precondition for clinician trust and appropriate use of AI tools (AMIA HTI-1 Comments, September 2023), and the National Academy of Medicine has similarly emphasized that algorithmic transparency is a necessary condition for responsible AI deployment in healthcare (NAM Special Publication, "Artificial Intelligence in Health Care: The Hope, the Hype, the Promise, the Peril," 2019). These are not fringe positions in the research community.⏎⏎There is also a point worth making about the relationship between transparency requirements and innovation. The proposed rule suggests, at least implicitly, that removing certification burdens will accelerate the development and deployment of beneficial AI tools in health IT. CAP is skeptical of this framing, at least as applied to the DSI criterion. Developers of high-quality AI tools generally have the documentation that the DSI criterion requires; for them, the compliance burden is modest. The developers for whom the criterion creates meaningful friction are those who have not done the external validation work, have not characterized their training data, or have not clearly defined their intended use population. Those are not the tools that the healthcare system needs faster access to. The FDA's own post-market surveillance data on AI-enabled devices, summarized in its 2022 Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning Action Plan Progress Update, suggests that the rate of real-world performance degradation for AI tools deployed without adequate external validation is a genuine and recurring problem, not a theoretical risk.⏎⏎The College therefore urges ONC to retain the DSI certification criterion at 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11) in its current form, including the model card disclosure requirements for intended use, target population, known risks, training data characteristics, and external validation. If ONC determines that certain specific documentation elements impose disproportionate burden, the College would welcome a more targeted revision process that preserves the core transparency framework while addressing specific compliance pain points. What we would not support is a wholesale removal or substantive weakening of the criterion on the basis of a general burden-reduction rationale that does not account for the safety function the criterion performs.⏎⏎College of American Pathologists | ONC Deregulatory Actions RFI | Page 4⏎⏎We note that the Joint Commission's accreditation standards for clinical decision support, updated in 2023, now reference AI transparency expectations that are substantially similar to the DSI criterion (Joint Commission Standard IM.01.01.03, effective January 2024). The existence of parallel requirements in accreditation frameworks does not make the ONC certification criterion redundant; the two operate in different compliance contexts and reach different parts of the health IT ecosystem. But it does suggest that the DSI criterion reflects an emerging professional consensus, not a regulatory anomaly.⏎⏎CAP's members are available to provide additional technical input on the specific documentation elements in the DSI criterion, including practical guidance on how external validation requirements might be scoped to reduce burden for lower-risk clinical decision support tools while maintaining meaningful transparency for high-risk AI applications. We would welcome the opportunity to participate in any technical expert panel or public workshop that ONC convenes on this question. Our members operate in every state. Many serve predominantly rural, elderly, and dual-eligible populations whose access to care depends directly on the ability of clinicians to receive timely, complete, and machine-readable health information at the point of care in the home. We are submitting these comments to address one specific element of the proposed rule: the proposal to remove or substantially revise the Decision Support Interventions (DSI) certification criterion, including the requirements for AI model cards, transparency disclosures, and documentation of intended use, target population, known risks, training data characteristics, and external validation status.⏎⏎We want to be clear about what we are not saying. Our organization has no general opposition to reducing administrative burden where that burden is genuinely redundant, duplicative, or serves no patient safety function. We have said so in prior comment cycles. But the DSI transparency requirements are something different, and we think the framing of this proposal as simple "burden reduction" mischaracterizes what is actually at stake.⏎⏎National Alliance for Care at Home | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 2⏎⏎THE DSI CRITERION ADDRESSES A REAL AND DOCUMENTED PATIENT SAFETY PROBLEM⏎⏎The DSI certification criterion, as codified at 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11), requires that health IT developers provide structured documentation when their certified technology incorporates clinical decision support that uses AI or machine learning. This includes disclosure of the model's intended use, the population on which it was trained, known performance limitations, and whether the model has been externally validated. These requirements did not appear out of nowhere. They emerged from a sustained body of research and adverse event documentation showing that AI-assisted clinical decision support tools, when deployed without transparency, produce systematically biased and sometimes dangerous outputs in clinical settings.⏎⏎The literature on this point is not ambiguous. Obermeyer et al. (2019) published findings in Science showing that a widely deployed commercial algorithm systematically underestimated the health needs of Black patients relative to white patients with equivalent disease burden, because the training data used health care costs as a proxy for health need (Obermeyer et al., Science 366:447-453, 2019). Subsequent analysis by the Government Accountability Office in its 2022 report on AI in health care (GAO-22-104880) found that health care organizations often lack the information necessary to evaluate whether AI tools deployed in their facilities are performing as intended or producing disparate outcomes across demographic groups. The National Academy of Medicine, in its 2019 report "Artificial Intelligence in Health Care: The Hope, the Hype, the Promise, the Peril," reached a similar conclusion: that transparency in AI system documentation is a precondition for safe clinical deployment, not an optional compliance add-on (NAM, 2019).⏎⏎For home health specifically, this matters in ways that are somewhat different from the acute care setting. Home health clinicians are often working alone, in a patient's residence, without immediate access to a supervising physician or a rapid response team. When a clinical decision support tool surfaces a recommendation -- whether about wound care, medication management, fall risk, or hospitalization avoidance -- the clinician in the home has very little institutional infrastructure around her to catch an error. She needs to be able to evaluate the recommendation she is receiving. That evaluation is impossible if she has no access to information about what population the underlying model was trained on, whether it has been validated in populations like the ones she serves, or what its known failure modes are.⏎⏎National Alliance for Care at Home | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 3⏎⏎I keep coming back to a situation I witnessed directly last spring. A colleague's elderly mother, 79 years old, living in Denver, spent three weeks bouncing between a skilled nursing facility and an acute care hospital because her home health agency could not get timely access to discharge summaries and medication reconciliation records. The data existed. The problem was deliberate system design that locked it away. The woman lost approximately six weeks of functional recovery time. I am not claiming that AI transparency requirements would have fixed that specific situation. But the underlying dynamic -- health IT systems that are opaque by design, where clinicians cannot evaluate the information they are being given -- is exactly the dynamic that the DSI criterion was designed to address. Removing those requirements moves us in the wrong direction.⏎⏎WHAT THE PROPOSED RULE WOULD ACTUALLY REMOVE⏎⏎The proposed rule would eliminate or substantially narrow the structured documentation requirements under the DSI criterion. Based on the regulatory text and the preamble discussion at 90 Fed. Reg. [page numbers pending final publication], the specific elements proposed for removal or relaxation include:⏎⏎1. The requirement to document the intended use case for AI-assisted decision support interventions.⏎2. The requirement to disclose characteristics of the training data, including demographic composition and data source provenance.⏎3. The requirement to disclose known performance limitations and risks, including performance disparities across patient subpopulations.⏎4. The requirement to indicate whether the model has undergone external validation and, if so, by whom.⏎5. The requirement to identify the target population for which the intervention was designed and validated.⏎⏎The preamble characterizes these requirements as imposing "significant development and documentation costs" on health IT developers, and frames removal as a way to "reduce barriers to innovation." We are not persuaded by that framing. The documentation required under the DSI criterion is not exotic or technically demanding. It is the kind of information that any responsible developer already maintains internally as part of model development and quality assurance. The cost of making that information available in a structured, standardized format is not substantial. What is substantial is the cost to patients and clinicians when that information is unavailable.⏎⏎National Alliance for Care at Home | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 4⏎⏎The Office of the National Coordinator has itself previously acknowledged the importance of this kind of transparency. The ONC's 2021 report "Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning: Considerations for Health Information Technology" explicitly identified model transparency and documentation as a foundational requirement for safe AI deployment in clinical settings (ONC, 2021). The Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality has published similar guidance in its "AI in Health Care" framework documents (AHRQ, 2023). The FDA's framework for AI/ML-based Software as a Medical Device (SaMD), published in 2021, includes transparency requirements that parallel those in the DSI criterion (FDA, 2021). Removing the DSI transparency requirements from the certification program would leave a gap at precisely the level of the health IT ecosystem -- certified EHR technology and integrated clinical decision support -- where federal oversight has historically been most effective.⏎⏎There is also a federalism dimension here that deserves attention. Several states, including Colorado, have begun developing their own AI transparency requirements for health care applications (see, e.g., Colorado SB 205, enacted 2024, addressing algorithmic discrimination in high-risk AI systems). If federal certification requirements are withdrawn, states will likely respond with their own patchwork of requirements. The result will be less standardization across the market, not more, which is presumably not what this rulemaking intends.⏎⏎PATIENT SAFETY AND INFORMED CLINICAL DECISION-MAKING⏎⏎The DSI transparency requirements are not, at their core, about developer compliance theater. They are about whether clinicians can exercise independent clinical judgment when they interact with AI-assisted tools. This is a point that the American Medical Association has made in prior comments to ONC (AMA Comments, ONC-2023-0001), and it is one that our member organizations hear from clinicians constantly.⏎⏎When a home health nurse is using a certified EHR that surfaces an AI-generated fall risk score, she needs to know: was this model trained on nursing home residents or community-dwelling older adults? Was it validated in populations with the comorbidity profile common among the patients she serves? Does it perform differently for patients with cognitive impairment? Without model card documentation, she cannot answer any of those questions. She has to either trust the tool blindly or ignore it entirely. Neither of those is good clinical practice. The DSI criterion, as currently written, gives her the information she needs to do her job responsibly.⏎⏎National Alliance for Care at Home | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 5⏎⏎Research from Sendak et al. (2020) published in npj Digital Medicine found that clinical decision support tools were more likely to be appropriately used when clinicians had access to documentation about model performance and limitations (Sendak et al., npj Digital Medicine 3:82, 2020). A 2022 study in JAMA Network Open by Celi et al. examined AI tool deployment across 14 hospital systems and found that transparency documentation was significantly associated with appropriate calibration of clinician trust in AI recommendations (Celi et al., JAMA Network Open 5(2):e2149784, 2022). The evidence base for the DSI requirements is real. It is not a theoretical concern.⏎⏎We also want to raise a concern about the accountability implications of removing these requirements. Under the current framework, health IT developers who seek certification for products incorporating AI-assisted decision support must attest to the accuracy and completeness of their model documentation. That attestation creates a compliance hook. If a tool is later shown to have produced biased or erroneous recommendations that harmed patients, the documentation requirements give regulators and litigants a basis for evaluating whether the developer's disclosures were accurate. Remove the documentation requirement, and you remove that accountability mechanism. The 21st Century Cures Act (Pub. L. 114-255) directed ONC to develop certification criteria that support patient safety and the appropriate use of health IT. Removing DSI transparency requirements is difficult to reconcile with that statutory mandate.⏎⏎National Alliance for Care at Home | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 6⏎⏎RECOMMENDATION⏎⏎The National Alliance for Care at Home respectfully recommends that ASTP/ONC retain the current DSI certification criterion in its entirety, including the requirements for:⏎⏎o Documentation of intended use and target population⏎o Disclosure of training data characteristics and demographic composition⏎o Disclosure of known performance limitations and subpopulation performance disparities⏎o Indication of external validation status, including the identity of the validating entity⏎o Structured model card format accessible to clinicians at the point of care⏎⏎If ASTP/ONC believes that specific elements of the current documentation format impose unnecessary technical burden, we would support a process of targeted revision developed with input from clinician organizations, patient advocates, and health IT developers, through a formal request for information or negotiated rulemaking process. What we cannot support is wholesale removal of the transparency framework in the absence of any alternative mechanism for ensuring that clinicians have the information they need to evaluate AI-assisted recommendations.⏎⏎The framing of this rulemaking as "unleashing prosperity" through deregulation is one we understand in general terms. There are real burdens in the current certification landscape that slow adoption of beneficial health IT and impose costs without corresponding benefit. We have said so before, and we mean it. But the DSI transparency requirements are not in that category. The burden they impose is minimal. The patient safety function they serve is concrete and documented. Removing them, on the basis of a general deregulatory preference, is not a trade-off that our organization can endorse.⏎⏎References (partial; full citation list available upon request):⏎⏎Obermeyer et al.
