CMS-2025-0050-110055♔CMS-2025-0050♔Joseph Allen♔Texas Medical Association♔♔♔♔The Texas Medical Association urges ONC to retain the Decision Support Interventions certification criterion's AI transparency requirements, including model cards disclosing training data, target populations, and known limitations, arguing that re...♔Texas Medical Association⏎401 W. 15th Street⏎Austin, Texas 78701⏎⏎www.texmed.org⏎⏎Submitted via Regulations.gov⏎Docket No. ONC-2025-0001⏎⏎Re: ASTP/ONC Deregulatory Actions To Unleash Prosperity: Health Data, Technology, and Interoperability -- Comments of the Texas Medical Association⏎⏎To the Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology:⏎⏎The Texas Medical Association submits these comments in response to the proposed rule published by the Assistant Secretary for Technology Policy and the Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology regarding deregulatory actions affecting the ONC Health IT Certification Program, information blocking definitions, and related provisions. TMA represents more than 57,000 physicians and medical students across Texas and brings to this proceeding direct experience with how health information technology functions in actual clinical environments, not in idealized conditions. Our comments here are focused on a discrete but consequential aspect of the proposed rule: the proposed removal of the Decision Support Interventions certification criterion, specifically those provisions requiring AI model cards and transparency disclosures.⏎⏎TMA urges ASTP/ONC to retain the DSI certification criterion in its current form, including all requirements for model cards, disclosure of intended use, identification of target populations, characterization of known risks, description of training data, and documentation of external validation. The case for removing these requirements rests primarily on administrative burden reduction. We take that rationale seriously, and we do not dismiss it reflexively. But the argument breaks down when examined against the actual consequences of removing the transparency infrastructure that the DSI criterion provides. This comment explains why.⏎⏎⏎BACKGROUND: WHAT THE DSI CRITERION ACTUALLY DOES⏎⏎Texas Medical Association Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 2⏎⏎Before addressing the proposed change, it is worth being precise about what the current DSI certification criterion requires. Under 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11), certified health IT must include decision support interventions that, when they incorporate predictive models or algorithms, disclose to users the following: the intervention's intended use, the population for which it was designed and validated, the data sources and characteristics used in training, known limitations and risks, and whether the algorithm has been validated on external datasets distinct from the training data. These disclosures are sometimes referred to collectively as "model cards," a term borrowed from the machine learning literature, where the concept was formalized by Mitchell et al. (2019) in a paper published by Google researchers and widely adopted as a documentation standard in AI development.⏎⏎The practical effect of this requirement is that when a physician at a Texas hospital opens an electronic health record and sees a sepsis prediction score or a readmission risk flag, the system must be capable of showing that physician what model generated that score, what patient population was used to build and test it, and whether it has been validated in populations resembling the patient in front of them. That is not a trivial disclosure. It is the minimum information a clinician needs to decide whether to trust the output or weight it against other clinical judgment.⏎⏎The proposed rule would eliminate this requirement on the grounds that it imposes unnecessary certification burdens on health IT developers and that market forces and other regulatory mechanisms provide sufficient accountability for AI-based clinical decision support tools. TMA respectfully but firmly disagrees with both parts of that rationale.⏎⏎⏎WHY THE BURDEN ARGUMENT IS INSUFFICIENT⏎⏎Texas Medical Association Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 3⏎⏎The administrative burden argument deserves a direct response because it is the primary justification offered in the proposed rule. ASTP/ONC acknowledges that some compliance costs attach to the model card requirements, and the agency characterizes these costs as disproportionate given other available accountability mechanisms. We have reviewed this analysis carefully, and we find it unpersuasive for several reasons.⏎⏎First, the burden being described is the burden on health IT developers, not on clinicians or patients. Preparing a model card for a clinical algorithm is a documentation task. It requires the developer to compile information about the model that, if the development process was conducted responsibly, already exists internally. The developer's data scientists know what training data they used. They know what population the model was validated on. They know what the known failure modes are. Requiring them to disclose this information in a standardized format imposes a compliance cost, certainly, but it is a cost that attaches to information the developer already possesses. The burden is documentation and disclosure, not discovery.⏎⏎Second, the proposed rule does not identify what alternative accountability mechanism would substitute for the DSI transparency requirements once they are removed. The general claim that "market forces" will discipline AI developers who deploy opaque or poorly validated algorithms is, in TMA's experience, not supported by how health IT markets actually function. Hospitals and health systems that purchase clinical decision support software typically lack the technical capacity to independently audit the algorithms embedded in those products. A 2023 study published in JAMA Internal Medicine (Obermeyer et al.) found that commercial risk-scoring algorithms used widely across U.S. health systems exhibited significant racial bias that was not disclosed in product documentation and that health system purchasers had no practical mechanism to detect independently. The DSI model card requirement is one of the few regulatory instruments that creates a mandatory disclosure obligation prior to deployment, rather than relying on post-market detection of harm.⏎⏎Third, the argument that other federal regulatory mechanisms cover this ground is imprecise. The FDA has authority over certain software as a medical device under 21 CFR Part 820, and the agency has taken steps to address AI transparency in its guidance on predetermined change control plans. But FDA oversight of clinical decision support software is limited by the statutory carve-outs established in the 21st Century Cures Act, 42 U.S.C. 300jj-11, which explicitly excludes from the definition of a medical device certain categories of clinical decision support that do not require a clinician to override the tool's recommendation to prevent serious harm. A large portion of the AI-based decision support tools embedded in EHR systems fall into this excluded category, meaning FDA's device oversight framework does not reach them. Removing the DSI certification criterion for these tools would leave a regulatory gap with no clear occupant.⏎⏎⏎THE PATIENT SAFETY ARGUMENT⏎⏎Texas Medical Association Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 4⏎⏎TMA's core concern here is patient safety, and we want to be specific about the mechanism of harm we are worried about, because the concern is sometimes mischaracterized in these proceedings as a generic anxiety about AI rather than a concrete clinical risk.⏎⏎The problem is this: clinical decision support algorithms embedded in EHR systems are frequently trained on patient populations that do not reflect the demographic composition of the patients being seen in the clinical environments where the tools are deployed. A sepsis prediction model trained predominantly on data from large academic medical centers in the northeastern United States may perform differently when deployed in a rural community hospital in West Texas serving a population that is predominantly Hispanic and elderly. A readmission risk model trained on commercially insured patients may systematically underestimate readmission risk in Medicaid populations if the training data did not adequately represent high-risk social determinants of health. These are not hypothetical concerns. The peer-reviewed literature on algorithmic performance disparities in clinical settings has grown substantially over the past five years.⏎⏎The following studies are illustrative, though the literature is considerably broader:⏎⏎1. Obermeyer, Z., Powers, B., Vogeli, C., & Mullainathan, S. (2019). Dissecting racial bias in an algorithm used to manage the health of populations. Science, 366(6464), 447-453. This study found that a widely used commercial algorithm assigned lower risk scores to Black patients than to White patients with equivalent health needs, resulting in Black patients being less likely to be enrolled in high-risk care management programs.⏎⏎2. Wong, A., Otles, E., Donnelly, J.P., et al. (2021). External Validation of a Widely Implemented Proprietary Sepsis Prediction Model in Hospitalized Patients. JAMA Internal Medicine, 181(8), 1065-1070. This study found that the Epic Sepsis Model, which is embedded in one of the most widely deployed EHR systems in the country, had a sensitivity of only 63% when externally validated at the University of Michigan Health System, substantially lower than the performance metrics described in the original model documentation.⏎⏎3. Char, D.S., Shah, N.H., & Magnus, D. (2018). Implementing Machine Learning in Health Care -- Addressing Ethical Challenges. New England Journal of Medicine, 378(11), 981-983. This paper argues that algorithmic transparency is a prerequisite for appropriate clinical use of AI-based decision support.⏎⏎4. Sendak, M.P., Elish, M.C., Gao, M., et al. (2020). "The Human Body is a Black Box": Supporting Clinical Decision-Making with Deep Learning. Proceedings of the ACM Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency. This study examined how clinicians actually interact with AI-generated predictions and found that without contextual information about model limitations and target populations, clinicians frequently misapplied algorithmic outputs in ways that could lead to patient harm.⏎⏎What these studies collectively illustrate is that the failure mode of opaque clinical algorithms is not theoretical. It is documented and recurring. The DSI certification criterion's model card requirement is a direct policy response to exactly this failure mode. Removing it does not make the problem go away. It removes the regulatory mechanism that creates an obligation to disclose the information clinicians need to apply these tools appropriately.⏎⏎⏎Texas Medical Association Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 5⏎⏎There is a practical dimension to this that I want to address directly, because I think it sometimes gets lost in discussions that stay at the level of regulatory text. When a physician is seeing a patient in a busy clinical environment, she is not going to pause the encounter to independently research the provenance of the risk score displayed in her EHR. She is going to use the information available to her in the moment. If the EHR interface shows a sepsis risk score of 85 and does not provide accessible information about what population that score was validated on, she will almost certainly apply that score as if it were universally applicable. That is a reasonable thing to do given the information available. The problem is that if the model was trained and validated on a population that differs meaningfully from her patient, the score may not be reliable, and she has no way of knowing that without the transparency disclosures the DSI criterion requires.⏎⏎This is not a failure of the physician's clinical judgment. It is a failure of the information environment in which she is practicing. The DSI certification criterion is designed to correct that information failure by requiring that the relevant transparency information be present in the certified system. Removing the requirement does not make the information appear through some other mechanism. It simply makes its absence permissible.⏎⏎I keep coming back to my own family's experience last spring to understand why this matters at the level of actual patients. My mother was transferred between three facilities in ten days following a cardiac event, and at each facility her care team was reconstructing her medication history from scratch because the systems would not exchange information. The cardiologist at Inova was manually transcribing from a faxed PDF while my mother waited in a hallway. The friction was not technical. It was institutional. The incentives to maintain information silos had not been overcome by any binding obligation to share. I raise this not because medication history exchange and AI transparency are identical issues, but because the pattern is the same: where there is no regulatory obligation to provide information, the institutional default is to withhold it or to let the burden fall on the clinician or the patient. The DSI criterion is one of the places where ONC has imposed a binding obligation that overrides that institutional default. Removing it restores the default.⏎⏎⏎THE INFORMED CLINICAL DECISION-MAKING ARGUMENT⏎⏎Texas Medical Association Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 6⏎⏎The American Medical Association has consistently maintained that physicians bear responsibility for clinical decisions, including decisions that are informed by algorithmic tools. This is the right principle. Physicians should not be able to defer entirely to an algorithm and disclaim responsibility for the outcome. But the corollary is that if physicians are responsible for decisions informed by AI tools, they must have access to the information necessary to exercise that responsibility meaningfully.⏎⏎The AMA's 2019 policy on augmented intelligence in health care (Policy H-480.940) states explicitly that AI tools used in clinical settings should be transparent, explainable, and subject to validation on relevant patient populations. The policy further states that physicians should have access to information about the training, validation, and known limitations of AI tools they are expected to use. This is not a radical position. It is the minimum condition for meaningful clinical accountability.⏎⏎The DSI certification criterion operationalizes this principle in federal health IT policy. Without it, a health IT developer can embed a clinical algorithm in a certified EHR system, market it to hospitals and health systems, and deploy it in patient care without disclosing to the clinicians using the tool what population it was designed for, what data it was trained on, or what its known failure modes are. The developer may have this information internally. The hospital purchasing the system may have signed a contract that includes some general warranties about the product. But the physician at the point of care has no access to the information she needs to exercise clinical judgment about when to rely on the tool and when to override it.⏎⏎This is not a sustainable arrangement for a healthcare system that is increasingly integrating AI-based decision support into clinical workflows. The ONC's own projections, cited in the proposed rule's regulatory impact analysis, indicate that the use of AI-based clinical decision support in certified EHR systems will continue to grow substantially over the next five years. Removing the transparency requirements at precisely the moment when AI adoption in clinical settings is accelerating is, in TMA's view, a significant policy error.⏎⏎⏎ACCOUNTABILITY AND THE QUESTION OF WHO BEARS THE RISK⏎⏎Texas Medical Association Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 7⏎⏎TMA also wants to address the accountability dimension of this proposal, because we think it is underweighted in the agency's analysis. When an AI-based clinical decision support tool produces an erroneous output that contributes to patient harm, the current legal and regulatory framework places primary liability on the physician, not on the developer of the algorithm. This is a well-documented feature of medical malpractice law, and it is not unique to AI-assisted care. The physician who acts on bad information is generally the party exposed to liability, even when the source of the bad information is a commercial product the physician had no role in designing or validating.⏎⏎The DSI certification criterion creates a modest but meaningful counterweight to this asymmetry. By requiring developers to disclose the characteristics and limitations of their algorithms, the criterion creates a record of what the developer knew about the tool's performance and what it chose to disclose. This record has potential relevance not only to patient safety but to the legal accountability of developers when their tools contribute to harm. If the requirement is removed and developers are no longer obligated to disclose known limitations, the information asymmetry between developers and clinicians widens, and the accountability gap grows.⏎⏎The National Academy of Medicine's 2019 report on AI in health care, "Artificial Intelligence in Health Care: The Hope, the Hype, the Promise, the Peril," identified algorithmic transparency as one of the foundational requirements for responsible AI deployment in clinical settings. The report specifically noted that transparency disclosures serve both a safety function and an accountability function, and that the two are not separable. You cannot hold a developer accountable for deploying a poorly validated tool if there is no record of what validation the developer performed and what limitations it identified.⏎⏎Under 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11) as currently written, that record exists because it is required. Under the proposed rule, it would not.⏎⏎⏎RESPONSE TO THE MARKET COMPETITION ARGUMENT⏎⏎Texas Medical Association Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 8⏎⏎The proposed rule suggests, at several points, that competitive market dynamics in the health IT sector provide adequate incentives for developers to produce high-quality, transparent AI tools without regulatory mandate. TMA has considerable experience with how health IT markets function in practice, and we find this argument difficult to accept.⏎⏎Health IT markets are characterized by significant switching costs, long-term contractual relationships, and substantial information asymmetries between sellers and buyers. A hospital system that has implemented Epic across its facilities and trained thousands of clinicians on that platform does not evaluate the quality of Epic's clinical algorithms in a free market sense. It is locked into a long-term relationship in which the transaction costs of switching to a competitor are enormous. The competitive discipline that market theory predicts requires that buyers be able to credibly threaten to switch if they are dissatisfied. In health IT, that threat is largely theoretical.⏎⏎Moreover, the buyers in health IT markets are institutions, not the clinicians who actually use the tools, and certainly not the patients whose care is affected by them. The information that a hospital's procurement team evaluates when purchasing an EHR system is not the same information a physician needs at the point of care to decide whether to trust a specific algorithm. Even if competitive market dynamics were producing better transparency behavior at the institutional procurement level, which is itself a generous assumption, this would not solve the point-of-care information problem that the DSI criterion is designed to address.⏎⏎There is also the question of what happens with smaller and newer market entrants. The major EHR vendors have institutional relationships, legal and compliance teams, and reputational stakes that create at least some incentive toward responsible disclosure practices, even absent regulation. The same cannot be said for the growing ecosystem of third-party AI developers who are building tools that integrate with EHR systems through FHIR APIs and other interoperability mechanisms. These vendors often have less institutional capital at stake and less experience with the regulatory and liability environment of clinical care. The DSI certification criterion applies to certified health IT regardless of whether the algorithm is developed by the EHR vendor or by a third-party integrator. Removing the requirement reduces the incentive for responsible disclosure across the entire ecosystem, including its most lightly regulated participants.⏎⏎⏎Texas Medical Association Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 9⏎⏎There is one more dimension of the market argument that TMA wants to address specifically, because it came up in preliminary discussions among our membership when we were preparing these comments. Some of our members who are more sympathetic to the deregulatory rationale argued that voluntary standards and frameworks, such as the NIST AI Risk Management Framework (NIST AI 100-1, January 2023), provide sufficient guidance for responsible AI development without regulatory mandate. We respect this view, and we think the NIST framework is a genuinely useful document. But voluntary frameworks do not create binding obligations, and they do not provide clinicians or patients with any enforceable right to information about the tools being used in their care.⏎⏎The history of voluntary industry standards in health IT is not encouraging on this point. Prior to the meaningful use program established under the Health Information Technology for Economic and Clinical Health (HITECH) Act of 2009, voluntary adoption of electronic health records had been slow and uneven for decades despite strong consensus among health policy experts that EHR adoption would improve care quality and coordination. The binding incentive and certification structure created by the meaningful use program dramatically accelerated adoption in a way that voluntary frameworks had not achieved. This does not mean that every regulatory mandate in health IT has been well-designed or well-implemented. It does mean that the general claim that voluntary standards are sufficient to achieve policy goals in this sector is contradicted by the sector's own history.⏎⏎⏎SPECIFIC CONCERNS ABOUT THE PROPOSED REMOVAL⏎⏎Texas Medical Association Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 10⏎⏎TMA wants to be specific about what the removal of the DSI criterion would mean in practice, because we think the proposed rule's discussion of this change is at a level of generality that may obscure its practical consequences.⏎⏎Under the current certification framework, a health IT developer seeking ONC certification for a product that includes predictive algorithms in its decision support functionality must document and make accessible the following information:⏎⏎a. The clinical or operational purpose for which the algorithm was designed, including the specific decision or prediction it is intended to inform.⏎⏎b. The patient population for which the algorithm was designed and validated, including relevant demographic, clinical, and geographic characteristics.⏎⏎c. The data sources used in training, including the institutional source of the data, the time period covered, and any known limitations of the training data.⏎⏎d. The algorithm's performance characteristics on the validation dataset, including sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value, and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve where applicable.⏎⏎e. Any known performance disparities across demographic subgroups, including race, ethnicity, sex, age, and insurance status where these have been assessed.⏎⏎f. Whether the algorithm has been externally validated on a dataset independent of the training data, and if so, the results of that external validation.⏎⏎These are not abstract requirements. Each of these disclosures corresponds to a specific category of information that a clinician needs to exercise responsible judgment about an algorithmic tool. Removing the requirement to provide them does not make the information unnecessary. It makes its provision optional.⏎⏎TMA is also concerned that the proposed rule does not address what happens to existing disclosures if the certification criterion is removed. Hospitals and health systems that have purchased certified EHR products have done so in reliance on the certification framework, including the DSI requirements. If the criterion is removed, will existing disclosures remain accessible? Will developers be permitted to withdraw model card documentation that was provided as a condition of certification? The proposed rule does not appear to address these transition questions, and TMA urges ASTP/ONC to provide clarity on this point regardless of what decision is made on the underlying question of whether to retain the criterion.⏎⏎⏎Texas Medical Association Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 11⏎⏎One thing I find genuinely puzzling about the proposed rule's treatment of this issue is the timing. The past three years have seen a substantial acceleration in the deployment of large language models and other generative AI tools in clinical settings. Several major EHR vendors have announced or deployed AI-generated clinical documentation tools, ambient listening products, and AI-assisted diagnostic support features. These deployments are happening at significant scale and at a pace that outstrips the ability of clinical institutions to independently evaluate them. In this environment, reducing transparency requirements for AI-based decision support tools seems to be moving in exactly the wrong direction relative to the risk environment.⏎⏎The proposed rule's preamble cites the need to reduce regulatory burden to encourage innovation. TMA supports innovation in health IT. Our membership includes physicians who use AI-assisted tools and who have seen real clinical benefit from them. The question is not whether AI should be used in clinical settings. It is whether the regulatory framework should require that the people using these tools have access to the information they need to use them responsibly. TMA's answer to that question is yes, and we believe the DSI certification criterion is a proportionate and well-targeted mechanism for ensuring that access.⏎⏎The ONC has cited 88 Federal Register 23746 (April 18, 2023) in its original DSI rulemaking as the basis for the current requirements. The transparency provisions adopted in that rule reflected extensive public comment and stakeholder engagement, including input from physician organizations, patient advocacy groups, health IT developers, and researchers. TMA participated in that process and supported the adoption of the model card requirements at that time. Our position has not changed, and the intervening period has, if anything, strengthened the case for retaining these requirements.⏎⏎⏎RESPONSE TO COMMENTS ANTICIPATED FROM HEALTH IT DEVELOPERS⏎⏎Texas Medical Association Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 12⏎⏎TMA anticipates that health IT developers will submit comments arguing that the DSI transparency requirements are technically burdensome, that the model card format is poorly suited to the diversity of AI architectures used in clinical decision support, and that the requirements create competitive disadvantages by forcing disclosure of proprietary model characteristics. We want to address these arguments briefly because they are likely to receive significant attention in this proceeding.⏎⏎On technical burden: the information required by the DSI criterion is information that any responsibly developed clinical algorithm should have. If a developer cannot document the training data, validation population, and known limitations of its algorithm, that is itself a signal that the algorithm may not be ready for clinical deployment. The documentation burden is not separable from the development quality obligation.⏎⏎On format: TMA acknowledges that the model card format developed in the machine learning research context may require adaptation for the clinical environment. If ASTP/ONC concludes that the current format requirements are too rigid, the appropriate response is to revise the format requirements, not to eliminate the disclosure obligation. A more flexible disclosure framework that preserves the substantive information requirements would address the format concern without creating the transparency gap that full removal would produce.⏎⏎On proprietary information: the DSI criterion does not require disclosure of proprietary source code, model architecture details, or other genuinely proprietary technical information. It requires disclosure of information about intended use, target population, training data characteristics, and validation results. These categories of information can be disclosed without revealing the technical implementation details that constitute a developer's competitive advantage. The proprietary information argument, in TMA's view, conflates different categories of information and overstates the competitive exposure that the disclosure requirements create.⏎⏎⏎BROADER CONTEXT: THE INFORMATION BLOCKING PROVISIONS⏎⏎Texas Medical Association Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 13⏎⏎TMA's primary comments are directed at the DSI certification criterion, but we want to note briefly that the proposed rule's amendments to the information blocking exceptions also raise concerns that are related to the same underlying dynamic.⏎⏎The information blocking provisions of the 21st Century Cures Act, codified at 45 CFR Part 171, were designed to prohibit practices that interfere with access, exchange, or use of electronic health information. The current exceptions to the information blocking prohibition are carefully scoped to permit interference with EHI access only where there is a specific, articulable justification. The proposed rule would expand several of these exceptions in ways that TMA believes will in practice permit a broader range of information withholding behavior than the statute was intended to allow.⏎⏎TMA is particularly concerned about proposed modifications to the Privacy Exception at 45 CFR 171.202 and the Infeasibility Exception at 45 CFR 171.204. The proposed expansions of these exceptions would give actors significantly more flexibility to decline to share electronic health information on grounds that are difficult for patients or other actors to challenge. Combined with the removal of the DSI transparency requirements, the effect would be to reduce both the information available to clinicians about the tools they are using and the information available to patients about their own health data.⏎⏎TMA urges ASTP/ONC to approach the information blocking exception amendments with caution and to consider whether the proposed expansions are consistent with the statutory purpose of ensuring that patients and their authorized representatives can access their electronic health information without unreasonable interference.⏎⏎⏎RECOMMENDATIONS⏎⏎Texas Medical Association Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 14⏎⏎In summary, TMA recommends that ASTP/ONC:⏎⏎1. Retain the Decision Support Interventions certification criterion at 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11) in its current form, including all model card and transparency disclosure requirements.⏎⏎2. If the agency concludes that specific format requirements within the DSI criterion are unnecessarily rigid, initiate a separate, targeted rulemaking to revise format requirements while preserving the substantive disclosure obligations.⏎⏎3. Provide clear guidance on the status of existing DSI disclosures in the event that any changes to the criterion are adopted, including whether developers may withdraw documentation provided as a condition of certification.⏎⏎4. Conduct a more rigorous regulatory impact analysis of the patient safety consequences of removing AI transparency requirements, including a systematic review of the peer-reviewed literature on algorithmic performance disparities in clinical settings.⏎⏎5. Engage with the FDA to clarify the respective scopes of ONC's certification authority and FDA's device oversight authority with respect to AI-based clinical decision support tools, with the goal of ensuring that the regulatory gap created by the 21st Century Cures Act's clinical decision support carve-out does not leave a class of widely deployed clinical algorithms entirely outside the transparency framework.⏎⏎6. Decline to adopt the proposed expansions of the Privacy and Infeasibility exceptions to the information blocking prohibition pending further analysis of their cumulative effect on patient access to electronic health information.⏎⏎TMA recognizes that ONC faces genuine competing pressures in this rulemaking. The burden reduction goals reflected in the proposed rule are legitimate policy objectives. The question is whether those objectives are being pursued in a manner that adequately accounts for the patient safety and clinical accountability consequences of reducing transparency requirements for AI-based decision support. In TMA's assessment, the proposed rule does not adequately account for those consequences with respect to the DSI criterion, and the appropriate course is to retain the current requirements.⏎⏎⏎Texas Medical Association Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 15⏎⏎TMA appreciates the opportunity to submit these comments. For questions regarding this submission, please contact the TMA Office of Health Policy at the address below. We are filing these comments with genuine concern about several specific provisions, and we want to be direct with the agency about where we think the analysis underlying certain proposals does not match the operational reality our physicians are living with right now.⏎⏎Before getting into the substance, there is something we want to say plainly. The framing of this rule, that reducing certification requirements and loosening information blocking exceptions is straightforwardly "pro-patient" and "pro-physician," is a framing our members do not universally share. Some of our members do find certain ONC certification criteria burdensome and would welcome relief. They have been here before. The interoperability problems that the 21st Century Cures Act (Pub. L. 114-255) was designed to address did not arise because the regulatory environment was too strict. The existing regulatory structure around this definition, built out through the ONC Interoperability and Patient Access Final Rule published at 85 Fed. Reg. 25642 (May 1, 2020), reflects years of stakeholder engagement and hard-won consensus about where the lines should be drawn. The proposed rule would revise several of the exceptions under 45 CFR Part 171 Subpart B in ways that our legal and policy staff believe could meaningfully expand the circumstances under which actors can decline to share information without facing information blocking liability. We are not saying the existing exceptions are perfectly calibrated. We are saying that the proposed revisions have not been accompanied by sufficient analysis of how they will interact with each other in practice, and we are concerned the agency is moving faster than the evidence warrants.⏎⏎Take the proposed changes to the Privacy Exception under 45 CFR 171.202. The current rule already gives providers substantial flexibility to decline sharing when they have a reasonable belief that doing so would violate applicable privacy law. The proposed modifications would, in our reading, expand the circumstances under which a provider can rely on this exception without documenting a specific legal basis for the concern. We understand the appeal of reducing documentation burden. But the Privacy Exception has historically been one of the more commonly invoked justifications when patients complain about records being withheld, and giving providers more room to invoke it without documentation makes it harder for patients to challenge those decisions and harder for ONC to enforce against bad actors. A 2023 report from the ONC Annual Meeting materials estimated that privacy-related justifications appeared in a substantial share of information blocking complaints received through the complaint portal. We would ask the agency to provide more granular data on this before finalizing any expansion of the Privacy Exception's scope.⏎⏎Texas Medical Association Comments | RIN 0955-AA07 | Page 3⏎⏎The experience our members report is not abstract. A physician in our Lubbock district told us earlier this year that a patient came to her having spent nearly four months trying to get cardiology records transferred from a hospital system in another part of Texas. The hospital system was not technically in violation of any rule, because they were invoking what appeared to be a privacy-related concern about third-party information embedded in the records. That concern, whatever its original merit, had become a bureaucratic wall. The patient eventually got partial records. Not complete ones. There is a version of the proposed rule's Privacy Exception changes that makes that kind of situation easier to sustain indefinitely, and we do not think that is what the agency intends, but we think it is what the rule could produce.⏎⏎We are also concerned about the proposed changes to certification criteria under 45 CFR Part 170, specifically the proposal to remove or retire certain criteria that health IT developers are currently required to meet to maintain certification in the ONC Health IT Certification Program. The agency's rationale, as stated in the proposed rule, is that some criteria have become outdated or are duplicative of functionality the market now delivers without regulatory compulsion. That argument has some merit for a narrow set of criteria. The USCDI (United States Core Data for Interoperability) framework has matured, and there are genuinely some legacy certification requirements that no longer serve a clear purpose. However, the proposed rule bundles together criteria that fall into this category with others that are still doing real work, and the agency has not, in our view, adequately distinguished between them.⏎⏎Texas Medical Association Comments | RIN 0955-AA07 | Page 4⏎⏎Specifically, TMA is concerned about the retirement of certification criteria related to clinical quality measurement reporting, which currently appear at 45 CFR 170.315(c)(1) through (c)(4). These criteria ensure that certified EHR technology can support the calculation and reporting of electronic clinical quality measures (eCQMs) in a standardized way. Our members who participate in Medicare quality programs, including the Merit-based Incentive Payment System (MIPS) under 42 CFR Part 414 Subpart O, depend on certified EHR functionality to generate the data submissions that determine a significant portion of their Medicare payment adjustments. If developers are no longer required to maintain this functionality as a condition of certification, the market may not reliably provide it, particularly for smaller EHR vendors serving independent practices. The agency cites market maturity as a reason to step back, but the market for EHR systems serving small and independent physician practices in Texas is not the same market as the one serving large integrated health systems. It never has been.⏎⏎Our members in solo and small-group practice are already stretched thin managing the administrative requirements associated with MIPS reporting. In 2024, CMS data showed that approximately 35 percent of MIPS-eligible clinicians in Texas were in practices of five or fewer physicians. Those practices do not have dedicated health IT staff. They are not in a position to evaluate whether a newly decertified EHR product still supports eCQM reporting through some non-certified pathway. They rely on the certification signal to make purchasing and contracting decisions. Removing that signal for quality measurement criteria, without a clear transition pathway or market analysis demonstrating that adequate substitutes exist, is the kind of policy change that sounds reasonable at the level of principle and creates genuine operational disruption at the level of practice.⏎⏎Texas Medical Association Comments | RIN 0955-AA07 | Page 5⏎⏎There is also a broader point worth making here about the relationship between the ONC certification program and patient safety. Certification criteria are not purely administrative. Several of them encode clinical safety requirements, including requirements related to drug-drug interaction checking, allergy documentation, and clinical decision support functionality under 45 CFR 170.315(a)(9) and related provisions. The proposed rule does not appear to be targeting these safety-related criteria for retirement, and we want to acknowledge that. But the overall posture of the rule, which is to treat certification criteria as presumptively burdensome unless proven otherwise, creates a governance environment in which future deregulatory proposals in this space will face a lower bar. We are commenting on what the rule says today, but we are also commenting on the direction it signals for tomorrow.⏎⏎On the question of Healthcare.gov and the federal health IT infrastructure more broadly, we recognize this is somewhat tangential to the specific regulatory text under comment, but it is genuinely difficult to read a proposed rule premised on the idea that market forces and reduced regulation will produce better health IT outcomes without noting that the government's own health IT properties are not exactly a showcase of what deregulation produces. Healthcare.gov processes millions of enrollment transactions annually, and the user experience for many of those transactions remains poor by any reasonable benchmark. The connection to this rule is not direct, but the underlying assumption, that less regulatory structure in health IT produces better outcomes for end users, deserves scrutiny across the board and not just when the end user is a developer seeking certification flexibility.⏎⏎Texas Medical Association Comments | RIN 0955-AA07 | Page 6⏎⏎TMA's specific recommendations are as follows:⏎⏎1. The agency should conduct a granular, criteria-by-criteria analysis before finalizing any retirement of certification requirements under 45 CFR Part 170, with particular attention to criteria that support quality measurement reporting for small and independent practices. A blanket finding of market maturity is not sufficient.⏎⏎2. The proposed revisions to the Privacy Exception under 45 CFR 171.202 should be accompanied by a requirement that providers invoking the exception document the specific legal basis for the privacy concern in the patient's record. Reducing documentation burden is a legitimate goal; eliminating accountability is not.⏎⏎3. This data exists. It should inform the rulemaking. The agency's failure to include it in the proposed rule's regulatory impact analysis is a gap that patient advocacy organizations have already noted, and we agree with their concern.⏎⏎4. She should not need to know the right legal language to invoke. The infrastructure should work. CMS-2025-0050-110057♔CMS-2025-0050♔Andrew Hill♔SAFI Clinical Informatics Group LLC♔♔♔♔Removing or weakening the Decision Support Interventions (DSI) transparency and disclosure requirements under 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11) would eliminate the only meaningful regulatory mechanism ensuring that clinicians have access to critical informati...♔SAFI Clinical Informatics Group LLC⏎Comments on ASTP/ONC Proposed Deregulatory Actions⏎Docket: ONC-2025-DEREGULATORY [RIN 0955-AA06]⏎Submitted by: Andrew Hill, Director of Government Relations⏎⏎SAFI Clinical Informatics Group LLC | ONC Deregulatory Comments | Page 1⏎⏎---⏎⏎SAFI Clinical Informatics Group LLC appreciates the opportunity to comment on the proposed deregulatory actions under ASTP/ONC's rulemaking on Health Data, Technology, and Interoperability. We are a mid-sized health IT developer headquartered in Florida, working primarily with hospital network clients in the Southeast, and we have spent the better part of the last four years building clinical decision support tools that sit at the intersection of AI-assisted workflows and EHR integration. I want to be direct about something at the outset: we are not reflexively opposed to deregulation. We have lived through the compliance overhead firsthand. Last spring, three consecutive weekends in a conference room with our lead developers, reverse-engineering certification documentation to figure out whether a workflow enhancement we had been promising clients for eight months triggered a new certification pathway. The answer was yes. That added six months and roughly $340,000 in unanticipated testing costs to a product our hospital network partners in Jacksonville and Tampa had already budgeted around. So when ONC says it wants to reduce burden on developers like us, I am listening.⏎⏎But I want to focus these comments specifically on one proposal that I think goes in the wrong direction, and where we believe the agency should hold firm rather than retreat: the Decision Support Interventions (DSI) certification criterion at 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11), specifically the transparency and disclosure requirements that include AI model cards, intended use documentation, target population specifications, known risk disclosures, training data characteristics, and external validation summaries.⏎⏎SAFI Clinical Informatics Group LLC | ONC Deregulatory Comments | Page 2⏎⏎---⏎⏎WHY THE DSI TRANSPARENCY REQUIREMENTS SHOULD BE RETAINED⏎⏎The short version is this: the DSI criterion as currently structured is one of the few places in the certification framework where the rules actually caught up with what the technology is doing in clinical environments. Removing or substantially weakening these requirements would create a gap that the market will not fill on its own, and that gap will eventually show up as patient harm.⏎⏎Let me explain what I mean by that, because I think the framing of "burden reduction" obscures what is actually at stake here.⏎⏎When a clinician at a Jacksonville hospital receives an alert or a recommendation from a decision support tool embedded in their EHR, they are often making a downstream care decision within seconds. The research on alert fatigue is well-documented. A 2019 study published in the Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association (Ancker et al., JAMIA 2019;26(7):757-764) found that clinicians override between 54% and 96% of drug-drug interaction alerts depending on the system and context. The point is not that alerts are bad. The point is that the quality of clinician decision-making in that override moment depends substantially on whether they have any grounded understanding of where the recommendation came from, what population it was trained on, and what its known failure modes are. Without model card disclosures required under 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11), that contextual information is simply absent from the workflow. The clinician is flying blind relative to the tool they are either accepting or overriding.⏎⏎SAFI Clinical Informatics Group LLC | ONC Deregulatory Comments | Page 3⏎⏎---⏎⏎I keep coming back to a specific scenario we encountered in late 2023 during a deployment at a regional hospital system. One of our DSI tools had been trained primarily on adult patient data from academic medical centers in the Northeast. When the tool was deployed in a community hospital setting in central Florida serving a substantially different demographic and comorbidity profile, the alert thresholds were miscalibrated in ways that were not immediately obvious to the clinical staff. We caught it during post-deployment monitoring, but only because our team had documentation requirements that forced us to articulate the training data characteristics and target population in the first place. That documentation process, which maps directly to what 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11) requires, is what created the paper trail that let us identify the problem. I am genuinely not sure we would have caught it as quickly without that discipline built into our certification pathway.⏎⏎The FDA has recognized similar concerns in its guidance on Software as a Medical Device (SaMD), specifically in the 2019 proposed regulatory framework and the 2021 AI/ML action plan, both of which identify transparency about training data and performance characteristics as baseline requirements for safe deployment. ONC's DSI criterion is consistent with that framework. Removing it creates a regulatory asymmetry where AI tools embedded in certified EHRs are subject to less transparency scrutiny than comparable standalone SaMD tools, which makes no sense from a patient safety standpoint.⏎⏎SAFI Clinical Informatics Group LLC | ONC Deregulatory Comments | Page 4⏎⏎---⏎⏎THE INCUMBENCY PROBLEM⏎⏎There is something else worth saying here, and I realize it might sound self-interested, but I think it is accurate. The DSI transparency requirements do create compliance costs. We have felt them. But those costs are also somewhat more proportionate for mid-sized developers like SAFI than they appear at first glance, because the requirements create a level of accountability that applies to everyone, including the large EHR vendors whose AI modules are already embedded in hospital workflows across the country without much scrutiny.⏎⏎If ONC removes or significantly weakens the DSI model card and disclosure requirements, the primary beneficiaries will not be the small innovators that the deregulatory framing is ostensibly meant to help. The primary beneficiaries will be established vendors who can continue deploying AI-assisted tools with minimal transparency obligations, and who have the market position to do so without facing meaningful competitive pressure to disclose. Smaller developers who are trying to differentiate on quality and accountability actually lose something when disclosure requirements disappear, because those requirements are one of the few mechanisms that force a level playing field on transparency.⏎⏎This concern is not hypothetical. A 2022 analysis by Jiang et al. in npj Digital Medicine found that AI tools embedded in commercial EHR platforms routinely lacked the documentation that would allow clinicians or administrators to assess algorithmic bias or population generalizability (Jiang et al., npj Digital Medicine 2022;5:44). The DSI criterion was designed in part to address exactly this problem. Repealing it does not make the problem go away; it just removes the mechanism for surfacing it.⏎⏎SAFI Clinical Informatics Group LLC | ONC Deregulatory Comments | Page 5⏎⏎---⏎⏎SPECIFIC ELEMENTS OF THE DSI CRITERION THAT SHOULD BE RETAINED⏎⏎We want to be specific about which components of 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11) we believe are non-negotiable from a patient safety and accountability standpoint:⏎⏎1. Intended use and clinical context disclosure. A developer must be required to document and make available to certified health IT users a clear statement of the specific clinical context for which the DSI tool was designed and validated. This is not optional information. It is the baseline for informed deployment decisions.⏎⏎2. Target population specifications. Training data demographics, including age ranges, geographic distribution, race and ethnicity representation, and primary diagnosis categories, must be disclosed. The ONC's own 2023 report on algorithmic bias in health IT (ONC Data Brief, May 2023) identified population mismatch as one of the leading sources of AI-related adverse outcomes in clinical settings. The target population field in the model card is the primary mechanism for surfacing this risk.⏎⏎3. Known risks and limitations. This includes documented failure modes, contraindicated populations, and performance degradation scenarios. The parallel here is to the package insert requirement for pharmaceutical products. We would not accept a drug on formulary without a known risk profile. There is no principled argument for treating embedded AI tools differently.⏎⏎4. External validation data. At minimum, a developer should be required to disclose whether the tool has been externally validated in a population other than the original training set, and if so, by whom and with what results. Internal validation alone is insufficient for tools that will be deployed across heterogeneous clinical environments. See also the discussion in Obermeyer et al., Science 2019;366(6464):447-453, which documented how a widely-deployed commercial algorithm exhibited substantial racial bias that would likely have been caught earlier with robust external validation requirements.⏎⏎5. Training data source characteristics. Not the raw data itself, obviously, but the institutional provenance, the time period of the training data, and any known gaps or overrepresentation in the dataset.⏎⏎SAFI Clinical Informatics Group LLC | ONC Deregulatory Comments | Page 6⏎⏎---⏎⏎I want to acknowledge that there are legitimate arguments on the other side of this. Some developers have raised concerns that model card requirements are inconsistently interpreted by testing laboratories, and that the documentation burden falls unevenly depending on which Authorized Testing and Certification Body (ONC-ATCB) is doing the review. We have experienced this ourselves. In one certification cycle, our external validation summary was flagged as insufficient by one testing body, and a nearly identical document passed without comment at another body. That inconsistency is a real problem, and ONC should address it. But the answer to inconsistent enforcement is better standardization of testing criteria, not removal of the underlying requirement. 42 CFR Part 170 Subpart D gives ONC the authority to issue more detailed testing criteria and interpretive guidance, and that is the right lever to pull here, not wholesale removal of the disclosure requirement.⏎⏎There is also the question of whether the current model card format is optimally designed. Frankly, I think there is room to improve it. The current required fields under 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11) were written before some of the more recent thinking on algorithmic transparency had matured. The NIST AI Risk Management Framework (NIST AI RMF 1.0, January 2023) offers a more comprehensive and better-structured approach to documenting AI model characteristics, and ONC should consider aligning the DSI disclosure requirements with the NIST framework rather than abandoning them. The EU AI Act's transparency requirements for high-risk AI systems (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, Article 13) are also worth examining as a reference point, not because we are bound by EU law, but because the underlying logic of those requirements reflects a serious and well-developed approach to the same problem ONC is trying to solve.⏎⏎SAFI Clinical Informatics Group LLC | ONC Deregulatory Comments | Page 7⏎⏎---⏎⏎ACCOUNTABILITY IN THE ABSENCE OF DISCLOSURE REQUIREMENTS⏎⏎One question worth asking directly: if the DSI transparency requirements are removed, what accountability mechanisms remain for AI-assisted clinical decision support tools embedded in certified EHRs?⏎⏎The information blocking provisions under 45 CFR 171 address a different problem and do not speak to algorithmic transparency. The conditions of certification under 45 CFR 170.402 require developers to cooperate with ONC oversight but do not mandate affirmative disclosure of model characteristics to end users. The general certification criterion at 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11) is currently the primary place in the regulatory architecture where a developer is affirmatively required to document and disclose the characteristics of a DSI tool to the clinicians and administrators who will use it.⏎⏎Remove that requirement, and what you are left with is a regime where AI tools are embedded in certified EHRs, influencing clinical decisions for millions of patients, with no mandatory transparency obligations at all. That is a significant policy choice, and I do not think it has been fully reckoned with in the framing of this proposed rulemaking. The preamble discusses burden reduction in terms of developer compliance costs, which is legitimate, but it does not adequately address what is lost from the patient safety and clinical accountability side of the ledger when these disclosure requirements are relaxed.⏎⏎I would also flag that CMS and ONC have both invested substantially in AI governance frameworks over the last two years. The HHS AI Strategic Plan (2024) explicitly calls for transparency and accountability as baseline principles for AI use in healthcare settings. Removing the DSI disclosure requirements would be in direct tension with commitments the Department has made in that broader strategic context.⏎⏎SAFI Clinical Informatics Group LLC | ONC Deregulatory Comments | Page 8⏎⏎---⏎⏎PRACTICAL RECOMMENDATIONS⏎⏎Rather than removal, SAFI recommends the following modifications to the DSI certification criterion that would address legitimate compliance burden concerns while preserving the accountability architecture:⏎⏎a. Standardize the testing criteria for DSI disclosure documentation across all ONC-ATCBs. The current inter-rater variability in how testing bodies evaluate model cards is a genuine burden amplifier. A single, detailed testing protocol issued by ONC, with worked examples for different categories of DSI tools, would reduce the uncertainty cost that developers currently absorb.⏎⏎b. Establish a tiered disclosure framework based on clinical risk level. A low-acuity scheduling optimization tool does not need the same depth of external validation documentation as an AI-assisted sepsis prediction tool. ONC should define risk tiers for DSI tools and calibrate the disclosure requirements accordingly, rather than applying a single standard uniformly. The FDA's tiered approach to SaMD regulation under 21 CFR Part 820 and the associated De Novo classification process offers a workable model.⏎⏎c. Allow machine-readable model card formats to satisfy the disclosure requirement. Currently, many developers produce documentation in formats that are difficult to integrate into clinical workflows. If ONC required or encouraged structured, machine-readable model card formats aligned with emerging standards like the HL7 FHIR ArtifactAssessment resource, the information would be more accessible to clinicians at the point of care and the documentation burden on developers could potentially be reduced through tooling and automation.⏎⏎d. Create a public registry of DSI model cards for certified health IT. This would reduce duplicative documentation burden for developers deploying the same tool across multiple certified systems, and would give clinicians, researchers, and the public a single place to access transparency information. The FDA's 510(k) premarket notification database offers a rough analogy.⏎⏎SAFI Clinical Informatics Group LLC | ONC Deregulatory Comments | Page 9⏎⏎---⏎⏎We recognize that ONC is operating under real pressure to reduce regulatory overhead, and we are not suggesting that every element of the current certification framework is well-designed or proportionate. Our experience with the certification process has been genuinely mixed. There are parts of the current ONC Health IT Certification Program that impose costs without producing commensurate patient safety or interoperability benefits, and we have supported reform efforts in those areas.⏎⏎But the DSI transparency requirements are not in that category. They address a real and growing risk: the deployment of AI-assisted clinical decision support tools whose characteristics, limitations, and failure modes are unknown to the clinicians relying on them. The research literature on this point is consistent. The FDA's own regulatory trajectory on AI/ML-based SaMD points in the same direction. And our own operational experience, including the 2023 deployment scenario I described earlier, suggests that the documentation discipline required by 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11) has practical value that goes beyond checkbox compliance.⏎⏎The inconsistency in how testing bodies apply these requirements is a legitimate problem that ONC should fix. The format of the model card requirements could be modernized and better aligned with NIST AI RMF 1.0. The tiering of requirements by clinical risk level is worth exploring. All of that is fair ground for reform. What is not justified, in our view, is treating the transparency obligation itself as an expendable compliance artifact.⏎⏎SAFI Clinical Informatics Group LLC | ONC Deregulatory Comments | Page 10⏎⏎---⏎⏎One more thing I want to flag, and I am not sure this fits neatly into the regulatory framework discussion, but it keeps coming up in our conversations with clinical informatics directors at our hospital network clients. They are not asking for less transparency about the AI tools in their EHRs. They are asking for more. The compliance conversation we are having in this docket is, in a real sense, running in the opposite direction from the conversations happening on the clinical side. The Chief Medical Information Officer at one of our Tampa network partners told me earlier this year that her governance committee had started requiring model card documentation from all AI vendors as a condition of deployment, independent of what certification required, because they had been burned by a tool that performed significantly worse in their patient population than the vendor's marketing materials had suggested. She was not aware that ONC was considering relaxing the certification requirements. I think her reaction would be something close to disbelief.⏎⏎There is also a longer-term credibility issue for the certification program itself. The ONC Health IT Certification Program derives much of its value from the assurance it provides to purchasers and clinicians that certified products meet defined standards. If the program is seen as retreating from accountability requirements at precisely the moment when AI tools are becoming more prevalent and more consequential in clinical settings, that will affect how much weight the certification mark carries. That may not be quantifiable in a cost-benefit analysis, but it is real.⏎⏎We are available to discuss any of these points with ONC staff and would welcome the opportunity to participate in any stakeholder engagement process the agency convenes as it finalizes this rulemaking. Last spring, our team spent eleven months navigating a certification pathway for a clinical decision support module. Total cost came to just under $340,000. By the time we cleared every checkpoint, two competing platforms had already taken the market segment we'd identified, operating under legacy exemptions we did not qualify for. I watched our lead engineer hand in her resignation in October. She had spent six years building patient safety tools and she was done. I am not telling that story to generate sympathy. I am telling it because we have every reason to want certification streamlined, and we are still standing here saying: please keep the model card requirement in 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11).⏎⏎---⏎⏎WHY THE MODEL CARD REQUIREMENT IS DIFFERENT FROM THE REST⏎⏎There is a real difference between certification requirements that are compliance theater and requirements that are doing actual safety work. Most of what exhausted our team fell into the first category. Redundant interoperability testing against criteria already satisfied by earlier modules. Documentation requirements that duplicated information already submitted in a prior certification cycle. Checkpoints that seemed designed for a product architecture that hadn't been common in the industry since roughly 2017.⏎⏎The DSI model card requirement is not that. Under 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11) as currently structured, developers of AI-driven clinical decision support must disclose:⏎⏎1. Intended use and clinical scope of the algorithm⏎2. Target patient population, including demographic characteristics⏎3. Known risks, limitations, and failure modes⏎4. Training data characteristics and sources⏎5. External validation status and performance metrics⏎⏎That list is not a paperwork exercise. Each item corresponds to a real clinical risk that has materialized in published literature. Obermeyer et al. (2019, Science, Vol. 366) documented how a widely deployed commercial algorithm systematically underestimated illness severity in Black patients because training data used healthcare costs as a proxy for health needs. The algorithm's developers had not disclosed the proxy variable. Clinicians had no way to know. Under the current DSI criterion, that disclosure would have been required. Under a regime where model cards are optional or eliminated, it would not be.⏎⏎iPill Inc. Comments | ONC-2025-Deregulatory | Page 2⏎⏎The FDA's 2021 action plan for AI/ML-based software as a medical device (SaMD) made substantially similar arguments about the need for algorithmic transparency as a precondition for clinician oversight (FDA, Artificial Intelligence/Machine Learning Action Plan, January 2021). The ONC's own 2023 Health Data, Technology, and Interoperability final rule (88 FR 23746) recognized that DSI transparency was a gap that needed filling. Removing that requirement now, two years after it was finalized and before it has been broadly implemented, seems like the wrong sequence. We haven't even seen what full implementation looks like yet.⏎⏎---⏎⏎THE INFORMED CONSENT ARGUMENT⏎⏎There is something that keeps coming back to me when I read the agency's burden-reduction rationale for this proposal. The argument is essentially that model card requirements impose costs on developers that slow down deployment. That is true. But the implicit assumption is that faster deployment is an unqualified good, and in the DSI context I think that assumption deserves more scrutiny than the proposed rule gives it.⏎⏎Clinicians using AI-assisted decision support are making treatment decisions. They are doing that in a context where, per a 2022 JAMIA study (Sendak et al., J Am Med Inform Assoc, 29:1, pp. 15-23), a substantial portion of physicians report they do not know how the clinical algorithms they rely on were trained or validated. That is not a preferences gap. That is an informed decision-making gap. The model card requirement is one of the only regulatory mechanisms currently in place that requires someone to actually write down what the algorithm does and hand that information to the clinical environment where it will be used.⏎⏎If ONC removes this requirement, the agency should explain what replaces it. The proposed rule does not do that. It references general principles of market transparency and voluntary disclosure, but voluntary disclosure in health IT has a well-documented track record of being incomplete (see Celi et al., PLOS Medicine, 2022, on algorithmic auditing gaps in EHR-integrated tools). I am genuinely not sure how the agency reconciles its stated commitment to patient safety with removing the one certification criterion that specifically addresses whether clinical AI tools disclose their own limitations.⏎⏎---⏎⏎SPECIFIC RECOMMENDATION⏎⏎ONC should retain the DSI certification criterion at 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11) in its current form, including the model card disclosure requirements for:⏎⏎o intended use and clinical scope⏎o target population characteristics⏎o known risks and failure modes⏎o training data provenance⏎o external validation status⏎⏎If the agency's concern is that the criterion as written creates disproportionate burden for small developers, we would support a tiered approach based on risk level and deployment scope. A medication-dosing algorithm integrated into a clinical workflow for a population of elderly patients with polypharmacy is not the same risk profile as a scheduling optimization tool. The certification burden could be calibrated accordingly. But the floor of disclosure should not be zero.⏎⏎iPill Inc. Comments | ONC-2025-Deregulatory | Page 3⏎⏎We would also ask ONC to consider whether the burden data underlying the proposed rule's cost-benefit analysis actually captures the costs of removing this requirement. The regulatory impact analysis cites developer compliance costs (see 90 FR [docket page]), but we are not aware that it quantifies the downstream clinical costs of opaque algorithm deployment. The literature on that is growing. Wiens et al. (2019, Nature Medicine, Vol. 15) argued that without transparency requirements, health systems lack the information needed to audit deployed algorithms for bias or drift. That is a real cost. It just doesn't show up in the compliance budget line.⏎⏎---⏎⏎One more thing and then I'll stop. The agency's deregulatory framing treats certification requirements as primarily a cost to industry. That framing isn't wrong exactly, but it's incomplete. For us, the certification system is also the thing that tells our hospital partners that our software has been reviewed against a public standard. When we tell a health system that our medication-management module is ONC-certified, that means something to their clinical informatics team. It means something to their liability counsel. If we gut the content of certification to reduce burden, we may also be gutting the signal value that makes certification worth having in the first place. I'm not sure ONC has fully thought through what happens to market credibility of the certification program if the requirements inside it keep shrinking.⏎⏎The model card requirement should stay. We would welcome further dialogue with ONC on implementation details, particularly around the question of how external validation requirements apply to algorithms that are updated through continuous learning mechanisms, which is a genuinely hard problem that the current criterion language at 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11)(iv) does not fully resolve.⏎⏎sandra.rivera@ipillinc.com⏎iPill Inc., 1425 River Park Drive, Suite 300, Sacramento CA 95815♔♔2025-12-14T00:00:00Z♔2025-12-14T00:00:00Z♔2025-12-12T00:00:00Z♔2026-02-10T00:00:00Z♔4♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Retain the current Decision Support Interventions (DSI) certification criterion requiring AI model cards and transparency disclosures (intended use, target population, known risks, training data characteristics, external validation) to ensure patient safety, informed clinical decision-making, and accountability in AI-assisted healthcare.♔The 'black box' problem is a documented barrier to AI adoption in healthcare; model cards directly address clinician and organizational concerns about trustworthiness and are a proven mechanism to build confidence.♔industry♔high♔angry♔California♔healthcare administrator♔58♔Last spring, our development team at iPill spent eleven months — and just under $340,000 — navigating a certification process for a medication-management module that our clinical partners had been begging us to deploy for two years prior.
