CMS-2025-0050-110064♔CMS-2025-0050♔Daniel Lee♔Policy Center for Maternal Mental Health♔♔♔♔The proposed removal or weakening of the Decision Support Interventions certification criterion (45 CFR 170.315(b)(11)) would eliminate critical transparency requirements for clinical AI tools, putting vulnerable patient populations—particularly A...♔Policy Center for Maternal Mental Health⏎1601 St. Francis Street, Suite 220⏎Rapid City, SD 57701⏎policycentermhsd.org | info@policycentermhsd.org⏎⏎Docket No. ONC-2025-0001⏎Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology⏎U.S. Department of Health and Human Services⏎200 Independence Avenue, SW⏎Washington, DC 20201⏎⏎Re: ASTP/ONC Deregulatory Actions To Unleash Prosperity: Health Data, Technology, and Interoperability -- Comments of the Policy Center for Maternal Mental Health⏎⏎Dear Acting National Coordinator:⏎⏎The Policy Center for Maternal Mental Health is a South Dakota-based advocacy organization focused on closing the care gaps that place new mothers at risk of adverse outcomes from perinatal mood and anxiety disorders. Our work brings us into regular contact with community health workers, obstetric providers, inpatient psychiatric facilities, and the care coordinators who are supposed to hold all of those pieces together. We are not a health IT vendor. We are not a certification body. What we are is an organization that watches, on a fairly regular basis, what happens when health information systems fail the women they are supposed to serve.⏎⏎I want to be direct about why we are submitting these comments. The proposed rule includes provisions that would remove or substantially weaken the certification criterion for Decision Support Interventions, the requirement that health IT developers disclose what their AI tools are actually doing inside clinical workflows. That specific change concerns us deeply, and I want to explain why from a ground-level perspective before turning to the regulatory substance.⏎⏎Policy Center for Maternal Mental Health Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 2⏎⏎Last spring, one of our staff members accompanied a mother in Rapid City who had just been discharged after a postpartum psychosis episode. Her obstetrician's office had no record of the inpatient psychiatric stay. The two systems, the hospital's EHR and the OB's ambulatory platform, simply did not communicate. Her care team was working without any knowledge of how close she had come. That gap was partly a data exchange failure. But we have since learned that the OB practice was also using a clinical decision support tool to flag patients for postpartum depression screening, and nobody at that practice could tell us what data that tool was trained on, what populations it was validated against, or whether it had ever been tested on American Indian patients, who make up a substantial portion of our patient population in western South Dakota. We asked. Nobody knew. There was no documentation available. Under the current DSI certification criterion at 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11), that kind of disclosure is supposed to be a condition of certification. The proposed rule would weaken that requirement, and that is what brings us here.⏎⏎⏎REGARDING THE PROPOSED REMOVAL OR REVISION OF DSI TRANSPARENCY REQUIREMENTS⏎⏎The current certification criterion at 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11) requires that certified health IT products using AI or algorithmically-driven decision support disclose the following to clinical users:⏎⏎1. The intended use of the intervention, including the clinical purpose and the population for which it was designed.⏎2. The characteristics of the training data, including demographic composition and the time period from which data was drawn.⏎3. Known limitations and risks associated with the tool's outputs, including performance disparities across demographic subgroups.⏎4. External validation information, if any exists, and the conditions under which validation was conducted.⏎5. A description of the target population for which the tool is appropriate, and populations for which it has not been validated.⏎⏎These are not burdensome disclosures. They are the minimum a clinician needs to make an informed judgment about whether to act on an algorithmic recommendation. The argument in the proposed rule is that these requirements add compliance costs and may discourage innovation by health IT developers. I understand that argument. I genuinely do. But the cost of ignorance in clinical AI is not theoretical. There is a substantial and growing body of evidence that clinical decision support tools can perform differently across racial, ethnic, and socioeconomic subgroups in ways that are not obvious to the clinician at the point of care. Obermeyer et al. (2019, Science, Vol. 366, No. 6464) documented how a widely deployed commercial algorithm systematically underestimated the health needs of Black patients relative to white patients with the same measured disease burden. The algorithm's developers did not disclose the disparity. Clinicians had no way to know. The DSI criterion exists, in part, because of findings like that one.⏎⏎Policy Center for Maternal Mental Health Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 3⏎⏎In the maternal mental health context, the stakes of this kind of undisclosed bias are particularly high. Postpartum depression and postpartum psychosis screening tools are being integrated into EHR workflows at an accelerating pace. Many of these tools were trained on datasets that overrepresent certain patient populations. The Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, which is the most commonly embedded screening instrument, has been studied in diverse populations, and the research literature (see, e.g., Gibson et al., 2009, Acta Psychiatrica Scandinavica) has documented that score interpretation norms may not transfer cleanly across cultural contexts. When a clinical decision support tool applies a cutoff score or a risk stratification algorithm to a patient in a tribal health clinic in Kyle, South Dakota, and that algorithm was trained exclusively on data from large academic medical centers in the Northeast, the clinician should know that. Under the current DSI certification rules, there is at least a regulatory expectation that they would. Under the proposed changes, that expectation is weakened.⏎⏎The proposed rule cites 88 Fed. Reg. 23746 and related ONC materials in support of a streamlined certification approach. We are not opposed to streamlining where streamlining does not sacrifice accountability. But the DSI transparency requirements are not paperwork for its own sake. They are the mechanism by which clinicians can exercise independent judgment about the tools that are increasingly shaping their decisions. The 21st Century Cures Act, at Section 3024, directed ONC to develop certification criteria that support transparency in clinical decision support. The DSI criterion is the operational expression of that directive. Removing or substantially weakening it is inconsistent with that statutory mandate, and we think ONC should say so clearly in its response to these comments rather than leaving the question open.⏎⏎I want to be clear that our organization is not categorically opposed to reducing certification burdens. There are provisions in the proposed rule that appear sensible. The adjustments to certain interoperability testing requirements, for instance, may reduce duplicative compliance work without meaningful clinical impact. We do not have a position on every provision in this rulemaking. What we do have a firm position on is the DSI criterion, because in the maternal mental health space, it is one of the few regulatory levers that creates any accountability at all for how AI tools perform in clinical settings.⏎⏎Policy Center for Maternal Mental Health Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 4⏎⏎There is also a concern I want to raise about the information blocking provisions, specifically the proposed changes to the exceptions framework under 45 CFR 171. The proposed rule would give health IT developers and providers somewhat more flexibility in how they invoke exceptions to the information blocking rules. In theory, this is about reducing administrative friction. In practice, what we have seen in South Dakota is that information blocking exceptions are sometimes used by health systems to avoid sharing behavioral health records with other providers in ways that are technically permissible but operationally harmful. The mother in Rapid City whose story I mentioned at the outset -- her inpatient psychiatric records were not shared with her OB's office partly because of system incompatibility, but also because the hospital had made a determination, under a privacy exception, that those records did not need to flow automatically. Whether that determination was correct under the current rules is a question our organization is not positioned to answer definitively. But loosening the exceptions framework without simultaneously strengthening the affirmative sharing obligations creates a predictable outcome: more gaps, not fewer.⏎⏎We recognize that ONC is trying to balance provider flexibility against patient access rights. That is a genuinely difficult balance to strike. But the proposed rule, as written, appears to move the dial in the direction of flexibility without a corresponding strengthening of baseline transparency and accountability requirements. Removing the DSI model card requirements while simultaneously loosening information blocking exceptions is a combination that, in our view, makes the clinical environment less safe for patients who are already poorly served by the existing system.⏎⏎Policy Center for Maternal Mental Health Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 5⏎⏎SPECIFIC RECOMMENDATIONS⏎⏎Our organization respectfully urges ONC to take the following steps in finalizing this rule:⏎⏎1. Retain the DSI certification criterion at 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11) in its current substantive form. If ONC believes that certain disclosure formats are unnecessarily burdensome, the agency should narrow the formatting requirements rather than eliminate the substantive disclosure obligations. The content requirements, training data characteristics, target population specifications, known limitations, and external validation information, should remain mandatory conditions of certification.⏎⏎2. Require that DSI disclosures specifically address subgroup performance. The current criterion does not explicitly require developers to disclose how a tool performs across racial, ethnic, or socioeconomic subgroups. ONC should strengthen, not weaken, this dimension of the disclosure requirement. This is consistent with the recommendations in the National Academy of Medicine's 2022 report on AI in health care (Artificial Intelligence in Health Care: The Hope, the Hype, the Promise, the Peril, NAM Special Publication) and with the Biden Administration's Blueprint for an AI Bill of Rights, which, whatever one thinks of its broader policy implications, correctly identified transparency and explainability as baseline requirements for AI systems in high-stakes settings.⏎⏎3. Do not finalize the proposed changes to the information blocking exceptions framework without a parallel rulemaking that strengthens affirmative sharing obligations for behavioral health records. The two issues are connected. If exceptions become easier to invoke, the compensating mechanism has to be a stronger affirmative duty to share, not a weaker one.⏎⏎4. Conduct, and publish the results of, a disparate impact analysis before finalizing any changes to the DSI criterion. ONC has access to certification data across a large number of health IT products. The agency should be able to assess whether removing transparency requirements would differentially harm patient populations that are already underserved by clinical AI tools. We are not aware that such an analysis has been conducted, and the proposed rule does not reference one.⏎⏎Policy Center for Maternal Mental Health Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 6⏎⏎A word about implementation. One of the arguments we sometimes hear from health IT developers is that model card requirements are difficult to fulfill because training data documentation is inconsistent or incomplete, particularly for tools that use third-party data sources or that have been updated multiple times since initial training. We understand that this is a real operational challenge. But the solution to that problem is not to eliminate the disclosure requirement. The solution is to require developers to document what they know and to explicitly flag what they do not know. A disclosure that says "training data demographic composition is not fully documented for versions prior to 2021" is more useful to a clinician than no disclosure at all. ONC should clarify in the final rule that incomplete documentation, if disclosed transparently, satisfies the criterion, rather than treating any gap in documentation as grounds for non-compliance. That kind of practical clarification would address the legitimate compliance burden concern without gutting the accountability function of the rule.⏎⏎I am also aware that some commenters on this proposed rule will argue that the DSI transparency requirements duplicate disclosures already required under the FDA's framework for AI-based software as a medical device. That argument has some surface plausibility, but it does not hold up on examination. The FDA's SaMD framework applies to a subset of clinical decision support tools, specifically those that meet the statutory definition of a device under 21 U.S.C. 321(h) as interpreted after the 21st Century Cures Act amendments. Many of the AI tools embedded in EHR clinical workflows, including the kind of risk stratification and screening tools we encounter in maternal mental health settings, do not meet that threshold and are therefore outside FDA jurisdiction. The DSI certification criterion fills a regulatory gap that the FDA framework does not cover. Removing it does not eliminate a redundancy. It creates a void.⏎⏎The Policy Center for Maternal Mental Health appreciates the opportunity to submit these comments. We are available to discuss any of the points raised here with ONC staff at their convenience. Our contact information is listed in the letterhead above.⏎⏎Respectfully submitted,⏎⏎Daniel Lee⏎Community Organizer and Policy Director⏎Policy Center for Maternal Mental Health⏎Rapid City, South Dakota⏎⏎cc: Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology⏎Docket Management Facility, U.S. Department of Health and Human Services⏎⏎Policy Center for Maternal Mental Health Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 7⏎⏎Note: This comment was submitted on behalf of the Policy Center for Maternal Mental Health. CMS-2025-0050-110067♔CMS-2025-0050♔Sharon Thompson♔Defacto Health LLC♔♔♔♔Removing AI model card disclosure requirements from the DSI certification criterion would eliminate the only reliable mechanism by which under-resourced rural hospitals can obtain structured, comparable information about the limitations and traini...♔Defacto Health LLC Comments | ASTP/ONC Deregulatory RFI | Page 1⏎⏎---⏎⏎COMMENTS OF DEFACTO HEALTH LLC ON THE ASTP/ONC DEREGULATORY ACTIONS TO UNLEASH PROSPERITY: HEALTH DATA, TECHNOLOGY, AND INTEROPERABILITY PROPOSED RULE⏎⏎Submitted by Sharon Thompson, Chief Financial Officer⏎Defacto Health LLC⏎Charleston, West Virginia⏎⏎---⏎⏎PRELIMINARY REMARKS⏎⏎Defacto Health LLC operates as a health system advisory and management services organization working primarily with rural and semi-rural hospitals across West Virginia and the broader Appalachian region. Our client hospitals are, without exception, the kind of facilities that federal health IT policy often describes in the abstract but rarely accounts for in practice: single-facility systems with thin operating margins, limited IT staff, and a patient population that has few alternatives if care quality declines. We submit these comments in response to the proposed rule published by ASTP/ONC, and we focus specifically on the agency's proposal to remove or substantially revise the Decision Support Interventions (DSI) certification criterion, particularly those provisions requiring AI model cards and associated transparency disclosures.⏎⏎We want to be direct: we support deregulation in principle. The certification backlog problem is real. The burden on small developers is real. The time-to-market delays that result from overly rigid compliance frameworks have real consequences for hospitals like the ones we serve. We are not submitting these comments to argue that the status quo is working well, because in our experience it is not. What we are arguing is that the DSI transparency requirements are among the certification provisions that should be kept, and that removing them would create a category of patient safety risk that no administrative burden reduction can justify.⏎⏎---⏎⏎THE DSI CRITERION AND WHAT IT ACTUALLY REQUIRES⏎⏎Before getting into the substantive argument, it is worth being precise about what we are defending, because the framing in the proposed rule sometimes conflates transparency disclosures with the broader certification overhead that does create legitimate burden. The DSI criterion at 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11), as it currently stands, requires that certified Health IT modules deploying AI-driven clinical decision support provide documentation covering intended use, target population, known limitations and risks, training data characteristics, and whether the model has undergone external validation. This is what the industry commonly refers to as an "AI model card," borrowing terminology that has been in wide use in the machine learning research community since at least the Google research paper by Mitchell et al. published in the Proceedings of the ACM Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency in 2019.⏎⏎The practical ask here is not enormous. A model card is a structured disclosure document. It does not require a developer to redesign their product. It does not require new interoperability interfaces. It does not require recertification every time a minor software update is deployed. What it requires is that a developer who has built an AI model explain, in reasonably plain terms, what the model was trained on, what population it was designed to serve, and what its known failure modes are. Clinicians are then supposed to have access to that information when they are deciding whether and how to act on a system-generated recommendation. That is the entirety of what we are asking ONC to preserve.⏎⏎---⏎⏎WHY THIS MATTERS MORE IN RURAL SETTINGS⏎⏎Defacto Health LLC Comments | ASTP/ONC Deregulatory RFI | Page 2⏎⏎---⏎⏎The argument for retaining model card requirements gets stronger, not weaker, as you move away from large academic medical centers. Here is why: a hospital system like Johns Hopkins or Cleveland Clinic has internal AI governance infrastructure. They have data science teams, clinical informatics departments, and bioethics committees that can scrutinize a vendor's AI model before deployment. A 120-bed regional hospital in Morgantown or Beckley does not have any of that. When a clinical decision support tool arrives in a procurement package, the people evaluating it are typically a hospitalist physician who is already working a 14-hour shift, a CFO who is trying to balance three competing capital projects, and maybe an IT director who came up through the network infrastructure side and has limited background in machine learning validation methodology.⏎⏎For those evaluators, the model card is not a nice-to-have. It is often the only structured, vendor-provided document that contains information about how the AI was built and what it might get wrong. Without it, the decision to deploy is made based on marketing materials, a sales demo, and whatever the vendor's account manager says over the phone. That is not a reasonable basis for a decision that will affect clinical care for thousands of patients.⏎⏎Last spring, our organization was advising a 90-bed hospital in southern West Virginia that was trying to select a sepsis prediction tool. There were three vendors in the running. One of them had a full model card that disclosed, among other things, that their model had been trained predominantly on patient data from urban academic centers in the Northeast and had not been externally validated in rural populations. That disclosure was directly relevant to our client's patient population, which includes a high proportion of elderly patients with complex comorbidities and a different baseline presentation profile than the training data reflected. The hospital ultimately chose a different vendor partly on that basis. They would not have had that information without the disclosure requirement.⏎⏎I want to be honest that this example also illustrates some of the friction the proposed rule is reacting to: the vendor with the full model card had been delayed in getting to market by about fourteen months because of certification processing times, and they told us directly that the documentation burden was a significant factor in that delay. So I am not pretending the current system is costless or well-calibrated. But the answer to that problem is to fix the certification pipeline, not to eliminate the disclosure requirement. Those are separable problems and they should be treated as such.⏎⏎---⏎⏎THE PATIENT SAFETY ARGUMENT⏎⏎Defacto Health LLC Comments | ASTP/ONC Deregulatory RFI | Page 3⏎⏎---⏎⏎The proposed rule frames the DSI changes partly as a burden reduction measure and partly as an acknowledgment that the AI transparency requirements were premature given the state of the market when they were adopted. We understand that framing, but we think it gets the timing exactly backwards. The AI clinical decision support market in 2024 is substantially larger and more consequential than it was when ONC first began developing the DSI criterion. The number of AI-enabled tools seeking certification has grown significantly. The complexity of those tools has increased. The stakes associated with their deployment have gone up, not down. This is precisely the wrong moment to reduce the informational requirements that allow clinicians and hospital administrators to make informed decisions about these products.⏎⏎The clinical literature on AI failure modes in healthcare settings makes this point with more precision than we can here. A 2022 study published in the New England Journal of Medicine by Wong et al. examined an early warning AI system deployed across multiple hospital sites and found that the model's performance degraded substantially in patient subpopulations that were underrepresented in its training data, including elderly patients and patients with certain chronic conditions. The performance degradation was not apparent from the vendor's internal validation data. It only became visible through independent external validation. This is exactly the kind of information that a model card's disclosure requirements are designed to surface. Without the requirement to disclose training data characteristics and external validation status, a hospital has no systematic way to know that this risk exists.⏎⏎The counterargument, which we have heard from some vendor representatives, is that the market will solve this problem: hospitals that have bad experiences with opaque AI tools will stop buying them, and vendors who provide better transparency voluntarily will gain a competitive advantage. We are skeptical of this argument in any healthcare context, but we are especially skeptical of it in rural healthcare markets where there are often only two or three vendors with products that meet a hospital's other functional requirements. Market discipline requires consumer choice, and choice requires alternatives. In many product categories relevant to small rural hospitals, the alternatives are limited enough that the market discipline mechanism simply does not function the way the theory predicts.⏎⏎---⏎⏎ACCOUNTABILITY AND THE INFORMATION BLOCKING QUESTION⏎⏎Defacto Health LLC Comments | ASTP/ONC Deregulatory RFI | Page 4⏎⏎---⏎⏎There is a secondary issue we want to raise that touches on the information blocking provisions in the proposed rule, though this is somewhat tangential to our primary argument. The proposed rule makes several changes to the information blocking definitions and exceptions that are intended to give providers and developers more flexibility. We generally support that direction. But we are concerned that if the DSI transparency requirements are removed from the certification framework, the practical effect will be that model card information moves from being a required disclosure to being a form of proprietary information that vendors can legitimately withhold under the trade secret exception in 45 CFR 171.301.⏎⏎This concern is not hypothetical. We have already had conversations with at least two vendors who, when asked informally about their model documentation practices, indicated that absent a certification requirement, they would likely treat their training data characteristics and validation methodology as trade secrets. One vendor's legal counsel was quite explicit that the company's position would be that this information constitutes proprietary business information. If the certification requirement disappears and the information blocking framework simultaneously provides a legal basis for withholding this information, hospitals are left with no practical mechanism to obtain it.⏎⏎We recognize that ONC may not have intended this outcome, and we are not suggesting bad faith in the rulemaking. But the interaction between the DSI changes and the information blocking framework deserves explicit attention in the final rule. At minimum, ONC should clarify whether AI model documentation falls within the scope of electronic health information for purposes of the information blocking regulations, and if so, what exceptions would apply. The Federal Register preamble to the proposed rule does not address this interaction, and the silence creates real uncertainty for hospitals trying to establish vendor contracts that include model transparency provisions.⏎⏎---⏎⏎THE CONTRACTING PROBLEM⏎⏎Defacto Health LLC Comments | ASTP/ONC Deregulatory RFI | Page 5⏎⏎---⏎⏎Since we are a management services organization that spends a significant amount of time helping hospitals negotiate vendor contracts, we want to offer a practical perspective on what happens when transparency requirements are left to contract negotiation rather than regulatory mandate. In theory, a hospital can simply require model card disclosures as a condition of any AI vendor contract. In practice, the ability to do that depends heavily on the hospital's bargaining leverage, and small rural hospitals have very little of it.⏎⏎When a 90-bed hospital is negotiating with a mid-sized health IT vendor, the vendor's standard contract terms are not really negotiable. The vendor has a master service agreement that has been approved by their legal department, and the account manager does not have authority to add non-standard disclosure clauses. Getting a custom provision into a vendor contract requires escalating to legal on both sides, which adds time and cost that neither party wants to absorb. We have seen hospitals simply give up on getting transparency provisions into contracts because the negotiation process became too burdensome relative to their other procurement priorities. The certification requirement solves this problem by making the disclosure a baseline condition that applies uniformly, regardless of relative bargaining power.⏎⏎This is, in our view, one of the strongest arguments for retaining the DSI criterion in its current form. The regulation is doing exactly what good minimum standards regulation is supposed to do: it levels the information playing field between large vendors with sophisticated legal teams and small hospitals that are trying to make good technology decisions under significant resource constraints. Removing it shifts the burden back onto the hospitals, and the hospitals that will feel that burden most acutely are the ones that can least afford to absorb it.⏎⏎---⏎⏎RESPONSE TO THE BURDEN REDUCTION RATIONALE⏎⏎Defacto Health LLC Comments | ASTP/ONC Deregulatory RFI | Page 6⏎⏎---⏎⏎We want to engage seriously with ONC's burden reduction rationale, because we think it deserves a direct response rather than a dismissal. The agency's position, as we understand it from the proposed rule, is that the AI model card requirements impose compliance costs on developers that slow certification timelines and may deter smaller, more innovative vendors from seeking certification at all. We accept that this is a real problem. The certification processing times we have observed in our own work are genuinely problematic, and we have seen promising vendors exit the market or abandon certification efforts because the process was too slow and costly relative to their business model.⏎⏎But the solution to certification delays is not to remove the substance of what is being certified. If ONC determines that the AI transparency disclosures are worth requiring, then the right response to certification bottlenecks is to invest in certification capacity, streamline the review process, or create a tiered or expedited pathway for developers who have already completed equivalent third-party assessments. Several of these approaches have been discussed in the health IT policy community and some have precedent in other regulatory domains. The FDA's Breakthrough Device Designation program, for example, allows expedited review for devices that address serious conditions without abandoning the substantive safety evaluation requirements. ONC could develop analogous mechanisms.⏎⏎What we cannot accept is an implicit trade where substantive patient safety protections are removed in order to reduce administrative friction. The DSI transparency requirements exist because there is a genuine patient safety rationale for them, a rationale that has not diminished with the passage of time. If anything, it has gotten stronger as AI clinical decision support tools have become more widely deployed and the consequences of their failure modes have become better documented in the literature.⏎⏎---⏎⏎A SPECIFIC CONCERN ABOUT THE PROPOSED ALTERNATIVE⏎⏎Defacto Health LLC Comments | ASTP/ONC Deregulatory RFI | Page 7⏎⏎---⏎⏎The proposed rule suggests, somewhat tentatively, that voluntary disclosure frameworks or market-driven transparency practices might serve as alternatives to the certification requirement. We want to be specific about why we think this is insufficient, because the argument is sometimes made in a way that sounds plausible in the abstract but breaks down when you look at how the market actually works.⏎⏎Voluntary disclosure frameworks in health IT have a mixed record at best. The ONC's own 2016 Health IT Safety Center concept, which was designed to create a voluntary reporting and learning system for health IT-related safety events, never gained the traction its proponents hoped for, in part because voluntary participation rates in safety reporting tend to be low when the information being reported reflects poorly on the reporter. There is no reason to think voluntary AI model documentation would behave differently. The vendors with well-validated models and clean training data will publish model cards voluntarily because it helps them sell their product. The vendors with poorly validated models or training data that raises questions will not, because disclosure would hurt them competitively. The result is that voluntary disclosure systematically surfaces information about the better products while obscuring information about the worse ones, which is almost exactly the opposite of what a transparency requirement is supposed to accomplish.⏎⏎The market-driven transparency argument has a similar structural problem. It assumes that hospitals can identify and reward vendors who provide better transparency, but that requires hospitals to have enough information to make that comparison in the first place. If a vendor is not disclosing its model documentation, the hospital does not know whether the absence of documentation reflects a problem or simply a different disclosure practice. The information asymmetry that the requirement is designed to address cannot be corrected by market discipline that depends on the very information that is being withheld.⏎⏎---⏎⏎RECOMMENDATIONS⏎⏎Defacto Health LLC Comments | ASTP/ONC Deregulatory RFI | Page 8⏎⏎---⏎⏎We are asking ONC to retain the DSI certification criterion as it currently stands with respect to AI model card and transparency disclosure requirements, including the provisions covering intended use, target population characteristics, known limitations and risks, training data characteristics, and external validation status. These requirements should not be removed or made voluntary.⏎⏎If ONC is concerned about the burden these requirements impose on developers, we would encourage the agency to consider the following approaches, which address the burden problem without eliminating the substantive disclosure obligation.⏎⏎First, ONC could create a standardized model card template that vendors complete rather than develop from scratch. This would reduce the documentation burden significantly while ensuring consistency across submissions, which would also make it easier for hospitals to compare products. There is existing work in this space, including the model card frameworks developed by Hugging Face and Google, that ONC could draw on rather than building something from scratch.⏎⏎Second, ONC could establish a reciprocity arrangement with recognized third-party AI auditors, so that a vendor who has completed a qualifying external audit does not have to duplicate that work for certification purposes. This would reduce the total compliance burden while preserving the informational outcome that the requirement is designed to achieve.⏎⏎Third, the agency could consider whether the recertification trigger for AI model updates could be narrowed to material changes in the model's intended use, training data, or validation status, rather than requiring recertification for minor software updates that do not affect the AI component. This is a legitimate source of ongoing burden that could be addressed without touching the disclosure requirements themselves.⏎⏎We are genuinely open to discussion about the mechanics of how the requirement is implemented. What we are not open to is removing the requirement on the theory that the market or voluntary practices will fill the gap, because our direct experience tells us that they will not.⏎⏎---⏎⏎A NOTE ON THE BROADER DEREGULATORY DIRECTION⏎⏎Defacto Health LLC Comments | ASTP/ONC Deregulatory RFI | Page 9⏎⏎---⏎⏎We want to close with a comment on the framing of this rulemaking, because the "Unleash Prosperity" framing in the rule's title is doing some work that deserves scrutiny. The premise seems to be that health IT certification requirements are primarily a constraint on innovation and economic activity, and that removing them will release productive capacity that is currently being suppressed. There is some truth in this, and we have already acknowledged that the certification burden problem is real.⏎⏎But the framing obscures the fact that some certification requirements exist precisely because the absence of those requirements would shift costs from developers onto patients and hospitals. When a vendor does not have to disclose its AI model's training data, the cost of that opacity does not disappear. It moves. It moves to the clinician who acts on a recommendation without understanding its limitations. It moves to the patient who receives care influenced by a model that was not designed for people like them. It moves to the hospital that is liable when something goes wrong and cannot demonstrate that it exercised appropriate due diligence in vendor selection. The administrative burden that is being reduced on the developer side does not vanish; it is redistributed to parties who are less equipped to manage it.⏎⏎We are not opposed to prosperity. We are not opposed to reducing administrative friction where it is genuinely unnecessary. What we are opposed to is a framing that treats all regulatory requirements as equivalent constraints on economic activity, without asking who bears the cost when those requirements are removed. For the DSI transparency disclosures, the answer is clear: the cost falls on rural hospitals and their patients, and those are exactly the parties who have the least capacity to absorb it.⏎⏎Defacto Health LLC appreciates the opportunity to submit these comments and remains available to discuss any of the points raised here with agency staff. Correspondence may be directed to Sharon Thompson, CFO, Defacto Health LLC.⏎⏎sthompson@defactohealthllc.org⏎⏎---⏎⏎Defacto Health LLC Comments | ASTP/ONC Deregulatory RFI | Page 10⏎⏎---⏎⏎One practical issue we have not yet mentioned that keeps coming up in our client conversations: even where hospitals have managed to get model documentation from vendors informally, the documents they receive vary so wildly in format and depth that comparison across vendors is nearly impossible. One vendor will provide a six-page technical document with performance metrics stratified by age and race. Another will provide a two-paragraph summary that describes the model as "validated for clinical use" without specifying what that means or against what population. Without a standardized format requirement attached to the certification criterion, the disclosure obligation produces information that is technically present but practically unusable for comparative purposes. This is a fixable problem, and it is worth fixing, but it requires the regulatory floor to remain in place first.♔♔2026-01-13T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-13T00:00:00Z♔2025-12-12T00:00:00Z♔2026-02-10T00:00:00Z♔11♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Retain the current Decision Support Interventions (DSI) certification criterion requiring AI model cards and transparency disclosures (intended use, target population, known risks, training data characteristics, external validation) to ensure patient safety, informed clinical decision-making, and accountability in AI-assisted healthcare.♔The 'black box' problem is a documented barrier to AI adoption in healthcare; model cards directly address clinician and organizational concerns about trustworthiness and are a proven mechanism to build confidence.♔industry♔high♔concerned♔West Virginia♔hospital CFO♔36♔Last spring, I watched our small regional hospital nearly walk away from a contract with a promising clinical decision support vendor because their product had been delayed eighteen months navigating certification backlogs — time we simply didn't have while managing post-pandemic staffing shortfalls. Docket ID: ONC-2025-0001. Submitted on behalf of the South Carolina Primary Health Care Association. If anyone needs the PDF version for the archive, contact me directly.⏎⏎---⏎⏎South Carolina Primary Health Care Association⏎Comments on ASTP/ONC Proposed Rule: Deregulatory Actions To Unleash Prosperity: Health Data, Technology, and Interoperability⏎Docket ID: ONC-2025-0001⏎Federal Register Vol. 90⏎⏎The South Carolina Primary Health Care Association (SCPHCA) represents a network of Federally Qualified Health Centers and look-alike clinics serving medically underserved communities across South Carolina. Our member centers collectively see over 400,000 patients annually, the majority of whom are uninsured or enrolled in Medicaid, and who depend on community health centers as their primary and often only point of contact with the health care system. We appreciate the opportunity to submit comments on the above-referenced proposed rulemaking.⏎⏎These comments address a narrow but serious concern: the proposed removal of the Decision Support Interventions (DSI) certification criterion, specifically the provisions requiring transparency disclosures and model documentation for AI-based clinical decision support tools. We are asking ONC to retain those requirements in their current form, and we want to explain in some detail why the communities we serve cannot afford to have them removed.⏎⏎BACKGROUND: WHAT THE CURRENT DSI CRITERION REQUIRES⏎⏎Before addressing the proposal, it helps to be precise about what is actually at stake. The DSI certification criterion, as finalized in the ONC Health IT Certification Program under 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11), currently requires that health IT developers seeking certification for AI-powered clinical decision support interventions provide a set of standardized transparency disclosures. These include documentation of the intended use of the tool, the target patient population for which the tool was developed and validated, known risks and limitations, characteristics of the training data (including demographic composition), and evidence of external validation. These are sometimes called "model cards" in the machine learning literature, borrowing a term from a 2019 paper by Mitchell et al. that has since been widely adopted as a documentation standard in responsible AI development.⏎⏎The proposed rule would remove this criterion from the certification program on the grounds that it creates compliance burden for developers and that the market will organically produce transparency without regulatory mandates. We think that reasoning is flawed, and we want to explain why from the perspective of what actually happens inside a community health center when a clinical AI tool is deployed without adequate documentation.⏎⏎WHAT AI TRANSPARENCY MEANS IN PRACTICE AT A COMMUNITY HEALTH CENTER⏎⏎Our member centers have limited IT staff. The typical FQHC in our network has one or maybe two staff members who handle anything related to health information technology, and those individuals are usually managing EHR configuration, reporting requirements for the Uniform Data System (UDS), and HIPAA compliance simultaneously. They are not in a position to independently audit the machine learning models embedded in their clinical decision support tools. They depend entirely on what the vendor discloses.⏎⏎When a vendor provides model documentation, that documentation shapes how clinical staff use the tool. If a risk-stratification algorithm was trained primarily on data from urban academic medical centers, clinicians at a rural FQHC serving a predominantly Black and Hispanic farmworker population need to know that, because the tool's predictions may not generalize well to their patient population. If an alert-generation tool was externally validated only on patients over 65, that matters when the tool is being used in a pediatric or maternal health context. These are not hypothetical concerns. A 2021 study published in JAMA Internal Medicine (Obermeyer et al., building on earlier work from 2019 in Science) documented that commercial risk-scoring algorithms used across health systems systematically underestimated health needs in Black patients by using health care costs as a proxy for health need, a choice that encoded historical patterns of underutilization directly into the model. The algorithm was widely deployed before that bias was documented externally.⏎⏎The question is not whether individual FQHC clinical staff can detect these problems on their own. They cannot, and they should not have to. The question is whether the regulatory framework requires vendors to surface this information proactively, so that it is available to the clinicians and health center administrators who need it. The current DSI criterion does exactly that. The proposed rule would eliminate that requirement.⏎⏎SCPHCA Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 2⏎⏎THE "MARKET WILL HANDLE IT" ASSUMPTION DOES NOT HOLD FOR SAFETY-NET PROVIDERS⏎⏎The proposed rule's rationale for removing the DSI transparency requirements leans on the idea that market forces and existing liability frameworks will incentivize vendors to provide adequate documentation voluntarily. We are skeptical of this reasoning in general, but we want to be specific about why it fails for safety-net providers.⏎⏎Community health centers are not in a strong negotiating position with large health IT vendors. The EHR market for FQHCs is dominated by a small number of vendors, and the leverage that a large hospital system might use to demand detailed AI documentation is simply not available to a 12-site FQHC network in rural South Carolina. When a vendor says "here is our tool, here is our standard contract," our members largely take it or leave it. The contract negotiation that might produce additional transparency disclosures at a well-resourced academic medical center does not happen at the same level for our members.⏎⏎There is also the question of what "voluntary disclosure" looks like without standardization. Even vendors who want to be transparent about their AI tools will produce documentation in whatever format they choose, using whatever terminology they prefer, organized around whatever metrics they find favorable to present. Without a standardized disclosure framework, that documentation is essentially incomparable across vendors. A clinician or health center administrator cannot look at two different tools and evaluate them against a common set of criteria. The value of the current DSI criterion is precisely that it establishes a common baseline, so that the disclosures mean something consistent across products.⏎⏎I want to be honest that I have some sympathy for the compliance burden argument in the abstract. Documentation requirements do take time and resources, and there are certification requirements in the ONC program that have accumulated over time without always being reassessed for proportionality. But the DSI transparency requirements are not a paperwork exercise. They are the mechanism by which the people using these tools get the information they need to use them responsibly. Removing them does not reduce burden in any meaningful way for the health centers that rely on this information. It shifts the burden, invisibly, onto patients who may receive care shaped by an algorithm whose limitations were never disclosed to anyone.⏎⏎SPECIFIC CONCERN: TRAINING DATA DOCUMENTATION AND HEALTH EQUITY⏎⏎The requirement to disclose training data characteristics, including demographic composition, is the piece of the DSI criterion that I keep coming back to. It is also, based on conversations with our member center staff, the disclosure element that they find most operationally useful.⏎⏎South Carolina has significant health disparities by race, geography, and income. Our member centers serve communities where those disparities are concentrated. When a clinical decision support tool is deployed in those settings, the question of whether the training data reflects anything like that population is directly relevant to patient safety. A tool trained on claims data from a commercially insured population will behave differently when applied to Medicaid patients with different patterns of prior utilization, different comorbidity profiles, and different access histories.⏎⏎The proposed rule does not explain why this disclosure requirement should be removed. The Federal Register preamble discusses compliance burden in general terms but does not provide any analysis of whether the training data disclosure specifically imposes disproportionate burden relative to its value. That omission is significant. Under any reasonable cost-benefit analysis, a disclosure requirement that directly informs clinical use of AI tools in populations at elevated risk of algorithmic harm should require a detailed justification for removal, not just a general invocation of deregulatory principles.⏎⏎SCPHCA Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 3⏎⏎We would also note that the Office of the National Coordinator has previously recognized the importance of AI transparency in health care. The ONC's own 2024 report on artificial intelligence in health care acknowledged that transparency and explainability are foundational to responsible deployment of AI in clinical settings. The proposed rule does not engage with that prior guidance or explain why the policy position has changed. That disconnect is confusing to our member organizations, who are trying to build internal policies around AI governance and are looking to federal standards for guidance.⏎⏎WHAT RETENTION OF THE DSI CRITERION WOULD ACTUALLY REQUIRE⏎⏎We want to be direct about what we are asking for, because sometimes in these comments processes the ask gets buried.⏎⏎We are asking ONC to retain the DSI certification criterion at 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11) in its current form, including all of the following disclosure elements:⏎⏎1. A clear statement of the tool's intended use and the clinical decisions it is designed to support.⏎⏎2. Documentation of the target patient population, including demographic characteristics of the population for which the tool was developed and validated.⏎⏎3. A description of known risks and limitations, including circumstances under which the tool's outputs should not be relied upon.⏎⏎4. Characteristics of the training data, including data sources, time period of collection, and demographic composition of the training population.⏎⏎5. Evidence of external validation, including the population and setting in which external validation was conducted.⏎⏎These are not novel requirements. They are consistent with emerging best practices in responsible AI documentation across the technology sector, with the model card framework described in Mitchell et al. (2019, Proceedings of the ACM Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency), and with the risk-based AI governance frameworks being developed by the National Institute of Standards and Technology under the AI Risk Management Framework (NIST AI RMF 1.0, January 2023). The FDA's discussion of AI/ML-based Software as a Medical Device (SaMD) in its 2021 action plan similarly identified transparency about training data and intended use as a baseline expectation for responsible deployment.⏎⏎These requirements do not impose unreasonable burden on vendors who are genuinely building responsible AI tools, because a responsible AI development process already produces this documentation internally. The burden falls primarily on vendors who have not conducted external validation, who do not know the demographic composition of their training data, or who prefer that clinicians not scrutinize the intended use limitations too carefully. That is not a burden worth protecting.⏎⏎SCPHCA Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 4⏎⏎A NOTE ON THE RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN DSI TRANSPARENCY AND INFORMATION BLOCKING⏎⏎The proposed rule addresses both certification criteria and information blocking exceptions, and while our primary focus is on the DSI criterion, we want to briefly note that these two areas are not fully independent. One of the functions of the DSI certification requirements is to ensure that the information needed to make responsible use of AI tools actually exists and is accessible to the health care organizations deploying them. If vendors are not required to generate and disclose model documentation as a condition of certification, that information may simply not exist in a usable form, regardless of what information blocking exceptions say about access rights.⏎⏎In our experience working with member centers on health IT procurement, the practical barriers to information access are often not legal barriers. They are practical ones: the documentation was never created, or it exists only in a format that requires technical expertise to interpret, or it is buried in a contract exhibit that nobody reads during implementation. The DSI criterion addresses those practical barriers by standardizing what needs to be disclosed and making disclosure a condition of certification. Loosening the certification requirements while also broadening information blocking exceptions creates a gap that the market is unlikely to fill on its own, particularly for safety-net providers who lack the leverage to demand documentation independently.⏎⏎I keep thinking about a situation I dealt with last spring, in Concord, New Hampshire, where a family spent weeks trying to piece together their teenager's psychiatric records after a transfer between two facilities that couldn't share his treatment history electronically. We eventually got the records by fax. Page 47 of 63. The information existed. It just wasn't accessible in any form that helped anyone make a clinical decision in time. That is what happens when interoperability requirements are treated as optional or burdensome rather than as the baseline they are supposed to be.⏎⏎The DSI transparency requirements are a different kind of interoperability. They are about making sure that the information clinicians need to use AI tools responsibly actually exists and is accessible. Removing them doesn't reduce burden. It moves the risk somewhere else.⏎⏎SCPHCA Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 5⏎⏎RESPONSE TO THE COMPLIANCE BURDEN RATIONALE⏎⏎The proposed rule's primary stated rationale for removing the DSI criterion is compliance burden reduction. We want to engage with that rationale directly rather than dismissing it, because it is not an illegitimate concern. Certification programs can accumulate requirements over time that impose real costs on developers without producing proportionate benefits. That is worth examining.⏎⏎But the compliance burden analysis in the preamble does not actually quantify the burden associated with the DSI transparency requirements specifically. It discusses the certification program in general terms. It does not present evidence that the model card and transparency disclosure requirements are disproportionately burdensome relative to other certification criteria, or that they have discouraged market entry in ways that have reduced the availability of AI decision support tools. Without that evidence, the compliance burden rationale is essentially speculative.⏎⏎By contrast, the potential harms from removing these requirements are reasonably well-documented in the literature. A 2022 systematic review in npj Digital Medicine (Celi et al.) examined AI tools deployed in clinical settings and found that a majority of published AI clinical decision support tools lacked adequate documentation of training data demographics, and that tools lacking this documentation were significantly more likely to show performance disparities across patient subgroups. That is a direct evidentiary basis for the disclosure requirements that the preamble does not address.⏎⏎There is also a regulatory coherence concern. The Biden administration's Executive Order 13960 on Trustworthy AI in the Federal Government, and subsequent OMB guidance on AI governance, established transparency and documentation as baseline principles for federal AI deployment. The proposed rule does not explain how removing AI transparency requirements from ONC certification is consistent with those broader federal AI governance commitments. That explanation seems necessary.⏎⏎SCPHCA Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 6⏎⏎We also want to note that the DSI criterion has not been in place long enough to evaluate its effects with any confidence. The 2024 ONC final rule that established these requirements has only recently begun to be implemented across the certification program. Removing a requirement before its implementation has matured, and before any systematic evaluation of its effects, seems premature. If there are specific aspects of the disclosure format or content requirements that are proving disproportionately burdensome, ONC has tools available to address that through sub-regulatory guidance or through targeted revisions in a future rulemaking. Wholesale removal of the criterion is not the only available response to implementation concerns.⏎⏎HEALTH EQUITY IMPLICATIONS⏎⏎Our member centers serve patients who have historically had the least access to quality health care and who are therefore most dependent on the health care system working correctly when they do access it. For those patients, the deployment of AI tools that perform poorly due to training data mismatch or inadequate validation is not an abstract risk. It is a direct harm.⏎⏎The health equity implications of AI in clinical settings are well-documented. A 2019 study in Health Affairs (Obermeyer and Emanuel) noted that clinical prediction models trained on historically collected data can encode and perpetuate existing disparities in care. A 2023 analysis in JAMA Network Open found that commercial sepsis prediction algorithms showed significant performance variation across hospitals serving different demographic populations, with systematically worse performance at hospitals with higher proportions of Black patients. The FDA's discussion of AI/ML SaMD has acknowledged that performance disparities across demographic subgroups are a known risk category requiring specific attention in development and validation.⏎⏎The DSI transparency requirements are one of the few regulatory mechanisms currently in place that directly address this risk at the point of clinical deployment. They do not eliminate the risk of biased AI tools. But they create a framework in which the information needed to identify and respond to that risk is available to the clinicians and health center administrators using these tools. Removing that framework in the name of compliance burden reduction, without any analysis of the health equity implications, is a choice that will be felt most acutely in the communities our member centers serve.⏎⏎SCPHCA Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 7⏎⏎We recognize that ONC is operating under a deregulatory mandate and that there is genuine pressure to reduce compliance burden across the health IT certification program. We are not asking ONC to ignore that mandate wholesale. There are certification requirements that could reasonably be revised or consolidated without impairing patient safety. But the DSI transparency requirements are not in that category. They address a specific, documented risk in a targeted way, and their removal would leave a gap that no other current regulatory mechanism fills.⏎⏎SUMMARY OF RECOMMENDATIONS⏎⏎To summarize the specific recommendations in these comments:⏎⏎1. Retain the DSI certification criterion at 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11) in its current form, including all required transparency disclosure elements.⏎⏎2. If ONC believes that specific aspects of the disclosure format or documentation requirements are creating disproportionate burden, address those concerns through sub-regulatory guidance or targeted revision rather than wholesale removal of the criterion.⏎⏎3. Conduct and publish a health equity impact analysis before finalizing any changes to AI transparency requirements in the certification program, consistent with HHS's stated commitments on health equity and algorithmic accountability.⏎⏎4. Explain, in the final rule preamble, how the proposed changes to AI transparency requirements are consistent with the NIST AI Risk Management Framework and with broader federal AI governance guidance from OMB.⏎⏎5. Provide an evaluation timeline for the DSI criterion before considering removal, given that the criterion has only recently been implemented and has not yet been systematically assessed.⏎⏎We are grateful for the opportunity to submit these comments and are available to discuss any of the issues raised here in further detail.⏎⏎Respectfully submitted,⏎⏎South Carolina Primary Health Care Association⏎Policy and Advocacy Division⏎⏎Contact: policy@scphca.org⏎⏎www.scphca.org/policy-comments [link may be broken in some browsers - contact office directly for PDF version]⏎⏎---⏎⏎Stephanie Adams⏎Community Organizer, South Carolina Primary Health Care Association⏎s.adams@scphca.org | (803) 555-0147⏎⏎[Note to policy team: I'm not 100% sure the JAMA Network Open citation date is right - someone please double-check before we file anything else referencing it. Our work spans clinical guideline development, payer policy analysis, and health IT interoperability research, with particular attention to how care fragmentation affects maternal outcomes. We submit these comments in response to the proposed deregulatory rule published by ASTP/ONC and want to address one specific proposal that concerns us directly: the potential removal of the Decision Support Interventions (DSI) certification criterion requiring AI model cards and transparency disclosures.⏎⏎We are not generally opposed to reducing administrative burden on health IT developers. There are provisions in this proposed rule that seem reasonable. But the DSI transparency requirement is not administrative overhead. It is a patient safety mechanism, and we want to be direct about that distinction.⏎⏎Policy Center for Maternal Mental Health | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 2⏎⏎THE DSI TRANSPARENCY REQUIREMENT AND WHY IT MATTERS FOR MATERNAL MENTAL HEALTH⏎⏎The current DSI certification criterion, established under 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11), requires that certified health IT include disclosures about AI-driven decision support tools, specifically: intended use, target population, known risks, training data characteristics, and whether the tool has undergone external validation. These are not bureaucratic checkboxes. For a clinician seeing a postpartum patient for the first time, they are the minimum information needed to use an AI tool responsibly.⏎⏎Here is the problem we keep running into in our work. Perinatal depression and anxiety are systematically under-detected in clinical settings. The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) recommends screening at least once during the perinatal period (ACOG Committee Opinion 757, 2018), and the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force reaffirmed that recommendation in 2019. Yet a 2020 study in Psychiatric Services (Byatt et al.) found that fewer than 20 percent of obstetric providers consistently follow through on that recommendation. AI-assisted screening and risk stratification tools are increasingly being deployed to close that gap. Some of them are good. Some of them are not, and the difference is not always visible to the clinician at the point of care.⏎⏎When a decision support tool has been trained predominantly on data from one population and then deployed in a different one, its performance can degrade in ways that are not obvious. A tool trained primarily on commercially insured patients at academic medical centers may perform poorly when deployed at a rural community health center serving a Medicaid population. If the clinician has no way to know that, she cannot adjust her reliance on the tool appropriately. The DSI transparency requirement is specifically designed to make that information available. Removing it would mean clinicians have less information, not more.⏎⏎o Intended use disclosure: tells the clinician whether the tool was designed for screening, for risk stratification, or for something else entirely.⏎⏎o Target population: tells the clinician whether the training data reflects patients like hers.⏎⏎o Known risks and limitations: tells the clinician where the tool is known to fail or underperform.⏎⏎o Training data characteristics: tells the clinician whether the dataset was recent, diverse, and representative.⏎⏎o External validation status: tells the clinician whether an independent party has confirmed the tool's performance claims.⏎⏎These five disclosure elements together take up perhaps two pages of documentation. We genuinely do not understand why removing them is being framed as burden reduction. The burden of producing that documentation falls on the developer, once, at certification. The benefit accrues to every clinician who uses the tool and every patient affected by the decision.⏎⏎Policy Center for Maternal Mental Health | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 3⏎⏎SPECIFIC CONCERNS ABOUT THE MATERNAL MENTAL HEALTH POPULATION⏎⏎The population we work with is particularly vulnerable to the harms that can result from opaque AI tools. A few specifics worth putting in the record:⏎⏎1. Postpartum depression affects approximately 1 in 8 women in the United States, according to CDC surveillance data (Ko et al., 2017, Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report). The actual number is likely higher because of underreporting.⏎⏎2. Black and Hispanic women have higher rates of perinatal depression and lower rates of treatment access. A 2021 analysis in General Hospital Psychiatry (Kozhimannil et al.) documented persistent racial disparities in both diagnosis and follow-through to treatment. If an AI screening tool has a higher false-negative rate for these populations, which is a known risk with tools trained on non-representative datasets, the clinician needs to know that.⏎⏎3. The window for intervention is narrow. Untreated postpartum depression at six weeks can escalate to a more severe episode by three months. A missed flag at one visit can mean a delayed diagnosis by weeks or months. The ONC's own 2023 report on clinical decision support noted that provider overreliance on algorithmic outputs is a documented patient safety concern.⏎⏎4. Perinatal mental health care is fragmented by design. Obstetric providers hand off to pediatricians, who hand off to primary care, and none of these clinicians necessarily has access to what the previous provider documented. An AI tool at each touchpoint may be operating on incomplete data, and without transparency disclosures, the clinician has no way to assess whether the tool's output is reliable given those data gaps.⏎⏎What I keep coming back to is this: the proposed rule acknowledges that the health IT certification program has sometimes created "unnecessary burden" (88 FR 23746). That framing may be accurate for some certification criteria. It is not accurate for DSI transparency requirements, and the rule does not make a compelling case that it is. The justification offered in the NPRM is largely that developers have found the disclosures burdensome to produce. That is a developer interest. It is not a patient safety analysis.⏎⏎Policy Center for Maternal Mental Health | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 4⏎⏎RECOMMENDATIONS⏎⏎The Policy Center for Maternal Mental Health urges ASTP/ONC to retain the DSI certification criterion as currently structured, with all five disclosure elements intact. If ONC believes the current format creates genuine implementation challenges, we would support a process to refine the format in collaboration with clinical stakeholders, including maternal mental health providers and patient advocates, before any element is removed or made optional.⏎⏎Specifically:⏎⏎1. Do not remove the external validation disclosure requirement. External validation is the only mechanism by which a clinician can assess whether a developer's performance claims have been independently confirmed. Making this optional effectively allows unvalidated tools to be deployed without any flag to the end user.⏎⏎2. Do not remove the target population disclosure. This is the single most important piece of information for a clinician assessing whether a tool is appropriate for a specific patient.⏎⏎3. If burden reduction is the goal, consider a standardized template for model cards rather than elimination of the requirement. The FDA's proposed framework for AI/ML-based Software as a Medical Device (SaMD) Action Plan (January 2021) provides a reasonable model for what standardized disclosure could look like without eliminating the substance.⏎⏎4. We also recommend that ONC consult the existing literature on algorithmic bias in clinical decision support before finalizing this rule. Obermeyer et al.'s 2019 study in Science (vol. 366, no. 6464) documented how a widely used risk stratification algorithm systematically underestimated the health needs of Black patients. That study did not involve maternal mental health specifically, but the mechanism it describes is directly applicable.⏎⏎One more thing worth noting: the 21st Century Cures Act's information blocking provisions were designed in part to ensure that patients and providers have access to the information they need for care decisions. 45 CFR 171.103 defines information blocking as a practice that is likely to interfere with access, exchange, or use of electronic health information. Removing transparency requirements from AI tools that directly influence clinical decisions sits uncomfortably close to that definition, at least in spirit, and ONC should think carefully about whether the deregulatory framing here is consistent with the statutory purpose of the Cures Act.⏎⏎www.policycentermhm.org⏎comments@policycentermhm.org♔♔2026-02-06T00:00:00Z♔2026-02-06T00:00:00Z♔2025-12-12T00:00:00Z♔2026-02-10T00:00:00Z♔4♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Retain the current Decision Support Interventions (DSI) certification criterion requiring AI model cards and transparency disclosures (intended use, target population, known risks, training data characteristics, external validation) to ensure patient safety, informed clinical decision-making, and accountability in AI-assisted healthcare.♔Removing transparency requirements creates unacceptable patient safety risks when AI systems make or influence high-stakes clinical recommendations without disclosed performance data or known limitations.♔advocacy_group♔high♔hopeful♔Alabama♔director of government affairs♔55♔Last spring, I sat with my daughter-in-law in a Birmingham hospital room two days after she delivered her first child, watching her struggle to articulate to a new attending physician what her OB had documented about her perinatal depression risk — because that record simply hadn't followed her across the hall to postpartum care.
