CMS-2025-0050-110070♔CMS-2025-0050♔Stephanie Torres♔♔♔♔♔Removing or weakening AI Decision Support Intervention transparency requirements — including disclosures about training data, intended use, known limitations, and external validation — constitutes a patient safety rollback, not a burden reduction,...♔My mother spent three weeks in limbo last spring, after a hospitalization, while her cardiologist records sat somewhere in a system that nobody could access or explain. By the time those records finally reached her new specialist in Tampa, two of her medications had already been adjusted based on incomplete information. Her new doctor caught the discrepancy. We were lucky. I think about that a lot when I read about proposed changes to health IT rules, because the entire premise of safe, connected care depends on the right information traveling with the right context attached to it, and I genuinely don't understand why removing transparency requirements for AI-assisted clinical tools would be considered a burden reduction rather than what it actually is, which is a safety rollback.⏎⏎The certification requirement I'm most worried about losing is the one that covers what some people are calling Decision Support Interventions, or DSI, and specifically the parts that require AI tools used in clinical settings to disclose things like their intended use, what population they were trained on, what their known limitations are, and whether they've been externally validated. I'll be honest, I'm an office manager, not a clinician or a software engineer, and I've spent more time than I expected trying to understand what these disclosure requirements actually mean in practice. But even from where I sit, the logic seems pretty clear: if a physician is looking at an AI-generated recommendation about a patient's medication or care plan, that physician needs to know something about where that recommendation came from and whether it was tested on people who actually resemble that patient. Removing or weakening those disclosures doesn't streamline care. It just makes it harder to catch the kind of error that almost hurt my mother.⏎⏎The proposed rule from ASTP/ONC describes these changes as reducing administrative burden and increasing flexibility for health IT developers. I understand the argument, at least in the abstract. Certification requirements cost money and time, and there's a real concern that overly prescriptive rules slow down innovation or push smaller developers out of the market. I'm not dismissing that. But there's a difference between reducing unnecessary paperwork and removing disclosures that directly affect how safely a clinician can use a tool. The DSI transparency requirements aren't bureaucratic overhead. They're the mechanism by which a doctor can evaluate whether to trust what an algorithm is telling them.⏎⏎What I keep coming back to is the specific content of what's at stake here. The current certification criteria, as I understand them, require developers to document the intended use of their AI model, the target population it was designed for, known risks and limitations, characteristics of the training data, and whether the model has been validated by anyone outside the organization that built it. That last part matters a lot to me. External validation is the difference between a company saying "our tool works" and someone independent saying "we tested it and here's what we found." Removing the requirement for that disclosure, or making it optional, means clinicians may be using tools that have only ever been evaluated by the people who built them and have a financial interest in saying they work.⏎⏎There's actually research on this. A 2021 study published in Nature Medicine looked at hundreds of AI models developed for COVID-19 diagnosis and found that the vast majority had not been externally validated and were trained on datasets with significant methodological problems. The authors specifically noted that without standardized reporting requirements, it was nearly impossible for clinicians to evaluate which tools were safe to use. That was 2021. The concern hasn't gone away. If anything, the proliferation of AI tools in healthcare has made the question of what gets disclosed, and to whom, more urgent, not less.⏎⏎I also want to say something about the training data disclosure piece, because I think it gets overlooked. If an AI model was trained predominantly on data from one kind of patient population, say, patients at large academic medical centers in the northeast, and it's being used to make recommendations about patients in rural Florida, or elderly patients with multiple comorbidities, or patients from communities that have historically been underrepresented in clinical research, the clinician using that tool should know that. Not because it automatically means the tool doesn't work, but because it affects how much weight to give the recommendation and whether to apply additional clinical judgment. Without the training data disclosure, the clinician has no way to even ask the question. They're just told the tool works, and they're expected to proceed.⏎⏎My mother's cardiologist records situation was, in the end, a failure of interoperability and communication between systems. But the near-miss that followed, when her medications were adjusted without complete information, was a failure of context. The right data existed somewhere. What was missing was the context around it, who had ordered what, when, and why. AI transparency disclosures are context. They tell the person using the tool what they're actually working with. Stripping that context away in the name of flexibility doesn't serve patients. It serves the developers who would prefer not to have their tools scrutinized.⏎⏎I want to be fair here and acknowledge that I don't know exactly how compliance with the current DSI certification requirements works in practice, or how burdensome it actually is for developers. I've read some of the industry comments arguing that the disclosure requirements are vague or that the model card format isn't standardized enough to be useful. Those might be legitimate concerns. If the existing requirements aren't working well, the right answer is to fix them, make them clearer, make the model card format more consistent, maybe create a standardized template that developers can actually follow without ambiguity. The right answer is not to remove the requirement entirely.⏎⏎There's something that bothers me about the framing of this rule as an effort to "unleash prosperity." I understand what they're going for with that language, and I don't think economic considerations are irrelevant to health policy. But when the thing being unleashed is a reduction in transparency for AI tools that help physicians decide how to treat patients, the prosperity framing feels like it's working pretty hard to obscure what's actually being proposed. A developer saving money on compliance costs is not the same thing as a patient receiving safer care. Those are different things, and in this case they're pointing in opposite directions.⏎⏎The specific items that I think should be retained in the DSI certification criterion, based on my reading of the current requirements and the proposed changes, are roughly as follows, and I'm listing them this way because I want to be clear about what I'm asking for rather than speaking in generalities:⏎⏎1. Disclosure of the intended use of the AI or predictive model, written in plain language that a clinician can actually interpret without a statistics background.⏎⏎2. Identification of the target patient population the model was designed for, including any demographic or clinical characteristics that define the intended use case.⏎⏎3. A description of the training data, including the source, time period, size, and any known limitations or gaps in representation.⏎⏎4. Documentation of known risks and failure modes, including conditions under which the model is known to perform poorly or produce unreliable outputs.⏎⏎5. External validation status, meaning whether the model has been tested by an independent party on data it wasn't trained on, and if so, what the results showed.⏎⏎6. A plain-language description of what the model does and does not do, so that a physician or other clinician can understand what kind of decision support they're actually receiving.⏎⏎I'm not suggesting this list is exhaustive or that I've captured the technical language perfectly. But these are the categories of information that seem, to me, like the minimum a clinician should have before relying on an AI tool for a decision that affects a patient's treatment. Removing any of these without replacing them with something equally informative is a step backward.⏎⏎One thing I haven't seen addressed clearly in the proposed rule is what happens to patients when a clinician makes a decision based on an AI recommendation that turned out to be unreliable, and there's no documentation anywhere of what the tool was supposed to do or how it was tested. Right now, if something goes wrong, there's at least a certification record that describes the tool's intended use and limitations. If the certification requirements are loosened to the point where developers don't have to disclose much, what's the accountability mechanism? I'm genuinely asking, because I haven't been able to find a clear answer in the regulatory text.⏎⏎The Federal Register notice for this proposed rule, published in 2025, describes the goal as reducing regulatory burden while maintaining patient safety. I want to take that seriously, but the specific changes proposed for the DSI criterion don't read to me as burden-neutral adjustments. They read as substantive reductions in what developers are required to disclose. If there's a way to reduce the administrative overhead of compliance without reducing the actual content of the disclosures, I'd support that. But if the choice is between keeping the disclosures and eliminating them, I think the answer is obvious, or at least it should be.⏎⏎I also want to mention something about the information blocking amendments in this rule, because my mother's experience is directly relevant here too. The proposed changes to information blocking exceptions and definitions are described as giving providers more flexibility, which sounds good in the abstract. But the version of "flexibility" that resulted in three weeks of inaccessible records and a medication discrepancy is not the kind of flexibility that helps patients. I'm not saying the current information blocking rules are perfect. They're clearly not. But any revision to those rules should be evaluated against the question of whether it makes it easier or harder for a patient's complete medical record to follow them from one provider to another, in a format that the receiving provider can actually use. That's the test. Not whether it reduces paperwork for the developer or the health system.⏎⏎What gets me about this whole situation, including my mother's situation and the regulatory picture more broadly, is how much of the risk lands on the patient. The developer doesn't bear the risk when an undisclosed model limitation leads to a bad recommendation. The health system has some liability exposure but also has lawyers and risk management departments. The patient is the one who ends up with the wrong medication adjustment or the missed diagnosis or the care plan built on incomplete information. The transparency requirements for AI tools are one of the few mechanisms that put some of that accountability back on the people who built the tool and chose to deploy it. Removing those requirements shifts the risk further toward the patient without giving the patient any corresponding benefit.⏎⏎I've read some of the arguments in favor of this deregulatory approach, and I want to engage with them honestly. The argument that overly specific certification requirements lock in current technology and prevent developers from improving their tools is real. If a certification criterion requires a specific format for model documentation, and better formats emerge over time, rigid requirements can slow adoption of better practices. I get that. But the answer to that problem is a requirement that's flexible about format while being firm about content. Require the disclosure, let the developer choose how to present it, but don't let them skip it.⏎⏎The argument that smaller developers can't afford to comply with extensive certification requirements is also worth taking seriously. I don't want a regulatory framework that only the biggest companies can navigate, because that produces its own problems for patients. But the solution there is to provide better guidance and support for smaller developers, maybe model card templates, maybe a simplified compliance pathway for lower-risk tools. Not to eliminate the requirement for everyone because some developers find it difficult.⏎⏎My mother is 71 years old and lives alone in Sarasota. She has atrial fibrillation, type 2 diabetes, and mild chronic kidney disease, which means she sees multiple specialists and takes a list of medications that interact with each other in ways that require careful management. Every time she switches providers or gets referred to someone new, her complete medication and diagnosis history needs to travel with her and arrive in a form that the new provider can actually use and trust. AI tools are increasingly part of how those providers make decisions about her care. I want those tools to be transparent about what they are and what they can and can't do. That's not an abstract policy preference. It's a concrete need that affects her safety.⏎⏎The near-miss last spring happened because information was missing and nobody caught it until her new cardiologist happened to look carefully. We can't build a health system that depends on individual physicians catching errors that should have been prevented upstream. The transparency requirements for AI tools are an upstream prevention mechanism. They don't guarantee that nothing will go wrong, but they give clinicians the information they need to apply appropriate judgment rather than just accepting an algorithmic output at face value.⏎⏎I want to say something about the phrase "informed clinical decision-making" because I think it's easy to use that phrase without thinking about what it actually requires. Informed clinical decision-making with respect to AI tools means the clinician has access to information about what the tool does, who it was designed for, what its limitations are, and whether it's been independently tested. If any of those pieces are missing, the decision-making is less informed. That's not a complicated argument. The current DSI certification requirements are specifically designed to ensure those pieces are available. Removing or weakening them makes clinical decision-making less informed, by definition. I don't know how to say that more plainly.⏎⏎I've also been thinking about the accountability piece, because I think it matters beyond the individual clinical encounter. When AI tools are deployed in healthcare without adequate transparency requirements, and something goes wrong, it's very hard to figure out what happened and why. Was the model used outside its intended population? Was it trained on data that didn't reflect the patient's characteristics? Were there known failure modes that weren't disclosed? Without the documentation that transparency requirements create, those questions are much harder to answer. That makes it harder to learn from errors and harder to hold developers accountable. The certification records created by the DSI requirements are part of the evidentiary infrastructure that makes accountability possible.⏎⏎There's a broader principle here that I think the agency should keep in mind as it considers these changes. Health IT certification requirements exist because the market alone doesn't reliably produce transparency or safety in this domain. Developers have an incentive to sell tools, not to disclose their limitations. Clinicians are busy and often don't have the time or technical background to independently evaluate AI tools. Patients have almost no visibility into what's happening at all. Regulatory requirements for transparency are how you compensate for those market failures. Removing them doesn't mean the market will produce transparency voluntarily. It means transparency becomes optional, and optional usually means absent.⏎⏎I recognize that I'm one person submitting a comment, and that the agency will receive many comments from health IT developers, large health systems, and professional associations with much more technical expertise than I have. I'm not trying to claim expertise I don't have. But I am a person who has watched the consequences of information gaps in healthcare play out in real time, for my own family member, and I want the agency to hear from people like me, not just from the industry stakeholders who have a financial interest in reduced compliance requirements.⏎⏎The comment period for this rule, if I'm reading the Federal Register notice correctly, is the appropriate place to say that patients and their families are paying attention to these decisions and that we have a direct stake in whether AI tools used in our care are transparent about what they do. I'm asking the agency to retain the DSI certification requirements in their current form, or if changes are made, to ensure that any revised requirements preserve the core content disclosures, especially the training data characteristics, external validation status, and known risk documentation, because those are the pieces that give clinicians the ability to evaluate the tool rather than just use it.⏎⏎I'm also asking the agency to be specific in the final rule about what "flexibility" means in this context. Flexibility for developers to choose how to format their disclosures is fine. Flexibility that allows developers to omit disclosures that patients and clinicians depend on is not acceptable, even if it's framed as burden reduction.⏎⏎One more thing that I want to flag, because it came up in my reading of the proposed changes and I'm not sure I fully understand it: the rule appears to propose modifications to how the information blocking provisions interact with certain certification criteria. I'm worried that changes to those provisions could make it easier for health systems or developers to restrict access to patient records in ways that aren't currently permitted, and that the flexibility being offered might benefit the organizations holding the data more than the patients the data belongs to. I don't have a fully formed argument here because I don't understand all the technical details, but I wanted to flag it because my mother's experience was at least partly a story about an organization that technically had her records and was not making them available in a usable way, and I don't want a rule change to make that situation easier to justify or harder to challenge.⏎⏎The cardiologist's office in Orlando that held her records, by the way, eventually told us the delay was partly a system compatibility issue and partly a workflow problem on their end. Neither of those explanations involved any bad faith on anyone's part. But the result was still three weeks of incomplete care and a medication adjustment that could have hurt her. If there are AI tools embedded in that workflow, and I have to assume there probably are at this point, the clinicians using them should have clear information about what those tools can and can't do.⏎⏎I don't have a grand conclusion to offer. I'm an office manager in Florida who got interested in health IT policy because of something that happened to my mother, and I've spent the last several months trying to understand enough about the regulatory landscape to say something useful here. What I've concluded is that the transparency requirements for AI decision support tools are worth keeping, that the argument for removing them is mostly an argument about developer convenience rather than patient benefit, and that the agency should be skeptical of any framing that treats reduced disclosure as equivalent to reduced burden without examining what gets lost when the disclosure goes away.⏎⏎If there are specific technical issues with how the current model card requirements are written, fix the writing. If there are compliance pathway problems for smaller developers, address those specifically. But don't use those problems as a reason to eliminate requirements that exist because patients and clinicians need the information they provide.⏎⏎My mother's new cardiologist in Tampa, who caught the medication discrepancy, did so because she asked careful questions and looked at the full medication list rather than just accepting what was in the referral summary. That kind of careful, skeptical clinical attention is exactly what AI transparency requirements are designed to support. The clinician who has access to a model card that says "this tool was trained on a population that excluded patients with CKD stage 3 or above" is in a better position to apply that kind of judgment than one who's just told the tool produces reliable recommendations. That's the whole point. That's what's at stake in this rulemaking, and I hope the agency takes it seriously.⏎⏎I should also mention that I attempted to look up the specific regulatory citation for the DSI criterion in 45 CFR part 170 while preparing this comment, and I found the cross-references between the certification program requirements and the information blocking provisions genuinely difficult to follow, which is itself a problem worth noting because if I, as a reasonably careful reader, am struggling to understand how these provisions interact, then clinicians and smaller health systems probably are too, and that's an argument for clearer rules, not fewer rules.♔♔2026-01-23T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-23T00:00:00Z♔2025-12-12T00:00:00Z♔2026-02-10T00:00:00Z♔11♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Retain the current Decision Support Interventions (DSI) certification criterion requiring AI model cards and transparency disclosures (intended use, target population, known risks, training data characteristics, external validation) to ensure patient safety, informed clinical decision-making, and accountability in AI-assisted healthcare.♔Removing transparency requirements creates unacceptable patient safety risks when AI systems make or influence high-stakes clinical recommendations without disclosed performance data or known limitations.♔individual_consumer♔high♔concerned♔Florida♔office manager♔43♔Last spring, I spent three frustrating weeks trying to get my mother's cardiologist records transferred to her new specialist in Tampa after she was hospitalized — records that supposedly existed in some system somewhere but that nobody could seem to locate or release in a usable format. CMS-2025-0050-110072♔CMS-2025-0050♔Mark Moore♔No Delays, No Surprises Coalition♔♔♔♔Proposed deregulatory changes to ONC's certification requirements for clinical Decision Support Interventions would dangerously reduce transparency about AI tools used in clinical care, leaving clinicians without critical information about trainin...♔No Delays, No Surprises Coalition⏎1320 E. Lincolnway, Suite 12⏎Cheyenne, WY 82001⏎⏎Submitted via regulations.gov⏎⏎Re: ASTP/ONC Deregulatory Actions To Unleash Prosperity: Health Data, Technology, and Interoperability (Docket No. ONC-2025-0001)⏎⏎---⏎⏎No Delays, No Surprises Coalition Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 1⏎⏎ORGANIZATIONAL CONTEXT AND SCOPE OF COMMENT⏎⏎The No Delays, No Surprises Coalition is a patient and consumer advocacy organization based in Wyoming, focused on health data transparency, interoperability, and accountability in clinical decision support. Our membership includes patients, family caregivers, and health system researchers across the Mountain West region. We write to address a specific and, in our view, serious concern embedded in the proposed deregulatory package: the proposed removal or weakening of certification criteria governing transparency disclosures for Decision Support Interventions (DSI), including the requirements for what are commonly called "model cards" in AI-assisted clinical tools. Our comments are limited to this question. We are not addressing the full scope of the proposed rule.⏎⏎We want to be direct about something upfront. Our organization was formed in part because of how abstract regulatory language can obscure concrete harm. The phrase "reducing administrative burden for health IT developers" sounds reasonable in isolation. But when you trace that logic to its endpoint, what it sometimes means in practice is that clinicians using AI-assisted tools will have less information about what those tools were trained on, what populations they were validated against, and what failure modes they carry. That is not a bureaucratic concern. It is a patient safety concern, and the distinction matters.⏎⏎BACKGROUND ON THE DSI CERTIFICATION REQUIREMENT⏎⏎Under 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11), the 2024 HTI-1 final rule established certification criteria requiring that health IT developers document specific attributes of clinical decision support interventions that meet the definition of a "predictive DSI." These disclosures, which ONC described using the "model card" framework popularized in machine learning research (see Mitchell et al., 2019, "Model Cards for Model Reporting," Proceedings of the FAccT Conference), must include the intended use of the intervention, the intended patient population, known risks and limitations, characteristics of training data, and results of external validation. The Federal Register publication of HTI-1 at 89 Fed. Reg. 1192 (January 9, 2024) describes these requirements in substantial detail and explains ONC's reasoning for each disclosure element.⏎⏎The proposed deregulatory rule under consideration now would, as we read it, substantially relax or eliminate these requirements on the grounds that they impose compliance costs on developers and may duplicate disclosures made through other channels. We understand the argument. We do not find it persuasive, and the sections below explain why.⏎⏎No Delays, No Surprises Coalition Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 2⏎⏎WHY THE MODEL CARD REQUIREMENT SHOULD BE RETAINED IN FULL⏎⏎The core argument for retaining the DSI transparency requirement comes down to something fairly simple: clinicians cannot make informed decisions about whether to rely on an AI-generated recommendation if they do not know how that recommendation was generated. This is not a novel concern. The medical literature on clinical decision support has documented for years that the "automation bias" problem, the tendency of clinicians to defer to algorithmic outputs even when those outputs are unreliable, is directly correlated with how much information the clinician has about the system's basis for its recommendation (Goddard et al., 2012, "Automation Bias: A Systematic Review of Frequency, Effect Mediators, and Mitigators," Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association; Parasuraman & Manzey, 2010, "Complacency and Bias in Human Use of Automation," Human Factors, 52(3)).⏎⏎When a predictive DSI surfaces a sepsis alert, or flags a drug interaction, or recommends a particular imaging pathway, the clinician who sees that alert needs to know at minimum: was this model trained on a population that looks like my patient? Has it been externally validated, and if so, on what dataset? What is its known false positive and false negative rate? Without that information, the clinician is not exercising clinical judgment in partnership with a tool. The clinician is simply deferring to a black box, which is exactly the outcome that responsible AI deployment in healthcare is supposed to prevent.⏎⏎The model card framework addresses this problem in a practical, standardized way. It does not ask developers to reveal proprietary algorithms or trade secrets. It asks them to document what the tool is for, who it was built for, and what its limitations are. A 2022 analysis by Sendak et al. published in npj Digital Medicine found that fewer than 15% of commercially deployed clinical AI tools provided sufficient documentation for clinicians to assess their applicability to a specific patient population. The HTI-1 requirement was a direct regulatory response to that gap. Removing it, or making it optional, would almost certainly return the market to that baseline.⏎⏎We keep coming back to a specific concern about the "other channels" argument, the idea that developers can disclose this information through vendor contracts, product documentation, or FDA regulatory submissions rather than through ONC certification. The problem with that argument is that it mistakes availability for accessibility. A disclosure buried in a 200-page vendor contract is not functionally equivalent to a standardized, queryable model card that a clinician or a hospital informatics team can review at the point of procurement or at the point of care. Standardization is the mechanism that makes disclosure meaningful. The ONC certification requirement achieves standardization in a way that voluntary or contract-based disclosure simply does not.⏎⏎No Delays, No Surprises Coalition Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 3⏎⏎TRAINING DATA AND EXTERNAL VALIDATION: THE SPECIFIC ELEMENTS THAT MUST BE PRESERVED⏎⏎If ONC is inclined to retain some version of the DSI transparency requirement while modifying others, we want to be specific about which elements we regard as non-negotiable from a patient safety standpoint.⏎⏎The training data characteristics disclosure and the external validation disclosure are the two elements we are most concerned about losing. Here is why each matters independently.⏎⏎Training data characteristics: Clinical AI models trained predominantly on data from large academic medical centers in the Northeast and West Coast have been repeatedly shown to perform worse when deployed in rural or frontier settings, in facilities serving predominantly Medicaid populations, and in institutions with different documentation practices (Obermeyer et al., 2019, "Dissecting Racial Bias in an Algorithm Used to Manage the Health of Populations," Science, 366(6464); Gianfrancesco et al., 2018, "Potential Biases in Machine Learning Algorithms Using Electronic Health Record Data," JAMA Internal Medicine, 178(11)). Wyoming, where our organization is based, is a frontier state with a largely rural patient population, a high proportion of critical access hospitals, and care patterns that differ substantially from the academic medical center environments where most commercial clinical AI was developed. A model trained on data from Mass General or UCSF may perform very differently at a 25-bed critical access hospital in Lander, Wyoming. Clinicians and procurement officers at those facilities cannot know that without training data disclosure.⏎⏎External validation: The distinction between internal validation (testing a model on a held-out portion of the same dataset it was trained on) and external validation (testing on a genuinely independent dataset from a different institution or population) is well established in the clinical AI literature (Collins et al., 2021, "Reporting of Artificial Intelligence Prediction Models," The Lancet; Wynants et al., 2020, "Prediction Models for Diagnosis and Prognosis of COVID-19," BMJ). Internal validation results are frequently optimistic and do not generalize. External validation is the standard that serious clinical deployment requires. The HTI-1 requirement to disclose external validation results, including the characteristics of the validation dataset, is not a paperwork exercise. It is the mechanism by which a hospital system can determine whether a vendor's performance claims are based on evidence that is relevant to their patient population.⏎⏎Removing either of these disclosure requirements would, in our assessment, materially reduce the ability of health systems, clinicians, and patients to make informed decisions about AI-assisted care. The compliance cost argument does not hold up against that tradeoff. A 2023 study in Health Affairs (Matheny et al.) estimated that the average cost of developing a model card-style disclosure for a clinical AI tool is between $15,000 and $40,000 per product, depending on complexity. That cost is real but modest relative to the total development and commercialization cost of a clinical AI product, which routinely runs into the millions of dollars. Framing the model card requirement as an undue burden on developers is difficult to square with those numbers.⏎⏎No Delays, No Surprises Coalition Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 4⏎⏎THE PATIENT SAFETY DIMENSION CANNOT BE TREATED AS SECONDARY⏎⏎There is something that genuinely concerns us about how the deregulatory framing of this proposed rule positions patient safety considerations. The rule's stated rationale is reducing burden and increasing flexibility. Those are legitimate policy goals in many contexts. But in the context of AI-assisted clinical decision-making, "flexibility" for developers often translates directly into less information for clinicians and patients. The tradeoff should be made explicit, and in our reading of the proposed rule's preamble, it is not.⏎⏎The Joint Commission's Sentinel Event Alert No. 69, published in 2023, specifically identified inadequate transparency about clinical decision support tools as a contributing factor in patient safety events. The ONC itself, in the HTI-1 preamble at 89 Fed. Reg. 1192, cited a substantial body of evidence connecting algorithmic opacity to adverse clinical outcomes. The FDA's action plan for AI/ML-based software as a medical device (January 2021) similarly identified transparency and documentation as foundational requirements for safe deployment. These are not fringe positions. They reflect a broad, cross-agency consensus that transparency in clinical AI is a precondition for safety.⏎⏎Walking that consensus back, even partially, through a deregulatory rule that reduces certification requirements is a significant policy step. We do not think it has been adequately justified in the proposed rule's preamble, and we urge ONC to reconsider.⏎⏎No Delays, No Surprises Coalition Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 5⏎⏎There is also a longer-term market dynamic worth naming. If transparency disclosures are not required through certification, the vendors who choose to provide them voluntarily are placed at a competitive disadvantage relative to vendors who do not. Voluntary disclosure regimes in health IT have a poor track record precisely because of this dynamic (Kramer et al., 2022, "Voluntary vs. Mandatory Health IT Transparency: Market Evidence from EHR Certification," Health Affairs Blog; cf. Mandl & Kohane, 2012, "Escaping the EHR Trap: The Future of Health IT," New England Journal of Medicine, 366(24)). Requiring disclosure through the certification program levels the playing field and ensures that competition among developers happens on the basis of actual performance rather than on the basis of who can most effectively obscure their model's limitations from buyers.⏎⏎We want to acknowledge that there is a legitimate question about how the certification requirements interact with FDA oversight for AI tools that also qualify as software as a medical device (SaMD). Some developers have argued, with some justification, that duplicative disclosure requirements across ONC and FDA create compliance complexity without proportionate benefit (see comments submitted to FDA docket FDA-2019-N-1185 by AdvaMed and CHIME). We take that concern seriously. The answer, in our view, is not to eliminate the ONC requirement but to coordinate with FDA to ensure that complying with one disclosure framework satisfies the other where the underlying information is the same. That is a workable path. Simply removing the ONC requirement is not.⏎⏎SPECIFIC RECOMMENDATION⏎⏎ONC should retain 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11) in its current form, including the requirements for disclosure of:⏎⏎1. Intended use and clinical context⏎2. Intended patient population⏎3. Known risks, limitations, and contraindications⏎4. Training data characteristics, including source institutions, time period, and demographic composition⏎5. External validation results, including characteristics of the validation dataset and performance metrics disaggregated by relevant subgroups⏎⏎If ONC believes that specific elements of the current requirement impose disproportionate costs, we would support a targeted review process that evaluates each disclosure element individually against the evidence for its clinical utility, with public comment on any proposed modifications. What we cannot support is a blanket relaxation or removal of the requirement on general deregulatory grounds.⏎⏎We would also encourage ONC to consider whether the current certification framework adequately addresses updates to deployed models. A model card that accurately describes a clinical AI tool at the time of initial certification may not accurately describe that tool two years later if the model has been retrained or updated. The HTI-1 rule's approach to this question, addressed at 89 Fed. Reg. 1284-1287, is a starting point but may need further development as the market for continuously learning clinical AI matures (Sendak et al., 2020, "Real-World Integration of a Sepsis Deep Learning Technology into Routine Clinical Care," JAMIA Open).⏎⏎No Delays, No Surprises Coalition Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 6⏎⏎One thing we have not seen adequately addressed anywhere in this rulemaking process is the question of what happens to patients who are harmed by a clinical AI tool whose limitations were not disclosed. Under the current certification framework, a health system that relied on a certified tool with known but undisclosed limitations has at least some basis for a claim against the developer. If certification no longer requires transparency disclosures, that accountability structure weakens. The liability implications of this proposed change deserve more attention than they have received in the preamble, and we would encourage ONC to consult with CMS and with HHS Office of General Counsel on this question before finalizing the rule.⏎⏎The No Delays, No Surprises Coalition appreciates the opportunity to submit these comments. Questions may be directed to Mark Moore, Research Director, at the address above or at mmoore@nodelayssurprises.org⏎⏎---⏎⏎REFERENCES (partial; additional citations available upon request)⏎⏎Collins, G.S., et al. Our work concentrates on health information access, interoperability gaps in underserved communities, and the policy conditions that produce those gaps. We submit these comments in direct response to ASTP/ONC's proposed deregulatory actions published in the Federal Register on April 22, 2025, and we focus our analysis specifically on the proposed removal of the Decision Support Interventions certification criterion, including the associated requirements for AI model transparency disclosures.⏎⏎I want to be straightforward about what is driving these comments. Last spring, my mother spent eleven days at Forrest General Hospital outside Hattiesburg after a cardiac event. When we attempted to transfer her complete discharge records to her cardiologist at the University of Mississippi Medical Center in Jackson, we were handed a CD-ROM and told the two systems simply do not communicate with each other. I spent three days making calls, filing written requests under 45 CFR 164.524, and ultimately hand-delivering a flash drive across two counties. Three days I could not afford, and that her recovery could not afford. I have a policy background. Most patients do not. The certification standards this proposed rule would weaken were finally beginning to change the incentive structure that produces exactly that kind of outcome.⏎⏎Our comments focus on one question: whether ONC should retain the Decision Support Interventions (DSI) certification criterion that currently requires health IT developers to disclose AI model cards, including information on intended use, target population, known risks, training data characteristics, and external validation status. We believe the answer is yes, and the remainder of this comment explains why in some detail.⏎⏎⏎THE DSI CRITERION AND WHAT IT ACTUALLY REQUIRES⏎⏎Before engaging the policy question, it is worth being precise about what the DSI certification criterion requires. Under 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11), certified health IT that incorporates predictive decision support interventions must provide users with access to a standard set of source attribute disclosures. These include:⏎⏎1.  The developer's name and the intervention's name and version.⏎2.  The intervention's intended use, including the target patient population and intended care setting.⏎3.  A description of the training data used to develop the underlying model, including the demographic characteristics of that training population.⏎4.  Any known limitations or risks associated with the intervention's use in populations that were underrepresented in training data.⏎5.  A description of whether and how the intervention has been externally validated, and if so, by whom.⏎6.  Contact information for the developer for purposes of reporting concerns or adverse events.⏎⏎These requirements were codified in the HTI-1 Final Rule published January 9, 2024 (89 Fed. Reg. 1192). They do not take effect for all certified products until January 1, 2026. ONC is now proposing to remove or substantially revise them before they have been fully implemented. That sequence is worth pausing on. We are being asked to evaluate the costs of a transparency requirement that the market has not yet had a full opportunity to comply with, based on burden estimates that were developed before compliance timelines had run.⏎⏎No Delays, No Surprises Coalition | ONC-2025-0002 | Page 2⏎⏎The proposed rule's preamble acknowledges that some stakeholders have raised concerns about implementation complexity. What it does not adequately address is the asymmetry of harm between the two possible errors here. If ONC retains the DSI criterion and some developers find compliance burdensome, those developers will incur costs that are, in principle, measurable and recoverable through product pricing. If ONC removes the DSI criterion and a clinician in rural Mississippi applies an AI-generated risk score to a Black patient whose demographic group was not adequately represented in training data, the resulting harm is not recoverable at all.⏎⏎⏎WHY AI TRANSPARENCY IN CLINICAL DECISION SUPPORT IS NOT OPTIONAL⏎⏎The Coalition's position is grounded in a straightforward observation: the integration of algorithmic decision support into clinical workflows has moved faster than the clinical evidence base supporting that integration, and the DSI criterion is one of the few regulatory mechanisms that creates accountability for that gap.⏎⏎Consider the scale of what we are discussing. A 2023 survey by the American Hospital Association found that approximately 56 percent of hospitals had deployed at least one AI-enabled clinical decision support tool. The FDA's 510(k) database as of March 2025 includes more than 950 authorized AI/ML-based Software as a Medical Device (SaMD) products. ONC's own 2023 Report to Congress on Health IT noted that predictive analytics tools are now embedded in EHR workflows at a large majority of U.S. hospitals, often without clear disclosure to the clinicians using them about how those tools were trained or validated.⏎⏎The research literature on algorithmic bias in clinical AI is substantial and specific. A 2019 study published in Science (Obermeyer et al., Vol. 366, Issue 6464) found that a widely deployed commercial health risk algorithm systematically underestimated the illness burden of Black patients because it used healthcare cost as a proxy for health need, and Black patients historically had less access to care and therefore lower costs. The algorithm was being used to allocate care management resources at hundreds of health systems. The developers were not required to disclose training data characteristics or known limitations. Clinicians had no way to know.⏎⏎A 2021 study in npj Digital Medicine (Char et al.) documented similar patterns in sepsis prediction tools, where model performance degraded significantly in patient populations that were underrepresented in training data, with no disclosure mechanism requiring developers to flag that limitation. A 2022 analysis published in JAMA Network Open (Gao et al.) found that fewer than 5 percent of published clinical AI studies reported model performance stratified by race or ethnicity, meaning the published evidence base itself is inadequate for assessing differential harm.⏎⏎These are not theoretical risks. They are documented, published, peer-reviewed findings about tools that are currently deployed in clinical settings serving Medicaid patients in Mississippi, Alabama, Georgia, and other states where our member organizations operate.⏎⏎No Delays, No Surprises Coalition | ONC-2025-0002 | Page 3⏎⏎The DSI criterion does not solve all of these problems. It does not require independent testing for bias. It does not create a federal adverse event reporting system for clinical AI. What it does do is create a floor of transparency that allows clinical users, health system quality officers, and patient advocates to ask the right questions. Removing that floor before it has been fully implemented does not reduce burden in any meaningful sense. It eliminates accountability.⏎⏎⏎THE ARGUMENT THAT THE DSI CRITERION IS BURDENSOME DOES NOT HOLD UP⏎⏎ONC's proposed rule and the associated preamble discuss compliance burden in terms of developer resource requirements: the time and cost associated with compiling model documentation, maintaining disclosure records, and updating source attributes when models are retrained. We take those concerns seriously. But the burden framing, as presented, has several problems.⏎⏎First, the burden estimates in the proposed rule are based primarily on input from health IT developers, not from health systems, clinicians, or patient advocacy organizations. The HTI-1 rulemaking record includes comments from organizations like Epic Systems, Cerner (now Oracle Health), and Veradigm describing documentation burdens. It includes far fewer comments from rural critical access hospitals describing what it costs them when a deployed AI tool produces systematically biased outputs that no one disclosed. Those costs are real, they are just not captured in the burden calculus the way developer compliance costs are.⏎⏎Second, the proposed rule does not distinguish between new requirements and requirements that responsible developers should already be meeting. Any developer deploying a predictive clinical AI tool at scale should, as a matter of basic product management, know what data the model was trained on, what population it was validated in, and what its known performance limitations are. If a developer does not have that information, the problem is not that ONC is requiring disclosure of it. The problem is that the tool should not be deployed in clinical settings.⏎⏎Third, the compliance timeline matters. The DSI criterion's source attribute requirements do not become mandatory for all certified health IT until January 1, 2026. The proposed rule would revise or remove these requirements before that deadline. That means developers who have already invested in compliance infrastructure would be disadvantaged relative to those who waited, and the entire market would have received a signal that transparency investments are not durable regulatory commitments. That signal will persist long after any individual rulemaking.⏎⏎⏎No Delays, No Surprises Coalition | ONC-2025-0002 | Page 4⏎⏎WHAT REMOVAL WOULD MEAN IN PRACTICE FOR MISSISSIPPI PATIENTS⏎⏎Our member organizations include patient advocates working with rural health clinics, community health centers, and Federally Qualified Health Centers (FQHCs) in Mississippi, Alabama, and Louisiana. The patient populations these organizations serve are disproportionately Black, elderly, low-income, and medically complex. They are also the populations most likely to be underrepresented in AI training datasets developed from large academic medical center records.⏎⏎When a clinician at a rural FQHC in Sunflower County, Mississippi uses an EHR-embedded sepsis prediction tool or a readmission risk calculator, they are making clinical decisions based on that tool's output. Under current certification requirements that take effect in 2026, they would have access to documentation telling them whether patients like their patients were in the training data. Under the proposed deregulatory changes, that documentation would not be required.⏎⏎The practical consequence is not abstract. A readmission risk algorithm trained predominantly on data from large urban academic medical centers in the Northeast may perform very differently on elderly Black patients with limited transportation access and high rates of food insecurity in the Mississippi Delta. If the clinician does not know this, they cannot account for it. If the developer is not required to disclose it, the clinician has no way to find out. The certification requirement was the mechanism that would have put that information in front of the clinician. Removing it removes the mechanism.⏎⏎I keep coming back to a figure from ONC's own 2024 Health IT Report: approximately 78 percent of rural hospitals in Mississippi use certified EHR technology, and the majority of those systems include some form of embedded clinical decision support. The DSI criterion was designed precisely for this context, where clinicians are using certified systems and relying on whatever information those systems provide.⏎⏎⏎SPECIFIC RECOMMENDATIONS⏎⏎The Coalition requests that ASTP/ONC take the following actions in the final rule:⏎⏎1.  Retain the DSI certification criterion at 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11) without substantive modification to the source attribute disclosure requirements.⏎⏎2.  If ONC determines that any revision to the criterion is warranted based on the rulemaking record, limit that revision to clarifications of terminology or implementation guidance, and do not remove the core requirements for training data disclosure, known limitations disclosure, and external validation status disclosure.⏎⏎3.  Maintain the January 1, 2026 compliance deadline. Extending the deadline is a less harmful option than removing the requirement, if ONC determines some relief is appropriate for smaller developers.⏎⏎4.  Publish, as part of the final rule or accompanying guidance, ONC's analysis of how the DSI criterion interacts with FDA's regulatory framework for SaMD under 21 CFR Part 820 and the 2023 AI/ML Action Plan, so that health IT developers have a clear picture of the full compliance landscape and do not treat ONC certification as a substitute for FDA oversight.⏎⏎5.  Commission an independent assessment, through the Office of the Assistant Secretary for Planning and Evaluation (ASPE) or a comparable body, of the differential impact of current clinical AI deployments on Medicaid populations, as a precondition for any future deregulatory action affecting AI transparency requirements.⏎⏎No Delays, No Surprises Coalition | ONC-2025-0002 | Page 5⏎⏎6.  Require that any future revisions to DSI-related certification criteria be subject to a dedicated comment period with explicit outreach to patient advocacy organizations, FQHCs, rural health clinics, and state Medicaid agencies, not only to health IT developers and large health system trade associations.⏎⏎We recognize that recommendation 5 in particular goes beyond the scope of the current proposed rule. We include it because we believe the absence of that kind of population-level impact assessment is itself a gap in the evidentiary record that ONC is relying on to justify deregulatory action.⏎⏎⏎THE INFORMATION BLOCKING DIMENSION⏎⏎The proposed rule also includes revisions to information blocking exceptions under 45 CFR 171. While our primary concern in these comments is the DSI certification criterion, we want to note briefly that the proposed changes to the Fees Exception and the Infeasibility Exception raise related concerns for patient data access.⏎⏎The Fees Exception revision, as proposed, would give health IT developers more flexibility to charge for certain types of data access that are currently required to be provided at no or limited cost. For patients and advocacy organizations attempting to access electronic health information on behalf of patients, this creates a potential new barrier. The Infeasibility Exception revision would broaden the conditions under which developers and providers can decline to fulfill data access requests on grounds of technical infeasibility. Both changes, taken together with the removal of DSI transparency requirements, point in the same direction: less information available to patients and clinicians about the AI tools being used in their care, and more flexibility for developers to restrict access to the underlying data.⏎⏎We do not have detailed technical comments on the information blocking exception revisions at this time, but we flag them as a concern and note that they compound the patient safety issues raised by the DSI criterion removal.⏎⏎⏎THE REGULATORY TRAJECTORY ARGUMENT⏎⏎ONC's preamble frames this rulemaking partly as a course correction, suggesting that the HTI-1 rule imposed requirements that were more extensive than the market was ready to absorb. There is something to this argument in narrow contexts, and I am not dismissing it entirely. Implementation timelines for some HTI-1 provisions were aggressive, and there are legitimate questions about whether smaller health IT developers have the resources to comply with every certification criterion on the same schedule as Epic or Oracle Health.⏎⏎But the DSI criterion is not a case where the requirement outpaced market readiness. The clinical AI market has been growing at roughly 45 percent annually since 2020, according to figures cited in the ASTP/ONC 2024 Health IT Industry Overview. Developers have been deploying predictive tools in clinical settings for years without transparency requirements. The DSI criterion was a response to a documented market failure, specifically the absence of any standardized mechanism for disclosing model characteristics to clinical users. The burden it imposes is the burden of documenting what responsible developers should already know about their own products.⏎⏎No Delays, No Surprises Coalition | ONC-2025-0002 | Page 6⏎⏎There is also a longer regulatory trajectory argument worth making. The United States is currently in the early stages of what will be a decades-long process of integrating AI into clinical medicine. The regulatory choices made now will shape developer behavior, procurement decisions, and clinical culture for a long time. If ONC removes the DSI transparency requirements in 2025, before they have taken full effect, the message to the market is that transparency is negotiable, that documentation requirements will be rolled back when developers push back, and that the certification program is not a durable basis for accountability. That message will be heard by developers, by health system procurement officers, and by the clinicians who use these tools. It will not be easily corrected by a subsequent rulemaking.⏎⏎A 2024 report from the Brookings Institution's Center for Technology Innovation documented exactly this dynamic in the context of financial services AI regulation: early deregulatory signals in the 2017-2019 period made it substantially harder for regulators to reimpose transparency requirements after documented harms emerged, because the market had organized around the deregulated state. There is no reason to think health care AI will be different.⏎⏎⏎ON THE QUESTION OF INNOVATION⏎⏎The proposed rule's title includes the phrase "Unleash Prosperity," and the preamble makes clear that one of its animating concerns is that certification requirements may be slowing health IT innovation. We take this concern seriously. Regulatory burden is real, and there are certification criteria in the ONC program that impose costs without commensurate benefits. We are not opposed to deregulatory action as a general matter.⏎⏎What we object to is treating the DSI transparency requirements as a burden without asking what those requirements are a burden for. They exist because clinical AI tools have documented differential performance across demographic groups. They exist because clinicians in rural Mississippi are using these tools without knowing what populations they were trained on. They exist because, without them, the only people who know the limitations of a deployed AI model are the developers who built it and the large health systems that negotiated custom validation studies. Everyone else is flying blind.⏎⏎Innovation in health IT is genuinely valuable. But innovation that produces tools with undisclosed performance limitations, deployed in clinical settings serving vulnerable populations without any transparency requirement, is not the kind of innovation that produces better health outcomes. The DSI criterion was designed to make innovation more accountable, not to stop it.⏎⏎No Delays, No Surprises Coalition | ONC-2025-0002 | Page 7⏎⏎I do think there is a version of this conversation worth having about whether the specific documentation format required by the source attribute disclosures could be streamlined, or whether the compliance timeline for very small developers could be extended. Those are reasonable questions. But the proposed rule does not ask those questions. It proposes to remove the substantive transparency requirements, not to refine them. That is a different action with different consequences.⏎⏎⏎RESPONSE TO ANTICIPATED COUNTERARGUMENTS⏎⏎We anticipate that commenters representing health IT developers will make several arguments in support of the proposed removal of DSI requirements. We want to address a few of them directly.⏎⏎Argument: The DSI criterion duplicates FDA requirements for AI-enabled SaMD.⏎⏎Response: This argument is incorrect as a factual matter. FDA's 510(k) clearance process for AI/ML-based SaMD does not require disclosure of training data characteristics or known performance limitations to end users in the clinical workflow. FDA authorization means a device meets safety and effectiveness standards for its cleared indication. It does not mean that clinicians using the device have access to information about how it performs in their specific patient population. The DSI criterion fills a gap that FDA regulation does not address. The two frameworks are complements, not substitutes.⏎⏎Argument: Market competition will drive developers to provide transparency voluntarily.⏎⏎Response: The history of health IT does not support this. Before the information blocking provisions of the 21st Century Cures Act (Public Law 114-255), health IT vendors routinely charged for data access and imposed technical barriers to interoperability, arguing that market competition would eventually solve the problem. It did not. The problem was addressed by regulation. There is no reason to expect that AI transparency will behave differently. The developers with the most market power have the least incentive to disclose limitations that might disadvantage their products in procurement processes.⏎⏎Argument: Clinicians already know the limitations of the tools they use.⏎⏎Response: The published evidence directly contradicts this. A 2022 survey published in the Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association (JAMIA, Vol. 29, Issue 4) found that fewer than 30 percent of clinicians at academic medical centers could accurately describe the training data sources for the AI decision support tools they used daily. At community hospitals and FQHCs, that figure was lower. Clinicians are not failing here because they are incurious or negligent. They are failing because the information is not available to them in any standardized form. That is exactly the problem the DSI criterion is designed to solve.⏎⏎No Delays, No Surprises Coalition | ONC-2025-0002 | Page 8⏎⏎⏎A NOTE ON THE RULEMAKING PROCESS⏎⏎The Coalition also wants to register a procedural concern. The proposed rule was published with a 60-day comment period. The HTI-1 rule, which established the DSI criterion being proposed for removal, had a 60-day comment period for a rulemaking that was substantially more complex and that established new requirements rather than removing existing ones. We believe that a rulemaking proposing to remove transparency requirements that have been the subject of significant public investment, both by developers preparing for compliance and by patient advocates working to educate their communities about new rights, warrants at least the same level of public engagement as the rulemaking that created those requirements.⏎⏎We are also concerned that the comment period did not include targeted outreach to patient advocacy organizations in rural and underserved communities. The Federal Register notice was published in standard form. No Delays, No Surprises Coalition became aware of this rulemaking through a listserv operated by the National Partnership for Women and Families. Many of our member organizations did not. A rulemaking with direct implications for patient safety in vulnerable populations should include proactive outreach to the organizations that represent those populations, not just to the health IT industry stakeholders who have standing relationships with ONC.⏎⏎The 21st Century Cures Act's patient access provisions at 42 U.S.C. 300jj-52 include language about ensuring that the interests of patients and consumers are considered in ONC certification program decisions. We believe a genuine commitment to that language requires more than a standard Federal Register comment period when the proposed action is the removal of patient safety protections.⏎⏎⏎SUMMARY OF POSITION⏎⏎The No Delays, No Surprises Coalition's position is that the DSI certification criterion requiring AI model card disclosures should be retained without substantive modification. The case for retention rests on the following:⏎⏎o    Clinical AI tools are currently deployed at scale in health systems serving vulnerable populations, without any standardized mechanism for disclosing model characteristics to clinical users.⏎⏎o    The research literature documents consistent, significant differential performance of clinical AI tools across demographic groups, with particular impact on Black patients, elderly patients, and patients in low-resource settings.⏎⏎o    The DSI criterion was designed specifically to address this gap, and its compliance deadline has not yet passed. There is no empirical basis for concluding that it is unworkable.⏎⏎o    The burden imposed by the DSI criterion is the burden of documenting information that responsible developers should already possess about their own products.⏎⏎o    Removing the requirement sends a durable market signal that transparency investments are not a stable basis for product development, which will depress voluntary transparency efforts for years after any individual rulemaking.⏎⏎o    The populations most harmed by clinical AI with undisclosed performance limitations are the same populations that have historically had the least access to health information and the least capacity to advocate for themselves.⏎⏎No Delays, No Surprises Coalition | ONC-2025-0002 | Page 9⏎⏎⏎The Coalition urges ASTP/ONC to retain the DSI certification criterion in full, to maintain the January 1, 2026 compliance timeline, and to resist the framing that transparency requirements are inherently in tension with innovation. They are in tension with a specific kind of innovation: the kind that deploys products with undisclosed limitations in clinical settings serving patients who have no way of knowing what they are relying on.⏎⏎There is a version of health IT deregulation that makes sense: reducing duplicative documentation requirements, streamlining certification processes that impose costs without producing usable information, and extending compliance timelines when market readiness genuinely lags. The DSI criterion is not in that category. It is a targeted, minimum-floor transparency requirement for a class of tools that are already causing documented harm in the absence of disclosure obligations.⏎⏎The experience my family had at Forrest General last spring is one data point. What it illustrated was that information gaps in health IT do not fall randomly. They fall on patients and families who are already navigating a difficult situation, who do not have the institutional relationships or policy background to demand better, and who are dependent on the decisions of developers and regulators they will never meet. The DSI criterion was one attempt to tilt that balance in a different direction. Removing it before it has taken effect is not a deregulatory efficiency gain. It is a choice about whose interests the certification program is designed to serve.⏎⏎The Coalition is available to provide additional information, participate in technical discussions, or connect ONC staff with member organizations working in rural Mississippi and the broader Gulf South region. We can be reached at the contact information above.⏎⏎No Delays, No Surprises Coalition | ONC-2025-0002 | Page 10⏎⏎For the record, we want to note that the Coalition submitted comments on the HTI-1 proposed rule in October 2023 (Docket No. ONC-2023-0004), specifically in support of the DSI criterion, and that those comments included detailed input from FQHCs in Leflore County and Harrison County, Mississippi about the clinical decision support tools in current use at their facilities and the absence of any documentation about training data or validation populations. We reference those comments here because the factual record they established remains relevant and, to our knowledge, was not specifically addressed in the HTI-1 final rule preamble's response to comments section.⏎⏎We also want to flag, for whatever it is worth procedurally, that the proposed rule's Regulatory Impact Analysis does not appear to include any estimate of the costs associated with clinical AI adverse events attributable to undisclosed performance limitations. The RIA estimates compliance costs for developers. It does not estimate the costs, in medical harm, delayed treatment, or excess utilization, of deploying AI tools without transparency requirements. That asymmetry in the cost accounting is, in our view, a significant methodological gap that ONC should address before finalizing any changes to the DSI criterion.♔♔2026-01-06T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-06T00:00:00Z♔2025-12-12T00:00:00Z♔2026-02-10T00:00:00Z♔14♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Retain the current Decision Support Interventions (DSI) certification criterion requiring AI model cards and transparency disclosures (intended use, target population, known risks, training data characteristics, external validation) to ensure patient safety, informed clinical decision-making, and accountability in AI-assisted healthcare.♔The 'black box' problem is a documented barrier to AI adoption in healthcare; model cards directly address clinician and organizational concerns about trustworthiness and are a proven mechanism to build confidence.♔advocacy_group♔high♔angry♔Mississippi♔senior policy analyst♔44♔Last spring, my mother spent eleven days in a Regional Medical Center outside Hattiesburg after a cardiac event, and when we tried to get her complete discharge records transferred to her cardiologist in Jackson, we were handed a CD-ROM and told the two systems simply "don't talk to each other."
