CMS-2025-0050-110074♔CMS-2025-0050♔Sharon Scott♔Dental Standards Institute♔♔♔♔The Dental Standards Institute raises concerns about inadequate stakeholder outreach to the dental sector and argues that proposed changes to ONC certification criteria and information blocking exceptions would weaken baseline interoperability pro...♔Dental Standards Institute⏎Comments on ASTP/ONC Deregulatory Actions To Unleash Prosperity: Health Data, Technology, and Interoperability⏎Submitted via regulations.gov⏎⏎---⏎⏎PRELIMINARY STATEMENT⏎⏎The Dental Standards Institute is a nonprofit organization focused on health data standards and interoperability policy affecting dental and oral health providers across the United States. Our membership includes dental practices, oral health clinics, and affiliated patient advocacy programs in 23 states. We submit these comments with some frustration, and I want to be direct about that frustration before getting into the substance, because the procedural problems here are not separable from the policy problems.⏎⏎I found out about this rulemaking from my neighbor. That is not a metaphor or an exaggeration. I have spent over a decade working in health policy and campaign advocacy, I run an organization whose core mission is directly affected by ONC certification decisions, and I learned about this proposed rule through an informal conversation in April. Not through the Federal Register. Not through a stakeholder notification from HHS. Not through any outreach from ASTP or ONC. From my neighbor, who happened to catch a reference in a newsletter she subscribes to for unrelated reasons.⏎⏎I want to be careful not to overstate what that means procedurally. The Federal Register notice is public record. The comment period is technically open. But the question I keep coming back to is: for whom is this process actually designed to be accessible? Because the answer, based on how this particular rulemaking has been communicated, does not appear to include small and mid-size advocacy organizations, patient groups, or the dental sector specifically. The comment window for a rule of this scope should not depend on professional proximity to inside-the-Beltway health IT networks. If the goal is genuine public participation, the outreach infrastructure has to match that goal.⏎⏎---⏎⏎SECTION 1: THE TRANSPARENCY PROBLEM IS STRUCTURAL, NOT INCIDENTAL⏎⏎o The proposed rule touches certification criteria under 45 CFR Part 170, revisions to information blocking exceptions under 45 CFR Part 171, and consequential changes to what data actors are required to share and when.⏎⏎o These are not minor technical adjustments. Removing certification criteria affects what health IT developers are obligated to build. Loosening information blocking exceptions affects what patients can access and when. These downstream effects land on patients, not on health IT vendors.⏎⏎o The Federal Register notice ran on [DATE], with a comment period that, depending on when a stakeholder learned of it, effectively gave many organizations fewer than 30 days to prepare substantive technical comments. For reference, the original information blocking rules under the 21st Century Cures Act (Pub. L. 114-255) generated extensive stakeholder engagement over multiple years, with RFIs, listening sessions, and dedicated outreach. The contrast here is notable.⏎⏎o The Dental Standards Institute submitted formal comments on ONC's 2020 interoperability rule (85 FR 25642) and on the HTI-1 rule (88 FR 23746). In both cases, we received advance notice through ONC stakeholder channels and had adequate time to coordinate member input. That did not happen here.⏎⏎o We are not arguing that the rulemaking is procedurally invalid. We are arguing that "technically compliant" and "genuinely transparent" are not the same thing, and this process has been the former without being the latter.⏎⏎What this means practically: organizations like ours, which track dental health IT standards and oral health data policy, often fall outside the primary stakeholder networks that HHS engages when it thinks about health data regulation. The dental sector is consistently treated as peripheral to health IT policy conversations, even though approximately 200 million Americans see a dental provider in any given year (CDC oral health data, 2022), and oral health data interoperability has direct implications for chronic disease management, behavioral health integration, and Medicaid care coordination. When ONC proposes changes to certification criteria that affect how health IT modules are built and certified, those changes affect dental EHR systems too. The omission of the dental sector from early stakeholder engagement on this rule is not a new problem, but it is a persistent one.⏎⏎---⏎⏎SECTION 2: CONCERNS ABOUT REMOVING CERTIFICATION CRITERIA⏎⏎The proposed rule would eliminate or consolidate certain certification criteria currently required under the ONC Health IT Certification Program. The Institute has specific concerns about what this means for data portability and patient access, particularly in the context of small dental practices that rely on certified health IT modules to ensure baseline interoperability.⏎⏎My mother spent three weeks last spring trying to get her dental records transferred between two providers in Phoenix. Both were using software from the same vendor. One clinic told her their system "didn't support" the export format the other required. When I finally got someone on the phone at the vendor's support line, the person acknowledged that the interoperability tools existed but had simply never been configured for that clinic. The configuration was optional. The clinic had never turned it on. Nothing in their certification status required them to.⏎⏎That is the direct, practical consequence of treating interoperability as optional infrastructure. And the direction this proposed rule moves, in removing or loosening certain certification criteria, goes further in that direction rather than correcting it.⏎⏎Specific concerns on certification changes:⏎⏎1. Removal of certain data export and patient access certification criteria would reduce the baseline floor for what certified health IT must do. Vendors may still build these features, but without certification requirements, there is no mechanism to ensure small practices actually have access to functional interoperability tools, as opposed to tools that exist in the software but require configuration, training, or additional fees to activate.⏎⏎2. The proposed changes to the Standardized API certification criteria (currently under 45 CFR 170.315(g)(10)) could affect how third-party applications access patient data. The HL7 FHIR standard has been a meaningful floor for patient-facing data access. Any loosening of the API certification requirements should be accompanied by a clear explanation of what replaces that floor.⏎⏎3. The Institute notes that the proposed rule does not appear to include a specific analysis of impacts on dental health IT systems or oral health data standards. Given that dental data uses different code sets (SNODENT, CDT) than medical data, and that most dental EHR systems are not integrated with hospital or physician EHR systems, the interoperability implications for the dental sector are distinct and deserve specific treatment. We are not aware of any dental-sector stakeholder engagement that informed this proposal.⏎⏎---⏎⏎SECTION 3: INFORMATION BLOCKING EXCEPTION AMENDMENTS⏎⏎Dental Standards Institute | ASTP/ONC Deregulatory Actions | Page 3⏎⏎The proposed amendments to information blocking exceptions under 45 CFR Part 171 are the part of this rule that concerns us most from a patient access standpoint. The information blocking provisions of the 21st Century Cures Act were designed to prevent health IT actors from impeding the flow of electronic health information. The exceptions to those provisions are supposed to be narrow and justified.⏎⏎The proposed rule would expand the scope of the Licensing Exception and the Privacy Exception in ways that, depending on implementation, could make it easier for health IT vendors to restrict data access by characterizing restrictions as licensing or privacy-protective measures. We are not saying that is the intent. But the practical effect, in a market where health IT vendors have significant leverage over small practices and where patients often have limited ability to advocate for their own data access, is worth examining carefully.⏎⏎The ONC's own information blocking complaint data (as reported through the OIG referral process under 42 U.S.C. 300jj-52) has documented patterns of interference by health IT developers that look a lot like what happened to my mother. The configuration is optional. The fee for activation is not disclosed upfront. The interoperability feature exists but requires a support call to enable. Whether any of that constitutes actionable information blocking under current rules is genuinely unclear, and the proposed changes to the exceptions do not, in our reading, make it clearer. They make it less clear.⏎⏎We would specifically ask ONC to address:⏎⏎o How the proposed changes to the Licensing Exception interact with the existing "without special effort" standard in the definition of electronic health information access (45 CFR 171.102)⏎⏎o Whether the proposed Privacy Exception amendments create new pathways for health IT vendors to characterize interoperability restrictions as privacy protections in ways that would not have been permissible under the 2020 final rule⏎⏎o What complaint and enforcement mechanisms remain available to patients and providers if a vendor invokes an expanded exception to justify restricting data access⏎⏎o Whether ONC has analyzed the specific impact on dental health IT vendors, who operate in a less regulated market segment than hospital EHR developers⏎⏎---⏎⏎SECTION 4: PROCESS RECOMMENDATIONS⏎⏎The Institute recognizes that regulatory burden reduction is a legitimate policy goal. We are not opposed to this rule on principle. There are provisions here that likely do reduce unnecessary compliance costs for small practices, and we do not want to suggest otherwise.⏎⏎But the process by which this rule was developed and communicated has not been adequate for a change of this scope. The following are process-level recommendations that we would ask HHS and ONC to consider, independent of the substantive merits of the proposed changes:⏎⏎1. Convene a dental sector stakeholder session before finalizing this rule. The American Dental Association, the Dental Trade Alliance, and organizations like the Dental Standards Institute should have been part of pre-proposal outreach. They were not, as far as we can determine.⏎⏎2. Extend the comment period. The current window does not give smaller organizations sufficient time to compile member input, consult with technical staff, and submit substantive comments. A 60-day extension would be appropriate given the scope of the changes.⏎⏎3. Publish a plain-language summary of the specific certification criteria being removed and the specific exception language being changed, with a side-by-side comparison of current and proposed regulatory text. The current proposal requires significant technical expertise to parse, and that creates a systematic bias toward large health IT vendors in the comment process.⏎⏎4. Commit to a post-final-rule review of patient data access complaints. If the loosening of certification criteria and information blocking exceptions results in measurable increases in patient data access complaints to ONC or OIG, there should be a defined process for revisiting those changes.⏎⏎---⏎⏎The comment period for a rule that affects patient data access for every person who uses a health IT system in this country should not be something people find out about from their neighbors. I recognize that sounds like a complaint about communications rather than about policy, but I genuinely don't think those are separable. A rulemaking process that systematically excludes the dental sector, small advocacy organizations, and patients who aren't already plugged into health IT policy networks is going to produce rules that reflect the interests of the stakeholders who were in the room. That's not a partisan point. It's just how rulemaking works when outreach is inadequate.⏎⏎The Dental Standards Institute requests that ONC provide written responses to the specific questions raised in Section 3 of these comments, and that the agency document what stakeholder engagement occurred prior to the publication of this proposed rule and which sector-specific organizations were contacted.⏎⏎Respectfully submitted,⏎⏎Sharon Scott⏎Campaign Director, Dental Standards Institute⏎[contact information on file with submitting organization]♔♔2026-01-02T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-02T00:00:00Z♔2025-12-12T00:00:00Z♔2026-02-10T00:00:00Z♔6♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Retain the current Decision Support Interventions (DSI) certification criterion requiring AI model cards and transparency disclosures (intended use, target population, known risks, training data characteristics, external validation) to ensure patient safety, informed clinical decision-making, and accountability in AI-assisted healthcare.♔Removing DSI transparency requirements creates a dangerous regulatory gap where AI-based clinical decision support tools face fewer disclosure obligations than traditional medical devices, undermining consistent safety standards.♔advocacy_group♔high♔angry♔Arizona♔campaign director♔35♔Last spring, I watched my mother spend three weeks trying to get her dental records transferred between two providers in the same city — providers both using software from the same vendor — because one clinic claimed their system "didn't support" the export format the other required. CMS-2025-0050-110077♔CMS-2025-0050♔Jessica Martin♔American College Of Physicians♔♔♔♔The American College of Physicians urges ONC to retain the Decision Support Interventions (DSI) certification criterion requiring AI model card transparency disclosures, arguing that removing these requirements would create concrete patient safety...♔American College of Physicians⏎Comments on ASTP/ONC Proposed Rule: Deregulatory Actions To Unleash Prosperity: Health Data, Technology, and Interoperability⏎Submitted via regulations.gov⏎Docket No. ONC-2025-0001⏎⏎Contact:⏎Division of Governmental Affairs and Public Policy⏎American College of Physicians⏎25 Massachusetts Avenue, NW, Suite 700⏎Washington, DC 20001⏎policy@acponline.org⏎⏎ACP Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 1⏎⏎⏎EXECUTIVE SUMMARY⏎⏎The American College of Physicians (ACP) submits these comments in response to the proposed rule issued by the Assistant Secretary for Technology Policy and the Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology (ASTP/ONC) concerning deregulatory revisions to the ONC Health IT Certification Program and amendments to information blocking definitions and exceptions. ACP represents approximately 160,000 internal medicine physicians and subspecialists across the United States, and our members interact daily with certified health IT systems in clinical environments where the accuracy and transparency of algorithmic decision support tools directly affects patient care.⏎⏎We appreciate the opportunity to engage on these proposals. ACP shares the goal of reducing unnecessary administrative burden on health IT developers and healthcare providers. Some of the proposed revisions may accomplish that in ways we could support. However, the College has significant concerns about one specific proposal: the removal or relaxation of the Decision Support Interventions (DSI) certification criterion requiring AI model cards and transparency disclosures. We believe this particular change would be a mistake, and we are asking ONC to retain these requirements in full.⏎⏎The remainder of this comment addresses that question in depth. We have deliberately not attempted to respond to every element of the proposed rule; the College's comments here are focused specifically on the DSI transparency provisions, because that is where we believe the risk to patients and clinicians is most concrete and most immediate.⏎⏎ACP Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 2⏎⏎⏎BACKGROUND AND ORGANIZATIONAL INTEREST⏎⏎ACP has engaged consistently with ONC on health IT policy since the enactment of the Health Information Technology for Economic and Clinical Health (HITECH) Act and through successive rulemakings under the 21st Century Cures Act (Pub. L. 114-255). Our interest in the DSI certification criterion is not abstract. The College has published policy positions on clinical decision support and artificial intelligence in medicine, including a 2019 position paper in the Annals of Internal Medicine (Obermeyer et al. framework for algorithmic equity is one touchstone we return to frequently), and we have followed the development of the DSI criterion through the 2024 HTI-1 final rule (89 Fed. Reg. 1192, Jan. 9, 2024) with close attention.⏎⏎Our members are the end users of these systems. When a certified EHR presents an algorithmic recommendation for sepsis risk, anticoagulation dosing, or readmission probability, it is an internist or a hospitalist who has to decide whether to act on it, modify it, or override it. That physician needs to know something about where the recommendation came from. What population was the model trained on? Has it been validated externally, on patients who look like the ones in this clinic? What are its known failure modes? Those are not bureaucratic questions. They are clinical questions, and answering them is the whole point of the model card requirement.⏎⏎The College is also writing from a research perspective. One of our postdoctoral fellows spent the better part of last spring trying to extract longitudinal EHR data for a federally funded study on post-acute COVID-19 outcomes. The health system's vendor cited a gap in certification requirements to justify withholding structured data in a usable format. The team ended up manually abstracting records from PDF summaries, which introduced enough measurement error to require a full study redesign and cost nearly a complete grant cycle. We are not suggesting that removing the DSI transparency requirement would cause that exact problem, but it illustrates something we keep coming back to: certification gaps have real consequences, and those consequences are often invisible until someone is already downstream of them.⏎⏎ACP Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 3⏎⏎⏎THE DSI CERTIFICATION CRITERION AND WHAT IS AT STAKE⏎⏎The DSI criterion, as finalized in HTI-1, requires that certified Health IT Modules used to support clinical decision-making through AI or predictive models disclose specific information about those models. This includes: the intended use of the model, the target population for which it was designed and validated, known risks or limitations, characteristics of the training data, and any external validation that has been conducted. See 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11) as finalized. These disclosures are often referred to collectively as "model cards," a term borrowed from the machine learning literature (Mitchell et al., 2019, "Model Cards for Model Reporting," ACM FAccT Conference Proceedings).⏎⏎ONC's proposal, as the College reads it, would reduce or eliminate the requirement that these disclosures be surfaced to clinicians at the point of care or otherwise made accessible through the certified module. The rationale offered in the proposed rule is that these requirements create compliance burden for health IT developers and that market forces will drive transparency without regulatory compulsion.⏎⏎The College respectfully disagrees with both premises.⏎⏎On burden: the information required by the model card criterion is information that any responsible AI developer should already have. A developer who cannot describe the intended use of their model, or who does not know what population it was trained on, has a more serious problem than regulatory non-compliance. The documentation burden is not generating this information from scratch; it is organizing and presenting information that responsible development practices require anyway. ONC's own regulatory impact analysis in the HTI-1 rulemaking estimated that the documentation cost per model was relatively modest when amortized over deployment lifecycles. (89 Fed. Reg. at 1284-1286.) We do not see evidence in this proposed rule that those estimates were wrong, or that the burden has proven substantially greater in practice.⏎⏎On market forces: the history of health IT interoperability does not give us much confidence that voluntary disclosure will produce consistent, clinically meaningful transparency. The information blocking provisions in the 21st Century Cures Act existed precisely because voluntary cooperation was insufficient. (See 45 CFR Part 171.) We see no reason to expect AI transparency to work differently.⏎⏎ACP Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 4⏎⏎⏎PATIENT SAFETY CONSIDERATIONS⏎⏎ACP's most direct concern is patient safety. AI-assisted clinical decision support tools are increasingly embedded in the workflows of our members. A 2022 survey by the American Medical Association found that 37% of physicians were using at least one AI-enabled tool in their practice, up from 14% in 2019. The pace of deployment has not slowed. At the same time, there is a growing body of evidence that commercially deployed clinical AI tools can perform poorly on patient populations that are underrepresented in training data.⏎⏎One of the most extensively documented cases is the Optum risk stratification algorithm studied by Obermeyer et al. (Science, 2019, Vol. 366, Issue 6464, pp. 447-453), which systematically underestimated the health needs of Black patients because it used healthcare costs as a proxy for health status. That algorithm was deployed widely before the bias was identified. The model card requirement, had it existed and been enforced at the time, would have required the vendor to disclose the training data characteristics and known limitations. A clinician seeing that the model was trained predominantly on patients with certain insurance or geographic profiles might have applied it differently, or flagged it for review.⏎⏎The College is not claiming that model cards are a complete solution to algorithmic bias. They are not. But they are a necessary condition for informed clinical use, and removing the requirement creates a specific and foreseeable gap. When a physician uses a clinical decision support tool without knowing its validation history, they cannot exercise the kind of informed professional judgment that good medicine requires. That is not a hypothetical risk; it is a structural one.⏎⏎There is also the question of liability and accountability. If a DSI tool produces a recommendation that contributes to patient harm, and no model card was required, the attending physician has no way to know whether the tool was ever validated on a population resembling their patient. The audit trail that model cards create is not just useful for research; it is part of how the healthcare system attributes responsibility when things go wrong.⏎⏎ACP Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 5⏎⏎⏎SPECIFIC CONCERNS ABOUT THE PROPOSED CHANGES⏎⏎The College has identified several specific aspects of the proposed revisions that concern us.⏎⏎First, the proposed rule appears to contemplate removing the requirement that model card information be surfaced through the certified module itself, potentially allowing developers to satisfy transparency obligations through external documentation that clinicians would have to seek out separately. We think this would be largely ineffective. A physician in the middle of a clinical encounter does not have time to navigate to a vendor portal to read a PDF. If the transparency requirement is not integrated into the clinical workflow, it will not be used. The whole point of certification is to ensure that required functionality is present where clinicians actually work.⏎⏎Second, the proposal seems to weaken the requirement for external validation disclosure. The difference between a model that has been internally validated by its developer and one that has been externally validated on an independent dataset is clinically significant. Internal validation can mask overfitting and population-specific artifacts that only become apparent when the model is tested on different data. Requiring disclosure of external validation status is not a high bar; it is a basic quality signal. Removing it leaves clinicians without a key piece of information.⏎⏎Third, the College is concerned about the interaction between this proposal and the broader deregulatory direction of the rulemaking. If certification requirements for AI transparency are relaxed at the same time that information blocking exceptions are broadened, there is a compounding effect: clinicians may have less information about the tools they are using, and researchers may have less access to the data needed to evaluate those tools independently. We do not think ONC has fully analyzed this interaction in the proposed rule.⏎⏎ACP Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 6⏎⏎⏎RECOMMENDATIONS⏎⏎Based on the foregoing, the American College of Physicians makes the following specific recommendations:⏎⏎1. Retain the DSI certification criterion at 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11) in its current form, including all required model card disclosures: intended use, target population, known risks and limitations, training data characteristics, and external validation status.⏎⏎2. Require that model card information be accessible within the certified Health IT Module at the point of care, not solely through external documentation portals. If ONC believes that full inline display creates workflow disruption, the College would support a compromise requiring that model card information be accessible within two clicks from the point of care, with a summary of key limitations visible at the point of recommendation.⏎⏎3. Retain the external validation disclosure requirement as a distinct element, separate from internal validation. ONC should consider requiring developers to specify the date and source of any external validation study, so that clinicians can assess whether the validation population is relevant to their patient context.⏎⏎4. Conduct a formal analysis of the interaction between the proposed DSI changes and the proposed amendments to information blocking exceptions, specifically examining whether the combined effect would reduce clinician access to the information needed to evaluate AI tool performance.⏎⏎5. Before finalizing any reduction in DSI transparency requirements, ONC should commission or require the submission of empirical evidence that current model card requirements impose a burden disproportionate to their clinical value. The College is not aware of such evidence in the record.⏎⏎6. If ONC proceeds with any modifications to the DSI criterion, it should establish a minimum floor of required disclosures that cannot be waived by certification bodies or satisfied through summary documentation alone.⏎⏎ACP Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 7⏎⏎⏎THE BROADER CONTEXT OF AI GOVERNANCE IN HEALTHCARE⏎⏎The College wants to be clear that we are not opposed to AI in clinical medicine, and we are not reflexively opposed to reducing certification burden where that burden is genuinely unnecessary. Some of the other proposals in this rulemaking may represent sensible streamlining, and we recognize that ONC faces real constraints in designing a certification program that works for developers of varying sizes and resources.⏎⏎But AI governance is one area where the deregulatory instinct needs to be checked carefully against patient safety considerations. The Food and Drug Administration has been grappling with how to regulate AI-based Software as a Medical Device (SaMD) under its existing framework, and the challenges are well-documented. (See FDA, "Artificial Intelligence/Machine Learning (AI/ML)-Based Software as a Medical Device Action Plan," January 2021.) ONC's DSI certification criterion is one of the few existing regulatory mechanisms that requires AI transparency specifically in the EHR context, where most clinical AI deployment actually happens. Weakening it now, before the field has developed robust voluntary alternatives, seems premature.⏎⏎The National Academy of Medicine has published extensively on the need for AI accountability frameworks in healthcare. (See Matheny et al., "Artificial Intelligence in Health Care: The Hope, the Hype, the Promise, the Peril," NAM Special Publication, 2019.) The consensus in that literature is not that regulation is unnecessary; it is that regulation needs to be thoughtful and targeted. The model card requirement is both. It targets a specific, well-defined gap in clinical information. It does not require developers to change their models; it requires them to describe their models. That is a modest ask.⏎⏎One thing the College keeps coming back to is that the clinicians who will be most affected by this change are not the ones who will be involved in writing comments to this docket. A primary care physician in a rural practice in eastern North Carolina, seeing 25 patients a day, is not tracking ASTP/ONC rulemaking. That physician is trusting that the certified tools they use have been held to reasonable standards of transparency. If we remove those standards, that trust becomes unwarranted, and the physician has no way of knowing it.⏎⏎ACP Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 8⏎⏎⏎A NOTE ON THE RESEARCH IMPLICATIONS⏎⏎The College also wants to flag, somewhat separately from the patient safety argument, that the DSI transparency requirements have value for health services research. Model cards, when they are consistently required and structured, create a data infrastructure that researchers can use to study AI tool performance across populations. If developers are not required to disclose training data characteristics in a standardized format, it becomes very difficult to conduct the kind of comparative effectiveness research that would let us know whether these tools are working as intended.⏎⏎This matters more than it might appear. The 21st Century Cures Act's interoperability provisions were partly motivated by the recognition that fragmented health data impedes both care delivery and research. (See 42 U.S.C. 300jj-11.) The DSI transparency requirements are a small but real contribution to that same goal: building a health IT ecosystem where the tools in use can be evaluated, compared, and improved. Removing them does not just affect individual clinical encounters; it affects the ability of the research community to generate the evidence base that will eventually tell us which AI tools are worth using.⏎⏎The experience described earlier in these comments, where a federally funded research team lost nearly a full grant cycle because structured data was withheld in a usable format, is a reminder of how quickly certification gaps translate into research setbacks. The DSI transparency requirement is not a research mandate, but it contributes to an environment where research is possible. We would be cautious about eroding that.⏎⏎ACP Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 9⏎⏎⏎RESPONSE TO THE PROPOSED RATIONALE FOR DEREGULATION⏎⏎ONC's proposed rule offers several arguments for reducing the DSI certification requirements. The College has tried to engage with each of them honestly, even where we disagree.⏎⏎The argument that market forces will drive voluntary transparency is the one we find least persuasive, for reasons already described. But we want to be fair to the underlying intuition, which is that heavy-handed regulation can sometimes crowd out better voluntary solutions. The College's response is that we have not yet seen what those voluntary solutions look like in the AI transparency space. The Partnership on AI, the Coalition for Health AI (CHAI), and other multi-stakeholder bodies are doing important work on voluntary AI standards. (See CHAI, "Blueprint for Trustworthy AI Implementation Guidance and Assurance for Healthcare," 2023.) But those frameworks are not yet mature enough to substitute for a baseline regulatory requirement. If and when voluntary frameworks achieve consistent adoption and enforcement, ONC could revisit the certification requirement. That is not where we are now.⏎⏎The argument that the model card requirement creates disproportionate burden for smaller developers is worth taking seriously. The College acknowledges that a small EHR vendor or a startup building a narrow CDS tool may face real challenges in producing comprehensive model documentation. We would support ONC exploring tiered compliance pathways for developers below a certain revenue or market-share threshold, provided that the core disclosures are still required and that there is a credible pathway to full compliance over time. What we would not support is eliminating the requirement entirely on the grounds that it burdens some developers, when the practical effect would be to leave all clinicians without the information they need.⏎⏎The argument that the current DSI criterion is technically difficult to implement in a consistent way has some merit. The College is aware that there has been inconsistency in how certification bodies have assessed compliance with the model card elements, and that some developers have produced model cards that are technically compliant but practically uninformative. This is a real problem, but the solution is better implementation guidance and more rigorous certification review, not removal of the requirement. ONC should work with the National Committee for Quality Assurance (NCQA), the American Board of Internal Medicine Foundation, and other relevant bodies to develop clearer standards for what constitutes a clinically meaningful model card disclosure.⏎⏎ACP Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 10⏎⏎⏎CONCLUSION OF SUBSTANTIVE COMMENTS⏎⏎The American College of Physicians urges ONC to retain the DSI certification criterion requiring AI model cards and transparency disclosures in its current form. The arguments for deregulation in this specific area do not, in our view, outweigh the patient safety and accountability interests served by the requirement. We recognize that this puts us in tension with the general deregulatory direction of the proposed rule, and we have tried to explain why we think this particular provision warrants different treatment.⏎⏎We are not asking ONC to expand the requirement or make it more onerous. We are asking ONC to keep what it already finalized after a thorough notice-and-comment process in HTI-1. The evidentiary record that supported the DSI criterion in 2024 has not been overturned. The patient safety rationale has not diminished. If anything, AI deployment in clinical settings has accelerated since that rulemaking, which makes the transparency requirement more important, not less.⏎⏎The College stands ready to work with ONC on implementation questions, including how to make model card information more practically useful to clinicians at the point of care. We have members with deep expertise in clinical informatics, health AI, and internal medicine who can contribute to that work. We would welcome the opportunity to engage.⏎⏎ACP Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 11⏎⏎⏎APPENDIX NOTE⏎⏎Appendix A: Summary of ACP Policy Positions on Clinical Decision Support and Artificial Intelligence in Medicine (2019-2024), including relevant excerpts from Annals of Internal Medicine policy papers and ACP's 2023 statement on responsible AI deployment in internal medicine practice.⏎⏎Appendix B: Bibliography of cited literature, including full citations for Obermeyer et al. (Science, 2019), Mitchell et al. (ACM FAccT, 2019), Matheny et al. (NAM, 2019), and CHAI Blueprint (2023).⏎⏎Note: Appendices referenced above are not attached to this electronic submission due to file size constraints on the regulations.gov portal. CMS-2025-0050-110078♔CMS-2025-0050♔Michelle Taylor♔NORC at the University of Chicago♔♔♔♔Removing the DSI certification criterion's AI transparency requirements—including training data characteristics, target population documentation, and known risks—would undermine patient safety by eliminating one of the few enforceable mechanisms f...♔NORC at the University of Chicago⏎55 East Monroe Street, 30th Floor⏎Chicago, IL 60603⏎⏎June 23, 2025⏎⏎Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology⏎U.S. Department of Health and Human Services⏎330 C Street, SW⏎Washington, DC 20201⏎⏎Re: NORC at the University of Chicago Comments on ASTP/ONC Deregulatory Actions To Unleash Prosperity: Health Data, Technology, and Interoperability (RIN 0955-AA06)⏎⏎To Whom It May Concern:⏎⏎NORC at the University of Chicago is an independent research institution that conducts rigorous, objective studies on health policy, health outcomes, and the performance of health information systems. Our researchers work with federal agencies, state governments, and private foundations to produce evidence that informs policy decisions affecting millions of Americans. We appreciate the opportunity to submit comments on the proposed rule and write specifically to address the proposed removal of the Decision Support Interventions (DSI) certification criterion as it pertains to AI transparency disclosures.⏎⏎NORC's experience conducting federally funded health services research places us in a position to speak with some specificity about what happens when health IT transparency requirements are weakened or inconsistently enforced. Last spring, a NORC postdoctoral fellow spent several weeks attempting to reconcile patient-level discharge data from two hospital systems in Miami-Dade County for an outcomes study funded by a federal agency. Both systems had represented their interfaces as FHIR-compliant under the ONC Health IT Certification Program. What the researcher found instead were proprietary field mappings that had no documentation, silently dropped variables, and a vendor contract clause that effectively prohibited the research institution from publishing comparative performance findings. One site had to be excluded from the study entirely, introducing selection bias that the research team is still working to address in the published limitations. We are raising this not as an isolated complaint but because it illustrates a structural problem: certification requirements that exist on paper but lack the specificity to enforce meaningful transparency do not, in practice, protect researchers, clinicians, or patients. The DSI criterion's AI model card requirements are, in our assessment, among the few provisions in the current certification framework with enough technical specificity to make a real difference.⏎⏎NORC at the University of Chicago Comments | RIN 0955-AA06 | Page 2⏎⏎The proposed rule would eliminate or substantially revise the DSI certification criterion that currently requires health IT developers to document and disclose certain characteristics of clinical decision support and AI-driven interventions, including intended use, target population, known risks, training data characteristics, and external validation status. ONC has framed this as a burden-reduction measure, and we genuinely understand the concern about regulatory overhead for developers. However, we believe the agency has not adequately weighed the patient safety consequences of removing structured AI transparency disclosures at a moment when AI-assisted clinical decision support is proliferating rapidly across inpatient and ambulatory settings. The FDA's 2021 action plan for AI/ML-based software as a medical device (SaMD) and the subsequent 2023 discussion paper on predetermined change control plans both acknowledge that the clinical risk profile of AI tools changes as those tools are updated, sometimes continuously, in ways that clinicians cannot observe (FDA, Artificial Intelligence/Machine Learning (AI/ML)-Based Software as a Medical Device Action Plan, January 2021; FDA, Discussion Paper on Predetermined Change Control Plans for AI/ML-Based SaMD, 2023). The DSI model card requirement was one of the few places in federal health IT regulation where that concern was operationalized into something a clinician could actually consult at the point of care.⏎⏎The research literature on this is fairly consistent. Obermeyer et al. (2019, Science, Vol. 366, Issue 6464) demonstrated that a widely deployed commercial algorithm used to allocate additional care systematically underestimated the care needs of Black patients because it used healthcare cost as a proxy for health need. The bias was not visible in the product's marketing materials and was only detected through independent research access to training data characteristics. Under the current DSI criterion, a certified health IT product deploying a similar algorithm would be required to document training data characteristics and known risks. If the proposed rule eliminates that requirement, the regulatory pathway for detecting analogous disparities before they affect patient care narrows considerably. We are not arguing that the model card requirement alone would have prevented the Obermeyer finding, but the absence of any structured disclosure requirement makes independent verification significantly harder.⏎⏎NORC at the University of Chicago Comments | RIN 0955-AA06 | Page 3⏎⏎We want to be specific about what the current DSI criterion requires, because the proposal in the NPRM treats it somewhat loosely. Under 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11), certified health IT products that incorporate predictive decision support interventions must provide end users with access to a description of the intervention's purpose, the intended patient population, the source of the data used to develop or train the model, information about external validation if any has been conducted, and a description of known risks or limitations. These are not burdensome disclosures for a developer who has done adequate pre-deployment testing. They are, frankly, things a responsible developer should already know about their own product. The argument that these requirements create excessive burden is, in NORC's view, an argument that some developers are deploying AI tools into clinical environments without having characterized their own products adequately. That is a patient safety concern, not a regulatory efficiency problem.⏎⏎We also note that the proposed rule does not provide a satisfactory alternative mechanism for ensuring that clinicians have access to AI transparency information if the certification requirement is removed. The NPRM references market forces and voluntary disclosure frameworks, but voluntary frameworks have a poor track record in health IT specifically. The information blocking provisions enacted under the 21st Century Cures Act (Pub. L. 114-255) were themselves a response to the failure of voluntary interoperability commitments. The ONC Cures Act Final Rule (85 FR 25642, May 1, 2020) established enforceable standards precisely because the prior voluntary approach had not produced adequate data sharing. NORC is skeptical that a voluntary approach to AI transparency will fare better, particularly given that competitive pressures create strong incentives for developers to minimize disclosure of model limitations. A 2022 systematic review by Reddy et al. published in npj Digital Medicine found that of 164 commercially deployed clinical AI tools reviewed, fewer than 30% had publicly available information about training data sources, and fewer than 15% had undergone independent external validation (Reddy S et al., npj Digital Medicine, 2022, Vol. 5, Article 150). Those figures describe the voluntary disclosure environment that currently exists. Removing the certification requirement would move the regulatory baseline closer to that environment, not away from it.⏎⏎NORC at the University of Chicago Comments | RIN 0955-AA06 | Page 4⏎⏎There is a specific concern about target population documentation that we want to address directly. Clinical AI tools are frequently developed using training data drawn from academic medical centers or large integrated delivery networks, which tend to serve patient populations that are wealthier, more English-speaking, and less medically complex than the populations served by safety-net hospitals, federally qualified health centers, and rural critical access hospitals. Without a certification requirement that the intended patient population be documented and disclosed, clinicians at those settings have no reliable way to know whether a deployed AI tool was validated on a population that resembles their patients. The Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality's 2023 report on AI in healthcare (AHRQ Publication No. 23-0013) specifically identified this generalizability gap as one of the primary patient safety risks associated with clinical AI deployment. The DSI target population documentation requirement is a direct regulatory response to that identified risk. NORC believes its removal requires a more thorough safety analysis than the NPRM provides.⏎⏎We recognize that ONC is operating under a broader deregulatory mandate and that there are legitimate arguments for reducing compliance costs on health IT developers. NORC does not oppose burden reduction as a general principle. There are certification criteria in the current framework that impose administrative requirements with limited demonstrated benefit, and a thoughtful review of those requirements is appropriate. However, the DSI AI transparency requirements are not in that category. The administrative cost of documenting intended use, training data, and known risks is low relative to the cost of deploying a miscalibrated AI tool in a clinical setting. A 2021 analysis by Sendak et al. in NEJM Catalyst estimated that a single incorrectly calibrated sepsis prediction model deployed across a mid-sized health system could affect care decisions for thousands of patients annually before the miscalibration was detected (Sendak MP et al., NEJM Catalyst Innovations in Care Delivery, 2021, Vol. 2, No. 5). The transparency disclosures required under the current DSI criterion are, in effect, a low-cost early warning mechanism. Removing them in the name of burden reduction is, in NORC's assessment, a poor cost-benefit trade.⏎⏎NORC at the University of Chicago Comments | RIN 0955-AA06 | Page 5⏎⏎We would also note a structural concern about the timing and sequencing of this proposal. The current DSI certification criterion was finalized in the ONC Health IT Certification Program's 2024 HTI-1 Final Rule (89 FR 1192, January 9, 2024). That rule went through extensive notice-and-comment rulemaking, and ONC received and responded to a substantial volume of public comment on the AI transparency provisions specifically. The agency's responses in the HTI-1 preamble reflect a considered judgment that model card disclosures were necessary to protect patient safety and support informed clinical decision-making. The current proposal to remove those requirements is, as far as NORC can determine, not accompanied by new evidence that the safety rationale underlying HTI-1's AI transparency provisions was mistaken. The NPRM does not cite new data on developer burden, new evidence that voluntary disclosure has improved, or new findings about the safety record of deployed clinical AI tools. The absence of that kind of evidentiary basis for reversing a recently finalized rule is something NORC believes the agency should address more directly in any final rule.⏎⏎NORC at the University of Chicago Comments | RIN 0955-AA06 | Page 6⏎⏎For the reasons stated above, NORC at the University of Chicago recommends that ONC retain the DSI certification criterion requiring AI model card disclosures, including intended use documentation, target population description, training data characteristics, known risks and limitations, and external validation status. If the agency determines that specific elements of the current disclosure requirement are genuinely burdensome without corresponding safety benefit, NORC would support a targeted revision process that solicits input from patient safety researchers, clinical informaticists, and patient advocacy organizations before any elements are removed. We would also recommend that ONC consider whether the external validation documentation requirement should be strengthened rather than weakened, given the evidence from Reddy et al. and others that independent validation is currently the exception rather than the norm for deployed clinical AI. NORC stands ready to provide technical assistance or participate in any stakeholder process ONC convenes on this question.⏎⏎One practical note: the research team involved in the Miami-Dade study referenced above encountered a specific problem that the current DSI criterion, even in its existing form, would not fully resolve, which is that the certification requirement applies to the health IT module but does not currently create a mechanism for researchers to access model card documentation outside of the certified product's end-user interface. For federally funded outcomes research that depends on understanding the AI tools embedded in the clinical environments being studied, some form of researcher-accessible disclosure pathway would be a meaningful addition to the certification framework. This is not a request NORC is formally advancing in these comments, but it is something the agency may want to consider as it thinks about whether the current DSI transparency framework is adequate for the full range of stakeholders who need access to this information, including not just clinicians at the point of care but researchers conducting post-market surveillance and health⏎⏎NORC at the University of Chicago Comments | RIN 0955-AA06 | Page 7⏎⏎services research on AI-assisted care delivery. The current structure creates a disclosure that exists inside a certified product but is not systematically accessible to independent researchers, which limits the ability of the research community to conduct the kind of independent post-deployment evaluation that the FDA's own AI/ML SaMD framework identifies as necessary. That gap is worth naming even if it falls outside the specific scope of this rulemaking.⏎⏎Sincerely,⏎⏎Michelle Taylor⏎Postdoctoral Fellow⏎NORC at the University of Chicago⏎mtaylor@norc.org⏎⏎NORC at the University of Chicago | 55 East Monroe Street, 30th Floor | Chicago, IL 60603⏎www.norc.org♔♔2025-12-22T00:00:00Z♔2025-12-22T00:00:00Z♔2025-12-12T00:00:00Z♔2026-02-10T00:00:00Z♔6♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Retain the current Decision Support Interventions (DSI) certification criterion requiring AI model cards and transparency disclosures (intended use, target population, known risks, training data characteristics, external validation) to ensure patient safety, informed clinical decision-making, and accountability in AI-assisted healthcare.♔Hospital and health system procurement teams need transparent AI model information to make evidence-based decisions about which tools to adopt and how to implement them safely in their local contexts.♔academic♔high♔concerned♔Florida♔postdoctoral fellow♔32♔Last spring, I spent three weeks trying to reconcile patient-level discharge data from two hospital systems in Miami-Dade County for a federally funded outcomes study — systems that, on paper, both claimed FHIR-compliant APIs. You cut the wrong corner in the name of efficiency and you end up paying for it in ways you didn't expect.⏎⏎So I'm not here to argue against improving data sharing. I want that. What I'm worried about is a different piece of this proposed rule, and I want to be specific about it.⏎⏎THE AI TRANSPARENCY PIECE⏎⏎There is a certification requirement in the current framework, I'll call it the Decision Support Interventions requirement, that says if a health IT system is using an AI or algorithmic tool to help a clinician make a decision about my care, there has to be a documented disclosure. A "model card" in the current language. That disclosure is supposed to include things like what the tool was intended to do, what patient population it was trained on, what the known risks are, and whether it's been externally validated.⏎⏎I am not a health IT expert. I run a machine shop. But I know what a model card is in the rough sense, and I know WHY it matters. When a doctor is looking at an AI-generated risk score or a flagged lab value or a clinical recommendation that came out of some algorithmic system, that physician needs to know where that output came from. They need to know if the tool was validated on a population that looks anything like me, a 65-year-old white man in rural Maine who has a particular cardiac history and takes a particular set of medications. They need to know if it was trained on data from large urban academic hospitals and never tested anywhere like my situation.⏎⏎The proposed rule, from what I can understand of it, is considering loosening or removing this requirement. And I genuinely don't understand why.⏎⏎MY CONCERNS IN PLAIN TERMS⏎⏎Let me try to lay this out because I want to be clear:⏎⏎1. If a clinical AI tool doesn't have to disclose its intended use and its training data characteristics, my doctor cannot meaningfully evaluate whether to trust it. She might not even know she's looking at an AI output.⏎⏎2. If there's no external validation requirement, a tool could be deployed in clinical settings based on internal testing only, which is NOT the same thing. Internal testing has obvious incentive problems.⏎⏎3. If the target population information is removed from the disclosure, a tool trained on, say, data from a large Boston hospital network gets applied to patients in rural Maine without anyone flagging that this might be a mismatch.⏎⏎4. The known risks disclosure is maybe the most important piece. Every tool has failure modes. If those failure modes aren't documented, the physician has no basis for knowing when to override the system's recommendation.⏎⏎I keep coming back to item 3 specifically. I live and get care in a rural area. Rural patients are CONSISTENTLY underrepresented in training data for medical AI tools. This is a documented problem, it's not speculation. If I lose the protection that requires someone to disclose what population a tool was trained on, I lose one of the few mechanisms I have to know whether that tool was built with anything like my situation in mind.⏎⏎WHY THE "BURDEN REDUCTION" ARGUMENT DOESN'T SATISFY ME HERE⏎⏎I understand the argument for reducing regulatory burden. I really do. I have filled out enough compliance paperwork in my own business to have genuine sympathy for the idea that some requirements create costs without commensurate benefits. But the model card requirement doesn't feel like that kind of requirement to me.⏎⏎What I keep hearing is that these disclosures are burdensome for health IT developers. OK. Maybe they are. But the burden falls on the developer once, when the tool is being certified, and the benefit flows to every patient and every clinician who interacts with that tool afterward. That is not an unfavorable trade-off. That is EXACTLY the kind of requirement that makes sense to keep.⏎⏎There's also something that bothers me about the timing. We are at a moment when AI tools in clinical settings are proliferating fast. I don't know the exact number but I've read that there are something like 600-plus AI-enabled medical devices that have received FDA clearance in recent years, and that number keeps growing. The LAST time to be loosening transparency requirements is when the technology is expanding this quickly and we don't yet have a long track record of how these tools perform in real-world diverse populations.⏎⏎If anything, the model card requirement should be getting more specific and more rigorous, not less.⏎⏎WHAT THIS LOOKS LIKE FROM A PATIENT'S PERSPECTIVE⏎⏎I want to try to explain what this feels like from where I sit, because I think the policy discussion can get abstract in ways that lose the human stakes.⏎⏎When I was in that exam room with the incomplete echocardiogram data, the physician was doing her best with what she had. She knew the data was incomplete. She told me that explicitly and we talked about what it meant for the decision we were trying to make. That transparency, even in a frustrating situation, meant I could participate in my own care. I knew what she was working with and what she wasn't.⏎⏎If an AI tool is generating part of the clinical picture and neither my physician nor I knows anything meaningful about where that output came from, how it was validated, what populations it was built on, that is WORSE than the thumb drive situation. At least with the thumb drive I knew what was missing. With an opaque AI output, I might not even know there's a gap.⏎⏎This is not an abstract concern. The whole premise of informed consent in medicine is that patients and physicians have enough information to make real decisions. An AI tool that generates clinical recommendations without any transparency about its provenance is a direct problem for that premise.⏎⏎THE SPECIFIC ASK⏎⏎I want to be direct about what I'm asking for here. I'm asking HHS and ONC to RETAIN the current certification requirements for Decision Support Interventions that mandate transparency disclosures including:⏎⏎o intended use of the AI tool⏎o the target population it was designed and validated for⏎o known risks and failure modes⏎o training data characteristics (what data it was built on, from what settings, what time periods)⏎o whether external validation has been conducted and by whom⏎⏎These are not exotic or unreasonable requirements. They are the minimum a clinician needs to use an AI tool responsibly. They are the minimum a patient needs to have any meaningful ability to participate in decisions about their own care.⏎⏎If the concern is that these requirements are burdensome in their current FORM, I am open to a conversation about how the disclosure format could be streamlined or standardized in a way that reduces compliance friction without removing the substance. But removing the substance is not the answer.⏎⏎A NOTE ON ACCOUNTABILITY⏎⏎One more thing I want to raise and I'm not sure exactly where it fits in the comment structure but it feels important.⏎⏎When something goes wrong in a clinical AI situation, meaning a tool generates a bad recommendation and a physician follows it and a patient is harmed, who is accountable? Right now that question is complicated enough even WITH transparency requirements in place. If we remove the requirement that the tool's training data and validation status be disclosed, it gets even harder to trace what happened. Was the tool applied outside its validated population? Was there a known failure mode that wasn't disclosed? You can't answer those questions after the fact if the information was never required in the first place.⏎⏎I spent thirty years in manufacturing. You might be able to technically operate without it but you have no business doing so.⏎⏎I'm a small business owner in Maine with a cardiac history and I've had direct experience with what happens when health data systems fail at basic information sharing. Our work puts us in daily contact with the interoperability failures that federal certification policy is supposed to prevent. We appreciate the opportunity to comment, though I want to be direct from the outset: this proposed rule contains a specific provision that our organization believes will cause patient harm, and we are asking that ONC reverse course on it.⏎⏎The provision in question is the proposed removal of the Decision Support Interventions certification criterion's requirement for AI model transparency disclosures, sometimes called model cards. The preamble to the proposed rule frames this removal as burden reduction. We read it differently. What ONC is proposing to eliminate is one of the only structured mechanisms through which a clinician, a patient navigator, or a patient advocate can find out what an AI tool was trained on, who it was designed to serve, and where it has been shown to fall short. Removing that requirement does not reduce burden in any meaningful operational sense. It transfers risk, and it transfers that risk specifically to the patients and communities who already have the least ability to absorb it.⏎⏎Dental Standards Institute Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 2⏎⏎BACKGROUND ON OUR ORGANIZATIONAL PERSPECTIVE⏎⏎Before addressing the substance of the DSI transparency requirement, it is worth explaining why a dental standards organization is commenting on an AI certification criterion that applies broadly to health IT. The answer is that our member programs are not siloed. Community health workers and patient navigators affiliated with our network routinely encounter decision support tools embedded in EHR systems used by primary care providers, hospital discharge planners, and specialist offices. When those tools produce recommendations, our staff help patients understand and act on them. We have a direct operational stake in whether those tools are transparent about their design and limitations.⏎⏎Over the last three years, our network has documented more than 40 cases where AI-assisted clinical recommendations appeared to conflict with patient circumstances in ways that were not immediately legible to the clinician or the patient. In several of those cases, the recommendation was later traced to a model that had been trained predominantly on data from insured, English-speaking adults in urban academic medical centers. The patients receiving the recommendations were frequently uninsured, Spanish-speaking, and receiving care in rural or federally qualified health center settings. This is not a hypothetical problem. It is a documented pattern, and it is exactly the kind of pattern that model transparency disclosures are designed to surface.⏎⏎The proposed rule cites 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11) and related provisions in the context of reducing developer compliance costs. We understand the compliance cost argument. Preparing a model card requires real work, and smaller developers face real resource constraints. But the cost argument does not address the safety question. The question is not whether model cards are easy to produce. The question is whether clinicians and patients are entitled to know what is inside the tools being used to advise their care. We think the answer to that question is yes, and we think ONC's own prior rulemaking supports that position.⏎⏎DSI TRANSPARENCY REQUIREMENTS: WHAT IS AT STAKE⏎⏎The DSI certification criterion at 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11), as it currently stands, requires health IT developers to disclose specific information about AI and clinical decision support tools, including intended use, target population, known risks, training data characteristics, and whether the tool has been externally validated. These requirements were finalized in the HTI-1 final rule published at 89 Fed. Reg. 1192 (January 9, 2024). At the time of finalization, ONC described them as necessary to "support transparency and accountability in the use of AI-driven decision support." That language is still in the regulatory record. The proposed rule does not explain what has changed to make that accountability less necessary.⏎⏎Dental Standards Institute Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 3⏎⏎What has changed, as far as we can tell, is that some health IT developers have expressed concern about the compliance timeline and the specificity of the disclosure requirements. Those concerns are legitimate in some respects. The implementation burden is real, particularly for smaller vendors. But the appropriate response to implementation burden is phased compliance timelines, technical assistance, or tiered requirements based on developer size, not elimination of the requirement entirely. Removing the requirement does not solve the underlying problem of uneven developer capacity. It simply removes the accountability structure and leaves clinicians and patients without the information they need.⏎⏎I want to be specific about what clinicians actually need from these disclosures, because I think the policy debate sometimes loses track of the clinical reality. When a primary care physician in Prince William County sees an AI-generated risk score or care recommendation appear in their EHR, they need to know at minimum:⏎⏎1. What patient population the underlying model was trained on, including demographic characteristics and payer mix.⏎⏎2. Whether the model has been validated in settings similar to the one where it is being deployed, and if so, by whom and when.⏎⏎3. What the known failure modes are, particularly for populations that were underrepresented in training data.⏎⏎4. Whether the model's outputs have been shown to vary in accuracy by race, ethnicity, language preference, or insurance status.⏎⏎Without that information, the physician is making a clinical judgment about a tool they cannot evaluate. They may trust it more than they should. They may apply it to patients for whom it was never validated. And when it produces a bad recommendation, neither the physician nor the patient will have the context to recognize what went wrong.⏎⏎The 88 Fed. Reg. 23746 proposed HTI-1 rule, and the subsequent final rule, both included discussion of algorithmic bias and health equity as motivating factors for the DSI transparency requirements. The proposed deregulatory rule does not engage with that record in any substantive way. It does not explain why the equity concerns that motivated the transparency requirements in 2023 and 2024 are now less pressing. It does not cite any evidence that the market has produced adequate voluntary transparency mechanisms. It simply proposes to remove the requirement.⏎⏎Dental Standards Institute Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 4⏎⏎THE EQUITY PROBLEM IS NOT ABSTRACT⏎⏎Last spring, I spent three weeks working with a Salvadoran family in Prince William County, Virginia, trying to get their elderly mother's medication records transferred between two clinics. Both clinics used certified EHR systems. The records never moved. When I finally reached someone who could explain the failure, they cited an exception buried in the compliance framework that even the clinic's IT coordinator had not heard of.⏎⏎That experience is not directly about AI model cards, but it is about the same underlying dynamic: accountability structures that exist on paper but fail in practice, and that fail most predictably for patients who have the least institutional power to push back. The DSI transparency requirements are an accountability structure. Removing them does not make the accountability happen through some other mechanism. It makes the accountability disappear.⏎⏎The health equity literature is clear on this point. Research published in Science (Obermeyer et al., 2019) documented that a widely deployed commercial algorithm used to identify high-risk patients for care management systematically underestimated the needs of Black patients relative to white patients with equivalent health status. The algorithm used health care cost as a proxy for health need, and because Black patients historically incurred lower costs due to reduced access to care, the model ranked them as healthier than they were. That study was published six years ago. The problem it documented has not gone away. The DSI transparency requirements were in part a policy response to exactly this kind of documented failure.⏎⏎If a developer had been required to disclose training data characteristics and known disparities in model performance, a clinician or a health system reviewing that disclosure might have caught the problem before deploying the tool broadly. That is the purpose of the requirement. It is not regulatory theater. It is information that has a direct bearing on whether a patient receives appropriate care.⏎⏎Dental Standards Institute Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 5⏎⏎SPECIFIC RECOMMENDATIONS⏎⏎Our organization asks ONC to retain the DSI certification criterion's AI transparency disclosure requirements in their current form as finalized in the HTI-1 final rule (89 Fed. Reg. 1192). If ONC determines that some modification is warranted to address implementation burden, we ask that any such modification preserve the following elements without exception:⏎⏎a. Disclosure of intended use and target population, including the demographic and clinical characteristics of the population on which the model was trained.⏎⏎b. Disclosure of known risks and limitations, including any documented variation in model performance by patient subgroup.⏎⏎c. Disclosure of external validation status, including whether the model has been validated outside the developer's own internal testing environment, and if so, in what clinical settings.⏎⏎d. Disclosure of training data characteristics sufficient to allow a clinician or health system to assess whether the model is likely to generalize to their patient population.⏎⏎These are not burdensome requirements in any absolute sense. A four-page standardized disclosure document covering these elements is well within the capacity of any organization with the technical resources to develop and deploy a clinical AI tool. The Food and Drug Administration has published guidance on predetermined change control plans and AI/ML-based software as a medical device (SaMD) that provides a useful parallel framework (FDA Guidance, January 2021, "Artificial Intelligence/Machine Learning (AI/ML)-Based Software as a Medical Device (SaMD) Action Plan"). ONC could adopt a similar standardized template that reduces the documentation burden without eliminating the transparency obligation.⏎⏎We also want to address the argument, which appears in some developer comments on the HTI-1 proposed rule, that model card requirements are premature because the science of AI transparency is still developing. We understand that argument, but we do not find it persuasive as a reason to eliminate the requirement entirely. The fact that disclosure standards are still evolving is an argument for continuing to refine them, not for abandoning them. Clinicians and patients cannot wait for perfect standards before they need information about the tools being used in their care.⏎⏎Dental Standards Institute Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 6⏎⏎THE BROADER DEREGULATORY CONTEXT⏎⏎We want to be careful not to characterize this comment as opposition to deregulation in general. There are provisions in the proposed rule that our organization supports or views with genuine neutrality. The proposed adjustments to information blocking exceptions, for example, are complicated, and we have not taken a position on every element of that section of the rule.⏎⏎But the DSI transparency requirement is different from most of the provisions in this rulemaking. It is not a process requirement that generates administrative paperwork without clinical value. It is an information requirement that generates disclosures with direct bearing on patient safety. The distinction matters. When ONC reduces documentation burden on developers by streamlining certification testing procedures, that is a reasonable efficiency measure. When ONC reduces documentation burden by eliminating patient-facing information rights, that is a different kind of action with different consequences.⏎⏎The proposed rule's preamble invokes the goal of "unleashing prosperity" through reduced regulatory burden. We do not object to that goal as stated. But prosperity in health care is not measured only by developer efficiency. It is also measured by whether patients receive care that is appropriate to their actual circumstances, by whether clinicians have the information they need to make good decisions, and by whether the tools deployed in clinical settings are subject to some form of accountability. The DSI transparency requirements contribute to all of those outcomes.⏎⏎I keep coming back to a specific number: 40. That is roughly how many cases our network has documented over three years where AI-assisted recommendations appeared to misfire in ways traceable to training data or validation gaps. Forty cases across a relatively small regional network. If that rate holds across the hundreds of health systems and thousands of clinical settings now deploying AI tools, the aggregate impact on patient care is substantial. Model transparency disclosures will not catch every problem, but they create the conditions under which problems can be identified, reported, and corrected. Removing that requirement forecloses the possibility of systematic accountability.⏎⏎Dental Standards Institute Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 7⏎⏎COMMENTS ON THE INFORMATION BLOCKING PROVISIONS⏎⏎Because our comment focuses primarily on the DSI certification criterion, we will address the information blocking provisions only briefly. Our network's experience with information blocking is substantial. The scenario I described earlier, involving the Salvadoran family in Prince William County and the medication records that never moved, is a direct information blocking failure. The records were held in certified systems that were nominally interoperable. The failure was a compliance failure, not a technical one, and it was enabled by exceptions that were too broad and too poorly documented to allow any accountability.⏎⏎The proposed rule's amendments to information blocking exceptions, including proposed changes to the Infeasibility Exception and the Licensing Exception under 45 CFR 171.202 and 45 CFR 171.303, concern us for the same reason that the DSI changes concern us: they move in the direction of less accountability, not more. The Infeasibility Exception in particular has been used, in our direct experience, to justify information blocking that appears to have no legitimate technical basis. Broadening or further clarifying that exception in ways that make it easier to invoke seems likely to increase, not decrease, the frequency of the kind of failures we document.⏎⏎We recognize that ONC may have legitimate reasons for some of the proposed exception amendments, and we are not in a position to evaluate every proposed change in detail. But we ask ONC to apply a consistent standard: any change to an information blocking exception should be accompanied by an analysis of how it will affect patients who are currently unable to access their records, and particularly patients in communities where information blocking failures are already disproportionately common.⏎⏎Dental Standards Institute Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 8⏎⏎The Office of Inspector General's 2023 data on information blocking complaints (OIG Report OEI-09-23-00380, December 2023) showed that a substantial share of reported blocking involved small and medium-sized providers, not just large health systems. Any changes to the exception framework that reduce accountability for smaller providers will have a disproportionate impact on patients served by those providers, who are often in rural areas or underserved communities. That is not a hypothetical concern. It is a pattern visible in the complaint data.⏎⏎We also want to note, without going into extensive detail, that the relationship between information blocking enforcement and AI transparency is not coincidental. A health system that blocks patient access to records is also a health system that is less likely to be transparent about the AI tools it deploys. These are related governance failures. A deregulatory approach that simultaneously loosens information blocking exceptions and eliminates AI transparency requirements is, in our view, moving in a consistent but problematic direction.⏎⏎CONCLUSION OF SUBSTANTIVE COMMENTS⏎⏎The Dental Standards Institute respectfully urges ONC to:⏎⏎1. Retain the DSI certification criterion's AI model transparency disclosure requirements as finalized in the HTI-1 final rule (89 Fed. Reg. 1192, January 9, 2024), including requirements for disclosure of intended use, target population, known risks, training data characteristics, and external validation status.⏎⏎2. If any modification to the DSI transparency requirements is considered, adopt a standardized disclosure template approach rather than eliminating the substance of the requirements, and provide a phased compliance timeline for smaller developers rather than removing the obligation entirely.⏎⏎3. Conduct a focused health equity analysis of the proposed DSI changes before finalizing, specifically examining the potential impact on patients in communities where AI tools trained on non-representative data are most likely to cause harm.⏎⏎4. Apply a patient-impact analysis to each proposed information blocking exception amendment, with particular attention to the effect on patients in rural, uninsured, and limited-English-proficiency populations.⏎⏎5. Publish the public comments received on the DSI transparency provisions separately from the broader deregulatory docket, so that the record on this specific issue is clearly visible and accessible for future rulemaking.⏎⏎Dental Standards Institute Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 9⏎⏎We want to close by saying something about the framing of this rulemaking. The title "Deregulatory Actions To Unleash Prosperity" is a framing choice, and framing choices have consequences. They shape what counts as a success metric and what gets treated as a cost. In this framing, a developer who no longer has to prepare a model card has been relieved of burden. A patient who no longer has access to information about the AI tool advising their care does not appear in the accounting at all. We think ONC should look carefully at whose burden is being reduced and whose protection is being removed.⏎⏎The AI transparency requirements in the current DSI criterion are not perfect. The disclosure templates are inconsistent across developers, the validation requirements are underspecified in some areas, and the enforcement mechanism is weak. Those are real problems worth addressing. But the solution to an imperfect accountability mechanism is a better accountability mechanism, not no accountability mechanism.⏎⏎Our network will continue to document cases where AI-assisted recommendations fail patients in our communities. We will continue to bring those cases to the attention of ONC, CMS, and other relevant agencies. And we will continue to advocate for the proposition that patients in Prince William County, and in every other county in this country, are entitled to know what is in the tools being used to advise their care.⏎⏎Sincerely,⏎⏎Sandra Hernandez⏎Community Organizer and Policy Director⏎Dental Standards Institute⏎1847 Commerce Street, Suite 310⏎Alexandria, Virginia 22314⏎shernandez@dentalstandardsinstitute.org⏎(703) 555-0194⏎⏎Dental Standards Institute Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 10⏎⏎APPENDIX: SUMMARY OF CITED REGULATORY AND SCIENTIFIC REFERENCES⏎⏎For the convenience of reviewing staff, the following references are cited in the body of this comment:⏎⏎o 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11), Decision Support Interventions certification criterion (as finalized in HTI-1).⏎⏎o 89 Fed.
