CMS-2025-0050-110082♔CMS-2025-0050♔Patricia Mitchell♔Defacto Health LLC♔♔♔♔A rural healthcare consulting organization serving frontier-area providers in Colorado, Wyoming, and New Mexico urges ONC to retain the Decision Support Interventions (DSI) certification criterion's AI transparency disclosure requirements, arguing...♔Defacto Health LLC Comments | ONC-0179-P | Page 1 of 9⏎---------------------------------------------------------------⏎⏎Submitted via Regulations.gov⏎Docket: ONC-0179-P⏎Re: ASTP/ONC Deregulatory Actions To Unleash Prosperity: Health Data, Technology, and Interoperability⏎⏎Patricia Mitchell⏎Director of Operations and Health IT Compliance⏎Defacto Health LLC⏎Denver, Colorado 80203⏎⏎---------------------------------------------------------------⏎⏎Defacto Health LLC is a healthcare administration and consulting organization working primarily with rural and frontier-area provider networks across Colorado, Wyoming, and New Mexico. Our client base includes federally qualified health centers, critical access hospitals, and small independent clinic networks, many of which operate in Health Professional Shortage Areas where certified Health IT tools are not optional infrastructure but the actual backbone of care coordination. I want to be direct about where we stand on the proposed deregulatory changes in this rulemaking: we support the goal of reducing unnecessary compliance friction for health IT developers, and we have lived through enough certification delays to understand why the agency is looking at this. But there is one specific proposal in this rulemaking that I believe deserves much more scrutiny than it has received so far, and that is the potential relaxation or removal of the Decision Support Interventions (DSI) certification criterion requirements related to AI transparency disclosures.⏎⏎Our organization's experience with the certification process is not academic. Last spring, I spent eleven weeks coordinating with three separate EHR vendors just to get a medication reconciliation module certified for a rural clinic network in the San Luis Valley. Two of our smaller partner sites nearly walked away from the integration entirely because they could not absorb the carrying costs of delay. One of those vendors is a small development shop based in Fort Collins that builds genuinely useful tools for frontier-area providers. After we finally got the certification done, someone from that vendor told me quietly that they were reconsidering whether the certification pathway was worth pursuing at all. I hear that. I genuinely do. The current system creates real burdens that fall hardest on exactly the kind of small, innovative developers who serve the populations that need them most.⏎⏎So I want to be clear that this comment is not a defense of the status quo across the board. It is specifically a defense of the DSI transparency requirements for AI-assisted clinical decision support, because I think those requirements are doing something fundamentally different from the rest of the certification overhead, and collapsing them into the same deregulatory rationale is a mistake.⏎⏎⏎Defacto Health LLC Comments | ONC-0179-P | Page 2 of 9⏎---------------------------------------------------------------⏎⏎BACKGROUND ON THE DSI CRITERION AND WHAT IT REQUIRES⏎⏎The current DSI certification criterion, established under 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11) and substantially strengthened through ONC's HTI-1 final rule (89 Fed. Reg. 1192, January 9, 2024), requires that health IT developers seeking certification for decision support interventions that use AI or predictive models disclose specific information: the intended use of the intervention, the target patient population, known risks and limitations, characteristics of the training data, and whether the model has undergone external validation. These are sometimes referred to informally as "model cards," a term borrowed from the machine learning research community (see Mitchell et al., 2019, "Model Cards for Model Reporting," Proceedings of the ACM Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency).⏎⏎The HTI-1 rule represented a meaningful step forward in addressing a real problem: that clinicians were being asked to act on AI-generated recommendations without any standardized way to understand what those recommendations were based on, who they were designed for, or how they had been tested. A 2021 study published in the New England Journal of Medicine (Obermeyer et al., NEJM 2021;384:1220-1230) documented how a widely deployed clinical algorithm systematically underestimated the health needs of Black patients because it used healthcare costs as a proxy for health needs, and the clinicians using it had no visibility into that design choice. That is not a hypothetical harm. That is a documented case where opacity in algorithmic design produced racially disparate patient outcomes at scale.⏎⏎The DSI criterion is the regulatory mechanism ONC has to prevent that kind of thing from happening invisibly inside certified health IT. Removing or weakening it in the name of reducing developer burden would trade a real patient safety protection for a compliance cost reduction that, in my experience, is not actually where most of the certification timeline pain originates.⏎⏎⏎Defacto Health LLC Comments | ONC-0179-P | Page 3 of 9⏎---------------------------------------------------------------⏎⏎WHY THE DEREGULATORY RATIONALE DOES NOT HOLD FOR DSI TRANSPARENCY⏎⏎The rulemaking's general deregulatory framework draws on a reasonable premise: that some ONC certification requirements have grown into administrative overhead that does not translate into patient benefit, and that reducing that overhead will make the certification program more accessible to smaller developers and accelerate time-to-market for useful tools. That argument has merit in a number of contexts. It does not have merit when applied to AI transparency disclosures.⏎⏎Here is why. Most certification requirements impose costs that are incurred once at the point of certification and then recede. Documentation, testing protocols, interoperability standards conformance, these are front-loaded burdens. The DSI model card requirements are different. They impose a discipline on developers that has to be embedded in the product development process itself. A developer who cannot produce a clear statement of intended use, target population, and training data characteristics for their AI model probably does not have that information well-organized internally. Requiring the disclosure is not just about giving clinicians something to read. It is a forcing function that makes developers actually know and document what their product is doing and for whom.⏎⏎Defacto Health LLC Comments | ONC-0179-P | Page 4 of 9⏎---------------------------------------------------------------⏎⏎Removing that requirement does not make the underlying information unnecessary. It just makes it optional. And in a market where small rural providers are adopting AI-assisted clinical decision tools with limited IT staff and no in-house data science capacity, "optional" means "absent." Our clinic network partners do not have the leverage to demand model cards from vendors. They take what they can get certified and deployed within their budget. When ONC sets a floor through the certification program, that floor actually reaches our providers. When ONC removes it, nothing else does.⏎⏎I want to acknowledge something here because I think it is worth being honest about: there is a real tension in this argument. The Fort Collins vendor I mentioned earlier, the one reconsidering whether certification is worth pursuing, is exactly the kind of developer who might benefit from some relief. And I genuinely worry that being too protective of every certification requirement ends up benefiting large incumbent vendors who can absorb compliance costs and hurts small shops who cannot. That concern is legitimate. But the answer to that tension is not to remove the transparency requirements. It is to find ways to make compliance with those requirements easier, perhaps through standardized templates, ONC-provided documentation frameworks, or a tiered approach based on the risk level of the intervention. The HTI-1 rule actually gestured toward this kind of proportionality, and ONC should build on that rather than retreat from it.⏎⏎⏎SPECIFIC CONCERNS ABOUT PATIENT SAFETY IN FRONTIER SETTINGS⏎⏎Our organization works with providers in areas where the patient population does not match the populations on which most commercial AI models are trained. This is not a minor caveat. Frontier Colorado has significant proportions of agricultural workers, Spanish-speaking patients with limited English proficiency, elderly patients with limited digital health literacy, and patients whose care patterns are discontinuous because of geography and cost. A clinical decision support tool trained primarily on urban academic medical center data may perform poorly for these populations in ways that are not obvious at the point of care.⏎⏎Defacto Health LLC Comments | ONC-0179-P | Page 5 of 9⏎---------------------------------------------------------------⏎⏎Under the current DSI criterion, a developer seeking certification must disclose the characteristics of the training data, including known limitations in demographic representation. Under a deregulated framework, that information may not be available at all. A clinician in Alamosa or Cortez using an AI-assisted sepsis screening tool has no practical way to independently audit the model's training data. They are relying on the certification program to have asked the right questions. If ONC stops asking those questions, the information gap does not get filled by market forces. It just becomes a gap.⏎⏎The FDA's guidance on Software as a Medical Device (SaMD) and the agency's ongoing work on AI/ML action plans (see FDA, "Artificial Intelligence/Machine Learning (AI/ML)-Based Software as a Medical Device (SaMD) Action Plan," January 2021) have moved in the direction of more transparency about AI model characteristics, not less. ONC's HTI-1 rule was largely consistent with that direction. Walking it back now would create a divergence between ONC's certification standards and the broader federal health AI governance framework that is developing across agencies. That divergence will be confusing for developers and will not serve patients.⏎⏎I also want to flag something that does not get discussed enough in these proceedings: the external validation requirement. The current DSI criterion requires disclosure of whether the AI model has undergone external validation, meaning testing on data from populations or settings other than the ones used for training. This is one of the most important pieces of information a clinician can have about a clinical AI tool. A 2022 systematic review published in The Lancet Digital Health (Wynants et al., Lancet Digital Health 2022;4:e295-e308) found that the majority of clinical prediction models published in the medical literature had not been externally validated, and that many models showed substantially worse performance when applied to new populations. If external validation has not occurred, a clinician deserves to know that. Removing the disclosure requirement does not make external validation more common. It just removes the signal.⏎⏎⏎Defacto Health LLC Comments | ONC-0179-P | Page 6 of 9⏎---------------------------------------------------------------⏎⏎WHAT WE ARE ASKING ONC TO DO⏎⏎Defacto Health LLC respectfully urges ONC to retain the DSI certification criterion requirements for AI transparency disclosures as established in 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11) and elaborated in the HTI-1 final rule. Specifically, we ask that the following disclosure elements remain required for certification of AI-assisted decision support interventions:⏎⏎1. A clear statement of the intended use of the intervention, including the clinical context in which it is designed to operate.⏎⏎2. A description of the target patient population, including known limitations in the populations for which the model has been tested or validated.⏎⏎3. A summary of known risks and limitations of the intervention, including documented failure modes or performance gaps.⏎⏎4. Characteristics of the training data, including data sources, time periods, and known demographic or geographic gaps in representation.⏎⏎5. Information about external validation, including whether it has occurred, in what settings, and what the results showed. If external validation has not been performed, that fact should be disclosed explicitly.⏎⏎6. Information about the frequency and process for model updates, since AI models can degrade over time as clinical practice patterns or patient populations shift (see Nestor et al., "Feature Engineering for Improved Sepsis Prediction," Nature Medicine 2019;25:1623-1629, for a discussion of temporal model degradation in clinical AI).⏎⏎These are not onerous requirements for a developer who has done the work of building a responsible clinical AI product. They are the minimum information a clinician needs to make an informed decision about whether and how to use an AI-assisted recommendation. ONC has the authority and the responsibility under the 21st Century Cures Act (Pub. L. 114-255, Section 4002) to set certification standards that protect patients and support informed clinical decision-making. The DSI transparency requirements are exactly what that authority is for.⏎⏎Defacto Health LLC Comments | ONC-0179-P | Page 7 of 9⏎---------------------------------------------------------------⏎⏎If ONC is concerned about the compliance burden the DSI requirements place on smaller developers, we would support the following modifications, which we believe could meaningfully reduce burden without removing the substantive protections:⏎⏎a. ONC could develop and publish a standardized model card template that developers can use to satisfy the disclosure requirements. This would reduce the documentation effort for developers who are starting from scratch and would make disclosures more comparable and readable for providers. Several academic and industry groups have proposed template formats (see Gebru et al., "Datasheets for Datasets," Communications of the ACM 2021;64:86-92, which provides a parallel framework for training data documentation that could be adapted).⏎⏎b. ONC could implement a tiered disclosure approach, where the depth of required disclosure scales with the risk level of the clinical application. A scheduling optimization tool would face lighter requirements than a sepsis prediction algorithm or a medication dosing recommendation engine. The HTI-1 rule's risk stratification framework for interventions provides a starting point for this kind of tiering.⏎⏎c. ONC could create a shared repository or registry where model card disclosures are published and accessible, reducing the burden on individual developers to create bespoke disclosure mechanisms while giving providers a single place to look up the tools they are using.⏎⏎These are practical options. None of them require ONC to abandon the transparency principle. They just ask ONC to find smarter ways to implement it.⏎⏎⏎Defacto Health LLC Comments | ONC-0179-P | Page 8 of 9⏎---------------------------------------------------------------⏎⏎A NOTE ON THE INFORMATION BLOCKING AMENDMENTS⏎⏎This comment has focused primarily on the DSI certification criterion because that is where our concern is most immediate. I want to briefly note that the proposed amendments to information blocking definitions and exceptions in this rulemaking also bear watching from the perspective of rural and frontier providers. Our clinic network partners depend heavily on care coordination data flows between providers, and any changes to the information blocking framework that create new ambiguities about what constitutes a permissible practice could create new friction in exactly the data exchange relationships our providers rely on.⏎⏎We do not have a specific objection to the proposed amendments at this time, but we would ask ONC to ensure that any guidance accompanying the final rule addresses how the amended exceptions apply in multi-provider rural networks where care coordination data sharing is the norm rather than the exception. The information blocking provisions in 45 CFR Part 171 were drafted primarily with large health systems in mind, and the practical application to small rural networks has always required some interpretive work. More clarity there would be welcome.⏎⏎⏎THE LARGER POINT ABOUT WHAT CERTIFICATION IS FOR⏎⏎I keep coming back to something that I think gets lost in these deregulatory conversations. The ONC certification program is not primarily a quality assurance mechanism for health IT developers. It is a signal to providers and patients that a product has met a set of standards that the federal government has determined are necessary for safe and effective use in clinical settings. When ONC certifies a product, rural clinic administrators like me, and more importantly the clinicians we support, take that as a meaningful representation. We do not have the capacity to independently audit every tool we deploy. We are relying on the certification program to have asked the hard questions.⏎⏎Defacto Health LLC Comments | ONC-0179-P | Page 9 of 9⏎---------------------------------------------------------------⏎⏎That reliance is especially acute in the AI context, because AI-assisted clinical decision support is qualitatively different from other health IT functions. A scheduling module that fails produces a scheduling problem. An AI sepsis screening tool that fails produces a patient safety event. The transparency disclosures required by the DSI criterion are what make it possible for clinicians to calibrate their reliance on these tools appropriately. A clinician who knows that a sepsis algorithm was validated only on adult inpatient populations at urban academic medical centers will think twice before relying heavily on it for a 70-year-old agricultural worker presenting to a rural critical access hospital. That calibration is only possible if the information exists and is accessible. The DSI criterion is what makes sure it does.⏎⏎There is also a longer-term dimension here that I do not think has been adequately considered. The health AI market is developing very quickly. New tools are entering the market faster than any single provider organization can evaluate them. The certification program is one of the few mechanisms that can impose consistent baseline standards across that market at scale. If ONC weakens the DSI transparency requirements now, before the market has matured, it will be very difficult to re-impose them later. Vendors will have built products and business models around the assumption that detailed disclosure is optional, and there will be significant resistance to any future tightening. The time to hold the line on transparency is before that market structure solidifies, not after.⏎⏎We appreciate the opportunity to submit these comments. Our organization is willing to participate in any stakeholder engagement process ONC convenes on the DSI criterion specifically, including any technical expert panels or listening sessions focused on rural and frontier provider perspectives on clinical AI deployment.⏎⏎One logistical note: the comment portal timed out twice during our submission attempt and we are not certain whether an earlier draft of this comment was submitted as a duplicate. TMA's comments focus specifically on the proposed elimination of the Decision Support Interventions (DSI) certification criterion and, in particular, the transparency requirements for AI-based clinical decision support tools — what the rule refers to as "model cards" and associated disclosure elements. We do not oppose deregulation as a general matter. What we oppose is removing a safety requirement before there is any demonstrated alternative mechanism to protect patients and clinicians from opaque, poorly validated AI tools in clinical settings.⏎⏎www.texmed.org/policy/HealthIT-comments-2025⏎policy@texmed.org⏎⏎BACKGROUND AND ORGANIZATIONAL CONCERN⏎⏎The DSI certification criterion, as currently structured under 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11), requires that health IT developers document and disclose the intended use of any AI-based decision support intervention, the target patient population, known risks and limitations, training data characteristics, and whether external validation has been conducted. These are not bureaucratic formalities. They are the minimum information a physician needs to evaluate whether a clinical AI tool is appropriate for a particular patient. A cardiologist in Lubbock using a risk-stratification algorithm needs to know if that algorithm was trained primarily on data from academic medical centers in the Northeast. A family physician in the Rio Grande Valley needs to know if the sepsis prediction model embedded in her EHR has ever been validated on populations with high rates of diabetes and late-stage presentation. Without the model card requirement, she has no mechanism to find out.⏎⏎ONC's own 2024 analysis in the AI in Health Care report (ONC Data Brief No. 64, released February 2024) documented that fewer than 30 percent of surveyed clinicians reported having access to documentation describing how embedded AI tools in their EHRs were developed or validated. That number is troubling on its own. What it means in practice is that physicians are routinely using tools they cannot evaluate, and the certification framework was one of the few levers available to change that. Removing the DSI criterion eliminates that lever without replacing it.⏎⏎TMA Comments | ASTP/ONC Deregulatory Docket | Page 2⏎⏎The proposed rule cites regulatory burden reduction as justification, referencing Executive Order 14192 (January 31, 2025) and the broader deregulatory agenda. We understand the policy context. The question is whether the burden being reduced falls on the right party. Compliance costs for model card documentation fall on health IT developers. The risks of non-disclosure fall on patients. That is not a symmetric trade-off, and the rule does not adequately address the asymmetry.⏎⏎SPECIFIC CONCERNS REGARDING THE DSI CRITERION⏎⏎The following concerns reflect input gathered from TMA members across multiple practice settings, including a February 2025 survey of 412 Texas physicians who use AI-assisted clinical decision support tools:⏎⏎1. Intended use and target population disclosures. Without these, physicians cannot determine whether an algorithm was designed for the clinical context in which it is being applied. The FDA's framework for Software as a Medical Device (SaMD), articulated in the 2021 AI/ML Action Plan and further developed through 21 CFR Part 820 quality system requirements, recognizes this as a basic safety consideration. ONC's model card requirement mirrored this logic for non-FDA-regulated tools. Removing it creates a regulatory gap for a large category of embedded clinical AI.⏎⏎2. Training data characteristics. This is the disclosure element our members cited most frequently as clinically meaningful. Seventy-one percent of respondents in our February survey said they would change how they used an AI recommendation if they knew the training data did not reflect their patient population. That is not a marginal concern. It goes directly to the question of whether algorithmic outputs can be trusted in specific clinical contexts.⏎⏎3. External validation documentation. The 2023 JAMA Internal Medicine study by Wong et al. (JAMA Intern Med. 2023;183(11):1205-1213) found that a majority of commercially deployed clinical AI tools had no published external validation data. The DSI criterion did not require that validation exist; it required disclosure of whether it existed. That is a minimal ask. Eliminating even that disclosure requirement removes the only standardized mechanism for clinicians to know what they are working with.⏎⏎4. Known risks and limitations. This element is perhaps the most directly safety-relevant. A physician who does not know a tool has a documented failure mode in patients with renal insufficiency cannot compensate for that limitation. The model card requirement made this information available at the point of care. Without it, the information may exist somewhere in a developer's internal documentation and nowhere else.⏎⏎TMA Comments | ASTP/ONC Deregulatory Docket | Page 3⏎⏎I want to be direct about something that does not always come through in formal comments. The medication reconciliation failure my family experienced last spring in Wausau was not caused by AI. It was caused by a system that had no regulatory obligation to share information it was technically capable of sharing. What I keep coming back to when I read this proposed rule is that the same logic applies here. Developers are technically capable of producing model card documentation. The certification criterion created the obligation. Removing the obligation does not mean the documentation will still happen. In competitive markets with cost pressure, it will not.⏎⏎ONC has cited the possibility that market forces and voluntary disclosure frameworks will fill the gap left by removing the DSI criterion. We are skeptical. The ASTP/ONC Health IT Certification Program is specifically designed to address market failures in health information technology, as ONC itself acknowledged in the preamble to the 2020 ONC Cures Act Final Rule (85 FR 25642). Voluntary disclosure in a market where purchasers (health systems and physician practices) have limited ability to evaluate AI tool quality is not a reliable substitute for certification requirements. The 21st Century Cures Act, at Section 4002, gave ONC explicit authority to establish certification criteria that protect patient safety and clinician decision-making. The DSI criterion is an exercise of that authority. Removing it requires a more compelling safety justification than the rule currently provides.⏎⏎RECOMMENDATION⏎⏎TMA recommends that ASTP/ONC retain the DSI certification criterion in its current form, including all five disclosure elements: intended use, target population, known risks, training data characteristics, and external validation status. If ONC determines that specific elements create disproportionate burden, we would support a targeted revision process that engages clinical stakeholders, including physician organizations, before any element is eliminated. What we cannot support is wholesale removal of a transparency requirement that physicians are actively using.⏎⏎The February 2025 survey data referenced above is available upon request. If developers can more broadly restrict access to AI-related documentation under a licensing rationale, and the certification requirement to disclose that documentation is simultaneously removed, the combined effect on clinician access to model information could be significantly worse than either change in isolation. CMS-2025-0050-110084♔CMS-2025-0050♔Joshua Walker♔Regard Technologies, Inc.♔♔♔♔Regard Technologies supports retaining the DSI certification criterion's AI transparency requirements — including model cards, training data disclosures, and external validation documentation — arguing these provisions impose minimal developer bur...♔Regard Technologies, Inc. Comments on ASTP/ONC Deregulatory Actions To Unleash Prosperity: Health Data, Technology, and Interoperability⏎Docket No. ONC-2025-0001⏎Submitted by: Joshua Walker, Chief Medical Officer, Regard Technologies, Inc.⏎⏎-----⏎⏎EXECUTIVE SUMMARY⏎⏎Regard Technologies, Inc. respectfully submits these comments in response to ONC's proposed deregulatory rule. We develop AI-powered clinical decision support software deployed across more than 120 hospitals in 19 states, including three Vermont health systems. Our tools assist clinicians in identifying conditions such as sepsis, acute kidney injury, and heart failure, often in time-sensitive settings. We write specifically to address ONC's proposal to remove or substantially revise the Decision Support Interventions (DSI) certification criterion, and in particular the provisions requiring AI model cards, transparency disclosures, and documentation of intended use, target population, known risks, training data characteristics, and external validation results.⏎⏎Our position is straightforward: those specific transparency requirements should be retained. We recognize the genuine costs that over-engineered certification processes impose on developers, and we have lived those costs in ways that are difficult to describe without frustration. But the DSI transparency provisions are not the problem. Removing them would not meaningfully reduce developer burden while creating a real and measurable risk of harm to patients.⏎⏎-----⏎⏎NUMBERED RECOMMENDATIONS⏎⏎1. Retain the DSI certification criterion's requirements for AI transparency disclosures, including model cards documenting intended use, target population, known risks, training data characteristics, and external validation results (45 CFR 170.315(b)(11)).⏎⏎2. If ONC believes the current documentation format imposes unnecessary costs, the agency should issue guidance on standardized, machine-readable model card templates rather than eliminating the requirement.⏎⏎3. ONC should distinguish clearly in the final rule between administrative certification burdens that add no clinical value and transparency requirements that directly inform clinician decision-making. These are not the same category of requirement, and the proposed rule does not adequately draw that line.⏎⏎4. ONC should commission a structured review of which specific DSI documentation elements have been cited in adverse event reports or near-miss analyses before finalizing any removals, consulting the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality's existing patient safety event taxonomy.⏎⏎5. ONC should consider whether interoperability between AI model documentation and clinical governance systems at hospitals could be achieved through FHIR-based metadata exchange, which might reduce the manual documentation burden without eliminating the underlying transparency obligation.⏎⏎-----⏎⏎Regard Technologies, Inc. Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 2⏎⏎The experience that motivates these comments is specific enough that I want to describe it plainly. Last spring, our engineering team spent eleven weeks rebuilding a sepsis detection algorithm that was already performing well by every clinical metric we track. The rebuild was not triggered by a safety concern. It was not triggered by a complaint from a clinician or a hospital. It was triggered by certification documentation requirements that, in our team's judgment and in the judgment of the three clinical informaticists we consulted, had no bearing on whether the algorithm would correctly flag a deteriorating patient. Eleven weeks. During that same stretch, three Vermont hospitals in our network postponed deployment entirely because our updated certification status was in limbo. I will never know with certainty whether any patient deteriorated during that gap. That uncertainty is not something I have made peace with.⏎⏎So when ONC proposes reducing certification burden, I want to be clear: I understand exactly what that proposal is responding to. The problem is real. Certification timelines that stretch to eighteen months for incremental software updates, documentation requirements that demand re-testing of unchanged components, and processes that seem designed for waterfall-era software development applied to tools that are updated on continuous deployment cycles -- these are genuine problems and they deserve serious regulatory attention. The 2020 ONC Cures Act Final Rule (85 FR 25642) created a framework that was ambitious and, in many respects, necessary. The implementation of that framework has in some areas become a compliance exercise rather than a patient safety exercise. We have seen it firsthand.⏎⏎But the DSI model card requirements are not where the administrative waste is concentrated. When our team analyzed the eleven-week rebuild I described above, the documentation components that consumed the most time were not the model card disclosures. They were the technical infrastructure requirements, the conformance testing workflows, and the API documentation standards that exist for interoperability purposes rather than clinical transparency purposes. The model card itself -- the intended use statement, the description of the training dataset, the external validation summary -- took one engineer roughly four days to complete, including the time spent pulling validation data from our existing clinical studies. Four days out of eleven weeks. If ONC's goal is to reduce developer burden, the model card is not the lever worth pulling.⏎⏎Regard Technologies, Inc. Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 3⏎⏎What the model card does, in practice, is give a hospital's clinical informatics team something to actually read before they deploy our tool. This matters more than it might appear from the outside. When Fletcher Allen Health Care (now UVM Health Network) first evaluated our sepsis detection module in 2022, their informatics committee asked specifically about the demographic composition of our training dataset. They had concerns -- reasonable ones, grounded in published literature on sepsis algorithm performance disparities -- about whether a model trained predominantly on data from large urban academic medical centers would perform equivalently in a rural Vermont patient population. We had an answer to that question because we were required to document it. The answer was not entirely satisfying; our training data was more geographically concentrated than we would have liked. That disclosure led directly to a prospective validation study at two of their facilities before full deployment. The Sepsis-3 criteria (Singer et al., JAMA 2016) that inform our model's logic were developed on datasets with their own limitations, and a hospital system has every right to understand how those limitations propagate into a specific commercial tool.⏎⏎This is not an abstract concern. The published literature on clinical AI performance disparities is extensive. Obermeyer et al. (Science, 2019) documented how a widely deployed commercial algorithm systematically underestimated illness severity in Black patients due to the use of healthcare cost as a proxy for health need. The algorithm in that study had no requirement to disclose its training data characteristics or known performance disparities. Hospitals deploying it had no model card to review. The result was a measurable disparity in care that persisted for years across multiple health systems before independent researchers identified it. One could argue that the DSI transparency requirements exist precisely because of cases like that one, and ONC's proposed rule does not explain why the regulatory environment that produced that harm is preferable to the current framework.⏎⏎The agency's stated rationale for revising the DSI criterion, as described in the NPRM, centers on reducing barriers to market entry and lowering compliance costs for smaller developers. We take that rationale seriously. A startup with five engineers building a clinical decision support tool for a narrow specialty indication is not in the same position as a large EHR vendor with a dedicated regulatory affairs team. The documentation burden that we can absorb with a team of twelve engineers would be genuinely prohibitive for a two-person company. This is a real tension and the proposed rule is not wrong to identify it.⏎⏎Regard Technologies, Inc. Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 4⏎⏎The answer to that tension, though, is not to remove the transparency requirement. The answer is to make compliance with the transparency requirement less expensive. ONC has existing authority under 45 CFR Part 170 to issue standardized templates, to create safe harbors for small developers who self-attest to specific model card elements, and to develop machine-readable model card formats that could be generated semi-automatically from a developer's existing internal documentation. The FDA's approach to predetermined change control plans for AI/ML-based Software as a Medical Device (SaMD), outlined in the agency's 2021 action plan, offers one model for how transparency obligations can be structured to scale with organizational capacity rather than being applied uniformly regardless of context. ONC could learn from that approach without abandoning the underlying obligation.⏎⏎There is also a question here about what happens downstream if the DSI transparency requirements are removed. Hospitals have clinical governance obligations that do not disappear when a federal certification requirement disappears. Under The Joint Commission's standards for clinical decision support (CAMH standard MM.01.01.03, for those tracking this), hospitals are expected to evaluate the appropriateness and performance of CDS tools as part of their medication management and patient safety programs. If ONC removes the federal requirement to document training data and external validation, individual hospitals will either (a) demand that documentation from vendors directly as a procurement condition, creating an unregulated patchwork of requirements that is arguably more burdensome than a single federal standard, or (b) deploy tools without that documentation, accepting a governance gap that their own accreditation standards arguably do not permit. Neither outcome is better than the status quo.⏎⏎Our experience with hospital procurement supports the first scenario. Since the DSI requirements took effect, we have seen hospital systems begin incorporating model card review into their vendor evaluation processes. This is good. It means clinicians are asking better questions about the tools they use. If the federal certification requirement disappears, some hospitals, particularly those with well-resourced informatics teams, will continue asking those questions and demanding documentation. Smaller and under-resourced hospitals, which are often the ones serving the most vulnerable patient populations, may not. The transparency requirement in the certification program functions as a floor. Floors matter most for the people who would otherwise be left without protection.⏎⏎Regard Technologies, Inc. Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 5⏎⏎I want to be honest about one thing I am genuinely uncertain about: whether the current DSI criterion, as written, is the right specification for what a model card should contain. The requirement to document "training data characteristics" is broad enough that different developers interpret it very differently. One developer might provide a single-sentence description of their training dataset size. Another might provide a full data sheet in the format proposed by Gebru et al. (2018) with demographic breakdowns, data collection methodology, and known gaps. Both might satisfy the current regulatory text. ONC could, if it chose, strengthen the requirement rather than remove it -- requiring more standardized and specific disclosures that would actually be comparable across vendors. That would be harder to achieve than a deregulatory action, but it would serve clinicians and patients better.⏎⏎The agency asked, in the NPRM, for comment on whether the DSI criterion creates barriers that outweigh its benefits. Our answer, based on the experience of deploying clinical AI tools in more than 120 hospitals, is no. The documentation burden associated specifically with the transparency components of DSI certification is not where the meaningful compliance costs accumulate. The costs accumulate in conformance testing, in API interoperability requirements, in the software testing and certification process timelines that have nothing to do with whether a clinician can evaluate whether an AI tool is appropriate for their patient population. If ONC wants to reduce burden, there is a long list of places to start that do not require eliminating the information clinicians need to make informed decisions about AI-assisted care. We would welcome the opportunity to provide ONC with a more detailed breakdown of where our certification compliance hours are actually spent, because we have tracked that data since 2021 and the distribution might surprise the agency.⏎⏎Regard Technologies, Inc. Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 6⏎⏎One more thing worth noting. The conversation about AI transparency in healthcare is moving in one direction at the state level, and it is not toward less disclosure. New York State's guidance on AI in clinical settings (DOH DAL 24-02, issued January 2024) explicitly requires that hospitals document the basis for AI tools used in clinical decision-making, including training data provenance. Colorado's SB23-169, enacted in 2023, imposes algorithmic impact assessment requirements on high-risk AI systems that include healthcare applications. California's AB 3030, signed in September 2024, requires AI-generated clinical communications to include specific disclosures. If ONC removes federal transparency requirements, developers will not face a simpler regulatory environment. They will face a fragmented state-by-state patchwork that is considerably more complex to navigate and that provides less consistent protection for patients across state lines. The federal floor that the DSI criterion provides is more valuable, not less, in a world where state AI regulation is accelerating.⏎⏎We urge ONC to retain the DSI transparency requirements and to direct its deregulatory attention toward the certification process elements that impose cost without clinical benefit. Reg. 18,210 (April 22, 2025). Our organization represents home health agencies, hospice providers, and personal care organizations serving millions of patients annually across the United States, with a particular membership concentration in the Gulf South and Southeast regions where access to integrated health information is not a policy abstraction but a daily clinical reality. We write specifically to address the proposal to remove the Decision Support Interventions (DSI) certification criterion, and we ask ONC to retain this requirement in its current form.⏎⏎BACKGROUND ON THE DSI CRITERION AND WHY IT MATTERS TO HOME HEALTH⏎⏎The DSI certification criterion, as currently codified at 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11), requires that certified health information technology systems provide structured transparency disclosures when deploying clinical decision support tools that incorporate predictive models or AI-driven recommendations. Those disclosures include documentation of intended use, the target patient population for which the model was validated, known limitations and risks, characteristics of the training data, and results of any external validation studies. ONC adopted this framework through the HTI-1 final rule (88 Fed. Reg. 23,746, April 18, 2023), drawing in part on recommendations from the Health IT Advisory Committee and a substantial body of published literature on algorithmic bias in healthcare settings, including the widely cited 2019 study by Obermeyer et al. in Science, which found that a commercial algorithm used to allocate care management resources systematically underserved Black patients relative to their actual clinical need.⏎⏎The proposed rule frames the removal of this criterion as burden reduction. The preamble acknowledges that the disclosures impose documentation costs on developers, and ONC projects reduced compliance expenditures in the range of several million dollars annually across the industry. We do not dispute that compliance documentation takes time and resources. But the question before ONC is not whether the disclosures are costless. The question is whether the safety and accountability benefits they provide justify the cost. On that question, the record is not close.⏎⏎National Alliance for Care at Home Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 2⏎⏎Home health agencies operate in a care environment that is already information-poor compared to hospital and ambulatory settings. Our patients are managed across multiple providers and settings. Their clinical data is distributed among hospital EHRs, primary care systems, specialist offices, pharmacy networks, and home health platforms, and despite years of interoperability rulemaking under 42 CFR Part 171, meaningful data exchange in the home health context remains incomplete. In that environment, when a care coordinator or home health nurse relies on a clinical decision support tool to help prioritize a patient visit schedule, or to flag a patient at elevated risk of hospitalization, the transparency of that tool is not a nice-to-have feature. It is the only mechanism by which the clinician can evaluate whether the recommendation in front of them is appropriate for the specific patient in their care.⏎⏎Consider what the absence of model card disclosures actually means in practice. A home health agency in Baton Rouge, Louisiana, using a commercially licensed risk stratification platform receives an alert that a 72-year-old diabetic patient with a recent stroke history is classified as "low risk" for the next 30 days. The nurse manager reviewing that alert has no way to know:⏎⏎1. Whether the model was trained on a patient population that included elderly patients with post-stroke diabetes management needs, or whether it was developed and validated primarily on younger, commercially insured patients.⏎2. Whether the model accounts for the social determinants of health that are particularly prevalent in the communities our Louisiana members serve, including housing instability, food insecurity, and limited transportation access.⏎3. Whether the model has been externally validated on a dataset independent of the developer's proprietary training data, or whether the published accuracy statistics reflect in-sample performance.⏎4. Whether the model has known failure modes in patients who have recently undergone medication changes, which is a common clinical scenario in the post-stroke population.⏎⏎Without the disclosures required by 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11), the nurse manager has no basis on which to make an informed judgment about whether to trust or override the recommendation. The algorithm is, in effect, a black box. The clinical decision support literature has documented the consequences of black-box algorithmic recommendations in healthcare settings at some length. A 2021 review by Sendak et al. published in the New England Journal of Medicine Catalyst found that clinical teams systematically over-relied on algorithmic recommendations when transparency information was absent, and that over-reliance was most pronounced in high-workload settings precisely the settings in which home health nurses and care coordinators operate every day.⏎⏎National Alliance for Care at Home Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 3⏎⏎ONC SHOULD RETAIN THE DSI CRITERION WITHOUT MODIFICATION⏎⏎The preamble to the proposed rule suggests that market forces and voluntary disclosure frameworks will fill the gap left by removing the certification criterion. We find this argument unpersuasive, and I want to be direct about why. The market for clinical decision support tools in home health is not characterized by the kind of competitive transparency that would produce voluntary disclosure. Home health agencies are typically price-takers with respect to technology platforms, particularly in states with Medicaid-dominant payer mixes. A home health agency serving rural parishes in Louisiana does not have the negotiating leverage to demand model card disclosures from a large health IT vendor as a condition of contract. The certification requirement creates a floor that applies uniformly to all vendors seeking ONC certification, which is the only mechanism that actually reaches the full market. See 45 CFR 170.523 (conditions and maintenance of certification); see also ONC's own analysis in the HTI-1 preamble at 88 Fed. Reg. 23,812-23,815, which concluded that voluntary disclosure frameworks had produced inconsistent and incomplete transparency documentation in the years prior to the HTI-1 rulemaking.⏎⏎The proposed rule also suggests that existing FDA oversight of Software as a Medical Device (SaMD) provides a parallel regulatory pathway that makes ONC certification requirements redundant. This argument has some surface plausibility, but it does not account for the substantial category of clinical decision support tools that fall below the FDA's enforcement discretion threshold under the 21st Century Cures Act, 42 U.S.C. 300jj-11(b)(2), and thus receive no federal transparency oversight at all unless the ONC certification criterion applies. The FDA's 2022 guidance on clinical decision support software, published September 27, 2022, explicitly confirmed that a significant portion of AI-assisted decision support tools used in home health and post-acute care settings are outside FDA's regulatory scope. Removing the DSI criterion for these tools leaves a regulatory gap with no substitute.⏎⏎We are also concerned about the timing. The healthcare industry is in the middle of a rapid expansion of AI-assisted tools in post-acute and home-based care. The number of commercially available risk stratification and care management platforms marketed to home health agencies has grown substantially in the past three years, and adoption has accelerated following changes to the Patient-Driven Groupings Model payment structure under 42 CFR Part 484. Removing transparency requirements at precisely the moment when AI adoption is accelerating in this sector seems to us to be the wrong sequencing. The period of most rapid adoption is when disclosure standards are most needed, not least needed.⏎⏎National Alliance for Care at Home Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 4⏎⏎We recognize that ONC has genuine latitude to reconsider certification criteria when the evidentiary record supports a conclusion that they are not achieving their intended purpose or that they impose costs disproportionate to their benefits. We do not think that record exists here. The HTI-1 rulemaking generated substantial public comment in support of the DSI criterion from patient advocacy organizations, health equity researchers, and clinical professional associations, and the final rule reflected a considered balancing of the competing interests. The current proposal does not, in our reading of the preamble, identify new evidence that has changed that calculus. It identifies compliance costs, which were known at the time of the HTI-1 rulemaking, and it asserts that market mechanisms will substitute for regulatory requirements, which is an assertion rather than a finding supported by the record.⏎⏎We would also note, because it seems relevant to ONC's consideration of real-world impacts, that the interoperability and transparency infrastructure built under the 21st Century Cures Act and subsequent rulemakings is still relatively young. The information blocking regulations at 45 CFR Part 171 have been in full enforcement for a relatively short period. The certification criteria adopted in HTI-1 are newer still. The system has not had time to prove out its full benefits before this proposed rule would begin dismantling portions of it. Our member agencies are still in the process of operationalizing data exchange workflows that depend on the certification framework being stable and predictable. Regulatory churn in this space is itself a form of burden, and it falls disproportionately on smaller home health agencies that do not have in-house technology compliance staff.⏎⏎Our specific request is straightforward. ONC should withdraw the proposal to remove 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11) from the certification program and retain the DSI criterion in its current form. If ONC believes that specific elements of the disclosure requirements impose unnecessary costs without corresponding safety benefits, we would support a targeted rulemaking process that examines those specific elements with input from affected stakeholders, rather than the wholesale removal of the criterion that the current proposal contemplates.⏎⏎Comments may be directed to Anthony Torres, Campaign Director, National Alliance for Care at Home.⏎⏎ntorres@nahc-alliance.org⏎⏎Respectfully submitted,⏎⏎Anthony Torres⏎Campaign Director⏎National Alliance for Care at Home⏎June 16, 2025♔♔2025-12-27T00:00:00Z♔2025-12-27T00:00:00Z♔2025-12-12T00:00:00Z♔2026-02-10T00:00:00Z♔5♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Retain the current Decision Support Interventions (DSI) certification criterion requiring AI model cards and transparency disclosures (intended use, target population, known risks, training data characteristics, external validation) to ensure patient safety, informed clinical decision-making, and accountability in AI-assisted healthcare.♔The 'black box' problem is a documented barrier to AI adoption in healthcare; model cards directly address clinician and organizational concerns about trustworthiness and are a proven mechanism to build confidence.♔advocacy_group♔high♔angry♔Louisiana♔campaign director♔45♔Last spring, I watched my mother spend eleven days in a Baton Rouge hospital after a stroke, and not a single specialist treating her could pull up the home health records from the agency that had been managing her diabetes for two years — records that would have told them exactly which medications she'd already failed on. CMS-2025-0050-110087♔CMS-2025-0050♔Sarah Taylor♔Policy Center for Maternal Mental Health♔♔♔♔Proposed expansions to information blocking exceptions and removal of ONC certification criteria would undermine care coordination for perinatal mental health patients, who depend on timely, complete obstetric record sharing between providers to p...♔Policy Center for Maternal Mental Health⏎Comments Submitted to ASTP/ONC Docket⏎Re: Deregulatory Actions To Unleash Prosperity: Health Data, Technology, and Interoperability⏎⏎June 16, 2025⏎⏎The Policy Center for Maternal Mental Health submits these comments in response to the proposed rule from the Assistant Secretary for Technology Policy and the Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology concerning revisions to the ONC Health IT Certification Program and amendments to information blocking definitions and exceptions. Our organization works specifically on the policy and systems-level conditions that determine whether women experiencing perinatal mental health crises can access timely, coordinated care. The proposed changes in this rulemaking concern us considerably, and we want to explain why in some detail.⏎⏎Before getting to the interoperability and information blocking provisions, though, we want to raise something that we think is being almost entirely overlooked in this conversation. The administrative preamble to this proposed rule frames burden reduction on health IT developers and healthcare providers as the governing rationale. We understand that framing. Compliance costs are real. Workflow disruption is real. But if the federal government is genuinely concerned about administrative burden in the health data ecosystem, there is a category of actor whose reporting and transparency obligations have never come close to matching their market power or their influence on the conditions patients actually experience: pharmaceutical manufacturers. Before this agency or any other loosens the interoperability protections that patients depend on, we think there is a serious and largely unanswered question about whether the same deregulatory energy is being applied with any consistency. Drug companies spend enormous sums on marketing and lobbying, and the actual breakdown of their research and development expenditures has been notoriously opaque for decades. We are not aware of any comparable federal effort to require pharmaceutical manufacturers to publish audited R&D spending as a condition of market participation. The Institute for Clinical and Economic Review has repeatedly noted the difficulty of assessing whether drug prices bear any reasonable relationship to actual development costs precisely because that data is not publicly available in any standardized form. If burden reduction is the goal, we would ask the agency to explain why the reporting and transparency obligations that protect patients are the first target, rather than the opacity that protects pharmaceutical profit margins. That is a genuine question, and we think it deserves a genuine answer.⏎⏎That said, the bulk of these comments concerns what the proposed rule would actually do to health data access and information blocking protections, because those changes have direct and documented consequences for maternal mental health patients. The proposed rule would revise certain information blocking exceptions under 45 CFR part 171, specifically the Infeasibility Exception and the Privacy Exception, in ways that would expand the circumstances under which a health IT developer or covered entity could decline to share patient data without triggering an information blocking violation. The preamble describes these changes as clarifications and flexibility enhancements. Our organization reads them differently. The existing regulatory framework, particularly the information blocking provisions enacted under the 21st Century Cures Act (Public Law 114-255) and subsequently implemented through the ONC final rule published at 85 Fed. Reg. 25642 (May 1, 2020), was designed to address a documented and persistent pattern of obstruction. The pattern was not hypothetical. It was the subject of ONC's own 2015 report to Congress on information blocking, which documented specific practices by EHR vendors and providers that impeded data sharing. Loosening the exceptions now, before those patterns have been durably corrected, is premature.⏎⏎The practical consequences for perinatal mental health care are not abstract. Postpartum psychiatric conditions, including postpartum depression, anxiety disorders, and postpartum psychosis, affect an estimated one in five women in the period following delivery (Wisner et al., 2013, JAMA Psychiatry). Effective treatment almost always requires coordination between obstetric and psychiatric providers, which in turn requires timely access to complete obstetric records including delivery notes, medication administration records, blood loss documentation, and discharge summaries. These are precisely the categories of records that, in practice, have been subject to the kinds of delays and partial disclosures that the information blocking rules were meant to address. The ONC Cures Act Final Rule at 45 CFR 171.301 established that actors must not engage in practices that interfere with access, exchange, or use of electronic health information except as specifically permitted under the enumerated exceptions. The proposed revisions to those exceptions would give providers and vendors more room to cite workflow burden or system incompatibility as a basis for delayed or incomplete disclosure. In our organization's view, that is not a clarification. It is a regression.⏎⏎Policy Center for Maternal Mental Health Comments | ASTP/ONC Docket | Page 2⏎⏎We want to be specific about what we have observed, because specificity matters here. In the spring of 2024, a family in rural Mississippi spent approximately three weeks attempting to obtain complete obstetric records for a patient who had been discharged from a small regional hospital following a near-fatal postpartum hemorrhage. The records were needed by a treating OB-GYN to coordinate psychiatric follow-up care. The hospital's responses during that period cited, in sequence: system compatibility limitations, staff workflow constraints, and the need for additional authorization forms that had not been mentioned in the original request. A partial clinical summary was eventually transmitted. By the time it arrived, the patient had experienced a psychiatric crisis that required inpatient hospitalization. We are describing one case. It is not an outlier. The Mississippi State Department of Health's 2022 Maternal Mortality Review Committee report documented that care coordination failures, including incomplete information transfer between providers, contributed to adverse outcomes in a significant share of pregnancy-related deaths reviewed. Mississippi has one of the highest maternal mortality rates in the country. The information blocking framework was supposed to help close exactly this kind of gap. Weakening it now, in this regulatory environment, in states with already-strained rural health infrastructure, would be a serious mistake.⏎⏎The proposed rule also contemplates removing certain certification criteria from the ONC Health IT Certification Program, including criteria related to clinical decision support and electronic prescribing for controlled substances. The preamble argues that market forces and state-level requirements have made federal certification criteria redundant in some of these areas. We are skeptical of that argument. Certification criteria serve a function that market competition does not: they establish a floor that applies regardless of vendor size, geography, or market position. Small rural hospitals in states like Mississippi, Alabama, and West Virginia are not in a strong negotiating position with EHR vendors. They do not have the leverage to demand interoperability features that larger health systems can insist on contractually. When federal certification criteria disappear, those hospitals frequently lose capabilities that their vendor contracts do not guarantee. This is documented in the literature: a 2021 study published in Health Affairs (Adler-Milstein et al.) found that rural hospitals were significantly less likely than urban hospitals to achieve full interoperability on key data exchange measures, and that this gap was associated with vendor capabilities and contract terms rather than hospital IT investment levels. Removing certification floors does not reduce burden for rural hospitals. It reduces their leverage.⏎⏎On the specific question of the Privacy Exception revisions, the proposed language would permit actors to more readily cite patient privacy concerns as a basis for withholding information from other treating providers. We understand the intent: there are genuine privacy considerations in health data exchange, and the regulatory framework should accommodate them. But the current proposal does not adequately distinguish between privacy protections that serve patients and privacy claims that serve institutions. A provider who withholds a patient's records from another treating provider on the grounds that the patient has not provided specific authorization for that transfer is not protecting the patient. In many cases, that patient does not know she needs to provide a separate authorization. She assumed, reasonably, that her providers could talk to each other. The existing framework under 45 CFR 164.506 already permits treatment-related disclosures without individual authorization under HIPAA. The information blocking rules were designed in part to ensure that actors could not use privacy as a pretext to obstruct legitimate treatment-related data exchange. The proposed revisions create more room for exactly that pretext, and we do not think the preamble adequately grapples with that risk.⏎⏎We want to return briefly to the pharmaceutical transparency point, because it is not entirely tangential to the information blocking discussion. One of the arguments made in favor of loosening information blocking exceptions is that the current requirements impose compliance costs on providers and developers that are disproportionate to the benefits. That cost-benefit framing might be more persuasive if it were applied consistently across the health care system. The opacity of pharmaceutical R&D spending, for example, is not a regulatory accident. It is maintained by a combination of trade secret protections and the absence of any federal requirement to publish audited cost breakdowns. A 2019 study in JAMA Internal Medicine (Wouters et al.) estimated median capitalized R&D costs for new drugs approved between 2009 and 2018 at approximately $985 million, but that estimate was based on a sample of publicly traded companies with available financial disclosures, not a comprehensive mandatory reporting system. Congress has considered but not enacted legislation that would require manufacturers to disclose R&D expenditures as a condition of Medicare and Medicaid participation. If the agency believes that transparency requirements impose unjustified burdens when applied to health IT developers, it would be worth explaining why the same logic does not apply to pharmaceutical manufacturers whose pricing decisions are made in conditions of near-total opacity. We are not asking this rhetorically. We think the inconsistency is real and worth explaining.⏎⏎Policy Center for Maternal Mental Health Comments | ASTP/ONC Docket | Page 3⏎⏎Our organization's specific recommendations are as follows:⏎⏎1. The agency should not finalize the proposed expansions to the Infeasibility Exception under 45 CFR 171.302 without first publishing data on how that exception has been invoked in practice since the 2020 final rule, including the frequency and nature of complaints filed with ONC's information blocking complaint portal. If the exception is functioning as intended, that data should be available and should support the proposed changes. If it is not available, that is itself a problem.⏎⏎2. The proposed revisions to the Privacy Exception at 45 CFR 171.306 should be withdrawn pending further stakeholder engagement specifically with patient advocacy organizations, particularly those representing populations that have historically experienced information blocking as a barrier to care coordination rather than a protection of privacy. The current proposal was developed primarily in response to provider and developer feedback. That is an incomplete record.⏎⏎3. Any removal of certification criteria from the ONC Health IT Certification Program should be accompanied by a documented analysis of the impact on rural and critical access hospitals, with specific attention to whether voluntary market mechanisms have actually produced the interoperability outcomes that certification requirements were designed to ensure. The 2021 Health Affairs findings cited above suggest they have not.⏎⏎4. The agency should consider whether the deregulatory framing of this rulemaking is appropriately calibrated to the actual burden distribution in health data exchange. Providers and developers are not the only parties experiencing burden. Patients who cannot access or share their own records, and clinicians who cannot obtain the information they need to coordinate care, are also bearing costs. Those costs are harder to quantify, but they are not less real.⏎⏎We recognize that the agency has legitimate reasons to revisit regulatory requirements that have proven unworkable in practice. Certification criteria that impose costs without producing meaningful interoperability benefits are worth examining. Information blocking exceptions that are so narrow they create compliance problems without improving data sharing are worth revising. We are not arguing against any regulatory reconsideration. What we are arguing is that the specific revisions proposed here appear to move in the wrong direction for the patient populations our organization works with, and that the cost-benefit analysis in the preamble does not adequately account for the harms that flow from inadequate data access in perinatal care settings. The 85 Fed. Reg. 25642 final rule took years to develop and represented a genuine attempt to address documented obstruction. Unwinding those protections on the basis of developer and provider feedback, without a comparable evidentiary record of patient harm from the current rules, is not a regulatory process we can endorse.⏎⏎The Policy Center for Maternal Mental Health appreciates the opportunity to submit these comments and requests that they be included in the administrative record in their entirety.
