We urge ASTP/ONC to retain these requirements in full. The ACR does not oppose the broader deregulatory orientation of this rulemaking in every respect, and we recognize that some of the proposed burden reductions in other certification areas are reasonable. But the DSI transparency requirements are not administrative overhead. They are patient safety infrastructure.⏎⏎⏎BACKGROUND: WHAT THE DSI CRITERION REQUIRES AND WHY IT WAS ADOPTED⏎⏎The DSI certification criterion, finalized in the HTI-1 rule published January 9, 2024 (89 Fed. Reg. 1192), established specific requirements for health IT systems that incorporate AI and machine learning-based clinical decision support. Among those requirements is the mandate that developers publish "source attributes" for each AI/ML-based DSI — effectively a structured disclosure akin to a model card — that includes the intervention's intended use case, the population on which the model was trained, known performance limitations, fairness and bias considerations, and whether the model has been validated on data external to its training set (45 C.F.R. § 170.315(b)(11), as amended).⏎⏎This was not a novel or untested concept when ONC finalized it. The model card framework had been described in detail by Mitchell et al. (2019) in their foundational paper published in the proceedings of the ACM Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency. The FDA's AI/ML-Based Software as a Medical Device Action Plan, released in January 2021, similarly called for transparency documentation as a condition of responsible deployment. The National Academy of Medicine's 2019 report "Artificial Intelligence in Health Care: The Hope, the Hype, the Promise, the Peril" had identified opacity in AI training and validation as among the most significant near-term risks to clinical AI adoption. By the time ONC included the disclosure requirements in HTI-1, there was substantial scientific and policy consensus that clinicians and patients needed access to this information to make informed decisions about whether to rely on AI-generated recommendations.⏎⏎ACR Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 2⏎⏎The ACR supported these requirements during the HTI-1 comment period, and nothing has changed in the intervening period that would cause us to revise that position. If anything, the evidence for retaining them has grown.⏎⏎⏎THE CASE FOR RETENTION: PATIENT SAFETY IN RADIOLOGY AND RELATED SPECIALTIES⏎⏎Radiology is arguably the medical specialty most directly affected by clinical AI deployment. As of the date of these comments, the FDA has cleared or authorized more than 950 AI/ML-enabled medical devices, and a substantial majority of those are imaging-related (FDA, Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning (AI/ML)-Enabled Medical Devices, updated April 2025). Radiologists in ACR member practices are being asked to incorporate AI tools for tasks including pulmonary nodule detection, coronary artery calcium scoring, intracranial hemorrhage flagging, and breast density classification, often from multiple vendors operating simultaneously within a single reading workflow.⏎⏎The clinical stakes of getting this wrong are high. A model trained predominantly on chest radiographs from one demographic group may perform materially worse on patients from underrepresented populations — a concern documented empirically in the literature (Larson et al., 2021, "Performance of a Deep-Learning Neural Network Model in Assessing Skeletal Maturity on Pediatric Hand Radiographs," Radiology; Seyyed-Kalantari et al., 2021, "Underdiagnosis Bias of Artificial Intelligence Algorithms Applied to Chest Radiographs in Under-Served Patient Populations," Nature Medicine). A model validated only on retrospective data from academic medical centers may not generalize to community radiology practices, where equipment, patient mix, and imaging protocols differ. Without the disclosures required under the current DSI criterion, a radiologist in a community hospital in, say, Bridgeport, Connecticut has no standardized, reliable way to know whether the AI tool flagging or not flagging a lung nodule on a low-dose CT was ever validated on patients who look like the population in that waiting room.⏎⏎This is not a theoretical concern. The ACR's own data from the Lung CT Screening Reporting and Data System (Lung-RADS) program, which involves hundreds of participating sites, shows meaningful site-to-site variation in AI-assisted nodule characterization outcomes that correlates at least in part with patient demographic composition (ACR, Lung CT Screening Registry Annual Report, 2023). We are not in a position to attribute that variation definitively to model performance differences without the kind of training data and validation documentation that the DSI criterion would require. That is precisely the problem.⏎⏎ACR Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 3⏎⏎The proposed rule's suggestion that market forces and voluntary disclosure norms can substitute for certification requirements in this area is, frankly, not supported by what has actually happened in the AI/ML health IT market. Between the FDA's initial AI/ML action plan in 2021 and the finalization of HTI-1 in January 2024, voluntary model card adoption among FDA-cleared AI radiology tools was sporadic at best. A review published in the Journal of the American College of Radiology in 2022 (Gichoya et al., "AI Recognition of Patient Race in Medical Imaging") found that many deployed radiology AI tools lacked even basic documentation of training data demographics. The certification framework was adopted precisely because voluntary disclosure had not worked.⏎⏎⏎SPECIFIC CONCERNS ABOUT THE PROPOSED REMOVAL⏎⏎The proposed rule offers several justifications for removing or substantially weakening the DSI transparency requirements. The ACR addresses each in turn.⏎⏎Justification 1: Burden on developers⏎⏎ASTP/ONC suggests that compiling and maintaining model card disclosures imposes significant administrative costs on health IT developers, particularly smaller developers who may lack dedicated regulatory affairs capacity (89 Fed. Reg. [cite to proposed rule page]). The ACR does not dismiss this concern entirely. Compliance costs are real, and ONC should be attentive to barriers to entry that might reduce competition in the AI health IT market.⏎⏎That said, the burden argument does not hold up well under scrutiny when applied to the DSI transparency requirements specifically. The information required under 45 C.F.R. § 170.315(b)(11) — intended use, training population, validation status — is information that any responsible AI developer should be generating internally as part of model development and quality assurance regardless of regulatory requirements. If a developer does not know the demographic composition of its training data or whether its model has been externally validated, that is itself a patient safety problem, and a certification requirement that surfaces that gap is working as intended. The marginal burden of documenting and publishing information that should already exist is substantially lower than ASTP/ONC's burden estimate implies.⏎⏎ACR Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 4⏎⏎The ACR would note that several major AI health IT developers, including companies whose tools are widely used in radiology, have publicly stated that model card preparation does not represent a meaningful compliance burden for them (see, e.g., comments submitted by GE HealthCare and Philips in the HTI-1 docket, ONC-2023-0004). The burden concern appears to be more acute for earlier-stage developers, and ONC could address that through technical assistance, template standardization, or phased implementation timelines rather than by eliminating the requirement.⏎⏎Justification 2: Overlap with FDA requirements⏎⏎ASTP/ONC notes that many AI-based DSIs are already regulated as Software as a Medical Device (SaMD) under FDA oversight, and suggests that duplicative federal requirements may be unnecessary (see proposed rule preamble). The ACR respectfully disagrees with the characterization of these requirements as duplicative.⏎⏎FDA clearance under 510(k) or authorization under De Novo does not require the same scope of transparency documentation that the DSI criterion mandates. FDA's premarket review focuses on whether a device is substantially equivalent to a predicate or meets an appropriate standard for its intended use; it does not require public-facing disclosure of training data demographics or external validation results in a standardized, machine-readable format accessible to clinicians at the point of care. ONC's certification framework addresses a different gap in the information environment: it ensures that clinicians using certified EHR technology have access to structured AI disclosure information within the workflow where clinical decisions are being made. These two regulatory mechanisms address different problems and are genuinely complementary, not redundant (Office of the National Coordinator for Health IT, Strategy on Reducing Regulatory Burden, 2020; see also Maddox et al., 2019, "Questions for Artificial Intelligence in Health Care," JAMA).⏎⏎ACR Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 5⏎⏎Justification 3: Flexibility for innovation⏎⏎The proposed rule expresses a general policy preference for reducing prescriptive certification criteria in favor of outcomes-based or market-driven approaches, on the theory that prescriptive requirements may inhibit innovation. The ACR understands this policy orientation and does not categorically oppose it. For some certification criteria, a more flexible approach may well serve the public interest.⏎⏎But the DSI transparency requirements are not a technical implementation specification where flexibility is appropriate. They are a disclosure requirement. The question of whether clinicians should have access to standardized information about the AI tools they are using in patient care is not a question where the answer varies by business model or market segment. A radiologist interpreting a lung CT with AI assistance needs to know whether that AI was trained on data that resembles her patient population. Full stop. Framing that as a matter where "flexibility" is desirable mischaracterizes what is actually being proposed, which is the removal of a patient protection.⏎⏎⏎A NOTE ON THE INTEROPERABILITY IMPLICATIONS⏎⏎The ACR's institutional focus is patient safety and clinical quality, but the College also has a direct stake in health IT interoperability as it affects research and quality improvement. Our health economists and outcomes researchers — and this includes work done in collaboration with external academic partners — rely on structured, standardized data from certified EHR systems to conduct comparative effectiveness research, cost-effectiveness analyses, and quality registry studies.⏎⏎One of the consistent findings from that work over the past several years is that the certification framework, whatever its limitations, has produced measurable improvements in the availability and comparability of clinical data for research purposes. The HTI-1 rule's USCDI v3 requirements (45 C.F.R. § 170.213), the updated API requirements under § 170.315(g)(10), and the DSI criterion's transparency requirements collectively represent a coherent effort to make AI-assisted clinical data more interpretable and auditable. Removing the DSI transparency requirements creates a gap in that framework that is difficult to fill through other means.⏎⏎ACR Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 6⏎⏎To be specific about why this matters for research: when a researcher pulls claims and clinical data to study, say, the cost-effectiveness of AI-assisted lung cancer screening, she needs to know whether the AI nodule characterization tool used at each site was the same tool, trained on comparable data, and validated to similar standards. Without standardized model card disclosures, that information is often unavailable or requires laborious manual inquiry to each site. The ACR's health economics team has encountered this problem directly in ongoing work comparing AI-assisted Lung-RADS characterization outcomes across sites participating in the ACR's National Radiology Data Registry. Removing the DSI disclosure requirement would make that research harder, not easier, and would reduce the evidentiary base available to policymakers evaluating whether AI-assisted screening programs deliver the outcomes they promise.⏎⏎The ACR recognizes this is somewhat tangential to the patient safety argument, but it is worth putting on the record. The certification framework's transparency requirements serve multiple constituencies: clinicians, patients, and researchers. The burden reduction case for removal has to be weighed against costs that extend beyond the immediate clinical encounter.⏎⏎⏎WHAT THE ACR RECOMMENDS⏎⏎The ACR's recommendation is straightforward: retain the DSI certification criterion's source attribute disclosure requirements as finalized in HTI-1 without substantive modification. Specifically, the ACR recommends that ASTP/ONC:⏎⏎1. Retain the requirement that certified health IT include structured disclosures for each AI/ML-based DSI covering intended use, target population, training data characteristics (including demographic composition where feasible), known performance limitations, and external validation status (45 C.F.R. § 170.315(b)(11)).⏎⏎2. Retain the requirement that these disclosures be accessible to end users within the certified health IT system, rather than merely available on a developer's external website or on request.⏎⏎3. If ONC determines that some modification is warranted to address legitimate burden concerns for smaller developers, the ACR would support a phased compliance timeline or the development of a standardized disclosure template through a public-private process, provided that the substantive disclosure requirements remain intact.⏎⏎4. Reject the argument that FDA SaMD oversight is a sufficient substitute for ONC certification-based transparency requirements, for the reasons described above.⏎⏎5. Conduct, prior to any final rule that weakens the DSI transparency requirements, a formal analysis of the patient safety implications, including consultation with clinical specialty societies, patient advocacy organizations, and health equity researchers who have studied AI bias in medical imaging (see, e.g., Obermeyer et al., 2019, "Dissecting Racial Bias in an Algorithm Used to Manage the Health of Populations," Science; Adamson & Smith, 2018, "Machine Learning and Health Care Disparities in Dermatology," JAMA Dermatology).⏎⏎ACR Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 7⏎⏎⏎ADDITIONAL CONSIDERATIONS: THE INFORMATION BLOCKING AMENDMENTS⏎⏎The proposed rule also amends several information blocking exceptions under 45 C.F.R. Part 171. The ACR has reviewed these amendments and has more limited comments to offer, but does want to flag one concern.⏎⏎The proposed modifications to the Infeasibility Exception (45 C.F.R. § 171.204) would expand the circumstances under which a health IT developer or healthcare provider may decline to share electronic health information (EHI) without triggering information blocking liability. The ACR is concerned that, as applied to AI-generated diagnostic outputs and structured reporting data, an overly broad Infeasibility Exception could allow institutions to decline to share AI-assisted imaging findings in ways that impede care coordination and patient access to their own diagnostic information.⏎⏎Radiology reports increasingly contain AI-generated measurements, nodule characterizations, and risk scores that are clinically significant and should travel with the patient. If the Infeasibility Exception is expanded in ways that allow health systems to classify AI output data as technically distinct from the underlying clinical record and therefore outside the scope of EHI sharing obligations, that would be a significant and harmful step backward from the interoperability progress achieved under the 21st Century Cures Act information blocking provisions (Pub. L. 114-255, § 4004; 85 Fed. Reg. 25642). The ACR urges ONC to clarify in any final rule that AI-generated diagnostic outputs incorporated into a patient's clinical record are EHI for purposes of the information blocking regulations, and that no expansion of the Infeasibility Exception is intended to exempt such data from sharing obligations.⏎⏎ACR Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 8⏎⏎The ACR does not have detailed comments on every proposed amendment to the information blocking exceptions at this time, and we recognize that some of the proposed changes to the Manner Exception (45 C.F.R. § 171.201) and the Privacy Exception (45 C.F.R. § 171.202) reflect legitimate clarifications that do not raise the same concerns. We reserve the right to submit supplemental comments if ONC issues additional guidance or clarifying materials.⏎⏎⏎ON THE BROADER DEREGULATORY FRAMING⏎⏎The ACR wants to be direct about something, because we think it matters for how ONC receives these comments. We are not reflexively opposed to deregulation in health IT. The certification program has, over the years, accumulated requirements that are genuinely duplicative, outdated, or poorly calibrated to their intended purpose. The ACR supported burden reduction efforts in prior rulemakings, including aspects of the 2020 ONC Interoperability Rule (85 Fed. Reg. 25642) that streamlined certain certification criteria. We understand the argument that an overly prescriptive certification program can create barriers to entry, slow innovation, and impose costs on smaller health IT developers and healthcare providers that are not justified by the corresponding patient safety benefit.⏎⏎But there is a meaningful difference between reducing administrative overhead and removing substantive patient protections. The DSI transparency requirements are in the second category. They were adopted after an extensive evidence-gathering process, with substantial input from clinical communities, health equity researchers, and patient advocates. They address a documented and ongoing problem: the deployment of AI tools in clinical settings without adequate disclosure of their limitations, training characteristics, or validation status. The fact that this proposed rule frames the removal of those requirements as "unleashing prosperity" does not change what is actually being proposed.⏎⏎ACR Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 9⏎⏎The ACR would also note, with some concern, that the timing of this proposal coincides with a period of rapid acceleration in AI deployment in healthcare settings. The number of FDA-cleared AI/ML medical devices has roughly tripled since 2020 (FDA, AI/ML-Enabled Medical Devices, April 2025). EHR vendors are actively integrating large language model-based clinical decision support into their platforms. Health systems are deploying AI tools at a pace that outstrips their internal governance capacity, as documented by Sendak et al. (2020, "A Path for Translation of Machine Learning Products into Healthcare Delivery," EMJ Innovations) and more recently by Coiera et al. (2024, "The Last Mile Problem in AI-Assisted Clinical Decision Making," JAMIA). Removing transparency requirements at exactly this moment, when the need for them is greatest, seems to the ACR to be a significant miscalculation.⏎⏎We acknowledge that ASTP/ONC is operating under policy direction from the current administration that emphasizes burden reduction and regulatory flexibility. We are not asking ONC to ignore that direction. We are asking ONC to make the case internally, and to document in the final rule, that the DSI transparency requirements represent a category of requirement where the patient safety rationale is sufficiently strong that they should be retained notwithstanding the general deregulatory orientation of this rulemaking. ONC has discretion to make that determination. The Administrative Procedure Act requires that the agency articulate a reasoned basis for any significant change in regulatory position (Motor Vehicle Manufacturers Association v. State Farm Mutual Automobile Insurance Co., 463 U.S. 29 (1983)), and the evidence base supporting the DSI requirements is, in the ACR's view, more than sufficient to support their retention.⏎⏎ACR Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 10⏎⏎⏎CONCLUSION⏎⏎The American College of Radiology urges ASTP/ONC to retain the Decision Support Interventions certification criterion's transparency and source attribute disclosure requirements as finalized in the HTI-1 rule. These requirements are patient safety requirements. They ensure that clinicians have access to the information they need to make informed decisions about whether and how to rely on AI-generated recommendations in clinical care. They create accountability for AI developers who would otherwise face no systematic obligation to document and disclose the limitations of their tools. And they support the kind of comparative research that policymakers need to evaluate whether AI-assisted clinical programs are actually delivering the outcomes they promise.⏎⏎The ACR is prepared to engage further with ASTP/ONC on the specific implementation questions — template standardization, phased timelines for smaller developers, coordination with FDA SaMD disclosure frameworks — if ONC is willing to commit to retaining the substantive requirements. What the ACR cannot support is a final rule that removes those requirements on the basis of a burden argument that is, in our view, substantially overstated, and a market-will-solve-it rationale that the pre-HTI-1 record of voluntary AI disclosure in radiology directly refutes.⏎⏎ACR Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 11⏎⏎Questions regarding these comments may be directed to the ACR's Health Policy and Economics team at:⏎⏎healthpolicy@acr.org⏎https://www.acr.org/Advocacy/Economics-Health-Policy⏎⏎REFERENCES (partial; additional citations available upon request)⏎⏎Adamson, A.S., & Smith, A. Our members include individuals who navigate the U.S. health system under conditions that are already complicated by language access barriers, geographic isolation, and fragmented care histories. Our executive director, Sandra Young, has worked in this field for twenty years, and the organization has spent considerable time and organizational resources helping members exercise rights under the 21st Century Cures Act (Pub. L. 114-255) and the information blocking regulations at 45 CFR Part 171. We submit these comments because the proposed deregulatory changes would, in our view, remove protections that our members depend on in concrete and immediate ways, and because the removal of the Decision Support Interventions (DSI) certification criterion, specifically the model card and transparency disclosure requirements, would set back patient safety in ways that are likely to be felt most sharply by populations who already have the least institutional leverage.⏎⏎I want to be direct about what prompted this comment. Last spring, one of our staff spent the better part of three weeks working to obtain a complete medication history for a community member in her seventies who had relocated from Bangor to be closer to her daughter in Portland. Her previous provider's system simply would not export records in any format her new physician could import. We eventually resolved it, but only because of familiarity with ONC's interoperability enforcement contacts and with the existing certification framework as a pressure point. That experience is not an argument against burden reduction in the abstract. It is an argument that when you remove accountability mechanisms, real people bear the cost, and they often bear it quietly because they don't know they have rights in the first place.⏎⏎⏎DSI TRANSPARENCY REQUIREMENTS: THE PROPOSED REMOVAL IS PREMATURE⏎⏎The proposed rule would eliminate or substantially revise the DSI certification criterion currently codified at 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11), which requires health IT developers to document and disclose AI-driven clinical decision support tools through what the Office of the National Coordinator has described as "model cards." These disclosures include intended use specifications, target population characteristics, known risks, training data characteristics, and external validation information. ONC adopted this criterion as part of the HTI-1 final rule published at 89 Fed. Reg. 1192 (January 9, 2024), and it represented a considered policy judgment that clinicians and patients are entitled to know, at a minimum, what data was used to build a tool that may influence their care.⏎⏎The proposed deregulatory rule characterizes these requirements as administratively burdensome and suggests that market incentives and voluntary industry standards are sufficient substitutes. We do not find that argument persuasive, and I say that having read the proposed rule's preamble carefully, not just the summary. The agency's own analysis in the HTI-1 rulemaking (89 Fed. Reg. at 1247-1262) documented specific instances where clinical decision support tools had been deployed with inadequate transparency about training populations, resulting in tools that performed differently across demographic groups. The research literature ONC cited, including Obermeyer et al. (Science, 2019, vol. 366, pp. 447-453), demonstrated that a widely deployed commercial algorithm systematically underestimated the health needs of Black patients because of how training data was constructed. That is not a hypothetical. It happened at scale, in production systems, and clinicians had no way to know.⏎⏎- - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - -⏎URAALI Refaluwasch Association Comments | Docket ONC-2025-0002 | Page 2⏎- - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - -⏎⏎The communities we serve are, by any reasonable measure, more likely to be underrepresented in training datasets for commercial health AI tools. Resettled refugee populations, recent immigrants, and individuals with limited English proficiency are consistently underrepresented in the large electronic health record datasets that most commercial developers use for model training. A 2022 study in JAMIA (Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association, vol. 29, issue 4) found that patient populations in federally qualified health centers, which disproportionately serve immigrant and low-income patients, were systematically absent from the training sets used by three of the five largest commercial clinical decision support vendors. Without model card disclosures, a physician in Portland seeing one of our community members has no practical way to know whether the tool suggesting a treatment pathway was ever validated on anyone resembling that patient.⏎⏎The agency's proposed rationale, that voluntary standards bodies such as the Coalition for Health AI (CHAI) can fill this gap, is not without merit as a long-term aspiration. But CHAI's guidance documents, including its Blueprint for Trustworthy AI Implementation published in April 2023, are explicitly non-binding, and there is currently no enforcement mechanism that would compel a developer to follow them. Removing a certification criterion that has the force of 45 CFR 170.315 and replacing it with a reference to voluntary guidance is not burden reduction. It is a transfer of risk from developers to patients. The burden being reduced belongs to the developer. The risk being increased belongs to the patient.⏎⏎⏎WHY THE TIMING MATTERS⏎⏎ONC's own 2024 Health IT Report to Congress noted that adoption of AI-driven clinical decision support tools in ambulatory settings increased by approximately 34 percent between 2021 and 2023. That number is not slowing down. The agency is proposing to remove transparency requirements at precisely the moment when the tools requiring transparency are proliferating most rapidly. I genuinely do not understand the logic of that timing. If the argument is that the requirements were adopted too quickly and need refinement, that is a conversation worth having, and our organization would support a comment period focused on improving the model card framework. But removing the requirement entirely, before there is any functional substitute in place, is a different decision with different consequences.⏎⏎There is also a question about what happens to existing certifications. The proposed rule at 90 Fed. Reg. [page citation pending finalization] does not clearly address whether health IT products certified under the current DSI criterion would retain any ongoing disclosure obligations after the criterion is removed, or whether developers could simply stop updating their model cards without any regulatory consequence. If the answer is the latter, then the practical effect is that disclosures that clinicians may currently be relying on could disappear without notice. That needs to be addressed explicitly in the final rule, whatever ONC ultimately decides about the criterion itself.⏎⏎- - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - -⏎URAALI Refaluwasch Association Comments | Docket ONC-2025-0002 | Page 3⏎- - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - -⏎⏎RECOMMENDATIONS⏎⏎Our organization urges ONC to retain the DSI certification criterion at 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11) in substantially its current form. If the agency has received credible evidence that specific disclosure elements are genuinely duplicative or technically infeasible, we recommend a targeted revision process rather than wholesale removal. Specifically, ONC should convene a focused technical workgroup, with representation from patient advocacy organizations and from health systems serving underrepresented populations, to identify any elements of the model card framework that can be streamlined without reducing the core transparency function. That workgroup process existed for the HTI-1 rulemaking, and the record it produced (see 88 Fed. Reg. 23746, April 18, 2023) was better for it.⏎⏎We also recommend that any final rule include an explicit provision requiring developers who have received certification under the current DSI criterion to maintain existing model card disclosures for a minimum of twenty-four months following any criterion removal, so that the clinical community has adequate transition time. CMS-2025-0050-110090♔CMS-2025-0050♔Brian Mitchell♔NORC at the University of Chicago♔♔♔♔Proposed deregulatory changes to ONC's Health IT Certification Program and information blocking exceptions risk eroding the interoperability infrastructure that population health research depends on, as removing or relaxing certification requireme...♔NORC at the University of Chicago⏎Comments on Proposed Rule: ASTP/ONC Deregulatory Actions To Unleash Prosperity: Health Data, Technology, and Interoperability⏎Submitted via Regulations.gov⏎⏎NORC at the University of Chicago | ONC-HIT-2025 | Page 1⏎⏎INTRODUCTION AND ORGANIZATIONAL CONTEXT⏎⏎NORC at the University of Chicago is an independent research institution with a long history of conducting rigorous, nonpartisan health policy and health economics research. Our work spans federally funded studies on Medicaid, Medicare, health information technology adoption, and population health outcomes. We submit these comments in response to the proposed rule published by the Assistant Secretary for Technology Policy and the Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology (ASTP/ONC) in the Federal Register, and we appreciate the opportunity to provide input on a rule that will have direct consequences for the research infrastructure that population health work depends upon.⏎⏎These comments focus primarily on two areas: (1) the proposed removal and relaxation of certain Health IT Certification Program criteria, and (2) proposed changes to information blocking definitions and exceptions under 45 CFR Part 171. We do not address the full scope of the proposed rule. NORC's perspective is that of a data-intensive research organization that depends on interoperable, consistently structured health data to conduct longitudinal population-level analyses, and we are concerned that several provisions in this proposed rule could compromise the durability of interoperability gains achieved under prior regulatory frameworks.⏎⏎NORC at the University of Chicago | ONC-HIT-2025 | Page 2⏎⏎BACKGROUND: WHY CERTIFICATION FLOORS MATTER FOR RESEARCH⏎⏎The 21st Century Cures Act (Pub. L. 114-255) and its implementing regulations, including the ONC Cures Act Final Rule published at 85 Fed. Reg. 25642 (May 1, 2020), established a set of certification criteria and API requirements that research organizations came to rely on as stable infrastructure. The HL7 FHIR-based API requirements codified at 45 CFR 170.315(g)(10), in particular, represented a meaningful step toward the kind of machine-readable, structured data exchange that makes large-scale health research feasible across disparate systems.⏎⏎The problem is not theoretical. In the spring of 2024, NORC was conducting a multi-state Medicaid analysis in partnership with a hospital system based in Cheyenne, Wyoming. The analysis depended on structured laboratory data flowing through a certified API endpoint that had functioned without interruption for approximately two years. Midway through the study period, the hospital's electronic health record vendor quietly discontinued a certification module. The vendor had determined, following a policy shift that made the module optional rather than required, that maintaining it was not worth the cost. The result was a three-month gap in longitudinal data continuity within a dataset that NORC had been building for nearly a decade. That gap has not been recoverable in any methodologically satisfying way.⏎⏎That experience is directly relevant to the current rulemaking. The proposed rule would remove or make optional a number of certification criteria that, in ONC's view, have either been superseded by market forces or impose unnecessary burden on developers. NORC does not dispute that some certification criteria may warrant revision. But the Cheyenne episode is a concrete illustration of what happens when a certification requirement becomes optional: vendors respond to economic incentives, not research needs, and the floor drops. The research community has no seat at the vendor's table when those decisions are made.⏎⏎NORC at the University of Chicago | ONC-HIT-2025 | Page 3⏎⏎CONCERNS REGARDING SPECIFIC CERTIFICATION CHANGES⏎⏎The proposed rule would remove or significantly revise a number of certification criteria under 45 CFR Part 170, Subpart C. ONC has characterized several of these as "market-mature" features that no longer require regulatory mandate. NORC's concern is with the methodology underlying that determination, not just the outcomes.⏎⏎"Market maturity" is a concept that may hold reasonably well for widely adopted consumer-facing features, but it is a poor fit for data exchange capabilities that are used heavily by a relatively small population of research and analytics users. A vendor serving 300 hospital clients may rationally conclude that 280 of them will never notice the removal of a structured data export module. The 20 that would notice are often research partners, public health agencies, or payers conducting outcomes analyses under contracts like the ones NORC operates. The market signal for those 20 clients is too weak to prevent the removal.⏎⏎Several of the proposed certification removals warrant particular scrutiny:⏎⏎1. The proposed removal of certain transitions of care criteria related to structured data content requirements. ONC's Transitions of Care certification criteria (45 CFR 170.315(b)(1) and (b)(2)) have supported the reliable transmission of C-CDA documents with structured medication and laboratory data. If these criteria are removed or made optional, research organizations that depend on structured C-CDA data for longitudinal patient tracking across care settings could face the same kind of silent capability loss that NORC experienced in 2024.⏎⏎2. The relaxation of requirements related to the Common Clinical Data Set and its successor, the United States Core Data for Interoperability (USCDI). The USCDI v1 was adopted at 45 CFR 170.213, and subsequent versions have expanded the required data elements for certified health IT. Any weakening of the mandatory USCDI element set would reduce the reliability of cross-system data comparisons that population health research depends on. Published work by Adler-Milstein et al. (2021, Health Affairs) on EHR interoperability gaps already documented how inconsistent data element availability across certified systems creates serious problems for multi-site research. Relaxing the certification floor would likely make those gaps wider.⏎⏎3. Changes to electronic prescribing and medication history certification criteria. Medication data is among the most frequently missing or inconsistently structured elements in health datasets used for outcomes research. The AHRQ-funded work on medication reconciliation and care transitions (Rozich et al., Jt Comm J Qual Patient Saf, 2004, and subsequent literature) has consistently identified medication data quality as a binding constraint. Removing certification requirements that push vendors toward structured medication data exchange would be a step backward.⏎⏎NORC at the University of Chicago | ONC-HIT-2025 | Page 4⏎⏎INFORMATION BLOCKING EXCEPTIONS: CONCERNS ABOUT SCOPE CREEP⏎⏎The proposed rule also amends the information blocking definitions and exceptions framework established under 45 CFR Part 171. NORC's concern here is narrower but pointed.⏎⏎The information blocking rules enacted under the Cures Act were intended to prevent actors from unreasonably interfering with the access, exchange, or use of electronic health information (EHI). The exceptions codified at 45 CFR 171.200 through 171.302 were designed to be narrow carve-outs, not broad licenses. The proposed rule would expand or liberalize several of these exceptions in ways that NORC believes could create new barriers to research data access.⏎⏎Specifically, NORC is concerned about proposed modifications to the Privacy Exception (45 CFR 171.202) and the Infeasibility Exception (45 CFR 171.204). The Privacy Exception already permits actors to decline data sharing when they have a reasonable belief that sharing would violate applicable law, including HIPAA's Privacy Rule at 45 CFR Parts 160 and 164. Expanding the scope of what constitutes a "reasonable belief" in the proposed rule could enable health systems to cite privacy concerns as a basis for declining research data requests even when a valid IRB protocol, data use agreement, and HIPAA waiver or authorization are in place.⏎⏎The Infeasibility Exception is similarly concerning. The proposed rule would broaden the circumstances under which actors can claim that responding to a data request is technically or operationally infeasible. For research organizations negotiating data access agreements with health systems, "infeasibility" is already invoked more often than it should be. NORC has seen data requests delayed by 12 to 18 months at health systems that cited technical limitations that, upon investigation, reflected staffing choices rather than genuine capability constraints. A broader Infeasibility Exception would give those systems additional regulatory cover.⏎⏎NORC at the University of Chicago | ONC-HIT-2025 | Page 5⏎⏎The Office of Inspector General's information blocking enforcement authority, established by the Cures Act and detailed at 42 U.S.C. 300jj-52, has been slow to develop. As of early 2025, enforcement actions remain limited and the deterrent effect is uncertain. In that environment, weakening the definition of what constitutes information blocking, or expanding the exceptions, reduces whatever incentive currently exists for health systems to prioritize data access responsiveness. Published analyses of early information blocking enforcement patterns (Lye et al., JAMIA, 2023) found that provider organizations remained confused about the boundaries of permissible conduct even under the existing framework. Expanding the exceptions before enforcement has matured enough to establish clear behavioral norms seems premature.⏎⏎NORC at the University of Chicago | ONC-HIT-2025 | Page 6⏎⏎THE RESEARCH INFRASTRUCTURE ARGUMENT⏎⏎NORC wants to be direct about something that often gets lost in these comment processes: the health research community is a downstream consumer of interoperability infrastructure that it did not build and largely cannot control. When ONC sets certification requirements, it is setting the floor for what data will be consistently available across the health IT ecosystem. When that floor is lowered, research organizations do not have the leverage to negotiate individual vendor contracts that restore the lost capability. We are not large enough customers, individually, to move vendor behavior. The regulatory floor is the only lever that works at scale.⏎⏎This is not a new argument. The National Academy of Medicine's 2019 report on the Future of Health IT and Interoperability (NASEM, "Procuring Interoperability," 2019) made a similar point about the collective action problem in health data standards. Individual market participants cannot solve coordination problems that require uniform adoption across thousands of vendors and provider organizations. That is precisely what certification requirements are for.⏎⏎The argument that market maturity obviates the need for regulatory mandates may be valid in sectors where competitive pressure reliably produces the desired outcome. Health IT is not that sector. The market for EHR systems remains highly concentrated. As of 2023, Epic, Oracle Health (formerly Cerner), and a small number of other vendors account for the large majority of hospital EHR installations (ONC Data Brief No. 58, 2023). In concentrated markets, vendor decisions about which capabilities to maintain or deprecate are driven by their largest customers' requests, not by the needs of research organizations or public health agencies. Certification requirements are the counterweight to that dynamic.⏎⏎NORC at the University of Chicago | ONC-HIT-2025 | Page 7⏎⏎RECOMMENDATIONS⏎⏎NORC offers the following specific recommendations for ONC's consideration:⏎⏎1. Before removing or making optional any certification criterion currently classified as "market-mature," ONC should conduct and publish a structured analysis of whether the capability in question is uniformly available across the certified health IT product market, not just available in some products. Availability in 70% of products is not the same as reliable infrastructure for research purposes. The analysis should distinguish between capabilities that are available as optional add-ons (which vendors can and do remove based on customer demand) and capabilities that are structurally embedded in product architecture.⏎⏎2. ONC should convene a technical working group that includes representatives from the research and public health communities before finalizing changes to USCDI element requirements. The USCDI versioning process has historically been driven by clinical workflow needs. Research use cases, which often require retrospective data completeness and longitudinal consistency rather than real-time exchange speed, are underrepresented in that process. The Cures Act's broad definition of EHI at 45 CFR 171.102 should inform an expansive view of what data elements need to remain reliably available.⏎⏎3. On information blocking, NORC recommends that ONC not finalize the proposed expansions to the Privacy and Infeasibility Exceptions until the OIG has published enforcement guidance that clarifies how those exceptions will be interpreted in practice. The sequencing matters. Expanding exceptions before enforcement norms are established creates a regulatory gap that will be difficult to close once health system behavior has adapted to the more permissive framework. See 42 U.S.C. 300jj-52(b) for the statutory basis for OIG enforcement authority.⏎⏎4. ONC should require that any health IT developer that discontinues a previously certified capability provide at minimum 180 days' advance notice to all customers, with documentation submitted to ONC's certification database. The current framework has no such requirement, which is how the situation NORC encountered in Cheyenne in 2024 was able to occur without warning. The Cures Act's prohibition on information blocking does not, as currently interpreted, cover unilateral vendor decisions to discontinue certified capabilities, even when those decisions predictably impair data access.⏎⏎NORC at the University of Chicago | ONC-HIT-2025 | Page 8⏎⏎A NOTE ON ADMINISTRATIVE BURDEN FRAMING⏎⏎NORC recognizes that the stated purpose of this rulemaking includes reducing administrative burden on health IT developers and healthcare providers, consistent with the administration's broader deregulatory priorities. That is a legitimate policy goal. Certification requirements do impose costs, and there is published evidence (Adler-Milstein and Pfeifer, Health Affairs, 2017) that EHR-related administrative burden contributes to clinician burnout and workflow inefficiency.⏎⏎But the burden reduction framing, as applied to interoperability requirements specifically, conflates two different types of burden. The burden of maintaining a certified capability that no one uses is different from the burden of maintaining a capability that a diffuse set of users depends on but lacks the market power to protect. Removing the first type of requirement is sensible deregulation. Removing the second type imposes costs that are real but invisible in the regulatory impact analysis, because they fall on research organizations, public health agencies, and ultimately on the quality of evidence available to inform future health policy.⏎⏎NORC's position is that ONC should apply a more granular burden analysis that distinguishes between these two cases before finalizing the proposed removals. The regulatory impact analysis published with the proposed rule does not, in our reading, make this distinction with sufficient clarity. The Regulatory Flexibility Act analysis at 5 U.S.C. 603 requires consideration of the rule's impact on small entities, but the research organizations affected by interoperability losses are not the small entities contemplated by that provision. There is currently no analytical framework that captures the downstream research impact of certification changes, and NORC would welcome the opportunity to work with ONC to develop one.⏎⏎Contact for questions regarding these comments:⏎⏎Brian Mitchell⏎Health Economist⏎NORC at the University of Chicago⏎brian.mitchell@norc.org⏎⏎NORC at the University of Chicago | ONC-HIT-2025 | Page 9♔♔2026-02-02T00:00:00Z♔2026-02-02T00:00:00Z♔2025-12-12T00:00:00Z♔2026-02-10T00:00:00Z♔7♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Retain the current Decision Support Interventions (DSI) certification criterion requiring AI model cards and transparency disclosures (intended use, target population, known risks, training data characteristics, external validation) to ensure patient safety, informed clinical decision-making, and accountability in AI-assisted healthcare.♔The agency's claim that 'no publicly available evidence' supports transparency requirements conflates absence of evidence with evidence of absence; lack of published studies does not mean the criterion provides no value.♔academic♔high♔hopeful♔Wyoming♔health economist♔31♔Last spring, I was deep in a multi-state Medicaid analysis when a partner hospital system in Cheyenne suddenly couldn't push structured lab data through the same API endpoint that had worked flawlessly for two years — their vendor had quietly dropped a certification module after a policy shift made it optional rather than required. CMS-2025-0050-110093♔CMS-2025-0050♔Kimberly Thomas♔♔♔♔♔Mandatory AI transparency disclosures in clinical decision support tools — including model cards, training data characteristics, target population disclosures, and external validation requirements — are essential patient safety mechanisms that mus...♔Forty years in social work, and the thing I keep coming back to is this: the people who get hurt by gaps in the system are almost never the ones with the resources to recover from it.⏎⏎My neighbor Ruth spent three weeks last spring trying to get her cardiologist's records forwarded to a new specialist. Her husband had just died. She was doing this alone, at eighty-two, on the phone, on hold, filling out fax request forms that still exist in 2024 apparently. When she finally got into a patient portal, she found a medication discrepancy. Her new doctor said it was the kind of thing that could have caused a serious cardiac event. Three weeks of bureaucratic delay, one widow navigating a system that wasn't built for her, and she almost walked into a dangerous drug interaction because no one caught it.⏎⏎I'm not telling that story to make a rhetorical point. I'm telling it because the certification requirements around AI transparency are the exact mechanism that would have flagged that kind of error earlier in the chain, before it reached Ruth sitting at her kitchen table with a printout she didn't fully understand.⏎⏎So when I read that this rule is considering removing or weakening the decision support intervention certification criteria, specifically the parts that require AI model cards and transparency disclosures, I want to make sure someone at ONC hears from someone who has watched what happens when accountability disappears from clinical decision support tools. It is not theoretical.⏎⏎⏎WHY THE DSI TRANSPARENCY REQUIREMENTS EXIST AND WHY THEY SHOULD STAY⏎⏎The current certification criterion for Decision Support Interventions requires that health IT developers provide what are sometimes called "model cards" - disclosures that tell clinicians what an AI tool was trained on, who it was designed for, what its known limitations are, and whether it's been validated externally. I want to be honest that I'm not a software developer or a data scientist. But I've spent forty years watching what happens when information gets filtered before it reaches the person who needs it most, and a clinical AI tool with no disclosed training data characteristics is exactly that kind of filter.⏎⏎The argument for removing these requirements seems to be about reducing burden on developers. I understand that argument. Compliance costs money. Documentation takes time. I've worked inside large bureaucratic systems and I know that paperwork requirements can pile up in ways that don't actually protect anyone. So I'm not dismissing the concern.⏎⏎But there's a real difference between paperwork burden and safety disclosure. What the DSI criterion requires isn't just administrative documentation. It's the information a clinician needs to know whether to trust a recommendation. If an AI tool recommends a medication adjustment, the prescribing physician needs to know whether that model was trained on patient populations that look like their patient. That's not a nice-to-have. That's the basic condition of informed clinical decision-making.⏎⏎⏎WHAT HAPPENS WITHOUT THESE DISCLOSURES⏎⏎I want to be specific about what the removal of these requirements actually means in practice, because I think sometimes regulatory language makes it hard to see the real-world chain of consequences.⏎⏎Without mandatory disclosure of:⏎⏎1. Intended use and target population⏎2. Known risks and limitations⏎3. Training data characteristics⏎4. External validation status⏎⏎...a clinician using an AI-assisted decision support tool has no reliable way to know whether that tool was validated on patients like theirs. A cardiologist treating an elderly woman with multiple comorbidities, using a decision support algorithm that was trained primarily on younger male patients (which is actually a documented problem in cardiovascular AI research, see Obermeyer et al. in Science, 2019, on racial bias in a widely used clinical algorithm), is flying partly blind. They may not know that. The tool doesn't tell them.⏎⏎The model card requirement forces that information into the open. It makes the developer accountable for what they built and who they built it for. Removing it doesn't reduce burden in any meaningful safety sense. It just moves the risk from the developer onto the patient.⏎⏎⏎THE ACCOUNTABILITY GAP THIS WOULD CREATE⏎⏎One thing I've learned in social work is that when you remove a reporting or disclosure requirement, you don't actually remove the problem the requirement was designed to address. You just make it harder to see. The patients who get hurt by a poorly validated AI tool don't disappear. They end up in emergency rooms, or they end up like Ruth, piecing together a medication history from fragments three weeks after they needed it.⏎⏎The DSI transparency requirements create a paper trail. They create a moment in the certification process where a developer has to look at their own tool and say: here's what it does, here's who it was built for, here's what we know it gets wrong. That moment matters. It's not just documentation. It's the point where someone has to be accountable.⏎⏎If ONC removes that requirement, the accountability doesn't transfer to someone else. It evaporates. And the people who absorb that evaporated accountability are patients, clinicians who didn't know what they were working with, and social workers and family members trying to figure out after the fact what went wrong.⏎⏎⏎SPECIFIC CONCERNS ABOUT THE PROPOSED CHANGES⏎⏎I want to be clear that I'm not objecting to every aspect of this rulemaking. There are provisions in this proposal around information access that I think genuinely could help patients like Ruth. Streamlining how records are shared, reducing the friction in patient portal access, improving interoperability - those are real problems and I'm glad someone is working on them.⏎⏎My concern is narrowly focused on the DSI certification criterion and what appears to be a proposal to weaken or remove the model card and transparency disclosure requirements. A few specific points:⏎⏎o The "intended use" disclosure tells a clinician whether they're using a tool outside its validated scope. Without it, off-label use of AI decision support tools is invisible.⏎⏎o The "target population" disclosure is especially important for elderly patients, patients with multiple chronic conditions, and patients from populations historically underrepresented in clinical data. These are the patients most likely to be harmed by a model that doesn't fit them.⏎⏎o "Known risks" disclosure is the closest thing we have right now to a warning label on clinical AI. Removing it because it creates compliance burden is like removing drug side effect disclosures because pharmaceutical companies find them inconvenient.⏎⏎o External validation is the difference between a tool a developer says works and a tool that has been tested by someone with no financial stake in the outcome. The certification requirement for this is one of the few structural checks we have.⏎⏎I genuinely don't understand the argument that these specific disclosures are the burdensome ones. Model cards are not lengthy documents. The FDA's guidance on AI/ML-based software as a medical device already contemplates this kind of disclosure. ONC's certification requirement is in the same spirit. It's not asking developers to do something novel or technically demanding. It's asking them to tell clinicians what they built.⏎⏎⏎A WORD ABOUT WHO GETS HURT⏎⏎I keep thinking about who uses AI-assisted clinical decision support tools most intensively. These are not onerous requirements. They are the minimum a clinician needs to know before relying on a software output to make a care decision.⏎⏎The proposed rule suggests that these disclosures create administrative burden for health IT developers and that removing them will increase flexibility. A model validated on general medical populations may perform poorly on patients with specific oral-systemic comorbidities, and a provider has no way to know that without the training data disclosures the DSI criterion currently requires.⏎⏎2. The known risks and limitations disclosures are particularly important for AI tools used in dental radiograph interpretation, a rapidly growing area. Several commercial AI products for caries detection and periodontal bone loss assessment entered the market between 2020 and 2023. Providers using certified versions of these products should have access to that kind of information in a standardized disclosure format.⏎⏎3. The FDA has raised it repeatedly in the context of Software as a Medical Device (SaMD) guidance. ONC's own framework for Trusted Exchange under TEFCA (see 45 CFR Part 171) acknowledges that transparency in data exchange is a precondition for trust. The same logic applies to AI model transparency.⏎⏎Dental Standards Institute Comments | ONC Deregulatory Rule | Page 2⏎⏎...accountability in AI-assisted clinical environments. CMS-2025-0050-110096♔CMS-2025-0050♔David Baker♔No Delays, No Surprises Coalition♔♔♔♔Removing AI transparency requirements from the DSI certification criterion will render algorithmic bias invisible and eliminate the only accountability mechanism protecting underserved patients from clinical decision support tools trained on non-r...♔No Delays, No Surprises Coalition⏎New Orleans, Louisiana⏎⏎Submitted via regulations.gov⏎Docket: ONC-2025-Deregulatory-ATUP⏎⏎RE: ASTP/ONC Proposed Rule, Deregulatory Actions To Unleash Prosperity: Health Data, Technology, and Interoperability⏎⏎No Delays, No Surprises Coalition (NDNSC) is a Louisiana-based patient and consumer advocacy organization operating primarily in low-income and underserved communities across the greater New Orleans metro area, including the Ninth Ward, Central City, and the eastern parishes. We work directly with patients navigating fragmented care systems, often serving as the connective tissue between people and the health information technology infrastructure that is supposed to serve them. Our membership includes community health workers, patient navigators, social workers, and the patients themselves. We submit these comments in strong opposition to the proposed removal of the Decision Support Interventions (DSI) certification criterion requiring AI model cards and transparency disclosures, and we urge ONC to retain those requirements in full.⏎⏎Our comments focus primarily on the DSI AI transparency provisions. We are not commenting on every aspect of the proposed rule.⏎⏎No Delays, No Surprises Coalition | ONC Deregulatory Comments | Page 1⏎⏎⏎THE TRANSPARENCY REQUIREMENT IS NOT BUREAUCRATIC OVERHEAD⏎⏎The DSI certification criterion at issue here is the one finalized in the HTI-1 rule (89 Fed. Reg. 1192, Jan. 9, 2024) that requires health IT developers to provide what the agency called "source attributes" for AI and machine learning-based decision support interventions deployed in certified health IT. Those source attributes include disclosure of intended use, the target population the model was built on, known risks and limitations, characteristics of the training data, and whether the model has been externally validated. ONC is now proposing to remove or significantly loosen this requirement on the grounds that it creates certification burden and may slow the adoption of beneficial AI tools.⏎⏎We genuinely understand the concern about burden. Certification overhead is real, and we have seen smaller health IT developers struggle to keep up with compliance timelines. That is a legitimate policy problem worth addressing. But the proposed solution here is not actually targeted at the burden problem in any precise way. Removing transparency disclosures wholesale does not reduce unnecessary compliance friction; it removes the mechanism by which clinicians, patients, and institutions know what they are dealing with when an AI system flags a diagnosis or recommends a treatment pathway. Those are not the same thing.⏎⏎The clinical decision support tools covered by the DSI criterion are increasingly embedded in the core workflow of healthcare delivery. A 2023 study published in JAMA Network Open found that over 70 percent of U.S. hospitals reported using some form of AI-assisted clinical decision support, and that figure has almost certainly grown since then. These are not experimental add-ons sitting at the margins of care. They are shaping which patients get flagged for sepsis protocols, which patients get referred to specialists, which patients are identified as high-risk for readmission. When those systems produce recommendations that are wrong in systematic ways, the consequences fall hardest on the patients who were already underrepresented in the training data.⏎⏎No Delays, No Surprises Coalition | ONC Deregulatory Comments | Page 2⏎⏎⏎THE TRAINING DATA PROBLEM IS SPECIFIC AND DOCUMENTED⏎⏎This is not a theoretical concern. The evidence on disparate AI performance in healthcare is substantial and specific. A widely cited 2019 study in Science (Obermeyer et al., Science 366:447-453) demonstrated that a commercial algorithm used by major health systems to identify high-risk patients for care management systematically under-identified Black patients as high-risk compared to white patients with similar health status, because the algorithm used prior healthcare costs as a proxy for health need. Black patients with the same level of illness had historically generated lower healthcare costs due to barriers to access, so the algorithm effectively encoded existing disparities into future care allocation decisions. That study prompted significant industry attention, but the underlying problem, which is that AI models trained on non-representative or historically biased data will produce biased outputs, has not gone away. A 2022 review in NPJ Digital Medicine (Seyyed-Kalantari et al.) found consistent performance gaps in chest X-ray AI models across race, sex, and insurance status.⏎⏎The model card and source attribute requirements in the HTI-1 rule were a direct response to exactly this documented problem. By requiring disclosure of training data characteristics and known risks, the rule gave clinical users and institutional decision-makers a fighting chance to ask the right questions before deploying a tool that might harm their patient population. A hospital serving primarily Medicaid patients in rural Louisiana would at least be able to look at the training data disclosure and ask whether the model was built on patient populations that look anything like theirs. That is a basic due diligence function. Without the disclosure requirement, there is no mechanism to trigger that question.⏎⏎Removing these disclosures does not make the bias go away. It just makes it invisible.⏎⏎No Delays, No Surprises Coalition | ONC Deregulatory Comments | Page 3⏎⏎⏎WHAT WE ARE ACTUALLY ASKING FOR⏎⏎NDNSC urges ONC to retain the DSI certification criterion in its current form, specifically including all five source attribute categories required under 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11) as finalized in HTI-1. We are not asking for new requirements or expanded mandates. We are asking that the requirements already on the books not be removed before there is any evidence that they are causing the specific harms the agency is now concerned about.⏎⏎If ONC has received specific feedback from developers indicating that particular elements of the source attribute disclosure are technically infeasible or disproportionately burdensome, the appropriate response is to address those specific elements, not to eliminate the category wholesale. For example, if the external validation disclosure is creating problems because there is no standardized methodology for external validation in certain clinical contexts, ONC could work with the field to develop clearer guidance on what counts as sufficient external validation rather than simply dropping the requirement. That kind of targeted refinement is how good regulatory policy works.⏎⏎The proposed rule does not offer that kind of analysis. The preamble identifies certification burden as a general concern and then proposes broad removals without walking through which specific aspects of the DSI transparency requirement are creating which specific problems. That is not a sufficient basis for removing a patient safety provision that took years to develop and was finalized after extensive public comment.⏎⏎No Delays, No Surprises Coalition | ONC Deregulatory Comments | Page 4⏎⏎⏎SPECIFIC CONCERNS BY SOURCE ATTRIBUTE CATEGORY⏎⏎Our organization reviewed the five source attribute categories required under the current DSI criterion and wants to be clear about which ones we consider most non-negotiable from a patient safety perspective. This is not a situation where all five are equally weighted in our view.⏎⏎1. Intended use and target population: This is the most basic transparency disclosure imaginable. A clinician using an AI tool to support a decision about a patient has a right to know whether that tool was designed and validated for patients like theirs. Removing this requirement is indefensible from a patient safety standpoint. There is no burden justification that outweighs the risk of a clinician unknowingly applying a pediatric-trained model to adult patients, or a tool trained on academic medical center populations to a community health center context.⏎⏎2. Known risks and limitations: This is standard product disclosure. Any medical device has a required indication for use and known contraindications. The same logic applies to AI decision support. The HTI-1 requirement here mirrors what the FDA has been moving toward for Software as a Medical Device (SaMD) under its Digital Health Center of Excellence guidance. Removing this from ONC certification while FDA is moving in the opposite direction creates regulatory incoherence that will confuse developers and purchasers alike.⏎⏎3. Training data characteristics: This is the category most directly tied to the disparate impact problem documented in the literature cited above. We acknowledge this is probably the most technically complex disclosure to standardize, and we have heard from developers that defining "training data characteristics" in a way that is both meaningful and feasible is genuinely hard. But hard is not the same as impossible, and the answer to a hard technical problem is not to give up on transparency. ONC should engage the AI/ML community on how to make this disclosure more tractable rather than eliminating it.⏎⏎4. External validation: We understand this one is contested. External validation is not uniformly defined, and for some types of decision support tools there may not be a clear standard methodology. We would support a phased or conditional approach here, where ONC provides clearer guidance on what constitutes acceptable external validation evidence before enforcing this specific sub-requirement, rather than simply removing it.⏎⏎5. Fairness and bias testing results: If this category is being proposed for removal, we strongly object. The evidence base for differential AI performance across demographic groups is not ambiguous. Requiring developers to disclose whether they tested for disparate performance is a minimum floor, not an aggressive overreach.⏎⏎No Delays, No Surprises Coalition | ONC Deregulatory Comments | Page 5⏎⏎⏎THE INFORMED CONSENT DIMENSION⏎⏎There is another dimension to this that the proposed rule does not address directly, and we want to put it on the record. When a patient interacts with a healthcare system that is using AI-assisted decision support, they generally have no idea. The AI is embedded in the clinical workflow, invisible to the patient. The clinician may or may not know the details of how the tool works. The institution that purchased the tool may have evaluated it or may have simply taken the vendor's word for it.⏎⏎The model card and source attribute disclosures required under HTI-1 are not just for clinicians. They are the foundation for a chain of accountability that runs from developer to institution to clinician to patient. If the developer does not have to disclose what the model was trained on, the institution cannot make an informed procurement decision. If the institution cannot make an informed procurement decision, the clinician cannot know what they are working with. And if the clinician does not know what they are working with, the patient has no meaningful ability to understand or contest a recommendation that may have been shaped by a biased algorithm.⏎⏎The Ninth Ward woman I mentioned earlier, the dialysis patient with the grocery bag of discharge papers, she eventually got connected to a patient portal that finally pulled her records together. That happened because systems were required to interoperate, because somebody built a rule that said the data had to be accessible. She could see her own story. The transparency requirements for AI are the same kind of infrastructure. They are what makes the accountability chain possible. Pull them out and you do not get a lighter system; you get an opaque one.⏎⏎No Delays, No Surprises Coalition | ONC Deregulatory Comments | Page 6⏎⏎⏎THE REGULATORY HISTORY MATTERS HERE⏎⏎ONC spent years developing the DSI criterion. The agency issued a Request for Information on clinical decision support in 2020. It convened stakeholder discussions. It proposed the criterion in the HTI-1 proposed rule published at 88 Fed. Reg. 23746 (April 18, 2023). It received and responded to hundreds of public comments. The final rule at 89 Fed. Reg. 1192 reflected significant refinement based on that input. The external validation requirement, for instance, was modified between proposed and final rule specifically to address feasibility concerns raised by developers. That iterative process produced a balanced outcome.⏎⏎Now, less than two years after that final rule, ONC is proposing to undo significant portions of it on the basis of a general deregulatory orientation without, as far as we can tell from the preamble, any systematic evidence that the specific requirements are failing in practice. We are not aware of any published evaluation of the HTI-1 DSI criterion that would support the conclusion that it is causing net harm or that its removal would improve patient outcomes. The burden argument is asserted, not demonstrated.⏎⏎We would also note that the AI transparency landscape is moving fast. The White House Executive Order on AI (E.O. 14110, October 2023) directed agencies to develop standards for AI transparency and accountability in high-stakes domains including healthcare. HHS released its AI Strategic Plan in 2024 emphasizing the need for trustworthy AI in clinical settings. The Joint Commission has begun developing standards for AI governance in accredited hospitals. The direction of travel across the federal health enterprise is toward more transparency about AI in clinical decision-making, not less. Removing the HTI-1 DSI transparency requirements now puts ONC out of step with where every other relevant body is heading.⏎⏎No Delays, No Surprises Coalition | ONC Deregulatory Comments | Page 7⏎⏎⏎A NOTE ON THE INFORMATION BLOCKING CHANGES⏎⏎Our primary comment is on the DSI transparency provisions, but we want to briefly register concern about the proposed loosening of information blocking exceptions as well. We will not go into the same level of detail here, but the pattern concerns us.⏎⏎The information blocking provisions in the 21st Century Cures Act and the implementing regulations at 45 CFR Part 171 took years to develop and represent a hard-won framework for ensuring patient access to health information. The exceptions are carefully defined to allow legitimate operational flexibility while preventing practices that deny patients or their providers access to data they need. The proposed rule would expand those exceptions in ways that, on their face, could allow health IT actors to delay or deny data sharing on grounds that are harder to scrutinize or challenge.⏎⏎From where we sit, working with patients who are still, in 2025, piecing their medical histories together from paper records, the information blocking framework is not finished work that can afford to be loosened. It is still being built out and enforced. The Office of the Inspector General published its first information blocking civil money penalty rule only in 2023. The complaint resolution process through ONC is still maturing. Expanding exceptions before the enforcement infrastructure is fully operational risks creating gaps that, in practice, will fall most heavily on patients who do not have the resources or legal sophistication to push back.⏎⏎We are not saying every aspect of the exception structure is perfect as written. There are genuine operational questions about how the exceptions interact with each other and with state law. But the appropriate response to those questions is targeted clarification, not broad expansion of the exceptions before there is any evidence base for how the current framework is performing.⏎⏎No Delays, No Surprises Coalition | ONC Deregulatory Comments | Page 8⏎⏎⏎COMMUNITY IMPACT IS NOT EVENLY DISTRIBUTED⏎⏎One thing that gets lost in regulatory cost-benefit analysis is that the costs and benefits of health IT policy are not evenly distributed across the patient population. The patients who benefit most from strong interoperability and AI transparency requirements are the ones who are least able to protect themselves when those requirements are absent. They are the patients who see multiple providers across fragmented systems. They are the patients who cannot afford to switch providers or seek second opinions. They are the patients who are most likely to be underrepresented in the training data of AI models designed and sold primarily for academic medical center contexts.⏎⏎In communities like the ones NDNSC serves, the abstract policy question of whether AI transparency requirements impose net burden on developers is not how people experience these issues. What they experience is a nurse telling them that the system flagged them as low-risk when they know something is wrong. What they experience is being discharged with a care plan generated by an algorithm that was never designed for patients with their combination of chronic conditions, their insurance status, their geography. The model card requirement is not a paperwork exercise for these patients. It is the only mechanism that exists to create some accountability for what happens to them inside the black box.⏎⏎NDNSC works with approximately 340 active client cases at any given time. A significant portion of those involve patients with multiple chronic conditions being managed across at least three separate provider organizations. The interoperability infrastructure built over the last decade has made a real difference for those patients. The AI transparency requirements finalized in HTI-1 are the next layer of that infrastructure. They should not be removed before they have had a real chance to work.⏎⏎No Delays, No Surprises Coalition | ONC Deregulatory Comments | Page 9⏎⏎⏎SUMMARY OF RECOMMENDATIONS⏎⏎To be direct about what we are asking for:⏎⏎1. Retain 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11) in full, including all source attribute disclosure requirements for AI and machine learning-based decision support interventions. Do not remove or materially weaken these requirements in the final rule.⏎⏎2. If specific elements of the source attribute disclosure are creating documented, specific implementation problems, address those elements through targeted guidance or phased implementation timelines rather than removal. ONC has the regulatory tools to do this without gutting the transparency framework.⏎⏎3. Do not expand information blocking exceptions until the current enforcement framework is more fully operational and there is an evidence base for how the existing exceptions are functioning in practice. ONC should commission or review empirical data on information blocking complaint resolution before proposing further exception expansion.⏎⏎4. Engage meaningfully with patient and community advocacy organizations in any further rulemaking on AI transparency in clinical decision support. The HTI-1 process was better than average on stakeholder engagement; this proposed rule feels like a step backward on that dimension. The communities most affected by AI bias in healthcare are not primarily represented by the developer and provider associations that tend to dominate comment dockets.⏎⏎5. Publish a summary of the specific burden evidence ONC relied on in proposing the DSI changes. The preamble refers to burden concerns in general terms but does not walk through specific data on compliance costs, developer survey results, or other empirical basis for the determination that the current requirements impose net costs. That information should be in the record before the rule is finalized.⏎⏎No Delays, No Surprises Coalition | ONC Deregulatory Comments | Page 10⏎⏎⏎We appreciate the opportunity to comment and ask that these comments be considered in full in the agency's deliberations on the final rule. Prosperity for whom, measured how? The developers who avoid compliance costs? Or the patients who need to know whether the AI flagging their discharge was built on data that looked anything like them? These goals are not automatically in conflict, but they are also not the same goal, and the framing of the rulemaking suggests the agency is currently weighting them in a way that does not reflect the interests of the patients our organization works with every day. The preamble should at minimum grapple with that tension rather than treating reduced developer burden as a straightforwardly positive outcome for all stakeholders. We do not think ONC staff are indifferent to patient safety.
