CMS-2025-0050-110097♔CMS-2025-0050♔Lisa Martinez♔♔♔♔♔Removing the AI model card requirements from the Decision Support Interventions certification criterion would eliminate clinicians' and patients' only reliable mechanism for determining whether AI tools were trained on and validated for their spec...♔FW: Comment submission re: ONC deregulatory proposal - AI transparency - please forward to docket⏎⏎-----Original Message-----⏎From: Lisa Martinez⏎Sent: Thursday⏎To: regulations@hhs.gov⏎Subject: Comment on ASTP/ONC Deregulatory Actions Proposed Rule - AI Model Card Requirements⏎⏎---⏎⏎My name is Lisa Martinez. I'm a social worker in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, and I've been doing this work for thirty years. I want to say something upfront: I'm not a health IT professional. I don't write code or design software. What I do is sit with people on some of the worst days of their lives and try to help them navigate a healthcare system that often feels like it was designed for everyone except them. So my perspective here is not technical in the way that an engineer's would be. But I've seen enough to know when a proposed change is going to hurt the people I work with, and I'm genuinely worried that removing the AI transparency requirements from the Decision Support Interventions certification criterion is one of those changes.⏎⏎I want to try to explain why, and I'll try to be specific rather than vague about it, because I think the specifics are what matter here.⏎⏎Last spring, I spent about three weeks helping a 74-year-old client in Milwaukee piece together her complete medication history after she was transferred between two hospital systems. Records that should have been available in minutes took days and days to surface, and by the time her care team had the full picture, decisions had already been made without it. That story is about interoperability, yes, but it's also about what happens when systems don't perform the way their designers promise they will, and when there's no mechanism to ask why. The AI transparency piece of this proposed rule is exactly that kind of mechanism. Removing it takes away one of the few levers patients and clinicians have to ask: what is this tool actually doing, who was it trained on, and does it apply to my patient?⏎⏎I keep coming back to that question. Does it apply to my patient?⏎⏎WHAT I UNDERSTAND ABOUT THE CURRENT REQUIREMENT⏎⏎The current Decision Support Interventions certification criterion, as I understand it from reading through the Federal Register materials, requires health IT developers to include what are sometimes called "model cards" when they certify AI-based clinical decision support tools. That means disclosing things like the intended use of the tool, the population it was trained on, known risks or limitations, and whether it's been validated against data from outside the original training set. I've also seen this described in the ONC Health IT Certification Program documentation as requiring information about training data characteristics.⏎⏎I want to be honest: I had to read several explanations of this before I fully grasped what it meant. But once I did, I thought, of course. Of course clinicians need to know this. Of course patients should be able to find out whether the AI tool recommending a course of treatment was ever tested on anyone who looks like them.⏎⏎The proposed rule would remove or significantly revise this requirement. The justification, as I read it, is something about reducing administrative burden on developers and giving them more flexibility. I understand the argument. I've been in enough policy discussions to know that burden reduction is a real concern and not always a euphemism. But I genuinely don't understand why the answer to developer burden is to take away the information that clinicians and patients need to make sense of what these tools are doing.⏎⏎There's a 2021 study published in the New England Journal of Medicine (Obermeyer et al., though the original work dates to 2019 in Science) that found a widely used commercial algorithm was significantly less likely to refer Black patients for additional care compared to white patients with the same level of illness, because the algorithm used healthcare costs as a proxy for health needs, and Black patients historically had been given less care and thus generated lower costs. The algorithm wasn't disclosed to clinicians in the way that the current DSI criterion would require. Clinicians using it had no idea it had this problem. This is not a hypothetical. This happened. And it happened in part because there was no requirement to say: here is what this tool was trained on, here are its known limitations, here is who it was validated against.⏎⏎If I told you that a drug had been approved without disclosing the population it was tested on or the side effects that showed up in trials, you would find that alarming. I don't understand why we're more comfortable with that information gap when the intervention is software rather than a pill.⏎⏎WHY THIS MATTERS FOR MY CLIENTS SPECIFICALLY⏎⏎The people I work with in Milwaukee are disproportionately elderly, low-income, and from communities that have historically been undertreated or mistreated by the healthcare system. A significant number of my clients are Black or Latino. A significant number have multiple chronic conditions. When I say "does this tool apply to my patient," I'm asking a real question that has different answers for different people, and the answer depends entirely on information that the model card requirement is designed to surface.⏎⏎I've had clients who were flagged by clinical decision support tools for certain risk categories, and when I've tried to understand why, the clinicians themselves often couldn't tell me. Not because they weren't trying, but because the tool didn't come with enough information to explain itself. The current certification requirement is an attempt to fix that. It's an imperfect fix, I'm sure, but it's something. Removing it makes the problem worse.⏎⏎I also want to say something that might sound like it's coming from a different direction than the rest of this comment. I've learned, sometimes the hard way, that easier access to health information cuts both ways. A client of mine, several years ago now, discovered that her mental health records had been shared far more broadly than she had ever consented to. That breach quietly closed doors for her in ways she's still dealing with. So I'm not someone who just reflexively says "more transparency is always better" without thinking about what that means for privacy and safety.⏎⏎But the AI model card requirement isn't about sharing patient data more broadly. It's about making sure that the people deploying and using AI tools know what those tools actually do. Those are very different things. And the concern about developer burden, while real, doesn't justify taking away that disclosure.⏎⏎WHAT I'M ACTUALLY ASKING FOR⏎⏎I want to be clear about what I'm asking, because I've read enough public comments to know that vague requests don't accomplish much.⏎⏎I'm asking ONC to retain the current Decision Support Interventions certification criterion that requires AI model cards and transparency disclosures. Specifically, I'm asking that the final rule keep the requirements for:⏎⏎1. Disclosure of the intended use of the AI tool, including the clinical context it was designed for and the specific patient population it was meant to address.⏎⏎2. Information about the training data used to build the model, including demographic characteristics of that data, so that clinicians can assess whether the tool is likely to perform well for their specific patient population.⏎⏎3. Disclosure of known risks and limitations, including any known performance disparities across demographic groups.⏎⏎4. Information about external validation, meaning whether the tool has been tested against data from a different source than the training data, and what those results showed.⏎⏎These aren't burdensome requirements in the abstract. They're the minimum information a clinician needs to use an AI tool responsibly. A developer that can't provide this information probably shouldn't be deploying the tool in clinical settings.⏎⏎I understand that ONC has cited administrative burden as a reason for this change. I'd push back gently on that framing. The burden of not having this information falls on patients, not on developers. When a clinical decision support tool makes a recommendation that turns out to be wrong for a particular patient because of a training data problem that was never disclosed, the person who bears that burden is the patient. And in my experience, that patient is often already carrying more than their share.⏎⏎A SPECIFIC CONCERN ABOUT EXTERNAL VALIDATION⏎⏎I want to spend a moment on the external validation piece because I think it's the requirement that's easiest to underestimate.⏎⏎External validation, for anyone reading this who isn't a data scientist, means testing a model on data that wasn't used to train it. It's important because models often perform much better on the data they were trained on than they do in the real world. A model trained on data from a large academic medical center in Boston might perform quite differently when deployed in a community health clinic in Milwaukee's near north side. That's not a hypothetical concern; it's a well-documented phenomenon in the machine learning literature. The 88 Federal Register page 75766 (from the 2023 HTI-1 final rule) acknowledged this concern explicitly in discussing the rationale for the DSI certification requirements.⏎⏎Without the external validation requirement, a developer can train a model, test it on their own data, get good results, certify it, and deploy it broadly without ever knowing whether it works in a different setting or for a different population. That's a problem. It's a problem that the current requirement is designed to address, imperfectly but meaningfully. Removing it in the name of burden reduction is, I think, a mistake.⏎⏎I'm not saying the current requirement is perfectly designed. I'm not an expert in machine learning, and I'm sure people with more technical knowledge than I have could point to ways the requirement could be better calibrated or more clearly specified. But "this could be improved" is not the same as "this should be eliminated." And the proposed rule, from what I can tell, is much closer to elimination than to refinement.⏎⏎WHAT I'VE SEEN IN PRACTICE⏎⏎I want to go back to something concrete for a minute, because I think the policy debate can get abstract in ways that lose sight of what's actually happening in clinical settings.⏎⏎In my work, I interact regularly with care coordinators, discharge planners, nurses, and occasionally physicians. Over the past several years, I've watched AI-based tools get introduced into more and more of the settings where my clients receive care. Some of these tools are genuinely useful. Some of them I'm less sure about.⏎⏎What I've noticed is that when clinicians are given information about how a tool works, what it was trained on, and where it might fall short, they use it differently than when they're just given a recommendation with a confidence score. They ask more questions. They push back when something doesn't fit the patient in front of them. They treat the tool as one input among many rather than as an answer.⏎⏎When that information isn't available, the dynamic shifts. Clinicians tend to either over-rely on the tool (because there's nothing to make them question it) or they ignore it entirely (because they don't trust something they don't understand). Neither of those outcomes is good for patients.⏎⏎The model card requirement is, at its core, a way of giving clinicians the information they need to use these tools thoughtfully rather than reflexively. That's worth something. I'd argue it's worth more than the compliance burden it places on developers, but even if you disagree about the relative weights, you shouldn't just eliminate the requirement without a clear sense of what you're giving up.⏎⏎I've also talked to a care coordinator at one of the Milwaukee hospital systems (I'm not going to name her or the hospital because I don't want to put anyone in an awkward position) who told me, back in early 2024, that her team had started using a new risk stratification tool and that she had no idea what data it was based on. She said she'd asked the vendor and been told it was "proprietary." She found that unsatisfying, as did I when she told me about it. The current DSI certification requirement is designed to prevent exactly that kind of opacity. Removing it takes away the leverage that makes "it's proprietary" an unacceptable answer.⏎⏎ON THE QUESTION OF DEVELOPER BURDEN⏎⏎I want to engage with the burden argument more directly, because I don't think it should just be dismissed.⏎⏎Health IT developers, especially smaller ones, face real compliance costs. Writing and maintaining model cards takes time and resources. Conducting external validation studies is expensive. I understand that. And I understand that ONC is trying to balance the interests of innovation against the interests of safety and accountability.⏎⏎But here's what I keep coming back to: the developers who are most likely to be burdened by these requirements are the ones who have done the least work to understand their own tools. A developer that has rigorously documented its training data, tested its model against external datasets, and identified its limitations is not going to find the model card requirement particularly burdensome, because they already have that information. The burden falls hardest on developers who haven't done that work.⏎⏎I'm not sure that "this requirement is burdensome for developers who haven't validated their tools" is a compelling reason to eliminate the requirement. If anything, it suggests that the requirement is working as intended, by creating an incentive to do the validation work before deploying a tool in clinical settings.⏎⏎I also want to note that the burden argument is almost always framed from the developer's perspective, and almost never from the patient's perspective. The patient who receives a suboptimal recommendation from an AI tool that was never validated for their demographic group also bears a burden. It's just not counted in the compliance cost calculation. That asymmetry bothers me.⏎⏎SOME THOUGHTS ON THE INFORMATION BLOCKING CHANGES⏎⏎I want to say a few words about the information blocking piece of this proposed rule, even though it's not my main concern here.⏎⏎I support efforts to improve patient access to electronic health information. I've seen too many cases like the one I described at the beginning of this comment, where critical information wasn't available when it was needed, to be anything other than strongly in favor of better interoperability. The scenario of my client's medication history taking days to surface when it should have taken minutes is not unusual in my experience. It's the norm.⏎⏎But I've also seen what happens when the systems designed to share information don't have adequate safeguards around what gets shared, with whom, and with what consent. The mental health records situation I mentioned earlier is one example. I've had other clients whose substance use treatment records were shared in ways they didn't anticipate or consent to, with real consequences for their employment and housing situations.⏎⏎So I'm supportive of the general direction of improving access, but I'd want to make sure that any changes to information blocking definitions and exceptions don't inadvertently create new pathways for sensitive information to flow without appropriate patient consent. I don't have enough technical expertise to evaluate the specific proposed changes in detail, but I'd flag that concern for whoever is reading this.⏎⏎The connection to the AI transparency issue is this: if we're going to move toward a world where health data flows more freely and AI tools play a larger role in clinical decision-making, then we need more transparency about what those tools are doing with that data, not less. The two changes are moving in opposite directions, and I don't think that's a coincidence worth ignoring.⏎⏎ADDRESSING THE SPECIFIC ARGUMENT ABOUT FLEXIBILITY⏎⏎One of the arguments I've seen made for removing or softening the DSI requirements is that it gives developers more flexibility to innovate. I want to take that argument seriously, because I think flexibility genuinely matters in a fast-moving field like health AI.⏎⏎But there's a difference between flexibility in how developers meet a requirement and flexibility in whether they have to meet it at all. I'd be much more comfortable with changes that said "here are multiple ways you can provide the required transparency disclosures, and you can choose the approach that works best for your product" than with changes that said "we're removing the requirement entirely." The proposed rule, as I read it, is much closer to the latter than the former.⏎⏎There's also a question of what "innovation" means in this context. If innovation means building better tools that work more reliably for more patients, then transparency requirements support that, because they create incentives to do the underlying work well. If innovation means being able to deploy tools quickly without doing that work, then transparency requirements are an obstacle. I know which kind of innovation I want in the healthcare settings where my clients receive care.⏎⏎I'm aware that I'm probably not the most sophisticated commentor on the technical details of certification criteria. But I've been doing this work long enough to know that when someone tells me a consumer protection requirement needs to be removed in the name of flexibility and innovation, I should ask: flexible for whom? Innovative in whose interest?⏎⏎WHAT GOOD LOOKS LIKE⏎⏎I want to be constructive here, not just critical. If ONC is genuinely concerned about the administrative burden of the current DSI requirements, there are ways to address that concern without eliminating the requirements.⏎⏎For example:⏎⏎a. ONC could work with stakeholders to develop standardized model card templates that reduce the documentation burden for developers while ensuring that clinicians receive consistent, comparable information across different tools. If every developer is filling out a different format, the information is harder to use even when it's available.⏎⏎b. ONC could create a public registry of model cards for certified AI tools, similar to the way that clinical trial results are registered, so that the disclosure serves a cumulative public benefit rather than just a one-time certification exercise.⏎⏎c. ONC could clarify what "external validation" means in the context of the DSI requirement, and provide guidance on how smaller developers can meet that requirement without conducting large-scale independent studies. There may be ways to allow for phased or surrogate validation approaches that are less burdensome while still providing meaningful information.⏎⏎d. ONC could establish a clearer process for updating model cards when a tool is updated or retrained, so that the disclosure remains current rather than becoming stale over time.⏎⏎These are not my original ideas. I've seen versions of all of them discussed in the health AI literature and in previous public comments on related rulemakings. I'm raising them here because I think they represent a more constructive path than simply removing the requirement and hoping that market forces will somehow produce the transparency that regulation would have required.⏎⏎I genuinely don't know whether ONC has the authority or the resources to do all of these things. But I do know that "this requirement is burdensome" and "therefore we should eliminate it" is not the only logical path. There's a version of this that keeps the protection in place while making it more workable. I'd like to see that version.⏎⏎CLOSING THOUGHTS (which are not really a tidy conclusion)⏎⏎I've been writing comments on federal health policy proposals for about fifteen years now, ever since the ACA rulemaking process, and I've gotten better at not expecting that any single comment will change anything. But I keep doing it because I think the cumulative record matters, and because I want there to be a clear account, somewhere in a public docket, of what the people actually affected by these rules thought about them.⏎⏎What I think about this one is: the AI transparency requirements in the current DSI certification criterion are not perfect, but they are meaningful. They give clinicians information they need to use AI tools responsibly. They create accountability for developers. They provide at least a partial answer to the question of whether a given tool was designed for and tested on patients like mine.⏎⏎Removing those requirements in the name of burden reduction trades a real protection for a speculative efficiency gain. I don't think that's a good trade, and I'd ask ONC to reconsider it.⏎⏎I'll also say this, because it's been on my mind as I've been writing this: the people who will bear the cost of this change are not the people who will bear the cost of the compliance burden it relieves. Developers will save time and money. Patients, particularly patients from communities that have historically been underrepresented in medical research and undertreated in clinical care, will lose one of the few tools available to them to ask whether the AI making recommendations about their care was ever designed with them in mind.⏎⏎I don't know how to make that trade-off come out differently in a cost-benefit analysis. I'm not an economist. But I know which side of it my clients are on, and I know which side I'm on.⏎⏎Thank you for reading this.⏎⏎Lisa Martinez⏎Social Worker⏎Milwaukee, WI⏎⏎---⏎⏎P.S. - I'm submitting this by email because the docket portal kept timing out when I tried to upload the document directly. The CAP is filing these comments because the proposed deregulatory actions would, if finalized as proposed, remove a certification criterion that the College regards as ESSENTIAL to patient safety and accountable AI deployment in clinical settings.⏎⏎The CAP focuses these comments on one specific question: whether ONC should retain or eliminate the Decision Support Interventions (DSI) certification criterion requiring AI model cards and transparency disclosures. The College's position is unambiguous. RETAIN THE DSI CRITERION IN FULL. What follows is a detailed explanation of why.⏎⏎BACKGROUND: WHAT THE DSI CRITERION ACTUALLY REQUIRES AND WHY IT WAS ADOPTED⏎⏎The DSI certification criterion, codified at 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11) and substantially revised through the HTI-1 rulemaking, requires that certified health IT systems deploying predictive decision support interventions disclose specific information about those interventions. The required disclosures include: the intended use of the algorithm, the target patient population for which the algorithm was validated, known risks or limitations associated with the algorithm's output, characteristics of the training data including demographic composition and data sources, and whether the algorithm has undergone external validation. ONC borrowed heavily from the concept of "model cards" developed in the machine learning research literature (see Mitchell et al., "Model Cards for Model Reporting," Proceedings of the 2019 ACM Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency), and the resulting criterion is, in the College's view, a reasonable minimum floor for what clinicians need to know before acting on an AI-generated recommendation.⏎⏎The reasoning behind the criterion was not complicated. When a clinician receives a sepsis alert or a risk score from an embedded AI model, that clinician needs to know whether the model was trained on data that looks anything like the patient in front of them. A sepsis prediction model trained predominantly on data from large academic medical centers may perform VERY DIFFERENTLY when deployed in a community hospital serving a different demographic population. This is not a hypothetical concern. Obermeyer et al. (Science, 2019, Vol. 366, Issue 6464) documented how a widely used commercial algorithm systematically underestimated illness severity in Black patients because the training data used healthcare cost as a proxy for health need, a choice that embedded existing disparities directly into the model's predictions. That study involved a real algorithm used by real health systems affecting real patients. The DSI criterion exists precisely to prevent that kind of silent, undetected bias from propagating through certified health IT.⏎⏎CAP Comments | ONC Deregulatory Actions | Docket ONC-2025-0001 | Page 2⏎⏎The proposed rule suggests, without providing substantial empirical support, that the DSI transparency requirements impose undue burden on health IT developers and that eliminating or substantially weakening them would reduce administrative costs while preserving patient safety through market mechanisms. The College respectfully but STRONGLY disagrees with both the burden characterization and the safety preservation claim.⏎⏎THE BURDEN ARGUMENT DOES NOT HOLD UP⏎⏎On burden: the information required by the DSI criterion is information that a responsible AI developer should already possess and document before deploying a clinical decision support tool. If a developer does not know the demographic composition of the training data used to build their algorithm, that is not a documentation burden problem. That is a development process problem. The CAP is genuinely puzzled by the argument that requiring developers to DISCLOSE information they should already have constitutes excessive regulatory burden. The cost of completing a model card for a properly documented AI system is trivial compared to the cost of deploying an algorithm that harms patients because no one asked the right questions about its validation.⏎⏎The College reviewed the regulatory impact analysis in the proposed rule and found the burden estimates for the DSI criterion difficult to reconcile with the actual documentation requirements. ONC appears to have relied primarily on estimates provided by health IT developers themselves, which creates an obvious incentive problem. The developers who would benefit most from eliminating the disclosure requirement are the same ones providing the burden estimates. The CAP would encourage ONC to seek independent verification of those figures before treating them as reliable.⏎⏎There is also a subtler point worth making here. The DSI criterion does not require developers to IMPROVE their algorithms or change their development practices. It requires them to be transparent about what those practices were. The burden, to the extent it exists at all, is the burden of honesty. The College is not sympathetic to the argument that honesty about AI development is too expensive.⏎⏎CAP Comments | ONC Deregulatory Actions | Docket ONC-2025-0001 | Page 3⏎⏎PATIENT SAFETY AND THE LIMITS OF MARKET MECHANISMS⏎⏎The proposed rule implies that market competition and voluntary disclosure can substitute for the certification criterion. Clinicians who want transparency information can demand it; developers who provide good transparency information will gain market share; the market will self-correct toward appropriate disclosure norms. The College finds this argument UNCONVINCING for several reasons that are specific to the clinical AI context.⏎⏎First, the information asymmetry in clinical AI is severe. A clinician receiving an alert from an embedded AI model typically has no practical way to evaluate the quality of that model without the disclosures the DSI criterion requires. Unlike, say, a consumer choosing between two competing products based on visible quality signals, a hospitalist managing fourteen patients on a busy floor is not going to independently audit the training data provenance of every AI tool embedded in their EHR. The DSI criterion solves an information asymmetry problem that market mechanisms cannot solve on their own.⏎⏎Second, the competitive dynamics in health IT do not resemble a well-functioning market in the relevant respects. Health systems make EHR purchasing decisions based on a complex mix of factors, AI transparency is rarely a primary driver of those decisions, and switching costs are enormous. A health system that discovers post-deployment that an AI tool embedded in their EHR lacks adequate transparency documentation cannot easily switch vendors. The DSI criterion creates a FLOOR below which all certified products must not fall, which is exactly the function that certification standards serve in markets with high switching costs and information asymmetries.⏎⏎Third, and the College considers this the most important point: the patients whose safety is at stake have no meaningful ability to participate in the market mechanism the proposed rule envisions. A patient who is harmed because a sepsis algorithm failed to flag their deteriorating condition because the model was never validated on patients with their demographic profile has no meaningful recourse through market competition. They cannot go back in time and choose a hospital that used a better-documented AI tool.⏎⏎CAP Comments | ONC Deregulatory Actions | Docket ONC-2025-0001 | Page 4⏎⏎WHAT THE COLLEGE'S MEMBERS ACTUALLY EXPERIENCE IN PRACTICE⏎⏎The CAP wants to be direct about what the DSI transparency requirements mean in practice for pathologists and for the multi-site research contexts in which laboratory data is increasingly being used.⏎⏎Pathology is an AI-intensive specialty. Computer-aided detection tools for digital pathology slides, algorithms that flag abnormal cell morphologies, risk stratification models that incorporate laboratory values alongside clinical variables, all of these are increasingly embedded in the workflow of modern pathology practice. CAP members are not abstract bystanders to AI deployment in health IT; they are among its most active users and, in many cases, among its most technically sophisticated critics.⏎⏎When a pathologist uses a computer-aided detection tool to screen digital slides for potential malignancies, they need to know: was this tool validated on slides prepared using the same staining protocols as our laboratory? Was it validated on a patient population that includes the demographic groups we serve? What is the false negative rate in the validation dataset, and was that validation dataset independent of the training data? These are not exotic questions. They are BASIC QUESTIONS that any competent pathologist would ask about any diagnostic tool, and the DSI criterion is what ensures those questions have documented answers.⏎⏎The College is aware that some health IT developers argue that model cards are technically challenging to produce because AI models are complex and their behavior is difficult to summarize in a standardized document. The CAP is not persuaded. If a model is too complex to describe in terms of its intended use, target population, known limitations, and training data characteristics, then it is probably too complex to deploy safely in a clinical setting. Complexity is not an excuse for opacity.⏎⏎CAP Comments | ONC Deregulatory Actions | Docket ONC-2025-0001 | Page 5⏎⏎SPECIFIC CONCERNS ABOUT THE PROPOSED ELIMINATION OR WEAKENING OF DSI REQUIREMENTS⏎⏎The proposed rule presents several options for modifying the DSI criterion, ranging from minor adjustments to substantial elimination of the transparency disclosure requirements. The CAP's concerns vary in intensity depending on which option ONC is seriously considering, but the College wants to be clear about its position on each major modification being discussed.⏎⏎Option 1: Eliminating the requirement for training data demographic disclosures.⏎⏎This is the modification the College finds MOST ALARMING. The demographic composition of training data is arguably the single most important piece of information a clinician needs to assess whether an AI tool is likely to perform well for their specific patient population. Removing this requirement would effectively gut the patient safety function of the DSI criterion. The College strongly opposes this modification.⏎⏎The evidence base for this concern is substantial. In addition to the Obermeyer et al. study cited above, a 2021 systematic review by Parikh et al. published in npj Digital Medicine found that fewer than half of published clinical AI studies reported the racial or ethnic composition of their training datasets. If voluntary practice in the research literature produces this level of underreporting, there is no reason to believe that voluntary market practice in the commercial health IT space would produce better results. The certification requirement fills a gap that voluntary norms have demonstrably failed to fill.⏎⏎Option 2: Replacing mandatory disclosures with a voluntary attestation framework.⏎⏎The College is skeptical of voluntary attestation as a substitute for mandatory disclosure, for reasons that should be obvious from the market dynamics discussion above. Voluntary attestation frameworks work reasonably well when there is meaningful external pressure to comply, either from sophisticated buyers who can evaluate attestations or from liability exposure that creates strong incentives for accuracy. Neither of those conditions reliably holds in the clinical AI market as currently structured.⏎⏎CAP Comments | ONC Deregulatory Actions | Docket ONC-2025-0001 | Page 6⏎⏎The proposed rule does not identify any mechanism by which voluntary attestations would be verified or any consequence for attestations that turn out to be inaccurate. Without verification and consequences, voluntary attestation is not meaningfully different from no disclosure requirement at all. The CAP would support a voluntary attestation framework only if it were paired with meaningful verification mechanisms and clear consequences for inaccurate attestations, conditions that the proposed rule does not appear to contemplate.⏎⏎Option 3: Narrowing the scope of DSI requirements to apply only to algorithms that meet a higher threshold of clinical decision influence.⏎⏎The College has mixed feelings about this approach. There is a reasonable argument that not every decision support tool embedded in an EHR poses the same level of patient safety risk, and that a tiered approach might allow ONC to focus transparency requirements where they matter most without imposing identical burdens on low-risk informational tools. The CAP would not oppose a thoughtfully designed tiered approach IF the criteria for determining which tier a given tool falls into are clear, objective, and not easily manipulated by developers seeking to avoid the higher-tier requirements.⏎⏎What concerns the College about the tiered approach as described in the proposed rule is that the tier definitions appear to rely heavily on developer self-classification. A developer who wants to avoid the transparency requirements has a strong incentive to classify their tool as low-risk, and the proposed rule does not appear to include robust mechanisms for ONC or third-party certifiers to challenge those classifications. The College would recommend that any tiered framework include mandatory clinical expert review of tier classifications for tools that generate patient-specific risk scores or recommendations, regardless of how the developer classifies the tool.⏎⏎INTEROPERABILITY AND THE RESEARCH INFRASTRUCTURE CONCERN⏎⏎The CAP also wants to address a concern that goes beyond the immediate patient safety question, though it connects to it. The DSI transparency requirements are not only about protecting individual patients at the point of care. They are also about maintaining the integrity of the research infrastructure that depends on certified health IT systems to generate reliable, documented data.⏎⏎CAP Comments | ONC Deregulatory Actions | Docket ONC-2025-0001 | Page 7⏎⏎Multi-site clinical research increasingly depends on data pulled from certified EHR systems. When those systems are certified to consistent standards, including standards about how AI-generated data elements are documented, researchers can make meaningful comparisons across sites. When those standards are weakened or eliminated, the comparability of data across systems degrades in ways that may not be immediately visible but that compound over time into serious methodological problems.⏎⏎The College is thinking specifically about outcomes research that incorporates AI-generated risk scores or diagnostic recommendations as variables. If the AI tools generating those scores are not documented to a consistent standard, researchers cannot evaluate whether differences in outcomes across sites reflect genuine clinical differences or differences in the AI tools being used. This is not a minor technical inconvenience. It is a FUNDAMENTAL THREAT to the validity of a large and growing body of clinical research.⏎⏎The HTI-1 rulemaking recognized this concern explicitly. The preamble to the HTI-1 Final Rule noted that the DSI transparency requirements were intended to support not only point-of-care clinical decision-making but also the ability of researchers, payers, and patients to evaluate the performance of AI tools across populations and settings (89 Fed. Reg. 1192, 1247-1249). The proposed deregulatory rule does not meaningfully engage with this research infrastructure rationale, and the College believes that omission is a significant gap in the regulatory analysis.⏎⏎The CAP wants to be specific about what research infrastructure degradation looks like in practice, because the proposed rule treats this concern abstractly if it treats it at all.⏎⏎Consider a multi-site study examining post-surgical complications in patients who received AI-assisted preoperative risk assessments. To analyze that data meaningfully, researchers need to know:⏎⏎1. Which AI risk assessment tool was used at each site.⏎2. What patient population the tool was validated on.⏎3. Whether the tool's risk thresholds were calibrated consistently across sites or whether individual sites customized the thresholds.⏎4. What training data the tool used, specifically whether the training data included patients similar to those at each participating site.⏎5. Whether the tool had undergone external validation and if so, in what populations.⏎⏎CAP Comments | ONC Deregulatory Actions | Docket ONC-2025-0001 | Page 8⏎⏎Without the DSI transparency disclosures, items 2, 4, and 5 on that list are simply unavailable through any standardized mechanism. Researchers would need to obtain that information through individualized outreach to each AI tool developer, assuming the developer is willing to provide it, which is not guaranteed. The certification requirement is what makes that information systematically available and what makes cross-site research feasible at scale.⏎⏎The College recognizes that this concern is somewhat different from the point-of-care patient safety concern, but the two are connected. The same transparency that protects an individual patient from being harmed by an algorithm trained on an unrepresentative dataset is also what makes it possible to detect, after the fact, whether a deployed algorithm has been causing systematic harm to particular patient populations. Without the disclosure, neither the real-time protection nor the retrospective detection is possible.⏎⏎THE ACCOUNTABILITY QUESTION⏎⏎There is one more dimension of the DSI criterion that the proposed rule does not adequately address, and the College wants to name it directly: ACCOUNTABILITY.⏎⏎When an AI-assisted clinical decision goes wrong and a patient is harmed, the transparency disclosures required by the DSI criterion are what make it possible to determine whether the algorithm contributed to the harm and, if so, how. Without documentation of the algorithm's intended use, target population, and known limitations, it becomes very difficult to establish whether the algorithm was used appropriately or whether the deployment deviated from the developer's own specifications. This matters for malpractice litigation, for quality improvement investigations, and for regulatory oversight.⏎⏎The College is aware that some AI developers are concerned that detailed transparency disclosures could expose them to increased liability. The CAP's view is that this concern has the causality backwards. Developers should be liable for harms that result from deploying algorithms in ways that deviate from the algorithm's validated use case. The transparency disclosures are what establish what the validated use case is. If a developer is worried about liability exposure from being transparent about their algorithm's limitations, the answer is not to eliminate the transparency requirement. The answer is to develop better algorithms with fewer limitations, or to deploy existing algorithms only within their validated scope.⏎⏎CAP Comments | ONC Deregulatory Actions | Docket ONC-2025-0001 | Page 9⏎⏎This is a point the College feels strongly about. The patient safety and accountability functions of the DSI criterion are, in a practical sense, inseparable. An algorithm that is transparently documented is an algorithm that can be held accountable. An algorithm that is opaquely deployed in a certified EHR system, with no standardized documentation of its intended use or known limitations, is an algorithm that exists in a regulatory and legal gray zone where accountability is nearly impossible to establish after the fact.⏎⏎RESPONSE TO THE PROPOSED RULE'S RELIANCE ON EXISTING FDA OVERSIGHT⏎⏎The proposed rule appears to suggest, in at least some passages, that existing FDA oversight of Software as a Medical Device (SaMD) provides sufficient safeguards to substitute for the DSI certification requirements. The College disagrees with this characterization for several reasons.⏎⏎First, the FDA's SaMD oversight framework applies to a relatively narrow category of AI tools: those that meet the definition of a device under the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act. Many clinical decision support tools embedded in certified EHRs are specifically designed to fall outside the FDA's jurisdiction under the clinical decision support software exemption established by the 21st Century Cures Act. The DSI certification criterion was designed precisely to fill the oversight gap for tools that are NOT subject to FDA oversight.⏎⏎Second, even for tools that are subject to FDA oversight, the FDA's premarket review process does not require the same kind of ongoing transparency documentation that the DSI criterion requires. A tool that received FDA clearance several years ago may have been validated on a patient population that looks very different from the patients in the health system where it is currently deployed. The FDA clearance does not update automatically when the deployment context changes; the DSI disclosures provide a mechanism for that ongoing transparency that FDA oversight alone does not.⏎⏎Third, the FDA and ONC have different regulatory missions and tools. Treating FDA oversight as a substitute for ONC certification requirements conflates two frameworks that were designed to do different things. The CAP would strongly encourage ONC to maintain the DSI criterion as an independent safeguard rather than delegating the transparency function to a framework that was not designed to serve that function.⏎⏎CAP Comments | ONC Deregulatory Actions | Docket ONC-2025-0001 | Page 10⏎⏎SPECIFIC RECOMMENDATIONS⏎⏎The College's primary recommendation is simple: DO NOT ELIMINATE OR SUBSTANTIALLY WEAKEN THE DSI CERTIFICATION CRITERION. The transparency disclosures required by 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11) serve patient safety, research integrity, and accountability functions that cannot be adequately served by voluntary market mechanisms, FDA oversight, or attestation frameworks without robust verification.⏎⏎If ONC concludes that some modification of the DSI criterion is warranted, the College offers the following specific recommendations for how those modifications should be structured:⏎⏎1. Retain ALL five core disclosure categories: intended use, target population, known risks and limitations, training data characteristics including demographic composition, and external validation status. Any modification that removes any of these categories would substantially degrade the patient safety function of the criterion.⏎⏎2. If a tiered approach is adopted, ensure that tier classifications are subject to independent review for any tool that generates patient-specific risk scores or recommendations, regardless of how the developer classifies the tool. Developer self-classification without independent review is not an adequate safeguard.⏎⏎3. Do not treat FDA clearance or authorization as a substitute for DSI transparency disclosures. A tool that has received FDA clearance should still be required to provide DSI-compliant disclosures, because the two frameworks serve different functions.⏎⏎4. If voluntary attestation is incorporated as an alternative compliance pathway, pair it with mandatory verification mechanisms and clear consequences for inaccurate attestations. Unverified voluntary attestation is not meaningfully different from no disclosure requirement.⏎⏎5. Require that DSI disclosures be updated when a tool is deployed in a new patient population or clinical setting that differs materially from the validated use case. The disclosure requirement should not be a one-time box to check at certification; it should reflect the actual deployment context.⏎⏎6. Maintain the requirement that DSI disclosures be machine-readable and accessible through standardized APIs, so that researchers and health systems can systematically retrieve and analyze disclosure information across products. This is what makes the research infrastructure function of the criterion possible at scale.⏎⏎CAP Comments | ONC Deregulatory Actions | Docket ONC-2025-0001 | Page 11⏎⏎The College is aware that these recommendations are more demanding than the proposed rule contemplates, and the CAP does not apologize for that. The DSI criterion addresses a genuine patient safety problem with a targeted, proportionate solution. The proposed deregulatory approach would trade a functioning safeguard for a theoretical market mechanism that the available evidence does not support.⏎⏎ADDITIONAL CONCERNS ABOUT THE PROPOSED RULE'S BROADER DEREGULATORY DIRECTION⏎⏎The CAP limits these comments primarily to the DSI certification criterion, but the College wants to note briefly that the proposed rule's broader deregulatory direction gives the College pause in ways that go beyond any single criterion.⏎⏎The preamble to the proposed rule frames deregulation as inherently beneficial, as a way to "unleash prosperity" and reduce burden on health IT developers. The College does not object to reducing genuine administrative burden where it exists. But the framing concerns the CAP because it treats the costs of regulation as self-evidently outweighing the benefits without adequately accounting for what those regulations actually do.⏎⏎The certification standards that the proposed rule would weaken or eliminate were not invented arbitrarily. They emerged from a long history of documented problems with health IT interoperability, patient safety failures attributable to poorly designed or poorly deployed clinical decision support tools, and systematic biases in AI systems that were not detected until after they had affected large numbers of patients. The burden reduction framing tends to make those historical problems invisible, treating the regulations as the problem rather than as the solution to a prior problem.⏎⏎The College is also concerned about the cumulative effect of multiple simultaneous deregulatory actions. Each individual modification proposed in the rule might seem modest in isolation. But the DSI transparency disclosures, the information blocking exceptions, the certification criteria for specific data elements, these are not independent. They form a system. When multiple elements of that system are relaxed simultaneously, the cumulative effect on interoperability and data integrity can be substantially larger than the sum of the individual modifications. The regulatory impact analysis in the proposed rule does not appear to grapple seriously with this cumulative effect concern.⏎⏎CAP Comments | ONC Deregulatory Actions | Docket ONC-2025-0001 | Page 12⏎⏎The CAP raised a version of this concern in its comments on the HTI-1 proposed rule (submitted October 4, 2023), where the College noted that the value of certification standards comes in large part from their consistency across products and over time. A certification standard that is subject to frequent weakening creates uncertainty for health systems making long-term IT investments and for researchers designing multi-year studies that depend on consistent data documentation standards. Stability has regulatory value, and the proposed rule does not appear to account for it.⏎⏎THE SPECIFIC CASE FOR EXTERNAL VALIDATION DISCLOSURE⏎⏎The College wants to spend a moment on the external validation disclosure requirement specifically, because this is one element of the DSI criterion that the proposed rule appears to treat as relatively low priority but that the CAP considers CRITICALLY IMPORTANT.⏎⏎External validation, meaning validation of an AI model's performance on a dataset that was not used in training or tuning the model, is the minimum acceptable standard for establishing that an AI tool generalizes beyond the data it was trained on. Internal validation metrics, accuracy figures calculated on held-out portions of the training dataset, are notoriously optimistic and frequently fail to predict real-world performance. Wynants et al. (BMJ, 2020, 369:m1328) analyzed 232 prediction models developed for COVID-19 and found that the vast majority were at HIGH RISK OF BIAS and that predictive performance in external validation was consistently worse than internal validation metrics suggested.⏎⏎This is not a COVID-specific finding. It reflects a general pattern in clinical AI development where models that perform impressively on internal validation fail to generalize when deployed in new settings or populations. The external validation disclosure requirement is what gives clinicians and health systems the information they need to assess whether a given tool has been tested in settings similar to their own. Without this disclosure, a health system has no standardized way to determine whether the impressive accuracy figures in a vendor's marketing materials are based on internal or external validation, a distinction that could be the difference between a useful clinical tool and a misleading one.⏎⏎The proposed rule does not appear to offer a compelling reason to weaken or eliminate the external validation disclosure requirement. The College strongly urges ONC to retain it.⏎⏎CAP Comments | ONC Deregulatory Actions | Docket ONC-2025-0001 | Page 13⏎⏎A NOTE ON PROCESS⏎⏎The College wants to make one observation about the process by which the proposed rule was developed, without suggesting any impropriety. The proposed rule is framed as a response to an executive order directing agencies to reduce regulatory burden. The CAP understands that agencies operate within political and administrative constraints and that responding to executive direction is a normal part of regulatory practice.⏎⏎At the same time, the College is concerned that the burden-reduction framing may have shaped the regulatory analysis in ways that underweighted the patient safety evidence. The HTI-1 rulemaking included extensive discussion of the evidence base for the DSI criterion, including citations to the peer-reviewed literature on AI bias, the documented failures of voluntary disclosure in the health IT market, and the specific patient safety harms that the criterion was designed to prevent. The proposed deregulatory rule engages with that evidence base much less thoroughly, and the regulatory impact analysis appears to give substantially more weight to developer burden estimates than to the patient safety benefits the criterion provides.⏎⏎The CAP is not suggesting that the agency acted in bad faith. But the College is asking ONC to ensure that the final rule reflects a genuine balancing of costs and benefits, not a presumption that deregulation is the correct outcome regardless of the evidence. That kind of genuine balancing would, the College believes, lead ONC to retain the DSI criterion.⏎⏎CONCLUSION REGARDING THE DSI CRITERION⏎⏎The College of American Pathologists urges ONC to retain the Decision Support Interventions certification criterion, including all five core transparency disclosure requirements, in the final rule. The criterion addresses a real patient safety problem, supported by substantial peer-reviewed evidence. The proposed alternatives, market mechanisms, voluntary attestation, FDA oversight, do not adequately substitute for a mandatory, standardized, verified disclosure requirement. The burden the criterion imposes on responsible AI developers is minimal; the burden it removes from clinicians trying to evaluate AI tools in their practice is substantial.⏎⏎CAP Comments | ONC Deregulatory Actions | Docket ONC-2025-0001 | Page 14⏎⏎The College is also asking ONC to be more transparent, in the final rule's preamble, about the evidence it considered and the weight it gave to patient safety evidence relative to developer burden estimates. The HTI-1 rulemaking set a high standard for evidence-based policymaking in clinical AI governance. The proposed deregulatory rule falls short of that standard, and the CAP believes the final rule should return to it.⏎⏎If ONC has questions about the College's comments or would like to discuss the technical details of the DSI criterion with CAP members who have direct experience deploying and evaluating clinical AI tools, the College would welcome that conversation. The CAP's contact for regulatory affairs is available at the address below.⏎⏎College of American Pathologists⏎325 Waukegan Road⏎Northfield, IL 60093⏎advocacy@cap.org⏎⏎CAP Comments | ONC Deregulatory Actions | Docket ONC-2025-0001 | Page 15⏎⏎CITATIONS REFERENCED IN THESE COMMENTS⏎⏎45 CFR 170.315(b)(11) (DSI certification criterion, as amended by HTI-1 Final Rule)⏎⏎HTI-1 Final Rule, 89 Fed.
