We have eleven clinical staff, a part-time compliance officer who splits time with two other practices, and a care coordinator who, as of last spring, was spending the better part of her week doing by hand what a piece of certified health IT software had been doing automatically. I want to spend most of this comment on one specific issue, because I think it is the most consequential thing in this proposed rule that does not seem to be getting enough attention in the public discussion: the proposal to remove or scale back the Decision Support Interventions certification criterion, specifically the requirements around AI transparency disclosures, model cards, and documentation of training data and known risks.⏎⏎I will acknowledge upfront that I have mixed feelings about parts of this rulemaking. I understand the argument for reducing certification burden. I have watched that burden cause real harm to small vendors in our region. Last spring, our EHR vendor, a company called Meridian Health Systems out of Lexington, pulled two interoperability features from their platform mid-contract cycle because they could not afford to run those features through the eighteen-month recertification process after updating the underlying code. Our care coordinator, Brenda Tolliver, spent the better part of three weeks in April and May 2024 manually reconciling medication records for patients transitioning out of inpatient rehabilitation. Records the software had been reconciling automatically. We lost two patients to follow-up gaps during that period. I mean we lost contact with them. We do not know if they are okay. That is the kind of thing that stays with you, and I understand why reasonable people look at certification timelines and say the current system is not working.⏎⏎But that experience actually cuts the other way on the DSI transparency question. Here is why.⏎⏎⏎SECTION 1: WHAT THE DSI TRANSPARENCY REQUIREMENTS ACTUALLY DO IN PRACTICE⏎⏎The Decision Support Interventions certification criterion, as currently structured under 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11), requires that health IT developers seeking certification for clinical decision support tools that meet the definition of a DSI disclose specific information about those tools. This includes the intended use of the algorithm or model, the patient population the tool was designed for, known risks and limitations, characteristics of the training data, and whether the tool has undergone external validation. These are the model card requirements, essentially, adapted for a regulatory certification context.⏎⏎What this means for a practice like ours, in practical terms, is that when we evaluate whether to adopt a clinical decision support module, whether that module is embedded in our EHR or offered as a third-party add-on, we have access to documentation that tells us what the tool was trained on, who it was validated for, and what the developer says it should and should not be used to do. That documentation is not perfect. I have read model cards that were vague to the point of uselessness. But the requirement that they exist at all creates accountability. It means our clinical staff can ask the question: was this tool validated on a population that looks anything like our patients?⏎⏎Kith and Kin, LLC Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 2⏎⏎⏎Our patient population is predominantly low-income adults in eastern and central Kentucky dealing with substance use disorders, co-occurring mental health conditions, and significant social determinants of health. A clinical decision support tool trained primarily on commercially insured, urban patient populations in a large academic medical center is not necessarily going to perform well for our patients. We know this because there is now a substantial body of published literature documenting exactly this kind of algorithmic bias in health AI. The 2019 Obermeyer et al. study published in Science (Obermeyer et al., Science 366:447-453, 2019) is probably the most cited example, but it is far from the only one. That study documented how a widely used commercial algorithm systematically underestimated the health needs of Black patients because it used healthcare cost as a proxy for health need, and Black patients with the same level of health need had lower costs because of reduced access to care. The algorithm was being used across a large portion of the U.S. health system before that analysis was published. There was no requirement that the developer disclose the training data characteristics or known limitations in any systematic, standardized way.⏎⏎The DSI transparency requirements are, in part, a regulatory response to exactly that kind of failure. Removing them, or making them voluntary, does not reduce that risk. It just means the risk is no longer visible.⏎⏎⏎SECTION 2: THE PROPOSED CHANGE AND WHAT CONCERNS ME⏎⏎The proposed rule, as I read the preamble language, suggests that the DSI transparency disclosures may be scaled back, made voluntary, or restructured in ways that give developers significantly more flexibility in what they disclose and how. The stated rationale is that the current requirements are burdensome, that they may be duplicative of other regulatory requirements, and that reducing them will encourage innovation by lowering the cost of certification. I want to take each of those arguments seriously, because I do not think they are made in bad faith.⏎⏎On the burden argument: yes, the current DSI requirements add time and cost to the certification process. I have heard this directly from Meridian Health Systems and from two other vendors we have worked with over the past five years. One of them, a small company that was developing a screening tool for social determinants of health, told me in early 2024 that the documentation requirements for the DSI criterion were the single most time-consuming part of their certification preparation. I believe that. I also think the solution to that problem is to streamline the documentation process, provide better templates and guidance, and potentially adjust timelines, not to eliminate the requirement that the documentation exist.⏎⏎On the duplication argument: the proposed rule suggests that other regulatory frameworks, including FDA oversight of software as a medical device, and potentially FTC oversight in some contexts, may provide sufficient guardrails that ONC certification requirements are redundant. I am genuinely not sure this is right, and I want to say that carefully because I am not a regulatory attorney. But my understanding is that FDA's current framework for software as a medical device focuses primarily on tools that meet the definition of a device under the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, and that a significant portion of clinical decision support software is specifically excluded from FDA oversight under the 21st Century Cures Act amendments. The exclusion in 21 U.S.C. 360j(o) covers software that displays, analyzes, or prints medical information for clinicians to independently review and does not acquire, process, or analyze medical images or signals from certain in vitro diagnostic devices. A large share of the AI-driven DSI tools now being marketed to small practices like ours fall into that excluded category. They are not FDA-regulated. If ONC pulls back on its transparency requirements for those tools, the transparency requirements effectively disappear.⏎⏎⏎Kith and Kin, LLC Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 3⏎⏎⏎On the innovation argument: I want to be honest here. I have heard the argument that heavy certification requirements push small, innovative vendors out of the market, and I think it is partially true. The Meridian situation I described earlier is real evidence of that. But I keep coming back to the question of what kind of innovation we are trying to encourage. If the goal is to get more AI-driven clinical decision support tools into small practices in rural and underserved areas, which I genuinely support, then we need those tools to be trustworthy. A clinician who cannot get basic information about what a tool was trained on, who it was validated for, and what its known failure modes are is in a difficult position. They are being asked to incorporate the tool's recommendations into clinical decisions without the information they would need to know when to trust it and when to be skeptical.⏎⏎Brenda Tolliver, our care coordinator, used a medication adherence prediction tool for about eight months before we realized it was performing poorly for patients who had recently been incarcerated. The tool was flagging those patients as low risk for non-adherence, which meant they were being deprioritized in our outreach schedule. We figured this out because Brenda noticed a pattern in her case notes, not because the tool's documentation told us about this limitation. When we eventually got documentation from the vendor, after asking specifically, it turned out the training data had very limited representation of recently incarcerated individuals. That information should have been in the model card from the beginning. It should have been part of what we reviewed before we adopted the tool.⏎⏎⏎SECTION 3: SPECIFIC RECOMMENDATIONS⏎⏎Kith and Kin, LLC urges ONC to retain the current DSI certification criterion requirements for AI transparency disclosures in their current form, or to adopt modifications that strengthen rather than weaken those requirements. Specifically:⏎⏎1. Retain the requirement that certified DSI tools include documentation of intended use and target population. This is the most basic form of informed procurement. A practice should know, before adopting a tool, what patient population the tool was designed for. This does not need to be a lengthy document. It needs to be accurate and standardized enough to be comparable across vendors.⏎⏎2. Retain the requirement for disclosure of known risks and limitations. Vendors know things about their tools' failure modes that clinicians do not. The certification requirement creates a structured mechanism for that knowledge to be shared. Making this voluntary will predictably result in most vendors disclosing the minimum.⏎⏎3. Retain the requirement for disclosure of training data characteristics. This does not mean releasing proprietary data. It means disclosing the general characteristics of the training dataset: what time period it covers, what care settings, what demographic composition where known, and whether the training population is likely to be representative of the intended use population. This is standard practice in responsible AI development and the certification requirement simply formalizes it.⏎⏎4. Retain the requirement for external validation documentation. A developer's internal testing is not a substitute for external validation. This is well established in the clinical literature. A 2022 systematic review published in The Lancet Digital Health (Wynants et al., Lancet Digital Health 2022) found that the vast majority of clinical prediction models published in the peer-reviewed literature performed worse on external validation than on internal validation, and many performed substantially worse. The certification requirement that developers document whether and how their tool has been externally validated is not bureaucratic excess. It is a check on optimistic internal testing.⏎⏎5. If ONC is determined to reduce the documentation burden, consider a tiered approach based on the clinical stakes of the decision support function. A tool that generates administrative workflow suggestions warrants less intensive disclosure than a tool that is influencing diagnostic or treatment decisions. But the tiering should increase transparency requirements for high-stakes tools, not reduce them across the board.⏎⏎⏎Kith and Kin, LLC Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 4⏎⏎⏎I want to add something here that does not fit neatly into a numbered list. There is a power asymmetry in the current market that these transparency requirements partially address. Large health systems with dedicated informatics teams and data science staff can evaluate AI tools in ways that small practices cannot. They can run the vendor's tool against their own patient data. They can look at performance stratified by race, insurance status, or diagnosis category. They can negotiate for detailed technical documentation as part of the procurement process. We cannot do any of that. We have eleven clinical staff and a part-time compliance officer. The certification transparency requirements are, for practices like ours, a substitute for the due diligence capacity we do not have. When ONC requires that a developer disclose training data characteristics and known limitations as a condition of certification, it means that information is available to us in a standardized form, even though we did not have the leverage to demand it in a procurement negotiation.⏎⏎Removing that requirement does not level the playing field. It makes the field more uneven.⏎⏎⏎SECTION 4: RESPONDING TO THE INTEROPERABILITY BURDEN ARGUMENT⏎⏎I want to spend a moment on the broader deregulatory framing of this proposed rule, because I think there is a conflation happening that is worth naming. The rule bundles together several different kinds of regulatory burden as though they are all the same kind of problem. Some of them are. The certification cycle timelines that caused Meridian Health Systems to pull their interoperability features are a genuine problem, and I support efforts to streamline those timelines and reduce the cost of iterative updates to certified modules. The information blocking exceptions framework has provisions that are genuinely confusing for small practices trying to figure out their obligations, and I support clearer guidance there.⏎⏎But the DSI transparency requirements are a different category of thing. They are not primarily a burden on vendors who are trying to update their software quickly. They are a mechanism for making AI-driven clinical decision support tools accountable to the clinicians and patients who use them. The cost they impose is real, but it is the cost of doing that accountability work. You cannot separate the cost from the function and then argue that removing the cost has no effect on the function.⏎⏎I have seen what happens when clinical AI tools are deployed without adequate transparency. I described the medication adherence prediction situation above. That was a real situation with real consequences for real patients. The tool was not malicious. The vendor was not acting in bad faith. But without a requirement to document and disclose the training data characteristics and known limitations, there was no structured mechanism for us to know what we did not know.⏎⏎⏎Kith and Kin, LLC Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 5⏎⏎⏎SECTION 5: THE PATIENT SAFETY DIMENSION⏎⏎ONC has stated, in various guidance documents and in prior rulemakings, that patient safety is a core principle of the Health IT Certification Program. See, for example, the preamble to the 2020 Interoperability and Patient Access final rule (85 FR 25642), which describes the certification program as designed to ensure that health IT performs reliably and safely in clinical environments. The DSI transparency requirements are an application of that principle to AI-driven clinical decision support. They exist because AI tools can fail in ways that are not obvious, that vary across patient populations, and that clinicians cannot detect without information about how the tools work.⏎⏎If ONC removes or weakens these requirements in the name of reducing regulatory burden, it is making a tradeoff. The tradeoff is: lower compliance costs for vendors, in exchange for reduced transparency for clinicians and patients. I think that tradeoff is wrong. I think it is wrong in the abstract, and I think it is especially wrong in the current moment, when the adoption of AI-driven clinical decision support is accelerating and the evidence base for many of these tools is still thin.⏎⏎I am aware that some commenters will argue that the market will solve this problem, that practices will demand transparency and vendors who do not provide it will lose business. I am skeptical of that argument for small practices in rural and underserved areas. We do not have a lot of vendor options. The EHR market for behavioral health practices our size in Kentucky is not particularly competitive. We largely take what is available and try to use it safely. The certification program's transparency requirements are part of how we do that.⏎⏎⏎SECTION 6: COMMENTS ON THE INFORMATION BLOCKING PROVISIONS⏎⏎I want to briefly address one aspect of the information blocking provisions in the proposed rule, because it touches on something that has affected our practice directly. The proposed rule includes modifications to the Information Blocking Exceptions framework, including changes to the Fees Exception and the Manner Exception. Our experience with information blocking has been primarily on the receiving end: we have had situations where a hospital network's EHR system declined to share patient records with us in a timely way on grounds that were, in our view, pretextual. Getting those records is material to our care coordination function, particularly for patients transitioning out of inpatient settings.⏎⏎I am not going to comment in detail on the specific exception modifications because I do not have enough technical expertise in that area to do so responsibly. What I will say is that any changes to the information blocking framework should be evaluated against the question of whether they make it easier or harder for small, downstream care coordination practices to access the patient information they need to do their jobs. Large health systems have legal teams and compliance departments and negotiating leverage. We have Brenda Tolliver and a telephone. Changes that give health systems more flexibility in how they respond to information access requests are not neutral with respect to the power dynamics in those situations.⏎⏎⏎Kith and Kin, LLC Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 6⏎⏎⏎SECTION 7: ADDITIONAL CONCERNS ABOUT REMOVING CERTIFICATION CRITERIA⏎⏎Beyond the DSI transparency question, I want to note a broader concern about the cumulative effect of removing certification criteria. The proposed rule removes a number of certification criteria on the grounds that they are outdated, redundant, or no longer necessary. I understand that argument in specific cases. But the certification program is, in part, a floor. It defines a minimum set of capabilities and standards that certified health IT products must meet. When criteria are removed, that floor gets lower. Practices like ours rely on that floor when we are evaluating products we do not have the technical capacity to evaluate independently.⏎⏎I am not arguing that every criterion currently in the program should be retained forever. Some of them probably are outdated. But the process of removing criteria should be conservative and evidence-based. The question should be: what harm, if any, results from removing this requirement? For the DSI transparency requirements, the answer to that question is: reduced ability for clinicians to make informed decisions about AI tools, reduced accountability for developers, and increased risk of undetected algorithmic bias in clinical settings. That is not a trivial harm.⏎⏎The question of whether that harm is outweighed by the benefit of reduced compliance costs is a genuine policy question, and I think reasonable people can disagree about it. What I do not think is reasonable is to treat the compliance cost reduction as the primary consideration and the patient safety implications as secondary or speculative. The patient safety implications are not speculative. They are documented in the literature and experienced in practices like ours.⏎⏎⏎SECTION 8: A NOTE ON SMALL VENDOR IMPACTS⏎⏎I want to return to something I raised at the beginning of this comment, because I do not want to be misread as indifferent to the situation of small vendors. I am not. The Meridian Health Systems situation was genuinely harmful to our practice and to our patients. The certification cycle timelines are a real problem. The cost of maintaining certification for multiple product versions simultaneously is a real problem. I have talked to enough small health IT developers over the past several years to know that the current certification program creates barriers that are, in some cases, preventing genuinely good products from reaching the market.⏎⏎But the solution to that problem is not to remove the transparency requirements for AI tools. The solution is to make the certification process more efficient, more predictable, and less expensive, while keeping the substantive requirements that protect patients. ONC has the ability to do both of those things simultaneously. Streamlining documentation templates, providing clearer guidance on what level of detail is required for model cards, creating a safe harbor for iterative updates that do not change the core algorithm, offering certification support resources to small vendors, these are all things that could reduce the burden on small developers without eliminating the information that clinicians need.⏎⏎I would also note that the transparency requirements, if well-designed, can actually benefit small vendors by creating a level playing field. A small vendor with a genuinely good, well-validated tool should want to disclose its training data and validation results. That information is a competitive advantage. The vendors who benefit from removing transparency requirements are not the ones with the best tools. They are the ones with tools they do not want scrutinized.⏎⏎⏎Kith and Kin, LLC Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 7⏎⏎⏎SECTION 9: BROADER CONTEXT AND THE CURRENT REGULATORY MOMENT⏎⏎I want to acknowledge that this rulemaking is happening at a particular moment in the development of health AI. The number of AI-driven clinical decision support tools being marketed to healthcare providers has increased dramatically over the past three years. A 2023 analysis by the Pew Charitable Trusts found that hundreds of AI tools are now being used in clinical settings across the United States, the majority of which are not subject to FDA oversight and are not required to undergo any form of independent validation before deployment. The ONC certification program's DSI transparency requirements are one of the few regulatory mechanisms that apply to a significant portion of those tools.⏎⏎At the same time, the evidence base for many of these tools is genuinely limited. A 2021 systematic review in NPJ Digital Medicine (Celi et al., NPJ Digital Medicine 2021) found that a substantial majority of published clinical AI studies used datasets that were not representative of the broader patient population, and that few studies reported performance stratified by race, ethnicity, or socioeconomic status. This is the environment in which ONC is proposing to reduce transparency requirements. I find that timing troubling.⏎⏎I want to be fair to ONC. I recognize that the agency is operating under significant pressure to reduce regulatory burden, and that there are legitimate concerns about the current certification program's effect on innovation and market competition. I do not think the people working on this rule are indifferent to patient safety. But I think the DSI transparency requirements are the wrong place to look for burden reduction, and I think the case for retaining them, on patient safety and equity grounds, is substantially stronger than the case for removing them.⏎⏎⏎SECTION 10: WHAT I AM ASKING FOR⏎⏎To summarize the specific asks from Kith and Kin, LLC:⏎⏎1. Retain the current DSI certification criterion requirements for AI transparency disclosures in 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11), including the requirements for intended use documentation, target population disclosure, known risks and limitations, training data characteristics, and external validation documentation.⏎⏎2. If modifications are made, err on the side of strengthening rather than weakening the transparency requirements, particularly for tools used in high-stakes clinical decisions.⏎⏎3. Pursue burden reduction for small vendors through process improvements, better guidance, streamlined templates, and adjusted timelines, not through elimination of substantive transparency requirements.⏎⏎4. Consider the cumulative effect of removing multiple certification criteria simultaneously, and evaluate each proposed removal against an explicit patient safety analysis.⏎⏎5. In any final rule, provide specific guidance on how the information blocking exception modifications will apply to downstream care coordination practices accessing patient records from hospital systems.⏎⏎⏎Kith and Kin, LLC Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 8⏎⏎⏎I want to close this section by saying something that I recognize is not a policy argument but that I think belongs in this record. The two patients we lost to follow-up in the spring of 2024, the ones Brenda was trying to track when the interoperability tool went down, those are real people. I do not know their names for privacy reasons, I only know the case numbers. But I know that one of them was in recovery from opioid use disorder and had just completed a twenty-eight-day inpatient program, and that the transition window immediately after discharge is when the relapse risk is highest. We were supposed to be reaching out. We were not reaching out, because Brenda was doing manually what the software had been doing automatically, and there was only so much time in the day.⏎⏎I tell that story not to argue that the certification program as currently structured is perfect, because it is not. I tell it because it illustrates what is actually at stake when health IT decisions go wrong. The stakes are not vendor revenues or compliance costs, though those matter too. The stakes are whether someone in recovery gets a phone call at the right moment.⏎⏎The DSI transparency requirements are a small but real part of the infrastructure that makes it possible to deploy AI tools responsibly in settings like ours. They should not be removed.⏎⏎⏎ADDITIONAL OBSERVATIONS⏎⏎There is one more thing I want to put in the record, even though it does not fit neatly into the main argument above. The proposed rule, in its discussion of the certification criteria being removed or modified, relies substantially on the argument that market forces and voluntary industry standards will fill the gap left by removing regulatory requirements. I have read that argument in several places in the preamble, and I want to register skepticism about it, specifically in the context of small practices in underserved areas.⏎⏎The voluntary standards argument works better in markets where purchasers have information, leverage, and alternatives. In the behavioral health sector in rural Kentucky, none of those conditions fully apply. Our information is limited because we do not have the technical staff to evaluate AI tools in depth. Our leverage is limited because we are a small practice with modest purchasing power. Our alternatives are limited because the market for behavioral health EHR and care coordination software for practices our size is not large or particularly competitive.⏎⏎When ONC requires transparency as a condition of certification, it shifts the information burden from the purchaser to the developer. That shift matters a great deal for practices like ours. When ONC makes transparency voluntary and relies on market forces to produce it, it shifts the burden back to the purchaser. For large health systems with sophisticated procurement processes, that may be manageable. For us, it is not.⏎⏎⏎Kith and Kin, LLC Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 9⏎⏎⏎I am also aware that this comment has focused heavily on the DSI transparency issue and has not addressed many other provisions of the proposed rule. That is intentional. I do not have the expertise to comment responsibly on all of the proposed changes, and I think a focused comment on the issue I know best is more useful than a broad comment that covers everything superficially. There are other organizations better positioned than ours to comment on the technical details of the certification criteria being removed, the changes to the Conditions and Maintenance of Certification requirements, and the modifications to the information blocking regulatory definitions.⏎⏎What I can speak to, and what I have tried to speak to in this comment, is the experience of a small care coordination practice trying to use certified health IT responsibly in a high-stakes clinical environment, with limited staff and limited technical capacity, serving patients who do not have a lot of margin for error in their care. From that perspective, the DSI transparency requirements are not an obstacle to good care. They are part of what makes good care possible.⏎⏎⏎ON THE QUESTION OF IMPLEMENTATION TIMELINE⏎⏎One practical matter that I do not see adequately addressed in the proposed rule: if ONC does make changes to the DSI certification requirements, what happens to tools that are currently certified under the existing requirements? Is there a transition period? Are currently certified tools grandfathered under the old requirements, or do they need to be recertified under the new ones? For practices that have already built workflows around certified tools, the answer to that question matters a lot. We spent a significant amount of time in 2023 evaluating and selecting a new care coordination platform specifically because it was certified under the current DSI requirements and the vendor had provided model card documentation we could actually use. If the requirements change, does that documentation obligation disappear? Does the vendor have any ongoing obligation to update the disclosures if the model is retrained?⏎⏎These are not rhetorical questions. They are practical questions that affect how we manage our clinical workflows and how we make procurement decisions going forward. The proposed rule does not provide clear answers, and I would ask ONC to address them in the final rule or in accompanying guidance.⏎⏎⏎Kith and Kin, LLC Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 10⏎⏎⏎I will also note, for what it is worth, that the model card documentation we received from our current care coordination platform vendor in late 2023 was genuinely useful. It was not perfect. There were sections where the language was vague in ways that made me suspect the vendor was not entirely sure how to answer the question. But it told us that the training data was drawn primarily from Medicaid-enrolled patients in the southeastern United States, which is at least directionally relevant to our population. It told us that the tool had been externally validated on a dataset from a community health center network in Appalachia, which is about as close to our patient population as we could reasonably hope for in a commercially available product. It told us that the tool had known limitations in predicting engagement for patients with active psychosis, which is relevant to our caseload. None of that information would have been in a voluntary disclosure. I know this because I asked a competing vendor for the same information and they told me they could not share it for proprietary reasons. The certification requirement is why we got the information from the vendor we chose.⏎⏎That is the practical difference between a mandatory transparency requirement and a voluntary one. And that is why I am asking ONC to retain the current DSI certification criterion requirements.⏎⏎⏎Respectfully submitted,⏎⏎Kenneth Perez⏎Practice Manager⏎Kith and Kin, LLC⏎Lexington, Kentucky 40507⏎kperez@kithandkinllc.com⏎(859) 555-0174⏎⏎⏎Kith and Kin, LLC Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 11⏎⏎⏎REFERENCES CITED IN THIS COMMENT⏎⏎Obermeyer Z, Powers B, Vogeli C, Mullainathan S. CMS-2025-0050-110102♔CMS-2025-0050♔Carol Thompson♔HEP, LLC♔♔♔♔Removing the DSI certification criterion would eliminate critical AI transparency requirements — including disclosures of intended use, target population, training data, and validation results — that clinicians depend on to safely evaluate embedde...♔HEP, LLC Comments on ASTP/ONC Deregulatory Actions To Unleash Prosperity: Health Data, Technology, and Interoperability⏎Docket No. ONC-2025-0001⏎Submitted by Carol Thompson, Director of Government Relations, HEP, LLC⏎⏎HEP, LLC | ONC Deregulatory Actions | Page 1⏎⏎June 23, 2025⏎⏎Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology⏎U.S. Department of Health and Human Services⏎330 C Street, SW⏎Washington, DC 20201⏎⏎Thank you for the opportunity to comment on the proposed rule. HEP, LLC is a consulting and advocacy organization that works with health IT developers, digital health companies, and care-delivery organizations across the northeastern United States. Our member base includes early-stage startups, mid-sized EHR vendors, and a handful of larger enterprise developers. We track federal health IT policy closely, and we engage with ONC's Certification Program on behalf of our members on a regular basis.⏎⏎I want to be direct about where we stand: we support meaningful burden reduction in the ONC Certification Program. Our members have been telling us for years that certain requirements add cost and time without producing proportionate clinical or safety benefits. We have heard those concerns, we take them seriously, and we think ONC is right to ask whether every current criterion is earning its place.⏎⏎That said, we have a specific and firm disagreement with one aspect of this proposal, and I want to spend most of this comment on it. The proposal would remove the Decision Support Interventions (DSI) certification criterion, which currently requires developers to provide AI model cards and transparency disclosures covering intended use, target population, known risks, training data characteristics, and external validation results. We believe removing that criterion would be a mistake, and not a minor one. The clinical stakes are real, the accountability gap is real, and the burden argument for removing it does not hold up when you look at it closely.⏎⏎HEP, LLC | ONC Deregulatory Actions | Page 2⏎⏎BACKGROUND ON THE DSI CRITERION AND WHY IT WAS ADOPTED⏎⏎The DSI criterion at 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11) was finalized as part of ONC's HTI-1 final rule, published at 89 Fed. Reg. 1192 (January 9, 2024). It requires that certified health IT include functionality enabling the sharing of standardized information about AI and algorithm-based decision support tools, including documentation of the tool's intended use, the population it was developed and validated on, known limitations or risks, and information about training data. The requirement was not invented from whole cloth. It drew on a substantial body of literature and prior regulatory work, including FDA's framework for AI/ML-based Software as a Medical Device and the National Academy of Medicine's work on algorithmic transparency.⏎⏎The purpose was straightforward. When a clinician sees an AI-generated recommendation in their EHR, they need to know something about where it came from. Is it validated on a population that looks like their patient panel? Was it trained primarily on data from large academic medical centers when the clinician is practicing in a rural federally qualified health center? Does the tool's developer acknowledge any known failure modes? Without structured disclosure, the answer to all of those questions is: the clinician has no reliable way to find out.⏎⏎HEP, LLC | ONC Deregulatory Actions | Page 3⏎⏎THE ARGUMENT FOR REMOVING THE DSI CRITERION DOES NOT HOLD UP⏎⏎The proposed rule characterizes the DSI disclosure requirement as a source of certification burden. I understand the argument. Certification timelines have been a real problem. Last spring, two of our member developers were on the verge of shelving a promising care-coordination tool because the certification process had stretched to nearly fourteen months. One of those developers, a small company in Burlington with a team of eight, ultimately laid off two engineers and scaled back to a single-state pilot rather than the regional rollout they had planned. That is a concrete harm. We are not dismissing it.⏎⏎But the DSI model card requirement is not where that fourteen-month timeline came from. When we talked through the certification queue with those developers, the delays were in interoperability testing, in the EHR association review processes, and in the ONC-Authorized Certification Body (ONC-ACB) backlog. The DSI disclosure documentation, by comparison, was a manageable lift. One of the developers told us their team spent roughly three weeks producing it, and that the process of writing it actually surfaced a few things about their training data that they had not fully documented internally. That is the requirement working as intended.⏎⏎We are genuinely concerned that removing the DSI criterion will be read by the market as a signal that AI transparency in clinical decision support is optional. It is not optional. It should not be optional. The AI tools being deployed in EHRs today are making predictions about sepsis risk, medication dosing, readmission probability, and care escalation. These are not low-stakes recommendations. When those tools fail, patients are harmed. When they fail systematically because they were trained on non-representative data, whole populations are harmed disproportionately.⏎⏎HEP, LLC | ONC Deregulatory Actions | Page 4⏎⏎The evidence on algorithmic bias in clinical AI is not speculative at this point. A 2019 study published in Science (Obermeyer et al., 2019, 366 Science 447) documented that a widely deployed commercial algorithm used to identify high-risk patients for care management systematically underestimated the health needs of Black patients because it used healthcare cost as a proxy for health need. The algorithm was not disclosed to the clinicians using it. They had no way to evaluate whether it was appropriate for their patient population. That is precisely the information gap the DSI criterion is designed to close.⏎⏎We are also aware of the FDA's proposed regulatory framework for AI-enabled devices, published in draft guidance in 2021 and updated in 2024, which specifically contemplates transparency obligations for AI tools in clinical settings. ONC's DSI criterion is complementary to that framework, not duplicative of it. Removing it creates a gap between what FDA expects of standalone AI devices and what certified EHRs are expected to disclose about embedded AI tools. That is an incoherent regulatory posture.⏎⏎HEP, LLC | ONC Deregulatory Actions | Page 5⏎⏎WHAT CLINICIANS AND PATIENTS ACTUALLY NEED⏎⏎I keep coming back to a conversation I had in March with a primary care physician who practices at a community health center in Montpelier. She told me that she had been using an AI-based screening recommendation tool embedded in her EHR for about a year before she found out, through a conference presentation, that the tool had been trained almost entirely on data from commercially insured patients. Her patient panel is predominantly Medicaid and uninsured. She had no way of knowing that from within the EHR workflow. She had to stumble across a research presentation to find out.⏎⏎That is not an edge case. That is the normal experience of clinicians using embedded AI in EHRs today, and it is what happens in the absence of structured transparency requirements. The DSI model card requirement would have given that clinician access to the training data characteristics at the point of use. It would have told her something about whether the tool was validated on a population that looked like hers. She could have made an informed judgment about how much weight to give the recommendation.⏎⏎HEP, LLC | ONC Deregulatory Actions | Page 6⏎⏎Informed clinical decision-making depends on being able to evaluate the tools you are using. That principle is not new. It applies to laboratory reference ranges, to drug package inserts, to diagnostic imaging reports. The idea that it should not apply to AI-generated clinical recommendations is, frankly, hard to justify on any clinical or ethical grounds.⏎⏎Patients have an interest in this too, though it is sometimes harder to articulate in a regulatory comment. When an AI tool recommends against a particular treatment or flags a patient as low-risk for a condition, that recommendation may shape what care the patient receives. The patient has no visibility into the algorithm that generated it. The DSI requirement does not give patients direct access to model cards, but it creates a disclosure infrastructure that can support patient-facing transparency over time, as patient access tools and portal capabilities continue to develop. Removing it forecloses that possibility.⏎⏎HEP, LLC | ONC Deregulatory Actions | Page 7⏎⏎SPECIFIC CONCERNS ABOUT THE PROPOSED REMOVAL⏎⏎We want to be specific about what we think would be lost if the DSI criterion is removed.⏎⏎First, the intended use documentation. Under the current criterion, developers must document the specific clinical use case the tool was designed for. This matters because AI tools are regularly used off-label, applied to populations or clinical scenarios the developer never tested. Without a formal disclosure of intended use, there is no baseline against which to evaluate whether a tool is being used appropriately.⏎⏎Second, the target population disclosure. This is, in our view, the most important single element of the model card requirement. A tool trained on data from large urban academic medical centers may perform poorly in rural or safety-net settings. A tool validated on adult patients should not be silently applied to pediatric populations. These are not hypothetical risks. They are documented failure modes in the published literature on clinical AI. See, e.g., Adamson and Smith (2018), JAMA Dermatology, documenting differential performance of AI diagnostic tools across skin tones.⏎⏎Third, the known risks and limitations disclosure. Developers are in the best position to know where their tools fail. They have access to internal validation data, to error analyses, to user feedback. Requiring them to disclose known risks is not an unreasonable burden. It is basic product accountability. The analogy to drug labeling is not perfect, but it is not far off.⏎⏎Fourth, training data characteristics. This is where the Obermeyer findings are most directly relevant. If a developer cannot or will not disclose basic information about the dataset used to train a clinical AI tool, that is itself a signal worth attending to. The DSI requirement creates a floor, not a ceiling.⏎⏎Fifth, external validation results. Internal validation is necessary but not sufficient. A tool can perform well on the data it was trained on and fail on independent datasets. External validation results, or the acknowledgment that external validation has not been performed, give clinicians and health systems meaningful information for procurement and deployment decisions.⏎⏎HEP, LLC | ONC Deregulatory Actions | Page 8⏎⏎We recognize that some developers find these requirements burdensome, particularly smaller companies with limited regulatory staff. That concern is legitimate. But the answer to that burden is not to eliminate the requirement. The answer is to provide better implementation guidance, clearer templates, and possibly phased compliance timelines for smaller developers. ONC has done this before with other certification criteria, and it works.⏎⏎If ONC is concerned that the DSI criterion as currently written is more prescriptive than necessary, we are open to a conversation about refinements. There may be room to streamline the format of required disclosures, to clarify which AI tools fall within scope, or to align the model card structure more closely with emerging industry standards like the model card specification developed by Google Research (Mitchell et al., 2019) or the nutrition label frameworks being developed by NIST as part of its AI Risk Management Framework (NIST AI RMF 1.0, January 2023). Those are productive conversations. Removing the requirement altogether is not a refinement. It is an abdication.⏎⏎HEP, LLC | ONC Deregulatory Actions | Page 9⏎⏎ON THE QUESTION OF MARKET SOLUTIONS⏎⏎The proposed rule's preamble suggests, at several points, that market forces and voluntary disclosure frameworks may be sufficient to ensure appropriate AI transparency without mandatory certification requirements. We respectfully disagree, and we want to explain why.⏎⏎Health IT markets are not well-functioning markets in the classical sense. Purchasing decisions for EHR platforms and embedded clinical AI tools are made by health system procurement teams and IT departments, not by the clinicians who use the tools or the patients whose care is affected by them. The information asymmetry between developers and end users is substantial. Developers know their training data, their validation results, their known failure modes. Clinicians and patients generally do not. Voluntary disclosure frameworks address this asymmetry only when developers choose to participate, which is to say they do not reliably address it at all.⏎⏎The track record of voluntary transparency in health IT is not encouraging. Before ONC's information blocking rules took effect under 45 CFR Part 171, voluntary commitments to data sharing were widespread and largely ineffective. The mandatory framework changed behavior in ways that voluntary commitments had not. There is no reason to expect AI transparency to work differently.⏎⏎HEP, LLC | ONC Deregulatory Actions | Page 10⏎⏎We have heard from some of our developer members that they would prefer to handle AI transparency through contractual arrangements with health systems rather than through certification requirements. We understand the preference. Contractual flexibility is real, and some sophisticated health systems are in fact negotiating meaningful AI transparency provisions into their vendor contracts. But most health systems are not. Most community hospitals, federally qualified health centers, and small practices do not have the negotiating leverage or the internal expertise to demand and evaluate detailed model cards from their EHR vendors. The certification requirement is what protects those organizations and their patients.⏎⏎There is also a level-playing-field argument here that we think deserves more attention than it has received. Developers who invest in rigorous validation and honest disclosure of limitations are at a competitive disadvantage relative to developers who do not, in the absence of a mandatory floor. Removing the DSI criterion does not just reduce burden on responsible developers. It removes the requirement from everyone, including developers who would prefer not to disclose training data characteristics or known risks. That is not a market outcome that benefits patients or clinicians.⏎⏎HEP, LLC | ONC Deregulatory Actions | Page 11⏎⏎RELATIONSHIP TO BROADER AI ACCOUNTABILITY FRAMEWORKS⏎⏎ONC's DSI criterion does not exist in isolation. It is part of a broader emerging framework for AI accountability in healthcare that includes FDA's oversight of AI-enabled medical devices, the FTC's enforcement authority over deceptive AI practices, and state-level AI transparency legislation that is moving forward in several jurisdictions including Vermont, Colorado, and California. Removing the DSI criterion at this moment, when the rest of that framework is still being built out, creates a gap that is unlikely to be filled quickly.⏎⏎We are also watching the Executive Order on AI, issued in October 2023, and the subsequent OMB guidance on AI governance in federal programs, issued in March 2024. Those documents reflect a federal policy direction that is broadly consistent with the DSI criterion's requirements. Transparency, documentation of training data, disclosure of known limitations, external validation - these are themes that run through the federal AI governance framework that the current administration has been building. Walking back the DSI criterion sends a contradictory signal.⏎⏎We understand that the current administration has a different posture on AI regulation than the previous one, and we are not naive about the political context of this rulemaking. But patient safety and clinical accountability are not partisan issues. The clinician in Montpelier who didn't know her AI tool was trained on commercially insured patients is not a policy abstraction. Neither are the patients she sees.⏎⏎HEP, LLC | ONC Deregulatory Actions | Page 12⏎⏎A NOTE ON THE CERTIFICATION BURDEN ARGUMENT⏎⏎We want to say one more thing about the certification burden argument, because we think it is being applied selectively in ways that do not serve the field well.⏎⏎ONC's Certification Program has real problems. Timelines are too long. The ONC-ACB backlog is a genuine obstacle for smaller developers. The cost of certification is prohibitive for some early-stage companies. We have documented these problems in previous comments and in conversations with ONC staff, and we will continue to do so. These are legitimate issues that deserve serious regulatory attention.⏎⏎But the solution to those problems is to fix the certification process, not to remove requirements that serve genuine clinical and safety functions. The DSI criterion is not where the certification timeline problem lives. Removing it saves developers three to four weeks of documentation work, at most, while creating an indefinite gap in AI accountability in clinical decision support. That is not a good trade.⏎⏎If ONC wants to reduce certification burden in ways that do not compromise patient safety, we would point to several areas that would produce more significant relief:⏎⏎1. Streamlining the ONC-ACB review process and publishing binding timelines for certification decisions.⏎2. Creating a formal expedited review pathway for updates to previously certified products that do not involve changes to certified functionality.⏎3. Providing standardized templates and implementation guides for documentation-heavy requirements, including the DSI model card, to reduce the interpretive burden on developers.⏎4. Establishing a small-developer assistance program, similar to what FDA has done with its Q-Submission program for medical device developers, to help early-stage companies navigate certification requirements without dedicated regulatory staff.⏎5. Revisiting the scope of certain interoperability testing requirements that generate significant time and cost without proportionate benefit.⏎⏎These are the areas where meaningful burden reduction is available. The DSI criterion is not.⏎⏎HEP, LLC | ONC Deregulatory Actions | Page 13⏎⏎We also want to note, briefly, that the framing of this rulemaking as "deregulatory" deserves some scrutiny. Removing requirements that protect patients from undisclosed algorithmic risk is not deregulation in the sense of removing unnecessary red tape. It is removing accountability infrastructure that the field spent several years building and that clinical users and patient advocates supported. That framing matters for how the rule will be received by clinicians, patient organizations, and the research community, and we would encourage ONC to think carefully about it.⏎⏎RECOMMENDATIONS⏎⏎To summarize our position:⏎⏎1. Retain the DSI certification criterion at 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11) in full, including the requirements for disclosure of intended use, target population, known risks, training data characteristics, and external validation results.⏎⏎2. If ONC concludes that modifications to the criterion are appropriate, pursue refinements through a separate rulemaking or guidance process that allows for full public comment, rather than eliminating the requirement in this rule.⏎⏎3. Provide standardized model card templates and implementation guidance to reduce the documentation burden on smaller developers without removing the underlying requirement.⏎⏎4. Engage directly with clinician and patient stakeholder groups on the question of AI transparency requirements before finalizing any changes to the DSI criterion, as those groups were among the strongest advocates for the requirement when it was adopted and have a direct stake in its preservation.⏎⏎5. Address legitimate certification burden concerns through process improvements at the ONC-ACB level, expedited review pathways, and small-developer assistance programs, rather than through removal of safety-related certification criteria.⏎⏎HEP, LLC | ONC Deregulatory Actions | Page 14⏎⏎We appreciate ONC's work on this rulemaking and the genuine effort to reduce unnecessary burden on health IT developers. We share that goal. Our members are health IT developers, and we have seen firsthand how certification costs and timelines can prevent good technology from reaching patients. That problem is real and it deserves real solutions.⏎⏎The DSI criterion is not the problem. Removing it would leave clinicians without reliable access to information they need to evaluate AI tools, leave patients without the accountability infrastructure that supports informed care, and send a signal to the AI development community that transparency in clinical decision support is negotiable. We do not think that is the signal ONC intends to send, and we urge the agency to reconsider this aspect of the proposal.⏎⏎HEP, LLC | ONC Deregulatory Actions | Page 15⏎⏎Questions and correspondence regarding this comment may be directed to:⏎⏎Carol Thompson⏎Director of Government Relations⏎HEP, LLC⏎carol.thompson@hep-llc.com⏎(802) 555-0147⏎⏎We are available to discuss any aspect of these comments with ONC staff and welcome the opportunity to provide additional information or technical input as the agency works toward a final rule.⏎⏎One thing I want to flag before closing, because it came up in our member calls and I am not sure it has gotten enough attention in the public comment process: the DSI criterion's external validation requirement has a secondary benefit that is easy to overlook. When developers are required to disclose whether external validation has been performed, and if so on what populations and with what results, it creates a de facto incentive structure for actually conducting that validation. Before the HTI-1 rule, several of our member developers told us they had been relying entirely on internal holdout set performance metrics because there was no external requirement to do otherwise. The certification requirement changed the calculation. That is a real safety benefit that would disappear if the criterion is removed, and it does not show up in any estimate of certification burden savings because it is a behavioral effect, not a paperwork effect.⏎⏎We recognize that ONC cannot always account for second-order behavioral effects in regulatory impact analyses, and we are not criticizing the agency for that. We are flagging it because we think it is genuinely important and because the developers who told us about it were being candid in a way they might not be in a formal comment. The requirement to disclose whether you have done external validation is, in practice, a meaningful prod to actually do it. That is worth preserving.♔♔2026-01-11T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-11T00:00:00Z♔2025-12-12T00:00:00Z♔2026-02-10T00:00:00Z♔11♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Retain the current Decision Support Interventions (DSI) certification criterion requiring AI model cards and transparency disclosures (intended use, target population, known risks, training data characteristics, external validation) to ensure patient safety, informed clinical decision-making, and accountability in AI-assisted healthcare.♔Hospital and health system procurement teams need transparent AI model information to make evidence-based decisions about which tools to adopt and how to implement them safely in their local contexts.♔industry♔high♔concerned♔Vermont♔director of government relations♔55♔Last spring, I spent three weeks in back-to-back calls with two of our member developers who were on the verge of shelving a promising care-coordination tool — not because the technology wasn't ready, but because the certification timeline had stretched to nearly fourteen months and their runway simply couldn't absorb it. CMS-2025-0050-110103♔CMS-2025-0050♔Linda Lewis♔Dental Standards Institute♔♔♔♔Removing the AI transparency disclosure ("model card") certification requirement from the ONC Health IT Certification Program would eliminate the only standardized mechanism ensuring clinicians can access critical information about the training da...♔Dental Standards Institute⏎Comments on ASTP/ONC Deregulatory Actions To Unleash Prosperity: Health Data, Technology, and Interoperability⏎Submitted via Regulations.gov⏎⏎Dental Standards Institute | ASTP/ONC Deregulatory Docket | Page 1⏎⏎---⏎⏎INTRODUCTION AND ORGANIZATIONAL STANDING⏎⏎The Dental Standards Institute (DSI) is a Georgia-based professional and consumer advocacy organization focused on health data integrity, care coordination standards, and patient safety across dental and medical care settings. Our network includes community health workers, clinical staff, and patient advocacy volunteers operating primarily in underserved urban and rural communities throughout the Southeast. We write to offer comments on the proposed deregulatory rule published by the Assistant Secretary for Technology Policy and the Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology (ASTP/ONC), with particular attention to the proposal's treatment of Decision Support Interventions (DSI) certification criteria and the transparency disclosures currently required of certified health IT systems that incorporate algorithmic or AI-assisted clinical tools.⏎⏎DSI does not oppose regulatory reform as a general matter. Administrative burden in health IT is real, and we have seen providers in our network spend significant staff time on compliance activities that do not clearly benefit patients. But the specific certification criteria governing AI transparency disclosures are different from most administrative requirements, and the proposal to remove or materially weaken them deserves careful scrutiny before any final action is taken.⏎⏎---⏎⏎THE CURRENT DSI CERTIFICATION REQUIREMENT AND WHAT IT ACTUALLY DOES⏎⏎Under the existing certification framework established in the ONC Health IT Certification Program, health IT systems that incorporate Decision Support Interventions must, as a condition of certification, disclose certain information about any AI or predictive model embedded in or connected to those interventions. The required disclosures include intended use, the target patient population for which the model was developed, known risks or limitations, characteristics of the training data used to build the model, and whether the model has undergone external validation (45 CFR 170.315(b)(11), as interpreted through ONC's 2024 HTI-1 Final Rule, 89 Fed. Reg. 1192 (Jan. 9, 2024)). These disclosures are commonly referred to as "model cards," a term borrowed from the machine learning literature where the concept originated (Mitchell et al., 2019, "Model Cards for Model Reporting," Proceedings of the ACM Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency).⏎⏎What the current requirement actually does, in practical terms, is create a floor. A clinician using an AI-assisted tool to evaluate, say, a patient's risk of sepsis or likelihood of readmission can at minimum ask: who was this model built on, and was it ever validated on patients like mine? Without the model card requirement, that question may have no accessible answer. The vendor may not volunteer the information, and the clinician may not know to ask. That is the gap the certification criterion was designed to close.⏎⏎The proposed rule suggests that removing or revising this requirement would reduce burden on developers and give the market flexibility to establish its own transparency norms. We understand the argument. But the market for health IT tools has not historically converged on transparency without regulatory pressure, and there is limited evidence that voluntary disclosure frameworks in this space produce complete or standardized information (Sendak et al., 2020, "Real-World Integration of a Sepsis Deep Learning Technology into Clinical Practice," JAMIA Open, 3(2): 326-334). What tends to happen instead is that disclosures appear in vendor documentation that clinical staff rarely read, or in marketing materials that describe model performance under optimal conditions rather than in the actual patient population being served.⏎⏎Dental Standards Institute | ASTP/ONC Deregulatory Docket | Page 2⏎⏎---⏎⏎WHY THIS MATTERS IN COMMUNITIES WE SERVE⏎⏎Our concern here is not abstract. In Vine City, a neighborhood on Atlanta's west side, DSI's community health team has worked with several safety-net clinics that rely on certified EHR systems incorporating risk-stratification tools. These tools flag patients for care management outreach, and the clinicians using them have, in our observation, limited understanding of how the underlying models work or who they were built on. When we've asked clinic staff whether they know whether the model was validated on a low-income, predominantly Black urban population, the honest answer is usually no. They trust the certification mark to mean something. They assume that if ONC certified it, someone looked under the hood.⏎⏎That assumption is partly what the DSI certification criterion was designed to justify. If the requirement is removed, the certification mark no longer implies anything about AI transparency, and the clinicians who rely on that mark as a proxy for trustworthiness are left without a signal they didn't know they were depending on.⏎⏎This matters for patient safety in a direct and documented way. Research on algorithmic bias in clinical decision support has found that models trained primarily on data from well-resourced health systems can perform substantially worse when deployed in underserved settings with different patient demographics and documentation practices (Obermeyer et al., 2019, "Dissecting racial bias in an algorithm used to manage the health of populations," Science, 366(6464): 447-453). The Obermeyer study found that a widely used commercial algorithm systematically underestimated illness severity in Black patients because it used health care costs as a proxy for health needs, and Black patients historically incur lower costs for the same level of illness due to systemic barriers to access. A clinician who knew the model's training data characteristics might have questioned its outputs. A clinician who had no access to that information had no basis for questioning anything.⏎⏎We are not suggesting that every AI tool embedded in certified health IT is biased in this way. But the whole point of the model card requirement is that we should not have to assume either way. The disclosure requirement makes bias detectable. Removing it makes bias invisible.⏎⏎---⏎⏎ON THE ARGUMENT THAT MARKET FORCES WILL FILL THE GAP⏎⏎The proposed rule's reasoning appears to lean, at least in part, on an expectation that competitive market pressure and industry self-regulation will produce adequate transparency norms without a certification requirement. We are genuinely uncertain how to evaluate that claim in the health IT context, because the market for clinical AI tools does not operate the way markets are supposed to in standard economic models. The buyers (health systems, clinics) often lack the technical capacity to evaluate model documentation even when it exists. The users (clinicians) are several steps removed from purchasing decisions. And the patients whose outcomes depend on model performance have no direct market role at all.⏎⏎There is also a practical problem with the timing of this proposal. The HTI-1 Final Rule, which established the current DSI certification requirements, was finalized in January 2024 and the compliance timeline for developers has been rolling out through 2024 and into 2025. Many developers are in the process of building model card infrastructure right now. Removing the requirement before that infrastructure is fully deployed means that the investment already made in compliance will have been wasted, while developers who held back waiting to see whether the rule would survive can claim they were right to wait. That is not a dynamic that rewards good-faith compliance.⏎⏎Dental Standards Institute | ASTP/ONC Deregulatory Docket | Page 3⏎⏎---⏎⏎SPECIFIC RECOMMENDATION: RETAIN THE DSI TRANSPARENCY CERTIFICATION CRITERION IN FULL⏎⏎DSI urges ASTP/ONC to retain the existing Decision Support Interventions certification criterion requiring model cards and AI transparency disclosures without modification. If the agency has received evidence that specific elements of the disclosure requirement are technically infeasible or produce information of no clinical utility, we would welcome a more targeted revision process that preserves the core disclosure categories while addressing identified implementation problems. But a wholesale removal of the requirement, or a shift to voluntary disclosure, is not a targeted revision. It is the elimination of the only regulatory mechanism currently ensuring that clinical AI tools used in certified health IT come with accessible, standardized accountability information.⏎⏎We recognize that this recommendation asks developers to maintain a compliance obligation that some have characterized as burdensome. We take that characterization seriously, and we would support ONC working directly with developers to reduce the cost of producing compliant disclosures, for example by developing standardized templates or machine-readable formats that reduce duplicative documentation work. The National Academy of Medicine's 2019 report on AI in health care specifically called for standardized disclosure frameworks as a precondition for safe clinical deployment (National Academy of Medicine, 2019, "Artificial Intelligence in Health Care: The Hope, the Hype, the Promise, the Peril"). Standardization reduces burden; elimination of the requirement removes the incentive to standardize at all.⏎⏎There is also a patient trust dimension here that does not get enough attention in regulatory cost-benefit analyses. Patients in the communities DSI serves are already skeptical of health systems that have historically underserved them. When they learn that AI tools are being used to make clinical recommendations about their care, the first question is usually some version of: was this built for someone like me? The model card requirement does not fully answer that question, but it at least creates the infrastructure for the question to be answerable. Removing it sends a message that the answer doesn't matter, and that is not a message any of us should be comfortable sending right now.⏎⏎---⏎⏎CLOSING OBSERVATIONS⏎⏎We want to be clear that DSI's comments here are limited to the DSI certification criterion and the AI transparency disclosure question. We are not in a position to comment comprehensively on every element of the proposed rule, and we do not purport to do so. Other organizations with different expertise are better positioned to address the information blocking exception revisions and other provisions of the rule.⏎⏎What we can say with confidence, based on our work in Atlanta-area safety-net clinics and with patients who have experienced firsthand the consequences of opaque health IT systems, is that the model card requirement is doing real work. It is not a paperwork exercise. It is the mechanism by which the question "who was this model built on" becomes answerable in a clinical setting. The Federal Register preamble to the HTI-1 Final Rule described the DSI transparency requirements as necessary to "support the safe and effective use of AI and clinical decision support" and to "enable clinicians to appropriately apply or disregard" AI-generated recommendations (89 Fed. Reg. 1192, 1286 (Jan. 9, 2024)). That reasoning has not become less valid since January 2024.⏎⏎The timeline for public comment on this proposed rule is tight given the scope of what is being proposed, and DSI notes that several of the policy questions raised by removing AI transparency requirements would benefit from additional public input specifically from patient communities and safety-net providers before any final action is taken. We would respectfully request that ASTP/ONC consider extending the comment period or convening a public listening session focused specifically on the DSI certification criterion and its implications for patient safety in underserved communities.⏎⏎REFERENCES⏎⏎Mitchell, M., Wu, S., Zaldivar, A., et al. The CAP represents more than 18,000 board-certified pathologists and is the world's largest organization of pathologists, serving as a resource-rich laboratory accreditation and proficiency testing organization. Pathologists are physicians who direct clinical laboratories, interpret diagnostic results, and increasingly interface with AI-assisted decision support tools embedded directly into laboratory information systems and electronic health records. This comment focuses on one specific concern: the proposed removal or weakening of the Decision Support Interventions (DSI) certification criterion, particularly the transparency disclosure requirements commonly referred to as "model cards" under 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11).⏎⏎CAP Comments | ONC Deregulatory NPRM | Page 2⏎⏎WHY THE DSI TRANSPARENCY CRITERION MATTERS⏎⏎The CAP urges ASTP/ONC in the STRONGEST POSSIBLE TERMS to retain the DSI certification criterion requiring disclosure of AI model characteristics, intended use, target population, known risks, training data characteristics, and external validation status. We are genuinely worried that removing or substantially relaxing this requirement will create REAL, MEASURABLE patient safety risks that the proposed rule does not adequately address.⏎⏎Here is the core problem. Pathologists and other clinicians are being asked to rely on AI-driven decision support tools embedded in certified health IT systems. Under the existing framework codified at 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11) and further described in the ONC HTI-1 Final Rule (88 Fed. Reg. 23746, April 18, 2023), developers of certified DSI tools must disclose specific information about how those tools work, what populations they were trained on, and what their known limitations are. This is not a bureaucratic box-checking exercise. It is, frankly, the minimum information a clinician needs to decide whether an AI recommendation is appropriate for the patient in front of them.⏎⏎The CAP is aware that ONC has cited administrative burden as a rationale for revisiting these requirements. We understand that concern. But the burden argument, at least as applied to the model card disclosures, does not hold up to scrutiny when weighed against the patient safety implications. A 2023 study published in JAMA Network Open (Obermeyer et al., JAMA Netw Open. 2023;6(3):e233417) documented that algorithmic tools deployed without adequate transparency disclosures produced systematically biased outputs for Black patients in clinical risk stratification. The FDA's AI/ML-based Software as a Medical Device (SaMD) Action Plan, released January 2021, similarly identified transparency as a foundational safety control. These are not abstract concerns. They are documented failure modes.⏎⏎CAP Comments | ONC Deregulatory NPRM | Page 3⏎⏎WHAT THE CURRENT RULE REQUIRES AND WHY EACH ELEMENT IS NECESSARY⏎⏎The existing DSI criterion at 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11) requires certified health IT to provide, for each intervention, the following categories of information (as specified in the HTI-1 Final Rule, 88 Fed. Reg. 23799-23812):⏎⏎1. Intended use and scope of the DSI, including the clinical workflows it is designed to support.⏎2. The target patient population, including any known demographic or clinical subgroups for which the tool has NOT been validated.⏎3. Known risks, including documented error rates and conditions under which the tool performs poorly.⏎4. Training data characteristics, including the source, date range, and population demographics of data used to develop the model.⏎5. External validation status, meaning whether the tool has been independently tested on data from institutions other than those used in development.⏎⏎The CAP wants to be direct: each of these elements is necessary, and they are not interchangeable. A disclosure that lists intended use but omits training data characteristics tells a clinician almost nothing about whether the tool is appropriate for their patient population. A 2022 analysis in NPJ Digital Medicine (Wiens et al., NPJ Digit Med. 2022;5:89) found that fewer than 12% of published clinical AI studies reported sufficient information about training data demographics to allow external readers to assess generalizability. The DSI model card requirement was designed SPECIFICALLY to address this gap in the real-world deployment context, where published studies are often unavailable or inaccessible to the clinician at the point of care.⏎⏎The CAP has particular concern about the external validation requirement. Pathology AI tools, including image analysis algorithms used for cancer detection and grading, are notoriously sensitive to the characteristics of the imaging systems and staining protocols used at the training institution. A tool validated only at a large academic medical center with standardized slide preparation protocols may perform VERY differently at a community hospital using different equipment. See, e.g., Bejnordi et al., JAMA. 2017;318(22):2199-2210 (documenting performance variation in pathology AI across institutions). Without the external validation disclosure, a pathologist at that community hospital has no way of knowing that the algorithm's confidence scores may be unreliable in their setting.⏎⏎CAP Comments | ONC Deregulatory NPRM | Page 4⏎⏎THE DEREGULATORY ARGUMENT DOES NOT ACCOUNT FOR THE CLINICAL REALITY⏎⏎The proposed rule suggests, at least implicitly, that market forces and voluntary disclosure practices can substitute for mandatory certification requirements. The CAP respectfully but firmly disagrees with this framing. Voluntary disclosure in health IT has a poor track record. Prior to the ONC Health IT Certification Program's interoperability requirements under 45 CFR Part 170, health IT developers routinely cited proprietary concerns to avoid disclosing interface specifications, a practice that contributed directly to the fragmentation problems documented in the 21st Century Cures Act's information blocking provisions (see 85 Fed. Reg. 25642, May 1, 2020). There is no reason to believe AI transparency will fare better under a voluntary regime.⏎⏎The CAP also wants to note something that has not received enough attention in the public discussion of this rule. Pathologists who serve as laboratory directors are legally and professionally responsible for the accuracy of diagnostic results generated in their laboratories, including results generated or influenced by AI tools. Under CLIA regulations at 42 CFR 493.1445, the laboratory director is responsible for the overall operation and administration of the laboratory, including ensuring test performance. If an AI-assisted diagnostic tool produces an erroneous result and the laboratory director cannot demonstrate that they had access to sufficient information to evaluate that tool's fitness for use, the regulatory and liability exposure is SUBSTANTIAL. The DSI model card requirement is, from this perspective, not just a patient safety measure. It is also an essential component of the accountability framework that laboratory directors rely on to fulfill their CLIA obligations.⏎⏎We want to be honest that the CAP does not have a fully formed view on every aspect of the proposed rule. Some of the proposed modifications to information blocking exceptions, for example, involve trade-offs that require more analysis than we have been able to complete in the comment period. But on the DSI transparency question, the CAP's position is clear.⏎⏎CAP Comments | ONC Deregulatory NPRM | Page 5⏎⏎SPECIFIC RECOMMENDATIONS⏎⏎The CAP urges ASTP/ONC to take the following actions in the final rule:⏎⏎o Retain the DSI certification criterion at 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11) in its current form, without removing or substantially weakening the model card disclosure requirements for intended use, target population, known risks, training data characteristics, and external validation status.⏎⏎o If ONC determines that some modification is warranted to reduce burden on smaller developers, any such modification should be prospective and limited, for example by phasing in requirements for lower-risk DSIs while maintaining full requirements for DSIs used in high-stakes clinical decisions such as cancer diagnosis, drug dosing recommendations, or sepsis prediction. The Agency's own HTI-1 preamble acknowledged at 88 Fed. Reg. 23802 that the model card format would need iterative refinement. Removing the requirement before that refinement process has run its course seems premature.⏎⏎o The final rule should explicitly address the intersection of DSI transparency requirements and CLIA laboratory director accountability obligations. ONC and CMS have not, to the CAP's knowledge, jointly addressed how these frameworks interact, and the gap creates uncertainty for laboratory directors trying to assess AI tools deployed in their facilities.⏎⏎The CAP would be glad to provide additional technical input, including through participation in any workgroup or technical expert panel ONC convenes to refine the DSI certification standard.
