The organization's work spans state-level insurance oversight and public health data infrastructure coordination across multiple jurisdictions. Delaware's experience is instructive here. Last spring, a regional salmonella cluster saw seventeen cases go untracked for nearly three weeks because one county's electronic case reporting pathway had quietly lapsed. The state epidemiologist walked through that failure in some detail, and what became apparent is that the fragility was not the technology itself. It was the absence of enforceable standards that would have caught the lapse before it metastasized into a three-week gap. The parallel to AI transparency requirements is not incidental.⏎⏎When a clinical decision support tool operates inside a health system without any standardized disclosure about what population it was trained on, what its known failure modes are, or whether it has been externally validated, the health system is in roughly the same position as that county with the lapsed reporting pathway. Nobody knows the gap exists until something goes wrong.⏎⏎---⏎⏎THE SPECIFIC CONCERN: DSI MODEL CARD REQUIREMENTS⏎⏎The proposed rule would remove or make optional the certification criteria requiring health IT developers to document and disclose:⏎⏎    o  Intended use of the AI or clinical decision support tool⏎    o  Target population for which the model was designed and validated⏎    o  Known risks and limitations, including bias-related risks⏎    o  Training data characteristics⏎    o  Results of any external validation studies⏎⏎Progress Federal Solutions urges ONC to retain all of these criteria as mandatory certification requirements. The argument for removal appears to be administrative burden reduction. That framing deserves a direct response: the documentation these criteria require is not bureaucratic overhead. It is the minimum information a clinician or a state health agency needs to make an informed judgment about whether a given tool is appropriate for their patient population.⏎⏎Delaware's cancer registry team has communicated directly that without standardized transmission and data quality criteria, they would be rebuilding data-sharing agreements essentially from scratch with every major health system transition. The same logic applies here. Without standardized model card requirements, every hospital system, every state Medicaid agency, and every insurer conducting utilization review that relies on DSI tools will have to independently negotiate what disclosures they need from vendors. Some will have the leverage to get them. Many will not.⏎⏎---⏎⏎Progress Federal Solutions | DSI Certification Comments | ONC Deregulatory Rule | Page 2⏎⏎---⏎⏎WHY "MARKET PRESSURE" IS NOT A SUBSTITUTE⏎⏎There is an argument circulating in some industry comments to this rulemaking that market competition will naturally drive vendors toward transparency, so federal certification requirements are redundant. Progress Federal Solutions finds this argument genuinely unconvincing, and not for abstract reasons.⏎⏎State insurance commissioners see the downstream effects of health IT deployment decisions every time a coverage denial is appealed and the underlying utilization management tool's logic is opaque. When a tool was trained primarily on commercially insured, urban patient populations and is then deployed to assess care appropriateness for a rural Medicaid population, the errors are systematic. They are not random noise. They skew in predictable directions. And without a model card requirement, the insurer often has no way of knowing this at the time of procurement.⏎⏎The market does not self-correct for harms that are invisible at the point of sale. A hospital purchasing a clinical decision support tool in 2024 cannot easily determine, without mandatory disclosure, whether that tool was validated on a population that looks anything like their patient panel. The vendor has no structural incentive to volunteer unflattering information about training data gaps or known failure rates. This is precisely why certification criteria exist: to make certain baseline disclosures a condition of market participation, not a voluntary courtesy.⏎⏎Progress Federal Solutions is also skeptical of the argument that existing contractual and legal frameworks are sufficient. Contractual disclosure requirements vary wildly by institution size and negotiating leverage. A large academic medical center may be able to demand and receive detailed model documentation. A rural critical access hospital almost certainly cannot. The certification framework is the mechanism that levels that information asymmetry, and removing it does not reduce burden so much as it shifts the burden from vendors to the health systems and public health agencies that are least equipped to absorb it.⏎⏎---⏎⏎PATIENT SAFETY IS THE APPROPRIATE FRAME⏎⏎There is a tendency in deregulatory proceedings to treat administrative burden reduction as an unqualified good, and Progress Federal Solutions does not dispute that unnecessary administrative burden is a real problem worth addressing. But the DSI transparency criteria are not a good candidate for removal on burden-reduction grounds, for a straightforward reason: the information they require is information that directly affects whether a tool is used appropriately or not.⏎⏎Consider the specific case of an AI-assisted sepsis prediction tool deployed across a hospital network. If the tool was trained predominantly on data from one demographic group and has a materially higher false-negative rate for another group, a clinician who does not know this will calibrate their clinical judgment differently than one who does. A model card requirement makes that information available. Removing the certification criterion does not make the disparity go away. It makes the disparity invisible.⏎⏎Progress Federal Solutions works with state-level stakeholders who are trying to operationalize AI tools responsibly under significant resource constraints. What they consistently report is that the absence of standardized documentation creates enormous friction at the procurement and implementation stage. Paradoxically, mandatory model card requirements actually reduce administrative burden for these stakeholders because they create a common information baseline that does not have to be reconstructed from scratch for every vendor relationship.⏎⏎---⏎⏎Progress Federal Solutions | DSI Certification Comments | ONC Deregulatory Rule | Page 3⏎⏎---⏎⏎SPECIFIC RECOMMENDATIONS⏎⏎Progress Federal Solutions recommends the following:⏎⏎1.  Retain the DSI certification criterion requiring model cards as a mandatory condition of certification, with no opt-out pathway for developers.⏎⏎2.  If ONC determines that some streamlining of the model card format is appropriate to reduce documentation overhead, Progress Federal Solutions would support a standardized template approach, provided the substantive content requirements (intended use, target population, known risks, training data characteristics, external validation results) remain intact and non-negotiable.⏎⏎3.  ONC should clarify that model card disclosures must be updated when a developer makes material changes to the underlying model, including retraining on new data or modifications to the model architecture that could affect performance characteristics. The current language on this point is ambiguous enough that some vendors have interpreted it as requiring disclosure only at initial certification.⏎⏎4.  For tools deployed in populations that have historically been underrepresented in clinical AI training data, including rural populations, Medicaid beneficiaries, and patients with limited English proficiency, ONC should consider whether additional disclosure requirements are warranted beyond the baseline model card criteria. This is an area where the current framework may be insufficient even if retained as written.⏎⏎5.  ONC should require that model card information be made available not just to health IT developers and health systems at the point of procurement, but in a machine-readable format that state health agencies and public health departments can access through standard data exchange mechanisms.⏎⏎---⏎⏎A NOTE ON THE PUBLIC HEALTH REPORTING DIMENSION⏎⏎Progress Federal Solutions also wants to flag a concern that has received less attention in the public comment period than it deserves. The proposed rule touches on public health reporting certification criteria in ways that could have cascading effects on state electronic case reporting infrastructure.⏎⏎Delaware's experience with the salmonella cluster is not unique. Gaps in public health reporting data pipelines are common, they are often invisible until they cause harm, and they are extremely difficult to remediate after the fact because the data that was not reported is simply gone. There is no retroactive fix for a three-week gap in case surveillance data.⏎⏎If the certification criteria that govern electronic case reporting pathways are weakened or made optional, the likely result is not a uniform reduction in burden across all health systems. The likely result is a bifurcated landscape where well-resourced health systems maintain high-quality reporting because they have the infrastructure and staff to do it regardless of certification requirements, and under-resourced health systems let reporting quality degrade because they no longer have a certification incentive to maintain it. The public health agencies that depend on that data, including state epidemiologists and cancer registries, will absorb the consequences.⏎⏎Progress Federal Solutions does not think ONC has fully modeled the downstream public health costs of weakening these certification criteria. The administrative burden savings to developers are quantifiable and will appear in the regulatory impact analysis. The public health costs of degraded case reporting data are diffuse, delayed, and harder to attribute. That asymmetry in visibility should not be mistaken for an asymmetry in magnitude.⏎⏎---⏎⏎The organization recognizes that ONC faces genuine competing pressures in this rulemaking and that some of the certification criteria under review may warrant revision. Progress Federal Solutions is not arguing for the status quo across the board. But the DSI model card requirements are not a good place to look for burden reduction savings, because the cost of removing them will be borne primarily by patients, clinicians, and public health agencies rather than by the vendors who would benefit from the reduced documentation requirement. The Delaware cancer registry team, for one, has already said they would need to rebuild data-sharing frameworks from scratch under a less standardized regime, and that is not a theoretical concern. That is a concrete operational prediction from people who manage these systems day to day and have direct experience with what happens when certification requirements⏎⏎Progress Federal Solutions | DSI Certification Comments | ONC Deregulatory Rule | Page 4⏎⏎lose their teeth.⏎⏎For questions regarding this submission, contact:⏎Progress Federal Solutions⏎Office of the Commissioner⏎lnguyen@progressfederalsolutions.gov♔♔2026-01-20T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-20T00:00:00Z♔2025-12-12T00:00:00Z♔2026-02-10T00:00:00Z♔5♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Retain the current Decision Support Interventions (DSI) certification criterion requiring AI model cards and transparency disclosures (intended use, target population, known risks, training data characteristics, external validation) to ensure patient safety, informed clinical decision-making, and accountability in AI-assisted healthcare.♔Removing transparency requirements creates unacceptable patient safety risks when AI systems make or influence high-stakes clinical recommendations without disclosed performance data or known limitations.♔government♔high♔concerned♔Delaware♔state insurance commissioner♔40♔Last spring, I sat across from our state epidemiologist as she walked me through what a gap in electronic case reporting infrastructure had meant during a regional salmonella cluster — seventeen cases went untracked for nearly three weeks because one county's reporting pathway had quietly lapsed. CMS-2025-0050-110107♔CMS-2025-0050♔Margaret Wilson♔The Pharmacy Health Information Technology Collaborative♔♔♔♔Retaining the DSI certification criterion's AI transparency and model card disclosure requirements is essential for patient safety and public health research integrity, as removing or weakening them would eliminate the only standardized mechanism ...♔The Pharmacy Health Information Technology Collaborative⏎Comments Submitted to ASTP/ONC⏎Docket: ONC-2025-DEREGULATORY RFI⏎Submitted by: Margaret Wilson, MPH, Senior Research Scientist⏎The Pharmacy Health Information Technology Collaborative (PharmHITC)⏎Columbia, South Carolina⏎⏎pharmhitc-comments@pharmhitc.org⏎⏎June 2025⏎⏎The Pharmacy Health Information Technology Collaborative appreciates the opportunity to submit comments on the ASTP/ONC Deregulatory Actions To Unleash Prosperity: Health Data, Technology, and Interoperability proposed rule. PharmHITC is a multi-stakeholder collaborative of pharmacists, pharmacy benefit researchers, public health scientists, and health information technology specialists whose work depends, in a very practical sense, on the functioning of the interoperability infrastructure that the ONC Health IT Certification Program has spent the better part of a decade constructing. We support efforts to reduce genuine administrative burden. We are, however, deeply concerned that certain deregulatory proposals in this rulemaking would dismantle certification requirements whose value has been demonstrated empirically and whose removal would create patient safety risks that are not adequately addressed elsewhere in the regulatory framework.⏎⏎The Collaborative's comments focus primarily on the proposed removal or revision of the Decision Support Interventions (DSI) certification criterion, specifically the provisions that currently require health IT developers to disclose model cards and related transparency documentation for AI-enabled clinical decision support functions. This is the question we are best positioned to address, and it is the one we believe carries the most consequential implications for patient safety and research integrity in pharmacy and public health settings.⏎⏎Before getting into the substance of the DSI criterion, some context about why PharmHITC is particularly situated to comment on this. Our researchers use certified EHR data feeds and pharmacy dispensing data to conduct population-level surveillance of medication safety signals, opioid prescribing patterns, and drug-drug interaction rates. When the health IT systems generating that data change their underlying logic, whether through updated clinical decision support algorithms, formulary decision tools, or drug interaction flagging systems, those changes directly affect what we observe in the downstream data. A change in a drug interaction alert threshold that isn't disclosed to us can look, in our surveillance data, like a genuine shift in prescribing behavior. We have experienced this. Last spring, PharmHITC researchers spent approximately three weeks attempting to reconcile an anomaly in opioid co-prescribing data from a regional hospital network in South Carolina, only to eventually discover that the network's new health IT vendor had updated its CDS logic in a way that changed which alerts were firing and, consequently, which prescriptions were being flagged, modified, or delayed at the point of care. The vendor had no obligation to disclose this change in a standardized way. There was no model card. There was no documentation of what the underlying decision logic was, what patient population it had been validated on, or what the known failure modes were. We lost approximately six weeks of reliable surveillance data during what the South Carolina Department of Health and Environmental Control later characterized as a period of elevated overdose risk in the region.⏎⏎The point is that this is not a theoretical concern about AI governance philosophy. It is a concrete, measurable problem that PharmHITC researchers encountered in the field, and it is exactly the problem that the DSI model card and transparency disclosure requirements were designed to address.⏎⏎The current DSI certification criterion, as established in the 2024 HTI-1 final rule (89 FR 1192), requires that health IT developers seeking certification for AI-enabled decision support interventions provide documentation covering: the intervention's intended use, the target patient population, known risks and limitations, the characteristics of training data including source, date range, and any known demographic skews, and whether the intervention has undergone external validation. This is not an onerous list. It is roughly analogous to what any peer-reviewed clinical study would require before publication, and considerably less than what the FDA requires for a cleared medical device. The argument that this constitutes excessive regulatory burden is one PharmHITC finds difficult to accept at face value, particularly given that the alternative, deploying AI-driven clinical decision support without any standardized documentation of how it works or who it was built for, carries risks that fall not on the developer but on patients and on the clinicians and researchers who rely on the outputs.⏎⏎The proposed rule appears to suggest, or at least leaves open the possibility, that the DSI transparency requirements could be relaxed, eliminated, or made voluntary as part of a broader effort to reduce certification burden on health IT developers. PharmHITC's position is that this would be a serious mistake, and we want to explain in some detail why we hold that view.⏎⏎PharmHITC Comments | ASTP/ONC Deregulatory RFI | June 2025 | Page 3⏎⏎the current transparency requirements are grounded in a documented body of evidence about the behavior of AI-based clinical decision support tools in real-world settings. The literature here is not ambiguous. Obermeyer et al. (2019, Science, vol. 366, pp. 447-453) demonstrated that a widely deployed commercial algorithm used to allocate health resources systematically underestimated the health needs of Black patients due to features of its training data, and that this bias was not apparent from the algorithm's outputs alone. It required access to information about the training data and model structure to even identify the problem. That paper has been cited in excess of 2,000 times and is now essentially standard reading in any health informatics curriculum. Obermeyer's findings were about a resource allocation algorithm, but the same logic applies with equal or greater force to clinical decision support tools used in prescribing, diagnosis, and treatment selection.⏎⏎A 2022 study in the Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association (Gianfrancesco et al., JAMIA vol. 29 no. 8) documented similar patterns in CDS tools used in rheumatology, finding that algorithms trained predominantly on data from academic medical centers performed substantially worse when deployed in community health settings serving different patient populations. The study specifically called for standardized disclosure of training data characteristics as a mechanism for identifying these deployment mismatches before they caused harm. This is precisely what the HTI-1 DSI criterion requires.⏎⏎PharmHITC's own research is relevant here. In a 2023 analysis of pharmacy dispensing data from twelve hospital networks across the southeastern United States (Wilson et al., Pharmacy Practice, forthcoming), we found measurable variation in drug interaction alert rates that could not be explained by patient population differences alone. When we were able to obtain information about the CDS tools in use at each network, including in a few cases where vendors had voluntarily provided documentation resembling what the DSI criterion now requires, we found that differences in training data recency and alert threshold calibration explained a substantial portion of the variation. Networks using CDS tools trained on data from before 2018 showed systematically different alert patterns for certain opioid-benzodiazepine combinations than networks using more recently trained tools, even controlling for patient demographics and prescribing specialty mix. Without access to training data characteristics, we would have been unable to identify this source of variation and would likely have misattributed it to genuine differences in prescribing practice.⏎⏎The reason PharmHITC cares so much about the model card and transparency disclosure requirements is precisely because our research methodology depends on being able to distinguish between changes in clinical behavior and changes in the health IT systems that observe and respond to clinical behavior. These are genuinely different phenomena, and conflating them leads to incorrect conclusions with real public health consequences. If a hospital network's CDS tool is updated and begins firing more opioid alerts because the underlying algorithm has been recalibrated, that is not the same as physicians becoming more cautious prescribers, even though both would show up as a reduction in opioid dispensing in our surveillance data. The DSI transparency requirements give us at least a fighting chance of distinguishing between these scenarios.⏎⏎We want to be honest about something here: the current implementation of the DSI criterion is imperfect. The requirements were finalized relatively recently, and the standard for what constitutes an adequate model card disclosure is still being worked out in practice. Some health IT developers have submitted documentation that is technically compliant but not particularly informative, with vague descriptions of intended use and training data that don't give clinicians or researchers much to work with. PharmHITC recognizes that ONC will need to continue developing and refining the guidance on what good disclosure looks like. We have some specific thoughts on that later in these comments. But the appropriate response to imperfect implementation is to improve the implementation, not to eliminate the requirement.⏎⏎We also want to acknowledge that there is a real argument on the other side. Some health IT developers, particularly smaller vendors who lack large compliance teams, have found the DSI certification requirements burdensome, and there is legitimate concern that high compliance costs could push smaller vendors out of the certified health IT market, which would reduce competition and potentially harm the providers who rely on those vendors. PharmHITC takes this concern seriously. We don't think it justifies eliminating the transparency requirements, but it does suggest that ONC should think carefully about how to structure those requirements to minimize compliance burden while preserving their protective function. A tiered approach, where the depth of documentation required scales with the clinical risk level of the intervention, might be one way to address this. We would support ONC exploring that kind of calibration. What we would not support is a blanket elimination or voluntary conversion of requirements that are currently producing real, if imperfect, accountability.⏎⏎The proposed rule's broader deregulatory orientation also raises concerns for PharmHITC that go beyond the specific DSI criterion. The proposal to revise or relax certain information blocking exceptions touches on issues that are directly relevant to our surveillance research. The existing information blocking rules, as established in the 21st Century Cures Act (Pub. L. 114-255) and the ONC Information Blocking Rule (45 CFR Part 171), already contain exceptions that can be, and in our experience sometimes are, used by health IT vendors to justify refusals to export data in standardized formats. The exception for "technical infeasibility" in particular has been invoked in ways that PharmHITC researchers have found difficult to evaluate, because there is no standardized mechanism for a vendor to demonstrate that a refusal is genuinely technically infeasible rather than simply inconvenient or commercially disadvantageous.⏎⏎PharmHITC Comments | ASTP/ONC Deregulatory RFI | June 2025 | Page 4⏎⏎The experience described earlier in these comments, where a regional hospital network's vendor refused to export data in the standardized format our data-sharing agreement contemplated, illustrates this problem concretely. The vendor's position was that their new platform didn't support the export format specified in our agreement. Whether that was a genuine technical limitation or a decision not to build that capability is something we were never able to determine with confidence, because there was no regulatory mechanism requiring the vendor to demonstrate which it was. Our project coordinator eventually traveled to Columbia in person to negotiate, and we ultimately negotiated a partial workaround, but we still lost surveillance data during a period when that data mattered for public health decision-making.⏎⏎The proposed rule does not appear to directly address this specific problem, but PharmHITC is concerned that loosening information blocking exceptions could make situations like this more common, not less. If the regulatory framework gives vendors more flexibility to define what constitutes a legitimate reason for not sharing data in standardized formats, researchers and clinicians who depend on that data will have less recourse when vendors make decisions that prioritize their own operational convenience over interoperability.⏎⏎Returning to the DSI criterion specifically, PharmHITC wants to offer some thoughts on what the Collaborative believes adequate model card documentation should contain, because we think ONC's guidance on this has room to improve and we want to be constructive rather than simply opposing the deregulatory proposals.⏎⏎The current regulatory text at 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11) specifies that developers must provide transparency documentation for AI-enabled CDS. In PharmHITC's view, the following elements are the ones that most directly bear on patient safety and research usability:⏎⏎1. Intended use statement: This should be specific enough to allow a clinician to determine whether the intervention is being used in a context it was designed for. "General clinical decision support" is not an adequate intended use statement. Something like "alert generation for potential opioid-benzodiazepine co-prescribing in adult outpatient settings, excluding patients in hospice or palliative care" is closer to what is actually useful.⏎⏎2. Target population characteristics: This should include the demographic composition of the population the model was trained on, the care setting (inpatient vs. outpatient, academic vs. community), and any known subpopulations for which the model's performance has been separately validated or found to be degraded.⏎⏎3. Training data date range and source: This is particularly important for pharmacy-related CDS tools because drug interaction databases, formularies, and prescribing patterns change substantially over time. A tool trained on 2015-2018 data may perform very differently than one trained on 2020-2023 data, and clinicians and researchers need to know which they are working with.⏎⏎4. Known failure modes and limitations: This is where developers most commonly provide inadequate disclosure. "The model may not perform as expected in all clinical contexts" is not informative. Developers should be required to disclose specific known conditions under which the model's performance is degraded, including patient subgroups, comorbidity combinations, or data quality conditions that are known to affect output reliability.⏎⏎5. External validation status: Has the intervention been evaluated by an entity independent of the developer? If so, what were the results? If not, that should be disclosed explicitly. PharmHITC researchers have found that a surprisingly high proportion of deployed CDS tools have never been externally validated, which is information that clinicians and researchers would almost certainly want to know.⏎⏎These elements are not unreasonably burdensome to document. Developers who have built their models responsibly should already have most of this information internally. The burden the DSI criterion imposes is primarily the burden of organizing and disclosing information that good development practice would generate anyway. If a developer cannot provide this information, that is itself informative, and arguably a signal that the certification should not be granted.⏎⏎There is a version of the argument for deregulation here that PharmHITC finds genuinely worth engaging with: the idea that requiring this disclosure through the certification program is not the right mechanism, and that market forces or liability rules or clinical governance requirements could achieve the same goal with less regulatory overhead. We have thought about this argument. We don't find it persuasive in the current environment, for a few reasons.⏎⏎Market forces work reasonably well when buyers have good information and can make meaningful choices. In health IT, neither condition is reliably met. Hospital systems and pharmacy networks are often locked into vendor relationships through long contract terms and significant switching costs, and they frequently lack the technical expertise to evaluate AI model quality independently. The information asymmetry between health IT vendors and their customers is substantial, and the DSI transparency requirements are, among other things, a mechanism for partially correcting that asymmetry. Removing them in the name of market flexibility would likely result in less competition on quality, not more.⏎⏎Liability rules are similarly incomplete as a substitute. Tort liability for defective medical software is still an area of significant legal uncertainty (see, e.g., the discussion in Cohen and Mello, JAMA 2018, vol. 320 no. 21), and even where liability exists in principle, the practical ability of harmed patients to identify and prove that an AI-enabled CDS error caused their injury is limited precisely by the lack of the kind of documentation the DSI criterion requires. You cannot litigate against a black box. The transparency requirements are not just good public policy in the abstract; they are a precondition for any meaningful accountability mechanism, regulatory or otherwise.⏎⏎Clinical governance requirements at the health system level are real and in many organizations are becoming more robust. PharmHITC is aware that organizations like the American Health Information Management Association and the American Medical Informatics Association have published AI governance frameworks that address some of these issues (AHIMA, 2022; AMIA, 2023). But these frameworks are voluntary, their adoption is uneven, and they do not create the kind of standardized, publicly accessible documentation that the DSI certification criterion requires. A health system that has robust internal AI governance processes may know quite a lot about the CDS tools it deploys, but that information is not accessible to researchers, patients, or the public unless there is a regulatory mechanism requiring its disclosure. The DSI criterion is that mechanism.⏎⏎PharmHITC Comments | ASTP/ONC Deregulatory RFI | June 2025 | Page 5⏎⏎One thing PharmHITC wants to say clearly is that we do not think every aspect of the current health IT certification program is well-designed or appropriately calibrated. The program has real administrative burdens that fall unevenly on different types of developers, and the pace of certification review has at times been slow enough to create genuine barriers to deploying beneficial innovations. We would welcome a rulemaking that addressed those problems. The DSI transparency requirements are not the source of those problems, and removing them would not meaningfully address them.⏎⏎The certification program's overhead costs are driven primarily by the testing and certification process itself, not by documentation requirements. A developer who has built a well-characterized AI model can produce the DSI disclosures in a few days. The meaningful costs are in the testing infrastructure, the authorized testing laboratory fees, and the ongoing surveillance and reporting obligations. If ONC wants to reduce burden on small developers, those are the areas where calibration would actually help. Eliminating transparency disclosures would reduce paperwork marginally while creating patient safety risks that are likely to generate far larger costs downstream, both in terms of adverse outcomes and in terms of the regulatory response those outcomes would eventually prompt.⏎⏎PharmHITC is also aware that there are proposals in this rulemaking or in adjacent discussions to shift some certification requirements to a voluntary or attestation-based model. We have significant concerns about this approach as applied to the DSI transparency requirements. Attestation-based compliance, where developers self-certify that they have met certain standards without independent verification, has a mixed track record in health IT. The history of meaningful use attestation under the Medicare and Medicaid EHR Incentive Programs included a substantial number of cases where providers attested to capabilities their systems did not actually have (see OIG Report OEI-01-11-00571, "CMS Oversight of EHR Incentive Programs," 2014). There is no reason to expect that vendor attestation for AI model cards would be more reliable than provider attestation for EHR functionality, and the consequences of inaccurate attestation in this context are potentially quite serious.⏎⏎The question of external validation deserves somewhat more attention than it typically receives in these discussions. The current DSI criterion requires disclosure of whether external validation has been conducted, but it does not require that external validation actually occur before certification. PharmHITC believes this is a gap worth addressing. For CDS tools that are intended to influence prescribing decisions for high-risk medications, opioids, anticoagulants, chemotherapy agents, and the like, the case for requiring at least some form of independent performance evaluation before certification seems strong. We recognize this is a more expansive requirement than what the current rule contains, and we are not asking ONC to adopt it in this rulemaking. But we want to note that the deregulatory direction of the current proposal moves away from this goal rather than toward it, and that concerns us.⏎⏎There is a specific empirical claim in some of the arguments for relaxing the DSI requirements that PharmHITC wants to address directly. The claim is roughly that the market for health AI is evolving rapidly, that regulatory requirements impose lag times that prevent timely deployment of beneficial tools, and that the costs of delayed deployment (patients who don't benefit from a useful CDS tool) outweigh the costs of inadequate transparency. This is a legitimate empirical question, and PharmHITC doesn't dismiss it out of hand. But the evidence that has been cited in support of this claim is generally thin, and the evidence on the other side is more robust.⏎⏎The documented cases of AI-based CDS tools causing harm or perpetuating bias are numerous and well-documented in the peer-reviewed literature. The documented cases of beneficial CDS tools failing to reach patients because of the model card requirement specifically are, to PharmHITC's knowledge, essentially nonexistent. The DSI transparency requirements were finalized in January 2024 (89 FR 1192). They have been in effect for a relatively short time. The claim that they are creating meaningful barriers to beneficial AI deployment is not well-supported by evidence at this point, and the precautionary logic cuts strongly in the direction of maintaining them while more evidence accumulates.⏎⏎We should also address the argument that the DSI requirements are duplicative of other oversight mechanisms, particularly FDA oversight of software as a medical device (SaMD). This argument has some surface plausibility but does not hold up under scrutiny. FDA's SaMD framework, as articulated in the 2019 Digital Health Center of Excellence guidance and subsequent documents, covers a subset of AI-enabled clinical decision support tools, primarily those that are intended to diagnose, treat, or prevent specific conditions and that are not subject to the "clinical judgment" exception in the 21st Century Cures Act. A large proportion of the CDS tools deployed in certified EHR systems do not meet the threshold for FDA oversight, either because they fall within the clinical judgment exception or because they are characterized as administrative or informational rather than clinical. The DSI certification requirements apply to this broader category of tools that FDA does not reach. They are not duplicative; they are complementary.⏎⏎PharmHITC Comments | ASTP/ONC Deregulatory RFI | June 2025 | Page 6⏎⏎The Collaborative also wants to register concern about the broader signal this rulemaking sends to the health IT industry. The certification program has, over the past decade, created expectations and incentives that have shaped how health IT developers build and document their products. Health IT vendors have invested in compliance infrastructure, in documentation practices, and in some cases in the underlying research and validation work that good documentation requires. Removing or weakening certification requirements mid-stream creates uncertainty about whether those investments were warranted and, more importantly, whether future investments in quality and transparency will be rewarded or simply disadvantaged relative to competitors who skip them. The long-term effect of a deregulatory signal in this space may be to shift developer incentives away from the practices that produce safe, well-characterized AI tools, and that shift would be difficult to reverse once it occurs.⏎⏎This connects to something PharmHITC researchers observe in our own data collection work. Over the past two years, we have seen a modest but real improvement in the quality of documentation that health IT vendors provide when we request information about their CDS systems. We attribute at least part of this improvement to the anticipation and then implementation of the HTI-1 DSI requirements. Vendors who know they will need to produce model card documentation for certification purposes have, in our experience, begun building the internal processes to generate and maintain that documentation. This is exactly the kind of behavioral change that well-designed regulation is supposed to produce. Walking it back now would not just eliminate the requirement; it would likely reverse some of the behavioral change as well.⏎⏎The specific question of training data characteristics deserves a bit more development, because we think it is underappreciated in the policy discussion. For pharmacy-related CDS tools specifically, the temporal validity of training data is a first-order concern. Drug interaction databases are updated continuously. New generic entries change prescribing patterns. Opioid prescribing guidelines have changed dramatically since 2016, with the CDC Opioid Prescribing Guideline updates in 2016 and then again in 2022 (CDC, 2022, "Clinical Practice Guideline for Prescribing Opioids") creating substantial shifts in clinical practice that would show up in training data in complex ways. A CDS tool trained on pre-2016 prescribing data would have a very different picture of "normal" opioid prescribing than one trained on 2022-2024 data, and deploying the former in a contemporary clinical setting creates risks that are not visible without knowing the training data's date range.⏎⏎PharmHITC has encountered at least three instances in the past two years where discrepancies in our surveillance data were eventually traced to CDS tools using outdated training data. In one case, a hospital network's drug interaction alert system was flagging a combination that current clinical evidence does not consider high-risk, generating alert fatigue that likely reduced physician responsiveness to alerts for combinations that are genuinely dangerous. In another case, the reverse occurred: a tool trained before a significant update to opioid risk evidence was not flagging a combination that current guidelines identify as requiring monitoring. Both of these problems would have been identifiable earlier if the vendor had been required to disclose training data date ranges as part of a certification model card.⏎⏎There is one more argument for the DSI requirements that PharmHITC wants to make, and it is perhaps the most straightforward one. Patients who are treated using AI-enabled CDS tools have no way of knowing that this is happening, no way of knowing how those tools were built, and no way of evaluating whether the tools are appropriate for their specific situation. The model card and transparency disclosure requirements don't give patients direct access to that information in most cases, but they create a public record that researchers, journalists, policymakers, and patient advocates can access and use to identify problems and advocate for improvements. This is a form of accountability that operates through transparency rather than through direct patient control, and it is the kind of accountability mechanism that is particularly important for technologies that are complex, opaque, and consequential.⏎⏎The argument that this kind of transparency imposes proprietary information disclosure burdens on developers is one PharmHITC has heard and takes seriously. There is a real tension between transparency and the legitimate intellectual property interests of developers who have invested in building sophisticated AI tools. But the current DSI requirements do not require disclosure of model weights, training code, or other genuinely proprietary technical details. They require disclosure of the kind of information that any responsible developer should be able to provide without revealing competitively sensitive implementation details: what the tool is supposed to do, who it was built for, what its known limitations are, and whether it has been independently evaluated. This is not a high bar, and the proprietary information argument should not be allowed to function as a reason to avoid accountability entirely.⏎⏎PharmHITC Comments | ASTP/ONC Deregulatory RFI | June 2025 | Page 7⏎⏎To be direct: PharmHITC's recommendation is that ONC retain the DSI certification criterion in its current form, including the model card and transparency disclosure requirements. We recommend against any proposal that would make these requirements voluntary, move them to an attestation-based model without independent verification, or remove them as part of a broader certification streamlining effort. We believe the costs of retention are modest and the benefits are demonstrable, and that the deregulatory arguments advanced in support of removal are not well-grounded in the available evidence.⏎⏎If ONC determines that some revision to the DSI requirements is appropriate, PharmHITC would support revisions that improve the specificity and usefulness of required disclosures, that create clearer guidance on what constitutes adequate documentation for different categories of CDS tools, and that potentially create a tiered structure where more intensive documentation is required for higher-risk interventions. We would not support revisions that reduce the scope of required disclosure or that remove the certification program's role in verifying that disclosures have been made.⏎⏎We would also strongly encourage ONC to consider how the DSI transparency disclosures can be made more accessible and usable for researchers. Currently, even where model cards exist, accessing them requires navigating certification databases that are not well-designed for research use. PharmHITC spends considerable staff time locating and reconciling certification documentation for the health IT systems in our study networks, and a more streamlined, standardized access mechanism would significantly reduce that burden. This is an area where ONC could reduce real administrative burden without compromising the protective function of the requirements.⏎⏎The Collaborative is aware that some health IT developers have raised concerns about the competitive implications of required disclosures, arguing that requiring public documentation of training data characteristics and validation status could disadvantage developers who have invested in rigorous validation relative to those who have not, by making the absence of validation visible. PharmHITC's response to this concern is: yes, that is partly the point. A certification program that does not distinguish between tools with strong evidence bases and tools with weak ones is not functioning as a quality signal. If the transparency requirements create competitive pressure toward better validation practices, that is a feature, not a problem.⏎⏎One thing PharmHITC would add is that the current DSI requirements, whatever their limitations, have created a common vocabulary for discussing AI model characteristics in health IT contexts. Developers, purchasers, clinicians, and researchers now have a shared framework for asking about intended use, target populations, training data, and validation status. This common vocabulary is valuable in itself and would be degraded if the regulatory requirement that anchors it were removed. Building shared language for AI transparency in healthcare has taken years and has involved contributions from ONC, from professional societies, from academic researchers, and from forward-thinking vendors. It would be a mistake to let that infrastructure erode.⏎⏎We want to close by noting that PharmHITC's concerns here are not primarily about regulatory compliance as an end in itself. The Collaborative's researchers use health IT data to answer questions that matter for patient safety and public health. When the health IT systems generating that data change in ways that are not disclosed, our ability to answer those questions accurately is compromised. The DSI transparency requirements are, from our perspective, a mechanism for ensuring that the health IT infrastructure we depend on remains legible and interpretable. Removing them would make our work harder and, more importantly, would make it more likely that AI-enabled health IT systems produce harms that go undetected because no one outside the vendor organization has access to the information needed to identify them.⏎⏎PharmHITC Comments | ASTP/ONC Deregulatory RFI | June 2025 | Page 8⏎⏎There is a version of "reducing burden" that genuinely serves patients and the healthcare system, and PharmHITC supports that goal. Eliminating the DSI model card requirements is not that version. The burden being reduced is primarily the developer's documentation burden; the risk being shifted is primarily to patients and to the public health researchers who depend on reliable, interpretable health IT outputs.⏎⏎PharmHITC is available to discuss these comments further and would welcome the opportunity to provide technical input on any aspect of the DSI criterion revision process. Researchers at the Collaborative have direct experience with the challenges of working with AI-enabled CDS tools in pharmacy surveillance contexts and can contribute practical perspective on what documentation elements are most useful for downstream users of health IT data.⏎⏎pharmhitc-comments@pharmhitc.org⏎⏎Submitted June 2025⏎⏎PharmHITC Comments | ASTP/ONC Deregulatory RFI | June 2025 | Page 9⏎⏎One additional point that didn't fit cleanly into the above: the proposed rule's discussion of the DSI criterion does not, as far as PharmHITC can determine, include a quantitative regulatory impact analysis that separately estimates the costs and benefits of removing the model card requirements specifically, as distinct from the broader certification streamlining proposals. The regulatory impact analysis in the proposed rule addresses aggregate estimated burden reduction but does not appear to isolate the specific burden attributable to DSI transparency disclosures or to estimate the safety and research costs of removing them. PharmHITC would request that ONC provide a more granular analysis in the final rule, including an estimate of the number of certified CDS tools currently subject to the model card requirement, the average compliance cost per tool, and an analysis of what categories of patient safety risk the requirement is intended to mitigate. Without that analysis, it is difficult to evaluate whether the proposed deregulatory action represents a reasonable cost-benefit tradeoff or simply a reduction in visible compliance costs at the expense of less visible but potentially larger downstream costs.⏎⏎The Collaborative's request is not that ONC treat the DSI requirements as untouchable. It is that any revision be grounded in evidence about what the requirements actually cost and what they actually protect against, rather than in a general deregulatory orientation that treats all certification requirements as presumptively burdensome. The model card requirements were put in place for specific, documented reasons. CMS-2025-0050-110109♔CMS-2025-0050♔Melissa Jackson♔ZeroTrusted.ai LLC♔♔♔♔ONC should retain the Decision Support Interventions certification criterion's AI transparency requirements — including model cards, training data documentation, and external validation disclosures — because removing them would eliminate the prima...♔ZeroTrusted.ai LLC Comments | ONC-2025-Deregulatory RFI | Page 1⏎⏎My name is Melissa Jackson, and I am the Health IT Director at ZeroTrusted.ai LLC, a health information technology firm based in New Mexico that develops behavioral health and care coordination modules for federally qualified health centers and rural health clinics. I want to address one specific piece of this proposed rule: the proposal to remove or substantially revise the Decision Support Interventions certification criterion, particularly the provisions requiring AI model cards, transparency disclosures, and documentation of intended use, target population, known risks, training data characteristics, and external validation status. I am asking ONC to retain those requirements in their current form. I want to explain why, and I want to be direct about where I think the agency's analysis has gone wrong.⏎⏎ZeroTrusted.ai LLC Comments | ONC-2025-Deregulatory RFI | Page 2⏎⏎Let me start with what this looks like on the ground. Last spring, our team spent eleven months and just under $400,000 preparing a behavioral health decision support module for certification under the existing DSI criterion at 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11). Three federally qualified health centers in rural Doña Ana County, New Mexico were waiting on that module. I mean that literally: clinicians at La Clinica de Familia in Anthony, at Hidalgo Medical Services in Lordsburg, and at a third clinic I won't name because we're still in contract discussions, were refreshing their inboxes waiting to hear when they could deploy. By the time we cleared the certification process, two of those clinics had already cobbled together a workaround using a legacy clinical decision support tool that was not designed for behavioral health populations, had no documented training data provenance, and had been built for a predominantly urban, commercially insured patient population. The interoperability problems that created downstream took months to untangle and are honestly not fully resolved even now. I am not recounting that story to generate sympathy for our company. I am recounting it because it is the exact kind of situation that the DSI transparency requirements exist to prevent, and because the argument I keep hearing for removing those requirements, that they are burdensome and slow time-to-market, is an argument I have lived inside for eleven months, and I still do not think it is the right conclusion to draw.⏎⏎ZeroTrusted.ai LLC Comments | ONC-2025-Deregulatory RFI | Page 3⏎⏎The core question here is whether the transparency disclosures required under the current DSI criterion, what ONC has been calling model cards in informal guidance and what the Federal Register notice at 89 Fed. Reg. 1210 describes as algorithm transparency information, are actually creating the burden the agency seems to think they are, or whether that burden is coming from somewhere else. Our experience is that the documentation itself is not the hard part. The hard part is that many vendors, including some larger EHR companies, do not have clean answers to the questions the model card requires them to answer. They do not have clear documentation of what population the training data came from. They cannot always specify the external validation status of an AI-assisted intervention. They have not always conducted the kind of prospective performance testing that would let them characterize known risks for specific demographic subgroups. The model card requirement is burdensome in those cases not because the paperwork is excessive, but because the underlying work has not been done. Removing the requirement does not fix that problem. It just makes the problem invisible to the clinicians and patients who are relying on the tool.⏎⏎ZeroTrusted.ai LLC Comments | ONC-2025-Deregulatory RFI | Page 4⏎⏎I want to be precise about what I mean by "the underlying work has not been done," because I think this is where the policy debate gets muddled. There is a substantial and growing body of evidence that AI-assisted clinical decision support tools deployed without adequate transparency documentation have caused direct patient harm through algorithmic bias. The study published in Science in October 2019 by Obermeyer et al. found that a widely deployed commercial risk-stratification algorithm systematically underestimated the health needs of Black patients, in some analyses by a factor that meant a Black patient had to be measurably sicker than a white patient to receive the same level of care management attention (Obermeyer Z, Powers B, Vogeli C, Bhatt DL, Mullainathan S, Science 2019;366:447-453). That algorithm had been deployed across health systems serving millions of patients before the bias was characterized. The authors were explicit that the lack of transparency around training data and intended use made it nearly impossible for health systems to identify the problem from the outside. The DSI model card requirements exist, in part, to make that kind of discovery possible before deployment rather than years after.⏎⏎ZeroTrusted.ai LLC Comments | ONC-2025-Deregulatory RFI | Page 5⏎⏎A second study worth flagging here is the 2021 analysis by Wiens et al. published in Nature Medicine, which looked at the generalizability of clinical prediction models across different hospital settings and found that model performance degraded substantially when applied to patient populations that differed from the training cohort (Wiens J, et al., Nature Medicine 2019;25:187-188, with follow-on analysis in 2021). The external validation requirement in the current DSI criterion is a direct response to exactly this problem. If a vendor can certify a clinical decision support tool without disclosing whether the model has been externally validated on a population comparable to the intended deployment setting, a rural FQHC in southern New Mexico has no way of knowing whether the tool's performance claims are meaningful for their patients. Our patients in Doña Ana County are predominantly Hispanic, many are monolingual Spanish speakers, a significant portion are agricultural workers with occupational health patterns that differ from the populations that most commercial AI tools have been trained on. If the transparency disclosure goes away, we are back to trusting vendor marketing materials, which is not a standard of evidence I would apply to a pharmaceutical and I do not think it is a standard we should apply to AI-assisted clinical decision support either.⏎⏎ZeroTrusted.ai LLC Comments | ONC-2025-Deregulatory RFI | Page 6⏎⏎I recognize that the agency has genuine concerns about certification burden and I do not want to dismiss those concerns. The eleven months and $400,000 I mentioned earlier are real. The clinics that were waiting are real. The argument that the current certification timeline creates delays that harm patients is an argument I have made myself, in this docket and in previous ones. But there is a difference between fixing the certification process and removing the content requirements. The model card components, specifically the intended use statement, target population description, known risks documentation, training data characteristics, and external validation status, are not the pieces of the certification process that took eleven months. The timeline problems in our experience came from testing infrastructure issues, from ONC Authorized Certification Bodies (ONCACBs) that had inconsistent interpretation of the functional criteria, from the time required to coordinate test data environments across multiple health system partners. None of those problems are solved by removing the transparency disclosure requirements. What removing those requirements does is reduce the information available to clinicians and patients at the moment of deployment, which is precisely when that information matters most.⏎⏎ZeroTrusted.ai LLC Comments | ONC-2025-Deregulatory RFI | Page 7⏎⏎ZeroTrusted.ai LLC Comments | ONC-2025-Deregulatory RFI | Page 7 (continued)⏎⏎I also want to address the argument that market forces and existing FDA oversight are sufficient to address AI transparency in clinical decision support without ONC certification requirements. I have heard this argument made by several larger health IT vendors in public forums, and I understand why it is appealing from a competitive standpoint, but I think it is wrong for a specific reason that has to do with the structure of the health IT market in rural and underserved settings. The FDA's Software as a Medical Device framework, as described in the agency's 2021 action plan and subsequent guidance documents, does provide a regulatory pathway for certain AI-enabled clinical decision support tools. But not all DSI tools meet the threshold for FDA oversight under 21 CFR Part 820 or the De Novo pathway. Many of the tools that are deployed in FQHCs and rural health clinics, the kinds of tools that help a care coordinator in Chaparral, New Mexico decide which patients to call back this week, fall into a regulatory gap where FDA oversight is limited or absent and the ONC certification requirement is the primary mechanism ensuring any transparency at all. If ONC removes the model card requirements from the DSI criterion, those tools will be deployed with no required disclosure of training data, no required characterization of known risks, and no required external validation documentation. The market will not fill that gap. The FQHCs and rural clinics that are the last resort for uninsured and Medicaid patients in places like Doña Ana County do not have the procurement infrastructure to conduct independent AI audits. They rely on certification as a proxy for safety review, and that reliance is not naive, it is a rational response to resource constraints.⏎⏎ZeroTrusted.ai LLC Comments | ONC-2025-Deregulatory RFI | Page 8⏎⏎I want to flag one more piece of the regulatory record that I think deserves more attention in this discussion. The ONC 21st Century Cures Act Final Rule, published at 85 Fed. Reg. 25642 (May 1, 2020), included the DSI criterion specifically because the agency found that existing transparency mechanisms were insufficient to support informed clinical decision-making in the context of AI-assisted tools. The preamble to that rule contains a detailed analysis of public comments from clinical professional societies, patient advocacy organizations, and health equity researchers, all of whom raised concerns about the risks of deploying AI-assisted clinical decision support without documented transparency. The concerns raised in 2020 have not been resolved. The evidence base for algorithmic bias in clinical AI has, if anything, grown more robust since then. A 2023 systematic review by Obermeyer and colleagues in the New England Journal of Medicine Catalyst found that algorithmic bias in clinical prediction models was documented across a range of clinical domains including sepsis prediction, readmission risk, and mental health crisis assessment (NEJM Catalyst, 2023). The behavioral health domain, which is our specific area of work, is one where the documented risks of deploying undertested AI tools on vulnerable populations are among the highest in the literature. I am genuinely not sure how the agency's analysis concludes that this is the right moment to reduce transparency requirements in that space.⏎⏎ZeroTrusted.ai LLC Comments | ONC-2025-Deregulatory RFI | Page 9⏎⏎There is something else I want to say that is harder to fit into a regulatory argument, and I will try to say it plainly. The patients who use the FQHCs in Doña Ana County are not well-positioned to advocate for themselves in federal rulemaking processes. They are working in the fields outside of Las Cruces, they are waiting in a waiting room in Chaparral, they are not filing comments in this docket. The transparency requirements in the DSI criterion are one of the few places in the regulatory framework where their interests are explicitly protected in a way that does not depend on them knowing to ask. When a clinician at La Clinica de Familia uses an AI-assisted tool to help prioritize behavioral health referrals, the model card requirement means that clinician has access to documented information about whether the tool was validated on a population that looks anything like the patients in that room. Removing that requirement does not eliminate the AI tool. It eliminates the disclosure. The tool keeps running. The clinician just no longer has the information they need to calibrate their reliance on it. I keep coming back to that specific gap, between what the tool is doing and what the clinician knows about what the tool is doing, because it is not a theoretical problem. It is a problem we have watched play out in real clinical environments, and the consequences are not abstract.⏎⏎ZeroTrusted.ai LLC Comments | ONC-2025-Deregulatory RFI | Page 10⏎⏎From a practical implementation standpoint, I also want to push back on the framing that the model card components are technically difficult to produce for well-designed AI systems. For a properly engineered clinical decision support tool, the intended use statement, target population documentation, and training data characteristics should be artifacts that exist before the tool is deployed, not paperwork generated after the fact to satisfy a certification requirement. If a vendor cannot produce those documents without significant effort, that is informative. It means the tool was built without the kind of rigorous development process that a clinical environment requires. The certification requirement is, in that sense, not just a disclosure mechanism, it is a quality signal. In our experience, some certification bodies have accepted relatively high-level training data characterizations while others have required detailed demographic breakdowns of training cohort composition. That inconsistency creates compliance uncertainty that adds cost without necessarily adding safety value. A more specific, standardized model card format, something closer to what Google's Model Cards for Model Reporting paper proposed (Mitchell et al., 2019, ACM FAccT), would actually reduce compliance burden while improving the quality and comparability of the disclosures. That is a reform I would actively support. What I cannot support is using compliance inconsistency as a reason to eliminate the requirement entirely, because the solution to inconsistent enforcement is better enforcement standards, not no standards.⏎⏎ZeroTrusted.ai LLC Comments | ONC-2025-Deregulatory RFI | Page 12⏎⏎I also think it is worth noting that the direction of regulatory travel in comparable jurisdictions is toward more AI transparency in clinical settings, not less. The European Union's AI Act, which entered into force in August 2024, classifies AI systems used in clinical decision support as high-risk systems subject to mandatory transparency, conformity assessment, and post-market monitoring requirements. The National Institute of Standards and Technology's AI Risk Management Framework (NIST AI RMF 1.0, January 2023) explicitly recommends transparency documentation including training data provenance and performance characterization as core components of responsible AI deployment in high-stakes domains. The FDA's 2021 AI/ML-Based Software as a Medical Device Action Plan calls for predetermined change control plans and transparency to users as foundational principles. The ONC DSI model card requirement is, in this context, a relatively modest disclosure mechanism that aligns with the direction that serious regulatory frameworks are moving. Rolling it back at this moment, when the deployment of AI in clinical settings is accelerating and the evidence base for algorithmic harm is growing, seems to me like a significant miscalculation.⏎⏎ZeroTrusted.ai LLC Comments | ONC-2025-Deregulatory RFI | Page 13⏎⏎Our specific request to ONC is to retain the DSI certification criterion at 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11) with all current transparency disclosure components intact, including the requirements for intended use documentation, target population description, known risks characterization, training data characteristics disclosure, and external validation status reporting. If the agency is committed to reducing compliance burden in this area, we would support a rulemaking process focused specifically on standardizing the format and granularity requirements for those disclosures to reduce ONCACB interpretation variability, rather than eliminating the underlying requirements. We would also support exploring whether certain disclosure elements could be satisfied through a standardized machine-readable format that reduces manual documentation effort without reducing information availability to end users. What we cannot support is a regulatory change that removes transparency requirements from AI-assisted clinical decision support tools deployed in settings where vulnerable patient populations have no other mechanism to ensure that the tools being used on their behalf have been built and validated responsibly. The clinics in Doña Ana County are not edge cases. They are the primary care infrastructure for a region where the median household income in several zip codes is below $25,000 and where the health IT procurement budget for an entire FQHC system might be less than what a single large health system spends on a software audit. The model card requirement is not a luxury for those settings. CMS-2025-0050-110111♔CMS-2025-0050♔Nancy Martinez♔♔♔♔♔Removing or weakening the Decision Support Interventions (DSI) certification criterion's AI transparency requirements would disproportionately harm vulnerable patient populations—including elderly, immigrant, and minority patients—by allowing clin...♔Response to ASTP/ONC Deregulatory Actions To Unleash Prosperity: Health Data, Technology, and Interoperability⏎⏎My name is Nancy Martinez. I'm a licensed clinical social worker based in Broward County, Florida, and I've spent the better part of twenty-five years helping people navigate health systems that were, frankly, not designed with them in mind. I want to focus my comment on one thing that I think is getting lost in the broader conversation about burden reduction: the proposed removal or scaling back of the Decision Support Interventions (DSI) certification criterion, specifically the parts that require transparency about AI tools, what I've seen referred to in the literature as "model cards" or algorithmic transparency disclosures.⏎⏎Last spring, I spent three weeks helping a 67-year-old Haitian woman in Broward County try to access her own cardiac records. She had limited English, she was undocumented, and she needed those records so a new cardiologist could actually treat her. Two different hospital systems gave us the runaround. We eventually got what we needed, but only because I knew which pressure points to push. Most of my clients don't have that. I tell that story not because it's directly about AI, but because it tells you something about the baseline: the systems that are supposed to help vulnerable patients are already failing them in basic ways. Layering in algorithmic clinical decision support without any transparency requirements makes that worse, not better.⏎⏎Here's what actually concerns me about the direction this rule is taking. The DSI certification criterion, as it currently exists, requires health IT developers to disclose information about AI-driven decision support tools: the intended use of the algorithm, the target population it was trained on, known risks and limitations, characteristics of the training data, and whether the tool has been externally validated (85 Fed. Reg. 25642 (2020), as subsequently updated). These aren't bureaucratic requirements for their own sake. They exist because a clinician using an AI-assisted risk scoring tool in a predominantly white, middle-aged male training dataset is going to get different outputs when that tool is applied to a 67-year-old Haitian woman with a history of hypertension and limited English proficiency. If the clinician doesn't know that, they can't adjust.⏎⏎The research on this is not ambiguous. Obermeyer et al. (2019) published a paper in Science showing that a widely used commercial algorithm systematically underestimated the health needs of Black patients because it used healthcare cost as a proxy for health need, and Black patients had historically received less care, so the algorithm encoded that disparity as if it were a biological fact. The algorithm had been deployed at scale. Clinicians using it had no idea. That's exactly the kind of thing that model card requirements are supposed to catch. I'm genuinely not sure how we look at that evidence and conclude that the right policy response is to make transparency optional.⏎⏎The argument I keep hearing is that these disclosure requirements impose a burden on developers, slow down innovation, and add compliance costs without clear clinical benefit. I want to take that argument seriously because I do understand that paperwork burden is real. But I've also seen what happens when patients are on the receiving end of opaque systems. When I ask a hospital system why a particular patient was flagged as low-priority for care coordination, I'm increasingly getting answers that amount to "the system recommended it." That's not an answer. That's an abdication.⏎⏎There's also a patient safety dimension here that I think gets underweighted in the burden-reduction framing. The FDA has been grappling with how to regulate AI/ML-based Software as a Medical Device (SaMD) for several years now (FDA, Proposed Regulatory Framework for Modifications to AI/ML-Based SaMD, 2019). ONC's DSI certification criterion was one of the few existing mechanisms that required any transparency about AI tools deployed in clinical settings, even when those tools fell outside FDA's jurisdiction because they weren't classified as devices. If that criterion is weakened or made voluntary, there's a real regulatory gap. I'm not a lawyer, and I won't pretend to know exactly where the jurisdictional lines fall, but I know enough to be worried.⏎⏎What I keep coming back to is the population I serve. The people sitting in my office are not abstract policy subjects. They include:⏎⏎1. Elderly patients with multiple chronic conditions who are often flagged by risk stratification tools as "complex" or "high-cost," which can paradoxically lead to them being deprioritized for some interventions because the system predicts they won't respond well.⏎⏎2. Patients with mental health histories that appear in their records and may be feeding into AI tools in ways nobody has disclosed to them or their providers.⏎⏎3. Immigrants, documented and otherwise, whose care-seeking patterns are shaped by fear and whose limited interactions with the health system may cause algorithms trained on utilization data to systematically miscalibrate their risk.⏎⏎For all of these people, the question of whether the AI tool a clinician is using has been validated on a population anything like them is not an abstract policy question. It's the difference between getting the right care and getting the wrong care.⏎⏎I want to be honest about something I'm less certain about. I don't have a perfect read on whether the current DSI disclosure requirements as written are the most efficient way to achieve transparency. There may be ways to streamline the format of model card disclosures, reduce duplicative reporting, or create standardized templates that lower compliance costs without eliminating the substance of the disclosure. I would genuinely support a conversation about that. What I cannot support is treating "burden reduction" as a sufficient reason to remove transparency requirements altogether, or to make them purely voluntary in a market where voluntary compliance has historically been uneven at best (see, e.g., Sendak et al., 2020, discussing barriers to AI transparency in clinical practice, NPJ Digital Medicine).⏎⏎There's also something that bothers me about the framing of this rule as "unleashing prosperity." I understand that's political language and I'm not going to spend too much time on it. But prosperity for whom? Health IT developers who no longer have to document what their algorithms do? Or patients who need to be able to trust that the tools shaping their care are working as advertised? Those aren't the same constituency.⏎⏎The transparency requirements in the DSI criterion are not complicated to explain to a clinician or a patient once they exist. What they say, in plain terms, is: here's what this tool is supposed to do, here's who it was built on, here's where it might fail, here's whether anyone has tested it outside the developer's own data. That's information that any reasonable person would want before relying on a tool to make clinical decisions. The fact that producing that information requires effort from developers is not a reason to stop requiring it. It's a reason to require it.⏎⏎I also want to note something about the information blocking piece of this rule, though it's a little tangential to my main concern. The experience I described with my client last spring, the three weeks trying to get cardiac records from two hospital systems, was exactly the kind of situation that information blocking rules are supposed to address. I'm cautiously supportive of changes that make it harder for providers to obstruct legitimate access to patient records. But I'm watching carefully to make sure that loosening those rules doesn't create new pathways for sensitive data, mental health history, immigration-related diagnoses, to flow in ways patients haven't consented to. The two issues are connected. If we improve access to records while simultaneously removing the transparency requirements that would let patients and providers know how their data is being used by AI tools, we've solved one problem by creating another.⏎⏎My request to ASTP/ONC is direct: retain the DSI certification criterion as it applies to AI transparency disclosures. Keep the requirements for intended use documentation, target population disclosure, known risk disclosure, training data characteristics, and external validation status. If there are specific formatting or compliance elements that are genuinely burdensome without adding clinical value, I'm open to hearing that case made with specifics. But the substance of the requirement, the actual obligation to disclose what these tools are and how they work, should stay. Removing it doesn't reduce burden in any meaningful way for patients. It just removes information that clinicians need to do their jobs and that patients deserve to have.⏎⏎I've been doing this work long enough to have watched a lot of health IT initiatives come and go. The ones that end up hurting the people I work with are usually the ones where efficiency was prioritized over accountability in the early design decisions, and nobody noticed until a lot of patients had already been harmed. I'm not saying that's inevitable here. I'm saying the DSI transparency requirements are one of the mechanisms that exists to prevent it, and I'd like to see some explanation for why removing them is worth the risk before that decision is finalized.⏎⏎References⏎⏎Obermeyer, Z., Powers, B., Vogeli, C., & Mullainathan, S.
