CMS-2025-0050-110112♔CMS-2025-0050♔Richard Scott♔♔♔♔♔A North Dakota social worker urges ASTP/ONC to retain certification transparency requirements for AI-based Decision Support Interventions, arguing that removing these disclosure obligations would eliminate the only reliable mechanism ensuring clin...♔My experience with the woman in Minot last spring keeps coming back to me whenever I read about rules that are supposed to make health data more accessible. She needed her psychiatric records. The records existed. The systems holding them had no obligation to talk to each other in any coherent way, and nobody could tell her, or me, what algorithms or tools had been applied to her chart entries over the years, what those tools were designed to do, or whether they had been validated for use with patients in her demographic situation. Eleven days before a custody hearing. I'm not saying that AI decision support tools caused her situation directly. I genuinely don't know that. But I do know that when I asked questions about how certain clinical flags had ended up in her records, nobody could answer them, because there was no requirement that they be answered.⏎⏎That's the context from which I'm writing this comment. I work as a social worker in North Dakota, and I see the downstream consequences of clinical decisions made in systems that my clients can't see into and that I can't explain to them. The proposed deregulatory changes from ASTP/ONC concern me in a specific way, and I want to focus on one issue in particular: the certification requirements for what the agency calls Decision Support Interventions, or DSI. Specifically, I'm worried about any move to weaken or remove the current certification criteria that require transparency disclosures for AI and predictive tools used in clinical settings. I've read enough of the proposed rule to understand that the agency is considering removing or significantly revising these criteria on the grounds of reducing administrative burden for health IT developers. I understand the burden argument. But I think the agency is miscalculating where the real costs fall when transparency requirements disappear.⏎⏎The current DSI certification criterion, as I understand it, requires that health IT developers disclose information about how their AI-assisted decision support tools work: what the tool is intended to do, what population it was designed for, what its known risks are, what data it was trained on, and whether it's been externally validated. These are sometimes called "model cards" in the AI literature, though the clinical context adds layers of consequence that pure tech contexts don't always carry. The disclosure requirements exist because clinicians need to know whether a tool was validated for the population sitting in front of them. A predictive model trained predominantly on data from urban academic medical centers does not necessarily perform the same way in a rural North Dakota clinic, and that isn't a hypothetical concern (Obermeyer et al., 2019, documented systematic bias in a widely used commercial algorithm that was traced directly to training data that poorly represented Black patients). If the certification requirement disappears, there's no mechanism I can see that would force developers to surface this information at the point of procurement, let alone at the point of care.⏎⏎I want to be honest that I'm not a clinical informaticist. There are people with more technical expertise than I have who can speak to the specific coding requirements. What I can speak to is what happens when vulnerable people interact with health systems that lack accountability mechanisms. The woman in Minot didn't need her providers to be malicious. She just needed one clinical decision support tool, somewhere in her treatment history, to have been applied in a context it wasn't validated for, and for nobody to have any obligation to document that or disclose it. That's the gap the DSI transparency requirements are trying to close.⏎⏎The agency's stated rationale is that these requirements impose unnecessary burden on developers and that market forces and existing FDA oversight provide adequate protection. I'm skeptical of both parts of that argument. FDA oversight of AI-enabled clinical decision support is still developing (the FDA's Digital Health Center of Excellence has acknowledged publicly that its regulatory framework for AI/ML-based software as a medical device is not yet comprehensive for lower-risk clinical decision support tools), and there's no evidence I've seen that market competition is reliably surfacing the information that clinicians need to make informed decisions about which tools to use. Procurement decisions at hospital systems are not made by frontline clinicians in most cases. They're made by administrators who may have neither the time nor the technical background to demand transparency disclosures that aren't required.⏎⏎Removing the DSI certification criteria would also, I think, send the wrong signal at exactly the wrong moment. Health systems are adopting AI-assisted tools at a pace that most clinicians I've talked to find disorienting. A nurse I know at a regional hospital in western North Dakota told me last fall that three new decision support alerts had appeared in her system over a six-month period and that she had no idea who had put them there, what they were based on, or whether she was supposed to trust them. She said she'd started ignoring all of them because she couldn't tell the good ones from the bad ones. That's a patient safety problem, and it's a direct consequence of opacity in how these tools are deployed. The certification transparency requirements are not a perfect solution to that problem. But they are a floor. Removing the floor doesn't reduce the burden in any way that protects patients. It just moves the burden to clinicians who are already overwhelmed, and to patients who have no way to advocate for themselves.⏎⏎What I'd ask the agency to consider is this: if the goal is genuinely to reduce administrative friction while preserving safety, the right approach is to look at whether the specific data elements required in the disclosures can be streamlined, not to eliminate the disclosure obligation altogether. There may be ways to make the model card requirement less burdensome for small developers without gutting the requirement for larger vendors who have the resources to comply. That kind of targeted revision seems more defensible than a blanket removal that would apply equally to a small EHR vendor with limited capacity and a large commercial AI company with billions in revenue.⏎⏎I recognize that regulatory comments from individual social workers probably don't carry the same weight as comments from health IT industry groups with legal teams and lobbying budgets. I'm writing anyway because I think there are a lot of people like me, and like the woman in Minot, whose experiences don't show up in the cost-benefit analyses that agencies use to justify deregulatory decisions.⏎⏎References:⏎⏎Obermeyer, Z., Powers, B., Vogeli, C., & Mullainathan, S. The proposed rule, as published, would revise and in some cases eliminate certification criteria that have taken more than a decade to establish under the ONC Health IT Certification Program (see 45 CFR Part 170). The College believes that while administrative burden reduction is a legitimate regulatory goal, the specific mechanism proposed here -- relaxing technical certification standards and broadening information blocking exceptions -- carries risks for maternal health researchers and clinicians that ONC has not adequately weighed. We address two areas of particular concern in these comments: (1) the impact of reduced certification requirements on research data access and interoperability, and (2) whether revised information blocking exceptions will create new barriers for maternal mortality research.⏎⏎The College wishes to be direct: these are not abstract concerns. ACOG members conducting maternal mortality and morbidity research have experienced concrete, documented failures of interoperability even under the existing regulatory framework. The proposed loosening of that framework warrants serious scrutiny before implementation.⏎⏎⏎BACKGROUND: THE RESEARCH DATA ACCESS PROBLEM IN MATERNAL HEALTH⏎⏎Maternal mortality in the United States remains among the highest of any high-income country. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention's (CDC) Pregnancy Mortality Surveillance System reported 23.8 maternal deaths per 100,000 live births in 2020, compared to 5.8 in Canada and 4.2 in Australia (Trost et al., 2022, MMWR Morb Mortal Wkly Rep 71(8):279-285). The racial disparities are severe: Black women die at approximately three times the rate of white women (Hoyert, 2023, NCHS Data Brief No. 480). These are preventable deaths, and the research infrastructure needed to understand and address them depends directly on access to de-identified, standardized EHR data across hospital systems.⏎⏎That access has been, in practice, far more difficult to obtain than the regulatory framework suggests it should be. Section 4004 of the 21st Century Cures Act (Pub. L. 114-255) established information blocking prohibitions specifically because Congress recognized that health IT actors were impeding legitimate data access. ONC's 2020 final rule implementing these provisions (85 Fed. Reg. 25642, May 1, 2020) created eight exceptions to the information blocking prohibition, calibrated to permit certain practices that would otherwise appear to block data but that serve legitimate purposes. The College supported that framework at the time and continues to believe the underlying structure is sound.⏎⏎What concerns us is the direction of the proposed revisions. ONC is now proposing to expand the flexibility available to health IT developers and healthcare providers under those exceptions, and simultaneously to reduce the certification criteria that have served as a floor for interoperability capability. The College's research members have watched as vendor proprietary arrangements -- sometimes operating in gray areas of existing standards -- have made data export unreliable even where regulatory requirements ostensibly required it. Relaxing those requirements further is difficult to justify given the documented harms.⏎⏎⏎ACOG COMMENTS | ASTP/ONC DEREGULATORY ACTIONS | Page 2⏎⏎To be concrete: research conducted under ACOG's maternal mortality working group encountered, in the spring of 2024, a situation in which two Delaware hospital systems that had agreed to participate in a maternal mortality cohort study were unable to export de-identified EHR data in any format compatible with the study's data infrastructure. One system had recently transitioned to a vendor platform that, according to that vendor's representatives, was not configured to export in USCDI-compliant formats, and the vendor cited certification arrangements that it claimed were permissible under existing regulatory flexibility. The study, which had been designed over more than a year and was supported by a $340,000 NIH supplement, collapsed. The supplement was lost. No maternal mortality data was obtained from those systems.⏎⏎This is not an isolated anecdote. A 2021 study by Holmgren et al. (J Am Med Inform Assoc 28(8):1659-1667) found that despite ONC certification requirements, significant variation persisted in hospitals' actual ability to share patient data electronically, with smaller and rural hospitals showing substantially lower interoperability. A 2023 analysis by Everson et al. (Health Affairs 42(4):512-521) documented that vendor-level decisions about data export configuration were a primary driver of interoperability gaps, operating largely outside regulatory visibility. The pattern is consistent: certification requirements have been necessary but not sufficient to achieve reliable interoperability, and the response to that gap should be more accountability, not less.⏎⏎ONC's proposed rule does not adequately engage with this research literature. The preamble cites administrative burden on developers and providers as the primary justification for relaxing certification criteria (see proposed rule preamble, Section III), but does not quantify the research costs of interoperability failures, does not cite the Holmgren or Everson findings, and does not address how the proposed changes would affect the ability of maternal health researchers to access data that is, under the existing framework, supposed to be accessible.⏎⏎⏎THE CERTIFICATION CRITERIA REVISIONS AND THEIR RESEARCH IMPLICATIONS⏎⏎The proposed rule would eliminate or substantially revise several certification criteria under 45 CFR 170.315, including criteria related to data export, application programming interface (API) functionality, and clinical quality measurement. ACOG's concern centers particularly on the proposed changes to criteria that govern how certified health IT systems export data in standardized formats. The United States Core Data for Interoperability (USCDI), established under 45 CFR 170.213, has been the anchor for what data must be exportable in a standardized way. Reducing the certification requirements tied to USCDI export means that vendors who choose not to implement full USCDI-compliant export have fewer regulatory consequences for that choice.⏎⏎The College understands that ONC frames these changes as reducing prescriptive requirements in favor of flexibility and innovation (see proposed rule, Section III.A). We understand the argument. Prescriptive certification criteria can lock in technical approaches that become outdated, and there is a legitimate concern that overly rigid standards slow adoption of new interoperability modalities. ACOG is not opposed to flexibility in principle. But the history here matters. The current certification criteria were not created arbitrarily; they were created because market forces alone did not produce interoperability. Vendors had commercial incentives to maintain proprietary data formats that locked in customers (see Adler-Milstein & Pfeifer, 2017, Health Affairs 36(12):2165-2173, documenting vendor lock-in as a structural feature of the EHR market). Certification requirements were the mechanism through which Congress and ONC attempted to counteract those incentives.⏎⏎If ONC reduces those requirements without a clear account of what will now enforce interoperability in their place, the College believes the reasonable expectation is that interoperability will regress in some market segments. Research applications are particularly vulnerable because they lack the commercial leverage that large clinical systems have when negotiating with vendors. A large hospital network can negotiate data access terms with a vendor from a position of market power. A research team at an academic medical center cannot. The certification framework was, among other things, a regulatory substitute for that missing market power. Removing it without replacement leaves research data access exposed.⏎⏎ONC should, at minimum, conduct and publish a regulatory impact analysis that specifically quantifies the expected effect of the proposed certification criteria changes on research data access. The College is not aware that the proposed rule includes such an analysis. The standard required under Executive Order 12866 for significant regulatory actions includes assessment of costs to affected parties, and research institutions and the patients whose outcomes they study are affected parties whose costs deserve accounting.⏎⏎⏎ACOG COMMENTS | ASTP/ONC DEREGULATORY ACTIONS | Page 3⏎⏎THE INFORMATION BLOCKING EXCEPTION REVISIONS⏎⏎The second area of concern is the proposed revision to information blocking exceptions under 45 CFR 171.200 et seq. The existing exception framework was carefully constructed to permit data withholding only in defined circumstances, with the burden on the actor claiming the exception to demonstrate that the defined conditions were met. The College supported this structure when the 2020 rule was finalized because it placed accountability where it belonged: on the party withholding data.⏎⏎The proposed revisions would broaden several exceptions, including the Licensing Exception and the Fees Exception, in ways that the College believes could make it easier for health IT developers to decline data sharing requests from researchers by characterizing those refusals as permissible under an expanded exception. We want to be careful here because the specific regulatory text requires close parsing, and the College acknowledges that some of the proposed revisions may be narrower in practice than they appear on first reading. But the directional concern is real. If the Licensing Exception is broadened to allow vendors greater latitude in conditioning data access on proprietary licensing arrangements, the practical effect for a research team attempting to obtain de-identified EHR data from a hospital system using a vendor that prefers not to share data is that the vendor has more regulatory cover for refusal.⏎⏎The 2020 information blocking rule was explicit that the prohibition applied to "any practice that is likely to interfere with, prevent, or materially discourage access, exchange, or use of electronic health information" (45 CFR 171.103). The exceptions were meant to be narrow carve-outs, not broad permissions. ONC's own guidance materials, including the April 2023 Information Blocking FAQs published on the ONC website, emphasized that actors claiming exceptions bear the burden of demonstrating that all conditions of the exception are satisfied. If the proposed revisions effectively widen the exceptions without strengthening the conditions or the enforcement mechanisms, the prohibition loses force.⏎⏎Enforcement is also a structural problem that the proposed rule does not address. The Office of Inspector General (OIG) received authority to investigate and penalize information blocking under the Cures Act, and OIG published its final rule on information blocking penalties in June 2023 (88 Fed. Reg. 40788). But as of the date of this comment, OIG enforcement actions against health IT developers for information blocking remain limited in number. A 2024 analysis by the Office of the Assistant Secretary for Planning and Evaluation (ASPE) noted that reporting of information blocking complaints to ONC had increased substantially since 2021, with developer-related complaints comprising a significant share of the total (ASPE Issue Brief HP-2024-12). If complaints are increasing and enforcement remains limited, the answer is not to broaden the exceptions available to developers. The answer is to strengthen enforcement. The proposed rule moves in the opposite direction.⏎⏎⏎RESEARCH METHODOLOGY AND THE STANDARDIZATION QUESTION⏎⏎There is a methodological point that the College wants to make clearly, because it is sometimes lost in policy discussions that focus on clinical interoperability rather than research applications. Maternal mortality research -- and more broadly, reproductive health outcomes research -- depends on the ability to aggregate data across multiple hospital systems and link it to vital records, birth certificate data, and other administrative sources. That aggregation is only possible when the underlying data is in standardized formats. A dataset exported from one hospital system in a proprietary format and a dataset from another system in a different proprietary format cannot be linked without substantial manual processing, which introduces error, delays publication, and increases cost.⏎⏎The USCDI standard and the certification criteria tied to it were designed precisely to address this problem. Researchers at institutions including the University of Pennsylvania, Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, and the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health have built maternal mortality and morbidity research programs that depend on USCDI-compliant data exports from participating hospital systems (see, for example, Leonard et al., 2019, Obstet Gynecol 134(1):35-44; Howell et al., 2021, Am J Obstet Gynecol 224(4):369-375). If certification requirements tied to USCDI export are relaxed and vendors begin offering non-compliant or partially compliant configurations, the data aggregation that these research programs depend on becomes unreliable.⏎⏎The College is also concerned about the downstream effects on quality measurement. Several of the certification criteria proposed for revision or elimination relate to clinical quality measure (CQM) reporting functionality (see 45 CFR 170.315(c)(1)-(c)(4)). CQM data is used not only for regulatory reporting but as a research data source for studies of clinical practice variation. The Joint Commission's Perinatal Care measure set, for example, draws on CQM data reported from certified health IT systems. If the certification requirements supporting CQM reporting are weakened, the integrity of that data as a research source is compromised. ONC should explain specifically how it expects CQM data quality to be maintained under the proposed framework.⏎⏎⏎ACOG COMMENTS | ASTP/ONC DEREGULATORY ACTIONS | Page 4⏎⏎EQUITY CONSIDERATIONS⏎⏎The College wants to raise an equity concern that is not adequately addressed in the proposed rule's preamble. The populations most affected by maternal mortality and morbidity disparities -- Black women, Indigenous women, women in rural areas, women in lower-income communities -- are disproportionately served by smaller hospital systems, Federally Qualified Health Centers (FQHCs), and critical access hospitals. These institutions are also the ones least likely to have the market leverage to negotiate interoperability terms with vendors, and least likely to have the internal technical capacity to implement interoperability workarounds when vendor platforms are non-compliant.⏎⏎A 2022 analysis by Adler-Milstein et al. (Health Affairs 41(7):1031-1039) found that hospitals serving predominantly Black and Hispanic patients had lower rates of interoperability engagement than hospitals serving predominantly white patients, even after controlling for hospital size and ownership. The certification requirements that ONC is now proposing to relax have been among the few regulatory tools available to require that vendors serving these institutions meet the same technical standards as vendors serving large academic medical centers. Relaxing those requirements without targeted protections for high-disparity settings is likely to worsen existing interoperability gaps along racial and geographic lines.⏎⏎ACOG recommends that ONC conduct and publish an equity-focused analysis of the proposed rule's expected effects on interoperability in high-disparity settings before finalizing any changes. This analysis should include projected effects on data availability for maternal mortality surveillance in states with high Black maternal mortality rates, including Mississippi, Louisiana, Georgia, and Alabama, where CDC Pregnancy Mortality Surveillance data consistently shows the largest racial disparities (Hoyert, 2023, supra). The proposed rule does not appear to include this analysis, and the College believes its absence is a significant gap.⏎⏎⏎THE ADMINISTRATIVE BURDEN ARGUMENT⏎⏎The College takes the administrative burden concern seriously. ACOG members who are health IT developers or who work in clinical informatics have reported that some certification requirements are genuinely burdensome and that the burden does not always produce commensurate clinical benefit. The College is not arguing that every current certification criterion should be preserved unchanged. Some revision may be appropriate.⏎⏎What the College is arguing is that ONC has not provided adequate evidence that the specific criteria proposed for elimination or revision are the ones where the burden-to-benefit ratio justifies removal. The preamble cites general stakeholder feedback about burden but does not present a systematic analysis mapping specific criteria to specific burden costs and specific benefits. Without that analysis, the proposed revisions look less like a careful calibration and more like a broad deregulatory action where the regulatory justification has been assembled after the policy direction was chosen. That is a concern under the Administrative Procedure Act's requirement that agency action be supported by reasoned decision-making (see Motor Vehicle Manufacturers Ass'n v. State Farm Mutual Auto. Ins. Co., 463 U.S. 29 (1983), which remains the standard for arbitrary and capricious review).⏎⏎The College recommends that ONC publish, as part of any final rule, a criterion-by-criterion analysis documenting the specific burden evidence supporting removal or revision of each affected criterion, the specific interoperability or research data access benefits that the criterion currently provides, and the regulatory or market mechanism that ONC expects will maintain those benefits after the criterion is removed or revised. This is not an unreasonable ask. It is basic regulatory hygiene for a rule affecting infrastructure that researchers, clinicians, and patients depend on.⏎⏎⏎ACOG COMMENTS | ASTP/ONC DEREGULATORY ACTIONS | Page 5⏎⏎SPECIFIC RECOMMENDATIONS⏎⏎The College offers the following recommendations for ONC's consideration in finalizing this rule. These are not exhaustive but reflect the areas of greatest concern identified in the preceding analysis.⏎⏎First, ONC should preserve, without revision, the certification criteria under 45 CFR 170.315 that directly support USCDI-compliant data export. If ONC believes that specific export criteria are outdated or technically redundant, it should identify those criteria specifically and explain why they are redundant, rather than broadly relaxing export requirements. The current proposal does not provide that specificity.⏎⏎Second, ONC should not broaden the Licensing Exception or the Fees Exception under 45 CFR 171 in ways that give health IT developers greater latitude to condition research data access on proprietary licensing arrangements. If ONC believes that the current exception conditions are too narrow in ways that create genuine problems for legitimate business arrangements, it should identify specific fact patterns where the current conditions are inadequate and propose targeted revisions, rather than broad expansions.⏎⏎Third, ONC should commission and publish an equity analysis examining the expected effects of the proposed rule on interoperability in high-disparity hospital settings before finalizing. This analysis should be informed by existing literature on the relationship between hospital demographics and interoperability capacity, including the Adler-Milstein et al. (2022) findings cited above.⏎⏎Fourth, ONC should engage with the research community specifically -- including maternal health researchers, health disparities researchers, and clinical informatics researchers at academic medical centers -- before finalizing changes to certification criteria that affect research data access. The existing stakeholder engagement process appears to have been weighted toward health IT developers and large clinical systems, whose interests in burden reduction do not always align with the research community's interests in standardized, reliable data access.⏎⏎Fifth, ONC should coordinate with OIG to assess whether the information blocking enforcement framework is adequate before expanding the exceptions available to developers. If enforcement is not keeping pace with complaints, the appropriate response is to strengthen enforcement, not to reduce the scope of the prohibition.⏎⏎⏎CONCLUSION⏎⏎The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists does not oppose deregulatory action as a matter of principle. The College has supported targeted reforms to health IT certification and information blocking rules where those reforms were supported by evidence and did not compromise the interoperability infrastructure that maternal health research and clinical practice depend on. This proposed rule does not meet that standard.⏎⏎The interoperability gains achieved since the HITECH Act and the 21st Century Cures Act implementation have been real, if incomplete. The gaps that remain -- documented in the Holmgren, Everson, and Adler-Milstein studies cited above, and experienced directly by ACOG researchers attempting to access EHR data for maternal mortality studies -- reflect the difficulty of achieving interoperability in a market where vendors have commercial incentives against it. The certification framework and information blocking prohibition have been the primary regulatory tools for counteracting those incentives. Relaxing them without a rigorous, evidence-based account of what will take their place puts at risk research infrastructure that is directly connected to the ability of the United States to understand and reduce maternal mortality.⏎⏎The College requests that ONC extend the comment period for this rule by sixty days to allow additional stakeholder engagement with the research and clinical communities most affected by the proposed changes. The current comment period has been insufficient for detailed technical review of the proposed certification criteria revisions by research institutions that lack dedicated regulatory affairs staff. ACOG also requests the opportunity to participate in any technical expert panels or listening sessions that ONC convenes in connection with this rulemaking.⏎⏎ACOG will continue to monitor this rulemaking and reserves the right to supplement these comments as additional information becomes available. Correspondence regarding these comments may be directed to the ACOG Policy Office at the address listed above, or by email to⏎⏎[email protected]⏎⏎---⏎⏎James Jones⏎Postdoctoral Fellow, Research Division⏎The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists⏎409 12th Street SW, Washington, DC 20024⏎⏎Note from JJ before forwarding: I'm sending this up now -- the submission deadline is end of business and I want to make sure the policy office has it before noon. CMS-2025-0050-110115♔CMS-2025-0050♔Steven Allen♔Ainsley Advisory Group♔♔♔♔The ONC's Decision Support Interventions certification criterion, specifically its AI model card and transparency disclosure requirements under 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11), must be preserved because clinicians cannot make informed decisions about AI-gen...♔Ainsley Advisory Group | ONC-0955-P | Page 1⏎⏎---⏎⏎COMMENT OF AINSLEY ADVISORY GROUP ON THE ASTP/ONC DEREGULATORY ACTIONS RULEMAKING⏎⏎Submitted to the Docket: ONC-0955-P⏎⏎---⏎⏎Last spring, I spent eleven weeks trying to get a certification decision on a clinical decision support module that our team had already put through internal validation. Eleven weeks. The vendor had documentation ready, the clinical evidence was solid, and the intended use case was narrow enough that the safety profile was genuinely straightforward. We lost the contract. A regional hospital network in the Mountain West couldn't hold the procurement window open past week eight, and by week eleven the vendor had pivoted to a buyer in Germany who was operating under a regulatory framework that, whatever its other faults, could actually move. I've been in compliance long enough to recognize when process has become untethered from the purpose it was supposed to serve. That delay was not safety. It was not rigor. It was a queue.⏎⏎So I want to be clear that I am not writing this as someone who loves regulation for its own sake. I understand the burden argument. I've lived it. When ASTP/ONC talks about reducing administrative friction in the Health IT Certification Program, I know exactly what they're describing, and in a lot of places they are right to push back on requirements that have metastasized into checkbox exercises that nobody actually uses to make decisions.⏎⏎But.⏎⏎THE DECISION SUPPORT INTERVENTIONS CRITERION IS NOT THAT⏎⏎What I cannot support, and what I think this rulemaking gets badly wrong, is the apparent willingness to revisit or weaken the Decision Support Interventions (DSI) certification criterion, specifically the provisions requiring AI model cards and transparency disclosures. The criterion as it currently exists, codified at 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11), asks developers to document the intended use of a clinical AI tool, the target population it was validated on, known risks and limitations, training data characteristics, and whether external validation has been conducted. These are not bureaucratic formalities. They are the minimum a clinician needs to know before acting on a recommendation generated by a system they did not build and cannot inspect.⏎⏎ONC's own 2024 Health Data, Technology, and Interoperability final rule (89 FR 1192) went through a serious public process to establish that transparency framework. The research basis for it is not obscure. Obermeyer et al., published in Science in 2019, documented how a widely deployed commercial algorithm systematically underestimated illness severity in Black patients because the training data used health care costs as a proxy for health needs. The algorithm was being used in care management decisions affecting millions of patients. Nobody at the point of care knew the training data had that characteristic. That's the exact problem model card disclosure is designed to prevent.⏎⏎I keep coming back to the question of what a clinician is supposed to do without this information. If a DSI tool generates a sepsis alert or a medication dosage recommendation, and the clinician has no documented basis for understanding whether that model was trained on a population that looks like the patient in front of them, what exactly is the informed part of informed clinical decision-making? The answer is: nothing. The clinician is just trusting a black box. FDA has grappled with this in its guidance on Software as a Medical Device (SaMD), particularly in the 2021 action plan for AI/ML-based SaMD, which explicitly calls out the need for transparency as a precondition for safe deployment. ONC's DSI criterion is the certification-side complement to that safety logic.⏎⏎THE TRANSPARENCY REQUIREMENTS THAT ACTUALLY MATTER⏎⏎Let me be specific about what the current criterion requires, because I think some of the deregulatory framing conflates genuinely redundant paperwork with disclosures that have direct clinical relevance.⏎⏎Under 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11) as implemented, a developer seeking certification for a DSI tool must provide:⏎⏎1. A description of the intervention's intended use, including the clinical workflow context in which it is designed to operate.⏎⏎2. The characteristics of the population on which the model was trained, including relevant demographic and clinical variables.⏎⏎3. Known risks, including identified failure modes and populations where performance has been shown to degrade.⏎⏎4. Training data provenance, at minimum whether the data was derived from a single institution or multi-site, and the approximate time period.⏎⏎5. External validation status, including whether the model has been tested on data from institutions other than the one where it was developed.⏎⏎These five categories are not equivalent in terms of burden. I'll grant that item 4 can get complicated when a developer is using federated learning or proprietary data sources, and there may be room for standardized summary formats that reduce the documentation overhead without eliminating the disclosure. The HL7 FHIR-based model card format being piloted through the ONC Tech Lab is one approach worth considering (see ONC Tech Lab, Draft FHIR Model Card Implementation Guide, 2023). But the answer to documentation complexity is not to drop the requirement. It's to make the format more workable.⏎⏎Ainsley Advisory Group | ONC-0955-P | Page 2⏎⏎---⏎⏎What I genuinely do not understand is the theory of patient safety that supports removing these disclosures. The deregulatory argument, as I read the proposed rulemaking, is essentially that the certification burden slows time-to-market and that market forces plus existing FDA oversight provide adequate safety assurance. I find that argument unpersuasive for a few reasons.⏎⏎First, FDA's SaMD pathway does not cover the majority of clinical decision support tools in the EHR ecosystem. The 21st Century Cures Act (Pub. L. 114-255) carved out a substantial category of CDS from FDA jurisdiction precisely on the assumption that ONC certification would provide the transparency layer. If ONC now pulls back on transparency requirements for that same category, there is a genuine gap. The Government Accountability Office flagged this in its 2022 report on AI in Health Care (GAO-22-104629), noting that the regulatory framework for clinical AI has structural holes that depend on both FDA and ONC doing their respective jobs. Weakening ONC's DSI requirements doesn't simplify a redundant system. It creates a hole in a system that was already being held together by the interaction between two separate frameworks.⏎⏎Second, the market forces argument has a specific empirical problem. Health systems, particularly smaller regional and rural systems, do not have the internal technical capacity to independently evaluate AI model performance. A 2022 survey published in the Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association (Sendak et al., JAMIA 2022, doi:10.1093/jamia/ocac072) found that fewer than 30% of health systems deploying commercial AI tools had conducted any independent validation before deployment. Those systems are relying on the developer's own documentation. If that documentation is no longer required to meet a certification standard, the health system has nothing to rely on at all.⏎⏎Third, and I want to be honest that this is more of a concern than a certainty, there is a real risk that removing the DSI transparency criterion creates a race-to-the-bottom dynamic where developers who want to obscure poor model performance on minority populations can simply decline to document it. I'm not saying that's what most developers intend. But the requirement exists in part because voluntary disclosure has not been sufficient. The Obermeyer 2019 finding was about a tool that had been deployed at scale for years before a researcher with access to the underlying data figured out what was happening. Certification requirements are what you have when you can't assume good-faith transparency.⏎⏎WHAT SHOULD ACTUALLY CHANGE⏎⏎None of this means the current implementation is optimal. In my eleven weeks last spring, I watched a certification process that spent a disproportionate amount of time on documentation formatting rather than substantive review. There is real room to streamline the administrative process around DSI certification without gutting the disclosure requirements themselves.⏎⏎Specifically:⏎⏎o Standardize the model card format using a machine-readable template, rather than requiring free-text narrative. ONC could adopt something close to the Hugging Face model card schema or the proposed FHIR-based format from the 2023 ONC Tech Lab work. This reduces developer burden while actually improving the usability of the disclosure.⏎⏎o Create a tiered review process where DSI tools with narrow intended use and low-acuity clinical context get a faster track, while tools operating in high-stakes contexts (sepsis detection, dosing recommendations, diagnostic support for serious conditions) get full review. The current process treats a scheduling optimization tool the same as a sepsis alert. That doesn't make sense.⏎⏎o Publish a public registry of certified DSI tools with their model cards, so health systems can access this information without going through each vendor individually. ONC has the infrastructure to do this. It would reduce the per-transaction documentation burden while making the information more useful.⏎⏎o Clarify the interaction between ONC's DSI criterion and FDA's SaMD pathway so developers aren't duplicating documentation across two separate regulatory processes. That's a legitimate burden reduction that doesn't compromise the substance of either requirement.⏎⏎What I'm not willing to support is treating the existence of any documentation burden as sufficient reason to eliminate the requirement. The model card disclosures exist because clinical AI has a demonstrated track record of performing differently across patient populations, and because clinicians cannot evaluate that risk without information. The requirement is proportionate to that risk.⏎⏎Ainsley Advisory Group | ONC-0955-P | Page 3⏎⏎---⏎⏎I recognize the deregulatory direction of this administration and I am not categorically opposed to it. Some of the other changes in this rulemaking, particularly around the e-prescribing and clinical quality measure certification criteria, probably do reflect genuine redundancy with state-level requirements and existing standards. I don't have a strong objection to revisiting those.⏎⏎But the DSI transparency criterion is different in kind. It's not a process requirement that got layered on top of existing market practice. It's a disclosure requirement for a category of technology that has a specific and documented capacity to cause patient harm when deployed without adequate transparency. Removing it doesn't reduce theater. It removes one of the few mechanisms we have for making sure that when a clinician acts on an AI-generated recommendation, they're doing so with at least a baseline understanding of what the system was built to do and who it was built for.⏎⏎The vendor we lost last spring built something genuinely good. I hope they find their way back to the domestic market. But the answer to certification delays is faster and smarter certification, not less of it. And if ONC is looking for places to cut, the DSI model card requirement is not where I'd start. The administrative overhead in that eleven-week process was almost entirely in scheduling and queue management, not in the substantive documentation review. Fixing the queue is the project. Eliminating the safety check to make the queue irrelevant is a different thing entirely, and I don't think anyone who has actually read the Obermeyer paper would feel comfortable with that♔♔2026-01-17T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-17T00:00:00Z♔2025-12-12T00:00:00Z♔2026-02-10T00:00:00Z♔6♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Retain the current Decision Support Interventions (DSI) certification criterion requiring AI model cards and transparency disclosures (intended use, target population, known risks, training data characteristics, external validation) to ensure patient safety, informed clinical decision-making, and accountability in AI-assisted healthcare.♔Hospital and health system procurement teams need transparent AI model information to make evidence-based decisions about which tools to adopt and how to implement them safely in their local contexts.♔industry♔high♔angry♔Nevada♔compliance officer♔45♔Last spring, I spent eleven weeks navigating a certification backlog for a module our team had already validated internally — a delay that cost Ainsley Advisory Group a signed contract with a regional hospital network that simply couldn't wait. CMS-2025-0050-110116♔CMS-2025-0050♔Linda Sanchez♔Texas Medical Association♔♔♔♔The Texas Medical Association urges ASTP/ONC to retain the Decision Support Interventions (DSI) certification criterion requiring AI model cards and transparency disclosures, arguing that removing these requirements would leave physicians without ...♔Texas Medical Association⏎401 W. 15th Street⏎Austin, TX 78701⏎www.texmed.org⏎⏎Submitted via regulations.gov⏎Docket No. ONC-2025-0001⏎[Federal Register Vol. 90]⏎⏎RE: Comments on ASTP/ONC Deregulatory Actions To Unleash Prosperity: Health Data, Technology, and Interoperability (Proposed Rule)⏎⏎Date of Submission: July 14, 2025⏎⏎---⏎⏎EXECUTIVE SUMMARY⏎⏎The Texas Medical Association (TMA) submits these comments in response to the proposed rule issued by the Assistant Secretary for Technology Policy and the Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology (ASTP/ONC). TMA represents more than 57,000 physician and medical student members across Texas and is one of the largest state medical associations in the country. Our members work daily at the intersection of clinical practice and health information technology, and they have strong, direct experience with the consequences of how certification standards are written, enforced, or removed.⏎⏎Our comments focus on one issue above others: the proposed removal of the Decision Support Interventions (DSI) certification criterion, specifically the provisions requiring AI model cards and transparency disclosures. We believe this removal would be a serious mistake, and we are asking the agency to retain these requirements in full. We are also raising concerns about the broader signal this proposed rule sends about the federal government's commitment to accountability in AI-assisted clinical decision-making at a moment when that accountability matters more, not less.⏎⏎We recognize that the stated goal of reducing administrative burden is a legitimate policy interest. There are real costs associated with certification requirements, and TMA has been on record in prior comment cycles acknowledging that some certification criteria have generated compliance overhead without proportionate clinical benefit. But the DSI model card requirements are not in that category. They are asking for something basic: that when a physician uses an AI-powered tool to help make a clinical decision, she has access to information about what that tool was trained on, who it was designed to help, what its known failure modes are, and whether it has been externally validated. Removing that requirement does not reduce burden in any meaningful sense. It transfers the burden onto the patient.⏎⏎---⏎⏎SECTION I: BACKGROUND AND ORGANIZATIONAL PERSPECTIVE⏎⏎TMA has been engaged with ONC's health IT certification program since its early development under the Health Information Technology for Economic and Clinical Health (HITECH) Act of 2009. We submitted comments on the 21st Century Cures Act Final Rule (85 Fed. Reg. 25642, May 1, 2020) and on subsequent rulemakings addressing information blocking, FHIR-based interoperability, and prior authorization. Our members have implemented certified EHR technology across a range of practice settings, from solo rural practices in West Texas to large academic medical centers in Houston and Dallas.⏎⏎The DSI certification criterion was introduced in the ONC Health IT Certification Program as part of efforts to bring accountability to clinical decision support tools, particularly as AI and machine learning began appearing inside certified EHR systems. The criterion at 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11) requires that developers of health IT seeking certification for decision support interventions disclose, through what are commonly called "model cards," certain characteristics of AI-based decision support: the intended use of the intervention, the population it was designed to serve, known risks and limitations, characteristics of the training data, and whether the tool has been externally validated (see also 88 Fed. Reg. 23746, April 18, 2023, discussing ONC's approach to AI transparency in certified health IT).⏎⏎These are not novel or unreasonable requirements. The concept of a model card was described in detail by Mitchell et al. (2019) in a widely cited paper published through Google Research, and similar disclosure frameworks have been adopted or proposed by the National Institute of Standards and Technology in its AI Risk Management Framework (NIST AI RMF 1.0, January 2023), by the Food and Drug Administration in its guidance on Software as a Medical Device (SaMD), and by the Coalition for Health AI (CHAI) in its Blueprint for Trustworthy AI Implementation Guidance. The idea that AI tools used in clinical settings should come with basic documentation is not a regulatory overreach. It is the minimum standard of care we should expect.⏎⏎---⏎⏎Texas Medical Association Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 2⏎⏎---⏎⏎SECTION II: THE DSI TRANSPARENCY REQUIREMENTS AND WHY THEY MUST BE RETAINED⏎⏎My work as a community organizer in Indiana is not the same as practicing medicine, but I have spent enough time in hospitals and in people's living rooms trying to untangle what went wrong with their care that I understand something about what it looks like when information is withheld. Last spring, I spent three weeks helping a family in our neighborhood try to access their mother's discharge records after she had a stroke. The records should have transferred automatically between the two hospital systems involved. Instead, the family needed faxes, a phone tree, and eventually a referral to legal aid before anyone would even tell them what forms to fill out. We got there eventually, but only because I knew how to push. Most families I work with don't know how to push, and they don't have three weeks. They give up.⏎⏎I keep coming back to that experience when I read this proposed rule, because what ONC is proposing to do with DSI model card requirements is structurally similar to what those hospital systems were doing with those discharge records. The information exists. The developers have it. They know what their tools were trained on. They know what populations were included in the training data and which ones weren't. They know whether the tool has been externally validated and in what settings. The question is whether they are required to make that information available in a standard, accessible format to the clinicians who are using these tools to make decisions about real patients. The proposed rule says no. We say that is wrong.⏎⏎To be specific about what is at stake: the DSI criterion as currently written requires health IT developers seeking certification to provide, in a standardized format, the following categories of information about AI-based decision support interventions:⏎⏎1. Intended use of the intervention and the clinical context for which it was designed.⏎2. The target population the tool was developed and validated for, including demographic characteristics of the training data.⏎3. Known risks and limitations, including documented failure modes and conditions under which the tool's recommendations should not be followed.⏎4. Training data characteristics, including the source, time period, and any known gaps or biases in the data.⏎5. External validation status, including whether the tool has been tested in populations or settings beyond those used in development.⏎⏎These disclosures are not asking developers to surrender trade secrets. They are asking for the same kind of information that any responsible clinician would want before incorporating a new tool into her practice. If a pharmaceutical company brought a new drug to market and refused to disclose what the drug had been tested on, what populations had been excluded from trials, and what the known contraindications were, no one would argue that requiring that information creates "unnecessary burden." The logic applies equally to AI-based decision support.⏎⏎The proposed rule does not articulate a clear rationale for why these specific requirements should be removed. The preamble references a general interest in reducing certification burden and increasing flexibility for health IT developers (see the proposed rule preamble, Section III.A), but it does not explain how the model card requirements create disproportionate costs or how their removal would benefit patients or clinicians. We would genuinely like to understand that analysis, because from where we sit, the burden here is not on the developers. It is on the physicians and patients who would be left using tools they cannot evaluate.⏎⏎---⏎⏎Texas Medical Association Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 3⏎⏎---⏎⏎SECTION III: PATIENT SAFETY AND CLINICAL ACCOUNTABILITY IN AI-ASSISTED CARE⏎⏎TMA is not opposed to AI in clinical practice. Many of our members use AI-powered tools for imaging analysis, clinical documentation, risk stratification, and care coordination, and some of those tools are genuinely useful. But the usefulness of a tool depends on the clinician's ability to understand its limitations. A physician who doesn't know that an AI risk stratification model was trained primarily on data from large urban academic medical centers may not realize that it performs differently in a rural community hospital serving a predominantly elderly, low-income population. She may follow its recommendations in good faith and produce worse outcomes as a result. That is not hypothetical. There is published evidence that algorithmic tools trained on biased or non-representative data produce racially and socioeconomically disparate outcomes in clinical settings (Obermeyer et al., Science, 2019, vol. 366, pp. 447-453; see also Char et al., NEJM, 2018, vol. 378, pp. 981-983).⏎⏎The FDA's Digital Health Center of Excellence has been grappling with exactly these issues in the context of Software as a Medical Device regulation, and ONC's DSI requirements were designed to complement that work by ensuring that the certified health IT layer, meaning the EHR systems through which most clinicians actually access these tools, carries appropriate documentation. Removing the ONC requirements does not mean the FDA's oversight framework will fill the gap. These are different regulatory regimes covering different aspects of the technology stack, and there are plenty of AI-based decision support tools that operate within certified EHRs without being subject to FDA oversight as SaMD.⏎⏎There is also a liability question here that TMA believes deserves serious attention. When a physician uses an AI-based tool embedded in her certified EHR and that tool produces a recommendation that contributes to patient harm, the question of what the physician knew, or could have known, about the tool's limitations is going to matter in any subsequent legal or disciplinary proceeding. Under the current DSI criterion, there is at least a documented record of what the developer disclosed about the tool's intended use, training data, and known limitations. If those disclosures are no longer required, physicians are left in the position of using tools whose characteristics they have no standardized way to evaluate, and bearing responsibility for outcomes that depend on information they were never given. That is not a fair or reasonable allocation of risk.⏎⏎We are also concerned about what removal of the DSI criterion signals to the market. Certification requirements shape developer behavior. When ONC certifies a product, it is telling the market that the product meets a defined set of standards. If AI transparency is no longer part of that standard, developers who have invested in building robust model documentation will face competitive pressure from developers who haven't. The race to the bottom in this space is not theoretical. We have seen it happen with other health IT standards that were relaxed or made optional.⏎⏎---⏎⏎SECTION IV: RESPONSE TO THE AGENCY'S BURDEN REDUCTION RATIONALE⏎⏎The proposed rule frames the removal of DSI transparency requirements as part of a broader effort to reduce administrative burden on health IT developers and increase flexibility in the certification program. TMA takes seriously the argument that some certification requirements impose costs without proportionate benefits, and we have supported streamlining efforts in other contexts. But the burden reduction framing does not hold up when applied to the model card requirements specifically.⏎⏎First, the information required by the DSI criterion is information that responsible developers should already have. If a developer has built an AI-based clinical decision support tool and cannot describe its intended use, the characteristics of its training data, or its known limitations, that is not a documentation problem. It is a product development problem. Requiring the documentation does not create the burden of generating the information. It creates the burden of making the information available, which is a very different thing.⏎⏎Second, the costs of non-disclosure are not borne by the developers. They are borne by clinicians and patients. A physician who spends time trying to evaluate an undocumented AI tool, or who makes a suboptimal clinical decision because she lacked information about the tool's limitations, is absorbing a cost that the developer was allowed to externalize. Regulatory burden analysis should account for where the costs actually land, not just the compliance costs visible on the developer's books.⏎⏎Third, we note that the agency has not provided a quantitative estimate of the burden savings from removing the DSI criterion, nor has it provided an estimate of the potential costs in terms of patient safety or clinical outcomes. The regulatory impact analysis in the proposed rule focuses primarily on the reduction in certification-related paperwork for developers. We would urge ONC to conduct a more complete analysis before finalizing this provision, one that includes the downstream costs to the health system of reduced AI transparency.⏎⏎We want to be honest that we don't have a perfect answer to every question about how the DSI requirements should evolve as AI technology changes. The field is moving fast, and there may be aspects of the current model card format that need updating. The National Academy of Medicine released a discussion paper in 2023 (Matheny et al., "Artificial Intelligence in Health Care: The Hope, the Hype, the Promise, the Peril") that raises useful questions about how transparency requirements should adapt to different types of AI tools and different clinical contexts. TMA would support a process in which ONC works with clinicians, developers, and patient advocates to refine and update the DSI requirements. What we cannot support is removing them entirely while that conversation is still happening.⏎⏎---⏎⏎Texas Medical Association Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 4⏎⏎---⏎⏎SECTION V: INFORMATION BLOCKING AND RELATED CONCERNS⏎⏎Although our primary focus in these comments is the DSI certification criterion, we want to briefly note our concerns about the proposed changes to information blocking definitions and exceptions. The 21st Century Cures Act established strong prohibitions on information blocking (42 U.S.C. 300jj-52) precisely because the voluntary interoperability ecosystem had failed to produce adequate data sharing. The information blocking exceptions that ONC established in the 2020 final rule were designed to be narrow and well-defined, so that actors who claimed an exception would need to demonstrate that their data sharing restrictions were genuinely necessary and proportionate.⏎⏎The proposed rule would expand certain exceptions and reduce documentation requirements for actors claiming exception status. TMA is concerned that these changes, taken together, could make it harder to identify and address practices that effectively block patients and clinicians from accessing health information, even if those practices don't technically violate the revised rule. The experience of families trying to access discharge records, or physicians trying to get referral information from a competing health system, is not ancient history. It is happening right now in communities across Indiana, Texas, and everywhere else. The information blocking provisions are one of the few places where federal law gives patients and clinicians real leverage, and we would be cautious about any changes that reduce that leverage before we have strong evidence that the current framework has been fully implemented and enforced.⏎⏎The Office of Inspector General finalized its information blocking civil money penalty rule in 2023 (88 Fed. Reg. 6872, February 1, 2023), and enforcement under that framework is still relatively new. We don't yet have a robust empirical record of how actors are responding to the penalty structure, which exceptions are being claimed and in what circumstances, or whether the exceptions as currently written are being used as intended or as loopholes. Making the exceptions broader before we have that record seems premature.⏎⏎---⏎⏎SECTION VI: NUMBERED RECOMMENDATIONS⏎⏎Based on the analysis in Sections II through V, TMA offers the following specific recommendations to ASTP/ONC:⏎⏎1. Retain the DSI certification criterion at 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11) in full, including all provisions requiring AI model cards and transparency disclosures covering intended use, target population, known risks and limitations, training data characteristics, and external validation status.⏎⏎2. If ONC believes that the current model card format requires updating to reflect advances in AI technology or changes in clinical practice, initiate a separate rulemaking or Request for Information process to gather input on how to refine the requirements. Do not remove the requirements while that process is ongoing.⏎⏎3. Commission an independent study, in collaboration with the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ) and the National Institutes of Health, of the clinical and patient safety implications of AI transparency requirements in certified health IT. The study should include analysis of documented cases where inadequate disclosure of AI tool characteristics contributed to adverse clinical outcomes, and should be completed before any final rule removing or substantially modifying DSI transparency requirements takes effect.⏎⏎4. Direct ONC's certification testing bodies to develop standardized testing protocols for DSI model card completeness, so that the transparency disclosures required by the criterion are evaluated against a consistent standard rather than left to developer self-attestation.⏎⏎5. Engage in targeted outreach to physician organizations, nursing associations, and patient advocacy groups to gather input on what information clinicians and patients actually need in order to evaluate AI-based decision support tools, and use that input to inform any future revisions to the DSI criterion.⏎⏎6. With respect to information blocking, do not finalize the proposed expansions of information blocking exceptions until ONC has completed a review of how the current exceptions have been used in practice since the 2020 final rule took effect, and has published that review for public comment.⏎⏎7. Publish, for each proposed removal or relaxation of a certification criterion, a specific quantitative analysis of the patient safety and clinical outcome costs associated with that removal. The regulatory impact analysis in this proposed rule does not include this analysis for the DSI criterion, and we believe it is required for informed public comment.⏎⏎---⏎⏎Texas Medical Association Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 5⏎⏎---⏎⏎SECTION VII: ADDITIONAL CONSIDERATIONS⏎⏎There is something worth saying about the framing of this proposed rule that goes beyond any specific technical provision. The title of the rule, "Deregulatory Actions To Unleash Prosperity," is a framing choice, and framing choices matter. They tell regulated entities, courts, and the public something about how the agency understands its own mission. When ONC describes the removal of AI transparency requirements as "unleashing prosperity," it is implicitly characterizing those requirements as obstacles to economic activity rather than as protections for patients and clinicians. We don't think that characterization is accurate, and we are concerned about what it signals for how the agency will approach future AI governance questions.⏎⏎The health IT market is not like most markets. Patients do not shop for certified EHR systems. They receive care from providers who use those systems, often without any meaningful ability to choose otherwise. The accountability framework built into the certification program is one of the primary mechanisms through which patients and clinicians can have some confidence that the tools being used in their care meet a defined standard. When that framework is weakened, the people who bear the cost are not the developers or the payers. They are the patients.⏎⏎TMA also wants to flag a practical concern about implementation timing. If ONC proceeds with removing the DSI criterion, health IT developers who have already invested in building model card documentation infrastructure for their certified products will face a confusing transition. They will have spent resources on compliance with a requirement that is then removed, and the market signal going forward will be that AI transparency is not something the certification program values. We have heard from some of our members who are also health IT developers that this uncertainty is itself a burden, and that they would prefer a stable, long-term framework over a cycle of requirements being added and removed. The most effective burden reduction would be to establish a clear, durable standard and stick with it.⏎⏎We are also aware that there are ongoing discussions at the federal level about a more comprehensive AI governance framework for health care, including work being done by the HHS Office of the Assistant Secretary for Technology Policy, the FDA, and the FTC. TMA believes that the DSI certification criterion is an important piece of that framework, and that removing it now would create a gap that will be difficult to fill later. Coordination across agencies on AI governance in health care is something we strongly support, and we would urge ONC to engage with those interagency discussions before finalizing any changes to the DSI criterion.⏎⏎One more thing, and I realize this is somewhat tangential to the technical regulatory question, but it matters to me personally. The families I work with in my community organizing role are not abstractions. They are people who are already navigating a health system that is often confusing, fragmented, and inaccessible. When AI-based tools are making recommendations about their care, and when those tools have been trained on data that may not reflect their demographics or their clinical circumstances, they have no way of knowing that. They trust that the system has been designed with their interests in mind. The DSI transparency requirements are one small way of making that trust a little more warranted. Removing them makes it less warranted, and I don't think that is a trade-off the agency has fully reckoned with.⏎⏎---⏎⏎Texas Medical Association Comments | ONC-2025-0001 | Page 6⏎⏎---⏎⏎SECTION VIII: CONCLUSION OF FORMAL RECOMMENDATIONS⏎⏎TMA respectfully urges ASTP/ONC to withdraw the proposed removal of the DSI certification criterion and to retain in full the AI model card and transparency disclosure requirements at 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11). We further urge the agency to conduct a more complete regulatory impact analysis that accounts for patient safety and clinical outcome costs before finalizing any deregulatory changes to the certification program.⏎⏎We appreciate the opportunity to submit these comments and are available to provide additional technical input, to participate in stakeholder discussions, or to facilitate engagement with our physician membership. Questions regarding these comments may be directed to TMA's Health Information Technology Policy division.⏎⏎Respectfully submitted,⏎⏎Linda Sanchez⏎Community Health Policy Liaison, Indiana Region⏎On behalf of the Texas Medical Association⏎⏎401 W. 15th Street⏎Austin, TX 78701⏎healthIT@texmed.org⏎www.texmed.org⏎⏎---⏎⏎APPENDIX A: Summary of Referenced Standards and Guidance Documents⏎⏎(Note: Appendix A, containing full citations and excerpts from referenced standards documents including NIST AI RMF 1.0, CHAI Blueprint for Trustworthy AI Implementation Guidance, FDA SaMD guidance, and OIG information blocking penalty rule, is referenced herein but not attached to this electronic submission.
